Ah, Tekken. A game I play since my childhood and that will always hold a place in my heart. If you're a Tekken fan like me or just a fighting games enthusiast, then you absolutely need to get Tekken 7. Here are the pros & cons:
Pros
+ The graphics are breathtaking, especially if you have a configuration that can handle the max settings
+ The larger than average roster means a bigger diversity of characters that you can choose from
+ The main story is awesome(albeit short)
+ Online mode has a tournament mode and revenge match system, which enables you to play against the same player, in ranked & player matches
+ Practice mode offers a variety of options that you can use to try out different situations & setups
Cons
- Character stories suck (except for a few ones)
- Katarina
- High learning curve, with over 1000 moves across the entire cast (i'm not exaggerating) to learn & remember, the movement & 3D aspect(side stepping), so you will need to put a LOT of time & effort to even get at a decent level (again i'm not exaggerating)
Overall, Tekken 7 is an incredibly fun and rewarding game that I reccomend for both veterans of the series and newcomers alike, if the latter are willing to put down the hours & commitement to get good. A great addition to an awesome franchise.

Wow, Kingdoms of Amalur was a GOOD game. From beging to end i never felt that this game really deserved the bad rap that it got. However I do understand that this game has its issues and there are far more polished and more sophistcated RPG titles out there. But i blieve the late 38 studios did a great job with this title, with this being its first and now only ever game the company has produced i blieve it deserves the cult status it has slowly achieved. The story, the lore and the characters is were this game really shines, its ingossing and it makes you feel like you are a part of the world, and i am truely hoping that one day a studio, perhaps Obsedian, will save the franchise and make a much wanted sequal.
Now, there are areas that may turn people away, the combat is invigorating at first but quickly becomes quite repedative, and many of the side quests feel like you are just visting the same dungeon and the doing the  same objective over and over again. Although if you just stick to the main quest, you shouldnt come across this problem. The crafting system is also very limited and is pretty forgettable with the game's competitors blowing it out of the park. But that said it isn't bad either. With the fast leveling up, it feels like the crafting becomes more of a novelty in the late game.
So in conclusion, 38 studios, now gone will not be forgotten with this hidden gem in Amalur. I blieve the narrative of the game alone is enough to warrent interest from a new studio to give this ip another chance. Over all a good game, with some sub par RPG elements but with an amazing story and lore. Well worth buying during a steam sale.

This is an oldschool first-person shooter, for good and for ill.
The levels are completely divorced from reality. There are lots of secrets to find, both by using odd-looking sections of the wall and by (rocket) jumping to places that don't really look like you should be able to access. The action is fast and insane. There's no saving heavy weapons for later: the game expects you to use the many kinds of rocket launchers at first opportunity. And if you do run out of rockets, you also have bullet weapons with infinite ammo at your disposal. All of this results in an first-person shooter of the kind we just don't see anymore. Scoring is slightly more complex than in old first-person shooters, with a combo system for killing enemies in quick succession.
On the other hand, some things that could safely have been left in the past have also been carried over. Enemies blend into the environment and aren't too smart, sometimes getting caught on geometry. It's hard to tell when you're getting shot and how much damage you're taking. The same casual approach to level boundaries that lets you search for secrets can also result in you jumping outside of the level with no way to get back in. There are lots of deathtraps and jumping puzzles (not necessarily a bad thing, but...) unfortunately paired with a checkpoint system (there are no manual saves) that might make you repeat sequences multiple times. The checkpoints are fairly well placed but it's still a pain to fall in lava and die after spending five or ten minutes carefully navigating a complex room.
Multiplayer seems pretty broken at the moment. Server browsing is sorted by geographic distance, not ping. And the ping shown during a match seems to be wrong. There is no way a ping of 40 should result in other players warping around and hitching constantly. If they ever sort this out, multiplayer seems like it could be very fast and very fun, but online play just doesn't work well enough to make it enjoyable at this time.
There are also some optimization issues. The game runs mostly perfectly for me, but occasionally I enter a room where the framerate drops to 30 or even 20 for no good reason. It's not enough to be a dealbreaker, but this is not the game for you if you refuse to play anything under 60 frames per second.
Still, I think the good far outweighs the bad in Rise of the Triad. There really is nothing quite like it: a well-done oldschool FPS with a shiny new coat of paint.

Bought it for $1.49 during Summer Sale. I'm extremely cheap when it comes to games (if it has no replay value, I almost always ignore it) but this game, IMO, is esaily worth up to $5. (Note: If I say $5, the comparable to a normal person that isn't as crazy cheap as me would willingly pay $7.50+ for it without hesitation). I only say $5 because I finished the game in one sitting and it took me about a total of 2.5 hours.
GAMEPLAY: It CAN be played with keyboard, but you might as well not even try it if you don't have a controller, it's just made for controller and has not even made an attempt to be optimized for PC/KBM. It plays like a very nice, fluid puzzle adventure. You don't get obvious neon arrows pointing you in the direction you need to go nor does it hold your hand through each challenge. If you're stuck, call on the big bro and he'll point out where to go, but that's about it. This is a huge thing for me, I hate how the new generation of games have become this baby-friendly style where everything is given to you, pointed out, or you have to just put down some more money to advance. Regardless, this game works nicely with a controller but it's up to the person controlling it, I had a hard time being consistent with controlling both brothers at once so sometimes my mind would confuse me and both brothers run the opposite way-happened about a dozen times throughout.
STORY: Extremely great story, I'd say it's more of an interactive movie rather than a game with a story. Plenty of cinematics and gameplay put side by side, alternating. I'm not a very emotional person but I definitely was saddened by the story.
GRAPHICS: I don't have a very nice PC but it played at a solid 60 FPS (with/without vsync) although I had some screen tearing throughout the ENTIRE game, just one horizontal blur going up and down my monitor the entire time, about 2cm tall. You can only change the resolution in the launcher and whether or not to have vsync, that's it.
Note: You can reassign the keys if you're using KBM but the controller keymapping is completely set, just plug n play for that.
All in all, great game, great story, meh graphics [options] (absolutely horrific PC port), very sad ending, I'd give it a solid 8/10 for being all those above but -2 for the bad port

This game is definitely a must-play for its powerful storytelling and beautiful backgrounds and level design. You control two players at the same time (or you can grab a friend) and embark on a journey to save your in-game father. Along the way, you learn how to navigate through levels through a single-player co-op that also takes you deeper into a beautiful story that gets you to feel emotionally committed to the young brothers.
I honestly believe that there will never be another game that I consider to have better storytelling in such a short yet fulfilling gameplay (~2-3 hours), and I really hope that whoever reads this review will not be scared of the controller requirement (you can definitely do this on PC, as I have) or turned away from the fact that there is no English spoken.
tl;dr: Amazing, powerful storytelling with gameplay and character development that surprises you and becomes lasting.

The walls are more climbable, but not really worth the climb.
The guns are handed out to specially designed classes (characters) but not really worth splitting up.
The Panties are everywhere, but so are the Cens*rs.
The hitboxes are as unresponsive as the original, but the controls are far more unresponsive than the original.
The movements are all dumbed down, forget gun-rolling, you're always sword-dashing.
The swords no longer block bullets from the waist up, they just sit in front of you stupidly while the bullets smack your face.
It's not a true successor to the original GunZ. It's got some flare, but when everyone uses the same characters as you there's no individuality because all the weapons are the same.
This game hasn't impressed me, and the people playing it feel the same. They feel like they want to go play the old GunZ.

F1 Race Stars is ALMOST a very good game. But ultimately it is frustrating and somewhat lacking in comparison to other top kart racing titles. It is fun to play as your favourite F1 drivers in cartoon form, with lots of nice power ups, and some truly original and very innovative racing modes which keeps interest levels high. The graphics are quite good, though of course they are meant to be very cartoon-like as opposed to photorealistic. Overall, there's a lot of good to be said about the game. It is certainly a challenge!
But here's the rub: the game is challenging in the most frustrating of ways. Firstly, there is essentially no difficulty level. The 1,000 vs. 3,000 cc only changes the speed of the cars. Facing the AI is like a baptism of fire. It is relentless, and one can win only with a mix of skill and luck (luck being by far the most important factor). I don't like to win every race, but when I lose I want to be able to remedy that by improving my skills. Not so in F1 Race Stars. You can be racing at your very best and come dead last by virtue of a bit of bad luck; likewise you can race like a drunkard and come first with a contrary amount of good luck. This, unfortunately, is a very nearly game-breaking fault. As a result, what could have been a classic kart racing title will be one to forget in comparison to a Mario Kart or Crash Team Racing. But all in all, it isn't a bad game. Fun but frustrating. 7/10.

An under the cover game, dwarfed by other releases such as the Elder Scrolls V: Skyrim, this game should be viewed in greater light and strength. An addictive expansive world fuelled by a real fantastical scenario and setting, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning brings strong RPG elements to an otherwise uncomplicated genre. Though this game is stuck between an MMO and a traditional RPG, its combat, crafting and magical elements make this game a strong condendor for anyone looking to play an addictive, massive world game. The downsides to this game may be considerable for some: the purely linear main campaign, the massive open world with no fast travel and lack of considerable and ultimately interesting quests. Nevertheless, it makes up for these pitfalls in interesting dialogue that is both well tohugh out and witty. It is a real blast for any gamer. 8/10

To start with, I would like to thank Rooster Teeth and Monty for bringing about the wonderful series and this game. My review will have the good, the not-so good, and what hopefully could be added or expanded. I will try not to sound too demanding or unappreciative because I understand a lot of work is put into this game, and I am truly thankful for it. Without further adieu.
What is good:
. Storyline type of quests (even diverged from the show)
. RPG and real-time action mix
. Multiple characters to choose from
. Multiplayer online
. Beautiful environment
. Vibes that are just about the same as the show
. Music that changes from one moment to the next
. Difficulty is accomodated for based on players
. Graphics settings can be varied, appealing to more players (potato settings saved me lol)
. Stats (amount of kills, etc. just interesting to see how I do. The competetive part varies with whether the individual would like that or not)
. Variation in enemies (sure the same ones come back, but new enemies were introduced constantly throughout the levels)
. Mini bosses (the slightly tougher grimm that make it a little more challenging but fun)
What is not so good:
. Camera angles are tight (for example, it doesnt go much higher than the horizon point)
. No save point from what I can see (I'm not sure how it can be implemented, but it would be nice not to start over after leaving a session, sorry if I missed anything)
. A few glitches on camera that sees through the floor or map entirely
. A few glitches with movement (like Ruby moonwalking lol)
. Somewhat linear feel (It would be nice to explore the environments a little more rather than moving down a specific path)
. A minor glitch where the volume effect when upgrading remains if someone upgrades during transitions between maps
Hopes for expansion/addition:
. More characters (like team JNPR)
. Expanded skill tree for higher levels (Maybe this is because only a part of the full content is out)
. A more interactive environment (Opening gates, bridges, and moving the bomb was neat but it would be even more impressive interactiong with the environment like how characters destroy/use/interact with it in the show to a certain extent)
. Just some minor platforming (it would make jump ability more useful besides mid-air attacks)
. Player Vs Player
. A lot more content (I love the game, and I guess time flew by because it felt quick, maybe it will expand along with the show, idk.)
. Boss fights (It would be awesome to fight something like the deathstalker or nevermore, or even some boss unique to the game)
. Lock on camera (it would make it more convenient for focusing on a specific grimm or object)
Overall, the game is definately worth buying. I acknowledge this game is still in early access so I hope my review will be noticed and that it will have some influence in further development. I do apologize if anything I have said is wrong, and I will be checking from time to time to update my reviews for this game. I am indeed enjoying the game as it is, and with early access along with future improvements, I can't wait to play the final version!

Twilight begins with an unnamed narrator (whom we later find out is Bella) giving a brief account about how she is about to die at the hands of a hunter. She is dying in the place of someone she loves, and the narrator does not regret any of the choices that brought her to this point. The past few months have been extraordinary, and she can’t complain.
Zip! Now we’re following the life of Isabella “Bella” Swan, our seventeen-year-old narrator. Bella is moving to Forks, Washington, to live with her dad. We later learn that she volunteered to do this so that she wouldn’t hold her mother back from spending more time with her mother’s new husband. Forks is isolated, cold, dreary, and wet, and Bella’s relationship with her dad is distant, since she was raised by her mother in Phoenix. Bella's new life is dull until she gets a glimpse of the Cullen family – five gorgeous, mesmerizing siblings who attend her high school. She learns they do not socialize with anyone but each other. One of the boys in particular, Edward, pays her close attention and seems to regard her with alarming hostility when she's forced to sit next to him in Biology class. The next day, he is absent from school.
Bella continues to adapt to her new life in Forks. She gets a lot more attention from boys than she was used to in Phoenix. She makes several friends quickly. A few days later, Edward finally is back in school. Now he’s friendly to Bella. His mere presence excites her. That afternoon in the school parking lot, a boy’s truck almost hits Bella after skidding on some black ice, but Edward uses his body as a shield in order to save her. Wait, how’d he do that?! Bella is totally baffled by this, but Edward refuses to explain his inhuman strength. She begins to have dreams about Edward, but at school, he gives her the cold shoulder. His behavior is very confusing, indeed.
Bella gets asked to the upcoming school dance by not one, but three boys, all of whom she rejects. The next day, Edward gets Bella to talk to him during lunch – for the first time he’s spending lunch apart from his siblings. Knowing that she's trying to make sense of his strength and how he saved her, Edward asks for her “theories” on him. Next, it’s let’s-figure-out-your-blood-type day in Biology class, and Edward’s skipping class. Bella becomes faint at the mere thought of blood, and gets taken to the nurse’s office (Edward appears outside and intercepts her from Mike, one of the guys who has a crush on Bella). Edward insists that he take her home.
That weekend, during a trip to a beach at La Push Indian reservation, Bella meets Jacob Black, who tells her about “the cold ones” (vampires). Word around the reservation is that the Cullens are vampires. When Bella gets home, she does some internet research and things start falling into place. Bella decides that she’s too in love with Edward to resist him, even if he is a vampire.
Soon after, Bella takes a trip to Port Angeles with a few friends, where she gets lost looking for a bookstore. Some thugs almost attack her in a dark alley, but Edward appears in his shiny Volvo and saves her. They have dinner together, and he drives her home. He reveals that yes, he is a vampire. Edward doesn’t want to be a monster, though, and actually only drinks the blood of animals. Bella knows now that he does thirst for her blood, yet she still is in love with him. Edward repeatedly warns Bella that she should be afraid of him and stay away, if she’s smart.
Edward and Bella take a mini-field trip together and spend the afternoon in a nearby secluded meadow, where Edward shows Bella that his skin sparkles in the sun (which is why vampires only come out at night or on cloudy days, which are common in Forks). They are completely in love. They kiss for the first time. Bella learns more about Edward’s family and their past. Edward struggles with abiding his morals (not tempting himself by getting close to a human) versus what he desires – to be near Bella.
Edward spends the night in Bella's bedroom, watching over her as she sleeps (without her dad knowing, of course). Bella visits Edward’s house, meets his family, and learns more about their “kind” – vampires who don’t feast on humans. They go back to her house where Jacob and his father Billy Black show up to see her dad (Billy and Charlie are friends). Being a Quileute elder from the La Push reservation, Billy knows about the Cullens' secret and is worried for Bella's safety. He warns her to stay away from the Cullens. After the Blacks leave, Edward returns in his brother's jeep to pick up Bella. They’re going to play baseball. It's a Cullen family bonding ritual, evidently.
While the Cullens are playing their crazy version of baseball (they're all incredibly strong and fast), three other vampires show up. One named James takes a liking to Bella (in the “I want to eat you” kind of way). Edward and his family get Bella away from James long enough to make a plan. They know that James is trying to track Bella, so Alice and Jasper (Edward's adoptive siblings) whisk her away to a hiding place in Phoenix, but James lures Bella to him by telling her that he has captured her mom. He’s about to kill Bella when the Cullen clan shows up. The only problem is that James has already bitten Bella. If Edward doesn't suck the venom-infected blood out of her, she'll become a vampire. Though it's difficult for Edward to control his urge to suck all of Bella's blood, he manages to cure Bella without killing her. The Cullens kill James and get Bella to a hospital, where she starts to recover from her many injuries.
Overall Bella’s OK, though banged up. She and Edward are more in love than ever. However, they argue because Bella wants him to bite her and make her into a vampire so that they can live together forever; Edward refuses. Regardless of their different species, they are devoted to one another completely.
In the Epilogue, Edward surprises Bella by taking her to the prom – she's horrified because she's uncoordinated and worried about dancing in public. Jacob shows up at the dance and delivers a message – Billy wants Bella to dump Edward. He also wants her to know that they “will be watching” (Epilogue.118). Anyway, Edward and Bella go outside to have some time alone – it’s twilight outside. Again, Bella asks Edward to make her into a vampire, and he refuses. Edward says to Bella, “I will stay with you – isn’t that enough?” and she replies, “Enough for now” (Epilogue.204).

All in all I feel like Mortal Kombat X is a good "show", it's great fun to see all the fatalties in the most horrific death animations you will see out of any game. I'll start this out by saying that the only game in the series I've played is Human Revolution. That game did an excellent job at creating a larger picture of a world with augmentations as a possiblity, and addressed that as a political and psychological issue. The way they handled it got a bit preachy, but playing that game I remember thinking that this is the real potential for video games as an art form. But this is a review of Mankind Divided.
I've just started the game, but so far the game does a great job continuing where Revolution left off. They start with a quick briefing and then throw you into the action. It's a true Deus Ex game, every objective has several different options for completion. Short version, if you liked Revolution, I highly recommend this game. Also, if you're like me and lost track of some of the plot in the previous game, there is a skippable video which summarizes what happened.

Welp...it's here.  I have to say, underneath the glaring performance issues, even with some of the heavier processes turned off, somewhat floaty jumping, mouse acceleration and terrible character animation, there is a very good game in here somewhere.  However, so long as there's a greedy cash shop (did they learn NOTHING from the reaction to Deus Ex: The Fall?) and unforgivably terrible day one dlc (this sort of thing is bad enough, but five bucks for a few easy to acquire items?  Really?) I can't find it in me to recommend this game.  If you do find you need to get it, do it when it's on sale, after all the obligatory AAA post release patching and apologies for their crappy release state.  I recommend not spending more than thirty bucks on it.
Update:  Ok, rating isn't changing.  The game is UNFORGIVABLY short even if you do EVERY SINGLE side objective as well as just dicking around as well.  Don't let my playtime fool you, that's with starting over more than halfway through on a harder difficulty and a different build with a few different choices but there really aren't that many choices at all, let alone big ones that affect the story.  Don't buy this game at all, they heavily sequel/DLC bait at the end of this pitiful game in the hopes of getting more money from you.  Make no mistake, this is just a better looking 'The Fall' and is NOT worth any support.  I only wish I could still get my money back.

I originally had this for my Xbox 360 as an arcade game, but that was YEARS ago. Toy Soldiers is a tower defense strategy based game revolving around WW1 based action figures fighting to the death to either destroy your base, or defend it. Your mission is to defend your base, or Toy Box from the enemy. Your Toy Box will take damage if an enemy troop reaches it, and if enough troops make it to your Toy Box, you loose the level. Along with numerous variants of troops (soldiers, tanks, planes, ect) you have a variety of turrets to deploy as well. From artillery to machine guns, to even gas, finding the perfect set is sometimes challenging
. For every enemy killed you gain money for upgrading turrets and repairing them. Your turrets will attack automatically, but you can control them to kill enemies while earning boosted money drops and damage. There are numerous maps to play through and a total of 3 campaigns to smash though, each having bosses and funny moments. For someone whose never heard about this fun and cool game, I HIGHLY recommend this game. 9/10

Just got done beating this game, its DLC and numerous side quests.  It's the most fun I've had with a game in quite a while and highly recommend it.  I'm a fan of action RPG games like Diablo, Skyrim, etc. but not too much of a fan of Witcher (too many lengthy story pauses) and Dragon Age (clunky keyboard/mouse combat).
This game has a great story woven throughout, and the excellent keyboard/mouse controls coupled with so many places to explore really won me over.   The level designs are excellent and each region of the game world really feels unique.  I also loved the reckoning mode which slows everything down and allows you to perform special kills which were very satisfying.  The character voice narratives are excellently done too.  Quest markers were easy to follow, and didn't experience a single crash during my entire playthrough, unlike with the Gothic and Sacred games which disappointed me in this regard.
If I had to give "slight" complaints, I would say the overabundance of purple unique items.  Making it more rarer to obtain these unique items would have given a greater sense of excitement when finding one.  Also, you will want to increase the difficulty which is not a usual practice of mine as I typically play games on Casual or Don't Hurt Me mode.  The easiest difficult option in this game is just way to easy.
Overall, an outstanding game for those PC gamers who want a great exploratory experience and fun combat to boot.  I work for a living and don't want to be overly challenged when I find some time to game, and this game really hit the mark.  I give this game a 10 out of 10.

Fantastic Fighting game. I wasn't much of a Tekken fan back in the day but something about 7 has made me fall in love with it. One of my favorite fighting games I have played.

Tekken is one of my favorite fighting game series. I've been playing the series since Tekken 2 (With Tekken 3 being my favorite one)
Im really impressed with how optimized Tekken 7 is considering this is the first time its on PC; alot of care and work was put into this port. The game runs on UE4 and is gorgeous looking; i run the game on Ultra Settings with my GTX1060 and the framerate is always constant and does not go below 60.
Most of the character roster returns (albeit some exceptions below), however theres alot more newcomer characters this time. They've added a campaign story mode which i thought was interesting (made me want to go read up on the tekken lore) and they added treasure battle which is wicked fun; you can unlock customization items with ingame money.
The controls are still the same from previous Tekkens however they have added new mechanics such as camera slowdowns,  wakeups, powercrushes, rage arts, and rage drives, essentially "supers". I didnt like these new editions at first but after playing for a while i actually like them; they're cool looking but also add variety.
Sound effects were on point but as for the music.... personally i dont like a majority of the OST, theres maybe a few tracks i like such as Infinite Azure and the customization theme. The PS4 version has Tekken Tunes where you can change most of the music to the previous tekkens sadly the PC version doesnt have it.
I do have some minor cons
- Some modes seem to be missing
- Missing characters canon wise: Lei, Christie, Anna, Zafina, Bruce, Mokujin, Ganryu, Julia etc
- While story mode was interesting i wish it was longer, also arcade mode has 5 stages compared to 9
Honestly other than that ive been enjoying Tekken 7, probably one of the best ones to come out.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a gigantic map of living, breathing npcs woven together by a glossy art style and quirky, sarcastic tones for every serious moment. It prides itself for having a wide selection of combat and adventuring styles, from a measly peasant to a brutal war-mage. You'll find loot for days and a fighting system that delivers satisfying crunches with every impact. I picked up six different builds before I settled on one that fit a medium-range capacity with all the abilities to deal with enemies of every calibre. The game punishes as much as it rains down riches upon you, the player. Keep your eyes peeled and your hands on your keyboard or controller, 'cause there's plenty of things to do from killing to talking to throwing out junk to getting blown up by that one annoying trap to crafting MORE gems to discovering an ancient ruin of a city to getting rejected by that one hottie of an elf. Don't ever trust the game to hold your hand; take what you get and give nothing back.
Copious praise aside, there were a few factors which tripped over and otherwise pleasant gameplay experience.
There were bugs galore, from broken quests to broken npcs to missing items to items stuck in your inventory. A few of the colour palettes used were neon-nized to the point of frying the rods and cones in your eyeballs. There was so much story in the form of books that if you were to read all that AND read the npc dialogue AND run around looking for treasure, you'd be in the space age before you finished. The skill slotting menu and subsequent settings metres were broken in that they wouldn't move when dragged. Lastly, THERE WERE ONLY 2 DLCS ;_______________;

I am really loving Torchlight 2 as kill-gather-skill-up game that doesn't take itself seriously. Torchlight 1 was an endless dungeon and I ended up incredibly bored since there was nothing but a hundred levels of dungeon below and the one camp above.  I quit playing around lvl 30.  Torchlight 2 makes you run around 'outside' battling monster after monster in various areas before you dive into dungeons to battle monster after monster, and it psychologically seems to make all the difference.
For that reason, Torchlight 2 is MUCH better than Torchlight and if you like running around smashing monsters, gathering loot, going into dungeons to do more of the same just so you can upgrade through points and game money *without* actually having to pay attention to every fine detail cause it really doesn't make or break the game if you choose wrong...then this game is the diversion for you.

If one has ever played a Diablo game and enjoyed it, or if one enjoys RPG's or light MMO's, one will love Torchlight two.

This game is one of those little gems you stumble upon from time to time. I hadn't heard about the game until I found it in a bundle and bought the bundle on the strength of how interesting this game looked. I was not dissapointed. Yes a playthrough can take under an hour if you rush, but it's a game that needs more playthroughs to get the full essence of what was done. Basically there's a mystery to solve, but unlike other games, which may pretend that you are in control, this game really does leave full agency up to you. You select which tools you want, you steer the conversations as you want and the conclusion you reach will be up to you. I would compare the style of the game to Consortium, another game I enjoyed. It's a style I'd refer to as 'short, but wide'. The story itself may only be as long as a movie, but there are many ways to get through it.
Is it a perfect game? No, not if you're expecting AAA production values, and some people may find the stealth a bit annoying (I didn't, and there are slippers you can find which help with that). But it is exactly what indie games and steam direct should be about. It's a fascinating little experiment in alternative story telling and game design and it's sad that games like this which show some creativity and originality get lost in amongst the spam of asset flips and cheap cash-ins. It must be a bit disheartening to see games that literally sell achievements and trading cards making money, whilst something you've laboured over gets ignored. An unfortunate by-product of a free market I guess, although still sad to see. But I wish the developer well, and hope they do make more games, as they've demonstrated good potential with what they did here. Maybe one day when they've hit the big time they'll come back and do a sequel to this.
As a side note, after thinking the few broken achievements would never be fixed, the developer showed up and removed the ones that weren't working, so this game is absolutely beatable now for those who enjoy hunting achievements. Always nice to add a game you enjoyed onto the 'perfect' game list. So if you've been holding off on playing/buying for that reason, worry no more.

Initial impression: a stylish mystery/adventure game with an intricate dialog system, lots of cool exploration and discovery, and some pretty fun stealth action. The game objectives in Karaski are structured nonlinearly, and different approaches to completing them lead to different endings—so in a way the player actually writes the story... Very cool design approach with a ton of freedom and replayability, I dig it. :)
Stealth and social engineering are equally important skill sets in Karaski. The ability to sneak around undetected is key at certain times, other times it may be a good idea to offer someone a bribe or pour them a drink. The branching dialogs are indeed rich and complex, and there are quite a lot of clues, quests, and other details to keep track of... Fortunately the interface and game options are really, really good, so managing all this complexity is pretty much a breeze.
What impressed me the most about Karaski was the beauty and quality of its execution. The stylized visuals and music conjure a vibrant game world, and all the small notes, clues, and story threads weave together to form an exotic tapestry of mystery and intrigue. Karaski has a unique style and flavor, and owns it completely—this game definitely has some swagger. If you love a good mystery (and are feeling a bit stealthy) then Karaski may just be your cup of tea!

You know how I said to go get the new Rise of the Triad? Don't. I just played thirty minutes of it and I already had to walk away with a bad taste in my mouth.
The game's Advanced Settings are located in the launcher menu and not within the game itself, so you're greeted to a nice motionblur and bloom after when you're able to resolve any framerate issues. Lovely. Can't do anything about the game's terrible lighting, though, which makes everything blend together and like you're peering at the game through squinted eyes. With rain splattering your screen.
Bad lighting also clashes with the grayish enemy models, which at a distance look superimposed and close up look like a rudimentary Blender job. Given how slow enemies move and react, the player moves WAY too fast. Yes, games like Quake1 and Doom moved plenty quickly too, as did the original RoTT, but play this game and compare it to those and you'll notice the discrepancy is far greater, which isn't helped by the aforementioned character model clashing. Weapon zoom instantly locks to ironsights, then slooowly zooms in, which is just weird. Your knife, meanwhile, has wonky hit detection. You have to aim directly at an enemy or else the hit won't register. Typical melee in shooters is achieved through some hitscan trickery by creating a delayed bullet at the location where you aim. It's just that this bullet is usually nice and wide so you don't encounter the issue RoTT has here. Not to mention that knives in the original game were used to free yourself from nets and were only found in certain statues. It's a standard CoD stabbing implement here.
Voice acting isn't just hammy, it's lazy ("Please, don't shoot me.") and it sounds like it was recorded with a computer mic. Your character, meanwhile, spouts off♥♥♥♥♥♥OH♥♥♥♥♥♥THAT'S GOTTA HURT ♥♥♥♥ YEAH♥♥♥♥♥♥THAT HURTS♥♥♥♥♥♥depending on who you choose at any possible action taken, whether it's picking up a pistol, killing something, or getting shot by something (what exactly is hurting you is unclear until you can make out just what is shooting from the murk).
Compounding the schlocky voice work is gore, which is overwrought to irritation. Blood splatters look flat and they make a point of making sure you just saw a pair of eyeballs hit the screen and slowly slide down as if it were some 6 year-old desperately tugging at your sleeve for you to see the crayon monstrosity he just scrawled in his coloring book. Intense! Environments are basic linear corridors, the classic sign of a mediocre shooter. This issue becomes more apparent when you start running into invisible walls and realize that you're forcibly restricted from backtracking, or when you start bumping into little ledges and things you can't even see, creating a claustrophobia that's completely out of place in the game. Their layout, along with how little white damage value numbers pop out of your enemies when you shoot them, give off the impression that this game was made in some programmer's spare time for a F2P FPS.
Which I guess isn't all that inaccurate. The game was developed by Interceptor Entertainment, who from what I gather was previously only known for being C&D'd for a Duke Nukem 3D remake. It's yet another entry that attempts to hitch a ride on the Retro Games Return bandwagon conducted by small-name game developers with no idea of what made the original games so great (the original RoTT's gore effects, for example, were more understated and gave it grindhouse charm despite that genre being associated with over-the-top action. Somehow it just doesn't work here). The loading screen factoids that can be found on wikipedia and the achievement "Dat Nostalgia," which rewards you for turning on the 'classic' soundtrack - which is actually just a bad rendering of the original music - provides testimony to this trend. Who's feeling dat nostalgia for a turbid reboot, anyway?
Oh, yeah, and enemies can shoot through doors and walls. Way to go level coders.

Deus Ex Mankind Divided is a really fun game, and is a satifying sequel to human revolution from what I played. I'm not really sure how bad it is on keyboard and mouse like everyone else is saying but I'm probably never going to find out since I don't hardly ever play with one.
My main problem with the game is that it is very unoptimized to the point I get lag spikes every once and a while. At one point the lag was so bad that the bank I was entering caused me to clip through the floor and die. Basically the whole area didn't load and when I reloaded my last save, I had to stand there for a good 15 minutes before everything loaded up correctly so I wouldn't end up clipping to my death again. I'm running a 12gb DDR3, 850 WATT PSU, fx-8350 4.0ghz 8-core processor with MSI Geforce GTX 960 2gb.
Some of the AI, I also question since I've been detected despite being out of sight. However it doesn't happen all the time so it's not too infuriating. It's just sometimes annoying when that rare moment pops up.
I'll continue to play this game because I really enjoy it despite the lag, and it really isn't lagging enough all the time to the point it's unplayable. I just hope that the optimization issue is resolved.
So do I reccommend this game. Well yes, and no. My only reason I would not recommend this is because of the lag. So when that's patched up I'll gladly give it a thumbs up.

Now, I'm not someone that reviews a game over microtransations, graphics and optimizations, I have my reasons for it.
To start this review off, I absolutely love the game, this is coming from someone that has never played the first game AND is playing on the hardest difficulty for my first blind playthrough. After playing through this game and having yet to finish it, once I finish it, I might go check out Human Revolution.
Aside from that, the gameplay is something that's thrown me back quite alot. From a slightly multiple-choice and exploration(-ISH, I USE ISH LIGHTLY) type of gameplay to a intense, stealth/non-stealth combat game.
Even after 13 hours, I still have yet to get comfortable with the controls, it's a bit wonky at times (for me) but I get used to it after a while. The controls are (as far as I know) fully customizable, setting up my own type of keybinds to suit my needs for a much better experience.
The story, I might screw this one up, as I have yet to play Human Revolution and the first Deus Ex game.
This game's story has me in a really blank spot right now, as I'm abit confused on what
is going on. Aside from the confusion and complete misunderstanding of most of it, it's a really interesting story that I'd love to learn more about, with the news papers and collectables in the game, I'm able to piece together certain parts to understand the story better.
Aside from what was said above, this part of the review isn't going to affect my opinion on the game, as I still recommend it for those that atleast agree with me on one or two of these certain points.
Microtransactions, oh boy here we go.
Yes, the microtransactions in this game seem really absurd, especially when it's main focus is to be a singleplayer game (I think, correct me if I'm wrong), but come on, this DLC for singleplayer is completely optional! You don't have to buy it, just ignore it and you'll have a great time in the game.
Graphics, not entirely something I care about much.
What I care about in a game, is gameplay and story, I don't care if there's fancy graphic settings or if there's special shader, I don't care about any of that. But overall, the game looks really great, I love the design it has. One thing that bothers me is what seems to be some type of film grain which is rather annoying at certain points with motion blur.
Optimizations, I'm touchy on this topic.
I can't entirely review the game on optimizations, as I'm sitting on a build that is able to run it on everything maxed with a average of 60 - 100 FPS. There's a couple dips to 30 - 40, but it's overall running well, plus I have yet to experience any crashing. For a GTX 1070, while it was a game released AFTER the 1070, I do kinda feel like it could use abit of some polishing for optimization, as I kinda feel I should be getting abit higher frame rates or no frame drops.
This is basically my review of Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, I really do love this game and recommend it to people that only care about the gameplay and story. If you're someone that really hates microtransations and wouldn't buy a game with it, then... I don't think this game's for you.

I love the horror genre and don't scare easily so I figured 0.49 wasn't much money to risk if I didn't like it. This is amazingly atmospheric and so engaging. I set the resolution to 1920x1080 and quality to Fantastic, turned out the lights and turned up my headphones. The graphics and audio are actually really good. The game has a dark, gritty feel to it so I'm guessing that's where all the bad quality reviews are coming from. The controls are wasd standard by default, but you can customize them to your liking. Movement felt pretty fluid with no lag. I became completely engrossed had more "wtf was that???" moments than I've had in quite awhile. When the HatMan ate my soul (on toast with jam?) and I turned on the lights to find out who put poo in my shorts, I was amazed that only 12 minutes had passed. I spent more time petting my cat to calm down than I did playing the game. No, I wouldn't pay 60 bucks for it, but I feel great about what I did pay. Do yourself a favor and get this.

While although this game is a slight letdown to anyone who has played the first GunZ game, it's still relatively fun. Since it's not a complete game I can only hope that the Devs listen to the community and bring back a playstyle that is based on skill and reactions.

The second part of the infamous Gunz game where it is known for its high skill cap and fast combat system with a various of weapons at your disposal. I played the first game and loved it but had to stop due to the amount of hackers that flooded it unfortunately. When I heard a 2nd game was being made I was pretty ecstatic knowing one of my all time favorite 3rd person shooter was making a reboot. Unfortunately... I was dissappointed.
Before I begin, this is a side-by-side comparison review between Gunz1 and Gunz2. For those of you who have NOT played Gunz1, then you will have NO idea what i'm talking about and won't know what I felt when playing this game. Though I do bring up other points that are a "by itself" case in terms of Gunz2 gameplay but that is up to you to decide if you agree with me or not.
Without further ado, here is my Gunz2 review:
First off... classes... WHY?
It's sad to say this game tried to mimic the currently famous/mainstream shooters like COD and BattleField by introducing classes that uses specific weapons and has different playstyles. To make it worse, if you want to play the other classes you need to proceed to buy them. Just... no.
Gunz1 was fun because you could buy w/e weapon you wanted, try out different combinations and play it your own way.
With the class system it chooses FOR you limiting your playstyle and forcing you to either make a new account or pay to play another character if you get bored with the one you've been grinding for who knows how long.
Oh wait did I say grinding? yep... there is a level system in this game.
Every other level or so you unlock skills that are a necessary core playstyle for your class such as... I don't know... being able to save yourself mid-air when an enemy knocks you up which was a clear distinction in Gunz1 if you were going against a bad player or not.
This also brings me back to playing the other characters... oh boy now you got to level THEM up to.
I wanted to play a 3rd person shooter and go crazy, not grind and be forced to level my character up to access his abilities to fully experience the CORE of the gameplay.
Gunz1 had a level system but each level unlocked new weapons for you to try out, NOT necessary skills.
This brings me to playstyle itself.
I've reached level 6 before stopping (reasons which i'll explain later) and noticed a distinct play style everyone incorporates. Rush the enemy, knock them down using melee combos, then proceed to fill them with lead using your gun.
You see in Gunz1 most of the time you did NOT see a gun pop out unless it was a quickdraw. Most of the time you would see people flying around everywhere with their swords out using wall-slash climbing techniques or butterfly sword fights. Melee is completely obsolete in this game other than to do what I've mentioned above and to use your .... *ughs* ultimates/active abilities.
Oh boy... lets bring in some abilities that takes about the same skill level of a 13 year old targetting a mob in World of Warcraft and give it 1-shotting capabilities. That's right folks. Once you reach 3 bars in your power guage, you get access to a specific class based ability that pretty much 1-shots or gets close to it if you land it... which is pretty much easy since every single melee hit manages to stagger you and the game isn't as fast paced as it used to be.
Speaking of fast paced... this game is slow as BALLS compared to Gunz1. Seriously, they literally dumbed down the gameplay for people of all skill levels can somewhat compete with one another. When the point of a game is to try and out play your opponent in terms of wit and playstyle and you dumb that down so there is hardly any learning curve and the combat system is generic and repetitive, you get Gunz 2.
Oh and what a way to complement the slow gameplay with laggy servers...
Laggy servers that are chosen beforehand in a system where a "host" is designated to provide a specific region that best optimizes the rest of the players internet stability. Just as warning, that internet stability is nonexistant 3 out 5 times where hosts are constantly being shifted to different players due to the horrible connectivity issues.
Pay to Win.
Yep folks, this is a pay to win game. Gear is HEAVILY weighted in this game where a gear difference is enough to shift a balance dramatically to one team. For example: if you were to have a stand off with the enemy without moving, the person with better gear WILL kill you before you even break his shield. In this aspect, outplaying the enemy means nothing since he becomes a versatile one-man army being able to TAKE hits and dish out twice as much damage than you can.
But wait, there's more!
The queue system and lobby system, I admit, is one of the better ones I've seen that incorporates it. It's fast, it's clean, and gets you in a game without any trouble.
HOWEVER, the matching system is broken to all hell. There is no brackets in this game, as far as I can tell, and you WILL get paired up with people 2x, 3x, 4x, 5x + level than you. This is the main reason I quit the game because I constantly got paired with high leveled people that HAD the gear, the ABILITIES for the class, UPGRADES to their armor, and so forth. It was entirely one sided in most matches I've played since there is always a high level in yours or the enemy's team.
I'm pretty sure there are more points I missed but constantly thinking about Gunz 2 just keeps filling me with dissappointment and anger.
As a disclaimer, this review is purely OPINION. That's right folks... OPINION. So if you get butthurt because you enjoyed the game and I didn't then keep your comments to yourself. If there are people out there who do find this game fun then good for you. I'm not bashing the people who play this game, I'm just stating my opinion on why this game could have been better and what they changed that should not have been changed in the first place.
Well that's that. I hope my review sheds some light on w/e woes you have.

I don't write reviews on a normal basis but I felt like I should on this occasion. RWBY:Grimm Eclipse is in early access for a reason. It's not finished. What's there is good but there are still problems. The optimisation definitely needs some work, even with my fairly powerful system (i7-4790k R9 390) I still get stuttering fairly frequently and occasionally the framerate will completely die (although this appears to happen at the same time for everyone in game so may be an issue with the servers rather than an optimisation issue), taking a few seconds to recompose itself. As a fan of the show I definitely feel like I get more out of the game than someone who doesn't watch RWBY but even so there's still a decent amount of replayability to it. The one campaign that's there at the moment only takes about an hour to finish with a reasonably competent team, a bit less with a really good team and a bit more with a not so good team. However, RTGAMES have said they're adding two more campaigns, a single player mode and a horde mode this year, along with some optimisation tweaks so hopefully they'll really add to the game. Overall I feel like this is a must have if you like RWBY and like to jump into a hack n slash every now and then, otherwise, maybe wait to see how the next few updates turn out.

This game squeaks by as a recommendation from me.  It's good, but not great.
Game play is primarily a first person narrative.  You awake on an airship just after an explosion and you walk and talk to people to figure out the culprit.  Sort of.  The game's greatest strength is also its biggest weakness because while there is a pretty dynamic story with lots of options to pick from, you are not figuring out the story as much as you are writing it.  You can pick anyone you want to be the culprit, even be the culprit yourself, the game might be like "these bits of evidence that you uncovered don't quite match, but hey whatever you want" then there's a bit of outro that tells how your choices affected the world.  That's brilliant from a creative standpoint, but rather dull from a gamer standpoint.  I want my choices to affect the world I interact with, not the overall world that my character goes on to live in.  The game itself is pretty non-consequential.
There's also some stealth elements, but they are pretty basic.  There's only two areas where you actually have to dodge guards.  The rest are just walking clockwise, and flipping a coin to guess if someone might see you when you leave a restricted area.  There are also 4 main "powerups" you can unlock as you play.  You get to choose these powerups as you go, and they affect how you enter certain rooms, sometimes restricting access to them.  It makes the gameplay seem less-linear, but really it only makes your backtracking non-linear.  The main areas are still unlocked in the same order.
Graphics and sounds are decent.  The game switched art styles between the alpha and the release version, so while it looks interesting it's also jaring to look out the window and see crayon clouds floating by.  There's lots of public domain music that you've heard in other games, so take that for what you will.
There are also, currently (v1.09), a number of small bugs.  Nothing game breaking, but a lot of the achievements are not working properly and that is disapointing.
If I can summarize with a popular arbitrary rating system, I'd give the game 6/10.  Just over the line of a game that might not be worth the price.  I do enjoy the developers ideas.  I intend to check out their other game, Post Mortem, to see how it aligns with this one, and hopefully their next title is just as promising.

is a first person adventure game which offers very simple gameplay mechanics, most of which are based around stealth and sneaking around. Still, what Karaski lacks in gameplay, it compensates in exploration, narrative, its characters and the player’s dialogue with them.
The game takes places aboard the Karaski, the first Commonwealth airship, as it makes its first flight. Despite being somewhat quiet at first, things quickly take a quick turn and someone ends up sabotaging the ship. It is up to you to investigate and determine who is responsible for the attack on this Commonwealth technological marvel. There are certainly a lot of plot holes left by the main story but these are filled by your dialogue choices, not only in terms of the world the game takes place but in terms of the history background of your character and others as well.
In this sense, sometimes it felt like I was actually playing at another time, in another place, in the same universe as
but in a context that reminded of
. Despite the fact that both have very distinct art styles and ways of telling a story, some aspects of Karaski did remind me of the whole nationalist propaganda that was present in
. Still, I must say that the game did fail to keep me fully immersed at times, either due to the clunky animations or due to the fact that I’m still not 100% sure if I like or dislike the visuals of the game. Eitherways, I must say that the music you hear coming from certain radios on the ship add a lot to the atmosphere and helps make the world a lot more believable.
Your investigation will be focused around 4 major characters, with each one representing a certain “group”. One is more inclined towards religion, other is a nationalist, another is the architect of the Karaski airship itself and the last one is one of the members of the board of the biggest railroad company, to whom the introduction of transportation of goods and people by air poses a great threat. You’ll spend a lot of your time sneaking around in places where you shouldn’t be trying to figure out clues and the potential motives for any of these suspects to have sabotaged the airship. In this sense, the game features a branching storyline in which your choices have their own consequences and, in result, the game has different endings which are a result of your actions.
In the end, I feel like from the small list of
that I have about the game there is only one that might be a deal breaker for some people, and that is the fact that the game has no voice acting, which can be exceptionally disappointing in a game that focuses on dialogue and narrative. Apart from that, I just don’t really stylized font of dialogues, which thankfully you can turn off and also the head bobbing. Like I’ve initially said, the gameplay itself is nothing to be amazed by, you’ll be leaning around corners to watch out for guards but once you get a hold of certain items the worry of getting caught where you’re not supposed to be on the ship quickly goes away.

It's October 1923, my name is Jan Kowalski and I am honored to be one of the first passengers onboard the airship A. A. Karaski. When I joined this miracle of technology, I was excited with curiosity, how it works and what I’ll experience during the flight. I actually thought that I would spend the entire journey in a bar on the upper deck sipping fancy whiskey with casual conversation. After boarding, I picked up a boarding pass, introduced myself to a guide of the airship and headed to my cabin. Well, was just going to, because just around the corner I somehow fainted and my plan was screwed a little. A lot.
I woke up in a store room somewhere in the lower deck. I was glad I’m alive, my head screamed with pain. When searching for a way out, I just remembered that the guide told me something about, that I will question a lot of people on various issues and it will depend a lot on what I’ll know about them. I would rather know, how to get out and complain to the captain, what happened to me. I want an apology and a big glass of whiskey! Right in the next room it became even weirder. There was a turned on radio speaking to me. So, the thing is, there's someone on the ship, who does not want it to reach its destination. And I'm here to solve this question. OK, well, but who is it and what he wants to do? And there are apparently wardens to immediately lead me out or arrest when they spot me.
So I crawled around the first warden through a ventilation shaft and ran into the next room. I have discovered a wounded technician, broken ship control panel bursting with fire and acid bottle with a glove near it. Someone wanted to sabotage the ship! I went back to the radio and was told that it could easily be me. Such stupidity… I had to find out what is really going on and who is to blame! I ran up on deck and immediately met Jean, enthusiastic journalist. All passengers apparently felt the turbulence and thinks that something strange happened to the ship. She asked me to cooperate in the investigation. But could I trust her?
I had to explore the entire ship, avoiding guards, sometimes even bribing them not to report me, pick locks into the private rooms, search the crates with cargo, scuff my knees in the air ducts, but also talk to all the people on board… one of them had to be a saboteur. Sometimes it wasn't easy, I had to share a bottle of booze with them and to force them to talk. It seemed that it had to be one of the big four, Mrs. Boyel, that weird doctor, designer of the airship Karaski or even the captain? And then these lost parachutes... I felt at the end like Hercule Poirot, but I found the person who was responsible for this ... I think so at least. Or was I wrong?
Karaski: What Goes Up, is a smoothly playable mix of steampunk adventure with stealth action, where the main thing is well written story with deep characters. Nonlinear progress and stylized graphics help to desire to explore all parts of the game and also thanks to multiple endings and achievements it’s fun to play it repeatedly. The only major drawback I see is the absence of voiceovers, which decreases immersion a little. Lift off!

Disclosure: Product provided via key for review at:
Karaski: What Goes Up… is an entry in a relatively rare genre, the immersive simulation. While it is a genre that has never had huge mainstream appeal, when done right it creates quite a compelling space.
CONTROLS (3.5/5)
Karaski is a social stealth game and plays a bit like a blend of a fairly basic stealth title and adventure game. Its stealth mechanics are not deep or refined, and mostly consist of making sure you’re out of line of sight before you do anything risky. That being said, the options available are generally more than adequate, though not mechanically interesting enough to be a reason to seek out the game.
Adventure elements play like most other first-person adventures, running around talking to people, digging through their personal effects for doodads and currency, and occasionally using what you find to get more access to the plot.
GRAPHICS/SOUND (2.5/5)
As a low-budget affair by a small development team it should surprise no one that the visual side of things isn’t very impressive. Karaski is visually Spartan, favoring big and exaggerated geometry in the level designs over small details.
Characters designs are similar, with ornaments like hats and beards distinguishing characters more than unique faces. I’d found there could also be some strange judder with the game when mousing over objects that could be interacted with.
There’s no voice acting, which can be a little distracting, but it does allow for characters to have a wider range of dialogue. Music seems highly inspired by the type of tracks you’d hear in old propaganda pieces and fits the game’s tone rather well, even if it does little to stand out.
Sound effects are a bit hit or miss, with footsteps drowning things out a bit too much, though it does make for good positional cues when sneaking around.
GAMEPLAY (3.5/5)
The airship Karaski is taking its inaugural flight as a demonstration of the might of the glorious Commonwealth, a fictional stand in for the U.S.S.R., and the player has managed to snag a ticket. As you are boarding, however, you are quickly bopped on the head.
From there on you can make the story your own as the game allows you to play it as just a temporary knockout, or perhaps it gave you amnesia. Soon a mysterious radio is asking for your help, offering another opportunity where you can also play along or craft your own backstory. The game is full of little moments like this that allow you to fill in the blanks of your past.
Regardless of whatever backstory you decide on, the main thrust of the plot has the player investigating the mysterious sabotaging of the ship. It seems someone doesn’t want the flight to be a success, and there are four prime suspects: the architect Karaski, whom the ship (and thus the game) are named for, the rebellious ship captain, the religious doctor that sees mankind flying as a sin, and the train magnate that could view airship travel as competition.
At the start of the game you’ll get to choose a tool you fancy, and these significantly affect the gameplay. A fake police badge will get you out of trouble and might coerce information out of people, while a lock-pick will get you into the many locked rooms you’ll find in the course of the game.
Most of these items can also be found later in the game, but some are well hidden. During my first playthrough, for instance, I never found the item that lets you unlock and navigate vents, which closed off a few story beats.
Players are given relatively free rein to explore the ship, provided you can uncover the tools needed to get there, though there are a few choke points in the story. Many things you do impact the fates of the various characters, so even if you’re given a side-quest that you think is helping, the effect of completing it may end up doing more harm than good.
Karaski’s stealth mechanics are probably the least interesting element of the game, with the story and the ways you can change it being the strong point. Wisely there is no combat or death if you get caught; instead you’re ejected from where you were trespassing.
You may be able to bribe your way out of trouble, though if you don’t, your suspicion meter will rise. That can affect the way characters view you. Some actually seem to like a bit of a nasty streak, and might open up more, while others will consider you with disdain.
While the story is enjoyable, it does feel a bit more limited compared to other standouts in the genre like Consortium or Last Express. There are only a few characters, and events are more oriented around the player rather than everyone sort of having their own life.
This makes repeat playthroughs less attractive as, while the tools of the trade change things up a little from a gameplay perspective, the story doesn’t appear to have much to offer beyond the end sequences.
There’s also some lovely end credits that players get to explore rather than watch, including an extra room that showcases elements of the game in an alpha state when the art style was much different.
OVERALL (3.5/5)
While Karaski: What Goes Up… is a bit rough around the edges, both visually and mechanically, it does offer a good mystery story with a variety of ways to approach it.

Take to the skies in this whodunit mystery. You will take on the role of a passenger on this one of a kind airship, but something has gone wrong. The airship has been sabotage, but who has done it. Was it you? Will you be able to uncover who did it? Will you be caught snooping around and have everyone expect you of doing this heinous act?
In Karaski: What Goes Up... this is exactly what you'll be doing. You will be playing through the game with your main mission being to get to the bottom of the mystery of the sabotage, but there are other quests that you can take on to perhaps pry information from other passengers. In this game you will have the chance to bribe guards to look the other way, entice passengers with the promise of alcohol, and of course gain tools that will allow you access to different areas of the ship.
I'm going to be honest when I first picked up this game I didn't really get into it. I was really just running around the airship aimlessly while getting frustrated, but when I tried again from scratch and really tried to sink my teeth in I found a game where I didn't know what was going to happen next. There is definitely the need for stealth in this game, and early on I got caught ALOT. Thankfully as I played more and more of the game I was able to develop strategies of how to move around the different sections nearly undetected.
This game was a lot of fun, and there were plenty of clues that you had to be on the look out for to help solidify your case against the evildoer. There were quite a few repeat clues scattered on the ship as well, but something tells me that these locations are just the places where random items are placed so that you can experience a unique playthrough each time you play. That's right folks the person who did it in one playthrough might not actually be the the person who did it, if you were to play it again.
Graphically there was definitely a good art style going on, however sometimes it did come off as cookie cutter in certain areas where the same assets were used over and over again. Not surprisingly it was mostly the NPC guards that were all the same, the boxes/trunks around the ship, the different bedrooms, etc. Sure there is going to be duplication of areas and items in real life, but I just feel like there should have been a little more for a personal effect in the different people's rooms.
One of the things I always hope to see is voice acting in the game, unfortunately this game does not have that component, and there are sections that have pretty lengthy conversation pieces that after a while you just want skip through and hope that they weren't too important. However that's usually when there's something key in finding out who did it.
This game might not be for everyone, there's definitely some rough spots to the game, and as I just stated there is A LOT of text to read at certain parts of the game, but I did enjoy playing the game, and I think many people out there would enjoy it as well. This game gets an 8.0 out of 10.

I had a lot of fun with Karaski: What Goes Up, I'm also a pretty big fan of mystery type stuff so I knew I'd enjoy it before going into it.
The game is a who done it type mystery game where you must solve a mystery revolving around the sabatage of a commonwealth airship. You do this by exploring the airship, collecting clues, conversing with the 4 suspects and ultimately choosing who you think is the perpetrator. The game is open ended in nature so your actions during the game have an impact on the outcome of the story.
The game also incorporates some stealth elements too but they aren't punishing in terms of consequences. If you happen to get caught exploring areas you're not supposed to you can try to bribe the guard to look the other way but if you don't have the coin they'll report you to the captain and your suspicion level will go up. If your suspicion level gets too high the crime may get pinned on you in the end so you'll have to be careful.
The game is a lot of fun and only takes around 4 hours to complete and up to 5+ if you discover everything the game has to offer. Definitely a game that's worth checking out if you're a fan of mystery type adventure games.
-Shaun Meyers (Kyo Akiara) out!

KARASKI: What Goes Up . . .
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

The “AA KARASKI” airship is the pride of the Commonwealth of Danube and the first of its kind. You will take part in its maiden voyage set for the 11th of October 1923, which is an entire five days floating in the sky. What a sensational way to go from one part of the Commonwealth of Danube to another. However, on the third day of this exceptional trip, you will wake up in an unfamiliar room with a rather strong headache (well, someone knocked you on your noggin pretty hard –that’ll do it!). You will find out very quickly that something is wrong with the airship. Someone tampered with the “AA KARASKI” and you need to figure out who is/are the culprit (s). Oh, by the way, how is your noggin?
Karaski: What Goes Up is an adventure / stealth game which takes place on the airship “AA KARASKI.” You will have to investigate and find out who is behind the sabotage. The story is very well written with great dialogues. As you interrogate people, you will be able to choose several options available to you. Depending on your response, it can affect your relationship which each person. At the start of the game, you will not have anything on you and you will not be able to open certain doors until you manage to get the “ lockateer”  tool. Other tools and keys need to be found in order to open ventilation shafts, wooden boxes and doors to restricted areas. Make sure you look everywhere and collect all the money and bottles of alcohol you can find laying around. Read as many newspapers and notes as you can; they will give you additional information on what is going on in the Commonwealth of Danube and give you some evidence too.
As you progress, you will receive quests to do. All of them are related to the suspects. Make sure you are not acting suspicious. Things like being caught by a steward when you are opening a locked door will arouse suspicion about you. Sometimes you can bribe them with money or a good bottle of grog. Oh, one more thing . . .  if you screen is shaking, it is not because of the alcohol, it’s because the airship is passing through turbulence!
Plenty of achievements in this game but most of them are hidden, which is good in regards to re-playability.
The graphics are good and I had absolutely no problem with resolution. The controls are responsive and easy to use. I prefer to use the Keyboard and mouse rather than the gamepad. The soundtrack is enjoyable.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good graphics
-	Great story & dialogues
-	Good soundtrack
-	Achievement and trading cards
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	Stewards can catch you pretty easily.
8/10
KARASKI: What Goes Up is a very good adventure game with a well-written story and dialogue.

This game starts with a somewhat interesting concept. You can choose between a mother and a father, which so far, the only difference that it makes is that your death scream is different. You're trapped in some kind of demonic ward, or should I say, a shadow ward? This ward is always changing, so you have to keep moving forwards all the time. You gotta collect pages, too, like in Slenderman games, but way more, and a few other items along the way like matches and levers. You pretty much run between corridors, and now and then, you'll hear some kind of whispering, telling you that there is an item in a side room. If you miss an item and leave the room, just keep running, there is no point in going back, it probably changed already.
The main enemy of this game, is the Hat Man, a being that from a distance kinda looks like a trenchcoat wearing guy with a hat, surrounded in a cloud of blackness and with a purple aura. Later on, he changes to something different, that's way faster and more persistent, adding a bit of fear to the mix.
That being said, the problem with these procedually generated games is that, sometimes, it's way too random. And in this game's case, sometimes you're going to be able to finish the game in less than 30 minutes, sometimes it's going to take way longer than that. It took me around 30 minutes for a room I needed to spawn. I even believed my game was bugged.
The game's atmosphere is kinda creepy at first, being chased by this creature that never stops. (Actually, he does, when you enter a certain kind of room, like stairs or the room with the pit)
It's got some weak jumpscares, too, like a ceiling light falling, or a wheelchair moving. The problem is, after running from the Hat Man for a while, and after seeing the same rooms and the same jumpscares over and over again over the period of....dozens of minutes....It kinda starts to get old rather fast. It's quite a short game, and it doesn't offer much. It's really, really cheap, too. So, all in all, it feels stale, and it gets old rather fast, but I did find it fun for a short while. Maybe playing lots of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ games myself kinda made me more tolerant to this kind of stuff, but, If it's on sale, why not? You could try it for yourself.

Little does the player's character know, the asylum has nobody in it, except for the Hat Man and his Shadow People. The main objective is to run through the asylum, collecting journal pages and avoiding the Hat Man and his Shadow People. All in all, this game had a lot of potential, but it was really wasted, just like my time playing it.

Ok after quite a few more hours invested in the game then when my first review was made I think Im going to take another pass at it. Once again cannot stress enough that steam needs a neutral button.
First off this game was not designed with wsad in mind. Even on the lowest setting the camera jerks around like mad. I could also spend an entire review complaining about the fov but many people have already done it much better than I ever could. Second the ui is absolute garbage. No effort was made to change the game into something pc friendly so you can only use 4 spells/abilities at once, and they are mapped to the same radial. I play as a jack of all trades and have 9 abilities, however im only able to use 4 in combat. 4. Diablo 3 had a better skill system than this.
And for some unfathomable reason the useless 12 slot radial menu only allows you to bind potions. Thats it. Im playing on hard and I have only ever had to use health potions, which you can use by pressing r already.
Wanna switch your weapons and try a different play style mid combat? Sure! Just press start, select items, select weapons, scroll all the way through what can be up to 70 weapons (you will never carry this many but thats how many backpack slots you have at first), select the weapon you want and bind it to either your primary or secondary weapon slot. 5 steps to switch weapons. And trust me, you will be doing this alot. So yeah the simple task of switching weapons completely breaks what little flow of combat there already was.
Moving on to design I honestly have no problem with either the combat or the art style. The combat is darksiders and the art style is wow. Nuff said
I want to balance all these cons with some pros now so here goes. The game is huge. At my current play time i havent even made it across half the game map, and I still have yet to head to either of the dlc maps. Also EA apparently has most of the voice actors from bethesdas works at their beck and call. Barry Dennen is always a welcome addition to any game.
And the story is... well its alright. I felt a little let down with the first 15 minutes of the the game building me up as this whole fateless resurrected badass with the power of a god and the ability to change destiny itself then be told to go find some flowers for some schmuck so he can fight off the local creatures (thats what Im here for damn it!).
But the characters they bother to give personality are kind of memorable: the drunken circus preformer trying to keep his troop together despite his wife/co-leader leaving him, the leader of a band of mercinaries more concerned with keeping his hold and troops in presentable condition than completing jobs. The storybook maiden doomed to play the part of a tyrant forever trying to break the cycle and giving you the chance to help her all the while the people who sent you after her begging you to make her keep her role because its "How the story is supposed to end." It all adds up.
So I leave you with this. If you can shoulder your way past the fact that its not even a port, just a complete copy of its console version than its worth checking out. Dont buy it at full price though. But then who does these days?
P.s thank you Coraline Castell for suggesting widescreen fixer. However the fact that a game this large lacks something as basic as a changable fov kind of speaks for itself.

Only played a short game but was quite impressed so had to write this short review. If there is one thing missing from todays game titles then its a decent amount of world war 1 games. Enter toy soldiers. This is an interesting tower defense type game set during world war 1 in Europe. Although you are playing on what is supposed to be a toy game, it feels very much like world war 1 during the trench warfare. You have a limited number of bases where you can place various weapons such as machine guns, mortars and cannons. The enemy, as in other tower defense games attacks in ever increasing waves. You have to protect your toy box (the core) from being destroyed. Each of the weapons will act on its own but at anytime you can take over them and target the enemy yourself. The more enemies you destroy the more currency you earn and therefore are able to place / replace more weapons. At the end of each campaign battle you unlock more authentic WW1 weapons to use in the next fight. The enemy attacks you with soldiers, cavalry and armour. The barb wire slows soldiers who die as they crawl through it. The tanks on the other hand just roll over them and if you don't place your weapon bases carefully its curtains.
If you like boys toys, WW1 and tower defense games then this is a must.
