As it is right now, this is a fun game despite how light on content it currently is, and I'm looking forward to what is planned for future updates.
- Combat is pretty simple: you have a melee and ranged attack, you can dodge and you have three special attacks. Simple enough to learn, even a team of novice players could take on a few dozen Grimm with no problems once they learn the attack patterns of each monster. Luckily the next update is set to add a bit more depth to the combat with heavy and counter attacks, as well as balancing the Grimm accordingly, which is great as I feel like it's a bit too easy right now.
- The campaign we have right now adds up to maybe around an hour of gameplay. I hope the other planned campaigns and horde mode will be enough to keep people engaged. That said, the MOBA-like micro-progression is already a good reason for people to keep playing. You can't unlock every skill, but its fun to play around with different skill setups and see how effective they are. I love the combination of micro-progression and the fast paced action of a co-op hack-n-slash, I think it works great
- The game looks great, which isn't much of a surprise since they're basically using the exact character and weapon models, as well as art style, as the show
- Overall performance is great, pretty much constant 60fps, until you start fighting more Grimm at a time. Playing solo, this isn't much of an issue since the difficulty scales and you'll be fighting maybe at most 15 or less enemies at any one time. But with a full or almost full lobby, the number of enemies definitely starts to hit your performance a bit, and I have a decent rig (though I'm sure someone with a more powerful PC than mine would handle this just fine). It's most noticeable when you're in the collapsed Mountain Glenn sublevels fighting a large amount of enemies, with some that explode upon death
Great to see RWBY expanding to other media forms outside of the show, and great job to the dev team creating basically the exact game I imagined should be made after seeing each of the show trailers way back in 2013, I'm almost certain Monty would have loved to see this game to completion

After having been playing this game for a little while I am ready with a review:
I like the overall feeling of the game, I definitely enjoy a game that lets people do dodge-offsets to chain combos, so the combat system is a great thing!
With the voice acting there are a couple of problems with the game itself actually cutting off dialogue, without any clicking of buttons, but just because of the level ending too quickly, this has been a problem in Chapter 1 consistantly. As well as other random voice clips just being cut off due to the game.
When you connect to someone where either you or them has a bad connection you are in for a bad time. I recently played with 4 people through the campaign and even though we got through it, then having to wait 2-3 seconds before your hits registered really messes with you when you try to attack and dodge away to rinse and repeat.
As for "optional paths" in the current campaign, then I'd really like to see both paths be open at all times in one way or another, as in Chapter 2 and 3 with unfortunate RNG you never really get to see the other places. since you are always following the intended path with the artifact. So at least make a way to get to both places all the times.
A way to create your own lobby from the start would be nice, so you can make sure you are the host, this is currently possible by creating a friend only lobby and then turning the friend only option off, but simple is always a good option to have.
I praised the combat system earlier, but it would be nice if there was some more "customization" to it, I guess, more ways to chain combos or more ways to use your secondary weapon to beat up the grimm.
Otherwise as a Roosterteeth fan and fan of RWBY I gotta say, this game really has the right feel to it.
*Edit*
To add to this review, as I have been playing more and finishing up more characters.
Blake's voiceclip is played when Weiss is the first to reach "Main Street" in Mountain Glenn, even when not even having Blake with you.
One thing I'd really like seeing fixed is the freeze mechanic. When an enemy is frozen they are still fully able to attack, it does not cancel anything, only once in a while. I've seen the boars being able to headbutt through their freeze time several time, both with Weiss' and Ruby's freeze mechanic.
I will keep on playing even though after these 9 hours, even when playing the different characters it's getting very repetetive. The thing keeping it fun is the community around the game and the random people you meet. I'd really like to see more content that utilises every nook and cranny of the map, since there is a lot of dead space in the game and invisible walls in places that aren't even needed, but with them removed it would add to faster paths through things if you know how to jump around.

I was given a copy of this game to review and even though it is admittedly not my preferred game type I found enough charm and cleverness to recommend it positively.
The game was lent an air of pulpy respectability by the themes being presented by the suspects even as they boozed and smoked and gossiped. Each represented a core belief system; faith in technology, business, religion, and nationalism albeit to different degrees and even sometimes with a bitterness at the core.I applaud the creator's efforts at making a believable background and that each of the main characters is largely more than the sum of their parts.
The gameplay and aesthetics remind me of The Ship:In both games stealth plays a large role although with Karaski you are utilizing it much differently and are not meant to kill or be killed. Bribery,lockpicks, and even slippers which somehow smother your footsteps enough to render you completely silent are your tools to solve the mystery of who sabotaged the A.A. Karaski.At first it seems exciting to have to listen to the footsteps of stewards and guards in order to avoid detection, but there are many ways to mitigate any effects of being caught and eventually I got lazy and stopped caring.
The writing shows elements of wit and humor, but it never really feels tense or dramatic and at times those "big ideas" feel shoehorned in to the plot.
The game boasts of replayability and perhaps there is truth to that but I doubt I will be playing it again any time soon. It must be said that the current asking price is too high for what the game gives you, in the end.

Do you remember the game Postmortem: One Must Die? It’s an indie adventure game that was awarded strong praise in some corners of the gaming press back in 2013. It was praised because it had well written and nuanced characters. Unfortunately not everybody on Steam appreciated that game and thus it has only received mix review scores. However, the development studio that made that game is Unbound Creations and they are back with Karaski: What Goes Up. It certainly appears that they’ve listened to the constructive feedback, both good and bad, from Postmortem and have put the lessons that they have learned into execution here. This is an adventure game with plenty of action and of course the characters are again written superbly.
At the very beginning of the game you are told something that is clearly ominous. You will be asked many questions. However, the correct answers are the decision that you make. The truth is woven by your decisions. Each of your actions has an impact and consequences follow. I’ve always enjoyed games that do this if they are able pull it off without making the player feel that regardless of the decisions that they made the story and its outcome would have remained the same. It’s incredibly difficult to make it work. To this end I believe that Unbound Creations really did well with this in the game.
The game is set upon an airship – the first ever airship in fact – and somebody has sabotaged it. You are potentially a prime suspect due to your proximity to it when you awoke from the concussion. The good thing is that it is entirely up to you to determine who did it, why they did it and how they did it. The great thing, in regards to replayability, is that there is more than one solution to the game and by that I mean that unless you play the same way – choosing the same options – you’re never going to play the same game twice.
The  graphics and the sound featured within Karaski are certainly apt and aide immersion. They’re not state of the art by any means but they have been carefully chosen. They follow the principle of ‘KISS’ – keep it simple stupid – so as to not take away from the game play, the story or the mystery of the game which are the clear and decided focuses of the game. The graphics are almost cartoonlike in stature and you’ll be able to notice this from the very beginning as you walk through the exhibition on the way to getting onto the airship.
If adventure and action wasn’t enough the game also introduces a well thought out stealth mechanic. When a steward, the doctor or other members of the ship can see you you need to be careful. If you get caught going into places where you should not be your level of suspicion will rise. This has a lot of impact on the way people will see you on board the ship. You may even find yourself being found guilty of a crime that you didn’t commit. It really is a great touch.
A feature on Karaski would be remiss if I failed to mention the humor. It’s present all throughout the game and helps provide the game a certain charm that really aides the player in wanting to continue playing the game through to the conclusion. For such a serious matter the lighthearted presentation really works. This is an enormous strength and demonstrates the depth of the writing to see beyond the base layers. There is humor and delight to be found in even the smallest of matters.
A rock solid adventure game with stealth play, a lot of well written humor, deep characters and a great narrative. Karaski: What Goes Up ticks all of the boxes.

Karaski: What Goes Up brings back the simplistic, yet comical style of Papers, Please, but in a 3D exploration model of an airship.
This is a simplified adventure game with no cut-scenes or video, yet still in classic 3D format. You interact with various objects with simplified controls that do not get in the way of the action. This creates a casual game experience that allows you to just run around the ship and search for clues, without trying to keep up with key-mapping. Clues, maps, and data are all kept at hand for you to retrieve on demand.
There is a large stealth element. The sound effects become part of the detective work, as you find yourself listening for footsteps to grow louder and then quieter again to monitor the passing of guards. You are able to lean left or right to peer around doorways, with the camera angle accommodating your changed angles.
I was surprised to see that not only did my choices matter, but even becoming suspicious by being caught snooping around caused me to be able to gain more info from shady characters like myself. The story line seems malleable to the character you create.
The story is filled with references to Steampunk genre subjects; like technology, religion, and progressive utopian dreams of a “Scientific” society.  The player chooses from a variety of responses to each of these topics in conversation, ranging from agreeable, to snarky (Think Deponia.) The player character also is allowed to choose buffs at various points in the narrative to choose a focus on conversation, mechanical repair, stealth/breaking & entering, for example. In this sense the game reminds me of Deus Ex, though on a simpler level. You are also able to choose how to respond to being discovered. You are able to bribe the npc’s to look the other way, or you may choose to be a bully.
The graphics are not as simple as point & click hidden object mysteries, or The Shivah.  Yet, it is not as complex as The Portal. It fits nicely in the same complexity of graphics as Stanley’s Parable.  Once I warmed up to the style of game, I soon became caught up in the story; probably because the ease of play facilitated simply doing the missions I was given. It makes solving the mystery enjoyable, rather than stressful, providing a lightly humorous spin on politics and revolt, with cartoon-style artwork.

Overall, the replay-ability is average, with achievements for playing through the different branches of choices. The game is suitable for most age groups, and simple enough for even the casual gamer. But, it is not a game for hard-core gamers who like complex games. The achievements are simple enough to be mastered by most gamers. Many gamers could complete a play-through in less than 3 hours. Karaski: What Goes Up...
Detective Stealth Game
Unbound Creations LLC
Plug In Digital
is a first-person detective stealth game developed by Unbound Creations LLC and published by Plug In Digital. I enjoyed the developer's previous title
, but it had many problems and the gameplay wasn't all that entertaining. However, they fixed all of that with this game.
The story is inspired by classic whodunit novels by Agatha Christie. You play as a Sir/Madame who partecipates to the first flight of the Glorious Commonwealth's airship. However, one day someone knocks you over your head and you wake up in the ship's lower deck, where someone sabotaged the engines and killed a guard. You find a two-way radio from which someone mistakes you for an Agent, and it orders you to discover who the culprit is.
As a fan of mystery novels, I loved every aspect of this game, from its mysterious setup, to talking with all the different people who are on the ship (passengers, bartenders, workers) and to the outstanding and satisfying ending where you will choose, based on the clues you found, who is to blame for damaging the ship. There are also political subplots, conspiracies, spies, and a lot of lore to further help you in your final decision.
The game is developed with the Unity engine, and it looks pretty darn good. It uses cell-shaded characters and locations for a more cartoonish and light-hearted feel. The areas that you explore feature some great steam-punk architecture and furnitures, and I loved exploring every inch of the map, from the Crew Deck to the Private Lounge and Bar. The only real issue is the walking animation of some characters, which looks more like they are floating rather than walking.
Your goal is to find enough clues by exploring the different decks, talking with the other passengers and picking up objects. Some areas of the ship are off-limit, which means that you must stealth your way through them, avoiding getting caught by guards. If they ever manage to tackle you, you can either pay them or talk your way out of it, otherwise a Suspicion Meter will start rising, and less and less passengers will start believing what you say to them.
The game is not all that hard, but even the slightest mistake (getting caught by the guards when trespassing, disagreeing with some you're talking to,...) will make you lose trust, and every character will start suspecting you of being the saboteur. However, if you are even slightly familiar with stealth games, you won't have that big of a trouble avoiding guards.
The soundtrack is really good: I really enjoyed listening to the music that was coming out of the radios, and, while it is royalty-free music, it further immersed me into this living and breathing world. There are however a couple of sound effects, especially when going to the ship's maintenance rooms, that are extremely loud and annoying.
Every time you play the game, there are different choices to make that will change the way other characters react to you, as well as a different culprit based on the clues you find hidden in the environments. There are also newspapers and letters that fully explore the game's universe, and many Steam achievements to unlock.
Overall,
is one of the better detective games I have ever played thanks to its interesting dialogue and layered characters. The focus on choosing how to get different information and the stealth section also improve the enjoyment factor, delivering a full experience that will satisfy fans of mystery and stealth games.

I purchased this game as part of the Humble Double Fine Bundle, so use that tint when reading this review.
Brutal Legend has oodles of theme, but can't quite decide what it wants for gameplay, and suffers accordingly.  You start out with your typical hack'n'slash, then it adds a driving element, and just when you are getting comfortable with that, you find that the major encounters are handled as real-time strategy battles.
There were a number of issues that really hurt my opinion of the game:
I set the game to normal difficulty and expected a fair challenge.  Instead, I found in some scenarios I could do nothing at all and succeed, and in others I had to figure out a precise series of RTS actions to lead to victory.  In some of the ambushes your party rushes off to death before you can even get under way.
On the upside, Brutal Legend features an amazing soundtrack and voice cast.  If you love heavy metal you might enjoy this game on theme alone.  In fact, you'll probably forgive all of it's blemishes for having Lemmy, Ozzy, Jack Black, Lita Ford, and many more.  I'm not a huge metal fan, though, so for all of its charm I just couldn't get past the glaring gameplay issues.

I have mixed feelings about this game.
[PROS] On one hand, it's a true Artwork (from capital 'A') dedicated to the long-gone Heavy Metal culture. Brilliant characters based on real Heavy Metal legends, sexy gothic girls, true-to-the-theme fantasy story, brutally awesome music (most of it being top chart of Heavy Metal), and legendary Tim Schafer's humour at its best.
[CONS] All this awesomeness is followed by arcadish game mechanics, terrible and slugish controls (which would make veterans of Unreal Tournament furious), artificial rudimentary RPG elements (oh c'mon, who would want to explore this bland landscape to find few dragon statues?), and very repetitive secondary missions.
[CONCLUSION] I would prefer Brutal Legends being a film instead of a video game. As an adventure it's unforgettable, but as an interactive experience - it irritates as much as it fascinates.

It took me 125 hours to complete this game (all side quests and DLCs included)! Well, that perhaps is no match for Elder Scrolls, but, still, it's a lot of content!
What looks and starts as just another ARPG, soon turns into immersive and beautiful open-world experience with overwhelming number of quests. And the cartoonish style is actually very beautiful, when you give it a closer look! The variety of landscapes and details – just exploring the game's world is rewarding on its own. (Take a look at my screenshots and you'll know what I'm talking about).
I believe it would be fair to say that, "Kingdoms of Amalur" is "Skyrim meets Mass Effect"... just without sexy lesbian shower scenes... and without choices that actually matter.
Well, about that... Choices - this aspect is actually one of the minor faults of this game. It gives the impression that you have to make moral choices that will affect your future, but (apart from few barely significant exceptions in some of the side quests) all those choices change is, whether you accept a sidequest and how the NPCs answer you. They don't affect the main storyline and don't lead to alternative endings - there are no alternative endings. On the other hand, you won't be regretting anything and wishing that you had done something differently.
Especially because you can change your class (!) at any point in the game and redistribute your skills and abilities ("skills" are boosts to your stats in this game and "abilities" are your class-specific skills). And, in this aspect, KoAR is rather unique. There are 3 traditional classes in this game: rogue, warrior and mage. Also, you can combine any two of them or all three of them. This system reminds me that of Mass Effect. The only difference is that your choice is not fixed in the beginning, but you specialise your character in one of the three directions with each next level.
What else? Loot. There's a lot of it! But only few items are actually worth something - as always in this type of games! But, contrary to Borderlands, for example, you won't be spending as much time sorting your inventory. Just put everything you don't need to junk right away. Then you can sell it or salvage to craft new items.
Crafting, exploring, potion brewing, lore stone searching (they grant stat boosts), side quests, faction quests (they grant valuable rewards in the form of cards), appearance customisation, improvement of your headquarters – there is really a lot of content in this game. And that might feel overwhelming sometimes. You just grow tired of this game, especially because at one point this game stops being challenging even on the hardest difficulty. And the enemies and battles start to feel the same. You just want to find out how everything ends. But it just doesn't. This game takes for what feels like an eternity.
My suggestion is to take breaks from time to time. Thus, when you return to it, it will still feel fresh.
Don't ruin the experience for yourself! Because the story is rich and interesting, the combat system is versatile, the skill trees are complex, the numerous kingdoms of Amalur are beautiful, the sidequests are unique (well, most of them), there are various factions of enemies and the game itself offers immersive fantasy adventure experience that will take you hours to complete.
If only the graphics were more realistic, the enemies were more challenging towards the end and there was no level cap (=40), this would have been the perfect game for me.
Nevertheless, 10 EUR well spent.
My overall rating: 9/10

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is an indie horror adventure game. You play as the father or the mother of a girl who has gone missing in an insane asylum. You arrive in the asylum to go looking for her, but there is nobody in the asylum except for a ghostlike creature called the Hat Man. You spend the game running away from the Hat Man and meanwhile collecting two kinds of items:
- diary pages written by your daughter, explaining a bit what's going on and what you need to do next
- items that help you advance e.g. at the very start there is a barricaded door => you pick up a nearby axe and use it to remove the obstacle
The asylum's hallways and rooms are continuously generated at random. So I didn't really like the fact that you couldn't rely on your memory and orientation skills to find your way in the asylum. You just need to keep running until you come across the item you need to advance to the next part of the asylum.
What I did like about 'The Hat Man: Shadow Ward' is that you get a short thrilling experience for nearly no money at all. When I finished the game, I was surprised to see I got the achievement for finishing the game in under half an hour. It seemed longer what with the running around through the endless hallways and what with reloading when caught by the Hat Man. But the game shouldn't have been any longer than it is, because it's too 'basic' to entertain for hours. Now, at the price of this game (and especially when on sale) I think it's certainly worth playing if you're into the horror-atmosphere type games and are willing to settle for a quick, cheap fix.

I've only recently gotten into the show, and when I saw there was a game in the making, I thought the action of the show would be perfect for a game. I immediately bought the game and played through it. After playing through the first campaign, I can see that this game has a lot of potential for players who are new to the show or fans. I'm not saying this game is bad in any way, but in my opinion, the game is not worth the price in its current state. In its current state, its very basic (Which is understandable for an early access game), but it is that potential that really is pulling the game up and giving this game the recommendation. Reading over the list of what's supposed to be in the next update, a lot of the problems I had with the game are being addressed. The main problems I had with the game now is that the combo system is very basic, and the levels of the first campaign are very similar.  With the basic combo system of the game, every character playes the same. With the type of game that this is, similar characters are understandable, however, making each one unique in their own way adds more replayability to the game, and it would complement the show since each character has a different fighting style. And with the objectives, they are mostly moving through a level and defending a point from a few waves of enemies and an escort mission. Again, this is a very early build, but I hope that the objectives get fleshed out, maybe adding epic boss fights with large Grimm or characters from the show.
But like I previously stated, some of these problems are being addessed, and in my opinion, the asking price is too much for the amount of content avaliable.
But please keep an eye on this one. It has the potential to be great.

Just a short and quick review here. Got the game for next to nothing on sale. If you're familiar with old tabletop wargames using miniatures, the title pretty much tells it all: You get a set of toy soldiers and other units from WWI era. The tanks have a little key on the side and look vaguely like old tin toys. I have a great fondness for these things, but that's me. I openly own and admit my admiration for tabletop wargamers with meticulously well-painted miniatures. It's fine for what it's supposed to be, but don't expect actual tabletop warfare of that nature. This is more of a romantic homage without the bits that really appeal to adult fans of the hobby. Still, it's not awful, just not for everyone. You get more of a tower defense game with specific points where you can place specific units. You can climb in and take over a given unit to improve accuracy and excitement, or you can just allow matters to run their course. You probably really need to get in there and fight to win. Strategic aspect of this game is very low, at least on easy. I'm not interested in playing this on a higher difficulty because I really don't see it being anything more than what it is: Arcade action with toy soldiers and various era-specific units. If you have a romantic interest in this type of thing, maybe check it out for a dollar or two. I like it okay, but I won't be playing it a lot. I'd rather play actual tabletop miniature games than this to be honest.

Star Rangers is a surprisingly interesting game.
Space exploration games are slowly demanding the spotlight, and this title is successfully shaping its path to success.
The game is still in a very Early Access stage, with many features and details to be added and fixed (which have been planned by the devs). Due to its current status I am unabe to properly label the negative aspects as such, hence they will be listed at the bottom of the review as a mere feedback and advice.
You start off by creating a character, modifying his appearance and picking a class, which will give you a bonus on several stats, along with unique skills and perks.
There are various missions available, accessible from a text based computer (you actually have to type the commands, a little feature that I found brilliant in terms of involvement), and they range from space exploration ones (planet discovery, debris cleaening etc) to planet related ones (build a particular structure, collect materials etc).
The game is vast, hugely vast. You have the chance to explore your favourite solar system planet and much more. In your aid there are different vehicles with their own particular function.
In my current game experience I only visited Mars so far (I've always been fascinated by the Red Planet). Reaching it was a wonderful experience and the landing process is brilliant, with speed balancing being a vital factor to properly reach the planet without destroying your ship.
Without further ado, I would like to talk about the exteremly positive aspects of Star Rangers, which also are the reason why you should definitely give it a try:
In the end, I would like to point out a few aspect that many need an optimization (which I am sure will be fixed as I have read them being planned in the future).
Am I recommending the game? Yes! Even though it may feel like being in a beta status, it's definitely worth the price, considering you will be paying for an in-development product that will only get better in time!

Mario Kart Clone?
Alright, i bought it and wanted a Mario Kart for PC... This is what I got:
21/25 Gameplay
14/15 Replayability
5/10 Fairness
6/10 Controls
9/10 Graphics
8/10 Sound
8/20 Multiplayer
-----------------------------
71/100
And here we go:
In F1 Race Stars you get a game similar to Mario Kart. Same Power-Ups, same Gameplay. There is not much to say about these two points. But why does it just have 5 points in Fairness?
The Damage System! If you get hit, you get damaged, if you get damaged twice you are half as fast as the others. And that until you reach the next Repair Boxes. And to drive into these you loose even MORE time! Unfortunately you can only turn off the Damage playing with friends.
This leads to the next point: Multiplayer. There is no working multiplayer in this game! Noone plays it, becuase the Match Making is bugged...But if your friends play it, you get a nice experience: you can choose everything- Damage, Power Ups, Special Things, Length... And then the game makes very very much fun!
Unfortunately this game had no racing wheel support. Just controller support. But a good thing to say about it is that the Controls are pretty easy (WASD+Shift+Space+Alt) and that you can play this game in Co-Op mode with a splitscreen and on 1 computer. But you have to have a controller for each person you wanna play together with, just one person can use the keyboard.
Because of the easy Controls, the Replayability is very good. Also this game has very many game modes, a campain with several cups on several roads and a quick race mode. I took away 1 point because of the eventual Rage Quits because of the (Un)Fairness.
The Graphic is pretty good, the maps look cool and the special effects are well detailed. Everything is in a pretty comic style and there is no violent. You can play it with your whole family (if you turn off the damage...I am already hearing your kids cry...) and your friends.
The only thing I have to fault is the sometimes angular graphics. The sound is nice, too, but it had a bit potential upwards.
TL; DR
This game is a Mario Kart for PC with an unfair Single Player Damage and no Online Community. Play with your friends or Offline and have fun! (See my Sonic all Star Racing Transformed Review which has 87/100 points before you buy!!)

ugh... it really PAINS me to have to give Mortal Kombat X a thumbs down it really does but I cannot in good conscience recommend this game at full price. it's not to say this is a bad game, on the contrary it's my personal favorite in the whole series but the greed of these developers nowadays is really starting to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off cause it really just holding the game back. but we will get into all of that in a little bit… let's start off with the good...
first off let me just say what a great game this is and that it is hands down my personal favorite mortal kombat game to date. i've enjoyed the living crap out of this game so far and i look forward to playing it even more in the future. the game's graphics are just gorgeous looking, the kombat itself is so smooth and fluent and the blood and gore is just horrifically gruesome and i just love every bit of it!!! it really feels like a next gen mortal kombat game. the main story of the game is a bit on the short side but it is still one hell of a ride. there's a total of 12 chapters and a total of around 50 fights, the story is told through beautifully crafted, long cinematic cutscenes in between each fight. the story is full of suspense and twist and an epic cliffhanger at the end making the wait for the next Mortal Kombat game that much more harder for me lol. in total it took me around 4 to 5 hours to beat it. as far as single player goes there is also challenge towers to complete, test your luck and an excellent training mode for beginners adding tons of hours of gameplay. there's also an extensive online mode to fight others in with factions wars and online leader boards and even “living towers” that are like challenge towers that changes daily and weekly adding even more fun. on the surfaces the game is excellent and is probably one of the best MKs in the franchise. there is certainly a wealth of stuff to do in this game and you will have a blast while doing it… but now it's time for the bad… and oh boy...
sadly Mortal Kombat X is littered with crappy and meaningless DLC. things like “easy fatalities” and crap cheap charters skins that look like they should've already been in the game to start with *cough* *cough* blue steel sub zero *cough* *cough* and just a pure lack of content compared to MK9. to start off with MKX has only 24 characters on disk (not counting goro sinces he is technically DLC) compared to MK9s 27 starting character roster. also some characters such as rain, sindel and baraka are present in the game with full move sets and everything but are not playable, its even been proven they could be threw mods. they most likely did it to put them as separate DLC you will have to pay for down the line just like tanya… i don't have a problem with DLC characters but paying for characters that are already in our game is just stupid, looking at you goro… also they gimped the krypt so you would be more likely to buy there "unlock everything” DLC. for those of you who don't know the krypt is a place where you can go to spend koins you have earned in the game to buy things such as new costumes for fighters and fatalities and brutalitys and a whole bunch of cool stuff to unlock and use in game. in MK9 it was really fun and cool to earn koins and unlock everything. here even in MKX they made you feel more involved with it by making it its own fun first person metagame you can play to unlock stuff. the problem with it in MKX is that they severely gimped koin earring big time... by the time i beat the campain of the game i had around 67,000 koins. sounds pretty good right? well in the new krypt i spent all of that within around 5 minutes and only unlocked a hand full of items… so over 5 hours of gameplay and i barely got jack sh*t... the average item now can cost any where from a 1000 to almost 10,000 koins and you earn koins at a much slower rate than mk9 so in other words it's practically impossible to unlock everything in the krypt without grinding away for weeks on end unless you buy the "unlock everything in the krypt pack DLC" for 20 bucks… which is a HUGE load of crap... i could go on all day but my point is if you pay $60 bucks for a new game like this i expect the DLC for the game to be legitimate downloadable content that adds on to my game, not this petty bullsh*t “free to play” style DLC that is borderline meaningless and at times feels like it gimps your game. this type of dirty business practices is really starting to sicken me and it needs to stop...
well now that all of that is out of my system it's time to wrap this up, overall Mortal Kombat X is a FANTASTIC game but its only flaw is that it's heavily pledged by greed. but if you can get this game on sale like i did off bundle star it's certainly worth it and you won't regret it, but i just can not recommend this game at full price with this kind of DLC, you're better off waiting for a sale and then buying its DLC with the money you saved so you can have the whole Mortal Kombat X experience. it's a great game but with a lot of bad business practices…

Guns, melee types, campaign (and its AI), lobbies, and features (that were not carried over from the original GunZ 1)
Currently compared to GunZ 1, second duel is extremely stripped of features including dodge rolls, ground slams, charge attacks, customized lobbies (such as melee only), less modes (and maps) available and more.
The game suffers from net code or hosting issues frequently and everyso often suffers from DDoS attacks from hackers, currently a significant game feature (tesla shops) is shut down for said reason. Unless I haven't noticed it yet the message telling people that a feature was shutdown gave no estimate of when it would go back up and was rediculously breif, combined with the fact that it was not explained ingame also made many players confused.
This being said the combat is fluid and fast, skill being a relevant factor. Melee is no longer broken so the 'martial arts' of korean, butterfly and dash styles are much more difficult to pull off and are generally not used this lets new players get in more easily. Although some features such as the lunge attack (double press R) are locked until level 8.
Although getting in may be easier, early game is very difficult. There is an option to do campaign to avoid this, however the campaign is boring, bland, buggy, repetative, tedious and generally shovel ware. It also believes difficulty is the same as being unfair, by giving enemies the ability to deal damage equivalent to another player shooting you with rush and swarm tactics to make up for their shoddy AI and inaccuracy (they also have horrible animations unlike the player animations). (This is a nightmare to deal with due to stun locking) I also ran into a bug which made them invulnerable and stationary.
Ironically unlike its name 'GunZ' there are very few gunZ with a choice of roughly 3 weapons for each category of: melee, secondary and primary with slightly varying %s. What makes this worse is the fact that unlike the original gunZ there are a lot more class locked weapon types.
Ivan's secondaries are limited soley to smgs meaning he can't use pistols(?), This is a glaring issue and forces you into a pay wall if you want to use other weapon types. At this point in time there are no shotguns or light machine guns as well and melee weapons consist mainly of fast hitting sword like attacks, the only outlier is the tank classes shield. I'm looking forward to great hammers and quarterstaffs.
Ultimates can be used once you build up enough energy, however when you are able to use energy it gradually fades away, this feature makes no sense and saps away your ability to perform any abilities if you don't use them within a time limit.
Unlike most games it is easy to grind cash and acheivements also award crystals and cash to be used in either of the two shops (tesla and normal). Items from the normal shop are permanent with durability, although if clothes are worn down enough repairing them can cost significantly more than if you were to just buy a new set of the same clothes. The tesla shop items can yeild much cooler loots, like new outfits or variant of the normal store's weapons with elemental effects or slightly higher stats with a slim chance that the object will become permanent.
Each class has 2 different abilities both of which are different depending on what class you choose, from exploding decoys to a straightline slash dash that instantly kills your opponent. The game is fairly balanced although it could use a couple tweaks.
Yes there are many issues with this game, this is likely attributed to it being in its infancy stage, even so I still recommend this. Not only is it free it's gameplay is intelligent, difficult and unique. It's graphics are also a well done and player movements are well animated.
If you are looking for a similar experience I would recommend warframe although that has less emphasis on PvP and melee and more on abilties and utility.
There are a lot of tactics to utilize in this game so keep your eyes peeled.

I have heard that this also works for chests, so looting everything too early will hurt you in the end.

I quickly found myself skipping through dialogue to reach choices to get past it, that often make no difference besides the next line the npc says. I even tried to make a few npcs hate me but nothing happened. (And apparently I am now lovers with some girl even though all I did was use her boat.)
The Persuasion skill, having 10 whole ranks, only affects the chance for you to succeed in rare, often pointless dialogue options, that you could just pass by quicksaving/loading. There are also a couple milestones in it, but all they do is slightly lower the cost of bribes for crimes.
- Equipment.
Many people say that upgrading your blacksmithing skill makes getting good gear too easy, but it seemed like the opposite for me. With max rank blacksmithing i only ever made a few items worth using since I could never find good materials , and ended up just selling all of my loot and purchasing better gear from shops.
Armor sets just stink. I have done a lot of exploring and looting but have never found more than 2 parts of a set besides when given to me. And even if I had, my gear would still be far better. Same story for most of the special weapons I get.
- Side quests are annoying.
There are a few I have done that I found interesting and enjoyable, but mostly it just became a case of skipping through, accepting everything, just doing them as I went to an area with an objective there.
This could also just be because I have played too many mmoprgs.
- Not enough variety in enemies.
Throughout the game you will be finding the same enemies even in far different settings, such as trolls, spiders, and pretty much any people. Even being in different reigons and factions, they will have the same attacks and skills.
- Plenty of annoying bugs and things that could do with improvement.
I have had quests break multiple times, even once before causing me to have to start a whole new game.
When you disable an enemy in reckoning mode, your character will still try to target them.
And many more little issues...

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is a must-have for gamers who love horror. I feel positively about most aspects of this game. First of all, the price. This game is very affordable at the price of £0.79, although I picked this up in a sale (£0.19!), and it is worth it! I feel this game is quite underappreciated for what it is. The plot of the game itself is interesting, but yet not very unique. A mental asylum is quite common to see in horror games, however, copying ideas can result in a better game overall (the way I feel about this game). In no way at all will I compare this game with other horror survival games such as Outlast or Alien: Isolation, but it must be said, this game is genuinely scary, what you'd look for in a horror game.
I feel the way this game's layout is set is great, for example, the beginning of this game has a few doors that I myself thought you'd be able to open, but cannot. This can result in disliking the game or liking it even more. For me, this tactic doesnt mean the map is too detailed, and I like that. Many times I've played games that have had too many places to go to, when in the end, all I had to do was go through the main door. Adding details like doors that canot be opened helps prevent wasting time, which is great, getting to the next point of the story without wasting time or lowering suspense.
Like I covered previously, the main obvious plot is not too unique, which isn't necessarily a bad thing at all! Having a man chase you through a mental asylum is, of course, going to be a common theme. (Please note, the actual story to this game is rather unique, and the fact it's based off a real life story makes it all the more scarier!).
The controls are easy to use, the game is not too basic nor complicated, and there are plenty of them (and they're rather familiar with other games). Graphics, textures are all fine, and the flow of gameplay compliments it well.
Overall, I really enjoyed this game. I appreciate games like these that are affordable, fun to play, not complicated and that give you a few hours of enjoyment. I'd strongly recommend this to people who enjoy horror games.

Driver Parallel Lines (2007) is one of those games that tried to infuse additional gaming elements into driving, in an attempt to recapture the magic of Grand Theft Auto III (released 2002!), but end up making a mess of it as there's just too much to do. Adding more varieties of activities, such as motorcycles and such did not help.
Driver franchise is about fast and furious driving in the 70's, where muscle cars roamed, and an undercover officer must infiltrate gangs, get cars, deliver hot cars, pursue suspects, and more. Driver: Parallel Lines tried to infuse a GTA3 gameplay into it by letting you get out of the car, jack more cars, and shoot suspects all with GTA like mechanics without dumbing down the car chases and evading police. However, the "free roam" it managed to give never quite felt as immersive as GTA3. The controls are twitchy, but responsive enough if you don't collide. It is however, the additional acrobatic elements that made the game into WTF category.
After going through a couple tutorial missions where you're given instructions on basic car control, shooting, locking on, strafing, and even shooting while driving, you're dumped in the deep end of the pool and told: go drive around and find some missions to make 1500 for your mechanic Ray. You have $100. Okay, there were three races at the raceway and the basic one will pay $500, but you can only choose one. I managed to drive to the airport and found a checkpoint race... Which is where the WTF came in. The checkpoints are easy enough, until where suddenly there's a ramp, one of the checkpoints was on TOP of the room. Apparently, my car is supposed to be able to do it fast enough so it sail over the top, land on the ramp on the other side, and somehow make a hard right onto next point. Except, my car is not light enough or fast enough to do it. I tried it about 10 times. Yet there is no way to quit out of the mission except going all the way back to main menu.
Oh, and if you flip your car? Jump out and jack a different car. But the mission must continue.
And yes, you *can* run over pedestrians in this game.
Driver San Francisco is a much more interesting game due to the "jumping" mechanism. Play that one instead. This one is way too frustrating to play.

NOTE: This game was given to me by the developer for review purposes. This did not influence my review in any way.
Karaski: What Goes Up is a first-person exploration adventure game, very similar in graphics and general feel to the Ship.
You play a passenger on the maiden voyage of the Karaski: the first airship built by the Glorious Commonwealth. But something goes wrong only days into the voyage and it falls to you to investigate and find the culprit, with the assistance of a strange voice on the radio.
Graphics - The graphics have a consistent feel to them, but they seem a bit dated, with simple, blocky models; fairly bland and sharply mapped textures; and occasionally wooden animations that sometimes seem to cause NPCs to become stuck on world geometry.
Sound - Music and most sound effects are good, with propaganda-style music playing in various areas that brought a smile to my face. Footsteps, though, which you'll notice a lot while sneaking on metal surfaces, sound particularly bad, like someone banging on a pipe with a hammer.
Gameplay - The gameplay seems to me quite similar to the Ship, but single player only and with a bit more focus on stealth. Controls are typical FPS (mouse to look, WASD to move, CTRL and Space to crouch and jump, etc), and for the most part it moves quite well, although given the relative scarcity of objects and simplicity of most of the world geometry I was a surprised that it stuttered a bit in places.
The game is played entirely on board the Karaski airship after some sort of sabotage. You must roam the corridors and explore the rooms of the various airship decks, keeping on the lookout for guards. Through exploration and conversation, as well as using a small number of objects in the right places, adventure game style, your task is to uncover the perpetrator while also deflecting suspicion from yourself.
Karaski plays more like an exploration game than an adventure game, though, but you'll need some FPS skills to successfully sneak past all of the guards without getting spotted and reported to the ship's captain. Unfortunately the stealth sections don't feel that natural to me, with world objects sometimes completely hiding you from view and at other times seeming to make no difference. Having recently spent a few hours playing Styx: Master of Shadows, I can't help but think the stealth system needs a bit more work.
Pros:
+ Interesting setting that I found cynically amusing, sort of like Papers, Please
+ Multiple plot turns that depend on decisions you make, promoting replayability
+ Lots of achievements, further promoting multiple play throughs with different goals
+ Trading cards
Cons:
- Stealth is a big part of the game, but could still use some work
- Somewhat dated-looking graphics; some frame rate stuttering in long hallways
- In-game text could use some proofreading. It's better than many indie games, but I caught a handful of errors in my first few minutes of play
Karaski is one of those games that's hard to pin down. I've played it for a few hours and I'm generally interested in finding out what happens next. The game world is interesting and darkly humourous, and I want to see where the story goes. But the stealth side of the game is a fairly key focus and it's not that much fun, especially when parts of the game have you travelling through large prohibited areas with multiple guards.
It's a good game, but with a bit more work could be a great one.

I was given a pre-release copy to test, but that won't affect my rating.
I enjoyed it, it's kind of like a mix of thief and a choose your own storybook. It took me around 6~ hours to beat it, and no parts were exactly hard, but the stealth felt fun/intense. Your primary method of tracking guards is using your own sound, so you have to kind of learn their pattern before you even see what the area looks like, which is neat.
That being said, stealth IS NOT the main part of this game. There's maybe 20~ guards total you need to avoid.

Karaski is a unique first-person adventure game with lots of exploration, investigation and stealth mechanics.
The game takes place roughly in the 1920s onboard the airship AA Karaski, the sole pride of the Commonwealth of Dunabe and the first of its kind.
Your name? Chose yourself. Your past? Unknown. When you wake up from what seems to be the result of someone hitting you over the head, you'll soon learn that the airship has been sabotaged by terrorists. The fact that you were near the crime scene instantly turns you into one of the suspects, so it's only in your best interest to find the real saboteurs.
A mysterios voice over radio gives you instructions, but who are they, and can you trust them? It doesn't matter, as you get thrown head over feet into a thick complot of either selfish, nationalist or economic interests. Everyone onboard of the airship seems to have is own motives for turning this first ever airship flight into a disaster.
Over the course of the game your main activities consist of talking to the various crew and passengers, scavenging for evidence, breaking into rooms, bribing or sneaking around guards to get into prohibited areas. If you aren't careful, your suspicion level will rise and your dialogue partners will be a lot less cooperative. Stealth is a big part of Karaski, so thankfully the game provides you with various tools like lockpicks, vent openers and more to make your life easier.
Pros:
- interesting characters with their own stories and motives for sabotage
- pretty & atmospheric art style and music
- various endings
- nonlinear, mission based gameplay
- very intuitive UI with tabs for suspects, clues, inventory and missions
Cons:
- sneaking can get dreadful at times, esp. if you have to find that
item in the middle of a prohibited area
- no spoken dialogue
- lots of running back and forth
- relatively few usable items
- very open ending
Will you find the true saboteur(s)? Will you even be able to save the airship? It's all up to you!
Recommended to true adventure game fans!

The last few years have seen a resurgence of adventure games. A genre once thought dead, or at least dormant got an injection of adrenaline from two sources: Double Fine (helmed by veteran adventure game designer Tim Schafer) and relatively newcomers Telltale. But giving those two fine companies ALL the credit for the resurgence of adventure games wouldn't be fair. Others have also done an amazing job keeping people interested in the genre. People such as the fine guys over at Cardboard Computer or Unbound Creations. Today we'll be talking about a game released by the latter (who also released the most excellent Postmortem: One must die)
Karaski: What Goes Up... is that game. The interesting thing about Unbound Creations is that their games don't focus all that much on puzzles, QTEs or life altering decisions. They instead chose to focus on people and small, personal stories. Karaski is a game about a magnificent airship which has experienced a catastrophic accident. But that's not really it... It's a game about the people in that airship, their motivations, their small quirks and what they did before they got onboard.
As an agent for an unknown organization you must discover what happened to the airship and who's the saboteur (or is it you?!) In order to accomplish your objective you can sneak, talk, intimidate or steal stuff. But there's nobody there to tell you exactly what happened, and nothing is set in stone. Your actions will dictate the ending, and you will decide what happened by yourself, after hearing what the characters have to say, or obtaining the information by other means. It's a game designed to be replayed, and in many ways it works similarly to a choose your own adventure book (or a Way of the Samurai game)
Will you discover what happened to the magnificent airship Karaski? Will you save the ship from certain doom? Or maybe you were the saboteur all along?

The exquisite storytelling found in Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons offers an experience seldom seen in modern games.
-a perfectly crafted story of love, courage and sacrifice that stays with you long after you've beaten the game
-powerful ending
-hauntingly beautiful soundtrack

-both brothers are interesting characters and it's easy to get attached to them
-good controls
-puzzles and platforming are pretty simple, so do not expect to be challenged
-can feel a bit slow during a few sections
-controlling both brothers at the same time takes a bit to get used to
While the simple gameplay is there just to pull the story forward the story is what makes this game truly exceptional.
At around 3/4 hours Brothers is an emotional rollercoaster through a gorgeous world with amazingly crafted levels: sadly for review purpose even briefly spoiling the story would diminish its strength.
I can say though that few games engaged and touched me as strongly as this one: the obvious love that went into creating such a beautiful and ultimately satisfying story deserves to be experienced by anyone with a beating heart.
Do yourself a favor and buy it.

I enjoyed my 3-4 hours completing this short game, or should I say interactive movie.  The story was excellent and definitely has emotional impact.  The puzzles were quite simple but the mechanic of controlling two characters using both the 2 analog controls was original and fantastic.  In fact the dual controls are so critical to the game they even play a part in the impact of the story towards the end.
However my first impressions of the game were terrible.  I spent 30 minutes trying to work out why my logitech dual controller would not work.  It turns out the Steam notice above should say " requires an XBox controller or installation of an XBox controller emulator to play".  Eventually I installed the XBOX360ce and was able to actually play the game properly.  This is one game that the keyboard (the default) is not an option, you will only have maybe 60% of the intended game experience.
Then, in my first 5 minutes of real play, the little brother fell between 2 hay bails  and became  stuck.  I couldn't continue and had to restart from a checkpoint.  Poor QA I have to say.  Along with the controller issue, I was becoming quite annoyed.
As I got about an hour or so in to the story my irritation died down thanks largely to the spectacular settings and sometimes breathtaking action sequences.  At the time I was thinking this would be a nice game for kids and adults to enjoy however that soon changed. The middle to later games have some darker themes, not for kids.
I generally prefer more gameplay and replayability in games but I realise this is a story driven game so I can't complain too much.  I'm unlikely to play this again anytime soon but I definitely recommend it as an experience,  just be aware of what it is and isn't.

First off, I'll say it's taken a few "drafts" for me to find the review I like. I'll keep it sweet and short.
The gameplay for the game is great. There are a few issues I have with it, like the mouse acceleration (which isn't actually mouse acceleration, but low Y-Axis sensitivity), but that'll be fixed soon (remember, this IS a console port, so give it a break). The combat and stealth feels very similar to Human Revolution, but better. Better how? Being able to customize your weapon on the fly helps with both of those aspects. Want to pick off a few enemies at a distance with a silenced, scoped assault rifle, then remove the silencer and trade the scope for a holo sight to go crazy on the rest of the enemies? Go for it!
The story is very good as well. The rift bewtween "Naturals" and "Augs" is very apparent, and the atmosphere is heavy. You feel peoples disgust of you when you walk around, be it some coomment or noise they make. Square and Eidos have done an amazing job with this world, and how the events of Human Revolution, and augments in general, have changed the planet. All of what they have done makes this world feel alive.
The soundtrack is even better than the one in Human Revolution. It helps set the mood for the Cyberpunk world they've created. Besides that, there's not much more to say about it. It's just awesome.
The only negatives I can think of are the issues with the Microtransactions and Pre-Order stuff. For me, these aren't an issue. If you play the game, you don't NEED the Praxis and Credits you can buy. Honestly, I'm not even sure why those are offered; they literally feel pointless. DO NOT let these small issues stop you from playing the game, it's absolutely amazing.
FINALLY, DO NOT LISTEN TO MOST OF THE NEGATIVE REVIEWS! Of course you should be wary of ANY game, but most of the negative reviews posted are from people who have almost ZERO playtime. One guy posted a review of all the things he didn't like with 0.6 hours of gameplay. That's not even enough time to complete the TUTORIAL MISSION!

Note: This review will not contain spoilers, or talk about the PC port and microtransactions (I got through the game just fine without them). This review is also focused on the Main Story, not any of the side content (yet) besides for Jensen's Story: Desperate Measures.
So I had just finished Deus Ex: Mankind Divided on "Give me a Challenge" (Normal) difficulty and had been a fan of the series since Deus Ex: Human Revolution. Let me say the game is great. It takes all good aspects from Human Revolution, polishes them, and adds to them. But there is a "con" (if you could call it that) which may surprise some people.
The gameplay is similar to Human Revolution, you have a city hub, this time Prague, and you can explore it freely doing main missions, side missions, Points of Interest (new addition), or whatever you would like. Looking around the city, hacking into control panels, and finding loot is all the same as Human Revolution. The tutorial is good and will teach peopl ethe mechanics of the game in an interesting way, using tutorial spaces where you can try out augmentations and weapons without consequence. But let me talk about consequences.
The Deus Ex series is known for it's decision-making in it's story. Mankind Divided is no different. There will be some tough decisions to make in the story of the game. This time, it is two years after the events of Human Revolution, once again as Adam Jensen. You come to Prague only for the train station to be bombed. The game also has a 12 minute catch up movie if you haven't played Human Revolution, but I highly suggest you go out and play Deus Ex: Human Revolution - Director's Cut for the experience.
Now, what is the "con"? It has one of the same cons as Deus Ex: The Fall. The ending. WHAT?! The ending is bad?! No, it is a ending depending on the choices you make, my ending was pretty good. But, the ending has a cliffhanger that looks like it wants to set up either a Season Pass or a sequel (the latter would be awesome!). Now this may sound boring, but watch the credits and mid-way through, you'll see what I mean.
Rating:
9/10-Awesome
Rating for Deus Ex fans:
10/10-Legendary

Been playing Tekken since I was a kid, started on Tekken 3, but the one I played the most was Tekken 5. This is the first Tekken I've played "seriously" and I find it a very easy game to pick up and play, but it has a huge skill ceiling that makes it very rewarding to play for hours. I can lose track of time just playing ranked at night, revenge matching until I get to the next rank. Definitely recommended for that alone.
Story Mode is a mixed bag. The narrator is garbage, but the scenes that are fullmotion are well animated, and the climax is more over the top than I thought an ending could be. But I did enjoy it for the one playthrough and I tolerated the narrator. The side stories are pretty lame though.
The offline modes are all what you'd want in a fighting game, and online modes seem to work fine. Customizations are servicable, but I think they would be expanded a bit to allow for more creative outfits. Minor gripes with Tekken 7's training mode is that there are no good ways to analyze frame data and instructions how to execute some moves without third-party sources.
Gameplay's the Tekken standard with new fun mechanics like slow-mo and rage attacks. No complaints, it's kept me playing the game for 135 hours, and probably will keep me playing for a long time to come.
In summary, it's my current favorite 3D fighting game. Absolutely pick it up if you are looking for a fighting game to play casually, play seriously, or play dressup with your favorite fighter for hours on end. I know I have. :3

I purchased this game as part of the Humble Double Fine Bundle, so use that tint when reading this review.
Brutal Legend has oodles of theme, but can't quite decide what it wants for gameplay, and suffers accordingly.  You start out with your typical hack'n'slash, then it adds a driving element, and just when you are getting comfortable with that, you find that the major encounters are handled as real-time strategy battles.
There were a number of issues that really hurt my opinion of the game:
I set the game to normal difficulty and expected a fair challenge.  Instead, I found in some scenarios I could do nothing at all and succeed, and in others I had to figure out a precise series of RTS actions to lead to victory.  In some of the ambushes your party rushes off to death before you can even get under way.
On the upside, Brutal Legend features an amazing soundtrack and voice cast.  If you love heavy metal you might enjoy this game on theme alone.  In fact, you'll probably forgive all of it's blemishes for having Lemmy, Ozzy, Jack Black, Lita Ford, and many more.  I'm not a huge metal fan, though, so for all of its charm I just couldn't get past the glaring gameplay issues.

I am currently enjoying this game.  It has a little bit for everyone... There is a lot of hacking and slashing with some racing, RTS, and RPG elements thrown in.  Add an awesome soundtrack, engrossing story, plenty of size quests, and awesome cameos and you have the most metal game ever!

I have mixed feelings about this game.
[PROS] On one hand, it's a true Artwork (from capital 'A') dedicated to the long-gone Heavy Metal culture. Brilliant characters based on real Heavy Metal legends, sexy gothic girls, true-to-the-theme fantasy story, brutally awesome music (most of it being top chart of Heavy Metal), and legendary Tim Schafer's humour at its best.
[CONS] All this awesomeness is followed by arcadish game mechanics, terrible and slugish controls (which would make veterans of Unreal Tournament furious), artificial rudimentary RPG elements (oh c'mon, who would want to explore this bland landscape to find few dragon statues?), and very repetitive secondary missions.
[CONCLUSION] I would prefer Brutal Legends being a film instead of a video game. As an adventure it's unforgettable, but as an interactive experience - it irritates as much as it fascinates.

As a remake of the spiritual sequel to the grandfather of shooters, I expected to be thrown back with old school style gameplay and level design. It definitely doesn't disappoint with that the levels have a ton of secrets, branching paths, keys for doors halfway across the map, and a lot of gameplay choices that died out since the 90s for example, reloading literally does nothing, and was just included for kicks. Ironsights were also thrown in, but outside of singleplayer you'll get destroyed if you use them. Multiplayer is a rocketfest, which can be frustrating at times, but once you learn your way around that's when it gets fun. The devs are the best part of the game, honestly there's lots of jokes thrown in, like the AI telling you to stick with a controller and text-to-speech in multiplayer (John Madden! John Madden!). However, it is a bit buggy on launch day, as I found myself getting stuck in walls a lot in singleplayer. I also can't really see a competitive future. But for what it is and what it tries to be, it's perfect.

In this beautiful politically-incorrect quest for various porridges, you play as one of five ultra-proficient members of the United Nations, of all things, who's out to kill as many communistic cultists as physically possible in the hunt for oatmeal, keys, and magic mushrooms.
Merely two minutes in, you'll realise that this IS a legitimate sequel to the original Rise of the Triad from back in '94. Most of the original gameplay elements are perfectly preserved: floating golden coins litter the landscape. Experienced enemies will feign death or surrender and then shoot you in the back. God mode and Dog mode are still very much in tact. Bowls of porridge and weapons of mass destruction still lie senselessly strewn about the complex. Of course, since the original Rise of the Triad was so ahead of its time in some elements, some of these things don't feel out-of-place at all in a beautifully-detailed modern FPS.. but some really do, which makes the game even more entertaining if anything.
Polished with hundreds of achievements and beautiful, futureproof graphics, this throwback to the good ole days of PC shooters not only contends with some of the best shooters of the past several years, but in some aspects, actually surpasses them. It's everything you could possibly have expected from a game called Rise of the Triad, and one of my most confident recommendations of the year. 10/10.

I know these marketing techniques and they usually don't influence me, but I still went ahead and bought this game for like 25 cents because, why not? One can argue that for the price any game is worth it, except The Slaughtering Grounds, but actually there's games that are pretty much similar or even better and they don't ask for a penny. With all due respect to the developers, this game is an attempt at being something and I can see it, but fails due to the large amount of bugs and many other problems. I'm really nit-picky so I will address a lot of things in this review that most people maybe don't have a problem with.
When booting the game, I recognize the Unity launcher right away. Me and Unity games usually don't go well, but I can't judge a game by it's launcher obviously... Then the game boots up and a crazy amount of FPS makes me almost certain I'm going to have tearing issues, so I check Settings, only to find out that there's no option for VSync. I thought this was a standard in game options by now! Key bindings are pretty simple and I did try to change the inventory up and down bindings to my mouse wheel and it doesn't work so I'll just stick to the T and G keys, I had never done that, and it's terrible.
Finally I choose Play, and I pick to play as the Father. Upon the first second of the game... there it is, the damn screen tearing all over the place. Quite hard to ignore but since most of the game is dark as hell, I give it a pass. So, I go upstairs, touch a book and the game has officially started. So the first complaint is, although I know a lot of people just skip it nowadays but, tutorials please. I had no idea what I should be doing and how should I progress, you can't expect me to rely on the internet to find out how to escape or kill a damn ghost that just clips through the wall and grabs you in the first SECONDS. Turns out I just needed to Zoom my lantern in her face and she dies.
Then it seems I have to pickup... pages? Wait isn't this like that game where you're in the woods and... yes it is. You're pretty much lying if you say this game isn't a copy of Slender: The Eight Pages inside 4 walls because it clearly is. What it does differently is the fact that this is randomly generated, and it works well for the most part. You go right pass 3 rooms, and if you go back the map has changed. This is actually very interesting and an idea that I found to be wasted on a game like this.
So you do get the book and those pages, and finally enter this sort of asylum, this is where you seek the pages that your daughter wrote, as this is some sort of dream that you got to save her from. Upon collecting the fifth page, when the little 5 green balls are lit now on my HUD (which I had no idea what they were for like 2 hours), the almighty, spooky and fearsome enemy spawns. One of the main flaws in this game is the so called "Hat man", because he's just laughable, he just floats and follows you trying to catch you. Which he will never do since you can outrun him easily. Then he despawns somehow. This is the whole game, or pretty much all of it. Then again I do say, the lack of tutorials make this game so much harder than it is, no one actually gives you any tips on how to evade the Hatman or even progress in the game. The journal pages do give you tips but I don't feel it's enough for the player to actually understand what he has to do. Just to clarify, the little orbs in the HUD indicate that a new item to progress in the game has spawned and is now placed in the random rooms, so you need to find 5 pages for each new item to progress in the game.
Another complaint I have is, sound effects. You might ask, what sound effects? Exactly, there's barely any. When I die, playing as the father by the way, the sound of me getting caught is of a woman, what the hell. Also, the Hatman himself hardly makes any kind of noise, he doesn't even make a sound when he catches you...
The Hatman spawns are literally the only thing in this game that makes it hard and infuriating to say the least. And when you get cornered there's no way to go, making it such a cheap way to make you lose. Since there's a lack of manual saving, you're only allowed to save if you find certain save points, but these are hard to come by and you will lose a lot of progress. Also, the worst thing is when you've made good progress and the Hatman literally just clips through the damn floor and kills you. That made me rage-quit this game so badly I actually was about to give up on this, but I still got to the ending because I like self-torture, and achievements.
The atmosphere is... good! Despite the game being flawed to hell, having a not-creepy-at-all enemy that's just annoying and the lack of sound effects, the atmosphere does feel tense, and the feeling of not knowing where you should go because the game is randomly generated does give it a feeling of anxiety, since you never know what's on the next room, it could be the spooky scarecrow or the next exit. But please take note, a scary game doesn't need to have the brightness of the ocean depths. Don't rely so much in darkness to make your game scary. I hate games that are way too dark. I know horror has to be dark, but I like playing a game, not just hearing it.

So this game takes place in New york and a little bit of New Jersey, The map is so big i would often find myself fast travelling instead of driving there, The police in new york are possibly the most brutal i have ever seen in a game if you start speeding and they see you they instantly pull out the shotgun and start shooting, The city of new york is big and stays true to most of the buildings locations in Real life new york how ever the city feels empty and Uninhabited there is nothing special about anything in the city the only thing I stopped my car at was to look at times square and even that felt dull, I should also mention the lack of a Jump feature I often found myself wishing Jump up onto a ledge instead of running around the long way to get up there, also Pretty much in any open world new york based games i play i always want to see the land marks but with this you can't even get to the statue of liberty! ok so now that i have had my little rant  lets talk story
You play as a guy who's only name mentioned is TK (The Kid) Anyway TK is doing small time get away driving,
so he gets hired by slink or otherwise the tut guy and sends TK into the life of hardcore crime, there were a lot of missions that had interesting gameplay mechanics like one mission for instance you have to face against a tank,
anyway so *SPOILERS* TK Gets framed and goes to Jail for 28 years *SPOILERS* When he finnaly gets out it's 2006 and he has one thing on his mind Revenge (Because why not) anyway so for the next few missions You're taking out all the people that betrayed you with a predictable plot twist along the way,
Now The story racks up to be about 9 hours long but that's all it really needed, you can explore the city for Jobs such as being a get away driver, checkpoint races, ect. Now here's the fun part car Customization, I have Spent a little while customizing my car to be the fastest there is and it really is quite fun speeding through the city Listening to Addicted to speed,
SO over all  Driver Parallel lines is a good game the Map is dull and boring and even more so during the 2006 era but it really makes up for it in it's Customization Era changes So i reccomend you get this game But just don't expect an amazing Action packed game of the year

Driver Parallel Lines is a largely forgotten game, and a relic of a different era. It was the unfortunate byproduct of Atari's mismanagement of the Driver series and as a result has largely become forgotten to time.
After Driver 3, fans of the series had lost interest in the franchise. And after Grand Theft Auto San Andreas, people had seen the franchise as outdated. In the friendly rivalry between the two companies, Reflections and Rockstar, Rockstar was the definite winner. And the fall from grace can be felt with this game.
Parallel lines isn't a bad game at all really. It has a unique premise and for it's time is very impressive. The game follows it's main character TK (an abrreviation for "The Kid") through two distinctive time periods, 1978 and 2006. The difference between these two time periods is the selling point of the game, as it takes place in a very stylized miniature version of New York city. Likewise the driving is fairly solid and the soundtrack is absolutely amazing.
Where it falls flat is it's production values. Parallel Lines was clearly a much more budget release, reusing the same engine as Driver 3 and only taking place in one city. Likewise the general gameplay isn't that polished and the physics benefit an arcade game more than a non-linear driving game. The on-foot sections also still feel out of place. The story to the game is also fairly muddy, and apart from very good cinematics doesn't hold your attention until the 2006 portion of the game. Where it starts to become more reminiscient of the Count of Monte Cristo.
It feels like a game that was released too late, it would've given Grand Theft Auto Vice City a run for it's money in 2002. But by 2006 next generation consoles were out, and the game just couldn't compete with it's competition from 2 years earlier.
For it's price, Parallel Lines is a fine game. But it's a fall from grace. The Driver series would never recover after Parallel lines. The franchise was sold off to Ubisoft, which made Driver San Francisco, a purely driving game as opposed to sandbox. Ubisoft ducked out of the race with Rockstar, and unfortunately remained stopped at the start line.
