Note: I'm only recommending this game because it's $5 and even lower than that on sales. I bought the PS2 version when it came out in 2006 and $60 is ludicrous for such a mediocre game. Yes, I'm calling it mediocre, I'm a huge Driver fan, I own Driver 1 for PC and I think I still have my PS1 copy somewhere. I own Driver 2 for PS1. I own Driv3r for PS2 and PC and the same goes for Driver: Parallel Lines.
The main problem with Driver:PL is that they've turned this into a GTA clone, which wouldn't be so bad if they'd actually cloned the good parts. Sadly they failed miserably.
+ The city looks amazing and really feels like you're actually in New York.
+ Two eras, 1978 and 2006, both of them feel different enough and come with new cars and music.
+ The cars handle much better than in any GTA game, which is what Driver games are all about anyway.
+ The game uses a licensed soundtrack and has some really good songs in it.
+ Cars look quite detailed and there's a good variety of them.
- The draw distance is really annoying, things will pop into view all the time, PC's in 2006 could've handled a draw distance slider.
- The story is pitiful. It makes no sense at times and downright offensive and inane. In 1978 you're a wheelman for hire (though you never actually get paid), in 2006 you're a terrorist who bombs the NYPD building to scare the the guy that ruined his life. Yes, all those innocent people in the building had to die because you want to send the guy that locked you up the message that he's not untouchable. In the other Driver games you're a police officer yourself, here you're a cop killing psychopath.
- You're never getting paid for missions, you don't even get a thank you from the people that you do missions for. This forces you to d races and other side-missions so that you can at least buy some ammo for your weapons.
- The weapons in this game are clunky and have ridiculous names and design. In the 2006 Era there's grenade launcher that shoots rockets and it's called the "RPG Weapon".
- The character and NPC models all look awful, don't blame this on the fact that this was a PS2 port, because even GTA 3 had much better looking models.
- The game is around 11 hours long. That's not much for an open-world game.
I know that there are a lot of cons about this game but for the low price of $5 and less, the pros outweigh the cons.

Early Access Review: as of 7/7/16.
I started to play this game and put only a couple hours into it playing the Lagoon Training missions.
There are 4 parts to this mission before you head to the space academy. First part is talking to a hologram, second go to another lab on the island and  talk to another hologram, run an experiment, build an ATV, drive to next station. at next station figure out how to grow plants and  then drive to next station ( which I drove around the island three times before I could figure out where it was), build a rocket ship then blast off to the space station in orbit. Once I got there......??? At first I had no clue, there's nothing there when you arrive to tell you to use the computer in the room you just spawned and it didn't seem obvious. (second time round I seen it and that's were i got the mission to go to Mars).
So, what I find the game currently lacking is telling me what I'm supposed to do. The instructions are not very clear, in fact the first time i joined a game I was in a drop ship and falling to Mars Surface and die three times before I figured out the controls to the ship. but just as soon as I landed the guy who's game it was left and it closed on me.... so.. that was when I tried to do my own game but found the Lagoon Training missions instead that will lead to the Mission to Mars!
Update 7/10/16
Got a chance to play a little bit on mars building. Once I got the hang of the controls its not too bad but the Camera needs to be fixed in first person view. The Base building and crafting system is unique. You can research blueprints and then using different equipment you can build other items, habitats, tools etc... the game in it's current state is glitchy and i've experienced a few crashes which is common for very early access games but the Devs have been communicating with me and doing a good job. Do you like toy soldiers? Do you love reading about the Great War? Do you like strategy games? Do you like FPSs ? Do you like WWI dogfights?
If you so, then try out 'Toy Soldiers.' This is a gem of a game. It's officially a tower defense game, but it really is a whole lot more. It comes off with a unique and  comfortable feeling to it - I was reminded many times of Battalion Wars on the Gamecube. Loading screens are toy soldier (miniature) boxes and the battles take place on dioramas- like a little kid is playing in his bedroom.
Players fortify certain areas with machine guns, Ack-Acks, howitzers, and other weapons as enemy soldiers, tanks, and planes (in a bonus stage even flying saucers and Feudal knights) assault your lines, attempting to reach your toybox. If so many get in, it's game over (never had it happen personally- but close [down to 1]). To help, players can assume direct control over any of said defenses, turning it into a awesome arcade-style gunning game. If that doesn't tickle your fancy, just plan your defense and watch the battle play out, or maybe personally take control of a tank or aeroplane to counter-attack the enemy lines. The starting campaign follows Great Britain, but a German campaign is unlockable (for den Kaiser!).
The sound of the game is perfect. Period music is played in the background of menus, creating a very nostalgic (yet happy) atmosphere. I really wish they offered the soundtrack. Sound effects are all spot on (from what I can tell).
The game is also very clean. No blood, swearing, etc., so it can be played by all gamers at any age. If soldiers are hit they burst apart into toy pieces (springs, cogs, etc).
This is a great game. If on sale, grab it. If not on sale, still grab it.
The safety of the toybox depends on you.

Toy Soldiers-
Its a tower defense game set in the theatre of WW1, its the subtle things that make this game so enjoyable. Apart from the setting embracing a "old 1900's" toy soldier skin, you play out the levels in theme boxes, if you look at the out of bounds zones you will see the lamps and table that the game has been set on which adds an interesting atmosphere. You can build all sorts of WW1 trench towers, from machine gun nests to gas and, if upgraded, flamethrower bunkers. What I really enjoy about this game that engages me beyond normal tower defense games is that there are tanks and bi-plane spawn zones that you can activate and become part of the fight, the same goes for the towers. You can, say, take control of an artillery piece and use the cannon, subtle note, if you hold down the left click instead of just click, you can guide the shell, to an extent, into its target which is really enjoyable. I would totally recommend this game to any tower defense player and even to some fence riding players since it grabs a bit of hybrid and control that keeps, even me, engaged in the battles!

When one speaks of the first World War, it simply comes to peoples minds of heavy usage of trenches that streatched for miles. For some history buffs and on lookers, they would think the same, but they would also know the more in depth fact that millions of lives were lost from the half a square mile between the trenches, or in other various locations around the globe. And lastly but ultimately, generals on all sides treating their army as if they were toy soldiers. My point being: nearly all generals thought that every citizen in their home country would be so infurated with national pride that thered be an exspendable, almost endless supply of recuirts.
Unfortunately, this caused the deaths of nearly 11 million people.
Anyway, this isnt a history lesson. That was just a little historical review of the games appropriate setting for that era.
Normally when you think of someone making a WW1 game itd be, needless to say, boring since the whole thing was a stalemate and that it was, but engagements went on for nearly weeks upon months. In Toy Soldiers, the battles that are chosen for each level are very accurately selected, and even the historical date and location and even some promises made by some generals who were there. but if you thik youll be waiting for 20 minutes at a time for something interesting to happen, youll find yourself proven wrong. The levels, in the least to say, get very epic at times, not only in scale but to the point where your brain is operating to manage all the incoming enemy waves. And trust me, theres not jsut simpel infantry and occasional tanks, there are several kinds of Infantry, Armored, Airborne, even bosses that are sometimes extrodianarily hard to defeat and each havign a unique look and style.
Your mission, is simply to defend your trench *cough cough* Toybox *cough* from these waves. Even at your desposal are several kinds of Machine guns, AA guns, anti infantry guns, and even occasionaly player controled offencive-defencive airborne and armor units of your own. And the really exciting part is that each can be upgraded to better defend yourself, and it quickly becomes somewhat of a mian side priority next to defeating the enemy.
Since i want to wrap this up in seperate sections so i dont make you lost, ill say the final conclusion setences:
1st: Toy Soldiers is a simple game. its setting, objectives, and graphics are respectable but this game isnt really striding to become the top game of tower defence or what you have since it really dosnt feel liek tower defence all the time.
2nd: If you love the feeling you get when you play a game and get this really sensational 'buzz' or 'drive' to get your brain operating fast and your attentions faster, this IS the game for you.
3rd: I have to add this part so you dont feel that the games soundtrack is on a loop; the games themes are randomly picked everytime you go to the menu. And unfortunately, theres only 3. But all quite good to say the least. Not everybody loves vinatge music from the early radio or record player era but i certianly do. So if your into pre, post, WW1 music, or anything between 1914 and 1939, you wouldnt mind this too much at all.
4th: I cant really say anything for the multiplay since it never really felt satisfying. its cool to play Offencive Defencive but it seemed a bit alien. if it was faster paced, id give it a good word but its not really to my liking unfortunately. All in All, im in nuetral stance for its Multiplayer mode, and its more up to you as far as what you feel towards it.
So if you wanna pass the time a bit, Toy Soldiers, is definately a game worth the money.
PS: i wont be leaving a review for Toy Soldiers: Cold War mostly for the fact that it kinda takes an odd turn down a GI Joeish world. And after playing it during the WW1 struggle, it really dosnt feel cool to jump to the 1950s through 70's. World War One is kinda my only perf for it. Howver, i would LOVE to see a coastal defence expansion, or a more broad spectrum as afar as fronts around the world. it would add so much more to the devine scale of the First World War.

Earlier this year, I gave a negative review to this game to join the rant band wagon.  Now, I am going to give my honest review.  However, I will only touch on the online a little, because that IS NOT GTA.
THE STORY:
I am by no means a fan of single player games.  I prefer online, co-op killing action.  With that being said, GTA V NEVER failed to grab my attention with the story.  You are given plenty of options throughout your playthrough (such as killing someone, or leaving them alive) that impact the game.  The characters are without a doubt some of the greatest voice actors in recent video game history.  There is not a character in the game that isn't unique, and each one has an incredible backstory that you learn more about when you progress through the game.  There are also random events throughout the game that keep even the most basic driving exciting.  If it was from story alone, this game would EASILY get a 10/10.
THE WORLD:
When it comes to the design and detail of Los Santos, I can promise that there is not a better open world in the gaming industry.  The colors are vibrant, the world feels alive, and the designs of certain areas are pure perfection.  Only games like "The Witcher 3" can compare, so if that is something that you have played, you will be able to appreciate this world.  The parodies are a major bonus as well.
THE GAMEPLAY:
I consider this the weakest link of GTA.  The hand to hand combat in the game is a major down grade from GTA IV, but the guns are a major improvement.  Everything feels very smooth for the most part during combat.  The cops function very well, and work as a cooperative unit.  The cars all feel amazing, and have unique traction and speed.
CUSTOMIZATION:
From clothing items, to paint jobs, GTA does not fail to embrace the freedom of choice.  You can completely change cars that you buy from the vast Internet that was created.
THE ONLINE:
GTA Online feels almost nothing like the actual game.  However, it is still one of the best open world games you can play with your friends.  It is not nearly as fun without friends though.  The Online also fails at producing a fair market.  The amount of money that you earn is not nearly enough to purchase what you want, and it has been a major complaint from the beginning.  It is a shame that they have not yet added more housing or heists, but there is still plenty to do.  Shark cards are ridiculously overpriced, so I would recommend staying away from them.  Hackers are also very common.
THE VERDICT:
GTA earns a 9/10!
The base game is absolutely amazing and the game is definitely worth the purchase.  IF you are going to play online, make sure to grab friends!

(Warning: Long Read. Skip down a bit to get to actual gameplay. Also, this review was made during the early access period.)
Oh my, where to begin? This is not a tale of victory over difficult odds, nor of battles hard won. This is not even a story of an epic last stand. Straight up, this game will cheat, trick, and break you. The creators of Dark Souls could take lessons.
My very first experience on this game was greeted by the title screen, which was..... interesting. After mashing the keyboard, it finally acknowledged my presence and allowed me entry to make my character, where perhaps the only good thing happened to me. In the form of a glitch. You see, for whatever strange reason it simply would not register that I had chosen a character. I clicked create, and nadda. So, in my annoyance I bounced back and fourth between the only two male characters in the game (jiggily boobies were quite tempting, though) clicking "Create" until I finally gave up on the game (the first time of many).
Upon my inglorious reentry back to the title, I came to meet the good friend of many GunZ 2 player so-I-hear, the Title Screen Crash error. Having totally reinstalled from the ground up and still unable to conquer this obstacle, I turned to that blessed fountain of information (among other things), Google. There, I discovered that pressing any key multiple times, clicking multiple times, or by holding a key down too long will cause this error at the Title Screen. (lol wut?) I'm not a developer, but I think something like that should have been caught before release. Seems a biggie, to me. Anywhosit, this left me in a interesting bind. See, the game didn't acknowledge me when I pressed a single key a single time. I tried, waited nearly five whole minutes (timed myself), and tried again till apparently I hit the magic number to cause the error. This happened roughly seven times, spanning over half an hour post-installation, and still no game play.
Finally, after much teeth-grinding irritation, I discovered that holding in three keys for about ten seconds and then letting go would let me in, and then I saw it. Remember that "good thing" I mentioned? Apparently because of the character select fiasco, it had registered BOTH characters as mine, allowing me full access to both of them. This seemed a nice enough peace offering from the game to forgive it, and so I did. Oh, how I regret it.
My very first match I had spent 4 out of 5 revival tokens, finding myself dropping like a fly with my inexperience. Losing over 30 hp to enemy attacks and picking up heals of only 10 hp left me on death's speed-dial the whole game. When my second game arrived and I ran out of the magic revive coins, I asked an all-important question. How to get more. My answer was "by lvling up (Not true!) or buying with irl (In real life, for the text-speak challenged) money". Holy Monty Python's Flying Circus, what a cash-grab. And here I was burning them up like candy, I may as well have been rolling up and smoking likenesses of Andrew Jackson. This game offers no team revival system, very few heals, armor that only reduces damage, and scours of stormtrooper-grade enemies who are bound to land a hit eventually. And it will hurt. I watched my whole team die again, and again, and again, winning my first match by sticking around in ghost-cam for our lvl 20 to win it for us. And she almost died 9 times. On level 1. Little much, isn't it?
I wanted to play Mr. Shield-Man, hiding behind my bullet-proof friend more often than fighting, finding myself unable to weave between bullets as other characters seemed to, and always out of lovely-lovely minigun ammo. The only reason I could survive at all was because of that magnificent creature.
Ah, yes. And then it began cheating. Invincible, unkillable enemies. Spawning right on top of you, frozen in their spot but still able to shoot. You could not hurt them, but boy-oh-boy did they hurt you. I lost 80 hp in one hit from a knife-guy who spawned behind me, spooking me into lowering my shield and getting eviscerated by gatling gun fire. I once spent a whole game trapped in a room because the door we opened (second level, I do believe) decided all on it's own accord to close itself, and never-ever-ever open again ever. Alas, this became simply too much to bear, and I promptly uninstalled.
In the end, if you desire a game such as this, which pits a team of four or so players against a wave of ever-fun-to-slaughter cannon fodder, with awesome acrobatics, speed, katanas, and epic guns, I have but one suggestion. Go pick up Warframe. Enjoy recharging shields, revives that resupply after 12-hours, teammate revives, and in truth never really having to spend a dime on it unless you want a cosmetic item or are just impatient. All in all it's a better, prettier, much more enjoyable, and less money-grabbing game. If you absolutely must play this, I highly suggest waiting till GunZ 2 leaves the beta stage.

This is my review after playing about 300 hours.
I love Tekken and I always have. But there are a few things that I hate about my Tekken 7 experience.
1. It's disappointing that there is is there no way to do a quick rematch when playing with friends online. We get to do it when we are doing a player match with a stranger in the 'Quick match' mode but when creating a session to play with a friend there is no option to do quick revenge matches and the time wastage is annoying to say the least. A counter argument would be, if revenge matches are allowed in session matches then other players in the session could have to wait indefinitely. Well, in that case we definitely need a new online vs mode for just 2 players.
2. It's frustrating to not be able to quit when you want from tournaments and session matches even when you are not playing. Why would you force someone to stay and watch a whole tournament even when he is knocked out? Why would there be no way to quit when two other players are fighting in a session match? You are forcing us to use Alt+F4 often in game.
3. When an opponent quits in the middle of a match it just leaves the screen stuck at the other person's system with the message 'Syncing', as if connection was lost due to a network problem and that wait is frustrating. You really should be instantly showing that the other person quit the game and give him the victory and close the match, the way it works in Mortal Kombat.
The above three are my MAJOR concerns with the game. Following are some minor ones.
1. When in warmup mode of online games and accepting fight requests, many times I get the message 'Fight request could not be sent'. I feel that sounds lame and misleading because what really happened is the other person declined the challenge. So that's the message we should see.
2. I am a Law player and I know that the Dragon's flight is extremely hard to connect in combos. Very few players in the world are able to connect it consistently and is almost impossible in online matches. And in spite of this difficulty the reward is nothing exceptional. Most characters get similar damage from their mid screen combos which are much simpler. My suggestion - make the Dragon's flight easier to connect in combos or more damage in combos with current difficulty.

This may be the best game you've never played.  Kingdoms of Amalur was a very solid game that came out at a terrible time.  It followed on the heels of Arkham City, Uncharted 3, Deus Ex, Portal 2, and of course Skyrim, and followed just a little too late for most people to really feel like dropping $60 on it.  It's critical mediocrity and tepid sales are probably a direct result of it's poor timing.
As for the game itself...
The story is solid, if not entirely original.  The gameplay follows a similar vein - it's a heck of a lot of fun really.  There's serious depth to the gameplay and also the world (a magnificent and beautiful world that you could spend weeks exploring).  In many ways it feels like the love-child of Skyrim and Fable.  If you liked those two games, this is a no-brainer.

In the first few hours of playing the game: I saved a teammate from an unknown threat, Randomly stumbled into my bosses apartment to find out he was gay, infiltrated an underground newspaper, broke into an apartment and had the house AI call the police, ran into a cybernetic hypnosis cult run by an augmented stage magician, fought mobsters in an underground casino, and robbed the most secure bank in the country. And I haven't even completed my first non-intro mission yet. The amount of detail between places you can go and data you can find on computers and pdas is awesome. For example, I was in a random house, and found out the owner had a vault in the bank, so off to the bank I went, and went through office by office, escalating my security privilege by a combination of hacking, finding pocket secretaries and finding keycards. I located the vault and used the code I'd found at the house.
This game is awesome. The gameplay thus far is a nicely improved version of what is in Human Revolution. (Although if you use controller, stick with the HR controller config)
The bad:
There were a couple glitches (as is expected when a game is released into the wild) - if you are crashing at the Train Station, turn graphics medium or low, and play through the scene. Then turn your graphics back up and enjoy.
The good:
Graphics are beautiful. I have mine set at high on my 970 and it runs perfectly. The Very High and Ultra settings seem designed to future proof the game for new graphics cards when they come out, and they will look insane (I accidentally started using Ultra settings) especially on 4k or higher screen resolutions.
Gameplay is as I said earlier what I expected: HR with new nuances to master. More augment variations, and more weapons. The AI seems a bit more intelligent than in HR, which is good, because "Give Me Deus Ex" is challenging, and not just the mode everyone with self-respect should play.
Breach is interesting and fun - But I will add more info later if Micro-Transactions become annoying.
Note: Not finished the game yet, but will update with any additional info when I do.

The sad thing is it's not that the game is bad, it's the actual game infrastructure and servers that are apparently so easy to hack and mod. Take Two and Rockstar have already taken down the most widely used cheat/exploit providers, which have nothing to do with openIV. OpenIV specifically gets you to create a mod folder that will only be used in single player. As far as I remember, trying to mod the game files within openIV without a mod folder for single player means the game won't even launch or it will crash on start up in online.
I was also speaking to a modder on the gta online chat the other day, asking him not to give me money etc, and I asked how modders could mod online so easily, and he told me it was script injection, which I'm pretty sure has nothing to do with openIV. If you want to add scripts you need an asi loader and so on and those files go into the game directory manually, not through openIV. I've only ever modded single player, and not for a while, but that's how it used to be.
Yes, modders are annoying as hell, but how much money do you really need to make? I bought gta5 on ps3 and pc, specifically so I could mod single player, as i had done with gtaIV and san andreas for years. Plus the pc community for gta5 is surely smaller than the console community, who have no option but to buy sharkcards and so on, so your revenue isn't going to exactly fall off a cliff. I think last year gta online through microtransactions alone had made over $1bn since it's lauch, without taking into account purchases of the game. As a short term solution, this might make sense to take two interactive, but the ammount of negative community feedback will surely hurt them long term, especially since they don't exactly have many big new games from big ip's out at the moment. Sad times.

I found this game quite pleasing in it's design and story. Though some people might find the game short, I found it stayed the right amount of time, in the sense that I can see myself replaying this game to completion once again later down my life.
Story-wise, brothers is pretty focussed and to the point. You play two brothers that go on a quest to save their father from an illness, and not much more is said, considering the characters talk an alien language, most of the story is told mostly through sounds, expressions and visuals.  Though the game does start with a rather simple story you are given a lot of lore through the locations the brothers explore. It fills the world and makes it rather rich adding to the storytelling. However I did find some events of the game predictable.
There is no actual combat in the game, but rather puzzles that need to be resolved through the joint efforts of both characters. You control both brothers at the same time using your keyboard or controller (I highly recommend using a controller for this game) areas are mostly context sensitive meaning you have one button to perform different actions depending on where you are.
There will be times where you might cross the brothers and forget what side controls who but it's not a major frustration that kills the experience (though I don't deny some envy to those who have no issues with this).
Music and sound are pretty well handled, giving the right tone for all locations in the game. I didn't come across anything jarring or out of place. Considering the lack of any actual native speaking language this is actually a huge positive as the music and sound effects do help tell the story better.
I did enjoy this games story and atmosphere, it took around 4 hours to complete and the game allows you to pick previous chapters to replay which is good for achievement hunting.

Crowborn's Review of Torchlight II
-
Ever since I was a boy, and got my hands on Diablo 1, I have been a fan of the hack-n-slash game-genre. Something about the game strung a cord inside of me, and I played it almost non-stop for years. Same with the sequel - it kept me busy through highschool and sane in the awkward years following when I was rampaging through life, trying to figure out what the 'eck I wanted to do. And so arrived the highly anticipated 3rd installment of the Diablo genre - to lackluster reviews. I picked it up immediately of course, but I were never able to enjoy it. It just seemed off to me, seemed strange, like an orange growing on an apple-tree, trying to fit in with the smooth green skinned fellas around it. But for me it failed at the deceit, and I put down the game after playing it for only a few months. Dissapointed and bereft of one of my favourite genres, I started looking around for substitutes. That's when I heard about Torchlight II.
I had noticed the series before, but for some reason never gotten around to trying it out. It was supposed to be a fairly good diablo-clone, and while I liked the genre, it wasn't until one of my dear steam-friends gifted me the game, that I actually managed to sit down and play it. I felt obliged to, so to say. And my were I pleasantly surprised!
Torchlight II is a really well made game. From the steam-punkish world, cross the interesting skill-sets, to the actio-packed maps - this game just breathes fun game design. Granted, the game is 'very' much a Diablo-clone, and anyone who ever played those games will immediately find everything intimately familiar. But that's not a bad thing. In fact, I find it darned good. I didn't have to read a bible of game-guides before daring to venture out in the the world of Torchlight, and hack and slash my way through the first pack of monsters I came across. It granted me immediate satisfaction and loads of fun.
It feels to me like the devs of this game did right, what the guys at Blizz did wrong. Torchlight II follows to a point the tried and true old recipe of hack-n-slash. They don't try to reinvent or alter the genre, but instead stick to what works and 'has' worked for the last two decades. You got your attribute-points, your skill-points, random loot, runes and enchantments to upgrade your gear, rewarding exploration, and a story-line that doesn't distract you from your dungeon-delving fun.
The game hearkens back to the good old days, and gives the players exactly what they expected - and a little more. It deserves a top grade, but due to an at times non-transparent stat-system and unbalanced characters, I have to subtract a few points. I give it:
8.5/10

So, the successor of GunZ: The Duel, GunZ 2: The Second Duel has your familiar maps and combat that revolves around a sword and a gun. But that is about as far as the games are similar.
The gameplay is in a different park. The fluid ground movement from the original is gone to be replaced by a stuttering dash while wall climbing and running has been simplified into  a periodic tap of the jump key. The versitility of the sword is gone with the block becoming nothing more than something to reduce hits to you from a distance while its short-range strength is unbalanced. If you land a hit while moving towards your opponent, you've won due to the flinch and the knockdown on the combo attack. This combo also makes the secondary on the sword, the flip, useless as you can't break it like with the flip. Weirdly, once a opponent gets knocked down, you can't melee them.
The change in the wallrunning and climbing, other than simplifying the game, could be explained be the introduction of a class system on G2 as not everyone has a sword, one of the classes even has a shield instead of a sword. When you first start the game, you're given the choice of which class you wish to play with a short description of each. Once selected, you're stuck with that class. You don't get to try before you buy or anything of the sort. HI THERE! Would you like a sword, dagger, bat or shield? K, thx, bye. If you don't like the class you chose, too bad, you're stuck with it for the next several hours of gameplay. Each class has three weapon types, a melee weapon, an automatic weapon, and a semi-automatic weapon (excluding one class which gets a flamethrower instead) all of which you carry with you at all times. Each class also has a different armour capacity, of which can be replenished in various locations around the map making classes with higher armour have a substantially better sustain.
Along with the class system comes leveling and skills, a system which I believe is unsuitable for this type of game. When you start a character you automatically get two class specific skills and as you level up you unlock more in a linear fashion, each of which uses some combination of the basic controls.
MAIET, the company who are developing GunZ 2, have decided to go with a p2p host system for this game which everyone knows is the perfect system for a shooting game... Given that the game is still in the works, this host system may become more bearable once it comes to a full release and more people are playing.
Questing is back, but it is dull and boring given the bland map design, horrible AI and the fact that it costs $2.50 to revive (first six revives on account creation are free) if you die, meaning that if you die in a party, you'll probably be spectating for 5+ minutes and I have to say that that is a VERY boring thing to do...
I've heard several people say that the game gets better as you level up and unlock different skills but for that to happen, you kind of need to play which I find hard enough to do in the first place...
I can't think of anything more to say about this game, so thanks for reading

Well, this one is quite a hard one for me.
For starters, it was a blast, like discovering a jewel that has been sitting in front of you all of the time without you noticing it. I was like, "Why didn't I know this game did exist at all?" And so I was really hooked to it for a couple of hours. A couple of dozens of hours.

So, at the end, I wouldn't recommend it. It gave me plenty of hours of enjoyemet a the star, but left me empty and a bit angry by the mid-end game.  If you can get it on sale (not very often, I think) go for it, but else, I wouldn't do so.

This review should hopefully cover all levels of interest with this game.
If you are looking to get into fighting games, Tekken 7 is a decent place to start.
I picked this up Day 1. I've been a Tekken loyalist since Tekken 2. In a nutshell, it's more of what fans of the series have come to love - and also despise. Simple, fluid fighting, wakeup/airplay combos - and over-the-top styling. Gameplay is simple enough for your less-cool non-Tekken-geek significant other to play after a couple of drinks - and also forgiving enough for casual fans to enjoy online play without getting the crap kicked out of them every single time.
What's really blown me away are the improvements to online play the devs have made since launch. Day 1: it was disconnect or timeout every other match. After the latest patch, I'm finding matches that click almost instantaneously. And, with the option to ask for a revenge match after every online game (initially, there was only one revenge match), you can really get into a grudge match groove with someone online - provided they're willing to go the distance.
Tekken's about the closest thing you can get to neutral ground when it comes to fighters. It doesn't overly punish players who don't input precisely like, say, Virtua Fighter. It doesn't structure itself around a rock, paper, scissors style of play like, say, DOA - and it absolutely doesn't take itself too seriously like, I don't know... Killer Instinct... or Rise of the Robots?
Tekken works like this: (assuming you're using a controller, which you should). The face buttons of your controller correspond to a limb (i.e., right hand and left hand would each get a button, as would left and right leg) and most special moves and combos are performed as a function of the combination of limb buttons you press. Many effective moves aren't difficult to execute for many characters, which is why the series has been tagged as a button masher in the past. I would suggest the game's practice mode to get started with a character, then maybe the other single player modes - but they really it can't teach you what you'd learn by fighing online. And I do think that's where Tekken 7 excels: its online mode... I mean... it's really good.
The omission of Lei Wulong on the character roster is glaring, maddening and a bit bewildering. I suspect (hope) he'll show up in a DLC - but, for the rest of you, there's a bum ton of good characters that fit most playstyles. Seriously, I have no idea why they didn't include Lei. He's been there since 2.
For those of you who do not want to play against human opponents, there is an acceptable number of game modes that might suit your needs. Treasure mode, for instance, is a kumite-style mode where defeating an opponent grants you cosmetic unlockables and personal prestige. That's fun. Then, there's a fairly well-executed story mode, which details the nonsensical events of the Tekken universe this go-round. No spoilers there from me. Lots of NANI?! and haymakers. Desu.
Final word: Being the first Tekken on PC, I was skeptical of another Japanese fighter on PC after D0A 5:LR - which, frankly, was crap. The publisher of that game is crap too. Screw them. They, and their stupidly overpriced, poisonous DLC can eat a bag of them. I loved DOA once....
It would be wrong for me to say this game isn't slightly overpriced for the North American market - but I'm a fan - and I really I doubt it will get Steam cheap for a while - particularly with the potential for a lot of DLC to appear in the future. Still, Tekken 7 is a game worth playing for anyone who has an interest in fighters. LONG LIVE TEKKEN!

As far as I remember, trying to mod the game files within openIV without a mod folder for single player means the game won't even launch or it will crash on start up in online.
I was also speaking to a modder on the gta online chat the other day, asking him not to give me money etc, and I asked how modders could mod online so easily, and he told me it was script injection, which I'm pretty sure has nothing to do with openIV. If you want to add scripts you need an asi loader and so on and those files go into the game directory manually, not through openIV. I've only ever modded single player, and not for a while, but that's how it used to be.
Yes, modders are annoying as hell, but how much money do you really need to make? I bought gta5 on ps3 and pc, specifically so I could mod single player, as i had done with gtaIV and san andreas for years. Plus the pc community for gta5 is surely smaller than the console community, who have no option but to buy sharkcards and so on, so your revenue isn't going to exactly fall off a cliff. I think last year gta online through microtransactions alone had made over $1bn since it's lauch, without taking into account purchases of the game. As a short term solution, this might make sense to take two interactive, but the ammount of negative community feedback will surely hurt them long term, especially since they don't exactly have many big new games from big ip's out at the moment. Things I love:
The combat is very fluid and smooth. All of the actions seem to flow into one another without any problems. Honestly the combat is gorgeous in a way, and that's ignoring the fact the graphics themselves are pretty great too.
The characters and their dialogue all seem to fit perfectly with their animated counterparts, which makes it feel like i'm following along on another one of their adventures. Plus Ruby always gives me a reason to smile.
The game fits well into the RWBY lore constantly adding more and more lore to the constantly growing world of Remenant. The story of Remenant doesn't start and end with the anime, nor is there nothing outside the walls of Vale just because the story hasn't really left the walls. There is a whole lot more to the world of Remenant than the anime tells us, and this game gives us another glimpse into their world.
The character skill trees gives us some variety everytime we start a match. I also personally love that quite a few of the skills are locked until certain in game requirements are met, which gives us a solid goal and a reason to play more to unlock all of their skills.
The number and difficulty of the monsters increase for the more players there are in the game, so when all 4 players are in the game, the battles quickly become very large and intense and bring me back for more.
The 4 members all have very different playstyles and abilities, so there is likely be someone everyone. For example, Ruby focusing heavily on utilizing her combos, while Yang focuses more on brute strength and the power of her fists.
Things that could be fixed, added, or improved:
(This is more like a personal message to RT.)
Framerate. Please. I know you are doing all that you can to fix these things which means a lot to someone like me who doesn't even come close to having a high end computer, so please keep working on it. I'm sure I'm not the only one who like to enjoy this game at it's best, but are unable to.
While I would definitely love more characters to be added just as much as everyone else here, I think you should definitely focus more on perfecting the game than adding more characters. Things like optimizing and tweaking what's already there, and also adding more and more to the games mechanics as time goes on like more combos and better control of the combos, blocking, depth, etc. When those new characters come out, I want them to be something that makes an already perfect game better.
How about fixing the targeting system? Trying to hit specific targets at a range is near impossible. I can't tell you how many times I tried to hit someone right in front of me with Ruby's dust blast skill, but it would instead sail straight over all of their heads and harmlessly hit a wall. This also includes Ruby's basic sniping attack. It tends to choose a target at random to hit, or no one at all. I can't speak much for the other characters though since I hardly use them. Ruby just fits me and my play style perfectly.
I also think you can improve the skill trees a lot. They are a great feature, but at the moment they are still rather limited. There isn't all that large of a variety when it comes to choosing skills and move variations. With more passive skills and a greater variety in skill move branching, I think it would be a lot of fun to try out all of the different combinations and how well the moves work together with one another.
Lastly, I think it would awesome if each character had some kind of combat mechanics unique to them. For example, Ruby could set up with crescent rose implanted into the ground and snipe at targets at a distance. Perhaps it would have a greater damage and armor penetration, but she would be unable to move while she is set up. Similar to how she does it in the Red Trailer.(Sorry if that doesn't make sense, hard to explain.) Perhaps Weiss would be able to use and plant glyphs in some way that would aid her in combat. Perhaps Blake could use some of her dust enhanced/elemental semblance shadows in combat. The ones she used against Roman at the end of Volume 2. These are just some ideas, but I hope I got my idea across.
ANYWAY. Sorry about the long rambling review. I normally don't write this much. I just want to throw out any ideas that could be used, and things that could be fixed, because I really want to see this game be the best it could possibly be. Truly, keep up the good work!
TL;DR: A great RWBY action/hack n slash game. It's not perfect, but it has a lot of potential and it will only continue to get better from here. And if you love RWBY i'm sure you'll enjoy this.

I'm going to start this out by saying that this is a really fun game it's great feeling to fight tons of grim as the characters of RWBY in a team based setting. I think the game-play is decently fun and the story is alright. So when you read the rest of the review, keep in mind that I DO like your game, I just think that it could be improved in multiple ways.
[If you are reading this to decide weather or not you want to buy it, stop here. The rest is for the developers.]
My major problems with this game revolve around how much so many parts of the game feel the same. After about the 10th time playing through the campaign I have almost completely memorized all of the encounters. My biggest suggestion to improve this feature is by potentially randomizing the spawn locations of the relics and boxes, and putting a small randomization in the spawn rates of the mobs that we will be fighting. Also, all of the characters feel, for the most part, the same. The abilities seem to be lined up like this: AoE Damage/Utility, high damage single target, long range damage. To improve on this you could potentially either make it so that each character has a truly unique move set, or give each character the option between 5 or more moves that they would simply chose 3 of. Another way to add customization and diversity is by allowing people to upgrade their character with bonuses to health/speed/skill damage/flat damage/ attacking speed/whatever you want (look at the mod system in Warframe to get a better idea of what I'm talking about[I'm not saying copy the whole system, just the general concept of mods and slots]). As for the basic attacks, I suggest looking up the game "Vindictus" and trying to implement an attack/combo system like they have for their characters. It doesn't have to be identical, but there is currently little point to doing anything other than spam left click with the occasional tap of shift to dodge or space to jump. Alternatively, you could take a note from, again, the game "Warframe" by implementing differences in the attack combos based off of movement or pauses in stead of right clicks. This might solve the repetitive nature of the current combat system and make the game a little more enjoyable, but that is not what I think the main problem of the game is. As far as I'm concerned, the main problem with this game appears to be intention.
As far as I can tell, your current intention with this game is to make a fun game for people to buy, play a few times, then drop. Decently fun, good deal, maybe pick up every so often to play with friends, but not anything truly amazing. THIS WOULD BE A TERRIBLE WASTE. This is a fact that I can not stress enough: this could be an amazing game that people will still be coming back to when RWBY is in season 10 (if the series has that many seasons), or potentially outlast the actual show! All you would have to do is follow a simple formula, and this game could go from an alright game that friends play every so often, to a game big enough to compete with AAA titles.
It may seem like this is to small of a game to ever grow to the sizes that I may have mentioned, but all you have to do is 1 simple*(not really that simple) thing: continue to release content. Add more campaigns, continue to release new characters(it's not like you have any shortage to chose from), add cosmetic options(either in sets or for individual slots like chest, boots, legs, head, weapon), and even survival modes. Another way to increase interest in this game is by introducing a competitive scene, by having endurance challenges and/or races in preset unique situations. The rewards could be in-game currency (I'll get to that in the next section), unique cosmetics, or even potentially real RWBY merchandise. Holiday events are also another way to get attention and returning players. If you continue to add content and host events, you will have people coming back to this game till the end of time.
Now you may be currently thinking "aside from appeasing our fan after the complete ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T WE JUST PULLED IN THE LAST TWO EPISODES OF SEASON 3!" (*takes deep breath*) "Why would we do this? New content is expensive to produce and there no assurance we would get that much out of it." In reality you could make it quite profitable in one of two ways. The first of which I will call the "EA approach" and the second I will call the "Dangerous but Loved approach"
The EA approach is quite simple, and DLC is the name of the game. Just look at Payday 2, a very simple game (that is in my opinion isn't even that amazing) that has lasted far longer than it should have by a constant stream of frankly impressive DLC and developing content. You could release characters in team based packs or individually, payed cosmetics, and a billion different other things that people could buy for a (pleasepleaseplease) low price. The good part about this method, you will almost certainly make money off of each expansion you release. The down-side, people will hate you. You'll be accused you being money-grabbers and probably lose a good portion off players and fans. This is not the method I would personally suggest. Instead I would suggest...
The Dangerous but Loved approach. The idea is that you release all of your expansions and DLC free of charge. Any new content that could affect game-play you give to all your players completely free. Now hold on just one second before you call this method financial suicide, you still could make decent profit this way, but it would require a significantly larger amount of work. The idea is that you would pump out as much cosmetic DLC as feasibly possible. You could buy these cosmetics either with direct money transfers or an in-game currency that you purchase with real money. These cosmetics could easily be costumes (like previously mentioned), but you could also offer alternate skill effects, such as changing the color, but you could really do anything to just make them look different. You could introduce pets that don't actually do anything, just follow you around and look cute. I'm sure you can see the reason this is called the Dangerous but Loved approach, there is a significant risk of not making as much money as you may expect, but those who can't afford that much can still enjoy the game at a very low cost. While it may seem that you might not even break even with this payment model, I would suggest you look at Grinding Gears Games. They are a small game company that popped up only a few years ago, and is using almost this exact same model for an entirely free-to-play game. You could also take a not from their supporter pack by releasing time limited exclusive packs of cosmetics and real life merchandise. With your current fan base and the quality of the game as it is before you make any of my previously mentioned changes (if you do that is), I have no doubt that this game would be able to survive on this model.
In the end I just want to say that I am a huge fan of RWBY, both the animated series and the game. I think that this game could be amazing if you put the work into it. IF you put the work into it. As it is not and in the direction it's going, I think it will be an alright game that I definitely wouldn't pay more than 15 dollars for, but I just want you guys to know what this game COULD be, and hope you take this opportunity to make this the truly amazing game it could be.
Edit: since I posted this I've noticed that the developers have made updates as to new combat systems being introduced soon and a new hoard/survival mode coming in soon. I'll have to wait untill they are released and then will update with what I think of them.

is a 4 player co-op based, hack-n-slash game based upon Rooster Teeth’s international hit animated series RWBY.  It is currently in early access, so the game is still being developed.
The game heavily relies on "intense combat action", like the Legend of Korra game.
During your battles with the "Grimm" enemies across familiar locations from the show, you will encounter brand new areas that were specifically designed for the game.
Ruby, Weiss, Blake, and Yang all look exactly like the original show, with very miniscule changes to the models.
The 3D anime-esq art style mimics the original shows art very nicely and at times, made me wonder if they were using the models made for the show.
I'm a huge fan of the show, and the detail on the character models made me feel like I could have been watching an episode.
While kicking♥♥♥♥♥as one of the iconic girls from "Team RWBY", the story will escort you through some areas that look both familiar and new to the series.
The new stages / areas feel like they could easily be a part of an episode that was cut from the original show, with each individual stage having almost as much detail as I expected from a "Brawler" type game.
Since the game is in early access, the story development is not yet complete, however, it does look promising.
As far as licensed game stories go, the writing is some of the best of the "Brawler" genre.
The writing heavily benefits from the minds behind Rooster Teeth and the original show, allowing the game to seamlessly fit into the RWBY universe as if it were yet another episode.
During your adventure with team RWBY, you will encounter new enemy types and a brand new villain designed specifically for the game.
While the new villain is interesting, the enemies fall prey to what I like to call "I'm here and I'm evil, so you should stop me" syndrome which is shared between most licensed games like the "Legend of Korra" game that launched earlier this year.
I can't fully explain the story in depth, as it is still a work in progress.
When the complete story is available, I will update the review with a more fleshed out story section.
While I'd personally like to see some of the other characters that have appeared in the show, you can currently only play as the 4 main protagonists from the RWBY series.
Ruby, Weiss, Blake, and Yang feel distinct from each other and the animation is reasonably fluid with only a few animations looking a little bit odd.
The character models are well detailed like the show, and retain the style of the original series.
This is great, as most anime or CGI animated licensed games seem to forgo the detail that makes the characters so likable in favour of trying to justify a new villain for the game.
During gameplay, your character will level up, granting you the ability to customize your character’s "Loadout" of attacks and skills.  While this is a welcome addition to the core gameplay, it feels a little too similar to the "Legend of Korra", DOTA 2, Rise of Incarnates and Heroes of the storm type of skill customization.
Despite the similarities, the MOBA-esq skill system needs to be refined and some abilities need to have some incentive to use them.  I found myself using the same attack pattern over and over again until it was just an ingrained habit just as I did with the Korra game.
While RWBY's co-op mode is fun with a friend, it can be easily ruined by huge lag spikes and some odd hit detection in some stages.  I'm sure Rooster Teeth will fix this teething problem, as they are patching the game on a reliable basis.  Whilst playing online co-op, I found that many players simply AFK'd for extended periods of time and did not contribute to the team.  In a game where teamwork is so crucial, it was very frustrating to find team members frequently MIA.   I'd like to see the developers address this issue, perhaps by creating an NPC or bot system when players AFK for an extended period so other team members aren't penalised.
While the game is in early access, I can't completely give the game a free pass.
There are some big problems that Rooster Teeth need to fix, including awkward hit detection, bad enemy placement, dumb as a rock AI and above all else, they need to add a support AI for AFK team members.
Overall, the game can be fun, challenging and interesting.
However, I'd wait untill the game is a bit further through it's development pipeline before jumping on board.

Simply put, give back OpenIV.

___
PROS
+ Amazing Environment
I cannot tell you how much I love the game's beautiful environment. I loved sitting down with both brothers just to see an amazingly gorgeous scene or a scene in which showed a bloody battle. I would love wallpapers of these "bench scenes" since they just really stand out. The first time I sat down at one of those benches, I had to let my friends know how beautiful the game is! I wish I could say more but I can't put how wonderful the visuals are into words! You just have to experience it yourself.
+ Excellent Story
There were a lot of parts that had me hanging on my seat. (Don't even get me started at that snowy village place!) The action made it different from other fairy tales and the story definitely had me wanting to play more each day. It had fairy tale cliches but even with those, I enjoyed the game a lot. Heck, I almost started crying!
+ Unique Gameplay
So it's either me or I've never played a game in which you use different keys/buttons on your keyboard/controller to control two separate characters... I'm not very civilized if I really haven't... Moving on! The controls are a bit confusing but as soon as you get used to it, you can definitely get through the game without dying... (Maybe.)
+ Simple Characters
It's basically your common brothers with a simple design, both with similar, yet different, outfits. They don't make the personalities complicated like the people on DeviantArt do with their OCs, but, due to the game devs making the characters speak their own language, we're left with what we see and are free to interpret what personality they have.
(Now I think I just wanted to add this in because hey, why not? Plus I feel like making some fanart of this since I love this game.)
___
CONS
- Confusing Gameplay
As I said earlier, even though the controls are unique, it's still a challenge. From my experience, I had a hard time moving both brothers northeast by pressing A and W along with the left and up arrow keys. I wasn't able to do that so I ended up walking either forward, left, right, or back. It's not much of a bother but there is one part you might get frustrated at so, watch out!

This game is rather short, clocking at about 3 hours. That said, those are worthy 3 hours.
VIsually this game is fantastic, with stylized and very atmospheric environments. The audio basically helps compose the atmosphere, and does a great job at that, but dind't seem to stand out by itself to me.
The gameplay, using each stick to control the respective brother was mind-screwing at first, but worked well once I got used to it. And with these controls you go through the areas solving a series of environment puzzles based on teamwork. None of them seemed difficult, but they kept me entertained.
The story, focusing on the titular brothers' journey to bring  a cure for their father's illness, starts whimsical and humorous, but takes on far more sober and depressing undertones later. The narrative is presented without the use of (comprehensible) dialogue, but through the interactions with the environment and characters, the protagonists' personalities are presented and explored extremely well. I just found it a little silly that whenever characters "talk" to each other it looks like The Sims.
In the end, this one of those interactive experiencies, and one well worth it.

An absolute wonderful game.  My experience with Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons is massively positive.  Albeit I had a hard time adapting to the controls throughout the entire game, it was nonetheless excellent.  The game follows two brothers on a quest to what is to be assumed "The Tree of Life" in order to help their ill father (don't worry this is hardly a spoiler).  The game takes you on a ride of emotions throughout the game and does so without ever saying a word...literally the game is not voice acted (atleast not in language that is understood), narrated, etc etc. and yet manages to tell an absolute brilliant tale.  This game is fairly short but I think it is better off that way.  It's puzzles aren't very challenging ( which is a plus for me :) ), but introduces a unique mechanic of puzzling that I, myself, have yet to see anywhere else on any other game that I have played.  I would definitely recommend this game to anyone looking for an adventure/puzzle game (hope I have used those titles correctly) with a wonderful story to add to it.

This review should hopefully cover all levels of interest with this game.
If you are looking to get into fighting games, Tekken 7 is a decent place to start.
I picked this up Day 1. I've been a Tekken loyalist since Tekken 2. In a nutshell, it's more of what fans of the series have come to love - and also despise. Simple, fluid fighting, wakeup/airplay combos - and over-the-top styling. Gameplay is simple enough for your less-cool non-Tekken-geek significant other to play after a couple of drinks - and also forgiving enough for casual fans to enjoy online play without getting the crap kicked out of them every single time.
What's really blown me away are the improvements to online play the devs have made since launch. Day 1: it was disconnect or timeout every other match. After the latest patch, I'm finding matches that click almost instantaneously. And, with the option to ask for a revenge match after every online game (initially, there was only one revenge match), you can really get into a grudge match groove with someone online - provided they're willing to go the distance.
Tekken's about the closest thing you can get to neutral ground when it comes to fighters. It doesn't overly punish players who don't input precisely like, say, Virtua Fighter. It doesn't structure itself around a rock, paper, scissors style of play like, say, DOA - and it absolutely doesn't take itself too seriously like, I don't know... Killer Instinct... or Rise of the Robots?
Tekken works like this: (assuming you're using a controller, which you should). The face buttons of your controller correspond to a limb (i.e., right hand and left hand would each get a button, as would left and right leg) and most special moves and combos are performed as a function of the combination of limb buttons you press. Many effective moves aren't difficult to execute for many characters, which is why the series has been tagged as a button masher in the past. I would suggest the game's practice mode to get started with a character, then maybe the other single player modes - but they really it can't teach you what you'd learn by fighing online. And I do think that's where Tekken 7 excels: its online mode... I mean... it's really good.
The omission of Lei Wulong on the character roster is glaring, maddening and a bit bewildering. I suspect (hope) he'll show up in a DLC - but, for the rest of you, there's a bum ton of good characters that fit most playstyles. Seriously, I have no idea why they didn't include Lei. He's been there since 2.
For those of you who do not want to play against human opponents, there is an acceptable number of game modes that might suit your needs. Treasure mode, for instance, is a kumite-style mode where defeating an opponent grants you cosmetic unlockables and personal prestige. That's fun. Then, there's a fairly well-executed story mode, which details the nonsensical events of the Tekken universe this go-round. No spoilers there from me. Lots of NANI?! and haymakers. Desu.
Final word: Being the first Tekken on PC, I was skeptical of another Japanese fighter on PC after D0A 5:LR - which, frankly, was crap. The publisher of that game is crap too. Screw them. They, and their stupidly overpriced, poisonous DLC can eat a bag of them. I loved DOA once....
It would be wrong for me to say this game isn't slightly overpriced for the North American market - but I'm a fan - and I really I doubt it will get Steam cheap for a while - particularly with the potential for a lot of DLC to appear in the future. Still, Tekken 7 is a game worth playing for anyone who has an interest in fighters. LONG LIVE TEKKEN!

For an early access title, this is quite playable. You'll understand the background of the game if you've watched the series (i.e., the Rooster Teeth youtube channel).
PROs
[+] Starting a game is easy; choose a character, then join or create a group
[+] Each character has a variety of abilities to experiment with
[+] Each character has advanced skills that will unlock after you've demonstrated prociency with the basic skills
[+] There is good game balance that scales well if you have less than four players on your team
[+] Though playing solo is doable, the game really shines when you have a full rwby team because each character carries strengths that, when combined, become quite effective against enemies.
CONs
[-] To find people that you've previously played with, you'll need to add players as friends through the Steam interface. However, such players won't show up on Steam's "Recently Played With" tab, so you'll need to note the player names within the game.
[-] There might be an issue with occasional d/c's from the server (see notes below). I find that I can be playing for a good long while, but suddenly find myself scrambling to rejoin. Note that you'll need a Steam friend on the team in order to find your team.
[-] Keeping in mind that this is early access, the game currently consists of a sequence of game areas that build an overall story, complete with cut scenes. However, since this is only "Chapter 1," you'll be playing this chapter...and having fun...but you'll be getting somewhat familiar with this chapter after a few playthroughs. Just so you know.
NOTEs
1. There aren't dedicated servers, so when you host a game, your system is the server. This might be an issue if you've joined a host that gives you bad latency (i.e., causing you to d/c).
2. Currently, when you start a game from scratch, all your experience is reset, and you will need to accumulate experience to earn skill points to allocate. However, special unlocked skills will remain unlocked between game sessions; you just need to earn the skill points to spend.

Torchlight 2 is a very solid Action RPG and a vast improvement over its predecessor, which I did not enjoy. Surprisingly, I found this to be a difficult game to get into at first. After a couple of tries, I finally found the "sweet spot" with the SynergiesMOD and a few others. As such, my review will not be based on the "vanilla" experience.
If you like the art style then the graphics are enjoyable, otherwise it's merely serviceable. The sound is solid, but largely uninspired. The story is horrible, but that's typical for this genre. So, Torchlight II is a game that's all about the gameplay and it delivers - mostly.
On the scale of ARPGs, Torchlight II is much closer to Diablo II than even Diablo III. Character progression comes in the form of points – both attribute and skill – that you “spend” to increase your stats, the potency of active or passive skills, and unlock new skills. Skills aren’t held to a classic tree, but there are also no skill synergies (Diablo II skills could be made more powerful by spending skill points in other related skills). Instead, skills have bonuses when they reach levels 5, 10, and 15. Character respec is present, but also limited (this can of course be fixed with mods). You can only “refund” skill points for a few of your most recent acquisitions. This is more than sufficient later in the game when you’re character is set on a particular path, but I would prefer more up-front flexibility until I’ve at least had a chance to try all of the skills – the last of which aren’t available until level 42.
In my opinion, the character classes are the weakest aspect of Torchlight II. Part of why it took me so long to get into the game was because I didn’t find any of the character classes to be particularly interesting. To make matters worse, each class’s skill “branches” feature skills that feel very similar. For example, the first skill available in each branch of the Emerbermage’s skill set are “Magma Spear,” “Icy Blast,” and “Prismatic Bolt.” So basically you can choose which color ball to lob at enemies. As the skill tree opens up there is more diversity available, but not as much as I would have liked.
Combat itself always feels very responsive and is fast-paced. It isn't difficult to die if you forget to pay attention to something or miscalculate. Outside of boss battles, combat is largely enjoyable and features some interesting change-of-pace and exploration mechanics that Diablo 3 has subsequently stolen. Specifically, I particularly enjoy finding “Phase Beasts,” which, when killed, open a phase portal to some type of mini-event. On the flip side, however, are the boss battles. These I found to be frustrating and cheap. Playing solo as a somewhat squishy character, it felt apparent that the mechanics were designed to accommodate multiplayer battles. I only had the opportunity to battle a boss with another player once, but it was far, far easier. In my experience, boss battles basically amounted to developing an attack pattern that allowed me to stay alive and do a little bit of damage. After a while I would eventually whittle down the boss’s health. It’s workable, but not enjoyable. To make matters worse, these encounters always take forever and deaths were frequent, for me at least.
Also worth noting is the loot. There is a plethora of equipment to be found, including sets and legendary items, at least purportedly. Unlike Diablo 3 where “legendary” items now drop every couple of hours, I have not found a single legendary item in Torchlight II. There are also NPCs who can enchant items to add further diversity.
The endgame is currently similar to Diablo 3. There is no “adventure mode,” but the game can be restarted in New Game Plus. If that doesn’t strike your fancy there are random levels available to play that are akin to Neplalem Rifts.
Overall, if you enjoy, or believe that you may enjoy, Action RPGs then it’s difficult not to recommend Torchlight II. It absolutely has its flaws, but many of them can be mitigated through the mods available on the Steam Workshop. For a base price of $20 and a sale price of $5 - $10 it’s hard to beat the value offered here.

Heroes & Generals is a F2P WW2 game with a vast variety of weapons, vehicles, camouflages, planes and tanks. This is most likely the best WW2 game you can get in its category. However I have a few things to address before you start getting into the game.
As a new player, you will find yourself thrown in a massive pit of doom as soon as you hit Gold MM (after 10-15h of playtime from my own experience) because everyone is rocking better weapons and better badges than you.
What can you expect, it's a free to play game. I've never really complained about this part of the game so I have little knowledge about what's going on. All I can tell is that prices for some items are really weird/ not logical. But I guess it's the way Reto wants to go in order to limit the appearance of such items in the game (ex: people running with MG42, M1/M2, AVS on Bronze MM). The only thing I could recommend is to increase salaries back to the previous build in order to be more new player friendly.
I don't want to lynch the devs for everything that is wrong with this game. It's a small company, they do what they can to provide us fun content. It can take them very long to push an update with little content and it saddens me to see people discrediting Reto for any little issue this game has.
But, sometimes I feel like Reto and the community aren't on the same page.
For example, the new plane update was nothing like I expected, what everyone expected. We were expecting, for example, p51 for the US, Bf110 for the Germans, Pe-3 for the SU. But instead we got recon planes which have no influence on a battle. They literally just shoot each others and that's it. Even if really fun to play, they can't bring anything else on a battle because of how weak (armor and firepower) they actually are.
Another example, they made it impossible to get on roofs now. I remember seeing myself on B2 on Forward Airfield trying to shoot down paratroopers camping on the roofs (because you can cap points on roofs which is stupid now that they removed the ability to counter it). And dont get me started about attic capping.
There are many other things like that and sometimes I wonder if Reto even fully test its game before pushing an update.
Moreover, Reto ninja nerfs features they don't mention in patch notes. Last time it was the credits earned per battle (which has now been explained unofficially), the window example explained above, etc.
On the bright side, Reto is making a lot of progress in order to address these issues (prototype server, gathering community feedback, etc.) and I can see them improve overtime.
As I said, this game wasn't made for casuals. Don't play this game in order to achieve or unlock things but play it for what it was meant to be, FOR FUN. And if you can overcome the first hours of grind, this is actually quite a decent WW2 game. Maybe even the best in its category. You can play with many different weapons, drive jeeps, halftracks and trucks, pilot tanks and planes, parachute behind enemy lines, etc. And the maps are huge. Sure it might be not so well optimized but I don't hear a lot of complains from people playing this game on a decent computer.
The least you can do is give Heroes & Generals a try, it's free and who knows, you might like it.

There are no other games like this.
It is futile to argue whether this game is good or bad. Lets say this game is bad. What alternaive do you plan to suggest? Witcher 3? Dark Souls? Baldur's Gate? Dragon Age 3? All of these alternatives are great, and you should definitely get them, but none of them can fill the niche that KoA:R belongs to.
KoA:R was the only action RPG with decent combat system before Witcher 3 came, and because Witcher 3 pretty much carves its own very specific niche, KoA:R holds its position still. KoA:R excels in one other area where almost all other games in its genre falls flat: it has a vibrant and varied art style. Unfortunately the same can't be said about its story and AI.
In retrospect, if you divide the soul of RPG into four determining factors, they will be:
1. Combat
2. AI
3. Art style
4. Story
There are few RPG games that are good at one or two of these, but none that is good at at least three of them. KoA:R is special becaue it is the only one that shines in the combo { Combat, Art style }. It also tops { Combat } alongside Witcher 3 and Shadow of Mordor. Incidentally, Witcher 3 tops { Combat, Story }.
KoA:R's art style might be great, but the Big Huge Engine does not live up to its name. Zones are segmented and the cities are pretty small. The battles are also not really that big. However, the world is vibrant and has a majestic feel to it. You can see when the developers ran out of budget to keep paying Todd McFarlane because Klurikorn and Alabastra are trash, and the DLCs switch to realistic art style.
There are also many minor factors like freedom of choice, crafting and potions, quality of open world, degree of role playing, etc.
If you can resist comparison with Witcher 3 and Dishonored, KoA:R has some degree of freedom of choice, but it is straightforward. Potions are boring, but crafting is awesome in this game. Every item can be dismantled into its core components, so you only grind for effect drop. Dashboarding is involved, but after finishing the Gravehal Keep, you don't even need to do that.
It is combat where this game excels. Magic, might, and stealth each is played in its own different way. Within each, every weapon type has its own set of awesome skills. You can also mix and match to your heart's content. My first playthrough had a magic build, with some rogue elements mixed into it. My second playthrough was with a pure rogue build, and it played like a totally different game. I am planning to have a third playthrough with a pure might build. Each of the three primary builds has its own faction, and for the sake of variety I suggest sticking to only your specific faction in each playthrough, (because the faction missions bring out the real fun of each playstyle).

I've gotten all the way to Tekken God Prime with one character in the "offline" portion of the game and that by itself was quite a lot of fun, and had me constantly forced to adapt and become better in order to beat the increasingly difficult CPU. Obviously the real worth of this game comes from the online portion, which has near limitness room for improvement and I'm looking forward to getting better with every fight, which is something I haven't experienced with a game before, but which is the driving force of a fighting game's replayability and I have to say Tekken nails that completely.

Lastly, if you were thinking of playing this on a keyboard, just know that while it is possible you will have to fight with the button mapping as it defaults to having two separate player controls on your keyboard and doesn't allow for mouse-buttons to be mapped. The game doesn't really mention this anywhere but I would highly recommend using a controller, since I tried out keyboard in the beginning and it's just incredibly awkward to use for any kind of reactionary gameplay as you can't use the mouse.
