Tekken 7 is a game I could talk about for a very long time, but I’ll try my best to keep this concise. I’ve spent the past half year playing this game nearly every day, meeting others who play the game, and listening to different types of people talk about it. There is a pretty diverse pool of opinions when it comes to the game, both negative and positive. I believe however, that these opinions can generally be divided into two categories. Opinions of the game, Tekken 7, that was developed as 3D fighting game for arcades, and opinions of the port to home console and PC, of that arcade game. As far as the Tekken 7 that was made for arcades goes, which is what that you experience when you play Tekken 7, the consensus of this game is incredibly positive. Personally, this is my favorite Tekken to date, and I’ve been playing them since the release of 3. Pretty much every gameplay addition put in this game was a positive change as far as I’m concerned, and many of those changes double in their positives as Tekken is now more fun to watch at a competitive level than it ever has been. The second category of opinions are about the home console/PC port of the game, which have been mixed. Honestly, if you are judging the game based off how good the home console/PC port is, I don’t think it’d be a stretch to say this is one of the most disappointing Tekken games yet. It runs fine, and the PC version tends to have good netcode, however, compared to previous entries the game is severely lacking in content, modes, and several other aspects. Fans who play this game casually are the most likely to disappointed with this game, especially coming off Tekken Tag 2 which had an enormous amount of content. I won’t list everything, but among the most glaring omissions, the game doesn’t have a team battle or survival mode, the customization is lacking more features and items than Tekken 6, and the endings for each character are of the lowest quality the series has ever seen. A lot of the content not in the game I would be willing to bet was cut because of the single player campaign this game boasts, which if you ask me was not worth losing anything over. The single player story mode in this game is incredibly lackluster, short, and often frustrating, as to make the game more challenging, the CPU will sort of break the rules of the game to get an advantage over you. There is much more I could go on about regarding both ways of looking at this game, but I feel I’ve covered the most important points.
In short, if you play fighting games to grow as a player, and know you’ll spend 99% of your time playing against other players or training, this is one of the best Tekken games yet and a prime example of the 3D fighting game genre. If you play fighting games for their content, story, or just to mess around, you may end up a bit disappointed, especially if you’ve played other Tekken games in the past, as this port doesn’t offer nearly as much content as other Tekken games. Personally, I love the game and will be playing it regularly for the foreseeable future, hopefully you can get similar enjoyment out of the game if you check it out.

Oceanhorn is unashamedly a Zelda Wind Waker clone.  Oceanhorn has the very similar music, artistic motifs, items, and enemies; some of these are even identical to those in the Zelda games.  The only noticable difference is Oceanhorn's unique, multi-tier terrain.  If you liked Wind Waker, or most any Zelda games, you'll probably like this one.
But Oceanhorn does have its flaws.  Movement is very sluggish, combat is incredibly easy, and the puzzles all almost exclusively just require you to push blocks to solve.  I think the biggest failure is that Oceanhorn really doesn't offer anything unique to make it stand out.  Oceanhorn is blatantly "okay" in every way.  Not bad, not great, just a game you'll play once and forget.

Decent game, it's more on the good than on the bad side; not worth it at full price but if it catches your eye it will entertain you during it's short-ish duration.
The ideas were good, and it's a fine exploring/collectathon, but every problem this game has is self-inflicted pain.
The game is very easy (which is not a bad thing in particular, just be warned if you want some challenge this ain't the one), both in terms of combat and puzzling, there are some nice ideas and setups for puzzles and I'd wish they'd done more with them, yet I'll give them a pass, they work perfectly fine.
When it comes to combat there is very little enemy variety. I don't think that's a huge issue considering the lenght of the game, but it becomes increasingly noticeable after some time.
The story and worldbuilding has some nice ground, and you can feel there's something beyond what you're seeing, it's just barely explored and feels like hollow or "you're just seeing this very narrow side of the story"; which makes sense in a journey's perspective, but feels like the world closes it's doors to you when it comes to an exploration game.
I was very into the game's premise. An ocean monster? ancient technology? Ruined cities? Totally my jam! But it doesn't provide anything that you've never seen before or with a decent amount of substance to make them stay in your head after quiting the game.
In roleplaying games, they say "the most interesting part about the story can't have already happened when you start", here you feel you're here for the scraps, and not in a "you reconstruct the story and make sense of it while defining the new direction the world will take" (which would be just one of many interesting ways to take a story like this), but in a "oh, let us tell you what happened and there's this one thing left to do, do it and everything will be fine".
Traveling from island to island, you just select your destination and wait. You can shoot at some ocasional enemies and crates that will appear but it's so little engaging you'll end up spamming the fire button in the general direction while doing something else. Most boring part of the game by far, I would've loved more items to use on board, things to do or freedom to move myself.
The boss battles were... the most disappointing part. You explore, fight, and make your way to the islands to find some unique enemies that poses a challenge and... every single encounter is summed up to "find out what's the gimmick, repeat over and over."
You're probably thinking "well, most games in the genre are similar", but Oceanhorn pushes the boundaries. Maybe one is remotely memorable, the ambientation (either hype before or thrill during) the battle is nonexistant, the arenas are generic terrain you're already tired of... and when I say they're gimmicky I mean they're more trick execution that battles. Every single one of them. The final battle was extremely short as well which left you with a feeling it ended before it even started.
Performance-wise it runs fine, could be better optimized but no mayor problems.
It doesn't support gamepads/controllers with direct input, you'll need to use a third-party to map the controls.
Fine game, would give it a recommend if it supported controllers and had a little more content for the price point, for what it is, worth it if interested and on sale.
PS. Forgot to mention there's voice acting in the game, which ranges from "good but needed a little more emotion and oomph" to "I honestly took my headphones off and felt more inmersed in the world reading the dialogues alone bad"

*Action based RPG (not a fan of turn based)
*Decent visuals, with consistent animation.
CONS
*Subpar controls
*Too many game mechanics are not explained. Travel mini game; how to switch spells; how to collect "bloodstones"; fishing mini game to name a few.
*The camera control for looking at the area at "different" angels allows you to turn the camera about 1 mm in either direction. In other words, anything you couldn't see before won't be revealed if you "move" the camera.
*During boss fights the camera rotates to keep the boss centered on the screen. This does not garent that you are facing the boss, nor are you able to see what is behind you (such as hostile enemies during the first boss battle).
*Boss battles are not "hard" per say, but expect to die often to BS you can't dodge/shield with no indication the attack is comming.
*The story is boring. The characters are forgetable. The finding new island is rediculous (Throughout the game you'll sail past the location of various islands that exists, but don't have the location for. Those locations appear as open water. This is a worthy buy if you ever see it on sale. Very rich lore, skill system gives you flexiblity in your playstyle, freaky challenging enemies (lots of variety in enemies, too) and a seemingly endless world to explore a loot. Sometimes it can get a bit tedious and not all of the side quests are interesting but overall you'll find something to sink your teeth into.

(most of my hours in this game are on Origin, not Steam)
A lot of users compare this game to Skyrim, when really it is more like a single-player mix of Torchlight II and Guild Wars 2. Tons of missions, deep crafting, combo-friendly combat, a huge game-world and genuinely interesting lore means a lot of time can be spent in Amalur.
Installed size on hard drive (with all DLC): 11.6 GB
Reckoning is rather like a single-player MMO, if that makes any sense. Looting, crafting and leveling are the primary attractions. There is a ton of loot; putting points into the “detect hidden” skill reveals secret rooms and passageways that have even more loot. You'll want to loot as much as you can, even armor sets that you won't use – put points into blacksmithing, disassemble the armor and weapons you don't want to get the parts, and craft something truly epic. Leveling up provides new abilities, new special moves for weapons. At the end of each leveling session, you get to choose a “Fate Card” with special bonuses. Fate Cards are not class-specific, meaning you can use them to create a warrior mage who equips heavy armor, or an archer can wield heavy weapons, or a thief / rogue who also has some magic. There are dozens of hybrid “Fate Cards.” And if you're not happy with how your build has turned out, visit a Fateweaver to “Remix your Fate” and reset your build so you can level up again with your existing points.
The world is huge. There are a lot of places to explore with side-missions hidden everywhere. The graphics are 2012 era DirectX 9: Colorful, bright, and occasionally low-res. The general comic-book style of the artwork hides some graphical shortcomings. And on the plus side, if you have a less-than-stellar gaming PC, the game will probably run just fine. (Back in the day, I ran it on a 1GB Radeon 6670 without issues). The soundtrack by Grant Kirkhope catches the ambiance nicely. The voice acting is generally good (though your hero is silent, a la Dragon Age Origins).
Not everything is excellent, unfortunately. Combat flows well, encouraging the use of different moves. Despite the many different skills and abilities at my disposal, once I found a way to dispose of mobs, I just stuck to that, and never really tried to change up my attacks. I won't say combat is easy – if you go into an area under-leveled, you'll die fast (even with potions). But once you're comfortable in the system, combat becomes just another chore. Fetch quests are repetitive. All exploration is done on foot – no horses. The dungeons are NOT copy / pasted; there's a lot of variety here. But the missions that use the dungeon and cave levels tend to follow similar patterns. If you try to do a completionist run of Reckoning, you'll need a titanic level of patience and dedication. Inventory management, frankly, s*cks. Oh, and jumping. You can't jump, except at prescribed places (“press F to jump”).
Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a great game if you love messing about in an open world while worrying about plot later. If you're looking for a go-anywhere, do-anything adventure (with the freedom to jump wherever you want), you'll probably be happier with Skyrim. Or online with friends in Guild Wars 2. Sometimes, though, a solitary, easy grind for loot is exactly what you want - and exactly what Reckoning provides.
On DLC:
The Weapons and Armor DLC provides three complete weapons sets that are accessible at the start of the game. While great to have, the things you craft will quickly surpass them in quality and effectiveness.
The Teeth of Naros and The Legend of Dead Kel are both large additions to an already massive game. Each provides a new campaign and entirely new areas to explore. Naros in particular is a great piece of DLC. Both have a lot of content in an industry where content-laden DLC are rare. Definitely worth it to get both.
Notes:
An EA account is NOT required. Though the game asks for an EA login on startup, you can simply click the X in the corner to skip the login. The game will play and save normally.
The company that developed Reckoning, 38 Studios, went bankrupt in 2013. The only support for the game is what you will find when trawling the forums.

And beautiful not only by the Art Direction. The soundtrack, with that imaginary language made so comprehensible through the staging and the scenes direction. The plot, that how so strong bound between the characters, the magic of this universe lulled with Nordic references, that constant cinematographic feeling that makes the transitions between game phases and cutscenes very smooth, without any clashes. That inventive gameplay, that kindly forces you to use both of your brain hemispheres as if you were playing an instrument.
I can't find the words to describe such a masterpiece... This game is simply formidable and extremely touching, in a similar way to the excellent Papo & Yo, but with... something better. If a notation was possible, I'd give it without any doubt a 20 outta 20. Yes. It's that good.
------------------------------------------------------------
En temps normal, si un jeu me remue de l'intérieur et me fais pleurer... C'est souvent bon signe.. Je pense pouvoir m'avancer et dire que Brothers est sans aucun doute l'un des plus beaux jeu auquel j'ai eu l'occasion de jouer ces dernières années, sinon le plus beau et le plus touchant.
Et beau non pas seulement en termes de DA. La bande son, avec cette langue imaginaire mais pourtant si compréhensible grace à la mise en scène et à la direction des scènes, le récit, le lien si fort qui uni les personnages, la magie de cet univers bercé de références Nordiques, le côté cinématographique constant faisant que les transitions entre les phases de jeu et les cinématiques se font tout en douceur, sans heurts. Les mots me manquent pour décrire un tel chef d'oeuvre... For a game as old and as indie as it is, this game is extremely good.
Basically a role playing game but with large scale combat and allies.
You have skills and levels and you can level up, but you're never a one man army. No quest markers at all, turning in a quest is not only timed usually but you have to track people down based on hearsay. Troops have morale and will lose morale if you keep losing.
You can train soldiers from dirt to gods if they live long enough through many battles, but you can still lose them.
Playing as a woman makes the game much harder, because everyone says you're ugly and doesn't want to give you anything.
Towns have unique supply and demands including exchange rates, so something worth a mediocre price at one city might have double the value in another.
Overall, I came in expecting nothing but I got so much more than I expected out of this game. Only downside to it is that it's kind of dated. Can't wait for Bannerlord.

Game with both very strong single player and multiplayer scenes.
Singleplayer
Long, fun and rewarding sandbox campaign where you can do or become whatever you want. Be a man of the people, help the little guys and purge brigands from their lands. Maybe sell your sword and sign your warband as mercenaries in service of one of the major kingdoms. Build up your renown and become a loyal vassal, and be awarded land. Build an anarcho-capitalist empire owning dyeworks, ironworks, and weaveries all over the land while enforcing the NAP on those pesky viking raiders with your Recreational Swadian Knights™
Multiplayer
Skill based matches in a variety of gamemodes including TDM, DM, seige and duel. Very large servers, sometimes upto 200 players. Napoleonic Wars DLC is where it shines, though, as there is a large and active community, aswell as community made regiments that participate in huge organized battles. Some are serious, others are more laid back and play for fun.
To conclude, Mount and Blade: Warband has a great amount of content and replayability for it's price. I'd recomend picking it up, even before Bannerlord (Warband 2) is announced to get a taste of what it will be like.

A lot of people are writing reviews for this complaining about how buggy it is. To those people, please go and look up the word 'TEST'. This is a beta test, of course it's buggy! Anyway, about the actual game. The out-of-game browser is a nice touch. I like being able to look at what I want to do and customize things before going into the game. The character design is top notch. Come on, a ninja with a scarf? It's like Raiden if you took away all that corny over-the-top cybernetic gear. The controls are easy to get into. Barely had to even read the tutorial to know what to do, especially with walljumping. That part is usually tricky in games but here, it's super easy. Fighting is also a blast. I use the first character with the sword and the rifle. Pulling off head shots is a blast and slashing people to fill up the Z meter and unleashing a devastating anime style death blow is fantastic.
However, the community is terrible. It's as bad as LoL. The very first five minutes I was in the public lobby, two different people launched bigoted comments. One person used the N word to describe people who use DSL, the other was an asian complaining about jews. Not a good sign. Playerbase can make or break the experience. I also hope (don't have high hopes) that this sequel will deal with hackers better than the original, which had a hacker in every single game. There was no such thing as a legitimate match in the original GunZ. Please, devs, for the love of god, deal with your hackers this time!
Some additional notes... The sound clips like when you get hit are extremely repetitive. It becomes grating to listen to after a while. Older video cards also seem to have an issue with rendering the game and randomly spazz out, showing the game world in a glitched state. The maps seem very poorly designed considering there are usually 4-8 people and they end up crammed into small warehouse looking zones. The original game had much better areas like the beach/cave level. I'm sure these things will be ironed out later.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a 2012 single-player action role-playing video game developed by Big Huge Games and 38 Studios, and published by Electronic Arts.
Before this game was released, it was touted to be designed by a former Bethesda Game Studios veteran Ken Rolston who had worked on the award winning Elder Scrolls Oblivion. Famed fantasy author R.A Salvatore created the lore and backstory for the game's universe and the artwork was done by Todd McFarlane who is famous for his work on the Spawn comic series. 38 studios itself was owned by former baseball pitcher Curt Schilling, who was known to be a very avid video gamer himself.
With such big names behind this title, how is the actual game itself?
Sadly, it can all be summed up in one word: Average.
Graphically, while the game was done by Todd McFarlane, it looked nothing like McFarlane's signature style of bold colours and harsh artistic lines. In fact, the whole game looks like a Fable clone artistically. While the locations can look quite nice at times, it gives an overall "Been There, Done That" feel. Especially for players who have played Fable.
Gameplay is also extremely linear. Every location in the game, every dungeon feels like a corridor. While the game gives you an illusion of an open-world, it never really is. You will be stopped by invisible walls, can only travel on certain allowed paths. Its so restrictive, that your character cannot even jump, and can only leap off ledges at certain designated points.
In every RPG, story is quite possibly the most important aspect, and surely a story by famed fantasy writer R.A Salvatore would be something special? Well...not really.
While R.A Salvatore tries to craft a very intricate universe with lots of backstory, most of it can only be found in lorestones, books and you actually need to go out of the way to read them to understand the lore behind it. I don't know about you guys, but video games aren't novels. I'd rather EXPERIENCE a story thru gameplay myself rather then read one when i'm playing a video game. The over-arching main story quest is also quite generic, and is actually rather short with only 13 quests in total. None of the characters are particularly memorable and there aren't any plot twists.
Now I wouldn't have minded if the main quests were full of depth but they simply are not. Most of them just directs you to go to a specific location, kill someone and rinse and repeat. If it isn't a search and destroy mission, NPCs will actually ask you to go to 3 completely different areas on the map to do basically the same thing before you trudge back to the NPC to continue with the story.
Considering there are no mounts in the game, you can understand how tedious it was to travel on foot to repeat the same thing 3 times. This is obviously used as a cheap way to artificially lengthen the gameplay time. Luckily there is a fast-travel option available, but you can only use it if you have been to the location before. I never once used fast-travel in an Elder Scrolls game, because each location in that title is unique with lots of explorable locations with interesting quests. With this game however, I was so bored of the generic story of the main quest and boring fetch quests type sub-quests that I fast travelled whenever I could.
With that said, the only saving grace of this title is the combat which is absolutely brilliant.
Combat movement is extremely fluid combined with beautiful animations makes combat a joy to play. It doesn't matter if you choose to swing a sword, use a dagger or cast a spell. All of them have unique and cool animations and are a joy to play with. It almost felt as if they spent all their budget on perfecting the combat but neglecting everything else that makes a RPG special.
This game adds a unique "Reckoning" mode for combat which is a mode you can activate to go slow motion ala Matrix style after accumulating enough to fill a meter to dispatch multiple enemies with flourish that will net you extra experience points. The game will go into a QTE mode where mashing certain buttons can net you even more experience points. While its cool to go all Matrix style on enemies for the first few times, the novelty does wear out after your 50th "Reckoning" mode and it quickly becomes just another way to farm Experience Points.
As I come to the end of this review, I feel that you should know that this was the only game developed by 38 Studios before they filed for bankruptcy. 38 Studios is no more. This also means that the future of this IP is in doubt. The last I read back in 2013, there were no buyers interested in this IP Franchise when they were doing an auction to sell off their properties. Do not expect to see a sequel or anything Amalur related anytime soon. (If ever.)
Overall Rating: 6.5 / 10

I'm not much of one for writing reviews; I don't do it often, and have no practice at it. But, what I can say here, is that for years I've been looking for a game that's centered primarily, if not wholly, around Celtic mythology, rather than generic European medieval fantasy or feudal Asian mythology. This game delivered, moreso than I could have ever thought a game could. Why there haven't been more games featuring such strong Celtic themes is beyond me, but Kingdoms of Amalur: Recokoning showed that it can be done, and done very well. I was definitely impressed with the story of the game.
As far as gameplay, things were pretty good. Combat and controls felt better with a gamepad than mouse and keyboard, but that's never been a dealbreaker for me. I feel there could have been more done with combos and chaining attacks, because combat felt a little static after awhile, but it wasn't awful. Most quests(but not all; here's looking at you, Til's Collection) were interesting and often felt like an interesting task, rather than a chore to do for XP. The main quest line especially was fun, interesting, and kept me pulled in to the game. Factions you could join in the game I felt were pretty mediocre, and are your generic warriors, mages, and rogues factions. Their quests were fun, but I never really felt like my character truely belonged to the faction upon joining. The one major downside I felt in the game was gear drops. Almost always, what you can craft at each level was better than anything you could find, even rare named pieces or sets. As for the DLC, Teeth of Narros had a fun main story line, but for the most part it felt drawn out and monotonous. The side quests were pretty boring, and involved a lot of backtracking. Legend of Dead Kell was much better, and felt more involved.
One more note: This game is LONG. And I really mean long, especially if you are a completionist and want to do all of the side quests.

I got this game as part of a Humble Bundle. This game was not the reason I got the bundle, thankfully.
Anyone who's familiar with
will see that Oceanhorn takes almost all of its ideas from it, down to the blue starting outfit, island travel, cannons, and more. I'd be able to look past this if the game offered much of anything inventive, funny, or novel. It disappoints me in every category, from gameplay to level design to story.
At first glance, this game has the makings of something good. Puzzle-oriented dungeons and so-so combat make the game seem inviting. As I played more of this game, I found so many shortcomings compared to other games in its genre. I'll cover these in order of importance.
Oceanhorn offers both keyboard+mouse controls and Xbox controller controls. I played the game using a DualShock3 and BetterDS3 to emulate an Xbox360 controller. Sometimes, the game glitches out and reverts to KB+M controls and won't re-detect the controller until you relaunch it. When the controls work, they're okay. No other game does this to me, so I'm sure it's Oceanhorn.
Movement is very clunky. The main character can jog at a very slow pace, and dashing is limited to a single direction at a time. Stamina is depleted upon dashing, and you'll be lucky to cross a screen worth's of distance before running out. It takes roughly 10 seconds from depletion to fully charged stamina. There may be stamina upgrades later in the game, but I couldn't take it by the time I beat the Elder Gillman boss. More on that later.
Despite being in 3-D, Oceanhorn is clearly built using self-contained 3D boxes, which is closer to 2-D design philosophy. They're not voxels (it's traditional polys), but the reuse of assets is apparent. That wouldn't be a problem to me if it felt good to move around in the levels. The standard running speed is too slow to dodge anything reliably, walking up and down stairs is like watching a snail travel, and a later item that allows for rolling expends your stamina too quickly to be of any use. Couple this with a clearly box-oriented world, and you have a game that looks 3-D, but would be better off in 2-D.
When you hold your shield up using the right trigger, your character faces the nearest enemy and can strafe... except it's the same speed as swimming (which also eats stamina like crazy). Also of note is your shield can barely defend against anything. Rocks, maybe arrows. That's about it. Aerial enemies can hit you from above, past your shield, too.
Next is interaction. Oceanhorn mimics Zelda once again by using a context-sensitive action button. When you pick something up, hold a direction and hit the action button again to throw it. Aiming in this game is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ due to being stuck in an isometric camera angle. Thankfully, the game will correct for you if you're aiming near anything important.
Spells are something that sets Oceanhorn apart from the games it copies. It adds a second layer of interaction to the game world, which is very welcome. Unfortunately, you must stand in place and aim a cartoon hand at what you want to cast the spell on. Most of the time, this works fine, but if you're aiming at anything from a distance, there's a good chance that you'll cast on the wrong item, wasting your mana. Spells are also expensive, so you'll need to avoid busting things until puzzles are solved if you want to conserve mana.
Frankly, it's apparent that Oceanhorn underwent zero competent play-testing. There are so many minor issues with this game that it becomes a big problem just to play it. There are numerous places where I shouldn't have been able to go, but the weird edge detection would send me into walls. Sometimes, I'd have to hit a button twice to register an action. This game should've been in testing for at least 3-6 months to iron out these issues. One time, I fell through a floor and into the Elder Gillman boss fight, but was unable to correct the camera or escape, forcing me to exit the game.
The same item that allows you to roll is also used to jump across gaps. That's a great idea, but actually *using* that ability, especially during its boss, is a crapshoot. You'll most likely end up rolling off the edge of things instead of jumping, even if you're stationary when using it.
Oceanhorn is not what I'd call a difficult game; nothing wrong with that, because it's fairly lighthearted and started out pretty solid. However, the difficulty in this game comes from knowing where to bomb things, or "dodging" boss attacks that have nigh-perfect accuracy. That is not a substitute for real difficulty! In fact, the Elder Gillman boss in general is a disaster. He hovers near you constantly, and rains boulder shards on you from a distance; one of which is guaranteed to hit unless you dash or roll in time. His freeze laser traps you for 5-10 seconds, and the mechanisms you activate are dependent on switches or using the dungeon item perfectly. On its own, this wouldn't be so bad; cheese bosses can often be cheesed back in return. Sadly, this boss is very efficient at staying in your face, and is difficult to hit with the statues that breath fire. The camera is focused on him the entire time, which makes it difficult to see where you're going. Pots and purple coral will obstruct your way, making this fight even worse.
Honestly, the story isn't that bad. It's your standard adventure game fare. Instead of a princess, you're looking for your dad, who went to face Oceanhorn. Or something like that. The writing is a little cheesy in places, but overall there's not much to complain about. I couldn't get attached to any characters in the 12 or so hours I played.
Graphics are easily the best part of this game, but even then they feel... odd. It has a sort of Unity/Unreal feel to it, with over-rendered textures on environments, but cartoony enemies and characters. Kind of an odd mix. My biggest pet peeve is the lack of meaningful camera control. You can "lean" the camera using the right stick, but it's never enough to see anything important, and you can't rotate the camera or switch to a top-down view.
While we're talking about graphics, let's discuss objects you can destroy. It's not apparent which piles of dirt or rocks you can bomb and which you can't. This is a problem that game developers fixed
. There's no excuse to not have some sort of visual cue -- even if it's minute -- to prevent the player from wasting bombs or other resources like mana. In fact, Zelda: The Wind Waker *has* clues that suggest hidden items, while Oceanhorn does not. The game does a shoddy job of conveying what it intends you to do, and which areas are accessible. There are tons of places that
like you can reach them, but are blocked.
Ultimately, Oceanhorn has the potential to be an enjoyable, light-hearted adventure game. Its light, unengaged story, frustrating controls and mechanics, and ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t-grade bosses prevent me from enjoying anything great that this game might have to offer later on. I suggest skipping this game entirely. Word is the developers are working on a sequel; I would wait and see on that before bothering to spend money on an experience that will leave you wanting to play Zelda instead. Other games in the genre just plain do it better. I'm normally a big supporter of indies, but this game was clearly rushed and lacks the polish needed for the game to shine.

TLDR: banning singleplayer mods is stupid, shark cards are the root of all evil (in GTA Online).
It all started great. I bought the game mostly for online, but people say the singleplayer is decent. Back in the beginning, online was pretty great too. More or less balanced weapons, somewhat reasonable prices on cars and weapons. Heists were a lot of fun while they lasted.
But as the time went on, it became more and more apparent that TakeTwo, or Rockstar, cares only about their own profit. As more and more Online updates came out, all hope was lost for any quality content™. Don't get me wrong, the content of updates looks great, and some of the updates are even fun to play. But, as it would happen, there is one big 'but'. Most of the content in these "free" updates is gated behind stupidly expensive entry purchases, paid with in-game money. And the only thing you can do is to grind for a few weeks or months for money, or cheat (and get caught and banned, most likely), or... Buy Shark Cards for real cash.
Now, I didn't mind the shark cards when the game came out. They seemed to be a fine way to let playes with little free time to quickly get enough in-game cash to get to all the content, like high-end cars and heists. Unfortunately, the developer or publisher succumbed to greed. The ability to sell shark cards led to the natural result - making updates that require players to buy shark cards to properly enjoy.
And this is not all. Modding has always been an important part of gaming scene. I've had lots of fun modding Skyrim, Fallout, and a bunch of other games. Modding support greatly increases longevity of a game, and GTA V would have been no exception. Until TakeTwo decided that singleplayer mods are illegal. They have been agains Online mods since the very  release of the game, and while I disagree with that stance, I could see where they are coming from (as usually, greed, shark cards aren't gonna sell themselves). It baffles my mind as to why anyone would be against singleplayer mods in a game that has no singleplayer DLC to speak of.
To sum up, TakeTwo has been (and still is) too greedy about their own game. Questionable sale practices, "free" multiplayer content essentially gated behind shark cards, stupidest stance on modding, all for very questionable benefit.
Do not buy this game. Do not support TakeTwo. They do not deserve it. And if you do, don't expect any truly free updates, and don't expect being able to mod it.

I enjoyed this game, but definitely went in knowing what to expect: short, easy, visual story telling and story driven.
My suggestions on who would like this game: anyone who considers video games a legitimate story telling medium and not just a distraction from the day-to-day grind. If you have ever argued with a friend, family member or colleague about how video games should be afforded the same respect as other media, such as film, TV, books or comics for their ability to tell stories, then you NEED TO play this game. My one other recommendation is to play it through in 1-shot if you can (2.5-3 hours), because it has a flow that is best maintained.
Brothers evokes a strong emotional response without high profile voice actors, famous IP tie-ins or 8 figure development budgets, just a simple quest of 2 boys (with a penchant for rock climbing and spelunking) to save their dad. The game doesn't explain to you what matters, it shows it to you, it doesn't tell you when to feel sad, it makes you feel it and acknowledge it. I would say it is the best use of the medium to date insofar as evoking a meaningful emotional reaction in the player.
The gameplay is simple to learn yet can be tricky to master, the puzzles are pretty easy to anyone who's played a handful of games, but cleverly executed and come with some nice visuals. Also worth noting is that it is possible to beat the game without getting a single achievement; they are all unlocked by doing little aside actions along the way that are not required to advance the game.
Overall an amazing value when on sale and worth picking up for anyone who takes their games seriously.

As a fan of horror both old and new, I am quite picky on what's truly horror and what's cheap jumpscares or an over abundance of gore. Out of these three things, this game is none of them.
There's absolutely zero build up into the creepy atmosphere. It literally just... happens. Except it's not so much creepy as it is bland. The map sets you on a fairly linear path at first, soon tossing you hallways and areas that all look the same until you're left wandering aimlessly in pursuit for... something to keep you from falling asleep.
The "monster" makes its appearance so quickly and so suddenly that it's neither horrifying nor slightly startling. I just kind of stared at it... dumbfounded. And I jump quite easily. I'm a big sissy.
Atmosphere - 2/10 "It could be worse... but just barely."
Voice Acting - 2/10 "Ditto."
Graphics - 4/10 "Gives you a sense of late 90's PC gaming horror, but causes a reflexive cringe upon looking out a window at a still life photo likely snagged off of Google."
Story - 0/10 "Cliché. Overdone. Nothing even remotely interesting."
Gameplay - 1/10 "Basic. Boring. Minimal interaction, too much aimless meandering."
Sound - 1/10 "Too much random hissing noises and weirdness that grates the nerves in your ears as opposed to filling you with any sense of terror or dread. Voices sound as if they were recorded via somebody's webcam mic. Sound quality in general is massively lacking."
All in all, I can't really complain for a sale price of 49 cents. Probably fun to goof around with for a YouTube vid or with friends. Otherwise, this game put me to sleep within the first 5 minutes of playing. However I ventured on, regardless, only to walk into a pit of spikes, suffer an agonizingly god awful screaming sequence and get told that I had to restart from the very beginning because I didn't save. Exited out. Uninstalled. Ain't nobody got time for that.

I was an advid player of the original GunZ for a good while. The game & its concept was new & refreshing for its time. A good balance of gun & swordplay. The anime style of design added to the flare & presentation. Combined with excellent map layout & exciting matches, GunZ was hard to put down once you got started.
Sadly, GunZ 2 goes in the complete opposite direction in terms of game mechanices. Yes, the concept & art style remains the same but the combat system has been slowed down considerably. I am almost certain that this was done to cater to more players that could not adjust to the fast paced slash & shoot combat style that the original offered. Movement speed has been dumbed down as well. Where you once could chain jumps, wall runs & dashes all in a single pass, this game has a delay between each action. So it doesn't feel nearly as fluint. To put blunty, the've gutted the advantage of being a skilled player to bring a more equal playing field.
It's a great game to try but I recommend my fellow steam gamers to go play the original. Even with all of the changes that have been made sinces its original release, it is a vastly superior product compared to this. The only players that will enjoy this game is new players to the franchise or players that excel with the dumbed down combat system.

A game with several good ideas but spoiled by a flawed execution. Reminded me of Tempest, but "unwrapped" to 2D. The risk/reward mechanic of allowing the "horizon" to be landed on and/or selectively destroyed to boost the combo multiplier is a nice addition to a shooter-type game. Even given the wide variety of enemy types I saw, the colour-coding scheme made it easy to determine at a glance what the basic tactics of each new enemy would be (i.e. shoot/land/destroy horizon).
The control scheme is where it kind of fell apart. Using an analog stick, moving at full speed frequently felt too slow to cross the wide play area fast enough. Conversely, there's a miniscule sliver of a "half-dead" zone where gently nudging the stick moves the ship - but it's much too easy to nudge the stick a micron too far and jump back to "full" speed. As a result, the bullet-hell precision-dodging sections of the game (e.g. 2nd boss) were nearly luck-based, as trying to gently adjust position to slip between two bullets would usually (but not always) send the ship flying at full speed sideways into another bullet. Danmaku + sloppy control + big hitbox =
The "breakout" bonus games were a fun change of pace, especially when combined with the horizon-flipping mechanic, but again, they felt clumsy and crude due to the lack of precise speed/position control. Plus, a between-stage minigame played purely for points seemed to not be too relevant in a game where just
from level to level was hard enough. Looking back, I don't think I was ever once consciously aware of how many "points" I had, or how fast I was earning them - my focus was purely on not abruptly losing both(!) lives to undodgeable swarms of bullets and having to restart the current stage
This game feels like it was designed for (speed-limited) mouse control, but was poorly retrofitted for a controller. This game might be improvable, but as it stands, it's just not that fun.

It has the skeleton of what made the single-player story fun, with none of the progression, compelling  story, or INTERESTING minigames. What the multiplayer does give is a sandbox. Also, there seems to be a lack of added content for the single-player experience despite Rockstar's promises of making some.
Do I recommend this game overall? It's hard to say. I'm switching my review to positive because of the potential recovery of mods for the game, but I'd say it's not worth more than the story, and for the money, witcher 3 is probably a better buy. But it is a GTA game, so it's got that going for it. If you haven't bought it yet, try looking at some single-player and multi-player gameplay. if you like it, pick it up ON SALE ONLY.

Say, are you a fan of SNES-era action adventures?
You are? And you like A Link to the Past specifically?
Well, you're probably gonna like this then!
Alright, let's get down to business. This game draws heavily from 3 Zelda titles.
Its core gameplay is very much like A Link to the Past.
Its world and transportation is more like Wind Waker.
It has an aquatic race that is *very* similar to the zoras from Ocarina of Time.
All of these are good things. However, Oceanhorn understandably does not reach the same level of quality.
It would be unreasonable to expect such, considering the aforementioned series is a first-party Nintendo franchise.
Still, Oceanhorn makes an admirable attempt. It may not be as expansive or as polished, and I personally do not care for the voice acting, but it is an overall decent game and I certainly do not feel sorry for buying it.

It's derivative, clunky to control, generic looking, and boring. I wanted to like it because it looks like a nice modern take on classic Legend of Zelda style games. And it does ape the style and item selection and most of the conventions of a Legend of Zelda game. But it just doesn't feel good to play. It's slow and clumsy, the area layouts have no flow to them and are not fun to explore, and the story and characters lack the charm of better games in this genre.
Playing this, i kept expecting that eventually the game would turn a corner and I'd get past the slow introductory phases of the game, at which point things would pick up. I don't know if that ever happens because I eventually ran out of patience.
One of the risks inherent in making a game which is so blatantly derivative of beloved classics, is that you may end up reminding the player of better games. Much of the time spent playing this, I kept thinking to myself that I'd be better off re-playing Link to The Past, or finding one of the other Zelda games that I'd never finished. Well my SNES classic arrived in the mail today so I'm probably going to do just that.
If you're looking for a decent Zelda-like with a good balance of new ideas and homages to the classics, I *do* recommend Anodyne.

The game is a little on the short side, the controls are glitchy/unresponsive at times (especially the KB/M controls), and the world design/game flow is a little rough (too much backtracking, not enough shortcuts to previously visited areas) compared to a real LoZ game. There's also one item you get literally right before the final boss fight that is used only once in that fight and nowhere else in the game. Feels like a major missed opportunity.
Overall though, I definitely enjoyed playing this game and can recommend it if you enjoy LoZ.

An enjoyable old-school spirited Zelda clone, with charming art direction and fun (yet familiar) gameplay. You play as a boy on a quest to find his father and destroy the sea monster, Oceanhorn.
The narrative progression is in the form of island hopping, with challenges and quests on each of the land masses that pop up on the world map. This is a good looking game when in play mode but the cut scenes suffer from some terrible animation and the story isn’t very engaging. The voice acting is mediocre but the music is wonderfully nostalgic and reminiscent of old-school JRPGs. Another problematic area is in the level design. Since the game refuses to hold your hand or even provide a quest log or journal, this makes for some frustrating amounts of back tracking or redundant island hopping. Even with these delays, ‘Oceanhorn’  is a fairly short adventure, taking an average of about 10 hours to complete. There’s a fair bit of replayability for completionists in the form of each of the islands’ three challenges or expanding the game world further with DLC islands.
On mobile devices, this is a highly recommended little adventure.  For other platforms? Worth a playthrough, especially in preparation for that solid looking sequel on the horizon.

Let me give you my review for casual players.
New Mechanics: Rage Art + Rage Drive, Power Crush
Rage Art is a new "Super" attack for all characters. It is armored, which means it will absorb any attack chucked at you until the startup animation is complete, and the actual super animation begins. You're only able to use this, once you're reached Rage mode. Rage mode is activated automatically once your health reaches a certain level.
Rage Drive is sort of like an "EX" attack from 2D fighters. It enhances a normal attack your character has, and gives it properties it other wise wouldnt. For example, maybe instead of stunning your opponent, you're granted a launcher for a combo instead. This can also only be activated, once in Rage mode.
Power Crush is a normal attack that has armor properties. Again, this means you are able to absorb a small amount of attacks. Every character has this, but some benefit more from others. As with anything in fighting games.
Now that we've gotten the new mechanics out of the way!
Stages:
Okay! If you're looking for some memorable stages, meh. Pretty much all of the stages are box shaped. There's nothing that really pops out at you. You have a volcano pit, a child's gym, an endless ocean you seem to glide over, and a stage similar to Street Fighter's Training Stage, if a tank shot a missle at the building it sat and, that missle blew the ceiling off.
Nothing extremely creative, or exciting. But there's enough variety here that you probably won't mind. Plus there's a good amount. So you'll enjoy what's here for what it is.
Characters:
So we have 5 or 6 new characters. They're all extremely newcomer friendly. So if you wanted an easy character to play with if you're new the the series, or fighting games in general. You no longer have just Asuka or Eddy Kappa. No but seriously, these characters are simple, and they're great editions to the roster for the reason they're implemented. Shaheen is my personal favorite of them all. But you also have Josie, Claudio, Shaheen, Gigas, Lucky Chloe, and one other I think I'm forgetting. Any whos, none of the new characters have interested character designs in my opinion. They look like Tekken Movie extras they just decided to throw in the game. Shaheen looks the most interesting out of all of them. But in all honesty he's just a stereotypical middle eastern guy. Chloe is a weeb. Claudio was in Bleach. Gigas is..... And Josie is a Philipino Art Major. I may have exaggerated.
Edit: Oh yeah, and Akuma. He does a lot of damage. If you've ever seen Street Fighter 4, they've copied and pasted that exact character, into the game. And I mean exactly, playstyle, animations, all of that. It's him and all of his glory, except he's playing by Tekken's rules. Nice job with him as a guest.
Soundtrack:
Tekken has been really big into the hippest electronic music since like, 2 or 3 I forget. They just know whats in, and what will fit their stages. If you enjoyed TTT2, OR T6... it's not as good as those. Honestly, I'm trying to sit here and think of a stage where I heard the music and it stuck with me.. but I'm honestly drawing blank. The soundtrack is just pretty average. If you don't enjoy any form of electronic music, you won't like it. It's all some form of electronic music. EDM, Techno, I believe there's some Trance or House in there. I love electronic music, so I definitely don't mind. But I've always heard much better from the Tekken Devs. It does it's job. The music ramps up during the third round, makes the matches more intense. The menu music is cathcy, but nothing will ever beat the customization theme from Tekken Tag 2.
Gameplay:
It's limb based. It's Tekken. 1 is your right hand, 2 is your left, 3 is your right leg, 4 is your left leg. You'll punch, and kick, and various other means of physical violence- your opponent. Until one of you has no health left, or the 60 second timer runs out. Do this until one of you wins a round 3 times, and there's your winner. You can also alter the setting, make it 1 round, 30 seconds, or 4 rounds 99 seconds. Whatever you'd like.
There's TREASURE BATTLE mode. It's survival, except instead of just playing beating your highest score. Your're playing, beating your  highest score, AND unlocking new items for your chartacters that you can cusotmize them with. You'll unlock clothing options, hit effects, hair, and michellaneous (probably spelled that wrong) tems. Button ups, Sun glasses, Toy Guns, Real Guns. Sun flowers, staffs, a cute little floaty fish that hovers around your characters head. Occasionally, you'll encounter a special CPU with a rare item. Beat them, and you get what they're offering. There's a lot here. So treasure battle is definitely a way to deck your character out, and simultaneously improve on your game.
Outside of that, there's TOURNAMENT MODE. It's exactly what it sounds like. Up to 8 players. One lobby. You can do best out of 3, best out of 2, or just one match. You all progress through the brackets based on these settings. Two matches go on at once, so once you've one, its on to the next. The loser's will spectate until the winner is declared, and the prize pot is won. The prize is gold, which you can use to buy unlockables, or assets for you characters you can customize them with. You also receive two lucky box, which are loot boxes you win at the end of games. They'll contain either assets, or more gold. You can't buy lucky boxes, they are not microtransactions, they are rewards for completing matches on, and offline.
RANKED MATCH. If you've ever played anything competitive, you know what a ranked match is. With the new patch, they've made it so ranked is now a deathmatch. This is what I've wanted in a fighting game for awhile, so I'm glad they added it. It's been in Korea at their arcades for ages! What I mean by "deathmatch" is you continue to play, until one of you decides that you've won enough, or lost enough. I believe at some point, however; once you've beaten someone's♥♥♥♥♥enough, you no longer affect their rank. Don't quote me on that though. It's great for players who like to learn matchup in a more demanding environment.
PLAYER MATCH. It's ranked match. Your rank is displayed, but isn't affected by wins or loses. You can matchmake all day, or join a lobby of six people. You all can text chat and play, Set settings to how you like. Preferences on connections, regions, private slots. Blah blah blah.
COLLECTIBLES. So you have collectibles, uhm. Concept art, Movies, Wallpapers. You collect these using the gold you earn in the matches you've played. They have unlockables from every Tekken game, so if you're an enthusiast- check it out! Lots of cool wallpaper worthy stuff. But I have seen a better collection in all honestly. It's just good they decided to include something like this in the first place.
Finally, STORY MODE. At this point, if you've read this far. You're definitely a casual lol. I can't explain the story to you very well. Because honestly, it wouldn't make sense to you. But Tekken is rich in lore. Just do some research on your on time. HOWEVER. This story mode, is pretty short. You follow the Mishima Saga, followng the events of the scenario campaign in Tekken 6. I don't play story modes in fighters. Only games I have, have been all NRS games. (Mortal Kombat/Injustice).
This one, has little surprises that were nice to see. Like a point near the beginning, where you're shooting an assault rifle at a wave of soldiers. You can also decide to fight them straight up instead. I have not completed, and I probably won't anytime soon. But they've made it accessible to newcomers with attack mapping. I've heard it's only two hours long. So meh. There are also character episodes for each character that work like a traditional arcade mode. With a non canon cutscene at the end of each. Which is about another two hours for everyone.
FINAL THOUGHTS. This is a great game. Out of space to ty lol

TLDR, it feels like Warframe, but worse in every way. My reasoning is the fast/parkourish movement systems, and the fact you have a melee weapon and two guns, both games have this.
Anyways, I'm going to talk about coop here, I don't like playing pvp when coop is available in a game. I tried it on here and it was bs to me.

1. Swords
Swords are ok until the enemy is on the ground, then you can't hit them on the ground with your sword, you have to pull out a gun to finish them, or wait for them to get up. In Warframe you can do much more with the swords right from the start, so there's that, and when enemies are on the ground you can HIT THEM WITH YOUR SWORD. +1 Warframe
2. Guns (at least for the Ivan? character at the start), have absolutely no feeling to them at all. They feel completely weightless and seem like they do no damage, all because there's a lack of it feeling like a... gun. You'd think a game called GUNZ would get that right. Real great because Warframes guns have some pretty good feels to them. +1 Warframe
3. Movement
The movement ingame is ok, wallrunning and jumping is fun, movement speed is ok, dashing works, though having a keybind+direction for dash would be nice instead of double tapping a direction key, at least an option for it. +1GunZ
BUT. Warframe does so much more. Wallrun, walljump, climbing, sliding, sprinting, rolling. And most of these you can do while shooting or using your sword. +1 Warframe

Yeah, the spawns on here are crap, the enemies blatantly spawn in right in front of you or on you, even though they have their own designated "spawn rooms", only a few spawn in there and run out at first, the rest spawn in front of you when going past. Warframe? Enemies spawn ahead of where you are. Never once have I felt bs'd because they come out of nowhere.
The enemies on Warframe all have their own unique abilities and strategies, they use cover actually and don't JUST rush you, though there are units that do that, for good reasons. +1 Warframe
5. Download size

I picked this game up on a whim, largely because a lot of my friends like the series.  Though this game is in early access, RTG  has done a fantastic job of making the game run smoothly on systems old and new.  Samapuma and I both played through all three parts of the first chapter on one of my old and one of my lower spec'ed laptops without the game overheating or lagging significantly and we had a blast playing it.  So, now to the meat of the review.
This game is very much a toast to fans.  Those who are familiar with the series will appreciate that most of the original voice cast were used and the character models are really well done across all resolutions.  Considering the series was made entirely in CG, it would be disappointing if that wasn't the case.  The character animations are smooth, and ultra settings look great, even on my old laptop, which is only sporting an HD3650 video card and a gb of video ram.
The music is subtle and has enough length and variation that you don't get tired of listening to it as you play through the game.  I would probably pick up the soundtrack if it was made available later on.  The backgrounds match what little I saw of the tv series.  Actually, I'd say they are a bit better.  The series had very simple backgrounds with not a lot of details, but the backgrounds and scenery used in the game are pretty well detailed and don't seem like they just spammed a single model everywhere to put things together.  Some sort of notation about the edge of the map and ledges you can and cannot fall off of would be nice, though.
The map layouts, despite the above notation, are pretty good and make good use of corners for hiding things without making it ridiculously hard on for more casual players, and use different levels and heights for various things rather well.  The only stage where I had a problem with the map was probably the third part where you are doing a very tedious task while fighting enemies.  I don't have a problem with the task specifically; it was a nice change of pace, but, since the radar does not have a minimap or indicator for quest objectives, the mission was a bit harder than it needed to be.
The gameplay is smooth on a controller and less-so without.  I'd not recommend playing this game without a 360 or XBOne gamepad.  Armed with a gamepad, the controls are pretty well done and fairly intuitive.  Once you get used to holding down the trigger in order to execute your specials, you'll most likely be in good shape.  There were no signs of input lag between when the button is pushed and the character indicates the move, and charging times for specials are reasonable.
The difficulty for this game is a bit all over the place, however.  Samapuma is a casual gamer and not particularly good at these sorts of games.  Once she got used to it, she was helpful, but still had difficulty with most of the enemies, and that's not a good thing.  The game scales pretty smoothly for having more players, but is becomes very button mashy and less experienced players may have trouble keeping track of what does what.  The characters seem to have a good bit of variation to their moveset, while keeping to every character having a melee and ranged attack.
In conclusion, this is a very good game, especially for an early release title, and I look forward to seeing what they add to the game as it grows and develops.  Things I'd like to see added to the game would be, perhaps, a character customization feature where you can make your own student at the academy, with either generic voice or none at all.  I'd be happy to just play my own character in this setting.  I'd really like for there to be some degree of difficulty setting.  Samapuma couldn't really fully enjoy the game because she was struggling against a lot of the monsters, especially the rolling ones and the bears later in the game.  A single player campaign with either AI allies or even just taking one of the characters out solo would be nice.  This would give players a chance to practice various characters without having to deal with more experienced players complaining about how they don't know how to play for multiplayer.  Keep it short and I'm sure people will still be encouraged to play the game online with others.

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is best described as "more okay than I expected." In a time where first-person horror games get dumped out left and right for a shot at YouTube viral status and a quick buck, I didn't expect more than a reskinned Slender-esque with a few cheap deaths. The Hat Man is still a re-skinned Slender-esque, but the reskin isn't too ugly, and the cheap deaths were mostly lacking.
In fact, the titular Hat Man is barely effective as a threat at all. He's so easy to hear and avoid that it's highly unlikely you'll run into him in a game-ending sense more than two or three times over the course of the entire game. The bulk of gameplay consists of scrounging around for journal pages and other items as you try to track down your daughter, who's disappeared from her room shortly before your arrival and a sudden turn of everything for the spooky.
The asylum that serves as the game's setting is fairly easy to navigate, but suffers from a lot of repetitive textures and room layouts, making getting lost a frequent concern. Eventually things shift to more of a basement, which suffers the same problem, and it's not difficult to miss some of the pages you need upon first pass. It's still not incredibly hard, but when you do have to backtrack despite thinking you've checked every possible room, it gets frustrating very quickly.
Aside from the daughter's journey, as spelled out in her journal, the reasons for what you're doing as her parent (you can choose mother or father at the start) are less clearly explained. Storytelling definitely falls short outside those journal bits, which are handily voice-acted so you don't have to read them yourself. Quick tip: Don't turn on the auto-reading of the entries, but listen manually each time, as the former seems not to pop the "listen to every entry" achievement.
My final verdict is that The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is mediocre at best. While I didn't hate it, I don't see why I'd suggest anyone else take it for a spin. At least it was really short.

I'm not much of one for writing reviews; I don't do it often, and have no practice at it. But, what I can say here, is that for years I've been looking for a game that's centered primarily, if not wholly, around Celtic mythology, rather than generic European medieval fantasy or feudal Asian mythology. This game delivered, moreso than I could have ever thought a game could. Why there haven't been more games featuring such strong Celtic themes is beyond me, but Kingdoms of Amalur: Recokoning showed that it can be done, and done very well. I was definitely impressed with the story of the game.
As far as gameplay, things were pretty good. Combat and controls felt better with a gamepad than mouse and keyboard, but that's never been a dealbreaker for me. I feel there could have been more done with combos and chaining attacks, because combat felt a little static after awhile, but it wasn't awful. Most quests(but not all; here's looking at you, Til's Collection) were interesting and often felt like an interesting task, rather than a chore to do for XP. The main quest line especially was fun, interesting, and kept me pulled in to the game. Factions you could join in the game I felt were pretty mediocre, and are your generic warriors, mages, and rogues factions. Their quests were fun, but I never really felt like my character truely belonged to the faction upon joining. The one major downside I felt in the game was gear drops. Almost always, what you can craft at each level was better than anything you could find, even rare named pieces or sets. As for the DLC, Teeth of Narros had a fun main story line, but for the most part it felt drawn out and monotonous. The side quests were pretty boring, and involved a lot of backtracking. Legend of Dead Kell was much better, and felt more involved.
One more note: This game is LONG. And I really mean long, especially if you are a completionist and want to do all of the side quests.

Buggy and extremely unpolished
-------------------------------------------
This isn't intended to be a AAA title, I understand that. But I do expect a game where at least some measurable effort has been put into it. I expect a sim to actually simulate what it is said to be a sim of. I just didn't find that here, and instead, I found a seemingly incomplete, too early to be released attempt to be a firefighting sim. There are too many things wrong with the game that break the immersion of it feeling like a firefighting simulation.
Had this been an early access game, I may have been able to see potential (and obviously, reviewed it differently). But because this is allegedly a complete game, it must be reviewed accordingly.
=== THE GOOD ===
The premise. To be honest, that's about all I could find good with the game. I do find the genre (rescue simulator) interesting and fun, but the premise only takes us so far...the mechanics, gameplay, ambiance, etc. all must come together to help immerse the player in the experience. The game just doesn't do that.
=== THE BAD ===
AMBIENT SOUND ISSUES
--engine sound cuts on and off despite there being no running vehicles nearby
--door sound opening/closing whenever a person is nearby in the station (despite no doors opening/closing nearby)
--no sound distance; all same level despite distance (with a couple exceptions of cars I found while I was walking on road, but even then, they cut in and out instead of properly fading in and out)
--repeat voice loops (constant "good morning" and "Man, another shift that seems like it will never end." On the way back from the event, he kept repeating "I could really do with another hour of sleep."  I didn't know firefighters complained so much about their job.
--roaring fire sound same for all fires, even an extremely small 1 box fire. That is, it doesn't matter if a building is on fire or if it is a shoebox, it's a roaring fire with the same sound effect 100% of the time
GRAPHIC ISSUES
--shading is bad on characters and other assets, more like smoke. It's difficult to describe, I've never seen a game do that before. I've changed the settings to see if it changes anything, it doesn't. I may post a screenshot to give an example.
--reflections don't make sense. You can see reflections of things (like people for example) at angles, distances, and heights that are physically impossible (walking through the tutorial will give you an example of what I meant, but perhaps I should upload a screenshot to illustrate)
--hose is non-existent once it is connected to water source. Nozzle appears in hand, but it is never connected to the hose. This is an immersion breaker.
--reflections in vehicle rear view mirror are non-existent (except for sometimes, the top 1/4 of the rear view mirror displays the sky, nothing more)
--100% of all civilian vehicles have darkest possible tint - can't see inside any vehicle
BAD AI
--walks randomly w/o meaning (back and forth down halls). They have no real tasks, they do nothing. They are just there to give the illusion that the facility is not empty, but it just doesn't work IMO.
--will continue to walk into obstacles (like a desk). Eventually they seem to stop...but it takes a little while before they figure out they can't walk through the desk, it's weird.
--colleagues do not actually do anything at all. They are there just for aesthetics (they do not put fires, they only appear to be doing so). The Steam home page advertises that your fellow firefighters do help you...but they don't. They don't do jack. The outcome of an event/emergency rests entirely with you...the other "people" there are just for show.
=== THE UGLY ===
GAMEPLAY
--Tutorial only takes you through walkthrough of the department, it does not teach you the operations of the vehicles, nor does it tell you anything about any of the tools you use in putting out fires. There's a fair amount of different equipment, but absolutely no training on how to use them or what it connects to, etc.
The tutorial does absolutely nothing more than what an in-game map could do. That is no exaggeration. There is no benefit that the tut gives other than showing you where rooms are and in some rooms, what can be found there (a couple items here, coffee maker here, etc.).
--Mouse sensitivity - despite having it on its lowest settings, it's still extremely sensitive, I had to use my control panel to adjust settings since game's settings are insufficient. 1st time I've ever had to do that in a game.
--Physics...high pressure hose does not affect any entity in game except fire. 100% of all entities are there for aesthetics only (gas cans, boxes, trash, etc.). There are no movable objects.
--Water...once it leaves the hose, it magically appears, never to be seen again. There is no water on the ground, no soaking walls, nothing. It leaves the hose and disppears into thin air.
--cars take ZERO damage when running into them. They stop (at least), but nothing else happens. Obviously this is not a demolition sim....but I expected at some some sign of damage or some penalty. There's not a scratch on any vehicle, not even the truck I'm driving.
--100% clipping when walking into cars (or them driving into you). They are "ghost cars" apparently.
=== CONCLUSION ===
This is a game I'd expect to be in very early access. Currently, there are many early access games that are further along than this.   The idea behind the game (being a firefighter faced with different emergencies) is great, but the application fails miserably IMO.  Far too many bugs, immersion breaking issues, and lack of polish in just about every area imaginable.
I had reasonable hopes for the game, but they were dashed by a poorly delivered product on almost every level possible.
IMO, the game is worth around $5. I doubt that many players will get more than a few hours of game play from it as it is tedious, buggy, doesn't make sense at times, annoying (eg sounds), and has too many immersion breaking issues.

I really loved this game. Beat it about 2 years ago and once I complete my new build Im going to beat it for the 2nd time. It's pretty much a Zelda clone but it's unique enough to be its own thing. There are a lot of puzzles, gorgeous animation and a small but decent story. It's very straight forward and the game play is enough to keep things interesting in between story arks. Give it a shot.

Oceanhorn has been an amazing experience for me. It takes the classic action/adventure formula and sprinkles in just a little bit of RPG leveling (though, not in the traditional sense). Your main character gets all of the usual moves - attack; block; magic; dash; etc. but the game is paced well enough that you get a new ability, item, or spell periodically enough to keep it interesting. Leveling up doesn't increase stats but instead improves your spells, increases your carrying capacity or grants a new ability. This offers a little extra motivation to fight the monsters along the way and not just run past everything. The puzzles are not too difficult but they were rarely boring and they were easy enough to execute once you figured them out. Many other games make putting the solution together more difficult than actually solving the puzzle, so I am glad Oceanhorn didn't do the same. I also like how the "drops" are prioritzed a little bit. If you're low on health the enemies are more likely to drop a heart for you. Low on bombs? They'll probably drop some bombs. It's a nice touch and saves you from running to town to constantly buy supplies. The graphics and sound are all done well, especially for a game that started on mobile devices. I have no real complaints, only a couple of minor frustrations. Having limited movement on the camera is a bit bothersome for a 3D game but it's clearly a choice the developers made based on the style of game. There is also a little bit of backtracking to be done but if you're going for 100% you're going to do that anyway. Also, the fishing mini-game had a couple of annoying "tricks" used by the fish, which didn't spoil the game but was still a minor frustration. Overall I really enjoyed Oceanhorn.
clearly inspired by Zelda: The Wind Waker, Oceanhorn is still enjoyable for the fans of the genre. I recommend it on sale.

This is not a terrible game.  It just is not a great game.  It is an average game that I found boring.
The game is made in Unity.  You can play as either the father or the mother searching for their lost daughter in the insane asylum.  There are voice overs, and the acting is competent.   It isn't terrible, but it isn't outstanding.  Like everything in this game.
As mentioned, the game is in Unity.  The engine is smooth.  The graphics are not outstanding, but it animates well.  Moving your character is intuitive, although I found the movement a little awkward at times.  When there is something you can interact with a little hand will appear, and that is when you click.
The entire game, however, is just a search for pages of your daughters diary.  There are a few mild scares, and the setting in general tries to be unsettling.  Walking around a generic assylum that was dark looking for paper.... well, it just got boring.
If the game is on sale and you have some time to kill for a very average horror experience, pick it up.  Otherwise there are better ways to spend your gaming time.

Best ARPG I've played to date. Why?
- Casual gamer Friendly!
- Although there is, what may seem at first, a limited number of classes the skill selection makes for at least 3 or 4 different sub-variations for each class. Replay value is great, although leveling is a test of patience. Capping taking roughly 2 complete playthroughs.
- Graphics are not as hard on the average CPU that us mortals can afford. I prefer stylized graphics over realistic graphics because they are never out of style or look dated like most other 3D games.
- It offers an Endgame consisting of Mapworks, a tool that allows you to run random dungeons of a level of your choosing (up to 105), and Tarroch's Tomb, a relentless 10 wave gauntlet that drops loot every wave you beat but disappears if you die (Wave 1 comprised of lvl 100 enemies and wave 10 of lvl 199 enemies).
- The loot system actually feels FAIR!!! *coughs* Diablo III *coughs*
- Moddability adds heaps to the game including a difficulty increase and class changes that increase replay value. Downside is modded game saves are different than stock and you can only play with people that have the same mods. Items can not be crossed from modded to unmodded.
- If you get bored or just want to test limits you can duplicate items for money or utility by using a stash and save file manuever. You could also use console to spawn items but you will be labeled as a cheater. The ability to do these cheats adds a lot to the experienced of a gamer that is NOT HARDCORE. Casual gamers need to be catered to too.
The only real downside I found was the relentlessness when making ability choices.
MARK MY WORDS: You cannot respec more than the last 3 abilities you leveled or chose. This means you must level up a character from scratch to try a different build and will probably have to make 2 almost identical characters to fix a stupid choice mistake you made on your first try at a class. Some people love this feature but I believe it would be better if you could just have 2 sub-class slots like you have in WoW or if you could get an option to reset points after completing the game. Just my 2 cents.
Please buy this and enjoy.

Although this game is laggy at times, it is still a very good game if you do not own an X-Box or PlayStation.
Here's how to stop or remove the lag:
Lower the resolution
Turn off fullscreen
Turn off window boxing
Lower the particle effects
You don't have to do all of these steps if your Mortal Kombat X isn't very laggy. A mistake some people make is turning on frame smoothing. ONLY use it if there is not possible way for you to make game run at more than 30 fps, otherwise it will just make the lag worse. The launch isn't really as bad as people say, and I think this game is worth giving a chance to. Even the keyboard controls aren't bad, and in my opinion, are easier than the console controllers (some people still might say otherwise), but if you want you can still plug in a USB controller, which is what I do when my friends come over. Only the intro cutscenes are the ones that get most of the lag, but everything else, gameplay and storymode cutscenes, are very smooth after you adjust the settings. So don't hesitate to buy this game, even if your computer is slow. The game isn't as good as the console versions, but is still worth getting if you're not able to get the consoles.

Pretty game with smooth combat and some breathtaking vistas.  I have played to the end as a Mage, and have only a few real issues.  I will not call them complaints, because I enjoyed the game and may dust it off again someday.  As a veteran RPG fan, I enjoyed the skill trees and equipment customization.  I was disappointed that I reached the level cap about halfway through the game, playing with all DLC active. Changing skills resulted in measurable changes to one's fighting style: swinging a warhammer and stumping around in plate armor feels nothing like hurling chakrams while flash-teleporting through a swarm of enemies to set them up for a blast of fire.  The voice acting was generally good, and the tutorial explained all the mechanics without being too heavy handed.  The Lore is well-spaced and well written, and completing a set of lorestones give a reward for bothering to listen to the entertaining stories scattered around the world.
If I had complaints, it would be that, first, some abilitiess are heavily overpowered.  Once I learned "meteor" and specced my fate to archmage, I pretty much pressed one button to end a combat.  Secodnly, some skills are under-used.  I never once needed to pick a pocket or advance alchemy past the point of being able to mix potions with four ingredients.   Thirdly, the sense of being in a single-player MMO is sometimes overwhelming.  There are repeatable fetch-quests, it is easy to join and advance in all factions (no matter your ability choices), and actually leading a faction seems to provide little to no benefit.
If you enjoy RPGs even a little, I highly recommend picking this up the next time there is a sale.  It may be rough, but it is a gem. Pity the publisher will never get to improve on the benchmark they've set.
