As we see newer and newer games come out, I'm extremely happy to see and experience a recent release game that has originality to itself.
Many releases that could be considered 'arcade themed' have bad habits of emulating older games with newer graphics and intuitive addons and features. However, the base for Horizon Shift is an original concept if I have ever seen one! Having dual side defense as a bullet hell theme revolutionizes the possibilities and overall experience with Horizon Shift, and recreates the same adventurous and intuitive experience that you lose after playing through the same style bullet hell game a hundred times.
The interface is free of bugs and crashes, and there are many small pieces that come together to perfect this already solid concept. Varieties of customizable gamemodes, and solid hardcoded game modes give exceedingly more and more gameplay to experience. Coming from the mindset of a gamer, you can feel many of the classic gamer wishes coming to a full realization with this game, as powerups are rewarding, game progression is solid and smooth, and even the tutorial is made to perfection, allowing a swift and smooth transition into the gameplay that goes steady at first to allow you to get bearings, and progressing into the challenging bullet hell theme we all love and enjoy.
To finish off this gem is the beautiful music, both engaging and intense, the gameplay goes hand in hand with each style and, in a sense, leads you through the levels. Just like a good soundtrack to a movie, you don't sit in the middle of the scene shouting how great the orchestral score is, but you become immersed and let it flow through the environment.
However, unlike a linear story game that comes to an end, Horizon Shift is a give and take experience. You give it your time and become progressively better, and you will have a blast and feel the classic accomplishment that you could feel in an old arcade. Thus goes the same way, that it could last you a few minutes if you don't give the game a chance. I believe that this isn't an experience to survive, it is an experience to merely take advantage of, and for only $5, its more than worth the price.

The Sims 2 is my favorite Sims version, hands down. I have sunk in a lot of hours on that clunker on how much IMPROVEMENT it had over the Original Sims and it's console counterparts. It introduces Aging, towns, the Supernatural, 3D archetecture, Floors, and just...so much stuff that it is hard to comphrend how many things it has done.
Sims 3, however...isn't that. It kinda...uhm...isn't really as fun.
Sims 3 looks and runs a LOT better than Sims 2, don't get me wrong. The visual design works in it's favor of making characters look realistic as well as adding a town that doesn't require a long-crack loading screen. But when I bought Sims 3 and started playing it, It felt empty rather than full.
Not once did I actually play the In-Game families, when in Sims 2 I took a big love of the single mom and her dedicated son, the three dudes and the little alien baby (...Just got that reference) And the Goth Family just being cool again. But with Sims 3, I cannot recollect a single memorable sim that just made me think: "Yeah, that WAS a fun family to play with". But...I GUESS you can play as a custom sim? You know, the one with only a dozen or two default hairstyles?
And let's get it out of the way. The Sims is just a dollhouse simulator for adults and kids, and we just like building our little 'family' to play around with. But with Sims 3, it feels more like a Lego simulator, where you have to buy all the hairparts and
the brick parts and the clothes parts and the blah blah parts, and all of them are just so god dang expensive!
Even without the price tag, each DLC actually kind of RUINS the main vanilla flavor of the Sims 3 base game. It use to be where ghosts and the unknown were strange scary things, where the threat of death can come at a moments notice and surviving through to old age means you are a cool dude. Now, there are werewolves running around my town with a full moon every few nights, a dozen deer just running around yukking it up, and FESTIVAL EVENTS ARE COMING UP even though you bought the DLC to just get the hairstyles! It just muddles the main point of where I just want to let my sim live a normal life, not to become a immortal werewolf fairy vampire who has the big bucks and is married to Chuck the plumber.
I would love a Sims game where you can actually customize the length of the hair, the fabric and length of the clothing, the dreams and desires of a Sim where the actions can't be overridden, I just want a Sim game where it just takes place in a house, and you raise a sim from being a baby sim into being a dead ghost sim. Just...please.
Would I reccomend this game: NO
The graphics and visual design are an improvement over Sims 2, but the Sims 3 feels downright stale and claustrophobic compared to the open sense of discovery with it's predecessors.
Suggestions to Game Devs: Try to focus on making a game where the character's personality actually defines how they dress and how they interact with others. It would be SO MUCH FUN to just have Sims interacting without our guidance.

"They were too busy focusing on whether they could, that they forgot to think whether they should."
Oh, this game has gone downhill so fast, so much that playing it now is painful.
What they hell happened to "Help us make the game you want to play", developers?
Ever since Devyatayev update around 6-7 months ago (the infamous Squad 2.0 update), this game has gone further and further down the drain, whilst you constantly tell us that it's "Working as intended", which is a blatant lie based on the general consensus of the playerbase, well, what's left of us.
I think "Working as  intended" should become your new tagline.
To give any potential user some basic background information, they first locked changing between squads, so if you were, for example in an Infantry Squad, you couldn't either switch to another Infantry Squad or a Squad of a different class (Tanker, Pilot, Recon or Paratrooper).
The addition of the Auxiliary seats makes no difference, mostly because you have to grind to unlock them, and they are set by the Squad leader, who could be a level 0 soldier (when you have a level 17 soldier a few xp off becoming a general). To make matters worse, the game then became full of paranoid players who wouldn't use said seats for fear the Squad Leader would kick them from the Squad (and this does happen).
You also locked weapons in combat, and removed captured weapons from the store. Locking weapons in combat was a fair move as it was a bug that people could, for example, swap their SMG on one soldier for a sniper rifle if needed, but you gave us no option to move weapons between characters, which you have been promising for a while now.
Then came Evenhart, where you added a load of unwanted 'Immersion changes', which just means it takes 1.7 years to get out of your tank (making anti-tank infantry even easier to play as), and give you motion sickness when zooming from first to third person view.
Then came Furness, where you 'Balanced' the tanks (it's not even close to balanced), and then added the 'Player Journey' add-on, which made changing classes for newer soldiers impossible, so you are now forced to buy them.
Then came Garmen, which revamped all the maps (instead of just the capture zones), making each map essentially the same (mostly forest with some urban combat at the centre), and mae it so you spawn in the middle of the woods with no vehicles.
Then came Hallowes, which closed off windows on houses (making roofs essentially unreachable camping spots for paratroopers), decreased the base salary and nerfed the M1/M2 carbine and MG42 into the ground, instead of to in-line with the other weapons.
Then came Ihlefeld, which introduced a massively reworked piloting system that makes flying the old planes nigh-on impossible, and getting a good score (hence a profit) pretty much impossible. Also came a load of undocumented price increases - 541k for a Level 0 Recon is insanity.
Sure, the latest update is decent, but all it really does is add in even more expensive things for players to grind in. If you hadn't introduced all the flaws in the game, I would be singing high praise for it - indeed I used to.
It's so sad to reminisce about how the game used to be even just a year ago, when you truly cared about your playerbase and promised us future updates (new factions, bipods, more vehicles and weapons and maps and so on), but now we can plainly see you only care about making a profit.

I will not call them complaints, because I enjoyed the game and may dust it off again someday.  As a veteran RPG fan, I enjoyed the skill trees and equipment customization.  I was disappointed that I reached the level cap about halfway through the game, playing with all DLC active. Changing skills resulted in measurable changes to one's fighting style: swinging a warhammer and stumping around in plate armor feels nothing like hurling chakrams while flash-teleporting through a swarm of enemies to set them up for a blast of fire.  The voice acting was generally good, and the tutorial explained all the mechanics without being too heavy handed.  The Lore is well-spaced and well written, and completing a set of lorestones give a reward for bothering to listen to the entertaining stories scattered around the world.
If I had complaints, it would be that, first, some abilitiess are heavily overpowered.  Once I learned "meteor" and specced my fate to archmage, I pretty much pressed one button to end a combat.  Secodnly, some skills are under-used.  I never once needed to pick a pocket or advance alchemy past the point of being able to mix potions with four ingredients.   Thirdly, the sense of being in a single-player MMO is sometimes overwhelming.  There are repeatable fetch-quests, it is easy to join and advance in all factions (no matter your ability choices), and actually leading a faction seems to provide little to no benefit.
If you enjoy RPGs even a little, I highly recommend picking this up the next time there is a sale.  It may be rough, but it is a gem. Pity the publisher will never get to improve on the benchmark they've set.

(N.B. : in the sake of honesty, I'll say that I've received this game for free in exchange of a review. I've tried to stay as equal as possible when playing the game, but keep in mind that I did not have to pay for it and that this fact might have act on my mind.)
Horizon shift is an old- school arcade type game that will definitely give you an eighties or early nineties feeling (you know, when you were raging while wiggling that stick trying to beat the bloody level you had spent all your week money on...)
You direct a small vessel along a line placed at the center of the screen. You can orientate your ship so it'll face up or down. Of course, you can shoot, and that's lucky since there will be a lot of ennemies that will be coming at you. Each time an ennemy comes in contact with the horizon line you're sitting on, it breaks it partially, making your moves more difficult. Fortunately, you can jump along that line, and you should learn quickly to use that trick because it will allow you to get a little speed boost. And if an ennemy is not trying to destroy your line ? Well, it's probably shooting à you, or dropping bomb...
Far away from a manic shooter, Horizon Shift still gives you a real feeling of challenge across its different levels. Even if it's probably not the best in the "arcade shooter" category, mainly since it stays quite simple (but not easy), especially in the graphic and sound department, if you want a game that will tingle both your nostalgy and challenging nerves, then, at around 5€, it's safe to say you won't feel robbed by Horizon Shift. Maybe you won't play it for long hours in a row, but it's the typical game you'll launch for a few quick rounds when you don't have time for a bigger game.

This game........sigh.
In Brothers a Tale of Two Sons, you guide two brothers on a quest to find a cure for their father who has become ill. The concept is a co-op adventure with yourself, the game dividing your controller in half, left side for the older brother and the right for the younger. Together you must work your hands in sync to overcome obstacles, dangerous paths, and occasionally sit at a random stone bench to take in the breathtaking view. In execution it works well, with simplified move, camera, and Action for either side. You realize that each brother has their own strengths, younger brother can fit through small areas, older brother is taller and stronger and can achieve feats the younger one cant. To encompass all who play, they created a "language" so that instead of engrossing yourself in dialogue, you actually delve into the story via scenes, body language, and the tone of their language. The visuals in the game are stunning, taking you from lush lazy green hobbit-like farmland to deep troll caves, to wispy peaks to a snow-covered mountainous town, all really having me wish for a full open world game to actually delve into this world the developers have created. The sound is excellent, using tones of light playfulness, in-your-seat tenseness, to ride-along action and solemn mourning. For this game to not have any names, "understandable" dialogue, being fairly short, and having a not-so-unfamiliar quest, this game pulled tears. Should you play this? Yes. Plain and Simple. It DESERVES your attention. This review comes with a caveat; I haven't beaten it. I've tried quite a few times, but I've only gotten to the level 27 boss. And while I don't like reviewing a game I haven't beaten, I seem to have hit a wall at level 27. But hopefully, some will still find this helpful.
The visuals with
are simple, yet clean with an interesting trait. Half of the small enemies and some bosses look like something straight out of a game from the old days of vector graphics. Think
or
and you'll have a good idea of what they look like. Other enemies and bosses have a distinct Adobe Illustrator look about them, in that they're made up with those same vector graphics, but the lines are fatter, they have a smooth gradient on/in them, or both. It's a very basic design concept, with ships that look more like logos or graphic design symbols, but it's executed pretty well with touches of animation and rotation. The backgrounds are the opposite of the sprites, in that they appear to be polygonal models of a rotating planet, of falling down various kinds of tunnels, a Skeletor/Kaos head that taunts you, and other assorted animated images. They are then under various transparent layers that feature lighting and lightning effects, 3D scrolling blocks, and so forth that creates a multi-layered backdrop to the action. They're also kept rather dark, so despite how busy they can get, they don't interfere with the visibility of the game sprites, or become too distracting.
The music in the game is an interesting mix of old and new when it comes to instruments. You'll hear synths that sound like they could've come from an NES or a Genesis system, distorted Rock/Metal guitars, distinctly 80s synths, beats that touch upon House and Trance, and it's all mashed together to create an Electronica soundtrack that's enjoyable to listen to as you play. The music also supports the frantic pace that develops as the game progresses, without going ballistic in tempo or having overwhelmingly loud/rapid-fire notes. So in this area, there's nothing to complain about. When it comes to the sound effects, they do their job well. Explosions, pops, clicks and hisses that work with the retro-like visuals are present without being overpowering (save for the bomb effect that's meant to be big). So here too, things are fine.
With the gameplay, this game mixes gameplay traits from the likes of
,
and shmups like
. You don't fly over landscapes or in outer space. Instead, you stay within the confines of a single screen, moving back and forth along a straight line; the horizon. You can only move along this horizon, be it above or below it. Granted, you can jump (yes, jump) over bullets, enemies and gaps in the horizon thanks to a bit of platformer gameplay infusion. But most of the time, you'll be finding yourself sliding to the left and right along the horizon line, shooting strait up and down at the enemies. And there will be plenty of enemies to shoot at.
Each enemy has its own kind of attack. Blue rockets follow you as they travel down/up, blue asteroids slam into your horizon and break part of it off (which also adds a multiplier for each section that's broken off), red rockets come straight down and then “run” along the horizon if they reach it, geometric shapes appear in swarms that come after you if they reach the edge of the screen, indestructible pods fire lasers that cross the whole screen, several ship-types spin so they fire in random directions... and trust me when I say, there are many more. These all show up in a succession of waves, with each sixth wave resulting in a boss fight.
The bosses come in different shapes and sizes, including crab and jellyfish-inspired ones, a large spaceship, and a six-sided... thing that splits in half. They also feature attacks that vary from simple and easily avoided, to nearly screen-covering blasts of waves and bullets that require small adjustments to survive. Beat the bosses, and you'll be treated to bonus stages with different layouts where you break blocks for extra points. But the enemies and bosses aren't your only foes. As if that all wasn't enough, the very horizon you move along will eventually fight you, as it begins drifting steadily up and down the screen in later stages. This adds to the game's already frantic and at times chaotic pace by that point in the game. Factor this in with the gradually more crowded waves of enemies, increasingly bullethell-like boss fights, platform jumps and whatnot, and there's a lot going on. But, you're not left helpless in all of this.
You can flip your ship above and below the horizon, allowing you a greater chance to avoid being hit by ships and the white shots that the horizon stops (the yellow shots pass through it, so beware). There are a several powerups that you can earn throughout the game that seem to drop when you either reach a certain number in your chain counter, reach certain scores, or when you use a bomb and kill a high enough number of enemies on-screen (I'm still not sure what exactly triggers a powerup drop). From extra lives, shot power increases, and shields, to combo multipliers, a mirror image of your ship on the opposite side of the horizon, and speed ups, there are a number of ways available to increase your chances of survival. Add in a screen clearing bomb to use once you've killed enough enemies to fill the meter along the bottom of the screen, and the aforementioned jumping ability, and you've got a nice arsenal at your disposal. Oh, and when you die, you get to keep your shot power ups, which is a nice (and needed) touch.
But, with all of that positive stuff said, there are a handful of blemishes on this game's otherwise pleasant, stylized face. The first of my issues with the game, is that it simply gets too busy later on. Between all of the enemy types crowding up the screen, the moving horizon, indestructible enemies (which are extremely annoying), varying bullet types, and big lasers that drastically cut down on your mobility when they fire, the game can easily become a frustrating one to play. It's not that it gets hard in a shmup way or a platforming way, it gets hard because you have a lot to try and keep track of as the screen gets increasingly more chaotic, crowded and sectioned off. Another issue for me, was the powerup system. It appears to be completely random, and at times, it can lead to very unfair playthroughs. As an example, I didn't get my first shot powerup until stage 19 on one play through, and that's not a good thing in a game that's part shmup in gameplay. My last big issue is with the sluggish way your ship begins moving from a complete stop if you use a digital pad/keyboard. While you come to a dead stop when using both digital and analog inputs, you gradually start moving up to full speed if you use digital. The analog controls mostly alleviate this if you quickly move the stick fully to the left or right, but with the digital controls, it feels like you're fighting with a dead zone that has no way to be eliminated. And that didn't sit well with me.
So what can we say about
? Between the positive qualities, and the several modes of play that are available and unlockable, there's plenty to enjoy here. It's an interesting game with a good amount of creativity in its visuals, diversity in its gameplay mechanics, and a nice soundtrack. It's also a game that feels like it's a few tweaks away from hitting its full potential. The slow-to-start digital ship movements and the random powerup system dim some of its shine, and the method of its difficulty increase later on will likely be a detriment to its replay factor for some. Yes, it's a fun game. But I think that perhaps it got a few too many ideas jammed into it for its own good, keeping it from being as fun, accessible and replayable as it could be.
Score- 7.8 / 10

Disclaimer - Just because I'm friends with the developer doesn't mean that I'm going to be doing everything I can to make it look better.  I'm rating this as is, no bias.
I first met Paul when I left a nasty review on another one of his games, Super Killer Hornet Resurection.  He friended me and asked what I did and didn't like.  I told him about the glitches and just the little things I flat out didn't like.  He didn't write me off, or say "that's not what everyone else thinks so I don't care".  He took my words, and asked for a sort-of playtest/review of some of his other games.  He gave me a key for Pester on Desura.  It was decent, but it could have been better.  Not gonna lie; I did like it better than SKHR.  I offered him ideas and suggestions on how to improve the feel of it and some mechanics.  Little did I know, he was listening, and he threw in a huge twist.  (note, I also tested Pressure.  I told him it didn't feel fair reviewing it since I didn't like the type of game to begin with.  If you don't like a genre, it takes a lot to change your mind.)
It started with the idea to make a Pester II.  Just a few mechanic and graphical enhancements; make the game play a little better and look a little better.  He sends me a key for this (again, no bias, just stating a fact.)  I thought at first that this was just a little side project he's been working on.  I downloaded and started the game.  I realized, he actually used a few of my suggestions for Pester on this.  However, I got thrown off when I realized it was platformer influenced.  I'm like, "How the actual ♥♥♥♥ can you combine a Danmaku (the actual name for bullethell/SHMUP) and a platformer?  That doesn't even make sense!"  Well, it plays good.  It's just that simple.  It actually plays good.  He took two genres that generally have NOTHING to do with each other, made them equal, and somehow made it work.  That alone I give him props for.
It's like a weird space invaders meets... I don't even know.  Mario?  Like, I'm actually almost in shock.  Anyways, it has a decent soundtrack, and is a fun arcade game that you may not play for hours on end, but will come back to eventually and inevitably.  I plan on coming back to it myself.  But the only way you would understand is to try it for yourself.
Congrats, Paul.  I think this one may make it.

In the interest of fairness and honesty, I will start by saying that I was gifted this game. I will do my best not to let that cloud my review.
This game is a very interesting marriage of features from old school arcade games, mostly shoot em ups.
The visuals seem to be inspired by asteroids, while the game play is inspired by numerous other games, from some rail games like space invaders to some elements of bullet hell games, to reflexive game play and decision making that seems to be unique to this game, or at least, rare enough for me to not have encountered it before.
The rail in this game being in the middle of the screen rather than on one side like the left or bottom, is something that has been used in the past but not nearly as successfully as it is here. The placement of the rail not only gives the game more depth but also creates room for some very interesting interactions and stunts; both making it more difficult and more enjoyable than it would have been otherwise.
The game's simple visuals and unique game play are tied in together seamlessly with silky responses and a perfect soundtrack (note that the silkiness is gone from the game when you are in a bonus level, it will be hard to 100% one of those). Your little ship responds to you perfectly, and for this game that is essential. It really is all about game play, there are no frills, just clean honest game play. At no point while playing the game have I come across game breaking add on or boosts either, something that exists in many arcade games and very much saps any interest in the game once acquired.
There is a number of different modes to play the game in, classic, arcade, survival etc. so the users have several choices on how to tackle the game, and they are mostly unlocked after playing the game only once on the starting mode, so I didn't have to torture myself to try them all out. The learning curve for the game was mountainous but the levels and bosses were not unreasonable, I would get owned by a level or a boss, restart, and from my previous play have learned how to deal with it, and later get owned by something else down the line and repeat - I got owned a lot...
Now, I myself am not particularly good with arcade games, so maybe my assessment of the game's difficulty here is not entirely accurate; but I found the game
challenging. Very rewarding once you get past a hurdle, but I feel justified in underlining that word back there.
I looked at some of the other reviews on this game, and my experience of the dev's work on other games was as gaucho marx's experience with his fixes here, there was genuine interest in player feedback. That is always appreciated by the community.
So again, I would like to remind everyone that I was gifted this game before I end my review
- Easy to pick up, learn the basics
- Responsive controls
- Excellent soundtrack
- Smooth overall game experience
- Great Support
- Hard to master
- Might make you cry
Altogether, if arcade games are your thing, you will love this game, and if they aren't you should still give this game a go, it might just change your mind

This is a short but beautifully designed platformer/RPG genre game. The world it's set in is quite well graphically depicted, although quite linear. The story itself is somewhat dark but I found it a very refreshing reminder that the world we live in is filled with tragedy but we still need to be brave and rise above it. As such the ending is a bit of an anti-climax but such is life.
It's also quite original and ingenious how the developers applied a simple control system to so many brilliantly engineered (but not too challenging) puzzles. I played it using my XBox 360 controller and I only needed the 2-joysticks and left & right triggers. I can't imagine playing this with a keyboard and mouse. I guess what really makes this game unique IMO is having to control two characters (sometimes doing obliquely opposition actions) at the same time; the analogy of the childhood game of trying to pat your head while rubbing your tummy comes to mind. And I stumbled over myself trying to get this right quite a bit but that's what made the whole experience challenging yet fun.
All in all I think it was a great game, just a little too short.

Strip away its unique art style and seemingly half-baked story and suddenly Oceanhorn looks a lot like a Zelda clone. The basics of item progression, exploration, combat, and dungeon design all resemble Zelda in one form or another, which is comforting. The formula of the Zelda series is tried and tested, and works in Oceanhorn's favor.
While Oceanhorn never reaches the same heights as the Zelda games it attempts to emulate, it still does a good job at designing a believable world full of enemies, dungeons, and general villagers. What attracted me to Oceanhorn was its art style; I am a sucker for unique art styles, and Oceanhorn did a great job in this regard.
Pros:
- Item progression is rewarding
- Island discovery and exploration is a lot of fun
- The art style is visually appealing and the colors pop
- The music and general sound effects are well-designed
- It is satisfying to access unexplored areas with newly-found equipment
Cons:
- Combat is a bit clunky
- The story feels half-baked
- Most enemies are far too easy to defeat
- Swords are able to slay enemies but can not break pots
- The camera, while it can swivel slightly, is often too restricted
- The open ocean is not freely able to be explored like individual islands are
- Aside from the last few encounters, the bosses are laughably easy to take down
Pros and cons aside, my time with Oceanhorn was enjoyable. Exploring dungeons and fighting enemies with an ever-increasing collection of equipment was satisfying, and chatting with the locals of the various islands for information was a joy. Oceanhorn is inexpensive and a lot of fun. I highly recommend checking this game out.

Probably one of the more underrated games on steam. Shame there won't be more of this series.
Graphics are nothing special, reminds me of games like Kotor and Mass Effect 1. They aren't bad, they're actually pretty pleasing to the eyes, but they wouldn't blow anyone away on release and certainly wouldn't nowadays.
Combat is probably one of the most fun experiences I've had in any rpg. It's generally pretty varied, tons of enemy variety, tons of weapons etc. When you unlock some of the better abilities (like the aoe fire spell as a mage) you actually feel like a badass killing machine. Very rewarding experience.
Haven't completely finished the game yet but main story and faction quests are all pretty entertaining. Not as good as some of the other rpgs I've played (like Kotor) but probably on a similar level to a Fallout or Elder Scrolls story. Not amazing but sufficient. Only complaint is that most of the side quests are very menial, some are decent but for the most part they all just send you in to some dungeon that is slightly different than the last one you went to. Still worth doing as they expand on the story if you're in to that kind of thing.
This is also a lot of content for the money. There's probably at least 60 hours worth of it if you do sidequests and DLC. It really is a shame this series is probably dead, if there was a sequel with a slightly better main story with more engaging main characters and improved sidequests/less repetitive dungeons it would probably be one of the best rpgs out there.
As it stands I would definitely recommend this game to anyone that enjoyed Bioware rpgs and similar games.

i have waited for a long time to write this review. was close in giving it a thumbs down.
when it first came out it was a mess. crashes, lagging, game did not even end properly. even after several patches. some of the patches were over 15gb, and the game still had issues. every time i started a round, it was a slideshow but was smoother during the fight with occasional freezing. even when my pc was not the best but still within the recommended specs.
but after a serious upgrade of my computer, the game runs actually really smooth. no problems, no lagging, crashes, freezing, nothing. so having new hardware does seem to do the trick, but this could be just for me. some people are still having issues even with the latest hardware.
the game it self plays really smooth and the combat is fluent. the characters look more believable now and the remarks they have for each other by addressing the opponent by name at the beginning of a round, is a very nice detail that was missing in the previous titles.
each character has 3 types of styles that includes weapons too. but it also has its downsides as well since certain moves you like/used in previous titles are not available in every style.
also new are the "brutalities" that can be performed when the enemy is low on health by just performing a normal button pressing, unlike the fatalities that can get obnoxious to perform. but they are, as expected for a MK game, very gory in an over the top way.
the really bad things are that you have to buy the characters instead of unlocking them. also there is a feature called "the krypt" were you wonder around in first person view to unlock tunes, costumes, brutalities, and more. "whats so bad about that?"; you ask. the koins you earn during combat..... sorry, Kombat.... arent very high and therefor a very slow progress to unlock everything. in other words: you are nearly forced to buy the krypt unlock DLC for 20$. which i did since i personally didnt like the krypt and also dont have that much time.
also certain costumes have to be bought instead to unlock them.
the story mode is also shorter than in MK9. it continues were MK9 left off but nothing really special with a rather forgettable story line and some characters since they arent really explained well. also there are these pointless QTEs that have no effect what so ever if you fail them.
what was very frustrating was that even when you buy the retail version as i did, it will download the entire game. i was really surprised to find only one disc in the box after reading that it is over 40gb. all the disc does is starting the download and thats it. it is not so bad for me since i have unlimited bandwidth but mine isnt really that fast and took nearly a day to download the entire game.
the only good thing with the disc version is; that goro was included and a cold war costume for skorpion.

The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is a first-person game developed by the company Game Mechanics with emphasis on survival.
+ Occasionally the game succeeds to scare the player.
o The randomly created corridors, rooms and items offer a certain replayability, but the multitude of negative points in the general presentation of the game decreases the motivation to play it again.
o Solid sound effects create a partially threatening environment.
- The player has to face only one threat in form of the Hat Man, which results in a rather low level of difficulty.
- The A.I. and general collision system of the antagonist is poorly implemented, e.g. it tends to get stuck in the wall.
- At the beginning the player leaves an axe behind, which negatively impacts the credibility of this ‘survival’ game.
- Sloppy story telling.
- No characterization of the protagonist.
- No voice acting during the entire game.
- Very short game that can be finished in less than 30 minutes.
Hat Man does not work out as intended, because it has been released in an unfinished state. After 30 minutes, which it takes to finish the game, you will only remember the weak A.I., repetitive level design and sloppy story telling. Therefore, the advertising slogan 'the scariest game of 2014' can be considered a blatant lie.
Estimated time for 100 % completion: +3 hours
Singleplayer achievements: 11
Multiplayer achievements: none

"Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons" is absolutely amazing in terms of the
. And, controlling two people at the same time is certainly novel.  No, you can't play this game by moving one person and then the other.  You must be able to move them both simultaneously (or nearly so) to be able to get through some areas. It can be played without a game controller.  I played the entire game using
(after remapping the keys), because my controller just died. I am sure that added to the time it took also.
I am glad I played the game, so I recommend it.  However, it is with some reservations.  (1) I would not recommend this to a very young person or to anyone that might be easily affected by negative imagery. Besides being heavy on emotional situations (sadness, despair, ...), there are areas I can only describe as gruesome.   And, the overall story is bittersweet. (2)  Don't buy it if you want hours and hours of game play. To really enjoy the game you must think like you are on travel and want to see all the sites, scenery, and animals.  That's important because the game is very easy to get through quickly. I did it in 10 hours, taking my time and getting all the achievements, and even replaying some really cool parts
.
(3) Would I play this through repeatedly like I did with Portal or Knights of the Old Republic?  No, I probably won't.  It doesn't have that kind of replay value. The story is very linear.
All that being said, I did enjoy the game and its artfulness.

The game is somewhat polished for an Indie title and it is no secret that it is heavily influenced and pays homage to The Legend of Zelda series, particularly the 2D titles, because there is little-to-no 3D gameplay here, and perhaps Wind Waker on a more superficial level. It is definitely pleasing from an aesthetic perspective, but the soundtrack is very forgettable. The gameplay is repetitive and unsatisfactory, if not awkward at times. There are no standout riddles or puzzles. On the surface, it tries very hard to replicate the design of Zelda games, but some questionable design choices will remind you of the power gap between Oceanhorn and a real Zelda game, or a well designed game in general.
In conclusion, this is a game that is playable and looks nice, but lacks the necessary depth to really stand out among the hundreds of indie games around it in the same space. I wish I could give this a "Meh", as it is not a bad game per se to go for a straight "No", but between the two, it's definitely not a "Yes". It is just a flat, average experinence that doesn't have any particular highs to warrant a recommendation.

You know, for a genre that's supposed to be "dead" according to some, there sure are alot of shmups these days.  I can think of tons of great ones on the PC, shmups of all types, from traditional to bullet-hell and otherwise, and then there's the mobile scene... who coulda known that it would turn out to be totally perfect for that genre?  Well, with a tablet anyway.  Even hyper-difficult bullet-hell games tend to be great on there.   But really, there's tons of them now and more keep coming.  Those saying it's dead need to actually LOOK before talking...  I've played so many of them to freaking death over the years, more than enough to know alot about the genre.
And the thing about this is that there are many of these, so many, but few of them are actually unique.  They might have somewhat unique or interesting scoring systems, but for the most part, they follow a certain set of traditional mechanics at their core.  I recognize 4 types of shmups: vertical, horizontal, horizon (not to be confused with this game, this is something totally different), and single-screen, and all four of these subgenres do this.  Now, that's not bad in and of itself, but still, unique games are rare.
This time though I can say that we have one that actually manages to be unique.  Horizon shift is a single-screen type, like many old arcade games.  No long scrolling levels, or scrolling of any sort.  Any given stage is entirely confined to one screen.  And you shoot things, and those things that are shot will explode.  This though, is where the similarities end.
This game does 3 seperate things that make it very unique.  Number one is the "horizon" for which it is named. This is a line that horizontally crosses the center of the screen (usually).  Your ship travels back and forth along this line.  Like many single-screen games, you move just horizontally, you cannot just go anywhere on the screen.  But what this also does is let you "flip" from one side to the other, so instead of facing upwards, you are facing downwards, and enemies can approach from either side.  So right there, you've got two things to be watching, and have to deal with this additional movement mechanic.   And this mechanic is important and central to... everything.  If you dont learn it, you will lose very fast.   Also enhancing the movement is the fact that you can jump (and double jump).  This too is another integral part of the game, and combining these two things makes up a huge portion of the challenge.
Number two is effects that can happen to the horizon itself.  Enemies in this game are color-coded... different colors do different things.  Blue enemies, if they come into contact with the horizon, will break off a section of it that they touch, leaving a gap.  Now, as falling to your doom is an amazingly stupid and embarrassing way to die in any shmup (really, who falls off a cliff in a shmup?), you really want to not fall through these.  The red ones do not destroy the horizon, but instead will cling to it in various ways.  Remember the super irritating bow-tie things from Tempest, way back when?  Yeah.  They're like THOSE.  Except nowhere near as bloody irritating.  You cannot attack them once they're attached, so you have to jump over them as they move around.  Green enemies just shoot at you, their bullets usually popping harmlessly if they hit the horizon.  And then there's the "solid" ones;  if these guys hit the horizon, well, it's like the ships in Space Invaders hitting the bottom of the screen: you're just plain dead.
Number three though is just how the scoring system works.  You have a "chain" counter that goes up as you destroy enemies.  This just keeps going up, until you spend it by using a bomb (which is charged over time, also by popping enemies).  But the unique part of this is the multiplier.  When a blue or red enemy makes contact with the horizon, your multiplier increases by one.  This is a risk-reward system... if you want high scores, you have to let some of these guys impact the horizon, adding greatly to the danger that you're in.  Waves in the game are fairly short, and the horizon is cleared and fixed between each one, but they're also pretty frantic, so this can build up and kill you pretty fast.  You have to know when to let something connect (and thus when to not shoot at it), and when to make sure it doesnt.  The multiplier resets between waves.  So when you combine all of this, with the movement and such... you've got alot of depth here, and it's quite well balanced.   In addition, every enemy type is unique in it's movement and attack patterns, so you need to keep that in mind too.  And to get the best scores, you need to keep that chain counter going as high as you can before finally firing off the screen clearing bomb.  If you die, you lose the chain and the bomb charge.
In addition to these things, there are bosses that appear every few waves, a variety of powerups to grab, and Arkanoid style bonus stages where you can earn some big points.
The game also features many different modes, and numerous options available to you, including screen effects such as scanlines or the "inverted" one that blazes with the force of a thousand stars.  The overall look of the game is a graphics style that's been pretty popular in recent years, sorta similar to that of Geometry Wars and many others, though without the violent flashiness of that game (so you can, you know, actually see what's happening).  The soundtrack is pretty nice too, by the way.
I dont know how long the main game mode is just yet, particularly because my controller keeps randomly disconnecting due to micro USB cables being cheap little snots. I could do with a pair of scissors right now, really.   But I suspect that there are a fairly large number of waves to go through.
So yes, it's safe to say that I can recommend this one.  It really is a shame to see that the game got buried by Steam's godawful store interface (surprise!), due to it usually wanting to only show "popular" releases (how the heck is this even determined?) so alot of players that might be interested in such a thing wont even notice it, because the blasted thing isnt even SHOWING it.   I think it deserves alot more attention than it's getting.
I say, if you like shmups of any sort, give this one a go.  For $5, you're getting quite a lot here, as this is one of those games that'll take many, many hours to get good at, and there's plenty of depth to it.   Highly recommended.

I swear to god, this is the best puzzle game ever created!
...Alright, that's a little unfair - it's the best puzzle game when including DLC. Which is a bit cheaty, since three of the DLCs are entire games outright packaged as DLC for store-related reasons. But either way, Guntro And The Epic Blunder is the DROD game you should definitely get first, since it's the easiest and intentionally designed to be friendly for new players. After this, the games get progressively harder and harder. REAL hard!
So why is it such a good game? Well, entirely because the puzzles are very, very clever. It's frankly astounding just how many radically different puzzles can be created from a really simple yet consistent system. We're talking in the thousands, here! DROD is a brilliant puzzle game masquerading as a hack and slash. It's turn based and you die in one hit, but so does almost everything else and you move first. In the main it's a game about timing and movement, working out how to get enemies in the exact place that you can kill them before they kill you AND how to avoid trapping yourself. There are a TON of elements which are mostly pretty intuitive and the interactions between them all can create incredibly complex puzzles.
Gunthro and the Epic Blunder is designed to be an easy introduction to the concepts of the series - the puzzles build up in difficulty slowly with intro areas to each major puzzle element allowing you to get familiar with them all. The puzzles are fun but do require a lot of thinking sometimes, with hints for most rooms (press Del by default). Often you'll stare for a while then be like "oh of COURSE!". The official Caravel forums are a friendly community with more hints for pretty much every room already on there - you can access more hints for the room you're on by clicking the ? button. The story isn't particularly amazing and the voice acting isn't professional, but it's still fun and works well enough to get you more immersed in the game with the occassional very funny moment.
The base game has a good amount of hours (not sure how much exactly because haven't finished yet) and then after that you have the DLCs, which were all originally released as full games and are full length with their own voice acting, story etc. There's also TONS of high quality free user created holds on the Caravel forums that will give you literally thousands of hours of game time if you find you enjoy the series. The DLC difficulty goes approximately from easiest to hardest (and from chronologically first to last) base game>KDD>JtRH>TCB, with the other game The Second Sky being latest and hardest.
If you enjoy puzzle games this series is definitely worth a try.
PS One important hint, backspace is undo but it works *while you're dying* so if you're like me and hit the wrong key and die a lot it's no big deal cause you can hit backspace during the death animation.

Disclaimer: I was involved in puzzle/level and story design in this game.
For that reason in this review I will mainly be discussing the DROD series of games as a whole (there are 5 in total and the underlying game mechanics and gameplay remain the same throughout for the most part)
In short, DROD is the most ingenious, fun, and diverse puzzle game I have played and is by far my favourite game of all time.
Good points:
- Fantastic and varied puzzles. These are turn-based, logical puzzles that don't depend on randomness or reflexes - all the information required to solve each room is available and all elements are fully deterministic, but this doesn't stop the puzzles from being fiendishly hard in some cases. In addition to playing to solve the puzzles themselves, there are often many additional challenges and secrets included, and the potential to play competitively (via an online highscore system)
- Clever and flexible puzzle elements: it would be possible to create a ton of puzzles based around a single element alone (for example, trapdoors, tar, mirrors or bombs) and many other puzzle games out there may indeed be based around similar individual mechanics (cf. Sokoban). However, with over 30 elements/enemies (including serpents, goblins, pressure plates, firetraps, spikes, rock golems, time travel tokens...) the number of potential puzzles and their complexity feels almost unlimited. The fact that user-made levels are still being made after over 12 years and fresh ideas are still coming out is a testament to this. This leads me on to:
- Level editor and user-made levels: I love playing DROD but perhaps get even more enjoyment from creating my own DROD levels, posting them on the forum and seeing how people respond to them. It's always rewarding to make a puzzle that others enjoy, or that stumps DROD veterans. When download DROD, you're not just getting the official levels that come with the engine, but the ability to play over 500 other usermade levelsets (called Holds in DROD terminology), some of which actually surpass the official levels in terms of challenge, if not quality in some cases.
- Story: Over the course of 5 games, and in-canon additional Holds ("Smitemasters' Selections", which will also be available on Steam in future) DROD has built up a fantastic story involving the adventures of the Smitemaster, Beethro Budkin, as he explores an underground world and encounters the mysterious Empire (a bureaucracy gone mad). It's a great, and ultimately pretty epic story, complemented by quirky humour and artwork.
- DROD community - The DROD forum
is fantastic. As well as a place to share discussions of DROD and get help with tricky puzzles (there is a "Hints and Solutions" board), and to share usermade holds, there's a lot of interesting activity that takes place outside this, including monthly Contests.
Bad/Not-so-good points:
- This particular set of levels ("Gunthro and the Epic Blunder") was specifically designed for newcomers to DROD. As such, it's a lot easier than the others (so may not be as much of a challenge for DROD veterans), introduces fewer puzzles elements than some of the other entries in the series and doesn't really add much to the storyline as a whole (which is concerned more with Gunthro's grandson, Beethro). It's also a bit a shorter than some of the others in the series. However, if you are new to DROD, I would say it's a great place to start.
- Voice acting - this is generally pretty good and humorous, but can be a bit amateurish at times. I don't really find this a problem myself, but others have commented on this before.
- Graphics - these obviously aren't as good as a lot of games out there. However, I think they suit the game well and I don't think AAA graphics are really required for a puzzle game like this.
- While I've complimented the puzzles, there is occasionally a tendency for some level designers to use less interesting designs. For example, "hack-and-slash" rooms, where you are simply tasked with killing hordes of monsters in the room without having to solve any actual puzzles. I prefer the more "linchpin-style" rooms, where there is a trick you need to figure out to solve the room. This is more of an issue in the first official DROD game (King Dugan's Dungeon) and less so in the later ones, including this one (Guntho and the Epic Blunder), but is also an issue in some of the user-made holds. Some user-made holds will also take advantage of more esoteric puzzle mechanics (cf. the subtleties of serpent movement) and base puzzles around these - if you're not familiar with the more indepth mechanics this can be frustrating, but again this isn't such an issue in the official holds.
- Difficulties getting into DROD: As alluded to above, there are 5 main games (each release with a different engine), a number of official additional levelsets, and a plethora of usermade levels, so it can be hard to know where to start. Added to this, the very first set of levels (King Dugan's Dungeon) is nowhere near as fun or polished as the later ones. That said, Gunthro and the Epic Blunder is probably the best place to start.
TL;DR - get DROD, it's great.

Note: I purchased this game several years ago but only just redeemed a Steam key for it.
Here's how DROD works: you have a dude with a big sword on a grid, with both you and your sword occupying one square each.  The game is turn-based, and on each turn you can move in eight directions, swing your sword clockwise or counterclockwise, or do nothing.  Every time you take an action all the enemies on the board also take an action according to whatever kind of enemy they are.  Your goal for each room is to clear out all the enemies, usually by smacking them with your sword, and make it out of the room afterwards.  It's very much like a turn-based puzzle version of the arcade classic Gauntlet, and while it sounds simple on paper, it is much harder than it sounds.
The series isn't much of a looker, but its depth is far greater than you would expect.  It's a serious brain-burner, with both a huge quantity of puzzles and a high level of quality in their engineering.  Levels are each made up of multiple rooms, and there is some degree of flexibility in solving puzzles since there is often a path around a room's puzzle and into the next room, so when you're stumped on one puzzle you can often find another one to work on.  There are also secret rooms to find and challenges in some rooms to solve the puzzles in certain ways, which in this Steam release award achievements.
GatEB is the first game chronologically in the series and was specifically designed to be a good entry point in the series.  The Steam version emphasizes that by making the later games DLC instead of separate releases (with the exceptions of the RPG spinoff and the most recent release, The Second Sky, which are standalone).  Playing the games in chronological order is recommended, not only because there is an overarching story, but because the difficulty gradually increases between each one.  There are also extra sets of levels called Smitemaster's Selections, which are sort of mini in-between episodes (a full series timeline is available
for those who want to play things in chronological order).  And finally, there is a whole community of fans who like to make their own levels and post them to the Caravel Games website, so there is a lot of free extra content available.
If you are a serious puzzle game fan, you absolutely owe it to yourself to check this one out.

This is the best puzzle game you've never heard of and I mean it. It will kick your♥♥♥♥♥ tickle your brain, and then serve your brain back to you for lunch. This version right here: "Gunthro and the Epic Blunder" was made for beginners to the series. It serves as a prequel to the long 4 (or 5, if you wanna put DROD RPG in the canon) game series that goes King Dungan's Dungeon, Journey to the Rooted Hold, The City Beneath, and The Second Sky. You can play all of the first 4 (this one and everything up to The City Beneath) in this package, making it the ULTIMATE DROD package. You just need to pick up The Second Sky on it's own.
But what is DROD? It's a Top Down, 2D Dungeon Crawl Puzzler. You play as a smitemaster, a janitor for hire that cleans out dungeons and dangerous areas with your trusty sword. Killing Roaches, Raithwings, evil eyes, and more is all in a day's work for a Smitemaster. But here's the kicker: You can move up, down, left, right, and any diagonal direction in between. And you can NEVER put away your sword. It's constantly in your hands, and you have to rotate it by 15 degree increments. Each movement of your body or your sword takes a turn, so you have to figure out how to work with the AI of enemies, the level structure, and the turn based nature in order to solve puzzles. It seems simple, but builds to extremes you never dream of.
But there's then the problem of the graphics. That is that they are strange to say the least. I know many people will be turned off by the graphics. And the cheezy, low quality voice acting also might turn people off. Or the strange music. Or the strange sound effects. But to me it's part of the charm. It's a pulpy fantasy story through and through and the music, sound, and goofy narration help to sell it.

i have waited for a long time to write this review. was close in giving it a thumbs down.
when it first came out it was a mess. crashes, lagging, game did not even end properly. even after several patches. some of the patches were over 15gb, and the game still had issues. every time i started a round, it was a slideshow but was smoother during the fight with occasional freezing. even when my pc was not the best but still within the recommended specs.
but after a serious upgrade of my computer, the game runs actually really smooth. no problems, no lagging, crashes, freezing, nothing. so having new hardware does seem to do the trick, but this could be just for me. some people are still having issues even with the latest hardware.
the game it self plays really smooth and the combat is fluent. the characters look more believable now and the remarks they have for each other by addressing the opponent by name at the beginning of a round, is a very nice detail that was missing in the previous titles.
each character has 3 types of styles that includes weapons too. but it also has its downsides as well since certain moves you like/used in previous titles are not available in every style.
also new are the "brutalities" that can be performed when the enemy is low on health by just performing a normal button pressing, unlike the fatalities that can get obnoxious to perform. but they are, as expected for a MK game, very gory in an over the top way.
the really bad things are that you have to buy the characters instead of unlocking them. also there is a feature called "the krypt" were you wonder around in first person view to unlock tunes, costumes, brutalities, and more. "whats so bad about that?"; you ask. the koins you earn during combat..... sorry, Kombat.... arent very high and therefor a very slow progress to unlock everything. in other words: you are nearly forced to buy the krypt unlock DLC for 20$. which i did since i personally didnt like the krypt and also dont have that much time.
also certain costumes have to be bought instead to unlock them.
the story mode is also shorter than in MK9. it continues were MK9 left off but nothing really special with a rather forgettable story line and some characters since they arent really explained well. also there are these pointless QTEs that have no effect what so ever if you fail them.
what was very frustrating was that even when you buy the retail version as i did, it will download the entire game. i was really surprised to find only one disc in the box after reading that it is over 40gb. all the disc does is starting the download and thats it. it is not so bad for me since i have unlimited bandwidth but mine isnt really that fast and took nearly a day to download the entire game.
the only good thing with the disc version is; that goro was included and a cold war costume for skorpion.

Let me get this straight, you want me to tell you a review about this game? Whoever you are, you might as well go to the curators, because if you've come for a review on this game, you've come to the wrong place. However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

This is a rather nicely made little arcade shooter in the style of classic coin-op machines of the 80s. It's not just a simple remake, though - it brings some new ideas on the table.
At first glance it resembles a space invaders that is mirrored at the ground line. Your mission: defend the horizon against waves of all kinds of alien crafts and other objects that fall into several color-coded categories. Beset from both above and below, you can swivel up and down, slide and jump and collect several powerups. Destroyed bits of horizon make it harder to move around but increase your score multiplier. Every once in a while you will encounter giant bosses and there are bonus levels that may remind you of some other classic games. There are several game modes available and multiple customization options for gameplay, music and visuals. Among other things you can go for crisp graphics, make things look pixelated or emulate a a CRT's scan lines.

When you look at Flump Studios’ games there’s a clear progression, title to title. From the low price, high value Pester, through to last year’s math-shooter, Super Killer Hornet Resurrection,  it’s plain to see that the one man studio from England is honing its craft. Studio owner, Paul Marrable, seems to have a thing for old school arcade shooters and his latest title Horizon Shift continues his affinity for the genre.
As with most of Flump’s other games you’ll be in command of a diminutive spaceship, taking down wave after wave of enemies whilst dodging a barrage of oncoming bullets. Like all of Marrable’s games, though, Horizon Shift has its own “hook”  – a little something to make it stand out from the rest of the crowd. This time around your ship is on a rail in the middle of the screen, the “horizon” if you will, but it’s actually not as restrictive as it may sound.
You can flip over to either side of the rail at any time you like, giving momentary respite from the incoming bullets, but it also doubles the challenge you’ll be facing. Enemies now swarm the screen from both sides meaning you need to be twice as aware of what’s coming for you. It’s a fairly tricky game that has chewed me up and spit me out over and over, but it’s never frustrating because of how cleverly designed your enemies are.
Horizon Shift‘s neon, vector-inspired enemies aren’t your usual mindless drones that thoughtlessly spread across the screen. They’re more clever than that, or  rather, the way in which they work with other enemies is. No single enemy type on its own would provide much of a challenge, but with each having their own abilities, the correct (incorrect?) combination can cause you major headaches.  There’s your bog standard enemy that shoots back at you, turret-like enemies that fire tricky patterns of bullets across the screen, larger swarms of enemies that act as one, and “breakers” that destroy part of your rail, meaning you’ll need to jump over a large hole to reach the other parts.
Things can get very hectic, very quickly, so it’s worthwhile to prioritise which enemies to take out first. Breakers and turrets are sure to cause the most problems, so I opted to take them out as soon as I could. Fortunately, there’s some simple power ups to help you, and you also have the ability to blast away every enemy on the screen, at the expense of your combo bar. There’s also a mirror power up which allows you to control a clone of yourself on the other side of the screen  for double the destructive fun! Bosses and mini games also make an appearance now and then, mixing up the gameplay formula a little, in a move I’ve come to expect from Flump.
Horizon Shift is easily the best thing to come out of Flump Studios. It’s a step up from the studios previous games, in all departments. Not only is it the most visually appealing game to come out of the company, it is by far the most challenging and enjoyable. SHMUP fans should eat this up.

Horizon Shift is a shoot em up that definitely looks different from other shooters.  On first impression the game might look simple, but after fighting through a few waves you'll quickly see how this game innovates.  Let's take a look at Horizon Shift in this first impression review.
It can daunting to look at so let me explain to you how Horizon Shift works.  The game is based on controlling the horizontal line in the middle of the screen.  You can point your ship up or down to shoot at enemies on the top and bottom.  Enemies come in waves and there are boss battles periodically.  Your goal is to survive long enough to pass each wave.  Enemies come quickly and in high variety and they will attempt to disrupt your horizon in different ways.  Some enemies will plant themselves on the horizon and make you move away.  Others will literally blow it up which will mean game over for you.    And of course if your ship comes in to contact with an enemy or their bullets, it's also game over.
Shooting and moving between top to bottom has a very slight delay.  And this isn't a technical issue, it's a design choice.  There is no room for error.  If your actions aren't on point you can't fudge your way through a situation.  It can be a bit of a bullet hell, even when you flip between top and bottom so memorization is key.
This game introduces new elements and it does it right.  The levels, the enemy design, and the art style were very carefully crafted.  It's fun, addicting, and challenging.  At no point will you feel like you had a cheap death.  You death is caused by you making the wrong move at the wrong time.  Levels go by quickly and even when you die, you jump right back in to the action.  So you find yourself addicted to passing levels one by one.  Every attempt is a learning experience and if you are persistent, you will beat those hard levels.  The most challenging levels will require you to memorize enemy patterns especially in the beginning of the wave so you don't get overwhelmed.
The art style is very basic, but attractive and it ties in to the gameplay.  Color and shape are important motifs because they determined how enemies will disrupt your horizon.  Green enemies will bounce off your horizon making them less lethal.  Red enemies will mount themselves on your horizon and move back and forth.  The blue enemies will blow holes in your horizon.  And the swarm will annihilate your horizon.  This effects the priority of who you will shoot first and which hits you can afford to take.  It's not game over if red and green enemies attack your horizon.  You can still survive until the end of the wave.  You also have a bomb meter on the bottom that fills up from killing enemies.  The bomb is kind of like a panic button, because it will clear all enemies on the screen temporarily.  So you have to strategically save it for the right moment when you can't possible kill all of the enemies.
Boss battles are bullet hell moments that remind me of Ikaruga or Jamestown.  Bosses have distinct patterns that you have to weave yourself through.  I actually found most of the early boss battles to be fairly easy, but fun.
Horizon Shift has a ton of options for variety and replay ability.  There's four different modes to choose from and three unlockable modes.  They all have the same levels, but it effects how you play through them.  You get to restart from the last wave you played from,k which is great for making progress even if your skills aren't top notch.  There's also high challenge options like survival where you get no lives and no checkpoints.  You can also crank up the game speed to twice as fast.   The high variety of modes make it customizable and also easy to pickup but hard to master.  The game also has many options for how you want the music to play out.  And the music is rockin.  It's a perfect soundtrack for a shoot em up like this.
Horizon Shift is the perfect blend of classic shmup but with innovative features.  There's plenty of options for replayability.  And the game is only $5 on Steam.  This is a game that you definitely want to play.  Subscribe to the Skilled channel for more game reviews.

Name: Horizon Shift
Developer: Flump Studios
Genre: Arcade Game pure and simple no beating around the bush with this one.
Personal Verdict: This game... made me cry.
Horizon Shift is an innovative arcade game that  combines elements of shoot em up, arcadey action and the brutality of the shoot em up genre. Now normally in this case we ended up with a hard version of games like meteor, galaga etc etc but like most arcade games from the new to the old Horizon Shift introduces elements that differ it from the competition, namely the Horizon element.
This game reminds me of asteroid, well chatting with the dev the whole graphic side is inspired by asteroid so that means it plays out wholly in wireframe style graphics art of yer olden days games. That said the background is pretty well done in my book and helps mesh it along with the music as you can see why later.
The music is awesomely psychedelic, which is to say it will serve to pump you up and make you drown in its varied synth like tune. Combine this with the trippy background and by the end of my numerous defeat I was feeling trippy as heck.
Make no mistake. This game is hard. Very very hard. Paul if you are reading this know the fact that I hate you very much.
On to the gameplay, so what makes Horizon Shift so unique? Well to start with lets talk about what it is not unique in. Its an arcadey game, you press z to shoot, x to jump and c to bomb like most games. Enemies are plenty and comes in a lot of variety and powerups, score, suddenly paid homage minigame appearing are all the standard stuff it does.
What it does bring to the table however is the Horizon mechanic. Your shiplike object resides in a line right in the middle of the screen and this line is not invincible. Some enemies will destroy your Horizon piece by piece if they come in contact with it and others will downright obliterate it resulting in an instant KO since the Horizon is the only solid platform for you to stand on. Let say that only part of the Horizon is destroyed you can still survive the stage by jumping over the gaps, a rather risky move seeing as the later levels are choke full of enemies and stage hazard.
In any case, enemies come from bottom and top side and barring one particular power up you can't really shoot up and down at the same time so you have to switch sides all the time to counter them.
Enemies come in many flavour, the one I dubbed invader simply because they ride on your Horizon and move along it killing you if you come in contact with them, swarmer who targets your Horizon and destroy it, shooter who spits out balls of death at you but are easily avoided for most parts, its the combination of invader and swarmer that usually ends your life.
If you somehow in an impossible way manages to finish the game, more modes are unlocked for you! So you can continue dying and earning score on the leaderboard.
Happy to say the game controls well, sure it is a bit hard to jump because sometimes you overshoots the gap but hey, it works and no misspressed ever occur to me.
Horizon Shift, a pretty fun arcade shoot em up with unique mechanic, should you get this game? Depends, if you like this sort of games then go for it. The game is not bad at all and the only con I could muster is my inability to get good at this game. Overall Enjoyable.

Horizon Shift is a bullet-hell wave based shooter. You are essentially on your horizon (no surprises) with your little space ship/gunner. The game play is very similar to that of Space Invaders except you have to do it on two sides of the horizon which at the best of times is a hectic war. You can collect powerups, sheilds and if you kill enough enemies, you get a "wipe the board" abilitiy which is a life saver at times.
The graphics and art style is that of an arcade game, and a style that I very much enjoy, you can also add different effects to the visual aspect such as an inverse effect to give your game a different feel.  The game is hard as nails, I have only managed to get a score of about 5500 so far, and that took a lot of concentration and effort, with a lot of rage quits. The game is surprisingly addictive; you will keep coming back for more as you just have to get past that one wave that keeps destroying you.
The only technical issue I had was the loading times. I was surprised to find that I had to wait at least 20 seconds for the game "load" from launching, and about 10 seconds each time you start a game.
I can recommend Horizon Shift as it is something different - it will keep you coming back for more, it's like a hot but horrible girlfriend, you know you shouldn’t keep going back to it, but the rewards are awesome.

In short DROD is considered by some to be possibly the best puzzle game series ever and so far I´m more and more inclined to agree. The mechanics of this series are superb thanks to the balance of freedom the movement system allows and often lenient but nonetheless challenging puzzle/room design. While there are places where one is looking for that single perfect move even deeper into the series the majority of rooms allow the player to freely experiment and explore the challenge ahead. Where time limits are present they feel natural and interesting as opposed to the game dev just wanting you to retrace their steps one by one.
Now as far as Gunthro and the Epic Blunder goes it is good to remember that even though the entirety of DROD is showing up on Steam at once these are all very extensive games and GatEB is both a good starting point into the series and a rather big game in it´s own right. I can easily recommend it to anyone, though looking back it may have been a bit on the easy side for me personally. The learning process is fantastic one way or the other as everything is predictable and you are free to both explore the mechancs at your own pace or go through the quite detailed in-game manual when unclear why something works the way it does.
Audiovisuals of DROD are highly refined, consistent and surprisingly enjoyable. I would describe them as tricksy and they are for me the exact correct mix of ridiculous and self-serious. Basically all of it is intentionally over-the-top but with none of the joke-y 4th wall breaking bs. Most importantly the music is absolutely fantastic for this style of game. It sounds great both looping for an hour in the background and for the 15 seconds you pay attention to it while staring at the screen looking for your next move.
I could go on and on about specific game mechanics, different room styles(pure puzzle/execution based/monster horde) and such but honestly I can´t be bothered for now so "it´s bloody fantastic in basically every way" is going have to suffice.

DROD is an epic series in the history of puzzle games. I'm not going to write a lenghty review, just a piece of advice: if you're not sure what to think of DROD, go grab the first game in the series, DROD: Architects' Edition, that is available completely free here:
You can also download a demo of any DROD game here:
Once you play it and inevitably fall in love with it, come back here or go their store and buy every DROD game they released, starting with this one.

First let me clear up that this is appearently the 4th game in the DROD series, but it's the first story-wise and also the easiest, so it seems to be a good entry point into the series. Parts 1-3 are supposed to come out as DLC to this game and then there's a whole second series, godmayhavemercyonallofus.
DROD is a pretty damn good classic puzzle game with a unique mechanic: the movement is the same as in roguelikes, except you cary a sword that you can rotate, which takes one turn as well. Hit a monster, it dies, get hit by anything, you die. The way you progress in this part of the series is mostly straightforward: clear all rooms of monsters and proceed. You can almost always clear a room once you enter it, so there's no backtracking or confusing giant dungeons where you have to run back and forth. Still it doesn't feel too linear, since there is an overworld map and it is not always prescribed which dungeon to tackle next.
The main selling point of DROD is clearly the puzzle design which is on top of its class. The mechanics are quite simple but applied in so many ways that thinking out of a box is almost always required. If you like hard puzzle games this is clearly for you. It might be compared to Sokoban-style games, but the puzzles are much more varied. If anyone played that game: they reminded me of the Puzzles in Lufia 2.
You have a barebones story which is kept alive by horrible but hilarious voice acting and very short sequences of some NPCs moving around. It's nice that it's there and it gives some atmoshpere to the various dungeons.
Two negative points: while you can create and download levels from the website and integrate them in the game to play them, the more convenient way of doing all of this inside the game itself is only possible if you become a member of Caravel Net, which costs money (quite little though, but the price of 10 Euro for a game that is a few years old might be already considered high by some).
The other negative point would be the sound effects, which are quite annoying and unfortunately not satisfying enough (when you kill enemies, clear rooms or dungeons, ...).
The game does not have support for a gamepad, I think the reason is that the developer thought diagonal movement is not precise enough (which is important for this game). However, I found a nice way to enable precise diagonal movement and implemented it with an AutoHotKey script. You can find the details
