I'm not even sure where to begin, I love the DROD series so much and this is one of my favorite entries.  It's a masterpiece!  As an indie game dev DROD has been a huge inspiration to me.  It features some of the absolute best level design and play mechanics out there.
This game is truly a hidden gem and deserves way more attention than it has gotten over the years.  On the surface, it may not look like much -the graphics are a bit cheesey, same with the dialogue -but rest assured this game is awesome and amazing where it really matters: the gameplay.
If you like puzzle games, chess games, critical thinking, tricky levels, and outside of the box thinking then you will most likely love this game.  Yes, it can be frustrating at times, but usually if you stop and take a step back and change your approach you can usually find the solution.
Drod is turn based but rarely feels slow.  When you move, everything else moves.  This allows you to stop and think when you need to or rush through a level if you want to and that really helps the flow of the game.  The puzzle design here changes wildly which really helps keep it a fresh experience from start to finish.  The introduction of one new element dramatically changes the way some levels need to be played.  Sometimes there will be the occasional puzzle that feels tedious but in my opinion that's true of most all puzzle games.  No others have managed to be as consistently fun to me as the Drod games.
DROD: Gunthro and the Epic Blunder is a fantastic mix of what made the first three DROD games so great.  It doesn't take long to start getting tricky.  If you're new to the series you may have a bit harder time adjusting and knowing what to do, but DROD is one of those games that even when you adapt to it; it's not going to be easy.  It's going to throw you curve balls and it's going to challenge you which makes it all the more a truly satisfying experience.
If you are totally new to the series, I would strongly suggest taking the time to fully customize the controls to your comfort.  I personally prefer to use the desktop/number pad settings and the arrow keys as my clockwise/counter clockwise swing.  This allows me to eat nachos and other power-up brain foods with my left hand while controlling the entire game with my right hand -which means DROD often earns the rare-but-highly-coveted title as my go-to lunch time game!
I could sing praises of this game and this series all day, but I've probably rambled enough about it.  Hopefully you love it as much as the rest of us DROD fans do!

.... This is just..... Hard to review in a sense in how to describe this game.
This game is good but bad at the same time in some sense; but the good over shadows the bad only by so much... I guess I'll begin with the bad.
Bad:
The story is boring: In the sense it's your basic adventure story, something evil from an old age of technology and other sh*t comes out of no where and threatens to destroy the world and it's kinda mediocore from there. Sacred places with extra races who are grateful you recovered their technology or home or something precious to them that they give you a treasure so near and dear tot hem that you abuse it for puzzles and your own amusement such as dropping rocks out of the sky onto villagers for the hell of it.
The sound cues are just as bad, with the exception of the music, which is ok and some of the puzzle solving sounds, everything else feels out of place... When I got the Earth medallion for example, the laser like sound didn't sound like power was flowing from it and it's just awkward silence from there witht he voice from the medallion coming out of it. There are a dozen other sound clips in the game that just dislodge the whole experience. EVEN THE VOICE ACTING IS JUST..... WHY?!
If it was just the programmers voice acting to their game like the developers in Two World where the teams don't know HOW to voice act; Then I can give it the benefit of the doubt and let that slide for now.
The Good:
While it isn't as BIG or impressive as the game it's cloning, Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker and Legend of Zelda, any top down zelda-like game; It does bring other ideas to the table the legend of zelda genre won't touch or hasn't touched on yet.
Experience points: Ok, show of hands, who here finds grinding tiresome after doing it for a while in turn by turn RPG's and who here finds grinding LESS tiresome just by going around and killing lots of badies just because you we're bored and nothing good was on TV... Well, Ocean Horn uses the later part of that experience and it kinda works. What do you gain from the leveling? Well; imrpessive buffs such as the ability to carry more bombs or carry more arrows and so forth. In Zelda you either had to buy that kinda stuff or earn it after a tedious minigame; which is fine, unless that mini-game was a pain and you needed to perfect it. It's nothing new in some other top-down Zelda Clones, but at least this one has a decent idea of how to go about it.
World: The world is kinda like a mix between Minecraft and Legend of zelda and weirdly enough, I'm ok with that. You have an area to explore, you can't fall from great heights which forces you to think about how you navigate your terreign and so on. When you travel from island to island, the ocean water kinda looks like real ocean water, nearly realistic that I have to give the developers points for details like this and the different biomes from island to island.
Magic: Before I get stomped on, I want to ask a simple question, Aside from Din's Fire, Nayru's Love, Faore's wind and Large spin attack among OTHER spells in the Legend of Zelda, have any of them interacted int he world that you had to use to solve multiple puzzles? I've only seen it A FEW times in both N64 game's and in Link's Adventure for the NES and that's it. In this game, the spells or at least the magic I've found so far has multiple uses from puzzle solving to simple combat. Earlier I mentioned a spell that dropped rocks out of the sky; that spell can be used to fight enemies since you can throw rocks at them while also it can be used to hit switches you can't normally reach due to some difficulty.
Misc: The monster designs are though out in terms of how you beat them and their complexitity grows with each new island you find and become more difficult to beat. The character models, while not well designed, are ok for the kind of game developed, Puzzles, when solved, don't take 10-20 SECONDS TO SHOW THE EFFECT OF WHAT HAPPENED AFTER YOU SOLVED IT..... Looking at you ocarina of time..... There's places to explore for loot, treasure and it's fun to kill stuff.
I already heard theres an Oceanhorn 2 ind evelopment and after seeing a screen shot of it; I have high hopes for this team toa ctually make a game that could probably rival Zelda. If you have the money and just beat breath of the wild while WAITING for the DLC to it to be developed, I would defiantly give this one a look to the end.

This game is the ultimate tribute to Heavy Metal and I recommend it to anybody likes that genre of music.
The story of Eddie Riggs, the roadie who is transported to the world of Metal by an ancient god is something different for once, there are several awesome characters, like Ozzy Osbourne as the Guardian of Metal, and of course there is the great soundtrack of 107 different heavy metal classics.
The gameplay is a mixed bag. On one hand it is an open world action game similar to GTA (cruising around, finding missions, doing missions), just a lot more empty, which is kind of disappointing (But the landscape is full of references to metal bands and album covers which is pretty awesome). But the fighting and driving around is pretty cool. There are collectibles and some repeating mini games like fighting off a horde of enemies or racing, which give currency which you can spend at the Guardian of Metal to upgrade your weapons, your hot rod and customize Eddie. And of course there are the story missions.
Later in the game, a strategy game part is added. You fight an enemy team and the goal is to destroy the enemy's stage (base). You have to collect Fans (resources) to build your troops which you can lead against enemy troops and ultimately to the stage. While the game unfolds you get a larger variety of troops and the battles get more difficult, but I never found them that much fun. Something was just lacking, probably the lack of strategic depth, since just spamming troops will usually lead to a victory. There is also a multiplayer part consisting of that mode, however I haven't played that.
The graphics are not the best ever, but the comic-y style works and the goofy character looks just match the style of the game.
Over all, as I said in the beginning, I 100% recommend this game to any Heavy Metal fan, for gameplay fans I can't really recommend it to anyone, since it's not a great specimen for any genres it tries to fit in. I still recommend it for the story and the characters.

Is it possible to set an entire game as my wallpaper? I only ask because the art style and world design in this game are phenomenal. Even though the technology is fairly standard, the art direction elevates the game's world from interesting to something special.
The story is a standard fairytale, but told brilliantly through gameplay and expressive character animations alone. One area near the end of the game goes above and beyond in this regard, and hopefully this isn't a spoiler, but I'm tagging it just in case,
.
The gameplay has you controlling two characters at once. Each is controlled with one analog stick and one trigger, for movement and interaction respectively. You mainly solve puzzles which require you to use both brothers' abilities to traverse the game's beautifully realized world.
If I had to complain, I would point out that I did at one point run into a progression-stopping bug, but it was easily remedied by restarting the level from the chapter select screen. I would also note that near the halfway point, the basic traversal began to feel a bit repetitive, though to its credit the game immediately introduced a new mechanic that complicated things and alleviated the repetition somewhat. Other than that, it can sometimes be a bit confusing if the brother who responds to the left stick is on the right side of the screen, or vice versa, but now I'm just nitpicking.
So, is it worth the $15? As glowing as my impression of it is, I don't think I can definitely say yes, and that comes down to its length. I beat the game in about 3 hours, and $5 an hour is not a great value proposition. That said, the game never overstays its welcome, nor does it feel rushed, so I can't hold the length against it. If you don't think 3 hours is worth $15, wait for a sale, but definitely play this gem.
P.S. The game requires a controller with two analog sticks. Come prepared.

So what we have here is a pretty nice merge of spectacle fighter and faux MMO.
The game really gives off a strong MMO vibe from it yet i consider it to be one of the best mergers of cRPG and Spectacle fighter to date as the items you are wearing affect your characters stats more than in real spectacle fighters.
The closest game i can compare Amalur to would probably be... The witcher 3.
In fact i could safely say it's a more goofy (them giant swords and hammers) and slightely less dark (still rather dark tho) cousin of TW3.
The game includes relatively extensive crafting where you disasemble various items for parts (that have stats) and put them back together in order to form the item you desire (assuming you have te right parts of course). You can even name them so i ended up running around with a greatsword i christened "Sharpened metal door" and its siblings "sharpened metal door mk 2" and mk 3.
The combat takes some hints from arkham but it's not a full on copy where you jsut stand in a crowd and hit the counter button every 2 seconds. Yu can do that here however its MUCH harder. You don't get any indicators and you have to parry at the very last moment to get a counter going.
The game is chock full of cntent as well. There are many side quests. So many in fact that after the first 40 hours i decided to stop doing htem altogether because i just ended up hilariously overleveled making most of the endgame a cakewalk.
This brings me to the downsides...
Problems with difficulty and level scaling.
The game is just too easy if you decide to do side quests. Even on hard i only ever had problems at the begining but after several zones cleared of quests my character became overleveled again. It's really hard to strike a balance where you are not crushing your opposition or being demolished by it...
This is corrected by a community mod but... do i really have to cheat (you need cheatengine to use it) in order to have a satisfyingly difficult experience with this game?
I really don't mean to sound elitist but even on hard the game is simply a cakewalk where you can literally oneshot enemies while laughing off their damage.
For the TES veterans out there... remember that one alchemist character you made? Yes the hilariously overpowered one. This is how silly overpowered your hero gets in KoA... well maybe without the movespeed and jumping.
All in all the game is great and mod irons out some of its problems.
if you see it on sale then by all means grab it. heck if you see it 75% off grab the collection because for all its flaws this is still a gem.

If you’re looking for a solid action-RPG to play, Kingdom of Amalur: Reckoning would be a great choice, but it’s not without its faults. My 89 hours at the point of this review are straight after completing the main storyline and the vast majority of the sidequests, but while I’ve enjoyed my time I won’t be going back to 100% or play the DLC any time soon.
The Good:
+ Combat is sharp, responsive and entertaining. I played a rogue/mage hybrid, using a combination of either daggers or faeblades, with a bow and magic to support throughout. Once you get used to the combat style, you quickly learn a series of useful combos. I only played briefly with some of the other weapons, but they seemed ok as well. I was using the Xbox 360 controller for Windows that worked really well.
+ The creators have put together an interesting world, with a few ideas that put it above the generic tropes it could have fallen into. Lore isn’t normally my sort of thing, but I felt more interested in the world than I do with similar games.
+ Loads of content. My playthrough was a fairly swift run, despite doing most of the sidequests, and I think I could have padded this out with an extra 10 – 15 hours if I was a bit more thorough. Sidequests are largely solid with a minimal number of fetch quests. The House of Sorrows faction questline towards the end of the game was a particular highlight for me.
However, it felt like the content became sparser as you got closer to the end – with fewer sidequests per area. I remember spending ages in the first area, but got through the final continent in no time at all. Might just be me though.
+ Loads of concepts. Blacksmithing, alchemy, two types of lockpicking, stealth, enchanting, hidden items, player housing, interesting collectables – the game feels like it has it all. Admittedly, each of the areas are fairly shallow, but they do help spice the game up.
+ The game is fully voice acted with the exception of the protagonist. I know this has annoyed a few, but to me it felt like a conscious choice by the devs to help the player project onto their character. Real choices in dialogue are fairly minimal and the consequences irrelevant, but the voice acting is consistently high quality and there is loads of backstory in the dialogue if you’re looking for it.
+ The graphical style holds a nice point between realistic and cartoony. The art is sharp and colourful throughout and works well.
+ The game performed well on my mid-range PC, with no slowdown at 1080p. I’ve read that many people had lots of technical issues with the demo, but these seem to have been resolved for the end product.  A couple of issues do creep in more towards the end of the game (getting stuck on scenery, interaction with some objects), but nothing gamebreaking at all.
+ Lots and lots and lots of loot. Most of it is fairly useless, but the illusion of variety holds strong in the items you pick up.
The Bad:
- I’m a fairly average gamer, and found the difficulty far too easy after the first 10 hours. Once you find your playstyle and learn how the limited number of beasties attack, you will be in cruise control for the rest of the game. The only times where the difficulty was higher was against mages, where their attacks can be harder to dodge and they also back away from melee types. This is quickly sorted by the ‘fateshift’ mode, which offers from stylish killing blows but removes any real challenge.
The difficulty completely fell apart in the last 10 hours for me, as I made my own equipment (without playing the system) that ended with me being so overpowered I was one-shotting most of the regular enemies with my bow.
The final boss also failed to land a single hit on me.
There is an attempt to up the difficulty by making the ‘harder’ enemies more frequent on the second continent, but it’s too little, too late in my mind.
It’s worth noting that I was aware of the issues around difficulty before starting, and played through the full game on hard. I’d recommend that everyone does the same if they are a vaguely competent gamer. A fan made difficulty patch is around if you are looking for more challenge, but I haven’t tested it.
I seriously doubt I would have finished the game on a lower difficulty, there would have been no challenge at all.
- Content repeats itself far too often, and disappointingly the developers failed to offer up even reskins to give the impression of there being more enemy types. This extends to the dungeons as well, which are limited to a few themes with only the minority feeling unique. Given the size of the world, this becomes a big issue around the midpoint of the game – I had to take a break from playing for a solid week to avoid getting bored.
- Like almost all games of its ilk, money becomes completely pointless after the opening 20 hours. I finished with about 12 million gold, and this was with salvaging all of the equipment in the last 15 hours. For perspective, the biggest gold sink for me were trainers, who only cost 45k each at the highest level.
I rolled my eyes after a quest to collect a set of books across the world, spanning about 60 hours of game time, rewarded me with 800 gold on my return.
- The main storyline is a disappointment. While I said above I enjoyed the lore of the world, the main storyline was about as bland as it comes – amnesiac protagonist travelling across the world to face the big bad. Amnesia can be played well, but you learn nothing of your past until the final 10 minutes, where one of your companions gives you a load of exposition. A really lazy effort in storytelling.
The main quest also suffers badly from being too sparse. You end up doing a larger quest in the story, but then get sent a few areas across the map before you can progress it further. After doing all the sidequests along the way, I’d completely forgotten what was going on by the time I reached the next point – this being the only game I was playing at the time.
- The camera, especially in combat, is slightly odd and far too low angle. While you do get used to it, it is a shame there is no flexibility.
Conclusion:
Reading the above, it seems like I don’t like the game. Quite the opposite – I really enjoyed my time playing and do recommend it. I think the negative points above stem from the fact that the game is close to greatness, and with a bit more time and direction Big Huge Games could have made something really special. It’s disappointing to see that they went under after finishing the game – although something this large is a huge task, especially for a first game. I would have loved to have seen a sequel to solve its issues – the finale also set up nicely for the proposed MMO if it was successful.
Overall, this game gets a recommendation from me. If you’re looking for a fairly light action RPG, you could do a lot worse.

DROD is basically chess on steroids with countless elements you can combine, and it's also brutally difficult (as is made especially apparent in the DLC for this game, namely JtRH, TCB, and SMS 1+2). Time after time again, I sit down stumped on a room and just feel dumb. I eventually concede and go on Caravel's forums to find the solution to the room.
But you know what?
It's fun as hell.
Not only that.
But it's !&@?ing amazing.
Seriously, DROD is a special game where every puzzle is crafted to be a fun experience. The many, many elements it has, can mesh together in different ways. And, heck, you even get to experiment with it yourself; you get yourself a level editor, for FREE. You don't even need to unlock it. It is a key part of the DROD engine, and you got it, pal.
Not to mention, with the CaravelNet system, you can literally have INFINITE holds to play as they come out regularly by the playerbase-- that is to say, this game's replayability is through the roof. Sure, Steam's version doesn't come with CaravelNet subscription, but that's only a small price to pay.
This game is, in my honest opinion, THE best game on Steam I've played, and I could sink years onto it and barely scratch the surface. The gameplay is simple to understand, but hard to master (especially on more brutal puzzles), and the writing is a great mash of silly, surreal humor based on the environment, and surprisingly serious scenarios (as becomes more apparent in JtRH, TCB, and the other DROD game on steam, TSS), all with a dopey lovable oaf at the center of it all who is determined to find answers to a few questions he had... and the many more he gets along the way, and later finds himself trying to stop a giant threat.
If you like puzzle games, try DROD. If you like strategy games, try DROD. If you like the Legend of Zelda, try DROD. And if you like quirky worlds, try DROD just for the worldbuilding it has. It's not a hidden gem, it's a hidden 50-ton hunk of solid gold hidden in plain sight, protected by a few dungeon roaches.

[NB: Although I have played less than an hour on this Steam version, I have have played many hundreds of hours of DROD in its non-Steam versions.]
DROD is hardly known, but is one of the best puzzle games around.   Anyone who likes logic puzzle solving -- who gets a kick out of su-dokus, multi-state mazes, chess problems or similar -- will love this game.
Like all great ideas, it looks simple on the surface.  Guide your character around a series of rooms, killing monsters with your sword.  Sounds cheesy: childish, even.  But beneath this unpromising exterior lies a game of immense subtlety and depth.
The game is turn-based, and the different monsters each have their own, predictable AI.  So you will often have to create chains of reasoning along the lines of "To kill that roach *there*, I need to hold open a door *here*.  But I can't do that myself without waking up the Evil Eye in the corner.  So instead, I need to lure a different roach into position to hold the door open for me.  Which in turn means that..." And so on.
The rooms are greatly varied -- some are purely logical rooms of the type I just described; others require skill at defeating a large host of monsters before they overpower you.  But all are fair, and there is plenty of help available online for most of the harder rooms.
DROD has been a part of my life, on and off, for many years.  It's one of the few puzzle games I return to again and again.  Highly recommended.

DROD is the best-kept secret in the world of indie games, despite the efforts of its fans. Descended from the line of tile puzzlers like Sokoban and Chip's Challenge, it combines simple turn-based core mechanics with a rich, varied, and elegant set of puzzle elements to build puzzles that will make your head spin but are just so rewarding to solve.
Gunthro and the Epic Blunder is the fourth of the five main DROD games to date, but it's by far the best place to jump in. It smoothly introduces the basics of DROD play - move and swing your sword to slay every monster in the room - before delving into deeper exploration of the more complex mechanics and challenging enemies. Most areas of the game both teach and test understanding of a specific puzzle element, like the wraithwing that attacks in swarms and flees when alone, the serpent that's immune to your sword but will die if it's trapped, or the golem that reshapes the puzzle as you play by leaving a pile of rocks where it dies. By the end, all the elements are combined into puzzles tricky enough to test even veterans of the series.
Even after you've reached the end of the game, DROD has more to offer. Finding and clearing the extra-devious secret rooms unlocks a difficult bonus area. The challenge system goes beyond your everyday achievements, asking you to devise alternate solutions to specific rooms with demanding requirements like not turning your sword or slaying a specific monster in a low number of turns. You can play for score, optimizing your solutions to clear each room in as few turns as possible. And you can play any of the hundreds of custom level sets developed by the community over more than a decade.
I've spent hundreds of hours playing the DROD games. I've worked out puzzle solutions while cooking, walking my dog and even in my sleep. I started drinking an extra cup of coffee daily to help me with The City Beneath. DROD may not be for everyone, but if it clicks for you, it might be your new favorite game. Every fan of puzzle games needs to try DROD.

It all starts so gently, you get placed on the centerline of what looks like a giant ping pong table that has had its' net removed. The game has a distinctly neon feel to it, with lots of wireframe overlaid over a 3D background and a thumping dance track that settles you in, you are told that the right thumbstick will flip you so you can either shoot up, or down (Geddit, the ship goes both ways... *ba-dum-tsh* ... I'll get my coat -
).
Initially a few blue wireframe asteroids come sailing from both directions, you hammer them with your dinky ship and it's lovely shooty bangs... and then the game turns the screws. Before you know it you're dealing with lasers cutting off sections of the playfield, rocks smashing off pieces of the centerline (meaning that if you navigate off of it, you're going to die horribly, you have a jump button for this purpose), and bullets that either cannot or CAN penetrate the centerline and thus mean that sometimes you can take cover, and sometimes you can't.
... and it was all going so nicely.
If it were -just- a case of shooting up or down, this would be straightforward enough and a reasonable game, but it goes far, far beyond that. The playfield will shift, changing the rules of the game with death beams which cut the field up into little pieces, side based turrets that plop doomspikes onto the centerline that you must either dodge or hop over. This game rapidly evolves past "Nice" and well into the realms of bullet hell, plus platform hell to boot. It's evil, but it's also brilliant at the same time.
Then layered on top of that is an appropriately excellent house/EDM set of tracks that easily warrant the purchase of the OST on top. They're designed to grow and change as you work through the waves, and do so beautifully, and they have real *punch*, which helps with the whole dancing arcade machine thing as you frantically hammer your way through the ever clustering waves of chaos and mayhem around the edges of your horizon centerline.
At the price point asked, and for what the game gives in return, you'd be -absolutely mad- not to take this one into your collection, especially if you're a fan of score attacks and arcade games in the vein of Beat Hazard Ultra, or Intake.
Verdict :

Now excuse me as I practice patting my head and rubbing my belly...

: The status of the PC port. My computer is pretty hefty, needs some upgrades done but it could run Witcher 3 at Ultra with almost everything turned on and still get over 60fps. With this, I'm on high, with MSAA off and I still get only 50fps. In addition, as has been stated on Reddit and the forums here, as well as experienced by myself, the game crashing for some stupid reasons that should never have gotten past testing. "Oh, you like Exclusive Fullscreen? Too bad, you're going to crash during an UNSKIPPABLE cutscene, forcing you to watch it every time you try". Like come on Nixxes, what were you smoking during your time at the office?
: Mouse Acceleration and some menu options. It's fine there's mouse acceleration, some people might enjoy that and that's the point of PC, for the ability to customize. What's not fine is there's no option whatsoever to disable Mouse Acceleration, not even via a config file like Human Revolution. That is an absolutely terrible decision and needs to be fixed. As well, this is just for every developer out there that does this, STOP USING PERCENT SIGNS FOR FIELD OF VIEW! Just stop, it's idiotic, we have no idea what it actually means, use actual numbers.
: Square Enix, stop chopping up games because you're a bunch of money grubbing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, just please stop. I'm fine with a bad ending, I'm fine with one that leads into a sequel, but I want a complete story, whereas all the reviews and all the people that have beaten it have stated, it just abruptly ends, no warning or even indication you're coming to the final mission, it just ends. I dealt with that in Deadwood, I don't need that in Deus Ex
: While I have outlined my issues up above with the port (Nixxes) or Publisher interference (Square Enix), the developers (Eidos) have done what they do best, make a good game. The game play is smooth, giving you a good grasp of your abilities as well as how you're able to go through an area the way you want. Want to kill everyone, go for it. Want to sneak through and do your best Solid Snake? Bloody well go for it, it's your choice. The city hub is properly big, there's tons of sidequests, some that are more engaging than the main story even. In summary, while the game is good and I am heavily enjoying it, I am giving it a negative review because of issues with the port and things like microtransactions in a single player game, I absolutely cannot condone microtransactions, let alone in a single player game. Mount & Blade: Warband is a great game.
It is set in a medieval era on a fictitious continent, with several competing kingdoms or factions.
You play the part of a wanderer who dreams of becoming a major player.
You start off with low-grade weapons, and have to earn the money to buy better ones (or you can get extra weapons by defeating your enemies).
You roam the land, helping villagers, defeating bandits, and doing other virtuous acts - or you may even decide to operate on the wrong side of the law by attacking innocent people, robbing, trade caravans, looting, and pillaging.
Or you may do a bit of both - maybe you might decide to be a law-abiding citizen by day and a crime lord by night.
As you go further in the game, you can start to recruit heroes to your cause, as well as hire men for your growing band of warriors. That's when things start to become a lot more exciting.
When you have a sizeable little army, you can lay siege to castles and have major engagements in the field.
The battles are carried out in third-person format, up-close and personal, as are various other tasks, whilst you direct your overall strategies via a map.
You can operate as a vassal of an existing leader, or you can operate on your lonesome - or become a vassal, but then break away to form your own fiefdom.
If you campaign hard with your forces right across the width and breadth of the continent, and defeat all of your enemies (making them bow before you, or die by the sword), then you can proclaim yourself as the ruling monarch for all the land!
Highly recommended.

If you're looking for a game that will test your platform-game skills, look no further.
In this game, you play as a swanky egg who, after a small mishap with a teleporter, is trying to find his way home. How will this egg get home, you ask? Through 40+ levels of pure hell. Jump through spikes, traps, and pits with only your egg-physics and persistence to carry you through. Pray to RNGesus as a certain tyrannical spectator sends his side-scrolling wall of death toward you with the ultimate goal of ridding your existence from the face of the eggy-Earth. This game has the ability to make you scream great warsongs of rage, but it can also make you cry tender tears of pure bliss. Do all of this with a wonderful sountrack playing in the background, sure to soothe any lost and broken soul.
So, do you think you have what it takes to help an egg return home?
Overall, I thought the game was a very enjoyable experience. Anyone who knows me knows that I am terrible at platform games, so this game was a real challenge for me... A challenge that I have beat! I will try to expand a bit on some of the things I liked the best about this game which include the story, the music, and the physics.
Those who have played this game may be thinking, "What? There's a story to this game?" To that, I have to say, "Yes! There is!" This game features a very simple, amusing, and wordless story about an egg who made a silly mistake and just wants to go home. It's very hard to not sympathize with this poor egg, but it's also hard to not chuckle a bit at his situation!
I know I'm biased, but the music is great! Sometimes I leave the game open in the background just to listen to it! I never thought I would be hearing Mozart's Oboe Concerto in a game like this, but I guess it's just the little things that take the cake. I think the music is very fitting to the game as a whole; it gives the game a very quirky, yet sophisticated feel to it. Needless to say, great selection of music!
For the physics of this game, all I can say is kudos to the developer. When I first started playing, I thought this game would be fairly simple because the egg would roll and jump like a ball... but I was horribly wrong. You play as an egg! Therefore, you roll and jump how an egg would! This offers a whole set of challenges and setbacks that you would have never even thought of experiencing. Sometimes when you try to move to the right, the way your egg-body is angled causes you to move to the left instead. Or maybe you are trying to jump over a large pit and need to gain enough momentum to make the leap... let's just say, good luck on timing that jump! I truly think that out of all the good things this game has going for it, the use of egg-physics is simply the best of them.
So, if you have a few bucks to spare, I'd definately recommend adding this game to your collection! It's a simple, fun game that offers very thoughtful challenges and plently of rage-quits.

I am not a fan of tower defence games usually, but this is a gem. The setting is brilliant too, and even an old stickler like me can overlook the historical inaccuracies (not that it was ever intended to be that sort of game) and really enjoy it.

If you're into multiplayer tower defense action, Toy Soldiers on the PC is not for you, as this port of the game which was originally released on the Xbox 360 is single player only.
However, if you can live with it being a single player only game, there is a fair amount of content for $10. Due to the fact that multiplayer was not implemented, Signal Studios included both DLC packs free of charge. DLC included, there are 3 playable armies spanning approximately 18 different levels. Presentation wise, the game has a very vintage, authentic, first world war feel, in areas such as the loading screen artwork, and the game soundtrack.
If you're like me and aren't too big on multiplayer gaming, or are a military history buff, then Toy Soldiers is a game worth checking out.

Oceanhorn is a fun little Gem of a game. It's truly a Zelda inspired game with elements of Windwaker, and a little classic SNES/Gameboy Zelda inside. The game is a lot of fun, yet simplified enough for anyone to pick up and play.  Controls work well, and surprisingly the voice acting isn't too bad for being on it's own merits. I want to give a very special shout out to the composer of the game. The music in this game is fantastic, and noticeably enjoyable to listen to. I would go as far to say that I would love to have an OST for this game.  Back to the game, the boss battles are fun and clever enough, using your progression as the tool to winning.  The game has a fair amount of meat on it, as of this review i'm nearing the end parts of the story; however, there is still a bunch of collectibles around the many islands to keep you busy and gaining Level Ups.  Yes, there are Level Ups too in this game, which reward you with new abilities, and stronger attributes, making grinding a factor as well if you want to beef up.
Overall, this is a fun game, and worth the price! I HIGHLY RECOMMEND this title, and I would love to see this turn into a series of it's own if it were in the interests of the Devs!
Oceanhorn looks a little bit like Windwaker and it does play a lot like other Zelda titles, although with less complexity. Yet still, it is a fun little gem.

A shadow person (also known as a shadow figure, shadow being or black mass) is the perception of a patch of shadow as a living, humanoid figure, particularly as interpreted by believers in the paranormal or supernatural as the presence of a spirit or other entity. Many methamphetamine addicts report hallucinations of "shadow people", as a result of sleep deprivation.
A number of religions, legends, and belief systems describe shadowy spiritual beings or supernatural entities such as shades of the underworld, and various shadowy creatures have long been a staple of folklore and ghost stories.
Although participants in online discussion forums devoted to paranormal and supernatural topics describe them as menacing, other believers and paranormal authors do not agree whether shadow people are either evil, helpful, or neutral, and some even speculate that shadow people may be the extra-dimensional inhabitants of another universe. Some paranormal investigators and authors such as Chad Stambaugh claim to have recorded images of shadow people on video.
Several physiological and psychological conditions can account for reported experiences of shadowy shapes seeming alive. A sleep paralysis sufferer may perceive a "shadowy or indistinct shape" approaching them when they awake paralysed, and become increasingly alarmed. A person experiencing heightened emotion, such as while walking alone on a dark night, may incorrectly perceive a patch of shadow as an attacker.
Many methamphetamine addicts report the appearance of "shadow people" after prolonged periods of sleep deprivation. Psychiatrist Jack Potts suggests that methamphetamine usage adds a "conspiratorial component" to the sleep deprivation hallucinations. One interviewed subject said that "You don't see shadow dogs or shadow birds or shadow cars. You see shadow people. Standing in doorways, walking behind you, coming at you on the sidewalk. These hallucinations have been directly compared to the paranormal entities described in folklore.
The explanation we get from skeptics and mainstream science - and who are usually people who have never experienced the shadow people phenomenon - is that it is nothing more than the active human imagination. It's our minds playing tricks on us... our eyes seeing things in a fraction of a second that aren't really there - illusions...real shadows caused by passing auto headlights, or some similar explanation. And without a doubt, these explanations probably can account for some if not many experiences. The human eye and mind are easily fooled. But can they account for all cases?
To call these entities ghosts demands first a definition of what we mean by ghosts.But by almost any definition, shadow people are somewhat different than ghost phenomena. Whereas ghost apparitions are almost always a misty white, vapor-like or have a decidedly human form and appearance (very often with discernible "clothing"), shadow beings are much darker and more shadow-like. In general, although the shadow people often do have a human outline or shape, because they are dark, the details of their appearance is lacking. This is in contrast to many ghost sightings in which the witness can describe the ghost's facial features, style of clothing and other details. The one detail most often noted in some shadow being sightings are their glowing red eyes.
The dark countenance and malevolent feelings that are often reported in association with these creatures has led some researchers to speculate that they may be demonic in nature. If they are demons, we have to wonder what their purpose or intent is in letting themselves be seen in this manner. Is it merely to frighten?
One interesting idea suggests that shadow people are the shadows or essences of people who are having out-of-body experiences. According to Jerry Gross, an author, lecturer and teacher about astral travel, we all travel out of the body when we are asleep. Perhaps, this theory says, we are seeing the ephemeral astral bodies of these twilight travelers.
People from our own future, another idea states, could have found the means to travel to the past - our time. However they are able to accomplish this incredible feat, perhaps in that state they appear to us merely as passing shadows as they observe the events of our timeline.
Even mainstream science is fairly convinced that there are dimensions other than the three we inhabit. And if these other dimensions exist, who or what (if anything) inhabits them?

The story is pretty good and the new characters that introduced to the Monkey Island universe are just as fun and favorable as the old characters. There is a hint that a second season was supposed to come into play, but I'm guessing when Telltale Games went to work on other games and started going with their choice driven stories, they put this one on the shelves, which is a shame because I would've loved to play through a second season and continue the adventures of Guybrush Threepwood. Let me start by saying that if you get your kicks from fast paced action,
explosive energy, and the frusration of constantly trying to one up your fiends
or your own personal best, Horizon Shift is for you. If you fall into this
categoy you can stop reading now and just go buy the game, seriously it's
pretty awesome and very addicting. After finding my bairings, I couldn't put
the thing down and found myself lost in a world of bright lights, booming club
music, and never ending frustration. Not the bad kind though, it was the
frustration of being so close to completing my next goal only to misstep,
causing my run to end just shy of my mark. Horizon shift has the characteristics
to make you grit your teeth in anticipation while propetually smiling the
entire time. The controls work great, the game runs smoothly, and as far as I
noticed nothing seemed to be broken. If I had to state any issues, it would be
the lack of multiplayer, and that once you play tournament mode, everything else
fails to be as entertaining. I would have liked to see something done for a co-op
or vs mode in some form, but sadly thats not here in any way. As for tournament
mode it's pretty easy to see just by watching what I mean. If the game had a more
random format rather than set wave types this might not be as big of an issue.
Regardless tournament mode is so break neck fast, and full of action that if
anything other than a pattern system existed, I feel it would be too dificult to
take seriously. Even the occaisional random meteor shower tends to be a bit much
at times.
Overall I'm giving Horizon Shift a B+. It does a fantastic job of differentiating
itself from all the other shoot em ups and bullet hells. And it's also very fun
and addicting. But it falls a bit short in that it lacks what seems like a great
opportunity for multiplayer, and it also becomes a bit stale in the modes other
than tournament mode once you give that a go. Even with that though I feel
tournament mode is enough to keep players coming back to try and top the scoreboards.

I've been meaning to update my review for a while now and since the new content release was today I figured I should go ahead and update my review. The combat system overall has improved greatly and it's easy to tell all the characters have a different fight style. You can now counter as well which is pretty helpful against some of the bigger enemies.
The dialogue has overall improved as well among all the charaters, including the professors. Overall the smoothness of the characters movenments has also gotten better. Before the sprinting felt a little weird but it feels much more smooth now. I have no complaints about the camera angles either.
The controls have changed a bit and that took me a bit to get use to personally but the controls are still fairly simple and shouldn't be a problem for new players. The story still seems to be interesting and I can't wait to see what direction this is going. We get to see more of the mutan grimm as well which is exciting. Overall the world itself is very beautiful.
One other thing I noticed was the character, Team RWBY, have also changed a bit in appearance. I find this to be an improvemnt as before when I would try to look at Ruby's face it was extremely white and really bright, making it almost impossible to actually see her face. Now it's not blidning and you can actually see what her face looks like.
10/10 would play again

I was extremely excited for this game when I saw the trailer and got the game on Christmas. The animation style is pretty much the way it is in the show and is pretty smooth. There are sometimes glitches with people going off the map but I'm sure that will get fixed and it hasn't actually been a big issue for me. I have gotten stuck in rocks before, however.
You can be Ruby, Weiss, Blake, or Yang. The characters all fight in similar ways but there are some differences, such as how fast each person shoots or runs. Everyone has their own skills they can learn and each character has their own dialogue so I recommend playing through as each character so you can go through it all. I noticed a lot of people saying they feel all of the characters fight the same and while I can see how they would say that I will have to disagree as I have played all the characters. Personally, I don't like the way Yang or Weiss fight. Ruby and Blake, however, are my favorite two character as far as the way they fight.
The controls are fairly simple once you learn them, though learning how to talk in game took me a bit longer. This game is pretty hack n slash but there does appear to be a very interesting story line. So, if you are a big fan of RWBY I recommend play the game so you can go through the story line. Currently it isn't complete and once you reach the end you'll probably be eager for more. Gotta love a good cliff hanger. I believe we can expect even more amazing things from this game.
You can play with yourself or you can play with three other friends. Playing with strangers is also an option. To play single player you do have to start a new game and create a lobby where only friends can join. Having an actual single player mode would be nice. Especially if there was a difficulty option in the single player mode since, in my opinion, the game is a bit too easy if you play alone.
The game difficulty does adjust if a player leaves, which is a plus. Like all multiplayer games there are people who are complete jerks and will steal all your kills or take all the artifacts. It's rather annoying but that is no fault of the developers. Don't get discouraged though. I have played several games with people who do actually work well with others and don't steal kills and share the artifacts.
When you leave the game, please note there is currently no save option so you will start back at the beginning with 0 exp.
All and all it's a good game and I 100% say any RWBY should play this. I would definitely get it before the price goes up.

As a gamer who appreciates a more casual approach in a game, Oceanhorn is a very solid and fun experience.
The puzzles, exploration aspects, achievement hunting and enemy difficulty were just right as I do not wish to be engaged in 5 minute extreme battles every time I fight a singular enemy - though the trend nowadays seems to be towards difficult encounters and challenging content. But I play games to relax and enjoy the experience - to that end Oceanhorn was perfect.
There was no crafting bloating the irritation and time wasting aspect to the game. There were no side quests mandatory to level up. Just a straight forward story-lite which guided you to all the different islands, dungeons and puzzles with various challenges which each give achievements.
I have around 14 hours playtime and 100% of achievements, out of a £5 investment so great time:cost value as well.
If you are after some Dark Souls level combat or difficulty, or a fully fledged Zelda-like experience, you will be disappointed with Oceahorn.
However if you can appreciate the simple-ness of the game and note its solid combat, level design, art style and puzzle design then you can easily get your money's worth out of this cheap, cute and refreshing game.

So I had done a review of this game before, but I feel like it is time for a new review of this game.
I can honestly say that this is one of the games I always go back to. Let's begin with the graphics, which are flawlessly done. The graphics give off a sort of cartoon art vibe similar to World of Warcraft, and with the atmospheric glow it definitely makes the gameplay feel magical. The controls are easy to master, and the combat is more like an art form crafted from the imagination Gods. Besides the visuals, the storyline is on point and the side quests are always interesting as well. Not to mention that the world is incredibly huge, but with the DLC's you get over 200 hours of gameplay added PLUS even more areas to explore. The difficulty of this game is also sometimes a challenge when it comes to bosses but what game isn't? Sometimes you really have to think about how to attack an enemy and there is zero God Mode which makes it even more time consuming. There are also numerous options to designing your character. The character customization is standard (not amazing) but the features for your character are incredibly large. You want to be a badass warrior but want to be a mage at the same time? You can do it. Mechanics are something every game has but not many games manage to use them as metaphor as elegantly as Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons does. In a game with relatively simple puzzles, no real dialog, and a basic plot structure it's this integration of player input that brings everything together and elevates whole above the sum of its parts.
Backing up a little, the mechanic in question is the control scheme which has the player moving each brother independently with the two sticks on a controller (incidentally this means a controller is required to play this game, at least properly). This is definitely a new experience and an utterly confusing one, at least at first and therein lies some of the beauty and elegance of this game. When the game begins and the brothers begin their journey the controls are unfamiliar and slow to use but as the characters grow and gain confidence on their adventure so does your skill with the controls. The direct correlation between player input and in-game progression is not something explicitly noticeable while playing but it absolutely is effective at maintaining immersion and points that would feel like "press button to pay respects" in other games turn into touching moments that feel natural. I could go on about the mechanics and their ties to the game but this is a review so I'll refrain.
While they are terrific, mechanics alone can not carry a game to greatness. Fortunately Brothers delivers pretty much across the board. The art style hits a great sweet spot between realistic and stylized and makes terrific use of the engines power with many deep, bright scenes given center stage through out. The story, while structurally simple, is full of emotion and heart with plenty of highs and lows through out. It's also not going to pull any punches, much the same as our real lives are not full of happy endings and endless summers. The world is lush and interesting. In so many games the world and the events happening in it revolve around your character but in Brothers you really feel like you're journeying through foreign lands as you pass through places where major events have already happened, are in progress, or seem destined to happen soon. Some people may feel like they're missing out but personally I loved this. It made me think and wonder about the world much like anyone traveling through it would, imagining a great battle and speculating on the tensions that caused it. To me this is better than some exposition or pages of text with lore that's filled with places, names, and dates that have no real meaning or context.
In the end Brothers: A Take of Two Sons is masterfully both poignant and subtle, uplifting and heart-wrenching. It does require that you own or can borrow a controller but it's absolutely worth the effort. Put shortly, I highly recommend this game to anyone and everyone.

Episode 2 is my favourite episode, because we get to meet Morgan LeFlay.
Episode 3 is pretty decent. I like the Brotherhood, but the manatee mating ritual puzzle can be a little tricky (why won't she love me?!).
Episode 4 is a little "meh". I enjoyed the court section and that thing that happens to Morgan (the sound design is really good in that section). On the other hand, the sponge feeding quest was confusing and needlessly fetchquesty: it didn't seem like the plot was advancing anymore. So, as a long, long time Monkey Island player, I bought this when it first came out. I ran it through once and it was.. meh. Ok. I come back to the original three games probably every couple of years, but in (wow) 8 years, this is the first time I've come back since release. I've thought about it a bit and I have a couple of good memories of puzzles that would bring me in, but there are so many flaws that I just can't work past.
The control system is a masterclass in clumsiness. You can either go all-mouse and you drag Guybrush around like he's a badly behaved puppy or you can use WASD keys. The WASD version is better, but for a point and click franchise like this, it feels inelegant. The dragging is just horrible. This is exaggerated by the map/area layouts, which uses 3D to staggeringly poor effect. I'm no luddite - game-franches can come to 3D and do a hell of a job (Ocarina of Time springs gloriously to mind), but Monkey Island has tried and failed badly at this. The first three games used gorgeous hand-drawn backdrops that I never felt impaired gameplay. Now I have juddering camera angle changes because I've walked partially to a point where I can't get past, or ugly movement around fences because WASD doesn't really work with paths from the offered perspective. It's great for punching folks as Batman, not so much for walking around a forest picking flowers as a pirate.
Another frustration is the single click action which robs the player of animus in the game. You click, Guybrush does whatever he's supposed to do. Gone are the moments of joy at realising you can try to 'Pick Up' Kate Capsize only for Guybrush to bring out some terrible chat-up lines. Now we're in simplistic nothingness territory. It might be easier, but it's a whole lot less satisfying.
The graphics are just ok - I'm not complaining about the quality or complaining they're a decade dated (I still play LOOM for gods sakes) but the graphics in this are just so generic. There are hints at style, but you could never claim it looks great or iconic.
The characters seem to have become game-standard cliches. Guybrush is heroic rather than an accidentally capable baby, Elaine is a shrill, complaining damsel rather than the strong character deciding whether to save Guybrush at the start of LeChuck's Revenge and LeChuck himself is just incoherrent.
In the first three games much of the humour came from falling down little dialogue trees and seeing people react to Guybrush's daft statements; here the dialogue options seem to be ignored most of the time in favour of pre-chosen remarks, which robs the player of the feeling of control as well as the humour that is the bedrock of these games.
I so wanted to come back to the game and realise I was just being silly, but no, it's not to be - Monkey island continues to be composed of three great games that are receding further into the depths of time. Don't waste your time.

Horizon shift is one of those "what if" kind of games that really bends what people typically think when it comes to a genre.  It combines elements from bullet hell shooters, and basic platforming elements (Being able to jump) Along with this, a totally unique yet simple idea of having a middle line be your playing field. The controls are great, the visuals are pumping and the music is really rad. Jason Heine of the EMU review really did a great job with this one.
Really worth picking up.

This preview was done with a key obtained from the developer.
Horizon Shift is a great twist on the shoot em up genre that feels like a breath of fresh air for the genre. The added mechanics add a bit of depth to the gameplay that I haven't seen in the genre, and it adds elements of platforming that makes strategic defense of your Horizon (the middle line of the screen that you move upon) rather important, due to it being able to be destroyed. Uniqueness in Enemy and variation of enemies add to this in particular with the combinations that can be created, where you have to make quick decisions on taking out one enemy rather then the other, and making a wrong choice can lead to problems for you very quickly. While it's a wave based shooter that I'd love to see more of a “random” mode from for variation over a period of time, for 5 bucks and the experience it gives, you more then get the return on investment in several ways.

This game is the ultimate tribute to Heavy Metal and I recommend it to anybody likes that genre of music.
The story of Eddie Riggs, the roadie who is transported to the world of Metal by an ancient god is something different for once, there are several awesome characters, like Ozzy Osbourne as the Guardian of Metal, and of course there is the great soundtrack of 107 different heavy metal classics.
The gameplay is a mixed bag. On one hand it is an open world action game similar to GTA (cruising around, finding missions, doing missions), just a lot more empty, which is kind of disappointing (But the landscape is full of references to metal bands and album covers which is pretty awesome). But the fighting and driving around is pretty cool. There are collectibles and some repeating mini games like fighting off a horde of enemies or racing, which give currency which you can spend at the Guardian of Metal to upgrade your weapons, your hot rod and customize Eddie. And of course there are the story missions.
Later in the game, a strategy game part is added. You fight an enemy team and the goal is to destroy the enemy's stage (base). You have to collect Fans (resources) to build your troops which you can lead against enemy troops and ultimately to the stage. While the game unfolds you get a larger variety of troops and the battles get more difficult, but I never found them that much fun. Something was just lacking, probably the lack of strategic depth, since just spamming troops will usually lead to a victory. There is also a multiplayer part consisting of that mode, however I haven't played that.
The graphics are not the best ever, but the comic-y style works and the goofy character looks just match the style of the game.
Over all, as I said in the beginning, I 100% recommend this game to any Heavy Metal fan, for gameplay fans I can't really recommend it to anyone, since it's not a great specimen for any genres it tries to fit in. I still recommend it for the story and the characters.

This game, whilst still being in a alpha/beta stage, is surprisingly fun and addictive. This might be stemming from my nostalgic memories of this game from long ago, but even so, I digress. The only downside to this game is a steep learning curve. If you've never played the first, or just a twitch or hair-trigger game, it's going to be a bit challenging.

I love this game, It's action packed and drops you right into the action. It has a nice tutorial at the begining to help those new players and even veterans of the original gunz get used to the controls and what is new in this sequel. I am a huge fan of the original gunz and hopefully they bring back the old gunz into steam but until then, we have a good game to play while we wait. It is a free game and while it does have an item shop, it is like team fortress in the aspect that the items are purely cometic and give you no real advantage. That is with the exception of the starter kits which are a bit expensive and over priced for equipment which you can easilly get within a few hours of gameplay.
Each of the four characters are specialized in what I call, "your style of gameplay". We have Ivan who is the overall all around character who specializes in long range with his sniper rifle, able to inflict instant kill headshots and his trusty katana for close range. Rena on the other hand specializes in close quarters melee fighting with fast paced movement and quick high damage melee abilities, not to mention the ability to use a clone to go invisible. Elena is the complete opposite of Rena though, she specializes in long range combat with an arsenal of assault rifles and granade launchers in order to keep her opponents at a distance, but she is no slauch when it comes to melee combat as she has her handy mace type weapons to stun her enemies who get within arms reach. Then we have Max which is basically a walking tank type character. His big brawn lets him take damage from melee weapons without flinching, enabling him to continiously fight back. When the enemy is at a distance, he can quickly equip his shield to block all incoming damage from the front.
Overall I give this game a high rating, and as the player becomes familiar with the playstyle, so does the gameplay. Higher levels prove to be much more difficult as more experienced players learn new tricks thanks to the revolutionary style combat. It's a game where you have to learn and be spontaneous in order to survive rather than sit in a corner camping and hope to get lucky. I give this game a 10/10 even after considering the current inbalance issues that have yet to be resolved. I encourage players to try this game out at the very least.

(PLEASE NOTE: This is technically not a "review" of GunZ 2, but more of an early impressions piece since the game is still in beta form. A follow up review will be made once the game is declared "finished" by MAIET.)
Full impressions:
After several years of waiting, MAIET Entertainment has finally released their high-action multiplayer shooter for (most of) the world to enjoy on Steam’s Early Access program. GunZ 2: The Second Duel is an online third person shooter about killing stuff with style. Players can run up walls, pull off acrobatic movements and switch between gunplay and melee combat on the fly. It's a sequel to the original GunZ: The Duel which came out back in 2003-2005.
or those that do not know: One of the biggest changes in GunZ 2 compared to its predecessor is the removal of K-Style and D-style: Two popular play-styles that significantly changed the overall flow of gameplay by allowing players to jump, dash, block, slash and shoot all at the same time. While this made the gameplay a lot more intense and exciting, it also brought weapon imbalance, made latency issues more apparent and even brought about health concerns from prolonged performance of these techniques, such as Carpal Tunnel.
MAIET thought long and hard about wanting to bring "style play" back for the release of GunZ 2, but came to the conclusion that it was too much of a hassle to bring it all back if they were going to achieve a more balanced shooting game.
With my extensive time spent playing the South Korean, Europe and Taiwan versions of the game (as if I couldn’t get enough of this game in my life…), it was now time for me to jump head first into the Steam Early Access for North America, just to see if there has been any significant changes made, as well as being able to play against others in my region of world.
---
First bit of disappointment that I had with the Steam version was that MAIET still has not included any initial character customization when selecting between the four available classes, which for some reason all have names attached to them unlike before. The Silent Avenger is now called Ivan, the Gunslinger is called Elena, the Shield Trooper’s name is Max and the newest class, the Shadow Dancer, is named Rena. Between these four classes, they each have many different strengths and weaknesses, but you still cannot select different hair styles or faces for them, unlike the original GunZ.
In the original GunZ: The Duel: Instead of different classes, players had access to a weight system, where they could select any weapon they wanted just as long as the player had enough weight space available to hold them all, and this was all dictated by the armor each character wore, so if a player had good armor, they could carry multiple weapons or heavier weapons. However, this proved to give a false sense of customization in the later levels due to the use of K/D-style limiting most loadout options.
Once I selected my character, I went through the tutorial which hasn’t changed very much since the EU and TW versions. After completion, one noticeable change was the inclusion of crystals and ores which can be earned from unlocking achievements, opening supply crates every hour and from dismantling equipment. These ores and crystals can be used to earn weapons and equipment from the tesla machine, which is basically a fancy gachapon system. And as much as I dislike gambling systems, the tesla machine is actually very fair in comparison to other gachapon systems, mainly because it actually shows a global number of chances to win each available prize. Once you understand how the tesla machine works, it’s quite possible to wait patiently for the prize list to drop as low as possible to increase your chances of getting the main prizes, which are usually permanent weapons or special costumes.
The three modes that are currently available in GunZ 2 include Team Deathmatch, Team Elimination and Time Assault:  While Team Deathmatch is fairly self-explanatory; Team Elimination is similar to Team Deathmatch except that players have one life per round. If you die during a match, you cannot respawn. Think of it like a typical round of Counter-Strike with bombing run or hostage capture mode, except that there’s no main objective other than defeating the enemy team… and that people can jump around the environment like something out of a Cirque du Soleil show.
The other available game mode is Time Assault, which is very much a straight forward Attack & Defend game mode where one team defends one of three target points on the map while the other team tries to destroy those targets. This mode and Team Elimination mode is where the gameplay truly starts to shine, as teamwork plays a big role here. Of course, it’s hard to engage in teamwork when the thought of trying to be a nonstop, badass, one-man army kind of action hero is so tempting, but it usually pays off.
As to whether or not GunZ 2 takes skill to play compared to its predecessor, I would answer that by saying: It’s debatable. Gameplay is now more focused on team play rather than solo performance, although it is still very possible to hold your own in solo situations, no matter which class you choose. As I’ve seen time and time again where players have been able to carry entire teams on their backs or have been able to clutch it out during a 1-on-4 situation during a team elimination match. These intense moments really show that quick wits are now what GunZ 2 is all about, rather than repetitious muscle memory and a shallow overarching strategy of “spot an enemy and K/D-style them as hard as you can.”
Personally speaking: After a few matches in normal mode, and having the opportunity of playing with people in my region, I would have to say that Gunz 2 is actually more difficult to play than Gunz 1. Without the crutch of insanely high mobility, I was forced to make decisions more quickly. I found myself dying a lot in Gunz 2 because of the difficulty of adjusting to the more team-based and snap decision making nature of gameplay. Some battles do get pretty mindless (especially up against grenade spamming Elena players and YOLO flamethrowin' Max players), but usually when you’re up against a full premade group, you really need to focus.
The biggest issue with the Steam version of GunZ 2 is most definitely the lag issues. It seems like MAIET didn’t get the memo that peer-to-peer connections do not work well in online video games outside of South Korea, since not every country out there is the size of a small state, and not everyone has access to T1+ internet connection speeds. Unlike most modern shooting games that use dedicated servers, GunZ 2 randomly assigns one player as the “host” before a match begins, which means that if the host lags, everyone lags. And even if the host has a decent connection, they will still have a major advantage over enemy players due to hitscan detection and registration time. If a player is not selected as the host, they will need to lead their shots constantly; otherwise they’ll be missing a lot of hits. This is especially noticeable when using Ivan’s sniper rifle, where it can take up to half a second or more for a shot to travel from point A to point B, and by the time the shot travels across the map, a target would have already moved from their position.
Overall, in its current state, it shows a lot of promise. Even with the direct removal of K/D-style, it still managed to give me the same thrill and excitement that the original GunZ gave me. If they can manage to develop some kind of netcode that can compensate for the latency issues before adding new content, then I could see GunZ 2 having quite a long life span.

Mount & Blade: Warband is a great game.
It is set in a medieval era on a fictitious continent, with several competing kingdoms or factions.
You play the part of a wanderer who dreams of becoming a major player.
You start off with low-grade weapons, and have to earn the money to buy better ones (or you can get extra weapons by defeating your enemies).
You roam the land, helping villagers, defeating bandits, and doing other virtuous acts - or you may even decide to operate on the wrong side of the law by attacking innocent people, robbing, trade caravans, looting, and pillaging.
Or you may do a bit of both - maybe you might decide to be a law-abiding citizen by day and a crime lord by night.
As you go further in the game, you can start to recruit heroes to your cause, as well as hire men for your growing band of warriors. That's when things start to become a lot more exciting.
When you have a sizeable little army, you can lay siege to castles and have major engagements in the field.
The battles are carried out in third-person format, up-close and personal, as are various other tasks, whilst you direct your overall strategies via a map.
You can operate as a vassal of an existing leader, or you can operate on your lonesome - or become a vassal, but then break away to form your own fiefdom.
If you campaign hard with your forces right across the width and breadth of the continent, and defeat all of your enemies (making them bow before you, or die by the sword), then you can proclaim yourself as the ruling monarch for all the land!
Highly recommended.

The strongest emotional response I've had playing a game, is in Brothers.
You traverse the world in unison. Together you'll solve simple puzzles and explore cobblestone villages, dingy mines, and a crystalline arctic ocean. It is beautiful.
The brothers' story is told without words we understand. We become familiar with them through their actions - one uses a lady's broom to dutifully sweep the porch, the other cheekily shows off by balancing the handle on his palm.
When you first control each brother with their assigned analogue stick, it is awkward. Janky and disorganized, you stumble over obstacles. You're uncomfortable - just as the brothers are uncomfortable working together - they've never had to. But as you improve at the pat-your-head-while-rubbing-your-belly controls, so do the boys. They begin to cooperate. It's this progress that highlights the bond they establish with one another as they forge ahead. It's the second best example of control mechanics having narrative purpose in Brothers.
The best instance, will simply leave you speechless.

Brothers was an amazing game. It has a wonderful story, although there is no actual narration or coherent language. It is a game that will pull at your heart strings. With that being said, I feel that the story would be more immersive and bring you closer to the characters if there were deeper character development. I understand the purpose was art and it was made this way for a reason. However, the emotions I felt, or wanted to feel, were no where near as intense as they would have been if I had felt closer to my charaters.
Nonetheless, this is a brilliant game.

I hadn't heard any of the hype about this game so was pleasantly surprised by it. It was focused, and just the right length. No dull repetition, endless side quests and tedium of my usual action/adventure genre. A lot has been said about the artistic beauty so I won't go there. What I loved was that each scene introduced something novel in terms of gameplay that I hadn't experienced before (maybe I'm not a seasoned-enough gamer). Dual flying a glider, rolling around in a cocoon, belay swigning, fanning predators away, dodging malicious roots, riding mountain goats. The interplay between the two characters was nicely woven into the plot. Puzzles were fun and not repetitive. I didn't find myself having to endlessly collect trinkets for some achievement, blow up yet another enemy, or pick yet another lock. Overall, a great experience.

Heartbreaking and beautiful, Brothers A Tale of Two Sons is a wonderful, unforgettable experience.
Its Storytelling striped down to its minimilistic roots, Brothers is a visually stunning, and surprisingly moving tale. Theres no real dialogue to speak of, the characters speak in gibberish though you understand what their emotions are. Simple, but it gets its point across. This carries over to the controls as well, where you control each brother by a thumbstick and that is the only control you have.
The only complaint i have is while there are many inventive moments with the control scheme, its often frustrating to control two characters at once. Thankfully the puzzles are fairly simple and dont require finesse. Thats besides the point though, the highlight here, is for its wonderful narrative. Music plays a big part here and gives a grand sweeping touch as well as sombre tone to the game. I wont spoil the story, but all i will say is that it will stick with you long past the ending.
Its a short game too, about 3 hours, but by the end of it you wont even mind. It feels just right and never overstays its welcome. The narrative power is what sells it, and in a sea of uninspired forgettable games, this manages to be unforgettable. I definetly hope to see more games like this in the future.
Highly recommended!

It's a very fun experience playing a new 3D fighting game.
However, the learning process to get better is very front loaded and requires a lot of studying on your part (particularly frame data, which might be a concept that most people skip over or don't ever quite understand). Plus there are multiple beginner mistakes you can make while learning, and repeatedly use something that doesn't actually work (i.e. a string that registers as a "combo" but isn't a NATURAL combo; set the second training dummy action to "guard all" and you'll see what I mean very quickly with those kinds of strings).
I still recommend this game because it's very well balanced and you'll easily find a character that you like and can relate to. It's very hard but very rewarding once you know what you're doing. You can carry all of the things you learn in Tekken 7 to any fighting game from there on and improve much faster.

I think the first thing that needs to be said is that while I do, in fact, recommend this game, I recommend it under the condition that it receives polish appropriate to a series as impactful and immensely popular as RWBY.
So far, Grimm Eclipse is like a flash project. Its very basic and the 'campaign' can be completed in less than an hour. What keeps it standing so far is the intriguing ways that it divides the skills of Team RWBY into different trees that all manage to feel cohesive and part of the RWBY universe.
The visuals are actually fairly nice, but the voice acting is flat and disappointing. They have some intersting mechanics that make me feel like there is more this game has to offer in the future. I do, however, have to strictly recommend this game only to die-hard fans. I don't regret the purchase myself, despite the current product being a bit underwhelming. I look forward to seeing what will happen with it in the future. I'm sure it goes without saying that RWBY fans have high expectations of a faithful adaptation of the late Oum's work.
