Was really on the fence for this one for a while, but after realizing how lacking the game actually is, I decided to give my thoughts on it. First off, the pros and cons:
Pros:
- It's finally on PC
- Core gameplay is fun. Its classic enjoyable Tekken action accessible to newcomers but rewards the patient people that bother learning the game and improving
- The online netcode seems to work fine, don't notice a lot of lag when playing online.
- There's a gallery mode that includes endings for every previous Tekken games, so you can get mostly up to speed (however games such as Tekken 4 and 5 that have cutscenes throughout the arcade modes, you're gonna be missing some context)
- Practice mode is mostly solid and useful
Cons:
- Everything else.
- Lack of content (Basically no offline gamemodes)
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ storymode
- ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story
- Long loading times
- Introduction of rage art (really wasn't necessary)
- Old favorite characters are excluded (Lei, Anna, Mokujin/Combot)
- No tutorial mode (the game is pretty hard to fully learn and master, and other recent games have bothered with adding tutorial modes that make the games much more accessible for newcomers, and more fun, so not seeing it here is a disappointment)
- I can't use my fightstick because only dpad can move through the menus (and you can't change what buttons use dpad in the options). Sure that's very much a nitpick and specific problem, but I can't be the only one having problems with that.
I have a hard time deciding where to even start, but I'll start out with pointing out the first thing that disappointed me; the lack of gamemodes. Ever since Tekken 2, one of the most fun things about playing it was in Team Mode with friends. Playing as 8 characters versus 8 characters was so much fun, when you pick the coolest ones and save your strongest for the last trump card. But no Team Battle here. Not even any survival mode. No time mode, no Tekken Force mode. There's an arcade mode, but that's just taken directly from the arcade version and that means it only lasts 5 fights. That's it. No endings either, only the five fights, credits, then back to main menu. Then you have treasure battle mode, which is just to rank up your character offline, but also gives a reason for the developers to milk out more playtime from the users, as you just endlessly fight in battles to unlock new equipment. There's little to no variation, some fights are spedup, some fights have double damage. That's it. Else it's just endlessly beating battles. But hey! There's Tekken Bowl mode for season pass buyers!
Next, the story mode is absolute garbage. Not only is the story basically not in spirit of the old Tekken games (there's a lot of the world being at war and global dangers, there's basically not even a tournament) but they also even retcon the game, pull characters out of their asses, and have the worst crossover ever that's basically just a flimsy excuse to put in a beloved character from another game to trick people into buying it. The story mode is very much like the recent Mortal Kombat games, even to include QTEs. And like only 3. There's 3 QTEs in the game for absolutely no reason. But if you don't care for the main story, there's also small stories for each character. And I mean small. 1 fight each, with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ending. No cinematic, just a♥♥♥♥♥♥conclusion to the fight and then back to the menu to select another ♥♥♥♥♥♥ story fight. Playing through arcade mode in Tekken 1 is more rewarding.
But like I said, the core fighting of the game is fun. Very little has changed, the two couple of things changed is adding Rage Art, and Rage Drive moves. Rage Drive moves feel alright, but Rage Art is basically just the super moves from Street Fighter games, or the X-Ray moves from recent Mortal Kombat games. Something NO other Tekken game had, and something they had absolutely no reason to add. Each character have an unique way of activating the Rage Art move, but what's the point when they added a button to do it instantly anyway? And you might say it adds more strategy to the fights, when you have to worry about the enemy making a sudden comeback, but I say it breaks the flow and makes it more infuriating to play, as tricking your opponent into wasting it is really tedious and makes for a lot of staring at each other. It was executed much better in Tekken 6, where a character simply deals more damage when they're low on health.
Another problem is that the game takes way too much time to load. I blame the high quality graphics. Sure they're nice to look at, but having to wait like 20-40 seconds for a match to start is too much. I have also encountered the game crashing twice, and even softlocking in a menu. Also problems with it not detecting audio devices. Another bothersome thing is that my own arcade fightstick uses the stick as an analog stick, but you can only navigate through the menus with the controllers dpad. But the game won't let you change the dpad controls. And my fightstick doesn't have any dpad on it, so I can't use the controller at all to play the game, unless I'm in a battle.
In conclusion, playing the fights in itself is as much fun as any other Tekken game, but it has been focused way too much on the online crowd, that it forgets to make it fun to play locally with friends on the same system, and not very rewarding to play through the story modes by yourself or do anything offline. If you're planning to only play online then it's fine, but I'd say the asking price of $50 is too much, when there's been other Tekken games with just as much content priced only at $15.

The setting is way more detailed than you'd expect from a hack'n'slash RPG. But don't count on complex dialogue trees, there are only a couple occasions when you have to make a decision at the end of a quest. The look of the game is appealing. Some beings are so adorable, it's a shame you have to kill them.
The best thing of course is the combat. There are quite a many abilities you can use, but you aren't overwhelmed, as you learn them one by one. And if you're bored with one class, you can respec your character. You can even create mixes of the two or all three classes as you like.
Even though this is an RPG, the attacks hit based on your reflexes and skill and not on percentages. It's like a fighting game where you have to know what attacks can you land on what enemies and how you can couter certain enemy attacks. You can meat an enemy with ridiculously high health, but you'll never find an enemy that has such a high AC that you are unable to hit it, because the possibility to evade them and hit them is always at you fingertips.
Now, it still has problems with stealth, as most RPGs I know (this game also loves grand entrances of the boss enemies that talk to you dramatically, while you try to sneak in, also enemies that spawn on you), but if your target is not a named boss, then you can go and stealth kill quite a bunch of enemies before they notice you, which might be very useful if there are mages among them (take them out first).
The theme of the early missions and the DLCs resonates very well with the theme of the game, which is borderline self aware, but in the last part of the game it's like a different writer. It's still  not bad writing, but it's like they forgot about how everything is about fate. And while there are hints about some kind of big twist at the end, I was utterly underwhelmed by the ending.
Warning: If you don't want the game to get ridiculously easy, don't play the DLCs until the end. If you level up in the DLCs, then you don't need any tactics or skill after that in the main game.
And remember: this is more of an action game than a storytelling game. If you like RPGs for the possibility of writing your own story, talking to NPCs, etc., this isn't for you. Even though you can talk to NPCs for hours, but most of them will be nothing more than them just talking about the setting and filling you in about the lore.

KoA: Reconing is a fantastic, underrated 3rd person, open world RPG.  The game features an excellent plot, huge world, combined with truly customizable character classes.   For those of you who don't know the story behind this game's development, it was founded by Curt Schilling (former MLB pitcher) who was a fan of games when he wasn't playing baseball.  He sunk a ton of his own money into trying to make this game (and franchise) great but in the end it was a bit too ambitious for a startup company and they went bankrupt after releasing the game.  What does this all mean?  Well, it means the game has AAA quality production values but is often overlooked.  In short, it's a hidden gem that most likely will never get a sequel, but is a really well done game.
The game's plot and setting are quite good overall.  As part of the world building, bestselling fantasy author RA Salvatore (the creator of Drizzt) wrote over 1000 pages of plot and backstory to make this world come alive.  The result is not your typical generic fantasy world, but a world with a rich history that isn't just the same old elves and orcs all over again.   I enjoyed the plot and setting of the game.  The main plot reveals rather slowly, but the last few chapters of the main plot are quite interesting.  Of course, there are TONS of sidequests and 4 full factions to explore as well, as well as two full expansions that are worth getting.
Graphically, the world is very beautiful and some of the cities and outdoor settings are quite unique.   My favorite was the city of Ysa, which was built into the trees.  It's hard to get a sense of the game's graphics due to the 3rd person nature of the game.  Just looking at screenshots doesn't do it justice because your character is always standing in the middle of the screen, but when you can pan the camera around and explore the worlds, it's beautiful.  Level design is also very solid.  There's tons of areas to explore, lots of secrets, and the world map and quest system keeps you from getting lost.   My one complaint about the level design is that your character cannot jump in most places, but can only jump from certain spots.  The game's soundtrack is memorable and sound effects are also high quality, as to be expected.
Combat is the main part of the game and luckily, it's very fun.  Unlike most RPGs, you truly are free to design a character that is exactly how you want to play.  You're not penalized for being a hybrid character, in fact you can prettymuch use whatever main and secondary weapons you like along with fighting styles, stealth, and magic skills.  Want to play a mage that wears robes and fights with a big hammer?  Sure, there's spells to boost your armor, heal, and a summons to help distract enemies in combat.  Want to play a stealthy assassin that uses magery to stun from afar.  Go for it!  You can also play a pure fighter, mage, or rogue and enjoy the game that way as well.  It's easy to respec your character when you want to try something different.  There's also a deep crafting system for potions, armor, and magic gems that you can get into or completely ignore.  The game also keeps the crafting skills separate from the combat skills, so you're not forced into going into blacksmithy as a warrior or gemcrafting as a mage, for instance.
Fighting enemies themselves is quite fun.  Most regular enemies are pretty easy to destroy, so your character feels quite powerful.  Luckily, the boss fights can be pretty difficult and are very epic!  Be prepared to mow over most weak enemies and have some challenges with the various boss fights.
The game features achievements as well and all of them work.  You can 100% the game in about 70ish hours, in one playthrough.  Luckily, there's a lack of super grindy achievements and a lot of them are fun to get.  You'll need both expansions to 100% the game, but I would highly recommend both expansions as well.  The bundle for the game goes on sale quite often, so pick up the deluxe edition!
There are a few negatives that I must mention.  The number 1 complaint about this game is that it is too easy.  If you do every faction, sidequest, and area in the main game and both expansions, you will reach the level cap far before the end of the plot.  To remedy this, I recommend playing the game on hard mode.  It does not make the game too difficult, it merely balances it out to be about the average difficulty for most games.  Even if you are someone who normally plays games on normal or even easy mode, I highly recommend playing on hard mode so that it's simply not a pushover.   I ended up playing the game for about 13 hours on medium difficulty before deciding it was too easy and starting over.  Just play it on hard to begin with.  There's also an achievment for beating the game on hard mode and if you find the game to be too challenging, you can always just level up or even lower the difficulty if you have to.
The game does feature a huge amount of optional sidequests along with 4 factions.  If you do every optional sidequest and kill every enemy that crosses your path, you will be overleveled before the end.  Therefore, I recommend doing   the main plot, all 4 factions, both DLC and a just a few sidequests.  Doing this will keep the game challenging to the end of the main story.  Also, after the main story ends you are still free to continue the game and play all of those sidequests.  The game actually has so much content that you could probably replay a second time doing only sidequests and level up to max.   It is also very easy to outmanuver enemies and run past them, which cuts down on the tedium of killing monsters that respawn after a day or two.  Another complaint I had was that the game tends to reuse enemy graphics quite a bit.  The enemies are well animated, but the game could use a bit more variety.   Finally, the last few areas of the game are pretty difficult and sort of turn into a potion swilling festival.
However, despite these drawbacks, the game is extremely solid overall and highly recommended.  If you enjoy open world style games, this is certainly one to pickup and play.  It has a detailed plot, a well developed world, beautiful graphics, fun combat, epic and challenging bosses, a complex but optional crafting system, truly customizable classes, a variety of powerful weapon choices, and is a huge kingdom to explore for many hours.   Just play on hard mode and don't do every sidequest and you're sure to enjoy this hidden gem of a 3rd person rpg!  If you enjoyed Skyrim, chances are you will like this game.  I would even go as far to say that the combat and boss battles are better in KoA!  Give this game a chance and you'll be glad you did.

Unapologetically inspired by The Legend of Zelda series, Oceanhorn is a fun, if fairly lightweight, adventure/RPG.
The game sees the player exploring a series of islands (with both overworld locations and buildings/dungeons) from an overhead perspective, fighting monsters with a small selection of weapons (most commonly, just a sword and shield) and solving simple puzzles. The combat is fairly straightforward 'hack-and-slash' in style, but remains satisfying, while the puzzles are generally focused around block-pushing and switches - these are seamlessly integrated into the world, maintaining a good level of variety in most situations.
Graphically the game is again farily simplistic in style, with its roots as a mobile port being clear, but that style has a certain charm to it and means that the game isn't very demanding on system requirements. The soundtrack works well to provide a fitting atmosphere, but I can't see it being anything that remains memorable long-term.
Coming in at around 10-15 hours to complete, the game doesn't outstay its welcome but still has enough content to feel substantial. A fairly extensive list of achievements provides an excuse to sink some more time into the game - many of these will come 'naturally' as you play, but there are a few with quite specific requirements that encourage experimentation. One thing that I'd recommend not getting too focused on is the fishing mechanic, as ultimately this brings little reward and is unfortunately based on randomness that does require 'grinding' to see out in full.
All in all, Oceanhorn gets my recommendation as a very approachable adventure - just don't come here expecting a great deal of depth to the game.

<Score : 6.5>
[Gameplay : 7/10]
The game is fast paced, very mobile, and adrenaline-pumping. There are four classes and a variety of play styles available, whether you like going in guns blazing, staying on the defensive, sniping, or outwitting your opponent.
Movement is less fluid than in GunZ 1, but that is not necessarily a bad thing. Dashing seems to be more about short bursts of speed, and wall running is a bit hard to control, though running around corners is a welcome addition to the chaos.
GunZ 2 offers a matchmaking system not unlike other shooters, but seems to do away with the custom game rooms of it's predecessor (this is a bad thing for me, and I expect it to be re-introduced). Players can solo queue or invite their friends to a party for normal and ranked gameplay. GunZ 2 seems to see itself as a MOBA (for whatever reason) in the manner that leaving a room after you have entered map selection results in a temporary punishment of not being able to queue for a few minutes. It also offers a(n unwanted in my opinion) surrender feature, which brings the game to a halt when you have to vote yes or no. This is especially annoying when you don't want the game to end, but it might as well end because you're getting killed while you have to press alt, move your cursor, click no, and press alt again to resume gameplay.
The three normal/ranked game modes are as follows;
Team Deathmatch - What you would expect from this game mode; Two teams going head to head on one of several maps. After you die, you respawn at your base. The objective is to reach the score limit before the other team. Much like TDM Extreme of GunZ 1.
Team Elimination - Homage to the Team Deathmatch mode of it's predecessor. Upon death, you then spectate the rest of your team as they fight for winning the round. This mode also offers several maps to play on.
Time Assault - Players are assigned to an attacking or defending team. The attacking team must break through two walls, and destroy an object at the end, the defending team must hold them off as long as they can. When the final object is destroyed, the teams are swapped, and the new attackers must break through in a quicker time than the first attackers.
This mode sadly only features one map.
The game also brings a Campaign mode to the table. Players can team up to play through different seasons of PvE combat, complete with very detailed maps, and intense boss fights. This campaign mode definitely one-ups GunZ 1's quest mode, in my opinion.
GunZ 2 also decided to take to a rental system for items. You can spend around 15k (just a few game's worth of money) to rent a new weapon for certain pre-defined amounts of time. They also included a Tesla Shop, which allows you to sacrifice various items obtained while playing for a chance at more rare items (some of them are even permanent!).
[Visuals : 8.5/10]
The graphics are very vivid, and bright, while still maintaining that grungey, almost steampunk look you would expect. The effects are extremely well done, and give you a sense of speed and power depending on what's happening. Ragdoll physics can be comical at times, but are a welcome addition, as they amplify the chaos of the game, whether it be slinging chairs across the room, or causing your targets to do triple-backflips when you blow their head off.
Character design, outfit design, and weapon design seem to have received alot of attention this time around. Though I expect more in terms of customization/vanity, the existing items look and feel great. The developers graced us with cool scarf cloth physics, and super jiggly boob physics.
Map design is quite impressive. The maps seem to be well-sized for their respective game modes, and offer alot to look at without being overly-distracting. The remake of the Mansion of GunZ 1 does it justice, as it takes the same basic layout, but brings a feeling of freshness. I fully expect more GunZ 1 tribute maps to come eventually.
[Sound : 9/10]
While I may not have much to talk about as far as sound goes, almost all of what I have to say is good.
If you were a fan of GunZ 1 music, you should expect to be a fan of GunZ 2 music. It brings back the same industrial rock feel, but incorporates elements of electronic, and even what appears to be some jazz fusion. This is one of the only games in which I opt to leave the background music on.
Sound effects for weapons and skills are solid, I have nothing to complain about. Voice overs for Campaign are welcome, even if they are not in english, though I look to seeing an english translation in the future.
My only real complaint with the sound in this game is that some sounds seem to stack for whatever reason. Sometimes when my character dies (it happens alot), I can hear the same voice clip play twice. It's nothing major, but still.
[Heritage : 7]
This game is a sequel. Alot of people will tell you not to treat it like one because it 'doesn't hold true to the original'.
However, I think that it does for many reasons, and here is why;
Though the developers all but did away with the one thing that made the original game popular (K-Style, cancels, etc), they still brought the high energy/skill oriented gameplay back. The learning curve may not be as steep as in GunZ 1 (a cliff), but it is still there. Yes there is more ease-of-access, it is easier to get kills without being an expert, but with time you can still learn the do's and don't's of good gameplay.
The overall game just FEELS the like GunZ 1. The only problems I have with it reside in the lack of fluid movement (which is what K-Style/cancels were all about) and the lack of custom game rooms (which provided a place for people to hang out without being super serious about every match, and even lead to the creation of new player-made game modes).
[Balance : 4]
Here's where the bad stuff comes in...
The various melee weapons feel like they have a real weight behind them, but they stun WAY too much, especially for the amount of damage they do. If you start to get combo'd, you have little chance of survival, even after you learn to parry. This isn't even taking into consideration the end of the combo, where you just get knocked off your feet.
Flip recovery now relies on a skill that you unlock, rather than being there from the beginning, which gives a clear unwanted advantage to higher level players, making it a struggle to play every game prior to then. This doesn't seem needed or justified at all. I find myself missing GunZ 1 safe-fall every time it happens.
Ranged weapons feel bland, with the exception of a few good ideas, but still they have their problems. The grenade launcher can fire too many shots within a small time frame, constantly stunning the player, and preventing escape. The flame thrower does way too much damage, and even leaves damage-over-time when you manage to escape.
Max is so overpowered that most players choose to never select him, and when players do, it leads to a quite ironic flame-war.
[Bugs : 4]
The game seems to crash from time to time, and even lag out for no reason towards the end of the game. The engine seems unoptimized, and the frames-per-second seem to drop considerably even on high-end computers.
<Ending Notes>
The game is fun, though frustrating at times with movement, inbalance, and bugs. As a fan of the IP, it could hold your attention, though you may at first be disappointed in the lack of cancels. I will, and would advise anyone to give the game a try, and tough it out until a later time when many of the game's problems are fixed.

TL:DR 70/100.  Go read initial review then look at my new rating.
OK so you read my intial review below?  Scroll down a bit then come back here.  Great huh?   Here we go...  Remember when I mention DLC and the quest for more money?  Haha, typical joke, everyone laughs.  Well♥♥♥♥♥♥..  Now I'm a little dissapointed in this experience.  Without ruining the ENDING, the game will do that for you on it's own.  Really...  OK.  Total give away.  The ending is♥♥♥♥♥♥  I mean worse than mass effect 3 ending.  By a lot.  You walk through a door, have a brief conversation, and then it's over.  It literally ends just like that.  It's OVER.  Game done!  "but what about ____???"  NO!!!  OVER.  "What the hell?  what about all those...?"  NO!!! OVER!  "What happened to character X?  Character Y?"  SHUT UP GAME OVER.  Roll credits.  We are done!!!!  fffffffffffffffff.  I really was loving this game (read initial review) until it slapped me in the face.  So short, so abrupt, so sad.  I still really enjoyed what I experienced, but I feel let down on length (that's what she said!!!).  I suppose i'll be like every other idiot in the future, paying money for DLC... (quest for more money wink wink).  It was everything I hoped for, then it dropped me off the roof.  Damn.
The story I can accept being left open.  Everything  after all is a business; there are deadlines to meet and shareholders to cater to.  Here come the sequels, DLC, expansions whatever...
Still worth the $60?  What's to compare it to, no mans sky? ;-)  For deus ex nuts like myself... i'm conflicted. Knowing then what I know now, I could wait. For casual gamers who want to play something like this?  Absolutely worth it.  For the deus ex fans, expect an immediate high, then an abrupt crash.
Additional stuff:
The sound track is still terrific.
Did you like the original from 2001?  Then you played Human Revolution, which you liked as well.  Since that is the case, you'll like this one too.  Though I have not completed the game yet, I feel as if I can write an accurate review based on what I've seen so far.
PROS: OUTSTANDING level design.  The architecture, colors, lighting, NPCs etc create a realistic, believable world loaded with details. The magazine covers, posters, ads, faces, fashion design and everything in between is second to none. The price alone is worth it just to see everything.  The voice acting once again, is very good, as is the dialogue.
--Minor spoiler--
Being a fan of the original, it was intriguing to see and hear some familiar characters.  Lucius (DeBeers),  Page, Manderly, Simons, Dowd and others. Glad they kept the spirit of the original in this one.
The missions are engaging and fun.  Again offering various ways to complete based on how you build your character, which leads me to...
CONS: Adam Jensen is overpowered.  The augs, including the new ones, make things too easy.  I'm guessing the makers really pushed for aug usage. Ammunition for your weapons is abundant, but you can chew through it very quickly, leaving you no choice but to augment your way through or around the fight.    Best bet for a challenge is to force yourself not to enable them.  While the AI is improved, it behaves very much like in mankind divided.  Did you open a door right in front of an enemy?  Did you put a giant crate in the hall that wasn't there 10 seconds ago?  Are you hacking a computer at the desk of an NPC who is sitting in a chair right in front of you?  No big deal!  The AI still will walk right up to the doorway of the room you broke into, stand there for a few seconds, then turn around and leave.  It is still very easy to hide from the AI.  Though when they find you, they are a little better at pursuing you.  For example, if you are caught in a vent, they will shoot at both ends in an attempt to flush you out. I found myself having to jump out of vents and run for cover elsewhere a few times I was caught.
Overall, none of the individual cons are big issues.  It's more like small negatives scattered about.
Final gripe is that the majority of the game takes place in Prague.  While you do go to other areas, they are brief, and you come back to the same locations.  Though because of the terrific world design, Prague is very sizable and still enjoyable to explore even after playing many hours.  There is also mention of other cities and locations in the conversations through the game, but we never go to those place.  Perhaps those will be in future DLCs (ahh, the quest for more money).  It just would have been nice like the previous games in the series to see different, larger places (Paris, Hong Kong, Hengsha etc.)
Other things to note:
It's back to unrivaled interactivity with cardboard boxes! Better yet in this go around, we get traffic cones galore!  Don't forget all those boxes of beer and desktop printers!
Being on a PC, I am not having issues I see others mentioning.  I don't have a top quality machine, as I am running a GeForce 960, but the game plays perfect on high (I let the game default for me) settings.  While it's not the ultra settings, the game still looks terrific.  If you are having performance issues, just lower some of the settings, it's not going to ruin anything.  Also, I have thankfully not experienced any crashes or obvious glitches.
Overall the pros most certainly outweigh the cons by a wide margin.  I absolutely recommend this game. Definitely worth the price, and I look forward to multiple playthroughs.  I give it a solid 85-90 out of 100.
This might be a decent gane, but it runs so poorly on the PC it's difficult to say.  Wait until the publisher sorts out how to run the game before purchasing.

Good, but damned expensive.  Especially considering:
∙ The game is relatively ancient.
∙ They're getting set to release a new version of the game.
∙ As soon as this version was released, they literally turned off support for the last version of the game.

Unfortunately, for a game that costs as much as this one does, they seem to have some pretty big major oversights:
∙ They have a micro-transaction system that isn't micro and requires buying points.
∙ Their in-game store does not work with the Steam Wallet.
∙ Some of the expensive content in their store could well - and probably should - be offered on Steam as DLC instead of from their store.
∙ The game should have Steam Workshop integration.
∙ They have a free toolset that will not work with the Steam version - unless  you're willing to edit your registry and perform a wide variety of other advanced tasks in order to trick it.
∙ The game has some pretty basic bugs, and have always had those bugs, and requires mods just to keep the game playable.
Please note most of the problems I've noted just wouldn't be "problems" if the game wasn't still so expensive.  For example:
∙ Simply releasing a version of the game with all the content available for it included in the purchase price, even at a cost of around forty dollars, would render my complaints null.
∙ Either making the base game "free" as in beer, and bringing the costs of the DLC down to no more than a few dollars each.

Stumbled upon this gem a while back. Fantastic time sink for anyone looking to lose hours of their day in a sytlistically dissimilar game.
It's a Hack&Slash RPG. This means that for those who like to fawn over the mechanics of combat in other RPGs, you may find some issues with this game. After a few hours, repitition does rear its' head if you only tend to play one type of the 3 main RPG classes (Spells and pointy hat, quick with a small stick and slow with a big stick).
That being said, the game rewards you immensely for spending skill points in all of the 3 main skill trees and usingthe varied types of weapons. Some of the attacks you can pull off with well timed spells after ranged/melee combos are simply outstanding.
Story doesn't usually rank highly on my list of things I think
to be good for a game to be good but it certainly helps, especially in an RPG. The main quest in Reckoning will send you all over the place in stages, typical to any modern fantasy title. It takes you on a monumental adventure, eventually taking on an enemy no one had a damn clue existed and saving the day etc. good stuff all around.
The world itself looks outstanding, however the only real issue I had with this entire game was the lack of ANY major verticality. The world is by no means planar, but the only transition between up, middle and down was if you interacted with the world to perform a jump into a roll landing from up above OR the world slopes down/up to meet the next area.
Even if the height difference is an inch, you can't simply step up to that height.
While released in 2012, the game has aged fairly well. Would absolutely recommend if it comes up in your Summer Steam sale or a normal purchase if you're simply looking for a solid game.

Playing through all the episodes of Tales of Monkey Island was a complete joy.
As a fan of the Monkey Island series, I have always been very skeptical of this release; so skeptical, in fact, that I refused to even give this game a try until now.
First off, If you are not a Monkey Island fan... I don't know if this is the right game to start with. There are loads of inside jokes and returning characters that the game expects you to know, and the dialogue (as always) does reference previous events in other games. This is definitely the one Monkey Island game that wouldn't stand on its own! Some parts of the story won't have the same impact on you if you haven't lived through at least one other Monkey Island adventure. The more games you played in the series, the more enjoyment you'll get out of this.
With that in mind, it's crazy how good this game is. My expectations were low, but this game should not be as good as it is. What you are getting with the Complete Collection is five episodes, each lasting about 2-4 hours depending on how long it takes you to figure out the puzzles. Generally speaking, the puzzles are pretty easy. You'll definitely not need a walkthrough to beat these episodes, but there's still enough challenge to get you stuck for a few minutes... Still, I wouldn't mind some harder puzzles. Don't worry though, the wacky Monkey Island style is still present, so don't expect any real-world logic to apply here.
I also think that the writing in general lives up to the Monkey Island name, as well! I was surprised by how engaged I was and how much I wanted to see the story through. Good thing all the episodes are already out, because I would have gone crazy if I had to wait for a new episode to be released due to the cliffhangers. Make no mistake, this could have easily been a normal Point and Click adventure game rather than an episodic release. It's not one of those 'separate stories that just kind of fit together'-kind of episodic releases, and playing just one episode wouldn't leave you satisfied.
Seriously, I have no complaints about this game at all, other than the fact that the ending felt a bit rushed. I won't say anymore than that, but you'll see what I mean. It's not terrible and definitely not a game-breaker, but... Yeah.

I'm a fan of the Mortal Kombat franchise, and was looking forward to this game since it was announced. I saw a great sale on it recently, so I decided "what the heck" and picked it up.
I avoided preorder, as a principle, and later decided not to buy the game during the Summer Sale due to all the horrible reviews it had, claiming it was broken on PC, has terrible performance, is a poor console port, etc.
Maybe that was true on launch. I wasn't there, and I won't make any wild speculations. Today however (August 2015), it is working perfectly fine on my predominantly
, with the only notable upgraded component being a GTX 680 from 2012. I've had no issues despite my old (read: slow) computer, my uncommon (read: buggy) hardware configuration, my 96hz 1440p (read: extremely demanding) screen, or my ancient 2007 install of Windows 7 (read: inefficient).
I am able to run on high settings, with a nice solid 96fps, with no bugs and no issues. The game looks pretty good, and it an obvious step up from MK9, which itself looked pretty great for a console port fighting game. Furthermore, there are a whole lot of options to customize; more in fact than most PC only games! It handles alt-tabbing just fine, etc.
The game works, it is fun, and it is a worthy successor to MK9. If you like fighting games, specifically Mortal Kombat, and your computer isn't a
toaster, there is really no reason to avoid this title at this point. The game might have had issues in the past, but people really need to get off the second hand hate train - there is nothing wrong with the game today.

I wanted to write a review that will hopefully dispell and bring clarity to why the game shares some mixed reviews there's going to be a somewhat important comment at the bottom so bear with me or skip to the end:
I'll start off first with what was the most common issue and how my experience compared: Performance and Graphicals.  It seems a great deal of people are experiencing a number of frame rate and quality issues. That leads me to believe that is a majority issue, and my experience of a fairly smooth and visually appealing experience to be a minority exception (I don't know if it made a difference, I put everything, and I mean EVERYTHING on max settings, and it seemed to actually smooth out the gameplay to my surprise. I also played fullscreen as well in 1920x1080 resolution) I'm not saying you WILL experience graphical issues with this game, or never experience them, I can only say my experience was very positive, it actually looked better than mk9 (of course there is a development gap) Keep in mind, steam refunds are usually pretty understanding when they have a game that has known performance issues for some.
Specs are AMD FX-8120 with Nvidia GeForce GTX 960 (EVGA) if you wish to know/compare.
That was the big one I wanted to get out of the way, now the second is online. Unfortunately, it does seem to fall a bit short with constant stutters and players being dropped constantly, I can hope it will improve over time, but if does seem a bit lacking for a game with a retail value of $60. But I digress.
Content, in a competition with MK9, MK9 will win every time, it had more game modes, more one player challenges, and even a longer story (MKX is about 4-5 depending on difficulty, but they did remove the one-sided tag fights in story too which is a mixed bag I feel). They still kept with the tradition of the Krypt, however they made it that quite a few of the koffins appear on a timer... which without a guide, can make it very easy to miss them, some of which contain alternative costumes. It seems like it would be an easy thing to fix... but has remained unchanged.  Furthermore, with MK9 you were given oodles of free DLC taking the form of characters, however in MKX, it is separated into fairly expensive chunks (if bought separately at retail) bringing the "real" retail value up to about $80. With characters like Terra and Predator who obviously didnt appear in the story, I dont find it a big deal. However, Tanya was among one of the characters in the story who they kept under chains, which seems a bit unfair. If it was mostly costume based DLC, I definitely would have no issues, but that's the business model they chose, im not going to criticize that further. On the topic of costumes, some of the alternatives are completely unachievable even with the WBID account, as for whatever reason, it will not recognize that you have completed the requirements (this research I obtained from forums, mostly to save me the time from doing do myself). Probably not that big of a deal, but if you wanted Injustice Skorpion or Ninja Mime Johnny, you might as well call that a console only exclusive.
One thing I did like that they changed up a bit was character styles, which emphasize or add special moves based on what kind of style you played the character as previously, I haven't gone too far in depth to find any balance discrepancies so far, but I'm definitely not an expert at the game so take that with a grain of salt. Also I feel the interractives in the game fall to short on what I call a dice roll to how they can turn the tides. I personally feel it would have been better without them, but it might have been introduced as a way for newbies to be able to pick up the game quicker.
Now here's the catch to all this: I got the game in a bundle with most of the DLC for $20, and that is definitely the price I would pay for this. Wait for this game to go on sale for at least half off, and you'll get your money's worth, otherwise you  might be overpaying for a game that has its usable content cut. Perhaps I'm spoiled by MK9, but MK9 really set the gold standard for future mortal kombat games in my honest opinion, and it would follow its predecessors should do the same. It's not a bad game for certain, from a fighting standpoint it has a lot to offer, but certainly not superceding what it set forth.

Brutal Legend is probably one of the most underrated games I've ever had the pleasure of playing.
In Brutal Legend you assume the role of Eddie Riggs (voiced by Jack Black).  The game is a fantasy/comedy 3rd person adventure in which a roadie named Eddie Riggs is killed and transported many many years into the future (or is it the past?) where "metal" is the rule of law, rock music has magical powers and the world is unrecognizeable.  The game is an odd mix of game types.  On one hand it's an open world action adventure game where you essentially fight bad guys with your huge metal axe or by rocking out on your "axe" which zaps nearby enemies with lightning.  On the other hand it's a RTS game because at a certain point in the game all of the large, story centered battles turn into rock shows in which you harness the power of rock to lay the smack down on your foes.  You summon soldiers of various kinds who have different abilities, direct them to attack your opponent's buildings, play guitar solos to activate special abilities and build merch booths to collect "fans" which act as your resources to upgrade the stage and recruit better soldiers.  You gain the ability to fly which you use to quickly traverse the battlefield and direct troop movements, or even land and do battle yourself in order to help your guys out.
Since the game is sort of an open world type game, there's the usual optional side quests, unique areas to explore, lore to find, and even special guitar riffs you can find that give you special abilities.  For example the "face melter" kills nearby enemies by literally melting their faces off.  You will even find a certain celibrity, the Prince of Darkness, AKA the "Guardian of Metal" in underground caves who will sell you upgrades to your weapons, your roadster, or even cool looking outfits and paint jobs.
The game is not without its faults.  I played through the game on a PC with integrated Intel graphics and while the game ran fine, there was a weird graphical glitch where peoples' faces would disappear.  There's a topic on the Steam forums listing some bugs in the game and the developers seem to have abandoned it, meaning there probably will never be any future bug fixes for this game.  That being said, I didn't experience any game breaking bugs , and when I was having that issue it was on a Linux PC (the game is natively available for Linux if you install Steam for Linux) so it could have been a sub-standard graphics driver for Linux.  Playing it on Windows with my newer AMD machine I haven't had any issues whatsoever.  The only bug I've ever experienced was the facial glitch on that one machine.  Also, the online multiplayer doesn't seem to be very active.  The last time I checked the servers were still up so if you and one of your friends want to play against each other you can, but don't count on finding anybody in "Matchmaking" to play with at random.
The story line is good enough to justify buying the game.  There's a love interest, family drama, and the hero is never recognized as such because he assumes the role of "roadie" where he sees his job as being the guy who stays behind the scenes to make sure everything goes smoothly while staying out of the spotlight himself.  To top it off there's just enough comedy, celebrity appearances and pop culture references thrown in here and there to make you giggle every once and a while.  The gameplay is pretty solid and Jack Black did a surprisingly good job of voicing the main character.  The background music is a mix of various types of rock ranging from death metal to classic rock.  The game is a fun little gem that very few people seem to have played.  I've beaten it on Playstation 3 and PC both, and I still log in once and a while just to go driving around in the Deuce listening to Black Sabbath and going off sweet jumps, lol.

Although there are a lot of puzzles, they aren't as amazing a Nintendo's originals.
Another downside of this game is that it doesn't explain how to use a new item. (As with zelda, you get a new item in a dungeon and the puzzles onward show you what you can do with it).
Then there is the fishing part: This minigame is HUGE downside of the game.
You are supposed to cast your fishing rod into water, wait for the swimmer to be pulled under water to start the minigame. Then you have to keep the fish centered in the screen by pulling it left and right. At the bottom of the screen is a display of the fish's stamina, which is really hard to drain and even can regenerate. Most of the time you try to catch the fish for a couple of minutes until it eventually escapes...
To sum up: Oceanhorn is a well made Zelda clone with a few downsides, but definitely worth buying if you are a Zelda fan!

**EDIT: After beating this game, I have found that this game is exactly what I asked for, albeit short, with seemingly cut content and with an ending that is both incredibly lack-lustre and appears as a tourniquet. I felt this game had a lot of content removed or re-worked over development, which may give reason to its 5 year development time, and if not, is simply too short for a single player, story-based game of this level of development to be justified.
This is a gorgeous game with a great ambition to create and tie into its story well (minus texture and facial animations being sub-par at times, among other things), but I feel that this game should have a lot more to it aside from what was included. I feel this game could be developed to have many more hours of content directly tied to the story, because for such a wonderful looking game - and with the awareness that the quality and attention to detail in the environments is absolutely oustanding and relatively unparralelled like the previous entry, "Human Revolution" - others like "The Witcher 3", with its incredible depth and length (although not as detailed), are over double the length of this. If resources were, at least, taken from developing "Breach" and possibly even the short stories, this game could have had a lot more content to play in.
Additionally, the "stories" feel out of place. I feel the stories could have been included into the main story in some capacity, but were left out because of either both Edios or Square, in this case. I still have not given them a serious look, as their inclusion as a menu item appears very disjointed and unnecessary, given that with some additional development - or even complete omission - the short stories could have either be integrated into the game or omitted entirely.
I still recommend this game, but I am disappointed with some of the decisions that were made with regards to length and story quality.
7.0/10; 9.0/10 if the story were longer and more developed. +0.5 without non-inteference-type microtransactions.
This could have been a truly incredible, landmark game for both its genre, its story-genre, and gaming in general (again, minus early DLC, with micro-transactions being up for debate (they are both optional, and - surprisingly - actually don't feel forced)). Although the story feels cut short, and feels as if Square Enix did so to be greedy, this is still a fantastic game.
Do not let my score fool you - there are great albums and movies that acquire scores such as this because of their potential being squandered, but it is a harsh-appearing rating only due to its shortcomings in the face of its excellence. If anything, wait until this game is about $40 before buying, as, although this game has some shortcomings, it is an incredible game to own.

I do like this game. It can be a bit buggy at times, and the PvP is terribly unbalanced, but the gameplay is really good. The PvE in it is really fun and hard, and it makes you think about how to progress instead of just plowing through. It will also kick you out of a server in the middle of a game, and not just you. Also be aware to not jump in the elevators. Everyone on the server will be forced to find/create/join a new room. But still, it is a good game. The combat is fluid, the classes are varied, and it's a good challenge. Most of the issues I have with it should be fixed in fairly short order, so even if you don't like it now, I would suggest picking it up eventually. And if you're a returning Gunz: The Duel player, I think you'll find that it is different, but not too much that you'll have no idea what you're doing. Over all for now, I give this game a 7.5 out of 10.

Alright, let's get the bad out of the way first:
- Yes, there's a lot of DLC for this game. The total cost is almost $500 to get all the content available on Steam. Even if you don't buy any of the Stuff Packs, which only contain decorative items, you're still spending like $340. There's even more in the online Sims 3 store, most of which is just recolors or redecorations of existing items, but there are at least a dozen premium items that add new functionality to the game...and they cost more than $100 total too!
- The game is VERY buggy and slow. Any time you have to change maps (Create a Sim, Change Outfits, any expansion lot, etc), you have to go through a loading process that can take a while too. Compounding the problem is the "Hidden Objects" Loading Screen game that EA uses to advertise Sims 3 expansions and stuff packs. Once you get in the game, you have to deal with memory leak issues, which means that the game will get slower and slower the longer you play. The problem isn't too bad if you have just the base game, but each additional DLC you add on, the slower it gets. As for the bugs, the list gets too long to mention here. The major ones that I have experienced are that some of the icons don't always load and the Sims will have severe pathfinding issues from time to time. Don't get me started on the minor issues though...
- Make sure you have PLENTY of space. The game itself takes about 32 GB of the hard drive you install it on, which could be rather important if you choose to install Sims 3 on a SSD, which would help with the long loading times I mentioned earlier. In addition to that, the saves and any custom content you download from Sims 3 Store can also add to the bulk. Saves + custom content generally installs itself in your Documents folder, which means anyone who has a small SSD for their OS will have to be careful, since they can take 10+ GB of space as well (my saves + custom content is about 9.7 GB).
Alright, so those are the major bad points I can think of. Do the good points outweigh the bad? Well lets see:
- The game is fairly addictive for me at least. Even though this game is officially a simulation, I treat this game more like a RPG, as you get to customize your characters (Sims), help them train their skills, get better at their jobs, go on adventures (expansion packs required for this part though), and various other things. Even though the game premise (simulating real life) doesn't sound like a particularly exciting thing to do, it actually is quite fun. Your Sims has six basic needs in game: Hunger, Fun, Bladder, Hygiene, Social, and Energy. Trying to satisfy all of those needs while simultaneously trying to get the Sims to get better at various things is a challenge that requires planning and a lot of in-game/real world time. Besides, as you improve your Sims and they get more money, they can buy more stuff...and who doesn't like (pretending) to buy more stuff?
- There's a fairly high degree of customization available in the game. Within the game itself, the number of items available *might* be fewer than in the past, but each item can now have variations, many of which you can customize yourself. In addition, even if you don't get any DLC, there's plenty of free customized content available to download online, and, if you are talented/feeling adventurous, you could always design your own.
Conclusion:
I really wish Steam had a recommendation system ranging from 1-5 stars instead of a simple Yes/No recommendation because getting the game is ultimately a tricky decision. You will definitely have to put up with a lot of various frustrations in the process of playing the game, and patience is certainly required. In addition, even though you can perfectly play the game without any of the DLC, I'm pretty sure that anyone who buys the game without any DLC is constantly going to be either tempted by all the additional features of the expansions or just simply bombarded by the blatant advertisement for the packs that EA sprinkles throughout the game.
Still, if you are willing to deal with these faults and temptations, the game is certainly very fun to play. As I mentioned earlier, the game is certainly a good simulation game, and it does include good RPG elements as well. If you've played Sims 1 and 2 before, you already know more or less what to expect here, and (excluding bugs) the game is certainly better in every way.
In summary, if there was a 5 star rating system, I'd probably give this game a 3.5. Great game, but certainly flawed in numerous ways.

I picked up Kingdoms of Amalur with high hopes from the reviews and screenshots.  It looked pretty and promised things like an open world, a well written interesting story, and dynamic combat.  Sadly, it was bland and left me with a bad taste as it failed to deliver on many of those promises.
The first thing that struck me upon starting up a new game was that the camera is horrific.  The field of view is nauseatingly narrow and there is inherent camera acceleration when using a controller (more on whyy I chose that over mouse & keyboard later).  It also tracks player movement in a seemingly random fashion.  Thankfully there is a third-party program called Widescreen Fixer that was able to give me a usable FOV, but the acceleration/lag was just something I had to get used to.  I also ran into a few glitches such as being teleported around the map and the camera going black until the game was closed and restarted, but thankfully nothing that persisted.
The summary touts the New York Times bestselling author several times, but this seemed like a celebrity endorsement more than an actual contributor.  The story through the main quest that I got through was very generic and I couldn't bring myself to care about any of the characters.  There are several dialogue choices for each NPC you can enter into conversation with, but it's basically just a list of common topics that they'll give a sentence or two on.  I started on the Teeth of Naros DLC and the story was slightly more inspired but not memorable enough to recall.
From a technical standpoint the graphics aren't anything special and the textures are rather blurry for a big budget game from 2012.  The art direction saves it, though, as most environments are unique and very appealing.  While the areas I progressed through during the main story were generic, they were still nice places to be, and the areas in The Teeth of Naros were actually very beautiful and one of the few things that kept me playing as long as I did.
Not really much to say here, unfortunately.  The sound effects were generally passable, but the combat sounds got very tiring due to the hack-and-slash nature of combat meaning you'll spam the same attacks a lot.  Music is a big factor in RPGs for me, and I can honestly say I don't remember a single track.  Nothing was offensive or made me want to turn the music off, but I found the score wholly forgettable.
The gameplay is very combat focused and the combat seemed pretty refreshing at first.  It's pretty hack-and-slashy but satisfying nonetheless.  The combos are few but easy and intuitive and the movement and attacks are relatively fluid.  Where it fell short was how repetitive it became after about 8-10 hours.  I went with a mage as I figured that would keep things more interesting with a variety of spells to mix up combat.  What I found was that it takes a while to learn new spells as you need to level up to earn ability points to unlock them and leveling is quite slow (I only just made it to level 12 in my playtime).  Not a big deal, though.  The bigger issue is that, with a controller, you can only bind four abilities at a time and it takes forever to bind anything new, basically meaning that you better pick your favorite four abilities and forget about the rest.  For a melee build this might not be a deal breaker, but when playing a mage, this is a mortal sin.
Why not use mouse & keyboard, then?  I'm glad you asked.  When I switched M&K (after disconnecting my controller as the game threw a fit trying to use the M&K with it still attached), I started by rebinding my keys, only to find out that a few keys cannot have actions bound to them and a few actions cannot be rebound.  Again, a mortal sin for a PC game.  I also encountered an issue where the 'move camera' buttons would automatically set themselves to whatever I chose for movement, meaning that as I tried to walk around, the camera would automatically move the same direction, overriding the mouse control, basically rendering it unplayable.  At least there was the promise of binding 10 abilities at a time.  Sadly, an unrealized one.
There is a large number of quests and a few of them were interesting, but many felt more like chores.  Thankfully for quests of the nature "kill X of this enemy and collect Y of this enemies pants that only drop Z% of the time and of course don't drop until you actually take this quest even though you've already killed dozens of them," the game has the decency to call them tasks instead of quests.  Shortly before quitting I decided my character would murder anyone who gave me a fetch quest/task.  This was the most interesting "quest" I had.  Another plus is that you can turn down pretty much any quest an NPC tries to give you, so at least you can avoid quest log clutter.
As for world interactivity, it felt very disconnected.  Harvestable plants shimmer to make sure you don't miss them and hidden caches show up on you map from miles away with an early perk, making exploration mostly pointless.  A lack of a jump key and lots of invisible walls also added to that disconnected feeling, keeping me from getting immersed in the world despite how pretty it looked.
So I've touched mostly on the negative points so far, but the most important thing, I think, is the fun factor.  Did I actually enjoy my time playing?  I've put over 800 hours into Skyrim and could go on for pages listing all the negative points, but the bottom line is I still have fun playing it.  As for KoA, I just didn't enjoy my time playing it.  I kept waiting for something to happen in the story to pull me in, but it just never clicked.  I've seen a few people call it a single player MMO, and I think that is the most accurate and succinct way of describing it.  It was like playing WoW on an empty server: unfulfilling.
I didn't expect KoA to revolutionize anything.  I've played Dragon Age: Origins, and you could say it was a very standard fantasy ARPG.  It didn't break any new ground, but it did everything it set out to do well.  If you're looking to scratch that MMO itch and you can look past the technical issues, I'd say pick it up on a deep discount, but to everyone else, I can't recommend it.

Do you want a game that could be compared as the arcade feeling The Elder Scrolls with with too many side quests to deal with? Then this game is right for you. At the start, you were a dead person, and resurrected by a gnome. Eventually you will be fated to be three archetypes: Warrior (representing Might), a Rogue (representing Finesse), or a Sorcerer (representing Sorcery). During your time, you may swap points around any, or all three of these fields to get a nice mix-match of what kind of character you want to build. Sounds great at the start, but sadly the further you go to see a pattern of go to this region and do mindless side-quests that may get you so sidetracked that you may forget what you were meant to be doing with the main storyline. Especially in my case when I took a year long break because of said mindless sidequests.
Combat system is not that bad, but it is not that great either. You are allowed to hold two weapons at a time, yet both, or any of the weapons do have a limiting combo system. Best way to describe is just pressing X X X or B B B with a hint of X "pause" X "pause" X. Catch my drift. Too bad the baddies in the game do not hold up in the variety party. Could be a good thing when you do not have to remember how enemies attack, and can anticipate any attacks.
After the combat comes the spoils, and it feels like the loot got spoiled. In the beginning, when you have nothing to use everything is great loot. By the time you come around your twenties or thiry levels the look; much like any dungeon crawler, can be sparse in quality. Even the armor sets could not hold a candle to some of the blue or even green armors that I had been picking up which makes you wonder if picking the lock of an average or higher difficult chest is worth the trouble.
Speaking of lock picking; there are skills you can either pick up from leveling or some NPCs that you meet along the way. Most of these NPCs may only teach you so much in skill levels that it can be hard to find ones that can teach you further deep into the high ranks; even at areas where it should be level appropriate. Otherwise, most of the skills can you help you further into your adventure especially one to find all the hidden goodies. I did wish the crafting skills could make armor that would of been your end all to be all armor or weapons.
Pros:
+ You got PLENTY to do
+ Though limiting archetypes, but you can mix them up
+ Gorgeous world even at this point of the review it still holds up well.
+ Decent skill system with worth while skills to achieve
Cons:
- Too many side quests, but it is up to you if you want to bother
- Lackluster loot at the end, and crafting weapon and armor is not much worth it. Shame...
- Not much variety of enemies, and not much variety of a combat system
Even though I said a fair share of gripes with this game, but I did played through to the end, even if it was a bit painful if you are one that wants to finish all the quests. Without a middle recommendation, I am still going to recommend, but during a sale.

Being a student project, the game already shows a surprising level of expertise and polish in its gameplay mechanics and story telling. It's a lot more than a tech demo or concept work as it exhibits everything needed for a full fledged game and more. In principle, Hollowed let's the player experience the five stages of grief wrapped in a well thought out puzzle platformer.
Marrying the gameplay with the story, the spirit Oco basically represents the five stages of grief of which the first four the protagonist Halia needs to utilise, or go through, to get to the last stage: acceptance. These phases for Oco to embody are chronologically introduced during the game:
It's not immediately clear that these phases are a manifestation of Halia's emotions tied to her grief. Much like the controls themselves, the story unfolds gradually and escorts the player through a learning process. The puzzle parts have the right difficulty level between easy and frustrating and initially impossible seeming sections can be beaten with ease after a few tries. With the exception of a few sparsely placed tutorial signs, learning by doing is the way to progress and that simply feels rewarding.
Dim colours and a moderate amount of polygons together with soothing piano music and subdued sound effects generate an atmosphere akin to a hushed dream. The world is full of tribal signs, shrines and spiritual beings, both favourable or potentially hostile. Regular occurring alterations of the perspective elicit switches of the depth of field in a scene which is not only neatly done but also advantageous to its story telling.
While unfamiliar control schemes and a few wonky animations make Hollowed harder to get into at first, the game unravels its elegance sooner than later. Its visual and auditory beauty but even more so the gameplay and underlying narrative are remarkable. It's an altogether excellent student game that can easily compete with other established puzzle platformers.

Hollowed is a short, but beautiful game. The story is not terribly original, but it is well told through subtle imagery and hints hidden in each of the many secret areas throughout the game. Both the music and the graphics are pretty, with the latter looking a bit low-tech, like something you would find in older console platformers, which only adds to the overall charm. The fact that all of this is free is dumbfounding. Despite the game only taking about 2-3 hours to fully complete, it is easily worth $10.
The only problem I found are the infuriatingly inconsistent controls. The puzzles and action sequences that require split-second chaining of different abilities to progress were absolutely rage-inducing. I would just find myself cursing under my breath throughout the entire game: every time Halia failed to pick up the Oco, or the Oco got stuck on scenery, or Halia suddenly drifted off the platform, or the Oco got stuck behind Halia, or any other of the many maddening glitches that just kept interfering with what is otherwise a great time. If the controls and the physics were on par with the presentation, Hollowed would have been a masterpiece.

Hollowed is a good game. And it's free.
If you've got a controller and an hour kicking around, then you've stumbled across a good use of both.
Thematically, Hollowed seems to take inspiration from mythological (Babylonian?) 'descents into the underworld,' where a character must overcome trials to recover someone they've lost. There's little philosophical narration going on, and Hollowed instead aims to present pleasing vistas, validating puzzles and a sombre mood overall - and excells at this most of the time. By the end, the story - light as it is - has some conclusionary weight and more meat to it than you might expect, allowing for interpretative thought similar to what INSIDE offers, but with less deviation and independently-viable readings.
In Hollowed, you play simultaneously as a side-scrolling character, and a more complex orb that can change its platforming properties to solve puzzles. The controls are initially awkward, but like Brothers and Thoth, you'll come to feel quite capable in little time. There are some shortfalls; like the ground occasionally eating your companion as it transforms from ethereal to corporeal, and some delay in switching between platforming properties as required by secrets and some of the main puzzles/sequences, but the regular checkpoints mostly resolve this. Different barriers (water, fog, some weird goopy thing) all affect the characters differently, and while I understood them by the end of the game, there was quite a bit of bothersome trial and error in what could have been demarcated more solidly.
I want to stress that the art and music really work excellently together. The denizens of the underworld, both the (presumably) 'hollowed' characters and the masters of the realm, are all interestingly pleasing to observe, while also menacing when the game wants them to be. The game is littered with secret areas that aren't overly 'secret' in the sense of hidden, but offer a satisfying sense of accomplishment once you platform your way to them. Each of them has been tailored to a little scene that makes them aesthetically rewarding, too.
In summ, it's a free student game, and if you like the store page facade, rest assured the game holds true to it.

There's no (intelligible) dialogue to speak of, and it doesn't need any. Between the game mechanics being flawlessly intergrated with the world and the implicit stories, there are a slew of little, inconsequential moments you can interact with, characters you can talk to, and even benches you can sit on for a breather, while the camera gives you a sweeping view at the picturest environments, which add up to a world that feels in turns vast, tangible, and breathtaking.
If you're into simple, artsy, and beautiful games, this is definitely worth your money.

The big daddy of the new Roguelite wave (arguably, Diablo 1 and its clones were the first roguelite wave). The first game to bring procedural generation, permadeath and a focus on emergent gameplay from classical roguelikes into a platformer. This is the remake, the previous pixelated free version is still available to download on the web, with source code.
Utterly perfect game design and level generation, with hilarious emergent moments. Yetis in particular can cause incredible chain reactions.
It's also very addictive: I dislike trying the same level over and over in classical platformers like Mario, once I meet a difficult spot and keep falling in the same hole. But this game is different: the levels change after you die, and it's up to you to use what you learned to make it through this time. I finished the free version of this game multiple times, that's just how engrossing it is.
Lastly and very importantly, it has none of that "meta-progression" bul***** that creates an artificial wall of stats between you and the gameplay in other roguelites I won't name (game impossible to finish until you grind enough, then the beginning is too easy). The only thing standing between you and finishing this game is your skills and knowledge, and however unlikely, you could possibly beat the game on your first go.
You do unlock shortcuts that let you go straight to lower levels to practice them, but to beat the game you really want to do it from the start to get a maximum of tools at your disposal.
My only regret is that I find the graphics and music less charming in this version than in the free version. But the framerate, controls have improved, and this one has even more content, and the addition of coop play.

This game is a mixed bag of a few funny parts but the rest boring. I will review this from a perspective of a loyal Monkey Island fan that has played and owns the first three.
A. Story - The story from Telltale games is okay but is kind of stupid is some parts. It does not flow as well as the first three nor does it feel engaging.
B. Canon/Lore of Characters - Telltale creates characters that are like a spinoff and not true to their original personalities.
1) Guybrush is now some heroic pirate who is known all over the Caribbean. Guybrush normal goofy childish side seems to have been minimalized now. He is mean and cynical in some parts of the game which is not like the original Guybrush we knew.
2) Voodoo Lady is now some manipulator of the entire story. In the originals she was like a helper/advisor only.
3) Stan - The voice of Stan is totally different than the originals and personality is totally different. Stan usually was funny and tried to swindle some money out of people, with arms waving everywhere through any dialogue. In this game he is not funny.
4) Elaine - She is somewhat of watered down version than her former self. In previous games she was more independent and strong.
5) LeChuck - Turns into some nice guy through most chapters then becomes evil again. The concept of him being nice is so outlandishly stupid or odd, that it just doesn't seem like the LeChuck we knew.
C. Consistency - Telltale does not follow previous lore or rules that the first three games set. An example is the Voodoo Lady mentions "You cannot get rid of pure evil" in Curse of Monkey Island. Being able to kill LeChuck in the end of this game doesn't truly fit. Another example is the contradiction when Guybrush gets his hand chopped of in Ch. 1 but magically gets it back in the end. That makes no sense.
D. Graphics - Telltale invented a more 3D interface. This gets really confusing and annoying because you easily can miss things. The original pixelated or even the special edition allows for a better visual point and click interface because the screen is more 2d and flat. The 3D characters look kind of ugly. The special edition of 1 & 2 and cartoon look of Curse of Monkey Island fit the characters and the story great. The 3D view of these characters makes them look odd.
E. Dialogue - Numerous times you are given a choice on dialogues and which to click, BUT frequently Guybrush will not say what you click. This only happened a couple of times in the first three because the dialogue would have been super rude or inappropriate.  In the 5 chapters here, it happens way too frequently so the choice you have on what you want Guybrush to say is already programmed in the game to say something else.
F. Interface - The first three games had choices like a) push b) pull c) pick up d) use e) talk etc. etc. This game you only just click on an item. You click an item and it automatically picks it up. It's like a toddler could play the game almost. This takes away from the game making it less engaging.  There are a few actions in your inventory but the amount of actions is reduced.
Overall, it depends on your expectations. I played the original Monkey Island 1, 2, & 3 over and over numerous of times in my childhood and introduced them to my wife. She likes 1, 2, & 3 but for both of us Telltale Tales of Monkey Island does not feel like the original characters and story we enjoyed. I would not recommend it at full price nor do I like it. If you want to purchase it, I would suggest do it only when it is on sale like we did during the summer sale. For us this was just disappointing and felt like a new artificial story that was not consistent with the original series.

I was too young to play the original two games when they came out, but I was introduced to them three years ago by a friend who thought I'd really like them and gave them to me for my birthday. I absolutely loved them, even though sometimes the out-of-the-box thinking required to solve some of the puzzles (a red herring? Really?) was a bit much for me. So naturally, having loved those two, I figured Tales of Monkey Island would be lovely as well and I purchased them.
I was very unsettled by the first episode because of the different animation and play style of this game versus the old ones. It took me a while to realize that I was unsettled because of how similar the style was to that of Sam & Max, another point-and-click adventure series by Telltale. They even used some of the same voice actors for some of the characters. Once I realized that that was what was bothering me, it was all fun from there.
Very few games really make me feel. With these games though, I laughed, I cried, and I fell in love (literally to all three of those). The new characters, along with the new development of old characters (especially Voodoo Lady), really stood out to me. I was sad for Morgan's unrequited love, deceived by LeChuck's tricks, and very amused by Guybrush's discomfort with the Voodoo Lady's past. The puzzles were very similar in style to the old ones, and truly required some thinking. Fortunately, I'd gotten better at it since the last time.
One thing I also liked was how self-referential the games were. It was just enough to make those who had played the original games feel rewarded, but not so much so that people who hadn't would feel left out. Despite the fact that the existence of these games basically entirely negates the ending of the second Monkey Island game (unless you consider these to just be more adventures of Guybrush and Chuckie), I still am very glad I bought these. It is a very rare thing to see a franchise picked up so many years later by different hands, and to still have it retain everything you loved about it then. Way to go, TellTale!
BEST PART OF THE GAME: They restore the visual for Stan's jacket to the way it was in the original Monkey Island game (not the sequel), so that his arms move but the pattern doesn't move with it. God bless the animators in this game. I missed basically every conversation with Stan because I was just staring at his jacket.

What can I say; it's Monkey Island. I had a few doubts at first, being a diehard fan of the original games, but Telltale has been able to capture the heart, humor, spirit, and charm of the original games perfectly while still providing its own unique spin. If you're a fan of the original games, a fan of adventure games period, or just want a game that can tease your brain just as skillfully as it splits your side, this is a game you can't miss.

Overall, I would recommend this game for previous Monkey Island fans. It feels right to hear Guybrush's voice again and be immersed in that world for an episode. I would be hesitant about introducing it to those not familiar with the earlier games.
