I highly reccomend this game if your into games that take A LOT of time to complete.
Now i will say this, this game is ever so slightly grindy, in regards to making money "at the start" but when you get into the game and gather enough cash and resources you can purchase businesses at the major cities which can give you an income every week, which will deal with the money issue in the game.
The combat is very intuative and is linked to mouse movement, if you have a sword or an axe and want to do an over head smash straight down into the head of an enemy, you have to left click and move your mouse up slightly, same goes for the right side and left side slashes as well... It might seem a bit confusing at start, maybe even irritating to some degree, but stick with it and give it a few fights and your slashing through your enemies so quickly your forget your even moving your mouse at all.
Now in regards to content, this game is FULL of content, for the price of £15 you are getting a steal.
In this game you are able to take part in large tournaments and fight in several waves of combat against multiple enemies and fight for glory and money, the base prize for the tournament is usually 250 Denars but if you have enough cash on you, and start chucking 100 denar bets on yourself each round that will easily climb to over 2500 denars each tournament, which is a good way to make cash quickly if your low on money.
Another way to gather cash quickly, is to raid enemy villages and steal their belongings, the villagers might seem to be living on the bread line so to speak, but after raiding their town your gather loads of top ticket items to sell for a huge profit, on average, im able to get about 3000 to 4000 denars just by selling their items in the cities at the marketplace... A good way to gather enough cash to purchase businesses.
The leveling up system is great and is full of ways to level up your characther as you see fit, and all of it falls into four main areas, Strength, Agility, Inteligence and Charisma... for example, if you want to run faster, and hit harder with your weapons, then put your level up points into Agility and Strength respectively.
If you want to be able to build siege ladders and lead more men to glory, then dump points into Inteligence and Charisma, you get the general idea.
Now a single man is unable to conquer the land by himself, which is why you need to gather an army... Which can be done in several ways... The cheapest way is to recruit villagers, they cost 10 denars each and on average you can get about three to five villagers in each town, occasionally your get only one or two villagers who want to join you and on rare occasions you get six or seven villagers in one go... Its a quick and easy way to gather an army, but these troops are not the best but will level up quickly at the start and improve their chances of survival with better weapons and equipment which each level they go up.
A more expensive venture is to go to the local taverns in the major cities and hire men from there, they might cost more money at the start but they are much more adept at combat and are generally worth their price in the tavern.
Finally, you have the hero's or unqiue followers, there are multiple followers in the game which you can recruit from taverns incuding, Bunduk, Klethi, Nizar and Jeremus who will join your army to fight alongside you and provide insight into the games world, they range in price from free to 500 denars but they can be modified the same way as your charachter, and you can change our their equipment at any point should you so desire, bear in mind some unique followers will only use certain weapons and can only wear armor up to a certain weight and strength value.
My advice, gather enough money, buy as many unique followers and men as you can from the taverns and give the enemy a run for their money and land.
In summary
Graphics 6 / 10 - at the time the graphics were quite simple but its not exactly an ugly game and the game itself shows its beauty in the amount of content available... As long as you don't expect the standard of graphics available when it was released back in 2010 you should be fine.
Content 9 / 10 - This game is full of content and your find new things to do in every playthrough and its worth the price for how much you get.
Sound 8 / 10 - The game is full of music and during combat your hear the woosh of arrows as they fly through the air, the squeaky, squelch as your sword smashes into the enemy, the horse galloping towards you and the battle cries of your soldiers as they run to battle and yell of victory when you kill every last enemy in battle... Music wise, the music is varied and fits the game perfectly, but there will be a time when you've heard every track in the game, but during battle the music really gets the blood pumping.
Gameplay 9 / 10 - Excellent gameplay is available for you, and combat wise its very intuative and gritty, your find so much to do in this game, you might just find yourself getting addicted to it like i am, and spend hours playing it.
Overall 8 / 10 - Overall this game is a must buy, the graphics aren't groundbreaking at all, but it suits the game perfectly and does the job it needs to in a great fashion... The amount of content available is breathtaking to say the least and i would say it is well worth the purchase price.

This is a short and sweet puzzle platformer, that everyone should play, who enjoyed Limbo or INSIDE.
The total playtime is around 2-3 hours and it's totally worth your time.
The story is told through the environment and unfolds more and more as you progress, just like in the aforementioned games.
The gameplay mechanics revolve around traversing through obstacles with the help of your physically manifested...(spoilers?) soul. Your soul is represented as a floating ball, that has 4 different properties that you need to toggle and cleverly switch and combine to progress through the stage.
I think it's open to interpretation what each aspect is supposed to be, but basically you have:
a red, fiery aspect that can push or pull you to places, which might represent temper/ drive/ ambition;
a black aspect, which is a heavy ball, that can be used as extra weight (maybe negativity/ guilt/ burden?);
a baby blue light aspect, that can float through small spaces and switch places with you (positivity/ freedom);
and finally a pink aspect, that, when toggled on, reveals an alternative route (imagination/ creativity?).
I never gave any thought to what these 'aspects' might be on my first and only playthrough, but as you reach the end and it becomes more evident, that it is indeed your soul, then you start to wonder...
Anyways..given that this game is free, it's amazing how much polish and detail these guys put in. Quite frankly, I think they could easily charge 5€ for it and it would totally be worth it. Great job guys.

Hollowed is a puzzle platformer where you play a Hollowed lady, Hollow, who is trying to save her beloved. You start the game in a dying world trying to save your beloved. However, you fail and the god of the story pulls out a little bit of Hollow's soul to form a tiny ball called Oco. Once you reach the end of the story, you have 2 default endings to choose from. I won't spoil it for you but I suspect that there's a 3rd ending.
Gameplay-wise, it's a confusing controller system where you have to simulataneously control your character, Hollow, with the left thumbstick and her floating soul, Oco, with the right thumbstick. Square, Triangle, Circle, X or ABCD are the 4 forms of Oco. L1 is the jump button. Left thumbstick is Hollow and Right Thumbstick is Oco. The main gameplay comes from Oco, who is able to change into 4 forms. The 1st form allows you to alternate between realities in a small bubble and bring over some parts. There will be markings to let you know that you can alternate realities. The 2nd form allows you to pull and catapult yourself over long distances. The 3rd form allows to swap positions between Hollow and Oco. The 4th form allows Oco to turn into a heavy solid ball, detach itself from your body and allow it to be tossed over a small distance.
Conclusion, do try it since it's free. The game is short and the puzzles are relatively simple to solve. Executing the actions with cavemen reflexes are the main problem.
1. It's Semi-Interesting
The interactions with Oco are fine but not so wow.
1. Unintuitive Controls
Jump is the L1 trigger. Can you imagine how difficult it is to have an action that affects your movement on the same hand that controls your movement?
2. Complex Hand Movements
Do you need to jump, transform, move and swap? Just try it and you'll know.
3. Wasted Background
It's just left to right in the foreground. The Background is greatly wasted in terms of gameplay.
1. Separate Oco from Hollow
If you separate Oco from Hollow, the possibilities for puzzle solving grows exponentially. E.g. You can fly Oco to a button high up on a cliff, then change Oco into heavy form to press the button.

I know I am going to get a ton of hate for this, but considering I was expecting the "Greatest Game of All Time" like so many people were saying, I have to say I was incredibly disappointed by this game.
First off, it was hard to get used to the controls. I understood them, and I thought the layout was nice (Each joystick and trigger controls each brother), however I found myself constantly getting mixed up between the two, causing the characters to run in all sorts of directions. This can be either very frustrating or very funny, depending on which person you are. I found it a bit of both
What really frustrated me was that this game was extremely linear and easy. This game is advertised as a puzzle game, and yet none of the puzzles got me thinking like a puzzle should. Most of them include holding down the trigger and pressing one direction on the joystick. A big problem is that each puzzle only has ONE way of solving it, and there is no room for player creativity. The game makes it clear that you will be going the way it wants to, and the on-screen characters will not hesitate to point in the direction you need to go. There are many times in this game where I was forced to do something that I either did not want to do or did not did not know why I was doing it (What if I didn't want to free that troll? There were many other ways I could've progressed without freeing a potential criminal).
There are also invisible walls EVERYWHERE. Throughout the game, there are cliffs and canyons that look dangerous, but there would be no way to fall, as the game will not let you. There are moments where you will be balancing on a thin log over a giant waterfall, and it may seem difficult until you realize that, no matter how much you push the joystick in the opposite direction, there is no way you can fall. There are even ankle-high ledges that are blocked by these walls, which strips the sense of freedom and adventure that the game is trying to make the player feel.
Lastly, as much as the story is praised by others, it is really nothing special. The premise has been used before (You are on an adventure to find a treasure that will cure your father of an illness), but it is fitting for the fairytale-like setting. My main problem with it is that it focuses too much on being emotional, rather than being thought-provoking. Yes, you may cry at some points, but there were not any moments that made me think and reflect. The ending was especially disappointing for these reasons.
To sum it up, I felt this game fell flat in what it, and its fans, were promising. The gameplay is limited and void of challenges, the story was not engaging for me, and the ending was unsatisfying. It definitely did not resonate with me like TotalBiscuit promised. The visuals are beautiful, though. I can't lie about that
Overall, this isn't a BAD game, but it does not even get close to "Best Ever" status. If you are into these short, story-driven games, I would recommend To The Moon. It does not have the scenery as Brothers does, but the story is much more intriguing and engaging, with a very solid finish.
If this game is on sale, then sure, pick it up. But don't buy into the hype. This is an average game. 6/10

Do you want a game that could be compared as the arcade feeling The Elder Scrolls with with too many side quests to deal with? Then this game is right for you. At the start, you were a dead person, and resurrected by a gnome. Eventually you will be fated to be three archetypes: Warrior (representing Might), a Rogue (representing Finesse), or a Sorcerer (representing Sorcery). During your time, you may swap points around any, or all three of these fields to get a nice mix-match of what kind of character you want to build. Sounds great at the start, but sadly the further you go to see a pattern of go to this region and do mindless side-quests that may get you so sidetracked that you may forget what you were meant to be doing with the main storyline. Especially in my case when I took a year long break because of said mindless sidequests.
Combat system is not that bad, but it is not that great either. You are allowed to hold two weapons at a time, yet both, or any of the weapons do have a limiting combo system. Best way to describe is just pressing X X X or B B B with a hint of X "pause" X "pause" X. Catch my drift. Too bad the baddies in the game do not hold up in the variety party. Could be a good thing when you do not have to remember how enemies attack, and can anticipate any attacks.
After the combat comes the spoils, and it feels like the loot got spoiled. In the beginning, when you have nothing to use everything is great loot. By the time you come around your twenties or thiry levels the look; much like any dungeon crawler, can be sparse in quality. Even the armor sets could not hold a candle to some of the blue or even green armors that I had been picking up which makes you wonder if picking the lock of an average or higher difficult chest is worth the trouble.
Speaking of lock picking; there are skills you can either pick up from leveling or some NPCs that you meet along the way. Most of these NPCs may only teach you so much in skill levels that it can be hard to find ones that can teach you further deep into the high ranks; even at areas where it should be level appropriate. Otherwise, most of the skills can you help you further into your adventure especially one to find all the hidden goodies. I did wish the crafting skills could make armor that would of been your end all to be all armor or weapons.
Pros:
+ You got PLENTY to do
+ Though limiting archetypes, but you can mix them up
+ Gorgeous world even at this point of the review it still holds up well.
+ Decent skill system with worth while skills to achieve
Cons:
- Too many side quests, but it is up to you if you want to bother
- Lackluster loot at the end, and crafting weapon and armor is not much worth it. Shame...
- Not much variety of enemies, and not much variety of a combat system
Even though I said a fair share of gripes with this game, but I did played through to the end, even if it was a bit painful if you are one that wants to finish all the quests. Without a middle recommendation, I am still going to recommend, but during a sale.

Salvatore fantasy novel equivalent of a Role Playing Game, in the sense that it's really pointless to suffer through unless you are a fan of the genre with more free time than it would take to experience all the better offerings out there.  Why?  Well, for starters Kingdoms of Amalur is basically a single player WOW clone.  This isn't a bad thing by itself, and it might even be a selling point for many (and I thought it would be for me).  However, it really doesn't work. First, there is a limit to how many fetch quests and kill quests and how much stupid narrative you really can suffer through by yourself before it all starts feeling like a drag.  Second, the world, while immense, also feels like a desolated patchwork of ideas that just never comes together the way WOW's world does.  And lastly, the game's mechanics just don't come together well, leaving you with a lot of trap build options and over-performing weapons/builds.  I haven't sunk enough hours in to finish the game (my guess is that I'm probably at around 25% mark so far), but what I've played so far really doesn't make me want to go back for more.  Uninstalled, and not recommended.

I am not normally a fan of tower defense titles but Toy Soldiers is a welcome exception to that rule.  Although the basic gameplay in Toy Soldiers is identical to other tower defense titles, what really makes Toy Soldiers stand out is both the World War I atmosphere and the ability to individually control any one of your placed structures in a first person manual mode.  This not only gives the gameplay and extra level of depth, but allows you to watch the battle unfold first hand as well as adding in the twitch element that most tower defense games lack entirely.  These two elements are both so well done that Toy Soldiers definitely stands head and shoulders above most of the similarly priced competition.  Although the Steam Overlay is supported, unfortunately the game only supports resolutions up to 1680x1050, which results in a less than sharp picture on a widescreen monitor.  Minor flaws aside however, Toy Soldiers is a must have game for anyone who is a fan of the genre.

Oceanhorn is a mediocre isometric Zelda Clone that was initially released for tablets.  The controls, production values and graphics are surprisingly good considering that fact, but the game is pretty wholly style-over-substance and limited by isometric view and tablet technology alike- and it's afraid to be ambitious and challenge the format as well.
Why isn't it recommended?  Well, you've got a lot of other choices for better zelda clones, for one.  For two, although they put in the work to render this playable with a 360 controller, the controls are going to feel weird for the whole of the game.  Lastly... well, there's just no ambition, original ideas or spark, here.  They made a damn fine tablet zelda clone, and that's kind of it.  The occasional voice acting isn't bad (although it sounds like the same guy each time) but it can't save the world's blandest adventure.  In addition, the hit detection is kind of poor and your character is ploddingly slow (limited running doesn't help, either)
If you buy this you won't be wasting 20 bucks, but you can do better.  I can't recommend it.

The game's presentation is like old school games.
Retro gamers would find the presentation style very familiar and nostalgic. This is a good point.
The art style might not be for everyone.
This is not good or bad. It is just a matter of preferences.
Musics are good and suit the game pretty well.
Although sometimes, somehow, even though they sound good, it feels like they lack some originality.
Default aspect ratio is 4:3 with fixed resolution in windowed screen mode.
Game's window can be dragged to change size and full screen mode can be enabled but no proper resolution scaling. This is a drawback.
I read from some reviews that this game was in development for so many years.
For indie game which usually has small development team and budget, it is understandable that there would be something unpolished.
Still, in this day and age, not being able to change resolution properly, it is kind of a little letdown.
The gameplay.
This is where this game really shines.
Player put characters in the stage and let them do their jobs.
Characters automatically perform actions according to their roles but that is not a bad thing at all, on the contrary, the combat system is actually pretty deep.
Various characters with various roles and skills, fast pace switching mechanism of characters/roles in response to the game situations and enemies' mechanics. Especially in later levels where bosses and even normal enemies have various tricks up their sleves and failure in responding or improper strategy can easily result in game over or hard situation to recover from. The fights can get very intense and challenging which is something I did not expect when I first saw the game's art.
I would call this game an Action/Strategy had the developers did not state it as a RPG. But that is understandable since various elements in the game such as ATB, characters' roles, strategies, skills set and level up system are not far from RPG's standpoint at all.
And like old school games, there are secrets and extras to be discovered, which brings back memories of retro games. This adds value to the game and is something that is hard to find in this era of DLC.
The game has its pros and cons. But ultimately, this game has the one quality that I consider to be the most important quality for a game, indie or not. It is fun.
Recommend.

Wanderjahr is a very nice “clicker” RPG. The graphics are very beautiful and seems inspired by games such as MapleStory. Gameplay consists of managing a roster of heroes during battles and swapping them out of tactical necessity when needed, as you can only have 4 on the battlefield simultaneously.
The heroes attack automatically, and you are in control of item/spell use and switching out heroes when needed. In between battles you spend the gold and stars you earned from killing monsters on buying healing items, technology/spells, and upgrades for your heroes. Unfortunately, there are no skill trees for heroes which was something I would have liked to see and thus upgrades are completely linear.
Story-wise, the game was a bit on the weak side (you apparently have to read the plot from the menu?). Additionally, some heroes seemed more useful than others (the “thief” class hero doesn’t do much damage and only helps steal an inconsequential amount of gold per attack). However, I did enjoy the art style in this game and the animations were very smooth. Some levels were very challenging, including the first bossfight. I also enjoyed the soundtrack of this game. Overall, I did enjoy the game for the few hours I’ve played it and would recommend picking it up on a sale or when more content/updates get added.

Hollowed is a puzzle platformer game that for some reason can only be played with a controller but works fine control wise. It does take a little getting used to, as the control scheme is not very typical, but once you get it, it flows well.
The game is also pretty short, but for a free game it fails to be a deal breaker. I beat the game personally in about 40 minutes or so, but I enjoyed it, and it might take longer or shorter depending how well you handle the game's various challenges.
Basically, you go through puzzles requiring you to use 4 different abilities tied to the spirit character you control along with your human character, and that is your tools the entire game.
Pros++
+Fun Simple Puzzle Solving
+Abilities are very obvious in how they work.
+Difficulty ramps up very nicely and evenly. I never felt the game did not prepare me for what came at me.
+Interesting Character Design
+It's Free. Duh.
Cons--
-Controller only, no Keyboard support. I personally use Controller on most things anyway, but I know many people like their keyboards.
-A little glitchiness with collisions sometimes.
-+The game doesn't outright tell you much at all, so you mostly have to figure out what a lot of things do or how they react, like if a thing is killing, you, or your spirit, or something else wrong entirely. Could be a positive or negative depending how you like your games.
Overall, I liked this short little puzzle romp. I felt challenged as I proceeded, and had a fun time! I wholeheartedly reccomend it for any fans of platformers or puzzle games.

Your protagonist will go through many a peril to reach her beloved, and my oh my, this is an enthralling experience and a real aesthetic pleasure.
There are, in fact, two protagonists, as you are simultaneously given control of your spiritual companion, an orb creature that provides you with four abilities to use. The gameplay is based on combining all four in order to work your way ahead and pass different obstacles. These abilities are interestingly unique, and make for extraordinary puzzles. The puzzles are quite
, and never cease to amaze with their ever-growing ingenuity. My heart literally skipped a beat every time I ran into a new predicament, and having to replay certain places over and over was actually a delight.
The controls feel slightly weird and unfriendly at the beginning, but you will likely get used to them very soon. However, the game gets really demanding at times, testing your quick thinking and memorizing abilities. Be prepared.
I really hope you guys and your game get all the attention in the world you deserve.

TL;DR: It's an alright game if you're just looking for something to scratch a third-person action itch for twenty hours or so, but there's really nothing that makes it stand out as anything special.
Combat itself is entertaining enough, but there's absolutely no depth to it - you have one basic attack per weapon type that can be chained together to a limited extent, and a couple of active abilities that scale so terribly you'll hardly bother using them. And since unlocking additional weapon moves is locked in to progress down the ability trees, you spend half the game without access to the more varied attacks, meaning that most of the time you'll just be hitting your attack button and blocking/dodging occasionally.
The combat balance is almost non-existent, enemies are almost universally completely trivial other than the occasional one who is an annoying damage sponge and does hilariously disproportionate damage, and there's only about a dozen different enemies who are palette swapped and recycled throughout the course of the game. The most challenging part of the combat is dealing with the abysmal camera, which has a mind of its own and loves to zoom right in on you when you're surrounded by enemies, only stopping to clip through the scenery and get stuck under the floor occasionally.
There's a variety of non-combat skills to choose from (lockpicking, stealth, persuasion and so on) which are generally either absolutely bloody useless, or hilariously overpowered. Depending on which ones you choose you can end up completely trivialising the game without even trying, but with a little care you can max out almost all of the skills anyway which makes any sense of choice completely redundant.
The ability trees are probably the highlight of the game, there's a lot of different abilities to choose from, and thankfully you can respec your character at any time to try different things out. Depending on how you want to play, you can either go deep into one of the trees (magic, might, or finesse, which broadly correspond to the standard mage/warrior/rogue archetypes) or split your points across two or even all three trees. Putting enough points into one tree or a combination of trees unlocks "destinies" which give you added stats and bonus abilities and can make different ability builds feel very different from each other. Ultimately, however, it's still limited by the shallow nature of the combat system, and however you build your character you'll inevitably end up spamming the same basic attacks over and over again.
The real issue is with the pacing of the game. Every single town you come across is chock full of completely forgettable NPCs who will bury you up to your eyeballs in fetch quests and kill quests which give no real rewards but make you slog all over the place anyway. Either you try and do everything out of an obsessive sense of completionism, or you get bored of that by the second or third town, rush through the main quests, and realise there's really not that much game under all that padding. There are half a dozen factions with their own sidequest chains that have a bit more structure to them, but none of them really add much to the game, and aside from some minor stat boosts it makes absolutely no difference to anything whether you do them or not.
Overall it's a thoroughly mediocre experience through and through, which never manages to be amazingly good or offensively bad. If you like third-person action RPG games it ticks pretty much all of the boxes, it does everything more or less adequately without ever really impressing, it all looks nice enough and there's a whole bunch of lore if you can be bothered to pay attention to it. Pick it up in a sale and it'll give you a good thirty hours or so of moderate entertainment, but it's a mostly unremarkable experience with next to no replay value.

But it isn't. You'll find yourselfe spamming the same 3 combos all the time while getting annoyed of hundrets of MMORGP-like Sidequests.
I heared you people love +/- Lists so here you go!
The Good
+ Character customisation. You really have a lot of options and skills to chose from. You can also customise the apperance of your charater but the options are very limited so don't expect it to be as complex as in TES-Games.
+ Voice Acting. Honestly i haven't seen the entire game but so far i think all NPCs where well voiced. With one huge exception. Your own character. All your character has are texts you can choose in Dialoges and the "uh" "uah" "ah" in combat. This actally doesn't bother me too much as it's already a common thing in a lot of RPGs.
+ Open World. There is actally a lot of loot and other stuff to look for. Would be a huge + if the game was genarally good.
+ Decisions. Yay! I cannot tell you how much effect they have on the world around you but at least you can make some.
The Meh
~ Enemies. Not much variety for such a huge world but many of them require unique strategies to deal with them without losing too much life. For many of them it's recommended to learn their attacks and how to counter them.
The Bad
- Generic MMORPG feeling. The Quests are getting boring after the first few hours and even if there is a huge effort to make the Quests interesing, it still felt like brainless EXP-grinding.
- Tons of Sidequests. Wait, how is that a bad thing? Well if the game isn't fun at all you don't want to waste hours over hours doing minor stuff so you can keep up with the level of your enemies.
- Combat. If the combat gets dull and boring in a game build around combat nothing else can safe the game from a bad score. The combat it repetitive and boring. At first it seems fresh and fun but after a few hours in you'll see how boring it gets when you spam the same stuff over and over again with the wepons(s) of your choice.
- Bugs. Tbh i haven't encountered any but i haven't made it far enough into the game to get to the buggy parts of it. Quests cannot be completed if you do stuff in the wrong order and things like that. So a lot of save slots are highly recommended.
- EA Account. Yes, it's one of those games where you have to make a third party account and have to be online to play a singleplayer game.
- Inventory. A barely sorted List of Stuff, that you can only extend buying a limited Number of Backpacks from some NPCs. This is the Part where you clearly see that this game is a console port.

: NetherRealm Studios, High Voltage Software
: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
==========
Since 1992 when the first Mortal Kombat was released, we've seen many entries in the iconic fighting franchise. Despite it's name, Mortal Kombat X is the 21st Mortal Kombat game to see release, but it is the 10th installment of the main storyline. Featuring some new characters, mainly the children of some of the more well-known characters, Mortal Kombat X picks up 2 years after Mortal Kombat 2011 (commonly referred to as MK9) left off. Shao Khan has been defeated, but Shinnok has returned to once again threaten Earthrealm. Just to name a few of the new characters-- Kotal Khan, D'Vorah, Erron Black, Jung Jin, Cassie Cage, Takeda Takahashi, Jacqui Briggs, and Ferra/Torr. A lot of the older characters return, but with new looks. Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden and more are all here. Other characters such as Kabal, Sindel, and Stryker make an appearance as well.
==========
MKX retains most of the features that we've come to expect from the series, with the addition of a couple of new ones. The game plays out similarly to
. You'll have a cutscene, followed by a slight transition to the in-game engine where kombatants say a line or two to each other, then you have the fight. Once the fight concludes, the winner says a one-liner, then the game transitions back to cutscenes. Story Mode plays out entirely like this, and it works very well. It's *almost* seemless, but those with a good eye will see the exact moment of transition.
Returning from
are the stage interactions. Scattered throughout each stage are objects you can use to your advantage, that range from dealing damage or making an escape. There was literally one stage where you can pick up and old woman in the background and chuck her at your opponent! These interactions do a lot of damage, but seemed to have been scaled back a bit due to how abused they were in
.
There are a variety of game modes, spanning singleplayer and multiplayer. Let's go over singleplayer initially. First and foremost is the Story mode. In this mode you go through several chapters, each one dedicated to a specific character who you'll use to progress through battles that advance the story. Story Mode took me approximately 4-5 hours to complete. While short, it's really fun. Next, we have the Towers, which is like the classic ladder arcade mode. There are 3 towers initially, each with a different number of opponents. There's Single Fight, where you just choose your character and an opponent and just duke it out. Next is Test Your Luck, where you face off against the AI with random modifiers. Lastly, there is a Training Mode where you are free to practice with any character you choose on any stage, with various settings for your AI opponent. They can fight back or just stand there as you practice combos.
Multiplayer has a few different modes, the most notably of which is the Ranked Ladder. Participating in these allows you to climb the ranking ladder to number 1. There is also the returning King of the Hill mode from
. Lastly there are Tower Battles where you face other players. I didn't play multiplayer very much, as that's not my thing typically, but what I did play ran satisfactorily. There was a small bit of lag but it did not impede my enjoyment and was easy to adapt to. This may or may not be a dealbreaker for some players.
One of the new features added with MKX are tokens. There are 2 types of tokens: Skip Fight and Easy Fatality. Skip Fight allows you to do just that: skip any fight that you choose, as long as it's in Story Mode. Use these when you happen to get stuck versus a certain opponent. When used, the game acts as if you had won the battle. The Easy Fatality Token allow you to execute Fatalities with an easy button press. Both tokens are earned by unlocking them in the Krypt, which is also a returning feature.
Another new feature is the addition of Fighter Variations. These are sort of like different styles, and each kombatant has 3 of them. Each variation gives access to certain abilities which help define the playstyle of the character. For example, Scorpion has a Shirai Ryu style, which gives him access to dual-swords, and he also has Hellfire, which gives him access to demonic hellfire powers.
Lastly, MKX features a Faction War. When you start the game you are able to choose between 5 Factions. Upon joining one, simply playing the game (in any mode) earns you Faction Points. At the end of every Faction War, the winner is chosen and all members of the winning Faction are rewarded.
==========
MKX looks just as good as its previous installment. Everything is rendered in great detail, and as a staple of every Mortal Kombat game...there is a LOT of blood! It wouldn't be Mortal Kombat without it. Mortal Kombat is known for its amount of violence and graphic brutality. Nothing has really changed since the last game, and that's a good thing. Some character have new designs or reskins, such as Sub-Zero, Johnny Cage, and even Raiden. The biggest difference I noticed was that of Johnny Cage. TL;DR version: Chapters 1-4 were fun games with a few moments of tedious repetitive walking here and there, 5 was a horribly drawn out game with too many cut scenes and too much walking back and forth between point a and point b (with a point c thrown in from time to time for 'variety').
I hate to give a Monkey Island game a thumbs down, I really do - but overall, this game left me feeling unsatisfied.  Which is a shame, because the first four chapters actually built up quite nicely.  I was entertained by chapters 1 through 4, and I was looking forward to the final chapter.  BUT that final chapter - ugh!  Before I go on to a part that's spoilery, I'd like to mention my two big non-spoilery complaints, which both boil down to: movement!
First: you can only move by holding down a mouse key or by using awsd - and you have to keep your finger on the key/button or he'll stop moving.  Boy is THAT fun through 5 frigging games.  Oh wait, no, no it's not.
Second: like every five feet you walk, the screen changes to a new viewpoint.  And that new viewpoint frequently ends up being from another perspective or angle.  And when that happens, here's what MAY happen with your movement:
- keeping your finger on the button you had it on may keep him moving in the direction you had him walking in this first place.  This is disorienting when you were holding 's' for down and suddenly Guybrush is walking right.  Removing your finger and re-pressing s will make it down, but that gets annoying with a lot of screen changes.
- keeping your finger on the button you had it on may start him moving in the wrong direction.  You are walking down on one screen, you move to the next and he's still moving down, only now there's nowhere to go.
- keeping your finger on the button may do nothing.  You move to the next screen which (miracle of miracles) still has you facing in the right direction, and yet you suddenly stop, and have to again remove and repush the button to make him walk again.
- moving just a LITTLE too close to certain areas may end up with you walking into them, frequently interrupting your (six thousandth) walk from one end of town to the other as you try and complete a quest
If there's any rhyme or reason to when each of the above happens between screens, I never found it.
Dear game makers: if you absolutely MUST pad your game's playtime by making us go over the same territory again and again and again and again AND AGAIN (I'm not kidding, the final chapter is almost entirely made up of trudging back and forth between 2-4 points) - the LEAST you could do is give us back the option adventure games used to have of being able to choose faster or slower walking paces.  Remember Space Quest?  Yeah, I know you do.  Sure, you'd murder yourself a few times walking straight into something horrible, but at least you could speed up and slow down as necessary.
And now for the complaints about the final chapter, which is wholly responsible for my reluctant thumbs-down of this game as a whole.
PLEASE DO NOT READ ON IF YOU WANT TO AVOID SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL CHAPTER. PLEASE DO NOT READ ON IF YOU WANT TO AVOID SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL CHAPTER. PLEASE DO NOT READ ON IF YOU WANT TO AVOID SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL CHAPTER. PLEASE DO NOT READ ON IF YOU WANT TO AVOID SPOILERS FOR THE FINAL CHAPTER.
Okay, ready?  So, the whole Voodoo Lady thing - what was up with that?  Oh, she's using us all.  You know what, let's just keep listening to her advice!  Well... okay, I guess it doesn't make a lot of difference, in that she doesn't really give any advice.  She either speaks in riddles that never actually mean anything, or outright says "hey take that thing, you need it, it does such and such."  And now that Lechuck is (surprise) vanquished (temporarily (surprise)) AGAIN, let's forget about going after the Voodoo Lady and like... killing her to stop her from doing all this♥♥♥♥♥♥again!  The whole idea of making the Voodoo Lady into some sort of quasi-villain without a MUUUUUCH better job of explaining it, or dealing with it in the end, was a terrible, terrible idea.  I don't mind the repetitiveness of Lechuck as a villain, he's funny, and that's great, but the Voodoo Lady thing just left a big weird unresolved mess at the end of the game.  Between that and retracing my steps about a billion times - oh! and staring at the screen waiting for Lechuck to punch me to the next place where I had to do something a billion times - it ruined my impression of the game as a whole.

There´s no denying this is a Zelda rip-off. If you re-skinned it could certainly pass for a handheld iteration of the franchise. It´s got heart pieces, dungeon with small keys and boss keys, dungeon items/spell as you progress, collecting powerful ancient artifacts necessary to defeat/reach the final boss. The question is, if it was  a Zelda, would it be a good one? Not really. Would it still be enjoyable? Hell yeah!
As far as "Zelda rip-offs" go, this was the best I´ve ever played. It keeps the light and colorful tone that makes you fell comfortable while playing it. The controls and gameplay are not particularly good, but you must consider this was originally a mobile game, and as far as gameplay goes when fighting enemies it doesn´t go far from what you'd expect in the handheld iterations.
Is does lack in story, though. Very simple plot, although there is a lore to the game.
Also, there isn´t really an open world, you sail from island to island without controlling a boat except for a "minigame" in which you shoot enemies and crates in the sea. I wish there was some sort of fast travel option, at least to know places, to skip this sailing bit.
The graphics are not particularly good, but the artwork and direction are very nice, there´s a pleasant atmosphere throughout the gameplay, and the soundtrack is just fantastic. Many developers don´t give the proper dedication to the soundtrack, and is this case it was one the things that made this game so enjoyable.
In the end, it was worth my buck, but it felt more like an experience than a full-fledged game. I was left craving for more. Not more of the same, but a more polished experience, a PC/console focused game, with better dungeons and better controls. Finally, they would do well with abandoning some part of the Zelda formula and risk trying out their own things, try to become a franchise of it´s own, and not just a mere tribute to another game.
It is not quite there yet, but Oceanhorn has what it takes to become the non-nintendo, multi platform Zelda we always craved for, and I have big expectations for the next installment of the series.

I know I am going to get a ton of hate for this, but considering I was expecting the "Greatest Game of All Time" like so many people were saying, I have to say I was incredibly disappointed by this game.
First off, it was hard to get used to the controls. I understood them, and I thought the layout was nice (Each joystick and trigger controls each brother), however I found myself constantly getting mixed up between the two, causing the characters to run in all sorts of directions. This can be either very frustrating or very funny, depending on which person you are. I found it a bit of both
What really frustrated me was that this game was extremely linear and easy. This game is advertised as a puzzle game, and yet none of the puzzles got me thinking like a puzzle should. Most of them include holding down the trigger and pressing one direction on the joystick. A big problem is that each puzzle only has ONE way of solving it, and there is no room for player creativity. The game makes it clear that you will be going the way it wants to, and the on-screen characters will not hesitate to point in the direction you need to go. There are many times in this game where I was forced to do something that I either did not want to do or did not did not know why I was doing it (What if I didn't want to free that troll? There were many other ways I could've progressed without freeing a potential criminal).
There are also invisible walls EVERYWHERE. Throughout the game, there are cliffs and canyons that look dangerous, but there would be no way to fall, as the game will not let you. There are moments where you will be balancing on a thin log over a giant waterfall, and it may seem difficult until you realize that, no matter how much you push the joystick in the opposite direction, there is no way you can fall. There are even ankle-high ledges that are blocked by these walls, which strips the sense of freedom and adventure that the game is trying to make the player feel.
Lastly, as much as the story is praised by others, it is really nothing special. The premise has been used before (You are on an adventure to find a treasure that will cure your father of an illness), but it is fitting for the fairytale-like setting. My main problem with it is that it focuses too much on being emotional, rather than being thought-provoking. Yes, you may cry at some points, but there were not any moments that made me think and reflect. The ending was especially disappointing for these reasons.
To sum it up, I felt this game fell flat in what it, and its fans, were promising. The gameplay is limited and void of challenges, the story was not engaging for me, and the ending was unsatisfying. It definitely did not resonate with me like TotalBiscuit promised. The visuals are beautiful, though. I can't lie about that
Overall, this isn't a BAD game, but it does not even get close to "Best Ever" status. If you are into these short, story-driven games, I would recommend To The Moon. It does not have the scenery as Brothers does, but the story is much more intriguing and engaging, with a very solid finish.
If this game is on sale, then sure, pick it up. But don't buy into the hype. This is an average game. 6/10

Brothers (we're going to just go ahead and leave off the completely unnecessary sub-title) is an amazing and unique experience. I really don't want to go into too much detail, because it's a game that really should just be experienced. And even though it's a console port, I didn't experience any issues.
Without going into too much detail, Brothers uses a rather original control scheme, but with a big payoff. Plenty of games have tried to come up with interesting mechanics, but I've never seen one so well integrated into the story. It can be a bit frustrating to get used to in the beginning, but the decision was made with good reason and really makes the difference between this being an interesting little adventure game and a great emotional experience.
The design in this game really deserves a special call-out. The game is broken into different set pieces, and they're all interesting in their own right, but some of them really shine. I had heard mention of certain parts of the game being really cool, and it really didn't disappoint.
Don't expect much in the way of action when playing Brothers, it's an adventure game that truly has a sense of adventure. I really can't recommend it enough, but I also recommend playing it in one sitting if possible. The game is only a few hours long, and it'll be much impactful if you don't take an extended break. Getting into the flow of the weird control scheme is a big part of what makes it so good.

: NetherRealm Studios, High Voltage Software
: Warner Bros. Interactive Entertainment
==========
Since 1992 when the first Mortal Kombat was released, we've seen many entries in the iconic fighting franchise. Despite it's name, Mortal Kombat X is the 21st Mortal Kombat game to see release, but it is the 10th installment of the main storyline. Featuring some new characters, mainly the children of some of the more well-known characters, Mortal Kombat X picks up 2 years after Mortal Kombat 2011 (commonly referred to as MK9) left off. Shao Khan has been defeated, but Shinnok has returned to once again threaten Earthrealm. Just to name a few of the new characters-- Kotal Khan, D'Vorah, Erron Black, Jung Jin, Cassie Cage, Takeda Takahashi, Jacqui Briggs, and Ferra/Torr. A lot of the older characters return, but with new looks. Scorpion, Sub-Zero, Raiden and more are all here. Other characters such as Kabal, Sindel, and Stryker make an appearance as well.
==========
MKX retains most of the features that we've come to expect from the series, with the addition of a couple of new ones. The game plays out similarly to
. You'll have a cutscene, followed by a slight transition to the in-game engine where kombatants say a line or two to each other, then you have the fight. Once the fight concludes, the winner says a one-liner, then the game transitions back to cutscenes. Story Mode plays out entirely like this, and it works very well. It's *almost* seemless, but those with a good eye will see the exact moment of transition.
Returning from
are the stage interactions. Scattered throughout each stage are objects you can use to your advantage, that range from dealing damage or making an escape. There was literally one stage where you can pick up and old woman in the background and chuck her at your opponent! These interactions do a lot of damage, but seemed to have been scaled back a bit due to how abused they were in
.
There are a variety of game modes, spanning singleplayer and multiplayer. Let's go over singleplayer initially. First and foremost is the Story mode. In this mode you go through several chapters, each one dedicated to a specific character who you'll use to progress through battles that advance the story. Story Mode took me approximately 4-5 hours to complete. While short, it's really fun. Next, we have the Towers, which is like the classic ladder arcade mode. There are 3 towers initially, each with a different number of opponents. There's Single Fight, where you just choose your character and an opponent and just duke it out. Next is Test Your Luck, where you face off against the AI with random modifiers. Lastly, there is a Training Mode where you are free to practice with any character you choose on any stage, with various settings for your AI opponent. They can fight back or just stand there as you practice combos.
Multiplayer has a few different modes, the most notably of which is the Ranked Ladder. Participating in these allows you to climb the ranking ladder to number 1. There is also the returning King of the Hill mode from
. Lastly there are Tower Battles where you face other players. I didn't play multiplayer very much, as that's not my thing typically, but what I did play ran satisfactorily. There was a small bit of lag but it did not impede my enjoyment and was easy to adapt to. This may or may not be a dealbreaker for some players.
One of the new features added with MKX are tokens. There are 2 types of tokens: Skip Fight and Easy Fatality. Skip Fight allows you to do just that: skip any fight that you choose, as long as it's in Story Mode. Use these when you happen to get stuck versus a certain opponent. When used, the game acts as if you had won the battle. The Easy Fatality Token allow you to execute Fatalities with an easy button press. Both tokens are earned by unlocking them in the Krypt, which is also a returning feature.
Another new feature is the addition of Fighter Variations. These are sort of like different styles, and each kombatant has 3 of them. Each variation gives access to certain abilities which help define the playstyle of the character. For example, Scorpion has a Shirai Ryu style, which gives him access to dual-swords, and he also has Hellfire, which gives him access to demonic hellfire powers.
Lastly, MKX features a Faction War. When you start the game you are able to choose between 5 Factions. Upon joining one, simply playing the game (in any mode) earns you Faction Points. At the end of every Faction War, the winner is chosen and all members of the winning Faction are rewarded.
==========
MKX looks just as good as its previous installment. Everything is rendered in great detail, and as a staple of every Mortal Kombat game...there is a LOT of blood! It wouldn't be Mortal Kombat without it. Mortal Kombat is known for its amount of violence and graphic brutality. Nothing has really changed since the last game, and that's a good thing. Some character have new designs or reskins, such as Sub-Zero, Johnny Cage, and even Raiden. The biggest difference I noticed was that of Johnny Cage. He looks almost like a whole new character with the same name, but it's still the same arrogant Johnny some of you love.
==========
Every character is fully voiced and each stage has it's own music. The music for the most part is largely ignored because of the action on-screen, but for the type of game this is, it works. There really isn't too much to say here, and for that I apologize.

This review contains no story spoilers outside of the game's basic premise.
Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons sat in my wishlist since I first created my Steam account. It went on sale for $3.74 (normally $15) so I grabbed it immediately.
Gameplay:
A controller is required and necessary for the primary mechanic of the game - simultaneously navigating the two brothers (each by one control stick and shoulder button/trigger) through platforming and solving puzzles. The highlight of the platforming for me was a section in which you are alternating swinging the brothers while they are tethered together by a rope.
There is no combat. This is not a game recommended if you enjoy hacking and slashing or learning attack patterns. Once you've gotten used to using both control sticks to move the brothers in unison the "challenge" aspect of gameplay is taken away almost entirely. Having said that, I do not consider these a negative, but something you should be aware of before buying.
Story:
Obstensibly, you're tasked with finding a cure for your father's apparent illness. You're not explicitly told anything, but fully utilizing it's medium and not pretending to be a movie, the Brother's story is expertly told and very emotionally rich.
Like the gameplay, the story is subtle, slow and contemplative. I happily stopped and sat the brothers at each bench you come across in the game. The slow sweeping shots of the environments you're entering as you do so perfectly convey the overall tone of the game perfectly.
The characters don't speak a real language, but you're able to pick up a wealth of emotion from the great art direction. Without giving anything away, there were some very clever mechanics used at the end that brought everything full circle and reinforced a feeling of loss that really moved me.
Conclusion / TLDR:
The game is short, but I can't consider that a negative. As I said above, I paid $3.74, but if I'd paid $15 I would not feel cheated by the experience I had. Brother's - A Tale of Two Sons is the exact sort of game that I got back into gaming to enjoy. If you appreciate games as an art form, you will thoroughly enjoy this game.

A short but beautiful game with a strong subtleness and meaningfulness in every detail proving how well a nice story and am interesting, immersive world full of wondrous creatures and places can be created only by the means of level/props design, character expressions and gestures and verbal accentuation (because there is no proper narration and the voice actors talk in a fake gibberish language). The other audio work is very good too - nice, eerie music and sounds that make the nature around you feel very much alive and believable.
The controls are interesting: You control two characters, each with one stick of your controller. The game is very minimalistic in this manner as you basically only move them around and have one "use" button for each of them - yet the ways how this was utilised in the game are pretty awesome, making you traverse the environment utilising some very unique methods. I wonder if this can be played with two controllers in co-op because it's just begging to be.
At it's core it's about growing up, getting strong, taking responsibilty, having faith, showing courage and empathy. The controls work interestingly into these themes as sometimes both characters rely on each other for their immediate survival. Letting lose of one stick or "use" button will doom the other character. It's charming and heartwarming how there is a rather constant "co-operation" between the characters and various creatures/inhabitants of this world too, making this very much a great tale full of wondrous events where everything and everyone has a meaning and purpose.

By now, you probably know if you like mousekillers. It's hard to have missed Diablo and its massive following through the years. Click on things, collect loot, repeat. Torchlight II is competent and not unattractive as a modern take on the genre; however, it makes some glaring design and balance errors which should take all but the core audience out of the picture. Ultimately, the game becomes a long and painful grind rather than an entertaining adventure.
First, the good: despite its budget nature, the game's consistent art style is charming. Spell effects can fill the screen and look appropriately intimidating. The bright colors serve the game well, and lightning effects add weight. It's not beautiful, but it's very appropriate. Similarly, many abilities are also well done. Dashing through enemies with the form of a shadow wolf is pretty satisfying, for example. The classes are varied, if a bit derivative, and cover pretty much anything you could want to do to enemies. Even within classes, there's unexpected variety: you may choose to equip your Berserker with a sword and an axe and eviscerate everything, or you may drop a wand in each hand and go with the Frost tree.
However, due to the game's design, you might not get to use what you really want. There are pretty large skill trees to be had, but no reason not to spec wholly into one ability or other. Certain abilities are obviously most powerful up front, but most abilities just require you to invest, invest, invest to produce a good chracter down the line. It's not fun at all, especially when you have to complete entire playthroughs before unlocking some core skills. You have little choice but to add a respec mod into your game simply due to the inane hassle of storing points to play later NG. There is also no way to make hybrid or fun builds which don't abysmally suck due to poor scaling considerations. Game balance is absolutely horrid to boot. Melee will have you one-shot by everything; ranged builds are fully superior in every possibly way. Entire difficulty settings are entirely dependent upon grinding out insanely-overpowered items from a lower difficulty and importing them through shared storage. If you fail to do this, you will be one-shot by just about every random spawn halfway through your first playthrough even built for absolute maximum durability.
Torchlight also fails to break any of the genre's weaknesses. The game still relies too heavily on one button for everything: move, attack, target, pick up. This caused problems in the heyday of the genre and hasn't gotten any better with time. There is no native gamepad support and limited third-party support, which is particularly annoying when classes like the berserker play exceedingly poorly with the mouse bound to every action in the game. Story still takes a backseat to the action, and there's not much reason to even pay attention to it as you go. Just click and loot and move on.
If you're a fan of mousekillers already, you'll probably enjoy Torchlight II despite its flaws. It checks all the boxes and doesn't look bad in doing it. However, if you're not really into the click-click-grind, the game isn't going to warm you to the genre. It suffers from muddled balance, poor story, furstrating design, and terrible grindiness that detract sufficiently from the experience to make it hard to recommend to non-fans. If you're taking the time to read reviews, the game probably isn't for you.

TL:DR:  Exceeded my expectations for a random free to play release on steam.
First Impression Gameplay Video:
You never really know what you're going to get when downloading a new free to play on steam.
Many times you'll find a student project or just random unity assets cobbled together, loosely knotted into something fairly reminiscent of a "game".  Worse case scenario you'll come across a heavy pay to win title suffocating with micro-transactions.
But that's not the case with Hollowed, which has me pleasantly surprised.
Hollowed has a mysterious atmosphere about it which benefits from the graphic style, audio, and gameplay mechanics.
A warning to keyboard and mouse enthusiasts: only controllers are supported.
Anyways, the game starts you off slowly, introducing the various mechanics of your spirit orb.. thing.
Each function you learn will become vital to solving puzzles and navigating this side scrolling platformer.
And it does it well.  The abilities are very unique, and the game feels original.
The story is interpretive and has no dialogue (none which I came across at least).
Even so, the story is conveyed well and comes across as quite artistic.
I encountered no bugs or graphical flaws and I actually quite enjoyed this game.
I plan to come back and continue the story at a later date.
Recommended.

In overall the game is fine purchace from sale. At full price it's slightly at the expencive if compring the complexity of the content to the price tag, but at decent sale, do buy the game. Greetings Again!  Today I review the fourth episode in the Rain Slick Precipice of Darkness Series and this one has been a long time past due for a review.  So, how does the conclusion of this four part game series conclude?  Read on dear listener, read on…
Gotta Catch’em All:  The game series continues to evolve, using a bit more of a ‘modern’ version of the 16bit era but the most dramatic change is the music, which to be honest…is kind of awesome.  It evoked some of the greatness I remember from scores in old school JRPGs.  The mechanics themselves stay the same but evolved as well.  No longer do you play with your party but monsters that you catch and put in your monster orb reminiscent of a series I’m sure we are all familiar with.  You spend about 70% of the game with two divided parties which both created some interesting interactions but also a slight frustration when it came to gear and leveling.
Funny quip here:  The game has some minor difficulty spikes and a much tighter control over money than the previous one but the game doesn’t force more than 4 members in any battle so you can easily focus on your favorites.  One slight issue was that it requires you to select a trainer which is a fancy accessory that improves stats for the monster as it levels.  This is a neat idea but could cause problems if the monster is leveled ‘incorrectly’.  Though I do not felt this impacted my game it is possible.  The game does do a great job at auto-selecting trainers for new monsters and I found this more of a ‘potential’ issue than a real one.  One thing I will say about this game is that the ending is worth it, in an interesting and charming way.
The end of the world:  One small annoyance I had with the game was the two party systems they had for most of the game.  It left me feeling like I was starting over when switching parties because they were not as high level.  This caused a bit of a lapse in judgment that comes naturally with RPG leveling.  Many times I’d have a monster die because I didn’t gauge their health or the enemy’s power correctly, mainly due to this.  Overall this was a minor annoyance however.  The only other real problem I have with the game is that it still lacks an option to lock in your previous command.  Yes I’m going to cast Rat Fever…like I do every turn.
So, do you buy this?  Well, if you have played the others sure.  If you haven’t, then I’d suggest you do that first.  But what of this game stand alone?  I actually think this is the best of the series story wise and the strongest mechanically but would caution buying this one without the others, mainly because of story reasons.  If you don’t care…then go right ahead.  Enjoy!

EDIT: I changed my evaluation to negative. While all the positive points below are still true, about halfway through the game starts having less interesting dialogue, more boring stretches (the under-underhell part being particularly pointless) and varies things up in combat a lot less. There was even a boring dungeon (Battlegrounds) where all enemies have exactly the same elemental resistance, which you can't target with any of your character until the end of that section. Now I can't wait to be done with the game, it just feels like a linear sequence of mindless battles where I repeat the same actions over and over.
-------------
Original review:
Really fun RPG even if like me you've not been a big follower of Penny Arcade comics or haven't played the previous Precipice of Darkness games (the previous one also by Zeboyd Games is recommended though, the 1st and 2nd not so much).
The story, characters, world and enemies are consistently wacky which kept me entertained so far and sometimes made me laugh (the fake "translated from japanese" part still makes me smile).
The combat system is interesting with several Zeboyd staples such as HP/MP and potions always being at max at the start of every fight. You keep getting new abilities at a decent pace. A lot of battles change the rules to shake things up, so you'll rarely get the impression you're bashing on the same kind of enemy over and over.
No random fights, either, and dungeon design is super-simple meaning you're unlikely to have to backtrack. This means you don't get the stressful aspect of trying to get your bearings in a huge dungeon while under constant attack and having to manage your resources - which honestly, can be fun if you're in the mood for it - but it also minimizes the amount of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t you have to go through to get to the next joke, which is what this game is mostly about.
You can hold B on the controller to speed up combat animations, which is very welcome - but thankfully there are very few no-brainer fights.
The only thing I don't like is that some abilities such as getting a buff on your first turn, after defending or in similar circumstances aren't displayed anywhere in the UI during battle, so you don't have all the info there to help you pick which ability to use. Also, even if you have discovered the elemental weaknesses of some enemies and meet them again, it still only tells you the number of weaknesses, not which one they have. The game could remember that for you instead of forcing you to take notes if you wanna play optimally (I didn't).

This game has a lot of novelty. The monsters you acquire are all quirky and fun, and the combat system is different enough from standard fare that it feels great for the duration of the game. The plot is a bit weaker this time around, trying a bit too hard to be over-the-top. The Soundtrack is solid.

It's certainly not a perfect game - especially when held up to the standards of parts 1 and 2 - but it's worth the asking price.  I don't like the combat system, and I don't like how empty the world feels, but it feels like Zeboyd was able to let loose in a way they couldn't with episode 3.

You love Pokémon games, absurd humour and want to see the thrilling conclusion to the Rain-Slick Quadilo... Quadro...
ology.
Possibly my favourite of the series, primarily for its off-beat style, variety of playable characters and depth of combat.
Zeboyd Games appear to have had a creative field day with this one. Where Episode 3 felt a little restrained, here they have flipped the desk and gone "screw this! I'm doing it my way!" - Want a demon train? You've got it! Want to play with a sentient vending machine? It's yours! Want to fight panda-duck hybrids? Why the heck not!
It's essentially taken everything from the previous game, fixing the weaker points and trying to dose it up with more fun and variety. In effect, it's no longer trying to mimic the first 2 episodes, but stand alone with its own style. The music's had a badass overhaul and the attack sounds are considerably more fitting; all-in-all leading to very satisfying and engaging combat, aided by an even greater cavalcade of silly foes and special conditions.
But the creativeness hasn't just extended to the world or visuals. The combat system has been given a fun rethink too. The characters now fight using a team of fun, yet cute, creatures (very much an ode to Pokémon) each with their own very unique edge and specialisation to bring, really pushing the game mechanics to creative new frontiers. Some are defensive healers, others item-oriented... one even boosts its allies whilst KO'd! There's plenty to mix-and-match and, much like the class badges from before, the designs are creative, absurd and pretty damn fantastic. For those who like to play with every character in an RPG... this is an absolute gold mine!
The humour is still rich as ever, pushing the boat out even further with the parodies and puns... including a group with their own theme song. I can't say much on it, but it's possibly one of the most bizarre, yet wonderful moments of the game.
All this does come at a price, however (there's always a catch). In all of the outrageous fun, it's lost the brooding noir from the other episodes, so has a very different feel to it. And despite the sprawling world, the plot is actually quite sparse. There's still a wealth of brilliant dialogue and laugh-out-loud moments but, other than a nice conclusion, there's not much in the way of twists or turns and a rather drawn-out finale. Neither are problems in and of themselves, but it ultimately depends on what hooked you into the series.
Still... it was a very satisfying end to an incredible series of games. Not the deepest, but almost certainly the most fun!

Mount&Blade possesses some dated graphics--even at its release it wasn't exactly cutting edge--but the core gameplay is unparalleled even a decade after its earliest iterations first became available to early backers in its nascent alpha state. When I first installed it I didn't end up stepping away from the computer for a full 24 hours. I was hooked, and my WASD hand was all but crippled. Considering it started as the passion project of a single developer M&B has accomplished great things, filling a void in the market for open world medieval combat. A void where it really (sadly) still stands alone.
For those unfamiliar M&B is an RPG without a core story or quest to be fulfilled. You truly determine your destiny, deciding who you want to be and what you want to accomplish within an ever changing world. Kings and lords battle for supremacy over towns and castles, all while you eek out a meager existence hunting bandits and protecting caravans until you build sufficient renown and loyal forces to catch the attention of one of those kings and swear vassalage... or strike out to forge your own empire under your own banner.
You can find and hire companions, woo and wed princesses, befriend and betray the lords of the land... but the heart of the game comes not from its relatively underwhelming dialogues and interactions, but from the combat. Cavalry charges breaking lines of infantry... archers raining clouds of arrows on advancing forces... and you, fighting dramatically in the midst of the carnage, or safely removed, commanding your men and watching as the ordered chaos unfolds before you.
This is a seminal game in its genre, with fantastic gameplay on its own, but it becomes far more potent once you delve into its rich modding scene. There is no shortage of incredible mods that completely reshape the game. Some, like Brytenwalda capture the gritty realism of its chosen era. Others like Gekokujo shift the game's aesthetic focus over to the samurai of Japan. Then you have incredibly ambitious mods like The Last Days, Warsword Conquest, and A World of Ice and Fire, which transform the game into alternate universes (Lord of the Rings, Warhammer, and Game of Thrones, respectively). And that's just the beginning. Even as an older game, this is still one that holds up against the test of time. It was never the prettiest, but when you're bathed in the blood of your enemies who can even tell?

At the moment I am 13 hours into the game and want to give a general first impression of this first release build.
First off the overall game is very much the same as the previous title Deus Ex: Human Revolution.  All the game mechanics come back in spades, with a few minor tweaks such as storage units in your housing that allow you to save items and so on.   So if you are familiar with the previous title you will find this game going along quite well.
Now for the basic pros and cons of this First release build:
Con
-Clunky:  The controls feel a tad bit inebriated. They are not entirely as responsive, or at times over responsive even after tweaking them.
-Crash To Desktop: The first CTD I had was in the CS after the tutorial where there is an explosion in a crowded area (You see it in the trailers) The next time I loaded it up and went through the CS it did not occur, from what I can tell the first time you play through the game you will get a few CTDs at these heavy populated areas and scripted events (still few and far between.) and after that they will play through fine.
-Menu interface not loading:  Next The first time I used the storage lockers in the house the menu failed to load that would allow me to use and exit them, I could use ESC to open the game menu and load the previous save, but nothing would let me exit the storage unit.  Again as with CTD, it only occurred the first time.  However with the Telescope furniture it occurs every time it is used.  Make sure to save prior to attempting any unusual furniture/device use on your first play through.
-Bad Acting:  The acting is very Japanese in style, over exaggerated movements, poor tactical choices in CS that are clearly meant to illustrate badassery to those who have no real experience in basic combat positioning, weapon firing, stances, use of real cover and so on.  On top of this the lip syncing is not even trying, and you will find the CS after the tutorial illustrates that this game was clearly written for another language first before being made in English as no one pauses for “none of us here….. Disagree with you.” Once you adapt to these things you will find that it’s a fairly good storyline thus far (not completed) and like the previous title the world building is great.
-Micro transactions locked per save:  Many other faux reviews are stating that a “single player game should not have micro transactions.” This is not true, as single player is the one game type that they are most acceptable in, you cannot Pay to Win when you have no one to play against.  Beyond that there is a serious issue with the MT items and Preorder items being locked to your singular save, which if you experience any of the issues such as Clunky controls you will have to overwrite if you wanted to do say a pacifist run.  This sucks for those that pre ordered those items, and anyone who may be interested in the cash shop, but it is certainly not a game breaking issue.  Simply don’t buy anything in the cash shop and play the game.
Pros:
-Style:  The city, the Ghetto, Abandoned mostly built hotel Resort Island, all of it really come to life in the game, and the attention to detail is great.  And while the game is still an expanded corridor game it has plenty of paths and avenues for either aggressive or infiltration play styles to get through without having to repeat the same option on a 2nd or even 3rd play through.
-Crafting:  The crafting system is simple, you get generic spare parts that you can use to craft items such as bio cells (energy cell) multitools and so on, and however these same parts are also used for upgrades on guns such as increasing ammo capacity, rate of fire and so on.  On top of this you still get the attachment pickups that you can add onto a weapon, templates for mines that you can socket grenades in and the like.  It is simple in overall design and gives the player a level of customization that can tailor each weapon to fit your play style a bit better.
-Items:  Items you drop to make space, and items enemies drop in general persist, so you never have to worry about them despawning when you run back to stash more gear in your lockers.  Simple enough feature that lets you collect all the little gadgets and guns without having to give up anything major other than the time it takes to go home and come back.
-True RPG: This game is simply a true RPG, you have even more options in conversations than the previous title, and every situation has multiple ways you could potentially get around it without having to fight.  Gone are the days of boss fights without any option to talk it out, or trick them to your side. While you can’t exactly make up a character to play as, as for as scripted RPGs go this is exactly the way one should be done.
-No Augs are redundant:  All of the augments, which are the games equivalent of perks/traits are useful in their own unique way.  None of them are redundant or overlapping, and with a decent sized selection of them you have all sorts of ways to tailor your character.  The new overheating mechanic for total Aug use is quite interesting as it balances out most of the highly powerful ones by requiring you to choose which ones to shut off at what time or suffer severe damage to your systems such as visual and audio distortion and out right damage.  It would be nice to get a few more types of augs, but the ones present are great.  On top of that the preexisting ones from the previous title still exist as 2/3rds of the aug options, and you start out with a decent number of them already unlocked, so you don’t have to have the magical reset that makes you a zero climbing back to hero option all over again.
Keep in mind this is just 13 hours into the game, having played the tutorial section twice.  Not done with the game by far, and many of the issues could be fixed, and should hopefully be fixed in the patches to come.
Edit: Side note, 30 minutes of cutscene (if you choose the recap video) before initial game play is a bit much, and underlines the issue with the generic steam refund timeline.  You wont know if you want to keep the game by the end of the tutorial which is going to get you over the 2 hour mark by the time you start playing the actual game.
