I have just finished my first full playthrough on Deus Ex difficulty and then played the Jensen Mission on I Never Wanted This difficulty. Overall, it's a good game, but right now it has massive performance problems - this is why it's not recommended for now.
- The Main Game -
The Story is decent, the voice over feels a bit rushed, the gameplay fits in with the idea of the game. There is only one problem: many areas extremely favor either non-lethal or lethal - If you chose to do the other one, you better be quick and be lucky because that solid railing is not gonna block visibility. Stealth is an option and it's a rewarding one. Killing is also an option and you get to make a nice pile of bodies - my record is about 38 bodies before it crashed.
- Jensen Missions - Desperate Measures -
Wow. This is like what, 5 minutes of gameplay with stealth/non-lethal? It's 15 minutes cutscenes and literally just arrive by train, go through corridors, open a door, have a cutscene, react accordingly to the prompts, get back to the train. Underwhelming.
- The Issues -
This game is an insult to a high performance gaming PC:
1. Only uses up to 3 cores of your CPU.
2. Videos occasionally halt for a minute or two since it decided to stop preloading.
3. None of the graphics options actually help with framerate - I had the same 5-109 range with high as i had with low.
4. Reflections are off sometimes - I understand that local reflections (SSR) can't perfectly reflect behind an object, but impossible reflections should still be filtered out. The train sequence for example has multiple objects that reflected Jensens face - even though he wasn't facing them.
5. Menus are a pain in the argh to use with mouse. Why exactly doesn't the mouse jump to the notification window? Using a keyboard or a controller is better for this.
6. Streaming issues: A lot of zones load in very late, resulting in objects flipping out and once even resulted in me getting slammed out of the world by a physics prop that got stuck in another one. Well played, physics.
That is all for now. Until Issue 1, 2, 3 and 6 are fixed, this stays on not recommended.

Hello everybody,
today i wan`t to show you an interesting game.
No, more than a game. It`s a journey you will never forget, if you play this game.
STORY
This is the story of two Brothers on a journey to help their father.
At the beginning of the story the father got ill and his sons bring him to a healer.
The problem is, he know a way to heal the father but it will take a very long journey.
The sons already lost their mother and don`t wan`t to loose their father, too, so they started the Journey.
GAMEPLAY
I never saw a gameplay like this before. You MUST have a controller.
With it you controll the 2 Brothers at the same time. One with the right half and the other with the left half of the Controller. The same time! Most of the parts of this game you must do Teamwork with the Brothers to get through the game. That sounds a little bit complicated, but it is very easy to control.
At the beginning it may be a little bit complicated, but after a short time you´re in and you can enjoy the game and it´s story.
GRAPHICS
The Graphics are really awesome. At the beginning it is nothing special. You are in a small village, with some people, normal village life. But the more you play, the Settings gets better and better and you can see how much work it`s in this game. I don´t wan`t to spoil, that is something you must see by yourself. The World of BROTHERS got many nice details and all the characters are very well animated.
MUSIC
The music is wonderfull and fits great into the Game Scenes. It also supports emotional moments very, very well.
ACHIEVEMENTS
Yes, Brothers have his Achievements, but these are special ones. Each one stands for a little situation you must find. For example, you have to make a special person dancing, or helping a Turtlemom to get her Babys back. Very nice Achievements.
PERSONAL CONCLUSION
Yes, this game did it. I`ve had some tears in my eyes and i´m not ashamed of it.This is more than a game. It´s like a movie or like a book. You follow the story and you laugh and cry with them. Each chapter you wan`t to know how it is going on. You can`t stop. And at the End of the Game you sit there, thinking about what you have experienced. Thanks to the Developer and publisher of this experience.
It was awesome.
TO YOU
If you like great storys with great graphics and music, this is for you.
If you are really emotional, don´t forget the tissue. You will need it.
This is really a game that should be in every collection.

For me these are the pros:
1. Atmosphere.
Indeed, it is not a legendary story which chains you down from dusk till dawn. But it has a certain calmness, a bit like being the main protagonist of those old tales which are were read to children from big old books.
2. Simplicity and still fun.
There is nothing complicated things in this game (maybe some puzzles?), but not a lot of skill points, inventory management, item augmentations, alchemy etc.  In spite of this still offers a decent relaxation.
3. Graphics.
I don't want to say that it has some uber hardcore graphics, but it has it's own "bright" style, which is kind of a refreshing after playing 200 hours of survival horror.
Cons:
I really can't say anything really bad about this game. But if you are the person who needs some legendary stuff, and to feel feel like a mighty warrior or fearful mage, please avoid this game. :)
As a summary: I really recommend this game to those who can enjoy a game without the urge to compare to other BIG titles in the industry.

To be perfectly honest? This game is sadly the worst of their 4 games so far. The New Monster system just didn't seem to work out, but also their Final Fantasy 3/6 [Depending on how you wanna see it] group switches always disrupted my game experience. In the end  I grew accustomed to  a group of monsters, and then readjustet again to another one, by itself no problem. But from basically Level 1. Jump,  finally getting stronger - jump back yay this again.
The Story is very good.
The Battles? Jokes. If I have to think about how to defeat a group of monsters effectively, I have run into the problem of the HP. The HP grows for your enemies is gigantic. The battles in the end felt like a drag I had to do. If that happens in an RPG with Fighting as a focus? Ouch.I don't mind beating the hell out of mighty creatures that outdo me if I don't think and just act, but that was the story of every Battle. SMT Persona 3&4 keep me more entertained on Maniac/Very Hard [Respective for the game] and even though I sometimes just wanna throw my PS/P/VITA around, it's still fun. This game does the exact opposite for me. I've seen this as a problem in the Precipice of Darkness 3. The Battles are dynamic yes, the Waiting bar system has been done well and offers strategical insight to when to use Delay attacks or when to leave that alone. I don't want a game where I can beat up a monster in One Turn [Makes battles redundant] but if I have to fight Battles with monsters on a Boss LVL HP all the time, for basic rewards and this continously and all the time it's bad. The Boss battles were just a sign for me that I get closer to the finish of this game. I had a blast with it when the Fish Force song came up, I even enjoyed the first two Character Group jumps, but... the "Master" system where they gain extra stats for level ups and skill based on which Pokémon trainer - woops, slip of tongue - you use seems to be mysterious. The Badge system where you could swap your Class on the fly in the PoD 3 is better. By a lot. Experiment every fight! Here... not so much. "Catching" new pokédudes [a Grotesque reference] seems like it's hardly worth the time. This sums it up for the Battle segment.
The Map looks Beautiful and by far the best overworld they have ever produced. If only Cthulu could've looked this good, that would've been a delicious experience Visual wise. The Character models look good. The Music blows, and earlier mentioned Fish Force track took the cake. The Battle Theme is so-so. The other themes were fitting and good.
But going back to the Themes - if you know the Cthulu Battle theme, everything just pales in comparison, so this is biased.
Extending the Item system by new senseful things ; Great Job 10/10 Please do that again. It was cool in 3, and even better in 4.
All in all it's a very funny game, but as you can see the negative section weighs a lot heavier. BoD7/Cthulu/PoD 3 were all better by a big margin. I recommend playing the earlier mentioned games in succession to see how they evolved and then compare it to this. Otherwise I can't recommend it. *Prays for the well being of Cosmic*

Huh... I really tried liking this game. It's an ode to The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker, which is pretty much the only Zelda I haven't played (much).
It just... Feel too much like a rip-off. Puzzles are complete jokes, combat is kind of awkward, the whole experience mechanic feels like an afterthought far from well thought, and the whole blocky-style make the game feel very restrictive at time, especially since you can't jump if it's two block high... Except in certain places, which makes it far from consistent.
So many things that makes Zelda a fun game (series) are missing from it. Almost no important NPCs, there's no special sound for breakable walls, and most of the things are far from intuitive, which made me looks at a walkthrough every hour or so.
Graphics are really nice, but that's only when you see them from afar, like in all those screenshot. In cutscenes, we get close-up of the characters and objects, and everything looks really bad. (Like at 2:10 in the video)
The story feel forced and generic, and that's without talking about the character who like my character way too much for absolutely no reasons. I just really like one or two story choices, but those were things appearing near the end of the game, huh.
At least sounds and musics are really nice, which make the thing at least a bit enjoyable.
While trying to be it's own thing, Oceanhorn ends up being in the shadow of Zelda.
In the end, it feels more like a rip-off of Zelda, trying to market to those fans who wants games like them on PC, and on mobile. (Since this is actually a mobile port, even if it plays well with a controller, or only a keyboard.)
If you're looking for a Zelda clone, try Ittle Dew, Bit Dungeon II, the Ys series, Secrets of Grindea, or even Darksiders.

Fun game. Nothing is really groundbreaking, but it has a lot of great features. It has been awhile since I played, but this is what I remember:
Pros:
- Large, open world full of towns, characters, and an occasioanal secret location.
- Combat flows very well. Weather it is one or ten enemies, you can disptach all of them quickly. The class structure is great for this.
- Fate mode is a cool addition to combat, and can get some strong experience bonuses.
- Ton of sidequests to complete while running around the world, though they will become repetetive.
- The DLC adds a lot to the game, with two new areas.
- Crafting so you can easily upgrade/customize your gear when you level up.
- Fast travel to already visted areas.
Cons:
- You level up really fast, and can easily reach the cap before finishing the story line. Avoid DLC until completing the story line to alleviate that concern (I did DLC about half way through)
- Dungeon design is very common, almost copy/pasted. Normally they are just a series of tunnels.
- While entertaining, combat isn't too difficult, and dying is almost unheard of, especially if you over level from side quests or DLC.
- Enimies don't really change throughout the game, and you don't really have to learn any real combat patterns (with my build I could just run in and nuke everything).
- The bosses seemed very straightforward and simple. They could have been harder.
- Main story is fairly predictable.
This isn't a hardcore RPG, and players looking for a challenge might find this game to be subpar. While that is true, if you are casually playing through some games, this is for you. You're guarunteed to spend a lot of time in this game if you play through it. This game is definitely worth it if you're just looking for and fantasy RPG to mess around in.

Have you ever played an MMO and thought to yourself "Wow I hate these other players in my MMO. WIsh I could play my MMO without another player bugging me"?
If this describes a thought you've had while playing mmo, Kingdoms of Amalur was made for you.  Kingdoms can be summed up the best as a single player theme park MMO. You wonder from hub to hub, collecting quests, becoming overpowered and collecting gear.
The story is pretty generic, you are risen from the dead as the "Chosen one" go save the world because I said so.
The story kinda just rebounds you from place to place, serving to keep you somewhat on rails like a parent who tries to keep their kid in line but then gives up and returns to ignroing them and drowning their sorrow in a bottle of cheap wine.
You won't get to drown yourself in cheap liquor but you will get to drown yourself in cheap side quests! While some of them can keep your intrest, most equate to fetch this, or go collect 20 bear arses.  The lore waivers from being strong to repeating eveyrhting we automatically know. Spoiler alert: Elves are somewhat Immortal♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
Combat is a thing, half way between really fun and annoying which equates to this weird outcome of "I like this in short bursts". You won't get it in short bursts, you'll get a lot of combat. You can't stop the combat. Your choice of combat is magic combat, sneaky knife combat with some bow, or Imma SMASH IT combat. If you want you can make all combat happen at once by becoming a jack of all trades or you can focus down on your role of combat. So you can be a Archemage or god king fisty mcpunch guy.
The graphics are pretty, the world is bright and colorful, and ruins and swamps are dark and spooky. One of my fav. parts of the game is the Crafting system. It's pretty standard but each weapon you craft is truly yours. You select the parts, and then get to name it. It adds a personal touch to the game and can draw you in.
So should you buy Kingdoms of Amalur?
If on sale, Yes, You can easily get 20 hours of fun out of it before you get burnt out.
If for full price, No unless you really want a single player mmo.

If you want an RPG that feels like it was made to be an MMO but with action combat, then you will love this game.  I bought this on another sale and absolutely loved my time with it.  However, there are some flaws.  If you love to explore like I do you may find that by doing this you are getting over leveled by the time you are ready to move on to the next area of the giant world.  The enemies respawn, so as your exploring and going back and forth you keep gaining EXP and that is why I say is the main reason it feels like an MMO.
There is the ability to craft some OP weapons that make your character seem like the mobs are difficult, so it is a tough balancing act for someone like me who loves to keep it challenging.
You have a special skill that quite frankly I had to use that allows you to go bezerk and slow time down.  Which I have to admit after failing on some of the bosses it was much needed for me to win.
There are so many achievments to unlock, and not required but fun to shoot for.
Now, my absolute favorite part is the Legend of Dead Kel expansion.  With this it not only adds another area with more quests and boss to fight, but it also adds a place where you can claim and create a little kingdom of your own.  It is definitely something new to do after doing the 100s of other quests in the game and quite refreshing for me.
Hope this review helps, and for the small price you can unlock hours of entertainment.

DXMD's worst crime is that it's basically just okay. 7/10. It's not as compelling as DXHR was, the environments aren't very interesting to walk around (Prague itself looks great, but most of the streets are really similar to each other.) No save import was a massive missed opportunity. Few really annoying bugs that you may notice as well, mainly with the inconsistency of the controls - when you come out of the hacking minigame to control a panel, sometimes WASD will move the cursor to select lock/unlock, sometimes it will be arrow keys, and sometimes it will be the mouse. Sometimes your HUD will disappear entirely. While the other games in the series had multiple tasks you could take early on regardless of builds, this one basically forces you to max out hacking as soon as possible, as quite a few of the early sidequests have level 4&5 terminals in them - and there aren't really enough multitools to get by. The new augs are super uninspiring too, with the exception of the Icarus Dash which is really fun. The majority of times where the new augs would have been useful you could basically apply any firearm to the situation and get the same result. Graphically the game looks decent, but there are some weird lighting issues during melee takedowns (playing on ultra with a GTX1080). All in all, I can't really say I hate the game, but at the same time it's not quite as awesome as playing DXHR for the first time. If you see it below the current retail price (£39.99 at time of writing), give it a go if you liked the other Deus Ex games. I couldn't recommend it currently at full retail. There's also a lot of controversy if you look at other reviews over DLC as well, and it admittedly does feel a bit like a rushed cash grab in some parts of the game.
Also, why does everyone keep their beer in drawers in this game?
Edit: after finishing the game, the london section is one of the best stealth levels I have played ever, and the final boss was pretty cool too.

Brütal Legend is Jack Black's open world, Metal Apocalypse, video game. His finger prints are definitely all over it which I was glad to see. He plays the main character who is a roadie, wielding his guitar as a ranged weapon and his literal axe as his melee weapon. It was a very entertaining game, I loved the voice acting and cut scenes. His humor comes through in a great way and in my opinion was the shining feature of the game.
There were some different styles of gameplay incorporated. In the main campaign there are some battles that turn into an RTS type of showdown. I was surprised by this at first but it actually played pretty well. I do have my problems with some of the gameplay though. The traversal was something that just didn't really feel all that great to me. The handling of the car wasn't so good and you would have to drive it in narrow places at times and that became very frustrating. I also thought they could have done a better job of incorporating combos in the hand to hand combat, it just didn't have that type of connected feeling where you could string together a bunch of attacks and counters.
Those beefs aside I did enjoy many different features in the game. You play guitar riffs, in a way that I thought was reminiscent of Ocarina of Time, to accomplish different tasks. You can pump up your army in the RTS mode, summon your car, or melt the faces off of your foes with a wicked solo. They also have a pretty sick upgrading system for your character and car that is introduced and run by someone that you might find familiar.
There were some really cool little legends that you can listen too that sound like some kind of Metal Mythology. I thought this was a nice touch and it gives some background to the strange land you find yourself wondering. All in all it was a very Jack Black game, and I totally enjoyed it and was glad to have given it a shot. It didn't strike me when it first released as something for me, but the almighty power of the Steam Summer sale made me reconsider. It proved itself to me as a legit video game and not just some celebrity endorsed junk.

Most games these days with "Simulator" in the title are joke games that are complete garbage. Okay, so this one is a joke game, but it might just be
joke game that started the trend of calling funky physics games "simulators." In Surgeon Simulator, you are performing a surgery using your fingers on the keys of the keyboard that control the fingers on your character's hand. It's outrageously clunky and would be rage fuel for a player in a very serious game. However, here, it's pretty hilarious trying to perform precise, life-saving surgery on a patient while having worse hand dexterity than a drunkard with his or her arm tied off with a too-tight tourniquet.
Just imagine performing an open heart transplant in a moving ambulance, and you accidentally drop the heart and it goes flying out the back doors of the ambulance onto the city streets behind you. I found it to be pretty darn funny, and it's one of those games you can just have fun with, or legitimately try to "git gud" and perform a proper surgery, despite the wonky controls. It's challenging and pretty fun. There are several surgeries to perform and they're pretty entertaining.

Monkey Island is one of my favorite video game IPs of all time.   The Secret Of Monkey Island was the first game I ever pirated.   I have played them all, I even played the SegaCD port of MI.    So when I heard they were making a whole new series, I was so thrilled I nearly made water in my pantaloons.   Then I got ahold of it, and well...I didn't hate it.   The problem is (and it's the same issue I had with Telltale's Sam & Max stuff) it doesn't feel like a legit Lucasarts Monkey Island game.   It feels like a fan-made game.   It's really close, and it was made with a lot of love by people who obviously adore and respect the series, and they even got all the voice actors!   But it just doesn't feel right.   It's like a cover band of your favorite band...they might rock out the hits and sound dead on, but it's still not the real thing.

So, erhm, this is probably for the entire collection, and I find it strange I never did this...
If you're thinking on playing this as your first point and click, please turn around and take a look at far better options. Perhaps the first games in this series :P They were even remade and upgraded with fancy new art.
If you played the others in the series, well, this is a fun and ok game, but nothing exceptional. But since you are a fan of the series this probably won't make you quit, but this isn't a old LucasArt game :)
It's still fun though, so HAPPY GAMING!

I feel like I would absolutely love this game if it had a little more polish. It's got some really good Zelda-esque aspects in here with the music being beautiful and all the people charming. But then it leaves out some really crucial Zelda-esque things (and I mean if you're going to go for it, go all the way).
The good:
+ Artstyle
+ Music
+ Story
+ Inventory/Item switching
The Bad:
- Movement controls are a bit sloppy
- Boss battles are boring
- There are unfixed glitches in the game that can really mess up your progress (for example, there was a boss that I could routinely get down to zero health and who wouldn't die. He would just fly around the boss room until I got impatient and let him kill me).
- The game is often vague on what to do and not in a "here is a puzzle to solve" way, but in a "you can find one of the most useful rings in dark souls by climbing out a hidden tower and these ruins that don't look climbable, so you can go back to this area you didn't think you could get back to with no real markers or hints beyond a crow watching you" way.
- It has the FF8 syndrome where you can get locked into a village with no way to level, get more hearts, get better weapons, etc. And you can't get off that island until you beat a boss. That glitchy boss I mentioned before. It sucked.
There is just barely enough for me to recommend this game and a lot of the good will it had built up was destroyed by the that stupid boss glitch. If you're looking for a Zelda-esque adventure on PC that reminds you of Windwaker without all the sailing, but with more boring enemies? This is your game.

I bought this after exhausting my content interest in LoG and LoG 2.  I have played Dungeon crawlers all the way back to the ASCII days.  However, I've also enjoyed the cult classic "Dungeon Master" on the SNES, and have revisted it throughout the years several times.

After several hours of frustrating play, I felt that there was very little to this game.  It seemed just too primitive, with no quest journal, virtually no guidance and almost no content.  I refused to quit though and have finally come to appreciate that it is indeed a retro game that is designed to thwart the player who does not listen closely for the click of a pressure plate, does not scan a wall carefully for signs of a button or something unusual about its state (compared to an "ordinary" wall), does not read notes and signs very carefully, pausing to think about what they might mean and keeping them in mind and he moves through the dungeon.  You cannot rush through this game.  You must literally crawl through the dungeon listening, watching and thinking all the time or else you will be frustrated as you fail to find out how to open a door or move to another level or find a treasure that makes the difference between your living or dying.  You must collect food and water and refresh your supplies or you will find yourself in trouble.  If you want an easy game, a game that you can cheat in and speed through, this game is not for you.  If, however, you miss the good old days of immersive dugeon crawlers, this promises to be a beaut.  It is a bit short, however, at least so far, on the number and intelligence of monsters encountered and the developers need to beef that up some.

Despite being written by R.A. Salvatore the story isn't really something to write home about BUT it manages to encompass game mechanics (class changes - see above) is definitely a big plus. Don't get me wrong, it's not a bad story, far from it, but it's not a nail-biter either.
The graphics are surprisingly good for a game that's 3 years old. The spell effects are nicely done and should you chose the magic path you won't be disappointed.
The world is HUGE. I remember reading prior to making the purchase that this game could easily have been a MMO. It's true. It's fairly diverse as well, from lush forests to deserts and cities.
I would recommend buying the game even at full price even if it is 3 years old because there's frankly a lot of content. It has most of the pros of big titles and very few of the minuses (voice acting is decent but not great, the camera is a bit screwey, enemy types are recycled).

Edit:
I've finished the game, and I really took the scenic route. Took me about 45 hours.
GP:
I have replayed some missions from scratch because non-lethal takedowns will sometimes glitch out and send a NPC model ragdolling through the textures, to its death. I also got F-ed by some game logic decisions that make no sense - I killed one single exo-suit cop (didn't know NL Takedown works on them), so at the end of the mission I got scolded for killing Augs by a completely unrelated character (the Golem mission).
In what regards combat and stealth mechanics I don't have much to complain about. It's pretty solid, with some small bugs here and there.
The Point of Interest missions are so easy to miss that they might as well not even exist. I thought that, like in previous DX games, junkies asking for money in exchange for info are completely optional, and you can find the things they're not telling you on your own. Nope. Missed most of them because of this.
The Immersion is completely broken by the need to travel back and forth between the two main city hubs. And since the game only revolves around these hubs, you'll have to make 5-6 trips between every main mission (if you're a completionist that is).
Prague has some pretty awesome level design, and just exploring can be a lot of fun (takes quite some time too). This said, if you see it all before taking the side quests, you'll have to back track a lot, because mission items are only activated once the quest starts. Also, when you return from main missions, some door locks are reset, even though there's nothing more for you to find behind them. This creates a lot of confusion and gets you wasting time in the most tedious way possible: hacking (hacking is pretty fun, yes, if you don't have to do it every 2 minutes for about 40 hours).
I miss the "quick trips to multiple cities" policy the other games had.
Story:
Soo the Illuminati want to get rid of augmented humans, and they've failed their first attempt. Aaand it's done. That's it. That's the game. It's done. Buy the next one.
No other DX game had such a lame ending. They all ended in world changing events with unbeleavable consequences. This ends with a teaser for the next game (Alex and Adam talking about what they're going to do next) and a news report.
To be completely honest, I found the side missions much more entertaining than the main thing.
Performance:
I run a GTX 970 and an i5 4690k with 16GB DDR3. I've done a combination of high/very-high/ultra settings, and it runs pretty well. Some lagging at the start of each sequence (after loading) but once a few seconds pass, everything is as smooth as it can be.
Got a single crash during a loading screen, but I assume that was because I alt-tabbed and watched an episode of South Park every time the subway loading sequence started :D
Overall:
The experience itself reminded me a lot of Dragon Age: Inquisition - it's an extensive, tedious slog with a few sweet spots here and there. Of the 45 hours I spent going through as much content as possible, I'd say I only truly enjoyed about 20 (which would normally take to finish the story and side quests without getting side tracked). While it has some qualities that are undeniable, some aspects in execution are mediocre and tedious.
I payed ~$40 for the game and the price is pretty fair I guess. I've seen worse things that are more expensive. That being said, this still leaves a lot to be desired, and fails to fulfill both the standards set by the DX franchise and those set by other producers who put games much better than this on the market, for better prices.
I'd go as far as to say I enjoyed DX2: Invisible War more. (Personal, subjective opinion, reeking of nostalgia)

Brütal Legend is a game that tries to combine hack-and-slash with real time strategy. The end result is a cluster♥♥♥♥ that lacks both the mindless brütality of butchering your way through hordes of enemies, as well as any real strategic depth. I ♥♥♥♥ing love metal, and the game's aesthetics and humor, character design, soundtrack - it's amazing. Everything about this game is amazing, except the gameplay. I really enjoyed the start of the game, where it plays solely like a hack-and-slash. Cranked up the difficulty to max and comboed my way through hordes of enemies, and fun bosses. But then the game shoves its weird psuedo-strategy thing in your face, and from that point on most of the game consists almost solely of these so-called "stage battles".
The strategy ultimately boils down to rushing down your opponent all day every day, with one huge blob of units. Even if there was room for more elaborate strategies than "send all the dudes forwards", your overview of the battlefield, combined with the hectic hack-and-slash pace of it all makes it impossible to stop and focus for any given moment. You'll find yourself in a situation, then, where you're just trying to charge at enemies and at least enjoy the hack-and-slash - only to realize that everything the game has taught you so far about combos, timing your blocks, and so on, is ultimately pointless. Your only way to make any sizeable difference in a fight is to use "Double Team" - ie. taking control of one or several of your units and spamming their one or two attacks. At least solos are still fun.
Bottom line, this game, on paper, might just be the best video game ever made. Though in practice it turns out that hack-and-slash and real time strategy simply do not blend. If we ever get a Brütal Legend which focuses solely on one type of gameplay at a time - preferrably the hack-and-slash - then I might just give the team my entire wallet and call it a day. Until then, might wanna dodge this one.

After playing for a few months, here's my honest review for the game.
Pros:
- NOT pay-to-win ( details below )
- Great game concept
- Large arsenal of weapons
- Multiple divisions of careers to choose from ( recon, paratroopers, etc. )
Cons:
- Too much grind
- Broken matchmaking system ( details below )
- Hard to progress without paying real money
- Imbalances between factions ( details below )
- Each update seems to bring the game one step BACKWARDS
- High maintenance costs take the fun away from beginners
How is it not pay-to-win?
- All items in this game can be bought with the in-game currency that you accumulate as you progress except war bonds which in my opinion are useless. If you ask me, I find it to be more of a pay-to-progress-faster kind of aspect.
Broken matchmaking system?
- You get placed into gold matchmaking, which is where you meet more experienced players, too fast. If that doesn't justify my claim, it makes you wait 5-30 minutes for a game most of the time from my experience. Also, yeah you might find yourself in a 3v9 situation very often.
Imbalances between factions.
- I acknowledge the fact that they are trying to make this game historically accurate but they are "trying" to the point where its just pure bias. Try comparing a 4.2x German scope to a 2.2 US scope, in a long range snipe. If the US player can aim/see the tiny pixel on his sights then yeah he might get the shot with some difficulties BUT most of the time the German gets the shot MUCH easier. There are a lot more imbalances to mention but here's one of them.
Conclusion:
Do I recommend the game?
- Few months ago I would've said yes but now I would have to say no.

Zeboyd Games has a reputation for really grabbing the unholy trinity of RPGs: Interesting premise, well constructed gameplay, and dirt cheap price. In the finale of Rain-Slick, they pull off one and a half. While the game retains its bizarre unpredictable environment, fast-paced action, humorous writing, and gains a killer soundtrack, it overstays its welcome rather quickly. Which sucks considering this is the longest game in the series.
Early on you're introduced to the UnderHell, which fits considering the fact that virtually everything is unoriginal and dull to walk through. The enemies are as creative as ever but it's horribly boring to go through, which sucks since one of the aims was to give the game a more epic scale with the addition of a world map. The job pin system is also replaced with a party of four different monsters ranging from a bro rodent - or brodent - to a living vending machine, which hits and misses. Similarly to the job pin system of the last game, each monster has its own playing style, but none really match up to the rather impressive ideas that came from the mundane made awesome job system, which in case you forgot, weaponized shoemaking and planted gardens that caused various effects as time passed. Ultimately they play very simularly. The difficulty ramps up nicely as well and offers a good deal of challenge as time goes on, which is nice, though early game feels very simple.
Ultimately, Rain-Slick 4 just motivated me with the desire to play 3 again since I had a much better time with it. While this game offered a great amount of unpredictable moments, it's much more predictable. If this was 3 it'd be running around in circles, then as you thought it would keep running it'd do a backflip or start talking in an incomprehensible language, or randomly combust. 4 just keeps running, sometimes changing speeds and direction but it's still moving and you know it's going to move. This works out for it somewhat well as endgame is a lot more predictable compared to 3's endgame coming near out of nowhere, and it finishes very strong too. It's just a lot of the middle faultered greatly.
I recommend this game if you want to see the conclusion of the Rain-Slick series, are looking for a somewhat enjoyable RPG to play, or just enjoy Zeboyd Games' games. I mean it's cheap, you really can't beat that.

Review originally posted here:
I noted that Precipice of Darkness 3 felt a little formulaic and repetitive after having played Zeboyd's other games. Fortunately, 4 aims to mix things up right off the bat. Not drastically, but enough to feel a little different.
In Underhell, monsters are far tougher than our characters are used to, so they must capture and train Underhell creatures using a Monstorb - so there's a bit of a Pokémon vibe going on. You can choose which trainer is attached to each monster, which determines the monster's secondary abilities and level up bonuses. You'll want to experiment with different combinations to grow your monsters and benefit from trainer passive abilities, but you can swap at any time. This training feature, coupled with a reduction in combat options, adds a new layer of strategy while cutting down on the option overload. You don't have ten combat abilities per class for three classes - this time at max level you have five or six combat abilities from each of two classes, with passive abilities making up the difference.
The new overworld map makes the game feel less like a series of corridors even though it actually changes very little. It's a trick of perception - there are a few optional areas, but for the most part the game is just as linear as the last one. It took me a while to notice, though, so points for that. And the map looks pretty cool too.
Visuals and music are more distinctive and unique this time around. Environments that might normally be cliche (like lava world and desert world) are made weird enough that they're still interesting. And then of course there are some more unique areas like the ice cream caverns and the world tree zoo. Many of the audio tracks have more memorable melodies and more interesting sounds - enough for me to be writing about it this time, where last review it was more like "I guess it did have music".
I had fewer laugh-out-loud moments in 4 than I did in 3. I guess the subject matter - killing the last remaining god to destroy the universe and create a new one - is a bit less conducive to comedy than the more typical (but still weird) adventures in the previous games. But slightly less funny doesn't mean worse because the writing is still great. Tycho becomes an NPC this time around, acting more directly to fulfill his plans, and that's OK because it allows him to finally become as mysterious and badass as he's tried to appear all along.
Precipice of Darkness 4 provides a mostly satisfying conclusion to the series. I was a little disappointed that I didn't get to see end result of Tycho's work, but on the other hand, it would've been pretty hard to depict in just a few minutes. Anyway, if you enjoyed 3 you'll definitely enjoy 4. Though the opposite is also true - if you didn't enjoy 3 you'll feel the same about 4.

Good concept, but very buggy. I have a newish gaming laptop, high end stuff, but it is very sluggish unless I turn the video settings down and lower the resolution. It should not tax it based on the fairly simple graphics of this game, so it must be poor coding. That does not really bother me, but what does is the fact that the save game feature often glitches. You load you last saved game, and all your players have lost everthing they own. All weapons, armor and inventory is gone.
My suggestion: Save often, and do not override one save, create a new file each time. That way, if a save is messed up, you can go to the save before it and not lose too much time.
Still, I love this style of game and keep at it. If you really liked the Legond of Grimrock I and II, you will like this game. It is not as polished and you have to be careful with the saves, but until the next Grimrock comes out (and there is no plan for that, at least that I could find) this is the only option out there that I know of.
Its early yes, but the amount of bugs and grahics issues coupled with the complete lack of common sense features tells me to believe that it best to wait before a purchase.

Afterwards I started up the game with the highest settings possible, and the interface looked atrocious, the buttons were all comically oversized and didn't provide enough options; but I digress, I started up the game and was immediately greeted with a five nights at freddys lights sound clip playing on loop; this was to be the most scary event of my adventure.
I left the elevator and went up some stairs, went into a room, wandered about it, left it as it wasn't very interesting, explored the rest of the area, went back in the elevator, contemplated suicide, went back into the room and found the silly looking book. The book exploded and I said: "Ok, now you have my attention, suddenly the funroom isn't looking very fun!" in a silly very non-serious voice, so I tried to leave and told myself that I haven't gotten everything yet. I didn't care, I'm not some OCD crackaddict who needs to collect everything, so I grab the flashlight on the table and try again; and to my horror I still have not collected everything. So I start cleaning up the pieces of garbage scattered on the floor thinking: "Hey, maybe I'm a janitor in this game" and suddenly I could leave. Oh also there was a black mage who tried to ambush me, but I slew him with my flashlight some how. So I wondered aimlessly for a while after killing a door with another silly dialogue, and admired all the five nights at freddys lights sound clip playing in every single light in the game.
Eventually I got really sick and tired of picking up papers and wandering empty corridors, but I perseveered because why not. So I saw this big guy with a hat floating towards me so I went over to talk to him and made a very girly scream as I stood there looking at him; please note, he did not attack me, but I had a heart attack or I got flung back in time to when I was in the fun house room. So I gathered the flashlight and the papers-
But then it happened.. The door. You have not collected everything.
I gotten everything, but I couldn't leave, and the black mages kept spawning- until suddenly a black mage spawned who was immune to my flashlight, and then the game locked up, and steam locked up, and I couldn't alt+f4 out of it, and I couldn't minimize out of it, and I said "Good Game" and, since I have a second monitor; I simply closed out of it in task manager. It unfortunately murdered steam along with it and thus I had to relaunch steam just to post this review.
I'll give it a 2/10; for the sake of black mages at the very start of the game. Next time use UFPS to manage your first person camera, and get some more original sound clips and make sure the game actually works.
I have no idea why this game is even on steam; it's something which would be better off sold for free; I mean come on; Swamp Sim is more scary and entertaining than this.
And now, now; I can predict what some of you may be saying; "It's only 19 cents, what do you expect from it?"
Just because something is cheap, and you should expect it to suck; does not make it worthy of being considered a good game, or a game that could possibly be recommended.

Runic did something that I didn't think was possible:  They out Dialbo'd Diablo.  If ever there was a game that you felt the itch to grind for better, and better, and even better loot; Torchlight 2 is that game.  I have always been big fan of the series, and I think that the Runic guys really outdid themselves on this one.  Sure, the story is not nearly as encapsulating, or epic as the Diablo franchise.  But, honestly, it's not really why most people play this game.  It's straight up a gear grinder's love affair.  That isn't to say that the story is terrible, it's not.  If anything the biggest issue with this game is that the story is just good, but fairly forgettable.
Where Runic really nails it is with the sheer amount of gear you will churn through in any given play session.  These guys too the loot algorithym that Blizzard introduced the world to back in Diablo, and cranked it up to 11.  It's pretty much a guarantee that if you think you found a good piece of gear, in about five minutes, there will be better.
And then there is the added bonus of having a pet that doubles as your extra bag slot, and as your battle-buddy.  I mean, who doesn't appreciate a bulldog that shoots a fireball out of his mouth after he summons five skeletal archers, a rampaging imp, and a slighty ragey ghoul?  And if you don't like that?  Add a different spell to him after he gets back from town selling all the crap loot you collected along the way.
Honestly, if you want a fantastic substitue for Diablo, I can't reccommend this game enough.  It might not have the legacy of the Diablo franchise, and it might not have the MASSIVE amount of freedom of Path of Exile, but it will not dissapoint fans of classic top-down click-fest loot hoarders out there.

As a player of the entirety of this series, I have to admit the fourth iteration of this mouthful-of-a-game had the smack of the anticlimactic. For a story that built up an arc over three games and more years, the story felt rushed and unexplained to the point of nonsensicality. It relies mightily upon the memory of the player—assuming, of course, they played the other games—and gives only the sparsest of details the to uninitiated. Having not touched the other games for well over a year before this, details were slow in returning. Worse by far was having an ending that left me feeling miffed and forsaken, as if my playing of this game were a duty that was all the reward I needed, and it was indeed not. The ending was so dissatisfying as to taint the memories of the past entries into the series, all of which I would label as anywhere from 'fine' to 'good' based on their own merit. If you want to finish this series, by all means, buy this game, otherwise, forego this title in favor of greener digital pastures.

I wasn’t a big fan of episodes 1 and 2, though I did have to give them kudos for the writing and animation. Episodes 3 and 4, however, combine elements from many classic RPGs such as Final Fantasy 6 and Grandia, all headed by the geniuses behind Penny Arcade AND Zeboyd, the dude who did the hilarious and addictive Breath of Death 7 and Cthulhu Saves the World games.
Episode 3 stays a little more traditional by trying to tell the story straight while involving different characters that come and go, various upgrades, a vast job system, and an interesting new MP system. Episode 4 takes a lot from that, but also adds in a sort of Pokemon style take on it, has a hell theme, and replaces jobs with trainer perks.
Both episodes are instant classics and well worth your time and attention. The best part is they’re already pretty damn cheap, but then you get them even cheaper by getting them in the package deal. I personally believe this is some of Zeboyd’s finest work and if you’ve checked out any of his previous games, these are a definite must for your collection.

My ultimate slant is about 6.5/10.  I lean more towards recommending it on the basis that it is at least a very good casual game that would probably keep younger gamers busy -- around 8-12.  For harder core gamers, it is a little too oversimplified.
The game has a very slick visual style (a couple of the monster models withstanding, such as the bird-like enemy) and the graphics run famously at maximum settings on my overclocked 2012 PC (3.4 GHz Intel i3570k tuned to 4.0 GHz clock) with a 2015 graphics card (Radeon R9 X290 OC).  It is gorgeously presented and utterly beautiful.  The reflections from the surface of the water are sublime and the environments are truly immersive.
The gameplay, on the other hand, doesn't live up.  Combat involves almost no manoeuvre and is a slog between holding down the block key and hammering the attack button.  From time to time it can be strategic to let go of the block key and dash away, although this is more often rewarded with an enemy stabbing you in the back than with any actual benefit to your character that it is usually meaningless to try.  When you unlock magic spells, you gain a moderate cost "magic missile" spell that never misses its target; enemies have almost no personality other than the size of their hit meter and how long it takes to hurt them.  The most inventive enemy in the game is one with a mask which can only be knocked off with this spell or by throwing an object at them.  The others are, more or less, simply hit point meters that walk.  This is made even worse by the fact that their AI is almost nonsense: they will either lock onto you and blithely pursue you, or will suddenly and arbitrarily go back into unaggressive wandering behaviour.  (If they wanted to create a morality play where I feel remorse for haplessly slaughtering non-hostile creatures, they succeeded there, at least. =))
To coin a phrase, it has a "none with a but" style.  None of the monsters are well-designed,
one of them is.  None of the puzzles are difficult,
one is.  None of the combat conveys a sense of danger,
the ogres do the first time.
Controls are a bit twitchy, since the mouse controls your point of aim and is often relative to your character instead of relative to the position it is on the screen.  (This part might be better with a gamepad.)  The game doesn't have the responsiveness of a purebred action-adventure game and is really more of a pure adventure game with interactive combat.  For instance, once you unlock the bow, trying to shoot a flying enemy that is south-southeast of you will result in many wasted arrows.  There is no first person aiming and thus no ability to carefully choose your target -- your arrows are auto-aimed to a rather ridiculous degree at times, especially as the threshold for where the auto-aim kicks in seems to be unreliable.  There is no locking-on of targets to specify which one you would truly prefer to attack.
The game appears to be remarkably short (I figure I'm at least a third of the way through after 4 hours of play), made longer only by grueling semi-interactive travel sequences.  Where the game with a very similar visual style would allow you to control your boat, this game is oriented more for auto-piloted navigation.  Your first travels between islands are pointless as there is no user interaction whatsoever, and could just as easily had been done away with entirely.  That they were included at all implies that the game was trying very hard to emulate another.  After your first travels, your character unlocks an ability that does unlock interactivity during the boat travel, but all it does is turn the boat travel into a tablet-like point-and-shoot minigame which has extremely little variety while your boat still travels on auto-pilot.
Unfortunately the slick visual presentation is the only shellac over top of a samey plot and astoundingly shallow character interactions.  The characters completely fail to motivate the player: they are entities in a world in the same sense that a psychopath might view people walking down the street.  For instance, there is an implied romantic attraction between your character and another about 25% of the way through the game, with absolutely
exposition or setup as to why.  Even Miyamoto's games, with no more than a couple dozen lines per character, managed to express emotional attraction -- this does not.  I literally put my face in my palm for this one.  Literally.  I barely watched the cutscene through my fingers while shaking my head and laughing.  The only character I felt a genuine sympathy for was the "last of the Owrus", after visiting a grave nearby his house after reading the sign in front of the house -- the best example of "show don't tell" story writing, which (most of) the rest of the game sadly missed the ball on.  The game does express a hint of poignance in the bleak backstory now and then, but there is too little exposition for it to be more than fleeting.
The puzzles are very simplistic.  Never once did I have to pause for more than a second to figure anything out.  For instance, avoiding any spoilers, the supposedly cryptic messages that talk about gaining a particular item from a green chest are obvious exactly what that item is.  The only time I ever got "stuck" in the game is because I failed to notice that I could blow up a single barricade on the desert island at the very beginning, and even then I figured it out simply by double-checking the areas accessible to me and testing areas for vulnerabilities.  One of the puzzles later on in the game, en route to collecting the shield, is quite obvious in intent and solution and made frustrating only by the clunkiness of the movement and aim controls, including a need to quickly and precisely target two sword swings and a spell as well as several jumps.  Perhaps a gamepad would have served me better here too.
With all of those negatives, you would assume that I absolutely hated the game, but the game is well presented enough that, chore of gameplay aside, it is strangely compelling.  The music is utterly fantastic.  The game manages to capture "fun" without actually being particularly well done, and that is remarkable on its own.  It is a gorgeous romp through varied locations and all extremely atmospheric, even if all are extraordinarily short.  The voice acting is phenomenal and incredibly professionally done (not sure what VAs the other reviewers are listening to, but mine were great ;-)), although the characters are so one-or-two dimensional that it is difficult to develop any particular attachment.  There isn't enough of character interaction to make the world come truly alive, but it is certainly alive enough to watch as an external viewer: peering through the looking glass without ever deciding to step all the way into the rabbit hole.
An advanced gamer will probably turn their nose up at it, but it would definitely be something you could point a child at for mindless fun.

The premise behind Oceanhorn's story is something you have probably seen a hundred times before, as the story kicks off with the hero's father leaving to save the world, only to put you in control of the hero with a quest to find your father and help him defeat Oceanhorn moments after. From there onward you'll experience an entire Zelda-like adventure, looking for the location and a way to defeat Oceanhorn and rescue your father. There is always something new to discover, but Oceanhorn's biggest miss is when you realize that all your discovery excitement that builds up as you move forward quickly goes back to zero once you realize that there are few things to experience besides the main story. There are sixteen different islands to visit, mostly serving as an essential part to the storyline, but only a few of those have gameplay value to encourage a full exploration such as Tikarel which serves as the main town where you can buy items and take on new quests. Unfortunately, the rest of many are only a one-time visit deal, as you can finish everything there is to see and experience in less than 15 minutes and never return to that island again. There are some activities such as finishing and completing the different challenges that might add a bit of variety, but even those feel repetitive and pretty basic to any RPG. The story itself has nothing much to offer as you can probably guess how it's all going to end from the very beginning, but nevertheless, the journey all the way to the final island is an enjoyable ride if you're willing to look past the repetitiveness and basic concepts.
Not only does Oceanhorn feel like a Zelda game, but it plays like one too; if you have played a Zelda game before the formula will seem very familiar to you: make your way to that dungeon, defeat the boss in order to obtain the item you need, return to town to gather more information about your next quest and repeat until you get to the end. Navigation is done via a Wind Waker-like boat mechanic that allows you to travel from one island to the next one using your boat, but there are very few things to do on sea, as the only thing to keep you preoccupied while you reach your next destination are the barrels and mines that randomly pop in front of you as you sail, but after a while, even those start to become more annoying than fun, as the whole concept becomes repetitive and unrewarding. On land, the gameplay is pretty basic, as you only have a few spells at your disposal and your sword attacks, but once you realize that some spells are only useful once for the boss battle that they were designed for, the whole adventure will only become more and more repetitive. There are only a few enemies that you will encounter throughout your adventures, most of which can be defeated with basic sword attacks that require no strategy at all, while the boss battles vary in quality, as some of them feel intelligent and rewarding, while others are just a very long game of poke-poke-hit. Apart from the main quest itself, there are few things to keep you occupied in your adventures and while locating all of the bloodstones feels rewarding in the end, that reward will probably come in too late as you would've already finished the game by then.
Not only does Oceanhorn feel like a Zelda game, but it plays like one too; if you have played a Zelda game before the formula will seem very familiar to you: make your way to that dungeon, defeat the boss in order to obtain the item you need, return to town to gather more information about your next quest and repeat until you get to the end. Navigation is done via a Wind Waker-like boat mechanic that allows you to travel from one island to the next one using your boat, but there are very few things to do on sea, as the only thing to keep you preoccupied while you reach your next destination are the barrels and mines that randomly pop in front of you as you sail, but after a while, even those start to become more annoying than fun, as the whole concept becomes repetitive and unrewarding. On land, the gameplay is pretty basic, as you only have a few spells at your disposal and your sword attacks, but once you realize that some spells are only useful once for the boss battle that they were designed for, the whole adventure will only become more and more repetitive. There are only a few enemies that you will encounter throughout your adventures, most of which can be defeated with basic sword attacks that require no strategy at all, while the boss battles vary in quality, as some of them feel intelligent and rewarding, while others are just a very long game of poke-poke-hit. Apart from the main quest itself, there are few things to keep you occupied in your adventures and while locating all of the bloodstones feels rewarding in the end, that reward will probably come in too late as you would've already finished the game by then.
There are some great tunes in here, and if you didn't know different you could say there were in the soundtrack of a Zelda game, but they do start repeating after a while and it does make it boring listening to the same thing all over again. The effects are enough to justify the means, but the voice acting is absent, not that the game would necessarily need it since the quests instructions are pretty clearly delivered via text dialogue, but it would've been nice to have that option, at least for the main cutscenes to make the whole missing father story more personal.
You can finish the whole game within 10 hours, add a few more if you're willing to revisit every island in order to gather all the bloodstones and complete all the challenges, but that's pretty much all of it, and since some skills are required to access a few areas, you can't complete everything in your visit visit, so you will have to deal with the repetitiveness of the main story first and then move on to the repetitiveness of the sidequests.
It's impossible to deny the fact that Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is a Zelda clone since it feels, plays and looks like a game in the Zelda series, but it's a pretty decent one, so if you liked Zelda and want more of it, Oceanhorn might prove to be an entertaining adventure for you. The game does come with its flaws and lack of content, but in the end it will prove out to be an adventure worth playing.

Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is an action adventure heavily inspired by The Legend of Zelda. To begin with the story, it's not anything special, so you'll just live with the fact that your father left you to destroy the expanding evil. As a good son, instead of being hateful, you become a powerful knight that will save the world and unite all races, surpassing your father.
But from what exactly you'll have to save the world? Well, from three types of steampunk machines and a possessed living fortress, and few native creatures like trolls or orcs, which also have pretty low variety. Overall, Oceanhorn is limited this way, as you'll meet just few distinct NPCs and beat them with one of two swords, bow, bomb or one of your five spells.
The steam page says it's also an RPG but I think that's overestimated. Even though there is a leveling system, there aren't many character levels and each level up brings you a passive bonus, e.g. increased amount of bombs or arrows you can hold. There isn't any inventory system and even though there is a currency system, you'll save money for later anyway, because only appealing items in shops are the (two) expensive ones. All cheap stuff in shops are arrows, bombs, mana or health refills but you won't need to buy these - anytime you are missing something, the game drops it for you from the next enemy, bush or vase.
Low difficulty is something that really disappointed me. All puzzles are laughably easy and neither the combat is challenging, especially after you claim the second sword. Bosses might seem scary but they are easy too, it's like they want you to win with a single repeating pattern: Do something to stun them, tap your slash button until they stand up, and repeat two more times.
There are height differences on islands but the level design is pretty limited, you can't even jump down the cliff if it's higher than a block. After about 5 hours of playtime, you'll at least learn to roll and jump between blocks close to each other. Anyway, the game holds your hand in most moments so nothing bad can happen to you and if you fail anyway, you just respawn at nearest checkpoint and dead enemies are still dead until you leave the location. The game also have problems with occasional crashes, it crashed every hour in average but it's not a big problem since the game saves your progress often.
It's not complex, it's not hard, so what? Oceanhorn feels like a food for completionists. It has a good amount of achievements and it motivates you to explore all the areas, to find every treasure (
). There are a lot of secret areas and there's also a well-made challenge system - Each discovered island shows you three new challenges that you can beat anywhere in the game. Those challenges varies from "kill X enemies" through "drown your enemy" to "catch your first fish".
There are two minigames in the game, fishing and sailing between islands. Fishing is completely optional but the sailing, that's something you'll have to do many times... and it's annoying. You set the place to sail to and there are boxes, mines and sea creatures in your way. To get through, you have a gun with unlimited ammo and attack speed - it just shoots everytime you tap the attack button. It's a boring playtime filler where you are just mindlessly shooting everything, that you can't skip.
The colourful graphic design is something that definitely stands up for Oceanhorn in the amount of negative facts around. At least if you don't mind that all characters look like kids. The soundtrack is fine, it contains average positive melodies that you won't mind listening repeatedly, but you forget them immediately after you finish the game.
Oceanhorn comes as a disappointment by many features - low variety of everything, poor story, low difficulty, very limited RPG mechanisms. But it has its positives, as it'll make many completionists entertained for being able to explore all the islands with many secrets and challenges. That's why I think it's worth recommending to people seeking relaxing and easy game, just don't expect much from it. If you think 15 € for this is too much, wait for sale - There'll be another one for sure, as it already was in 1 dollar tier of Humble Bundle.

Oceanhorn is a mixed bag; it's definitely more good than bad, but it's clear that there is a lot of unutilized potential in it's design.
The most notable quality of the game is that it's derivative; of The Legend of Zelda to be specific, though that comparison is drawn quickly and immediately by anyone who has a passing familiarity with the Zelda franchise. Unlike many similar indie designs, Oceanhorn doesn't feel like an homage or a tribute (much in the way that Ittle Dew or Binding of Isaac do) -- instead it feels like a somewhat randomly curated collection of Zelda artifacts, patched together in to... something, without really knowing what all those pieces were meant to do in the first place. While it is an enjoyable playthrough, the game shows its most promise in the rare moments where it isn't trying to shoehorn another Zelda trope in to it's structure.
The story hurts the most of the trouble; many of the characters are direct references to Zelda staples, but they lack any of the history or context of that series, so instead of feeling like they contribute, they just end of feeling hollow or forced; the villain, for example, reads as a Gannon cliche, not as an evil peer. And in an effort to create gravity, many ridiculous plotholes are developed -- we're told that the world is in terrible shape, but we never see it; the Gillmen have been waiting for help for centuries, but it's not clear why they haven't sought help; the Sky Islanders watch everything, but are completely in the dark about anything meaningful (not to mention that they have advanced technology, but couldn't figure out a safe way to get to the ground). Heck, the game even tells you that you're liked in town, and drops a romance in your lap, which is crazy because when it happens you're little more than a pot-smashing drifter in town.
And with all the mirroring between Oceanhorn and the Zelda games, there is an unfavorable light cast on all its rough edges. The camera doesn't really work; there's mismatch between the overwrought dialog and its subtitles on several occasions; there's numerous small glitches and inconsistances that can ruin whatever it is that you're doing. And if Oceanhorn stood on its own, I'd probably be comfortable ignoring all of that; it's just how firmly planted in the shadow of another series the game chose to be that makes these issues pop to the fore.
That all said, it's a reasonable length for a good adventure; it's most tedious parts are either optional or far apart; and the game oozes with a respectible amount of polish. I think the dev team put some serious elbow grease in to brewing this game up, and they realized the concept admirably. They just need to get much further away from their inspiration before they decide to build.

Rating: 6/10
Overview: Isometric RPG
Similar Games: Legend of Zelda
The Good:
+ The artwork looks great
+ Game controls really well
+ Killing enemies and completed challenges rewards you with experience giving you some upgrades per level increase.
+ Music and sound effects
The Bad:
-The game's biggest flaw is the level design. Every 'island' you visit is one large complex, confusing puzzle that looks and feels the same in every regard. The puzzles are not nearly as well design as its counterpart that it's trying to rip-off and halfway through the game it starts feeling like a chore rather than fun.
- Selecting an island to travel, has you sailing in a ship that looks eerily similar to that in Legend of Zelda Wind waker. However you don't actually control the ship, the game does that for you while you shoot from a canon, destroying the same enemies over and over again. It was fun in the beginning but like the rest of the game it starts to feel derivative after a while.
- Story and characters feel very uninspired.
- Boss Battles are boring and frustrating to play.
Conclusion.
Oceanhorn is HEAVILY inspired from the legend of zelda series, and while that may be a good idea the game fails in its execution. If Steam had a 'meh' option I would probably choose that. Sadly I will give this game a negative review, because although the game is certainly competent in certain regards the fact that it tries so hard to be like Legend of Zelda and misses the mark is what really hurts it at the end.

As a guy who grew up playing Dungeon Master on Amiga 500, I can say, this game is a nostalgia trip. It took me back to those days, in many ways. Now where do I start, you begin the game in a conventional manner of choosing your party and other things.
After that, that's where the game actually starts, you aren't given too many clues on what's ahead, you have to pay attention to the dialogue, pay attention to your enviroment and read all the books and scrolls in order to get a gist of things especially those that will come in handy later.
The controls take a bit of getting used to but it's intuitive once you do so, same with the inventory management and in general the gameplay.
The visuals are gorgeous, in a late 90s/early 00s way, when things were beginning to be pretty but you still had to use the imagination to fill in the blanks.
Gameplay is straightforward for anyone who has played Wizardry, Dungeon Master and other first person RPG classics, it's relatively straightforward for those who haven't, as the tutorial explains everything you need to know.
You explore, solve puzzles, combat monsters but the most impressive thing about the game, it's FILLED to brim with secrets, chances are that instead of progressing in the main story, you'll land up in a whole lot bunch of secrets instead, because the game rewards curiosity and exploration.
This game certainly has potential and the devs really pay attention to their feedbacks and bug reports, so i'm sure the game will be even better with time.

But he keeps coming back needing replacements for the same organs, meaning that Nigel's hospital is distributing faulty organs.
And why does Nigel need instructions on how to move his hands? He must have some serious brain issue. This could be a direct result of his drug abuse. He intentionally shoots himself up with the patient's numbing agent to get a buzz during his operations. This is known to be intentional, because he has another syringe filled with the medicine to counteract the effects of the numbing agent. It harms the patient, so there is no reason to have it with him. Also he has no assistant.
My theory is that he's insane, has locked himself in the operating room, and is playing with the organs of his dead patient. But the game presents him as some sort of prestigious surgeon. But that's just my opinion.

I would HIGHLY recommend this criminally underrated game. I haven't played as much as I would have liked on the PC version, but I played this game to death on the 360. I'm hard-pressed to think of any major complaints about Amalur. It's got a big world to explore, tons of quests and factions to join, a great crafting system, fantastic combat, and a superb character progression/skill system. I've got to go into detail about the skill system because it's one of the best I've ever used in an RPG.
Amalur's skill/progression system lets you seamlessly blend together aspects of different builds effectively. All talents are broken down into Might (warrior), Finesse (rogue), and Sorcery (mage), and you can focus on one, mix the two, or even build into all three. If you focus on one, you'll be able to reach the higher-tier abilities faster. Whereas if you divide your build you'll have more variety and options in combat, but it will take longer to reach those endgame skills. You can mix as many or as few skills as you'd like; there are no wrong choices. Not only that, but as you build through the trees you get "Destinies" that you can change at any time. If you focus on Might abilities, you'll get Destinies that boost your Might abilities. If you mix together, say, Finesse and Sorcery, you'll unlock Destinies that compliment both of those styles. Each combination of skills has a corresponding Destiny branch, and each branch has its own unique feel that subtly changes your passive buffs/abilities. And on top of it all, if at any time you'd like to respec your character and start from scratch, you can do that for a small in-game fee (albeit one that grows slightly more expensive each time you do it, with the first one being free).
In addition to your main talents/abilities, you get specific skills (think things like crafting, lockpicking, persuasion, etc.) that further define your character.
The combat is also some of, if not the very best combat I've played in an RPG. Each class archetype (might, sorcery, and finesse) has three different weapon types to spec into. Each weapon type really does feel completely distinct from one another, having their own unique combos, timing, feel, and weight. A warhammer may seem similar to a greatsword on the surface, but when you actually have them in your hands, they feel quite different. You can have any two weapons equipped at the same time, and switching between them is as simple as pressing one of the two attack buttons. Primary weapons go on one, and secondary on the other. You can be mid-combo with a greatsword, and press the secondary attack button to immediately switch and attack with a bow.
This game is filled to the brim with content. Places to see, people to meet, dungeons to explore, and loot to plunder. Great combat, great RPG mechanics, and a ton of variety and options.
I truly feel like this is one of the most underrated games of its time and I would encourage anybody who is a fan of RPGs to give this game a shot.

Amalur is a brilliant game to get lost in. I found myself wandering the world embracing all the unique landscapes of regions in Amalur. The aesthetic and colour to the game is magnificent, and I always found myself appreciating the variety of regional areas the game had to offer. Each has it's own lore, story, quests and tales, beautifully dictated by the lorestones scattered about the world.
Lorestones are superb, and I found the voice acting brilliant for specifically the lorestones. Although it lacks in dialouge and it is apparent that many voice actors were reused for several character, which I understand due to the vast world Amalur has to offer. There's hundreds of unique NPC's with unique dialogue to keep you interested, and Amalur never lacks in conversation with NPCs from region to region.
Each region is unique, but I feel like I need to elaborate on this more. Every place you go to has it's own unique story and urban legends, many containing quests pertaining to these. Some of my favourites and ones to look out for are Canneroc (a spider infested town, with a strange woman at cause) and The Red Marches (a strange cult has swooped in and slaughtered an entire town, why.) These are just two instances of what makes Amalur a great game and examples of the hours of content you can obtain from it.
Another thing is that the lore is huge, and you have to earn it. Lorestones are the main source of knowlege throughout Amalur, although their are quite a few books located throughout the world containing information also. But Lorestones are convenient and a nice addition as you don't need to read an in-game book and pause for a few minutes to learn something new about Amalur. You also get a small bonus for completing a 'set' of lorestones, which encourages you to learn the full story.
Then there's the combat. The combat in Amalur is so fast-paced and exciting, with so many combos. I love it. I played as primarily a warrior on my PC playthrough, but I remember how satisfying been a mage was in this game, which is what a lot of games tend to miss out on. Also, stealth didn't feel that overpowered for once, as, while you could one shot normal creatures, been undetected the entire time was hard to pull off.
Amalur is not without it's flaws though, as their are many bugs in the game. Especially quest bugs, such as dungeons respawning as soon as a quest is finished...while still in the dungeon. This can potentially break certain quests or bring characters you've just completed a quest for to their untimely demise. Another bug I ran into during my PC playthrough is that audio would cut out during Reckoning mode, and stay that way occasionally. Only a restart seemed to solve this problem.
Another problem is that the main quest is pretty drab, The main quest has it's high points, but the entire premise is cliche (you're the only one that can save the world, you're the only one who can control their own fate, save us all!) But, I found the characters quite likeable, but I felt like they could of been fleshed out a little more. Amalur kind of feels like an MMO with the tons of quests but very little fleshing out of characters. It feels as though everyone is insignificant to you, which I guess they technically are if you think of the main quest plot.
What amazes me about Amalur the most though is how it can appeal to all sorts of players. When I originally played the game on XBOX all I cared about was the combat and the boss-fights and all the unique weapons and armors in the game. But when on my PC playthrough I took the time to learn about the story of each region, and the overall lore of the world. This made me appreciate the game a lot more, but made me realize that Amalur can appeal to both the casual and hardcore loremaster players that are attracted to modern RPGs.
Amalur somehow makes a blend of fluid combat, an expansive world and interesting lore to appeal to the adventures, fighters, and scholars in each of us. And it's
