The Penny Arcade games underwhelmed me almost immediately with its first two entries, but once Zeboyd Games got its hold on the license, I've loved every minute of the last two games.  Penny Arcade 3 and 4 calls back the nostalgia of older JRPGs, especially of FF and CT, but they introduce so much originality that you could hardly hold them for relying on rose tinted glasses alone.  Compared to the JRPGs of yore, PA4 requires very little grinding, and you recover all HP after each battle.  Also, you are welcome to use skills as often as you like, as your MP resets to 0 with each battle (MP grows steadily every turn or with special skills).  This lends each battle a uniqueness of its own, as there is very little mindless button mashing.  Enemies are difficult and even random battles CAN kill you if you don't think through your strategy.  These games also include a ton of customization with the myriad of classes and monsters you can unlock... there are even secret items, classes and monsters for the inquisitive to find, along with the requisite JRPG secret boss that is much more difficult than the normal story boss.  The dialogue is nonsensical and pretentious, and I found myself ignoring much of it... I'm not really a fan of PA's humor anyway, and these RPGs hammer that into my head by taking itself just a little too seriously.  Still, PA3 and PA4 were great games for me, purely out of its gameplay and mechanics alone.

The epic conclusion of the Penny Arcade saga.
Story- Tycho has destroyed the universe, the team has been separated, Gabe and Dr. Blood fighting each other for millions of years and all end up in a world below hell itself. So now Gabe must try to reunite with the others and find Tycho in this nightmarish world as he seeks to slay the final god to fullfill his goal of recreating exsistence. Yeah, this one gets ambitious. A+
Grapics- The characters in the game are recycled from the 3 game but the world is completely new and surprisingly well done and very nice to look at. Most of the caves and towns that you can explore look essentially the same but major dungeons are diverse and well crafted. B-
Sound- Sound effects are same recycled from the 3rd game but the music is extreamly well written, some of the best in the series. B+
Gameplay- There is more freedom to explore the world and enjoy hell and its sights as well as uncover it's many secrets (and there are many secrets to be found). The battles are different taking on more of a Pokemon style where you send out minions to fight for you. Each creature has their own talents as well as inherit talents from their respective trainers. There is a bit more strategy involved as well for an overall improved combat system. B+
Overall- This was, overall, the best in the series and a very welcome and satifying conclusion to the series. Everything was wrapped up so beautifully that it is teatering on my top 10 best ending in video games list it was that good. Highly recommended overall. B+

I played this because it looked like The Legend of Zelda games, but I didn't know how closely it was going to try to be Zelda.
The game is fine--albeit mediocre--as it is. It's sailing from island to island, finding three magical items to defeat evil; you go through dungeons, solve puzzles, defeat enemies and bosses, and find treasures--there's even fishing. The game is worth a playing if you already have it (my reason for having it, is it being in a bundle) and really want to play a Zelda game.
Islands are found through NPC dialog or the main narrative, and that's great, I enjoyed "finding" new islands by talking to people, but the islands are so tiny, sometimes with hardly anything on them, and that would be okay if sailing wasn't so time consuming and boring after the first few expiditions. Sailing is bland, as its an on-rails event where you take a minute or two to shoot obsticles in your way (bombs, boxes, barrels, an enemy). It wouldn't be so bad if you didn't have to sail back and forth for backtracking--which this game has lots of.
Dungeons are uninspired and extremely simple, with minimal mental effort to solve 'puzzles.' Usually, there's a tombstone hinting how puzzles are solved and where items are. Monsters are very lacking in variety, which is fine, but you're hardly ever in danger of them unless you let them hit you or they're invincible--but running away always seems to be an option. Bosses are different; the few bosses I've faced so far are either really easy, or...really easy but take long.
Oceanhorn: Monsters of Uncharted Seas could have been something great if it had more original ideas. All items, songs, style, and stories, seem to be heavily inspired by Zelda to the point where it's just "Legend of Zelda: Oceanhorn." I really hope Cornfox & Bros make another game, because they have potential, they just have to be a Zelda-like game, rather than a Zelda-clone (and if you're going to be a Zelda-clone, you're having people expect something equal to it).
The upside is that it makes me appreciate the Zelda series more.
Edit: After a very annoying boss battle, that was more cheap (nothing to do with skill or learning patterns--patterns seemed random and timing changed, and shields glitched out--, it just seemed buggy) than anything. I'm a little more weary of recommending this, but don't let that sway you.

Oceanhorn is another Zelda-clone game, although it's implemented differently. Between all Zelda games, this game is more like Phantom Hourglass, with some difference. Although i don't want this review to be Zelda-Oceanhorn comparison, i guess i can mention some similarities and differences between the two. Both games has "sailing" minigame, where you can go to other islands and sail, which there might be some obstacles and enemies that you can shoot along the path, minus the upgradeable ship, pirates, and travelling merchant ship which sells you items and a heart container (however, there is an island who sell the heart container). Both also has tricky puzzle and creative boss battle (only some bosses in Oceanhorn can be considered like that, though).
--
Well, enough blabbering about Zelda, since i want to review this as its own game.
Oceanhorn serves you with its outstanding UI at the start. The font and style really matches so well, not to mention a beautiful soundtrack in the beginning. However, i must say that i was quite dissapointed soon after i start the game, because the 3D models isn't as good as the UI. The models look stiff and some facial expression (especially Neeti, a girl in an island) looks weird. The hero always looks angry. I know it's quite hard to make a facial expression, but if you decided to use one face from the start to finish, it better be a bright one. Also, some animations looks weird. One example is on the cutscene when the hero sleeps.
Although i said before that Oceanhorn comes with a beautiful soundtrack in the beginning, i have to say, that i forgot most of the soundtracks in there, or maybe i didn't notice there is a soundtrack at all. The soundtracks are quickly forgotten. There is no difference playing it muted or not. Well, graveyard island might be an exception though, because it's quite creepy.
If you think that Oceanhorn comes with a beautiful and captivating story, you are mistaken. The ending only gives me a "huh?" feeling, since it didn't capture an ending moment perfectly (for those who have played this game, i just didn't like the fact that they are talking normally like nothing happened). The story is already set from the start, with some details in each of the cutscenes. In the middle of the story, they made a pair out of nowhere, and it's not romantic at all, even if they are put together in the night sky watching fireworks. But luckily, cutscenes are skippable and you can rewatch it anytime.
Well, since i said that the models, soundtrack, and story are a no, maybe you are wondering as why would i recommend this game. Simply put, with all the defects, i am still satisfied with the gameplay. Let me elaborate.
Most puzzles are creative enough to make you think, and there are some collectables which require you to solve some puzzles first. I must admit that i can't solve some puzzle and have to consult a guide somewhere, but it's not to a point where it's frustating enough and you have to see a guide in order to solve all puzzles.
Talking about puzzles, i must say that i was quite mad with the control at the start because you can't jump, only to find out that you can only jump after obtaining an item, which soon disappoints me because of the odd jump mechanism. You can only jump through one gap (you can't jump up and down one level). Also, you will roll if you can't jump, which makes you to really have to go through the corner in order to jump. I ended up stopping and jumping instead of running/walking and jumping because of that, which looks weird.
You can bomb some places to reveal a new path (and it doesn't looks bombable at all). However, it makes me stuck on some point. Although i have bomb the spot before, it didn't collapse, which makes me have to consult a guide to look for a new path, only to find myself to bomb the very same spot.
There are two collectibles, namely heart pieces and bloodstone. You might be wondering at the start on how to collect bloodstones (and it's quite annoying to do once you find out how to), though. There is an item to track bloodstone and although you can't track heart pieces, this game has a completed guide which you can consult to. However, i am quite dissapointed that you have to retrack all the way just to recollect all the collectibles after you can jump because it takes time as the map is quite big and travelling between islands costs time.
Although i must say that the final boss is quite dissapointing (it's easier than all the bosses in the game), the others are quite enjoyable. Okay, maybe the first boss is easier because it's similar to a boss in Zelda game (i forgot which), but it's still weird to think that the final boss is super easy if you already know what to do. The other bosses are more creative imo, especially that shadow thingy, because it has two phases. I was expecting the final boss to have something like three phases, but it's only two dissapointing battles.
. There is a fishing minigame in this game. Luckily, it's quite easy. You can get the fish you are looking for in less than 5 tries. However, some fish are exclusive in an area and most fishes took quite long to catch. There are some "specials" in some fishes which can make it harder, but overall, it's just the same as catching other fishes.
There is also a minigame where you are traveling between islands. You just need to shoot everything and it's relatively easy though. However, in my opinion, it's taking quite a long time, especially on the "cutscene" when it docks, which can't be skipped.
. There are some challenges which is linked to steam achievement and you can unlock it in other island. Sadly, you can't see the achievement list in one go because it's only listed by 3 in every island. Some challenges can be done as you progress the main story and some needs you to grind a little or do a certain trick.
This game is great for casual gamers and can be 100% quickly. The challenges aren't hard and doable.
Should you buy this game?

Oceanhorn is essentially The Legend of Zelda with a reskin, so inevitably comparisons are going to be drawn.
Zelda works as a franchise because it has buckets of charm. It's quirky, imaginative and full of life. This is just about as close of an imitation as you can get without calling the protagonist Link and giving him a green tunic with a hood, but it has none of the appeal of it's ancestor.
The Zelda games were designed to consistantly amaze you. In Ocarina, climbing Goron mountain for the first time, exploring the Zora water caves, even travelling across the world on horseback, all of it is inspiring and innovative. The worlds tell their own stories. This has none of that. It's a mediocre copy/paste of Windwaker that does nothing particularly special to cement it's own place.
Just about the only things it has going for it are a pretty decent soundtrack (which is never really complimented with spectacular scenary or tense circumstance) and the fact it's on PC and the Zelda games are not.
There are far worse games in existance, but why settle for this when it is decidedly average.

Got it on Humble Bundle where this game was just a bonus.  If you can get it cheap, then it's a good play-through, but otherwise, I wouldn't recommend it.
- silent hero who's default and only expression is a scowling face.  Has zero personality; a robot could replace him and it would be an improvement.
- there's a lot of excellently voiced dialogue in the game, except the story is so boring that it's really hard to care for any of these characters or their motivations.  Even the ending doesn't really resolve anything.
- several levels where you can get stuck while exploring, stamina gauge that limits your mobility for no reason, cheap boss fights offset by cheap items/spells, windwaker world map that serves no purpose other than to artificially prolong the game, fetch quests that require you to carry items slooooowly from point A to point B, legendary sword that is famed for its power yet a common rat can withstand two hits
This game had a lot of potential.  It has all the pieces for a great game, and yet somehow all the flaws amalgamate to a disappointing experience.  Overall, it's a zelda clone devoid of the things that make a Zelda game good.

I'm going to start by saying I loved Human Revolution and continue by saying that I can see this games potential to match it. However, due to the egregious use microtransactions and single use items (and improper explanations of them) combined with very poor performance I'm very tempted to refund the game (for reference, I'm having to run the game in 720p on medium to get a fps over 30 where I can run most current games in 1080p at 60fps on medium to high). From what I've experienced of the gameplay so far, it feels like just more Human Revolution but some of the systems feel clunky and I'm not a fan of the cover system this time round. This, coupled with the poor framerate and low graphical fidelity is making the gameplay feel stiff, although there is a lot of choice in the style of gameplay. Additionally, I'm finding the story less gripping than my first playthrough of HR and some of the dialogue is a little cheesey. All in all, a game that has great potential but has been spoiled by some poor marketing decisions and poor performance. I'd say get it if you like DE:HR, otherwise wait for a price drop, and do not buy the season pass, it’s a rip off.
Edit: After todays patch, I've seen a big increase in performance. The game has been stable at 1600x900 at mostly high at over 40fps. Reducing the UI size makes the screen feel a lot less cluttered although it still feels messier than HR. Using workarounds such as an early game save will mean you'll always have access to the single use items (my biggest problem with the game is the inclusion of these items, everything else could have been forgiven but single use consumables in a single player game are ridiculous and its a huge shame). I've decided not to refund the game, because whilst it may not be as good a game than DE:HR it is still a good game, just not one worth £40.

Dungeon Kingdom is very well made and very difficult dungeon crawler where you create a team of four characters from various classes like warrior, priest, and mage, including combinations of these, and as a unit this group must tackle the various puzzles, obstacles, and enemies the game throws at you.
Your team functions as a single unit in movement, and movement occurs along an invisible grid, meaning you can only go in one of the four directions. Control is done by keyboard and turning can also be done by keyboard, or by mouse.
The game has very hard puzzles that require you to actually pay attention to hints dropped by other characters or found in books, or quick on the spot thinking to manipulate obstacles, levers, and the like.
Everything happens real time, including the combat. Physical combat (hand-to-hand or swords) is done by clicking on the hand icons of the various characters, they will then strike directly in front. Magical combat can be done the same way if you've prepared quick spells.
On to magic: the game uses a combine system of runes that requires some learning, but can quickly become intuitive. For example, fire + breath/wind = fireball. Once you've succesfully created/cast a spell, it gets added to a quick list for future access.
As the game happens in real time your characters will also get hungry and thirsty, eventually losing health points if you don't take care of their needs. This adds an extra challenge to the game.
The difficulty of this game is high, but that will hopefully change somewhat as the game gets closer to release. The game is currently in early access, and there are some elements that don't seem as polished in the current build. NPCs don't actually appear in the world, but suddenly pop up as a portrait with (mostly voiced) dialogue. All portraits, including the player portraits, appear to be photoshopped photos of real people, this gives a somewhat strange effect. On the one hand it is realistic and still fitting to the game world, on the other hand it gives the odd effect during dialogue scenes where the game stretches and otherwise deforms the faces to give the illusion of speaking.
On a technical level, the game runs smoothly, with a constant framerate. Soundeffects are effective, nothing special there yet but no real bad picks either. Graphics are really good, with good lighting effects and nice effects on spells.
I can definitely recommend this game for anyone who is familiar with dungeon crawlers like Legend of Grimrock,  Might and Magic, or Wizardry. It already hits all the notes that draw me in to that genre and despite not being as polished yet as a full scale release, there is enough here to already give a fun, if really challenging experience.

Disclaimer: I’ve been somewhat involved in the making of this game as a tester and translator.
Dungeon Kingdom is an indie dungeon crawler in the vein of Dungeon Master and Legend of Grimrock. It is currently in Early Access, but for being an early version it is pretty well playable. All the key features are there, the systems (fighting, magic, resting, eating/drinking, levelling) are in place. The graphics are very pretty and compare well with recent 3D RPGs.
The Early Access version offers two main environments. The game starts in the wintry city of Barimbar during night-time, where the streets are deserted and you first learn of a looming menace: the Guild of Magic which protects Barimbar is in danger from a rival faction, and betrayal abounds left, right and centre. After recruiting your party of 4 you are sent to the great temple to fulfil a mysterious prophecy and aid the Guild. The temple level makes up the bulk of this version, featuring the beautiful upper levels and some run-down, maze-like lower levels where you’ll encounter both puzzles and fights.
The puzzles in this early stage aren’t too difficult, and paying attention to books and scrolls and thus the “lore“ of the world is definitely rewarded. The fights work alright too, but this is where the EA’s biggest issue lies. The AI still has some problems and occasionally prefers to wander around the room and take hits instead of actually fighting back. There are some balancing issues as well, but these are actively being fixed already, as seen in the first update two days after launch.
A special feature that many other crawlers lack is the physics system. Many objects are flammable, items have a weight, they can be thrown and roll around on the floor. This makes for some nice options for both puzzles and fights. Sometimes passageways and buttons are hidden behind curtains that can be traversed, making them sway in the air, or burnt down. Levels are continuous, which means that you can climb ladders, jump down pits, or throw items through them, all without any loading in between. One time I managed to kill a monster by luring it onto a rug and setting it on fire with a candle. Stuff like this is very satisfying and fun to experiment with.
Obviously a lot of content in terms of levels is still missing from the EA version, but spring 2016 is still some time away. The content right now makes for around 4 hours of gameplay. So if you like dungeon crawlers and would like to witness the development of an indie game, give this one a shot!

This is a game where I wish Steam had a "maybe" option instead of YES or NO. I'm putting yes just because that feels more fair than putting no, but here's my hotughts. I didn't play for too long obviously, and I like a lot of what I see, but there's a handful of things that make me want to wait until it comes out of early access and is fully and officially 'released'!
VOICES: Some of the earlier parts of the game appear to be voiced, not sure if more will be or just some bits, but honestly this one of those things.. Ya kinda gotta go all in or go home. In this case I'm assuming their budget and voice cast options are limited so, as far as voice, I say go home. Put your focus into good and compelling writing rather than voicing a few characters in a mediocre fashion! It'll pay off way more.
ART/AESTHETIC: The character portraits look like some paint overs of stock photos and, frankly, they're not bad. But when engaging in dialogue with some characters the potraits are mashed and contorted to give the illusion of expression and speaking and.. it really just doesn't look good. I applaud the developer for trying to add more like that but it just looks super strange; maybe this is something that'll be improved, but I frankly don't know that I've ever seen the warping thing done well for mouth movements and facial expressions for dialogue. The painted protraits look just fine, let them do the talking for you - we as players can imagine them moving, don't hamfist it in via weird morphing and smushing of things around.
GAMEPLAY: Movement is good, the game itself looks nice as far as the environments and all. I'd love to see some more character options as far as races - as is there's a swathe of humans, a dozen or so elves, two dark elves, one dwarf, one halfling, one "labian" wolf-type character, and a small trio of "other". It's not a bad mix, but it'd be nice to have at least a couple of each options, i.e. someone can make a halfling dominant party or similar, and not be forced to choose other races, or be able to mix whatever combo they like. Basically, at least four of each, ideally?
CONTROLS: I'd love to be able to remap controls but there seemed to be no ability to do so - In this style of grid-based movement I prefer A and S to turn, and Q and E to strafe, but their controls are locked to Q and E turn, and A and S strafe. It'd be nice to be able to customize these as we see fit. Maybe in the launcher? The in game menu didn't have the option, anyhow.
And speaking of, the controls are a tad inconsistent and not intuitive. Left clicking picks up an item in the world, but uses an item if in your inventory, rather than pick it up, so that creates some "oops I used a potion/read a scroll/etc." moments when you're trying to navigate things. It'd also be nice to be able to drop items on a character's portrait and it go into their first open inventory slot; instead you have to open the inventory, which removes visibility of other character's/inventory/hands/portraits, and gives you their bag slots.
UI: I think the dev could size down the inventory UI and keep visible your hands/your parties hands, and even make at least the first row of your party's bags visible for ease of moving stuff around, as is it definitely is a bit clunky.
I'm really on the fence - I almost wanna refund it and wait til' it's finished and out, but I do like a bit of what I'm seeing. Honestly a lot of my thoughts here aren't big game breakers, but all together it's enough to kinda be just annoying enough that it leaves me uncertain. A more intuitive menu/UI would be great, and it'd be nice of hitting ESC closed bags/stat screens/etc. as you'd expect, but instead it pulls up the game menu, which takes several seconds to slowly pop into view and then pop back out, which creates some annoying moments if you open it by accident when trying to close out something else quickly.
When it comes to games of a particular style I strongly feel like devs should take what we know works - Might and Magic, Grimrock, etc.- and build on that as far as controls go. There's control schemes we're used to and as a result expected ways for it to work; don't reinvent that wheel. By all means do nuts on the magic and items and skills and all that, blow our minds with that, but don't make your controls rigid and kinda wonky. :D Recreating that doesn't add anything to your game, it just frustrates folks. Mimicking control functionality is one of the best things you can "take" if anything, in my opinion, when it's done well repeatedly elsewhere. The left-click varying functionality is really what threw me off the most, and the lack of ability to adjust or change controls from within the game.
MAP: I also think the lack of ANY kind of map is a mistake. I know, I know. I grew up on grid paper and walked uphill both ways on dial-up and all that too, it's okay. But you have to realize that, these days, it's just not the same. I don't think I could even find a pen lying around, much less graph paper or something to draw up maps with, and as the developer said themselves, due to the 3D nature it'd be near impossible to map well.. But that also kinda begs the question, if it's that hard to make a map of it, how are we expected to navigate it without reasonably well and not just end up running circles and just dying?
Some kind of compromise seems necessary here. At the VERY least I think a rough 'area map' that designates where you are and the rough size/shape of space is enough, something to at least help people navigate around in a general sense and be able to find entrances/exits/etc., while not being a perfect grid-by-grid representation necessarily. Or heck, I kinda like the DS/3DS Etrian method of giving you the tools to draw up your map, it was a clever way to provide both maps and mapping
Edit: I just loaded it up and got the Unity launcher to check the inputs there.. You can adjust controls.. sorta? You can adjust the horizontal and vertical, but there's no options to change the turn bindings, which default to Q and E; they aren't even shown, in fact. :( I understand that there are often limitations when working with particular engines, but that kinda stuff can be a real sticking point, as it's awful frustrating to have to constantly remind oneself that what is usually turn is strafe and vice versa.
I feel like there's a pretty good 'heart' here as far as a solid Might and Magic/Grimrock/etc. dungeon crawler, but there's just enough polish missing that I'm really just not sure.
I also am kind've a grump and I hate to see just four classes. Maybe it's from a decade of playing MUDs and other RPGs and being so horribly tired of the SAME things, but just seeing heavy melee/light melee or range/divine caster/arcane caster as my only options just.. well it makes me sad, it smacks of a painful lack of desire to try and mix things up a bit.. There seems like there may be some hybridization which changes it up a little, but I'm not sure how much with what I've poked at thus far.
I do like the atmosphere and aesthetic of the game itself, it's solid. I like that you can peer down into pit traps and such, that opens a whole new venue for puzzles, and I like that, for example, hanging cloth on the wall can be set alight; that opens yet another angle for puzzles and secrets if there are a variety of physics interactions (lightning, fire, ice, etc. for manipulating the environment?) I don't know how much of this exists or is used in the game, but it's promising in any case to see that kind of thing!
TL;DR - I kinda like, I think I could totally like it with at least a few minor adjustments, you may totally like it, but I also think there's enough little snags that may just bother the hell out of you. Depending on what's left to change before "release" they may totally mop up all these little things, or maybe they'll carry on over to release and it'll remain kinda annoying.

PROS:
Very close to true open-world with rewards for exploring
TONS of quests and sidequests including multiple faction lines
Visually pleasing Fable-like graphics
Combo chain attacks
Crafting system for equipment and potions
Usual thief/mage/warrior options as well as some minor encouragement to try duel-specing
Interesting NPCs with really fantastic voice acting
Really fun story
CONS:
Not very well balanced
Buggy: some repeating crashes, quest marker glitches, etc.
Download the widescreen fixer if you want to save yourself from getting dizzy
Overabundance of quests+respawning mobs+in-game mechanic to increase xp+not great scaling system = you can easily overlevel yourself
Stuff that feels unfinished: quest items that get perma-stuck in inventory, can't craft accessories, etc.
Equipment crafting system at higher levels requires a lot of luck (read: quicksave/reloading) but even at highest levels can't beat found/bought equipment in all cases
OVERALL:
If you want a game that will absorb you for a good number of hours as you run around talking to a million people, navigate massive towns, do crazy numbers of sidequests, and get immersed in a fantasy world that's a little less Tolkien and a little more Fae, you'll enjoy this game.
However, those who care more about mechanics will have complaints. It's very easy to get overleveled, which can make all those many quests feel a bit like dull repetition. I discovered that I'd missed a whole faction quest at low level because I didn't realize I was allowed in an area, but because scaling maxes based on area, I spent the whole time OHKOing everything and then didn't even make enough money to offset my equipment repairs.
Speaking of equipment:
So, you can craft equipment out of pieces you buy or salvage by breaking down other equipment. Salvage works on a somewhat random system that can require dozens of reloads to get what you want. At high blacksmith skill, you can work an enchanted gem into an item so that, when you salvage it, you MIGHT get a crafting piece with the stats of the gem (or a little better).
However, you can find and buy equipment with gem "sockets" which allow you to freely (at a small cost until you max gem-crafting skill) swap gems into and out of that equipment. And those pieces can also have inherent bonuses of their own. There's also a top-tier rank of gems that only fit into a slot that can only exist on a chestpiece, that can't be crafted into a homemade armor.
So, you could spend a ridiculous amount of time crafting items, reloading until you salvage what you need, and then crafting your masterpiece equipment, but it would only get you close - not all the way - to the best armor you could find just by getting a lucky loot from a kill. And the "unique" and "armor set" items can't be salvaged and don't have gem sockets, so while the gimmick of the set bonus might be nice in early game, by halfway through the game such items are just money that's taking up inventory space.
I have a LOT of little complaints, which by themselves don't seem like much but added together feel clunky:
- The lockpicking minigame has only a few preset unlock positions, but the "wiggle" time on a wrong position is so low that you still need to stock up on a million lockpicks to play a broken minigame
- Repeatable sidequests ("Tasks") can't be turned off, so the quests markers will always show, the items will sit in your inventory, and they'll take up space in your quest log (and I've run into bugs that seem to trigger on having too many quests currently open)
- You can't change the game resolution unless a character isn't loaded and you're at the main menu. This is never explained anywhere and drove me crazy.
- The game is ridiculously dizzy with the spinning camera in close-up. If you get this game, check the game guide with information on downloading the free widescreen fix utility because otherwise you won't survive.
- Walking back through entire dungeons because there's no shortcut back to the entrance, or, worse, when there's an exit into an outdoor space for the boss fight but for some reason you can't fast-travel from it.
THE BOTTOM LINE
I could go on for a while about the issues I have with this game. I think that if EA took the time to release a patch or two, this could be a really great game. However, when I hit post, I'm going to go back to playing (and finishing) this game, so overall, I recommend.

Over 50 new vehicles along with tons of other content have been added in updates since the game released on PC, but none of it is available in singleplayer.  The only way to access this content is via online multiplayer, where you have to slowly grind for ingame money or pay real money for pricey "shark cards".  Many of the cars cost over a million ingame dollars before you even customise them, and $100 of real money only gets you 8 million ingame dollars.  This is on top of the game still costing $60 years after release and rarely ever going on sale.
Previously it was possible to enjoy update content in singleplayer through the use of mods, however the game's publisher has recently begun cracking down on singleplayer mods and threatening legal action against the creators of said mods.
The best part of GTA to me has always been the extensive freedom to experiment with lots of cars and weapons and other neat toys in an expansive sandbox world, and all these restrictions are unprecedented for the series.  All development focus now seems to be on monetizing the online multiplayer, and I am fearful for the future of this series.  At this point I cannot recommend the game to anyone who doesn't have limitless disposeable income to get around the MMO-style grind, since massive amounts of the game's content is unavailable in singleplayer for seemingly no other reason than incetivizing multiplayer microtransactions.

Ok since having the game from its debut in its early access form I gotta say this game turned out to be a dissapointment overall. It's not terrible but for what RT want you to spend for this game you are much better off using your money eslewhere. Regardless of whether the game is unfinished what ultimately should make this game fun for the 3 hours of playtime you'll have per campaign run isn't (yes £15 for 3 hours if you only play this once).
Combat is repetitive and dull with very linear combos that leave no room for creative thought. If you've played any other game in this sort of genre (Dynasty Warriors seems closest imo) you have this same system of basic attack strings but could use one string to easily lead into another creating larger combos (I.E X>Y to knock the enemy into the air then X>X>X>Y for another 4 hits with a powerful finish while juggling the enemy). This woud have made combat so much more appealing over bash x y and b to win. It's not terrible and what they have does work. It's just been done better elsewhere.
RWBY Grimm Eclipse also loves hallways. In every level from Chapter 1 to 10 you progress by following a liner path, beating up some Grimm (or robots), then proceed down the next hallway. One positive though is that on occassion you may wind up entering different pathways than previous attempts through the same levels, offering different groups of enemies to encounter.  A great idea, except for the fact that these alternative paths are essentially another hallway.
And the story? Bland, Forgetful, and ultimately adding nothing amazing to the world of Remnant. There were some great ideas here and there (tinkering with Grimm to create mutated abominations was something I appreciated if only to make the Grimm more threatening) but the villain was there just to be there. Heck I don't even think the game explains what the Villain's true objective was. He was just making Mutant Grimm FOR SCIENCE!!!! But no reason was given as to why he wished to make these Grimm and what they were for. I remember him saying 'they were truly superior lifeforms and other reasons' but honestly that was about all you get. In summary this story needed more fluishing out and development to be considered interesting.
Music is usually instrumental versions of the OST from Volume 1 and 2 (don't recall anything from 3 which would make sense as this takes in between V2 and V3). It's good♥♥♥♥♥♥and if you like it in the show you'll like it here. I think I recall hearing; Time to Say Goodbye, Die, Caffeine, Red like Roses (Part 1 and 2) etc. No 'I Burn' though which is a bummer.
The game also has a basic level up system. Earn EXP by beating Grimm, Finding Artifacts, achioeving objectives, and you level up to gain points, to improve special attacks, health, aura, stun length etc. Some special bonuses I think were supposed to be there to substitute for the character's Semblance (Yang's second wind which recharges her ultimate if her Aura is depleted, while in the show as she takes damage her attacks get stronger). But I think not having the semblance in this game is a majorly missed opportunity. Flushing out each characters abilities with their semblances could have created a deeper level of strategy with each of the ladies. For example in Multiplayer Weiss could have used her glyphy's not just for projectiles but also for buffs on her teamates (V2 where Weiss increases Blake's speed to destroy the missles). Alternatively Yang could have been given a buff which increased her attack in cordination with the amounf of damage she has taken in an encounter (use her Aura as a measurement for this maybe?) Although I'm not a video game developer so perhaps this may have been alot harder to implement than it appears.
Regardless I feel RWBY Grimm Eclipse is not only a dissapointment for fans, it's a dissapointment for the game itself. This had potential to be a good representation of what makes RWBY so appealing to its fanbase in a video game. The game isn't terrible, it just isn't memorably good either. Despite this I don't think the fault is entirely with the development team on this one. In fact I have to give major props to the reponse time of the team who developed this game, and their communication with the community was great. However this game feels 'rushed' and as a certain other franchise that follows a blue hedgehog smashing robots has taught me, rushing usually ruins a potentially good game. Wait for this game to go on sale if you still wish to purchase it.
In the mean time I'll sit and wait for the next RWBY video game project with the hope of it being a better success (fighting game possibly???)

Definitely a Zelda clone, and definitely not a bad one, either.  However, the fact that the camera is in an isometric view rather than top-down that can't be (from what I can tell using a controller) rotated, combined with a rather hilly landscape means tht there will be some things that you can't see in the game.  Sadly, that sometimes includes both you and hazards. Of course, that is my only real gripe, as the other controls are well-mapped (to the point that it really FEELS like Zelda), the landscape - well. seascape - itself is beautiful (tho it REALLY should have emulated Wind Waker more, IMHO.  I liked sailing to my destination myself, rather than picking an island and just going there with what amounts to a minigame or five along the way), the music is nice to listen to, and the story is also good (even if I find some dialog lacking). It's a good game, don't get me wrong, but it really pales in comparison to the series that rather obviously gave the creators inspiration.  Play it if you need a Zelda fix right now but don't have access to any actual Zelda games, or if you want something a LITTLE different from them.
EDIT:  After doing a casual playthrough, I have disturbing news for those looking for a cheap Zelda-like experience:  A liesurely stroll through the game doing a bit of exploration in optional areas gives you a 71% completion rate in just over 7 hours of playtime.  I would estimate that a 100% playthrough would only take about 10 hours.  Considering that is less time than an average LoZ game, I am a little disappointed.  Still, it is respectable given the price.  Still recommended, but know you're basically getting a truncated game in comparison to LoZ itself.

Heavily inspired by Link/Zelda games Oceanhorn slowly, eventually, groggily delivers an adventure. It doesn't quite get close to Link but the inspiration is there. The early parts of the games feel like if you injected Link with horse tranquilizers and fed him 50 muscle relaxers and gave him toddler toys as a quest. The game just never decides it's identity between ultra-casual young child adventure with no repercussions or something much more broad and deep with semi-complex puzzles and story nuances. And I think it struggles at that in a gameplay sense, at least in part, because of it being a mobile/tablet port. But thankfully by the second half it does evolve to a game with some average difficulty and challenges that most definitely a small child could not complete. Its just a very broken flow and stride to get there. A stride that was always a few steps too slow for my liking.
The world and story is complete though. And combat and puzzles do become quite fun. There's a fun adventure to be had. The pacing, or lack there of, pushed me into wandering and grinding. I'm not big on arbitrary video game "achievements" or "trophies" but going for them all in this game majorly contributed to my fun factor. What you get out is what you put in with Oceanhorn. You have to make a concerted effort with the game, but I think it was worth it.
There's more I could complain and nitpick about too. The fishing system is absolutely silly. The gun on the boat should've just been mounted to explain why you don't get to have it anywhere else. The boat travel in general could've had more variety. Blah blah blah. The point is, the game has issues. But never did I consider quitting or did any of them ruin my time. Quintessential casual controller game.
Swords, bombs, arrows, keys, treasure chests, and baddies! There's fun to be had if you want it. Just keep grand and lofty expectations in check.

At first I took the subtleties of this game's story as a Zelda inspired creation. However, it wasn't long before I started to enjoy the game in it's own right. It reminded me more of an old Playstation game by the name of Alundra more than Legend of Zelda. There is as much exploration and puzzles as there is adventure and fighting. Oceanhorn's story doesn't take too long to get into and honestly if I put down the game for a few days I would forget what I had to do despite the ability to review previous cutscenes. It's a really cool isometric game that deals with exploring various islands in a water ridden world.
The story was solid and never deviated far from the main goal of finding your father and defeating Oceanhorn. There were side quests a plenty along the way that brought you a little closer to your goal. Some featuring puzzles that required very little thinking, quick or otherwise. The general fighting was simple but gave you a few ways to approach how you would kill enemies. Boss battles took a slight learning curve before understanding their combat patterns. What I find surprising in this adventure RPG was the pace that it went.
This wasn't by any means a long game. The majority of my time was spent backtracking to find stuff or remember to do one of the quests when I ran into a road block. Clues were scattered around areas that alluded to other locations which I'd ultimately neglect to explore, which made things tedious. I noticed a few things that could have improved my experience.
One of the things I would have liked was a notebook that maybe jotted semi useful information that you found on your journey so that maybe I could remember where the honey was located without having to go back to the source to get information on particular items needed to progress. Another thing that I found a little mundane about it was the actual traveling between islands. You don't have the freedom of navigating yourself rather you select a route that your boat moves along. I did appreciate the obstacles in the water that I had to be vigilant and shoot with my cannon but after the 10th time it was repetitive to the point of boring because there was so much back and forth travel happening. It would have also been nice if your character was able to interact with people he met on the sea. With so many islands you really wonder why the sea was so barren.
Despite the critical observations I did enjoy this game the time I did spend playing it. the visuals were beautiful the controls tight and the music was well done. The atmosphere and pace of the gameplay was all one note with the exception nearing the final boss. This would be a nice game for anyone interested in Zelda-esque adventure.

Overall I enjoyed this game but there's a lot of +/- to it. I finished at about 24 hrs playtime and that's with a little achievement hunting. I mostly ignored the fishing.
+/- Lovely graphics but not a lot of variety.
+/- Puzzles are really easy which could be good or bad depending on what you're looking for.
+/- Controls felt a little clunky with keyboard/mouse. Might be better with controller.
+/- You get spells but casting them felt slow and awkward so I only used them when forced to.
+/- Combat not very challanging except for boss fights.
If you're looking for an adventure game that's not too hard then you'll probably enjoy this. I would recommend waiting for a sale though.

Summary: The fourth installment vastly improves over every element from episode three, with a much more coherent and identifiable plot, a battle system revamped with much more input from the player, a soundtrack that is decently done, and a greater emphasis on the adventure and roleplaying aspects of the game. It spends less time trying to serve itself up as a novelty of the 16-bit era RPGs many of us grew up with and instead craft its' own identity. Granted, some may quickly feel alientated from the approach it took for its' battle system (similar to Pokemon), but it's much more solid experience than previous installments. On its' own merits I'm recommending the game, I think most people will have a good experience and enjoy it. 3.5/5
So surprisingly, most of the faults I identified in the previous review for PAOtRSPoD 3 have actually been changed for the better in four. It's still a world full of 2D sprites, still a battle system more akin to Final Fantasy than anything else, and still full of the same humor and writing style from the previous installments. The biggest change you'll find is that the characters you were previously using, Moira, Tycho, Gabe, are all now "trainers" and will be in charge of a host of different monsters to control. Now this will sound amazingly like Pokemon, even the ability to change out monsters  with another mid-battle makes it seem ever more so, but the game fully recognizes this. There is even one satirical approach to a reocurring Jesse-and-James (from the Pokemon show)-type nemesis throughout the episode. It was minimal to the story, didn't really affect the pace of the game, and really is a sidenote, but still it shows that the developers were aware of the similarities. Besides this, the items are all fairly the same, spells and effects unchanged, and the WAIT-CMD-ACT phases of battle identical to the last installment.
Now the plot from three is summed up in the first few minutes of the game and that was actually very helpful. Three was incoherent and made little-to-no-sense, but the synopsis wrapped things up and put everything into focus. It's kind of ironic that things just seem to make more sense in this new world filled with monsters, demon trains, and flying daewhales than the city of Arcadia, but it does. I feel that the ending was a bit incomplete and may have just opened a window for succeeding episodes, but still there was a set objective, a defined mission that made the game easier to follow. There is still a limited amount of character development, not to mention there is virtually none for all the monsters you capture, but it is still a marked improvement.
The game is still fairly linear, but the ability to explore and more importantly the reward factor in doing so has greatly improved. You will find items, chests, and new monsters to "train" as you scour for every alternate pathway and random cave on the overworld. I've felt that in the previous games that the reward-to-time ratio was vastly low and in many cases not worth it, but spending the extra time walking around for hidden chests can be rewarding. There are now shops and towns, NPCs, and random dungeons to explore, which adds a greater depth to the world and although the effects of this is superficial, it does add some variety to the monoity of just dungeon-crawling all game.
In alot of ways, I feel that this should've been the type of game that was done for #3. I think that there was more effort put into this title and that the last game was kind of written off and pushed out. By no means is this game a masterpiece though with all the praise I've poured over it, it's just a vast improvement on everything that series failed on previously. There are still much better games out and the game can easily be covered in about 8-9 hours. It's not life-changing or particularly deep, but I found it enjoyable. There is limited replayability, the battle system could honestly have been just revamped instead of swapped with the monster trainer approach, and I feel that the game is still linear and falls short of being on par with the gems of the 16-bit era.  One part of the game that blew me away was the soundtrack. The music is a hundred times better and I'll probably end up keeping a few of the songs for casual listening. The Airship and Tycho themes in particular were well done.
With these points in mind, I'm recommending this game for the masses, it's a game I might recommend to certain gamer friends and in general you'll probably find something worthwhile along the way. 3.5/5

Reviews seem to pretty all over the place with this game - so I'm going to throw out my experience thus far in hopes that it helps someone.
First and foremost, I HIGHLY advise that you check out Total Biscuit's video beforehand. It does a very good job at highlighting the features that this game has to offer. Did they port this game to PC, yeah obviously. But there are small minor details proving that the devs do still have PC gamers in mind. Watch the video for further clarification.
There are a few things that we know exist 1) being DLC and 2) being performance issues (like low fps and mouse acceleration).
The DLC I won't even touch, it's simply becoming a trend and I won't let it warp my opinion in what could potentially be a great game from start to finish. The performance on the other hand, I can touch on. This game looks great, just keep in mind that you have to tweak settings. I originally had issues, but after reducing shadows to medium and turning off MSAA I am now reaching 60+ FPS stable on high settings. This is with a 970. I'm not saying that other people won't have problems with different components, just that under the right circumstances the game DOES run well and chances are there are further steps you can take to improve performance. Most people immediatly hop on here to complain and don't try to troubleshoot.
With that aside, focusing on the game itself. I have only played a small amount so far, but the detail is fantastic. The conversation options, the exploration, looting, STEALTH GAMEPLAY, all the stuff you would expect from Deus Ex is still very much there. The game is fun and you can tell the devs put a lot of thought and effort into it, straight from the getgo. I'll try to update this review later with more of my experiences and findings!
For those of you having issues I really hope that you can find solutions through research. If not, chances are the devs will have a fix out very soon. As I said before, they do seem to care, based on some of the features we've been given.

Tekken 7 is a 3D fighting game, where instead of the regular 2D plane, you will be fighting in a 3D environment. Like all fighting games, your goal is to knockdown an opponent by draining their HP completely, or by draining as much HP as possible before the time runs out. Since the game takes place in a 3D arena, movement in this game will not only cover the conventional move forward and backward, crouching and jumping, but it will also cover side steppings, where you will move around the opponent in a circular motion. This is very crucial for Tekken as you may want to dodge some strings, leaving the opponent open for a counter attack. You can also dash forward and backward, and if you hold forward for a long time, the character will enter a run state. Certain characters also have their own types of sidesteps and dash movement, which are able to be followed up with a certain input or combination of inputs, for example, Kazuya's wave dash. By just standing, holding back or holding down-back, you are able to enter a guard state, though they can only block certain moves. Holding down forward allows you to slowly crouch forward to your opponent, though if you do this input right when a low attack is about to land, it will parry it, opening a combo chance.
Mechanic wise, there are 4 attack buttons, each button corresponding to a limb. Depending on the characters, certain combination of buttons pressed in a quick sequence or together in a combination will produce different things, for example, a string of X-X-Y will yield a quick jab combo string, while X+A will yield a grab. Different moves have different properties, for example a attack that has a high property will hit a standing or jumping opponent, but will completely whiff on crouching opponent. Similarly, attack with mid properties are able to hit both standing and crouching opponents, but are able to be blocked, and finally low attacks hit opponents who are either not blocked or doing a standing blocked, but are blocked by a crouch block, or be completely negated by a low parry. Pretty much each character have their own special parry, other than the universal low parry, that are able to negate an attack with a counter attack of your own. When your HP is lowered up to a certain value, you will be able to access Rage Art, which are practically your super move, and a Rage Drive, which is an enhanced move that yields certain properties.
Story-wise, it basically continues the Mishima feud from the previous Tekken game. Since some characters have some storyline which does not fit into this Mishima feud plot, their story is more of a mini episodes that will cover what they are doing during this period. Other than story mode, the offline content also contains an arcade battle, like the old Tekken games where you fight a series of AI until you reach the final boss, practice mode to practice combos, blocking movement etc, and finally, treasure mode, where you fight AIs continuously until you lose or quit this mode. Everytime you win, you will earn fight money and a free customization item, which you will use to dress up your characters. If you win a special fight or a fight under a special condition, you will get to win more items. There is a VS mode, though its meant to be played offline with another player. Online mode have 3 modes, which are ranked, where you try to rank up in the leaderboard by beating other people, player match where you fight other people without taking into consideration of ranks, and finally tournament mode, where you can gather a group of people to fight each other, tournament style. Among all things, online mode will be the feature you will spend the most time in, followed by practice mode, unless you just like fighting AIs.
One thing great that Tekken 7 did, unlike Street Fighter 5 or Dead or Alive 5, is keyboard mapping. For a keyboard scrub like me, this is a godsend. SF 5 and DoA 5 lack these features suprisingly, and it's really troublesome when the keyboard layout they give causes ghosting, and the only way around it is to use a 3rd party remapping tools, or buy a stick or pad. Another thing it did well is that unlike SF 5, you can play offline mode without any server disconnection error. One thing that irks me about SF 5 is that the game will disconnect you from whatever session you are in, even if you are playing survival mode or story mode or trials. Imagine reaching stage 99 on Hell difficulty in Survival mode, only to have your progress cut off due to server disconnection. Tekken 7 does not suffer from this. You can play treasure mode all the way to Tekken God Prime rank, and if your Internet gets interrupted during that session, you won't lose any fight money or title progress. Online is great when it's smooth, pretty much most of the matches are playable without significant delays or lags. And finally, the customization. This game offers tons of customization. You can dress up characters as well, other characters, for example, Alisa as 2B. The customization is also able to dress a character to the point where you can dress up King as a masked Dwayne Johnson from the Tooth Fairy, along with the fairy wings and tutu. The roster of characters here is pretty huge as well, from returning characters like Jin, Heihachi, Kazuya, all the way to newcomers like Kazumi and god damn Akuma from the SF series.
While majority of the online matches are smooth, sometimes a match while having 5 bars of connection, will drop to 4 or below, causing some lag and jitter. Sometimes disconnects also happens, and fight requests appear to not reach your opponent, despite both parties accepting it. Offline content here, is pretty much very limited. For starters, there's no versus AI mode here, except for pretty much arcade and treasure mode, and those will get stale really quickly. Arcade is only 5 matches, after that its done, as compared to the old arcade mode, which takes about 8 rounds or so. Story mode is, unfortunately, extremely short. You can finish it all in about 2 hours or so. The character story modes, I am not sure should it even be called that, since they are freaking short, some videos, 1 match fights, and another video, and you are done with it. Seriously? Even most of the SF 5 character stories are slightly longer than that (slightly as in about 1-2 minutes longer though). Tournament mode is barely played since its broken as the host can disband the entire tournament by leaving this mode. It's also very hard for beginners like me to get it, since some stuffs are practically hidden and need to be discovered online, for example moves frame data, some hidden follow up moves or movements etc. Moves that are safe, best pokes etc have to be found out on your own or from the game community.
Overall, despite its flaws, its an awesome fighting game. I am getting bodied everywhere by everyone I met, yet I am seriously enjoying it. It's a great game for casual to drop in and punch people in the groin, but to fully understand the game, the road to mastery is really, really long. I would highly recommend it if possible, unless you are into those offline modes completely, then I guess you can give this game a shot, but you may want to try other games like DoA 5, Mortal Kombat or Injustice for so, since their offline contents are much more than Tekken 7 have to offer.
A soild 8.5/10 from me. Highly recommended.

It took me a while to get into this game, something of a couple of months, playing off and on, not really paying that much attention to the game, wondering exactly,
Why is it that this game is so praised?
Then just about a week Gog had a promotion offering the original Mount & Blade for free, I thought, maybe I should play that first.
I got absorbed by it, the combat was one that gave me the feeling of being part of a "classic battle", similarly to ones that you read about in history books, the game recreates that feel in a perfect way.
So from that I went back to play Warband.
I went ahead and just sunk maybe ten hours or so into the freaking thing.
There are three different types of buildings in the game, cities, villages, and castles.
Inside the castles at first there's not much you can do, you can from time to time recruit some powerful units but it will cost you a lot of money, maybe encounter lords which are the rulers of different areas on the map, and/or their wives, the ladys, as the game calls them, with them you can do a lot later in the game, you can either start massive battles, in which you pin hundreds of enemies against your equally large army, or alternatively you can play into the "diplomacy" and political aspect of the entire thing, convincing certain lords to join your party, while in other cases you can simply insult them, or maybe even capture them after a prolongued and brutal fight.
The villages serve much more as the opening for new players, and veteran ones, to set foot on certain possibilities that the game offers to you.
On one side you can recruit in most of the villages a lot of peseants and poor farmers, they might not be the most powerful units in the game but after a couple of fights against looters, deserters, plus expending some time as members of your clan, and/or army, this same units can, then, be upgraded into more powerful ones, requiring not only time to spend in battle, and inside your army, but also requiring money, or gold, in order to upgrade them, after that their monthly cost to sustain them will also become more expensive, at the end of each month (in-game) you're required to provide an ammount gold to pay your party/army for their services in battle.
This may sound complex, but I assure you, the game does an incredible job explaining this to you, naturally, as you play, there are no "pop ups" with different tool tips that tell you exactly how all of this works but there's a lot of "natural learning" coming from this.
Then there's the cities that serve as probably the largest and most important buildings in the game, they not only offer the option to recruit powerful units, but also they allow you contact lords and ladys similarlly to the castles, offer you access to different types of merchants, which can sell you weapons, horses, armor, or general goods to purchase, and to sell, and also they offer you lodging, allowing you to stay for a price that seems random depending on your relation with the clan that rules, over said city.
You can also take on quests that for the most part, also, seem random, but not procedurally generated, meaning that there's care put into the quests, as simple as they can be, while at the same time offering enough variety to spread them all around different characters.
The real meat of the game tho, comes from how utterly incredible the game can be in letting the player, subconsciously fill in the blanks, and the "ruff edges" that the game has.
It is no secret, and it is something that you can even see from screenshots, that this game hasn't withstand the sands of time graphically.
But what the game doesn't offer in graphics, or animation, compensates tremendously in aesthetic, music, and gameplay, so even if the game doesn't succeed in trascending it's experience superficially, internally, what this game offers, it's essentially one of the best classical war/battles simulators to ever come into existence so far, in this medium.
It is a joy to play this game, the combat feels incredibly well, while jumpy in some cases, and seemingly rudimentary in others, the game does a fantastic job in actually giving the player the feel of being in an actual past battleground, watching countless of enemies smashing against one another, swinging aimlessly your sword against them leaving you, your horse, and them, all covered in blood.
I must say just as a small compliment, that the game's "gore" system it's really well made, it's incredibly simplistic and while there's not really any sort of "gore" in it, meaning dismemberments, beheadings, etc...
Whatever...
The game does cover the textures of your enemies, and of yourself, with spurts of blood, making the combat both satisfying as it is brutal, think of something like what Assassins Creed Unity did, only in a more clean, and simplistic way, it is a joy to even watch how something so small, so ambiguous can change the feeling of a core gameplay mechanic so radically.
And that's just the ground battles against armies, pinned in both sides of a massive battlefield that constantly changes in fauna as well as in climate, giving even something like the scenario in which you play an incredibly unique, as more than interesting strategical feel to it, in a particular one, I happen to be at the opposite end of what was a battlefield composed by a flat open space, dividing the opposite one with a river which you needed to cross in order to meet the opposite army spawning at the top of a mountain, at one point I standed in one of the few edges that finished my battleground with the division of the river, giving me a clear sight towards the mountain, as my enemies charged I kept shooting arrows, again, and again, taking a couple of them out,  in grave desperation, the rest, fell a small stept into the river, allowing me, possitioned in the "higher ground" to even at close range, shoot at them with my bow and arrows, taking a large part of their army by myself.
I cannot tell you how did that felt, it seemed like that scene in Sin City when they ambush Manutes men.
A massacre, but a beautifully crafted, and planned one at that.
I think what attracts a lot of people to this game is the fact that the game offers much but it's "ambigous" enough in it's presentation as well as in it's design to let the player fill in the blanks of it's own flaws, this is in a lot of ways an incredibly flawed game, but it works so well when it comes to how all of its issues somehow provide enough room for in which ones own imagination can run wild, that the feeling that the game actually gives you it's one of pure rawness and trueness in battle design.
Any battle design.
It's kinda like an old blues tune of some kind, while even the voice of the artist singing breaks sometimes, in pain, you can thrive in the empathy that you share understanding how he felt.

This game changed my life.
Before playing Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons, I always wanted a brother. I was a quiet kid in school. I silently cried all the time. I went through a Goth phase, a Punk phase, and a Christ phase. But they were all band-aids over my wound which was not having a brother. Plus my mom was killed during a New Years Eve. My parents were partying really hard, and she was trampled by a zebra that had snorted drugs. My dad went to jail.
Anyway, I was lost after high school. Sometimes I visited my dad in prison, but I didn't know what to do with my life. So I got a job at the nearby Krispy Kreme. I didn't eat any of the stuff we sold because I didn't want to die from what we injected into the donuts, but I put them on display and sold'em to other sad people. And, I kinda liked their sadness; but it wasn't brotherhood. I bet many of them had brothers.
One day, while crying and playing Dota 2, a Mexican guy typed something about Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons and that I was a noob or something. I told him to eat a♥♥♥♥♥♥and reported him for being Mexican. We lost the match, and I cried. Then, when I closed the game, there it was, Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons. It was a game! About the joys of having a brother, it seemed; I had to play it.
It turned out to be even more than what I thought it would. I won't spoil any details, but just know that it let me go through the entirety of what brotherhood must be in real life. Brotherhood with your own blood. And the ending—don’t worry, no spoilers--near the end of the game, something happens to your brother, my brother, and you get to do something to him. It was the best moment of my life.
Since then I've quit my job at the Krispy Kreme. I've been at community college for almost a year now, and I have all A's. I don't even cry around other men anymore. All because of that random Mexican guy, mentioning this work of art. I now know what it’s like to have a brother.

A 2.5D Zelda clone for the PC that isn’t quite as good as Zelda.
You wanted more?
Fine.
Oceanhorn is a game about a kid who is looking for his dad. His dad took off to face off with Oceanhorn, the last of the Living Fortresses, great monsters which were left behind by an ancient civilization. Your goal is to go from island to island in search of your dad.
The core gameplay is very familiar to Zelda fans – you have a sword and a shield. You wander around stabbing stuff. While the game has 3D graphics, it is fundamentally 2D – indeed, it is a major gameplay mechanic that you can fall down one “floor” worth of blocks, and can only go up via stairs. This is pretty much how all the dungeons are arranged, and numerous puzzles center around your inability to jump.
This is not a sophisticated game – you walk around and slash stuff with your sword. There is no Z-targeting or anything of the sort, but the game does have a sort of auto-aim feature.
Over the course of the game, you acquire items – bombs (for blowing stuff up), a bow and arrow (for shooting targets to trigger stuff, as well as certain enemies), a fishing rod (because what is Zelda without fishing?), boots (for jumping over one-square gaps)… really, exactly the most basic items you’d expect in a Zelda game. You also get spells – a fire spell, a spell that drops stuff on switches, an ice spell to freeze stuff which seemed unnecessary, a cure spell that I only used on the final boss, and a black hole spell that is super overpowered but useless on bosses.
That said, the game is pretty easy, and the puzzles basic. There’s nothing here that you haven’t seen before many times.
And that’s really the problem with the game – it is nothing new. It is just a kind of mediocre Zelda-ish game that doesn’t do anything new, just sort of treads the usual ground. The bosses are nothing impressive, the ordinary enemies are mostly boring and samey (and you find them a lot – there isn’t a whole bunch of variety, having even less variety than Zelda games), the environments didn’t feel that varied (you’re on a bunch of islands, but few of them feel unique)… really, there’s just very little here to excite you.
It isn’t bad, and the voice acting is decent (even if the script is often not great), but there’s just little here to get excited about. You’ve probably played Zelda, and if you haven’t, this isn’t a great introduction to the genre – games like Darksiders felt like they were much more interesting new interpretations of the Zelda formula than this was. This was same old, same old, and fairly mediocre. There’s nothing great about it, and while it isn’t bad, there’s little to recommend.

There's some good and some bad about this game honestly, but I would say overall a worthwhile experience. It's one of those things where there are weird little things that stand out like a sore thumb in an otherwise excellent piece. Oceanhorn is very Zelda-esk, which is what I went in looking for, what with the slowly unlocking new gear to open up new areas around the world. It also has an actual leveling system, which is nice, although it doesn't do a ton, it mainly just upgrades the number of bombs or arrows you can carry and whatnot. The challenge system is nice and provides an easy way to track achievements in a way that gives in game experience points. The story is kind of meh, but they don't shove it down your throat and generally just let you go explore. There are quite a few instances where they don't tell you about something and you're supposed to kind of just figure it out. That is to be expected from this kind of game, but there were several times where I had to utilize something in a way I wasn't even aware was possible and that was a bit frustrating since it wasn't clear. My main gripe with this game is the movement mechanics. I understand what they are going for, but it feels almost moronic to get stopped by 1ft high rocks CONSTANTLY and not being able to fall down more than one ledge space at a time. I feel like if they had given it more physical depth, it would have been a more immersive experience since it really pulls you out of the game when you have to navigate in ridiculous fashions that no normal human being would ever have to deal with. You also have to unlock the ability to jump via an item, which is stupid, and it only lets you jump horizonally across one space and not vertically at all. The movement structure also causes some confusion about progression since the rules get bent a bit here and there. Like you can normally only drop down 1 tier, but in certain spots to progress you have to drop down 2 or 3 and you weren't thinking you could even do that. The boss system is solid and very refreshing. It is something that genuinely awards paying attention and trial and error. The boss battles themeslves are actually extremely easy, but only if you know what you're doing. For instance, I would go into a boss battle and die over and over again until I learned something new and then I could go in and kill it without almost any problems at all. The fishing system in this game seems forced and pointless. You don't gain anything by doing it and it is complete random luck and there are far too many achievements revolving around fishing. My goal was to 100% this game and I got to the last few achievements and was just like NOPE. I see no enjoyment in running all round the world looking for fish and hoping they are the right kind. I was also a bit bummed that the sailing in this game is on rails and not open world. It doesn't feel bad or anything, but I didn't expect it to lock you on your path. Overall an enjoyable game though that satisfies the Zelda itch for a good price. I picked mine up in a Humble Bundle or something, so it was only a few dollars and it was money well spent.

If you haven't played the predecessor to this game (Rain-Slick 3), then you should look up reviews for that game.  If you have played 3, then there are two reasons you might be considering this game: 1) you're interested in the ending to the story or 2) you enjoy old school, 8/16-bit turn-based, menu-based RPGs.
With regard to the first reason, this game is quite similar to its predecessors from a thematic standpoint.  The story continues from where the last game left off and there is closure.  The dialogue maintains its humor along and the narration retains its cryptic, Tycho-ness.  If you enjoyed this aspect of the Rain-Slick Precipice so far you won't be disappointed.
If you remove the Penny Arcade references and focus on the mechanics however, I am convinced you will find it as disappointing as I did.  Combat is repetitive and boring.  This is how I felt about the previous game, but the problem is exacerbated this time because there are noticeably more encounters.  You have the ability for open world exploration, but each individual *instance* is very limited with nothing to do except fight in a linear manner from point A to point B.
You can adjust difficulty on the fly throughout the game and I found myself frequently toggling between Veteran and Insane.
All in all, I don't regret purchasing this game for $5.00.  If you're not invested in the story though, I recommend going through and playing an actual old school RPG.  I recently finished Final Fantasy 4 and am working through Final Fantasy Dimensions, and both are easily more fun and rewarding than this game.  I would recommend you play those first, even with the latter costing 4x as much.

The conclusion to the Rain-Slick Precipice of Darkness saga takes it a long ways away from its beginning. Following on the indie coattails of Rain-Slick 3 (also from Zeboyd), the team raises the stakes and brings the story to a final, satisfying close.
This game presents more like a Pokemon or other copy-cat monster trainer RPG (I guess, no personal experience), but the mechanic doesn't diverge too far from the basic party system of PA3. It does give you more characters with distinct personalities and play styles to work with, and that makes a big difference by the end of the game.
At times the narrative gets a bit wobbly in the sense that it's just not clear what's going on, but it's never too disorienting for long. In that regard, the pacing of the story is pretty unbalanced. For instance, there's a big plot revelation in the final scene of the game that really ought to have come much sooner. These are minor flaws, yes, but it makes the game feel rushed.
This series is well worth playing. It's an ambitious project spurred on by a team of people who have spent most of their adult lives discussing video games and I like to see that. It captures the humor of Penny Arcade brilliantly and, of course, is laced with plenty of in-references (but is rarely obtuse about it).

Over 50 new vehicles along with tons of other content have been added in updates since the game released on PC, but none of it is available in singleplayer.  The only way to access this content is via online multiplayer, where you have to slowly grind for ingame money or pay real money for pricey "shark cards".  Many of the cars cost over a million ingame dollars before you even customise them, and $100 of real money only gets you 8 million ingame dollars.  This is on top of the game still costing $60 years after release and rarely ever going on sale.
Previously it was possible to enjoy update content in singleplayer through the use of mods, however the game's publisher has recently begun cracking down on singleplayer mods and threatening legal action against the creators of said mods.
The best part of GTA to me has always been the extensive freedom to experiment with lots of cars and weapons and other neat toys in an expansive sandbox world, and all these restrictions are unprecedented for the series.  All development focus now seems to be on monetizing the online multiplayer, and I am fearful for the future of this series.  At this point I cannot recommend the game to anyone who doesn't have limitless disposeable income to get around the MMO-style grind, since massive amounts of the game's content is unavailable in singleplayer for seemingly no other reason than incetivizing multiplayer microtransactions.
