So far it's very good. An improvement over Human Revolution in terms of what you can do in the game and the number of pathways to an objective. Content of the game is spectacular, in terms of how the game plays I think it is great. You will not be disappointed. Also, a lot more options this time if you want to choose a combat oriented build and overall the combat in the game feels much nicer. Graphically the game looks very good and with the number of options it has I expect it to be a test benchmark for awhile. I can only imagine what it looks like at 4k with settings cranked to Ultra.  I think a lot of the problems people are experiencing with performance are due to thinking they can crank everything up on their 970/ i5 builds because that's what they are used too. It's clearly better optimized for AMD cards, but on High settings with all optional settings turned on except for motion blur (which I hate)  i'm able to achieve stable 60fps at 1080p. I've not seen it drop once.  I did try running the game at all ultra once and was able to get a mostly stable 30 fps, but it wasn't ideal and I could't really tell the difference  between it and High. Had to take screenshots and find small individual differences. I imagine if you plan on playing it on a 4k monitor you would probably be benefited by choosing Ultra, but based on performance results no consumer cards really stand this game up at a stable 60fps 4k Ultra. I'm sure there will be some performance increases when the DX12 patch comes out. All of this doesn't mean the game has been problem free though. Quite the contrary. Hard crash upon first arriving to Prauge during a cutscene that I resolved by cranking everything down to low and turning vsync off. No idea why this happened, but I was able to get past it. Had an in-game tip that stayed in the middle of my screen and forced me to re-load after getting my first set of praxis kits at the book store, but the bug didn't replicate thankfully so I was good after that. Everything else has been peachy.
Note about Micro-Transactions: The game includes them, but in the same manner as Dead Space 3 I totally forgot they were there. Completely unnoticeable and the game doles out scrap and praxis kits at a rate that you won't need it ever unless you are lazy and want to fast track your success, and at that point I wander why you bother playing but to each their own. The tactical and assault dlc you see on the store page are included with the pre-order version along with a short story mission. It's not really the best content so don't feel like your missing out on anything.
0/10, microtransaction store don't have options like "turn off mouse acceleration", "add framerate" or "turn off crashes". Only some useless in-game items.
Other than the train station crashing issue, the port is fine. People with bad computers nuking the steam reviews.

The short and skinny: This game features the art style of World of Warcraft with the open world and quest style of Skyrim. It has huge replay value and is immensely enjoyable, even with some bugs here or there.
Kingdoms of Amalur is both a unrivaled triumph and a missed opportunity. As you play the game you can easily fall in love with it and you'll find an absurd number of things to do in the open world enviroment. Truly there are maybe 5x more quests than you'll need to move through the main story and level up. This allows you to the freedom of turning down quests you dont think would be fun or a waste of time. Or it lets you focus your efforts in a few places and save the other quests for another play through. This really lengthens the replay value of the game. Really the only thing that prevents this game from being as good as or better than skyrim is the absolute zero mod support. Unlike games that don't fully support modding, Amalur simply locks it out without heavy hacking. In that regard the game has no longevity like Skyrim. Which brings me to one problem: the game is buggy and the company that made it has gone bankrupt. There will be no patches to fix anything as even the rights to the game are in arbitration in bankruptcy court. If the game had mod support, players could have patched the bugs, but without it...you have to live with them. Some are more annoying than others but what can you do?
Over all the game is amazing. It really makes me sad to know there will be no sequel as the state of rhode island owns the rights to this title while trying to make up for losses from the bankruptcy. You can google the details on it if you like. The end result is no sequel and no future for Amalur. Its such a good game too... its maddening. It has some quirks and so on, but over all the game is amazing. I can't believe I waited so long to try it. I felt like I missed out. I guess better late than never, right?

I've played this quite a bit, and overall have to say its one of the better free to play experiences out there. It's not pay to win, although you can pay (a lot) to cut down on the grind. It's got lots of funny quirks (some of which are actually really great) such as having to physically move your character in order to pan side to side when prone, the ability to hide in vehicle turrets, attaching AT/health/ammo crates to vehicles for your teammates, whistling to get a ride (or trick a baddie), and a movement system that thankfully seems much less "floaty" than it did in beta but still can cause "bunnyhop syndrome".
Overall, I'd recommend this game for a casual FPS game that's got good teamwork, a fairly decent environment for a multiplayer game, and an approachable learning curve. If nothing else it's well worth a download and trying out for 20 hours or so. Also, steam hours don't reflect reality, I played this for several hundred hours/years before the game was placed on Steam.

Tekken 7 is a 3D fighting game, where instead of the regular 2D plane, you will be fighting in a 3D environment. Like all fighting games, your goal is to knockdown an opponent by draining their HP completely, or by draining as much HP as possible before the time runs out. Since the game takes place in a 3D arena, movement in this game will not only cover the conventional move forward and backward, crouching and jumping, but it will also cover side steppings, where you will move around the opponent in a circular motion. This is very crucial for Tekken as you may want to dodge some strings, leaving the opponent open for a counter attack. You can also dash forward and backward, and if you hold forward for a long time, the character will enter a run state. Certain characters also have their own types of sidesteps and dash movement, which are able to be followed up with a certain input or combination of inputs, for example, Kazuya's wave dash. By just standing, holding back or holding down-back, you are able to enter a guard state, though they can only block certain moves. Holding down forward allows you to slowly crouch forward to your opponent, though if you do this input right when a low attack is about to land, it will parry it, opening a combo chance.
Mechanic wise, there are 4 attack buttons, each button corresponding to a limb. Depending on the characters, certain combination of buttons pressed in a quick sequence or together in a combination will produce different things, for example, a string of X-X-Y will yield a quick jab combo string, while X+A will yield a grab. Different moves have different properties, for example a attack that has a high property will hit a standing or jumping opponent, but will completely whiff on crouching opponent. Similarly, attack with mid properties are able to hit both standing and crouching opponents, but are able to be blocked, and finally low attacks hit opponents who are either not blocked or doing a standing blocked, but are blocked by a crouch block, or be completely negated by a low parry. Pretty much each character have their own special parry, other than the universal low parry, that are able to negate an attack with a counter attack of your own. When your HP is lowered up to a certain value, you will be able to access Rage Art, which are practically your super move, and a Rage Drive, which is an enhanced move that yields certain properties.
Story-wise, it basically continues the Mishima feud from the previous Tekken game. Since some characters have some storyline which does not fit into this Mishima feud plot, their story is more of a mini episodes that will cover what they are doing during this period. Other than story mode, the offline content also contains an arcade battle, like the old Tekken games where you fight a series of AI until you reach the final boss, practice mode to practice combos, blocking movement etc, and finally, treasure mode, where you fight AIs continuously until you lose or quit this mode. Everytime you win, you will earn fight money and a free customization item, which you will use to dress up your characters. If you win a special fight or a fight under a special condition, you will get to win more items. There is a VS mode, though its meant to be played offline with another player. Online mode have 3 modes, which are ranked, where you try to rank up in the leaderboard by beating other people, player match where you fight other people without taking into consideration of ranks, and finally tournament mode, where you can gather a group of people to fight each other, tournament style. Among all things, online mode will be the feature you will spend the most time in, followed by practice mode, unless you just like fighting AIs.
One thing great that Tekken 7 did, unlike Street Fighter 5 or Dead or Alive 5, is keyboard mapping. For a keyboard scrub like me, this is a godsend. SF 5 and DoA 5 lack these features suprisingly, and it's really troublesome when the keyboard layout they give causes ghosting, and the only way around it is to use a 3rd party remapping tools, or buy a stick or pad. Another thing it did well is that unlike SF 5, you can play offline mode without any server disconnection error. One thing that irks me about SF 5 is that the game will disconnect you from whatever session you are in, even if you are playing survival mode or story mode or trials. Imagine reaching stage 99 on Hell difficulty in Survival mode, only to have your progress cut off due to server disconnection. Tekken 7 does not suffer from this. You can play treasure mode all the way to Tekken God Prime rank, and if your Internet gets interrupted during that session, you won't lose any fight money or title progress. Online is great when it's smooth, pretty much most of the matches are playable without significant delays or lags. And finally, the customization. This game offers tons of customization. You can dress up characters as well, other characters, for example, Alisa as 2B. The customization is also able to dress a character to the point where you can dress up King as a masked Dwayne Johnson from the Tooth Fairy, along with the fairy wings and tutu. The roster of characters here is pretty huge as well, from returning characters like Jin, Heihachi, Kazuya, all the way to newcomers like Kazumi and god damn Akuma from the SF series.
While majority of the online matches are smooth, sometimes a match while having 5 bars of connection, will drop to 4 or below, causing some lag and jitter. Sometimes disconnects also happens, and fight requests appear to not reach your opponent, despite both parties accepting it. Offline content here, is pretty much very limited. For starters, there's no versus AI mode here, except for pretty much arcade and treasure mode, and those will get stale really quickly. Arcade is only 5 matches, after that its done, as compared to the old arcade mode, which takes about 8 rounds or so. Story mode is, unfortunately, extremely short. You can finish it all in about 2 hours or so. The character story modes, I am not sure should it even be called that, since they are freaking short, some videos, 1 match fights, and another video, and you are done with it. Seriously? Even most of the SF 5 character stories are slightly longer than that (slightly as in about 1-2 minutes longer though). Tournament mode is barely played since its broken as the host can disband the entire tournament by leaving this mode. It's also very hard for beginners like me to get it, since some stuffs are practically hidden and need to be discovered online, for example moves frame data, some hidden follow up moves or movements etc. Moves that are safe, best pokes etc have to be found out on your own or from the game community.
Overall, despite its flaws, its an awesome fighting game. I am getting bodied everywhere by everyone I met, yet I am seriously enjoying it. It's a great game for casual to drop in and punch people in the groin, but to fully understand the game, the road to mastery is really, really long. I would highly recommend it if possible, unless you are into those offline modes completely, then I guess you can give this game a shot, but you may want to try other games like DoA 5, Mortal Kombat or Injustice for so, since their offline contents are much more than Tekken 7 have to offer.

This game is one of the best Medival RPGs even though it's gotten quite dated. Overall, great game that lets you play in many ways and offers great replayability.

Despite it still in beta, there are a lot of glaring problems with the game so far.  Most everyone you'll run across in the game are already experienced and have bought new characters to stomp newbies with.  As far as character design goes, there's very limited customization as opposed to GunZ: The Duel.  Weapons are tied to a single character of which you can only pick one; the other three you have to buy.
Speaking of the characters, the four of them have a unique skill set to each of them.  Ivan is an assassin, equipped with a sword, submachine gun, and sniper rifle; Rena is a gunslinger, who specializes in dual pistols, daggers, and submachine gun like Ivan; Elena, the demolitionist, is equipped with a (better) submachine gun, grenade launcher, and a club; and Max, the shield trooper (aka tank) equipped with a flamethrower, vulcan gun, and shield (duh).  My beef, however, lies with Elena, for one.  Her basic submachine gun, the Typewriter (an obvious reference to the Thompson submachine gun with a drum clip), is way too accurate in comparison to the real-life weapon (the Tommy gun is actually very inaccurate, hence the spray-and-pray tactic used when shooting it).
There appears to be only one main server for all the players, which results in some very nasty lag, especially if the match host  lives on the other side of the globe.  Hopefully, this issue will be resolved with dedicated servers per region.  Another issue I'm worried about is hackers/exploiters.  What drove a lot of legitimate players away from GunZ was hackers, using aim bots, trigger bots, lag switches, etc., to ruin the day of many dedicated players.  Hopefully MAIET will have some sort of anti-cheating system to counter this, since none existed in the original game.
Speaking of the game, the famous exploit "K-Style" has largely been removed in favor of smoother acrobatic animations.  However, the movement animations have been heavily streamlined, as quick movement has been reduced to dashes only.  So far as I have seen, there's no tumbling anymore when equipped with a gun.  I liked the first GunZ for the "gunslinger" style of using a defensive roll while still being able to shoot your weapon.  That's all gone for now (you can still shoot while dashing, but it doesn't look as cool), so I expect some players will want to see those neat diving animations back.
Matchmaking is currently a joke.  If you're new to the game, expect almost all of your matches to be a guarantee that someone who's ten levels above you will be on the opposing team.  They have better weapons, better equipment, and actually know what they're doing when using the acrobatics in the game.  Be prepared to be utterly frustrated in getting stomped by veterans over and over again while scratching your head, wondering where they suddenly appeared from (partially due to the aforementioned lag).
Overall, GunZ 2: The Second Duel has a lot of potential, but for right now, the game is kind of a mess (aside from some grammatical errors in English).  With unfair matchmaking, lag woes, very limited customization, and the potential threat of hackers/exploiters, it may be worth taking a look if you're a fan of the first game, but I'd steer clear of this one until some major updates come out down the road.

Firstly, enemies. There are barely any bosses and a severe lack of mini-bosses of any sort, leaving you to spam click your sword through low level enemies in every dungeon without any real threat to your annoyance. The Graveyard, Riptide, Old Fortress... none have a boss of any sort. Just the same ol' boring low level enemies. Not only that but pretty much every boss could just be taken down by a few bomb throws from across the arena. Very boring.
Secondly, level design. The trailers don't lie: the levels are small and cramped. But alright, you can still do great things with that limitation. Sadly Oceanhorn doesn't. The puzzles can barely be called that, and yes this is coming from a puzzle lover who's crack is a challenge that could take hours to figure out, but holy applesauce this game... There is more than a couple instances where the 'puzzle' is literally a box right next to the switch. The 'increased' difficulty for puzzles in this game just seems to be: add more boxes and switches sitting next to each other.
This game feels like it was made for young children with its 'difficulty'. The only reason I have so much time on this is because it was an easy grab for achievements and it felt like it would be an embarrassment to not have them all with how trivial it is. The amount of time is because of how slow it is to move around, fishing, & the time it takes to skulk about an area murdering all of one type of enemy.
Thirdly, the story. While the main points are fine and dandy... there's a huge problem with everything else that gets one emerged in the game. There are no interesting or fun interactions with any NPC and despite them never doing anything, learning anything about you, knowing anything about what's happening, the game forces an advancement in their generic uninteresting NPC comments as if they are all omniscient. There are promises of a fun side note/reaction to something you've done, like the “Don't break the pots” sign or the “You will never reach Master Level” sign sitting right next to the 'Master Adventurer' but just... nothing. It's all glossed over.
Another example is Neeto. No introduction convo, she doesn't acknowledge you're different than the regular townsfolk, yet when you meet her for the 2nd time suddenly she's waiting on the docks for you to arrive and help her cause you're the only one she can count on. Really..? It goes even further with the fireworks scene with her acting like she's the protagonists girl friend, asking to be taken to see the world, and then the kid gives her the super special thing he just got! Wat... Where did that all come from? Where did any of these relations come from? We never get to see, participate, or develop any of it. This game, in my opinion, is the symbolism of how metal survived since its creation. Metal vs New Wave, Metal vs Grunge, Metal vs Emo Rock, and always, Metal will triumph. You must like Heavy Metal to enjoy this game. The soundtrack is pure metal, the theme and environment is all metal and gothic inspired. The story and dialogue is pretty funny with the main character voiced by and based off of Jack Black. It is an open world game of which you will spend a good amount of time in your car to get around. Side missions are a bit repetitive asking for either defend a group and kill the enemy, signal a mortar, go kill certain beasts, or race this irish fishman. The main mission incorporates multiple missions that are interesting in that it plays out as a tug of war style game where you have to convert spirit piles to your side to build up your fan count which you in turn spend on units and try to take out the enemy stage while protecting your own. I found this concept entertaining, but those who don't may not like the game all that much.
The combat is basically hack and slash, pressing different combinations of your mouse buttons or utilizing guitar solo's for power ups and abilities. There are a decent amount of upgrades and and purchases so you can customize your weapons to some extent and your looks.
Overall it is a very fun playthrough, very little issues past how annoying it can be to do the races and your car gets knocked off course by the racer or because of a tiny bump. The cutscenes are a bit derpy on visuals and voice sync but nothing bad. When the gothic scenary and enemies come in, that for me was the most enjoyable. Would love to see another version of this game, perhaps using techno or any electronic music.
Personal experience score: 9.5/10
Story: 9/10 - It was actually interesting and different considering everything revolves around the heavy metal environment. It wasn't epic but had a good amount of humor.
Sound: 11/10 - Amazing soundtrack from top artists in the heavy metal industry. Cutscenes have some strange sound though that shouldn't be there
Graphics: 7/10 - A bit outdated and basic even for 2013. The cutscenes have some derpy animation and voice out of sync.
Controls: 9/10 - Great overall, driving the car in the races is probably the only fault with the controls as it feels hard to maneuver
Game Length: 5/10 - Short unfortunately, around 20 hours if you really get into the exploration. Otherwise it will be more around 13.

This game is awesome.
A rogue-like platformer. You descend into the depths of the earth, making your way through various themed levels which grow gradually more difficult. Along the way you collect items like bombs, rope, and weapons, kill monsters, rescue puppies in distress, blow stuff up, and DIE A LOT. I have died 312 times so far, without completing the game once.
Like I said, this game is awesome.
PROS
+ Tons of fun. I've played nothing else for the past two or three weeks.
+ Highly challenging. When I started playing, I could barely make it out of the mines. Now I've gone all the way to the end, but I haven't beat it yet. I will, though!
+ Catchy music. Always good. Really sets the tone. You can tell what the theme of the level is by the music.
+ Plays well both single player and multiplayer.
+ Always entertaining. I may be ready to throw my controller across the room because I just made a stupid mistake, but instead I can't help keep playing.
CONS
- None
CONCLUSION
This game may not be drop-dead gorgeous. It may be incredibly difficult. It may be frustrating. But it's one of my favourite games of all time. I will keep coming back to this game, I know. It will never grow old.
FINAL RATING: 7/7

Solid old fashioned RPG fun.
That's the description I keep thinking about all the time I've been playing. In fact I'm having too much fun to admit this game has flaws - which it definitely does but I just don't care. Because there's that itch and it's being thoroughly scratched, and if you need proof just start counting how many times I'm about to use the word fun. ;) And if counting isn't your thing, there is an actual demo (shocking, I know), so ignore me and try the game yourself.

So why is it fun? Being able to mix and match any class you can come up with is fun. Respeccing anytime you feel like it (for a fee) is fun. The loot is good, diverse and stays interesting. Exploration is very much rewarded. And alone these elements mean: "I just found an interesting legendary item in a chest behind a weird crevice that I had no reason to go to, but it's not for my build. Let me respec for a moment and try it out". And that's just fun. :)
This game gets compared to Skyrim a lot (and trashed for that reason), but it does combat, classes and abilities so much better than Skyrim. For starters, the combat is actually entertaining. Gets a bit on the easy side if you hunt down the side quests, but it feels satisfying and enjoyable - neither unnecessarily complex nor simple button mashing. There is no huge enemy diversity, but what there is gets the job done in forcing you to try different tactics. Stealth and ranged are rather disadvantaged systems because of how often enemies mob you, but magic is really well done, sword play and daggers are fun, and some of the more interesting weapons, like the middle-range chakrams and the faeblades, have been given a lot of love. In fact all classes and class mixes work well (stealthy assassins aside), which doesn't happen often enough in RPGs, so feel free to create the weirdest mix you ever came up with.
The crafting systems don't reinvent the wheel but they are both intuitive to use and deep enough: The alchemy is useful and the experimenting process works well, blacksmithing admittedly becomes a bit obsolete on higher levels, and gem crafting is more or less what you'd expect, but still helpful with later game weapons.
The map is big without feeling unmanageable, and there's a lot of game there: many side quests, some with follow ups, much to discover if you just run down a random path in the forest, long main quests and a decent number of mostly smaller dungeons that manage not to be too boring. So length-wise this is a fair value for money proposition, but it's also not so long that it overstays its welcome.
I'm also really enjoying the story, but it won't be for everyone. If you ever read anything by R.A. Salvatore (Drizzt from Forgotten Realms, DemonWars, etc) you will know what to expect: Pulp, generic fantasy, with occasional interesting flashes, decent if not overly original world-building and lore, a "working writer's" kind of prose, but rather enjoyable nonetheless - if you like that kind of stuff. Personally I am loving it, but the disclaimer remains. Just don't expect real choices or fancy dialog trees.
All in all, there's not too much to complain about. There are the occasional problems with weird camera angles, the way maps deal with over-/underpasses can be annoying, and that dispelling rythm mini-game you have to use to unlock some chests was a really bad design idea. But those are just pet peeves. I encountered no weird bugs or crashes, the game runs smoothly on a low to mid range computer, and the UI is workable. Both controller and mouse/keyboard played fine for me, so pick your poison.
So in case you still didn't get my memo, Kindoms of Amalur is simply fun to play. :) If you like traditional crpgs with a bit of an MMO aroma (just without the pesky other humans around), ignore the horrible name and give the demo a try.

Obviously it's "optional" but you'd be fool to think that this doesn't affect the development process (weapon prices are picked by developers, and developers who make money selling extra credits may be tempted to increase the prices a little bit too convince more people to buy extra credids with real cash).

I really wish there was a Meh button for this rating system. As far as a game goes this one is enjoyable and entirely playable. However, there are some glaring weaknesses I want to point out. If you're a veteran to the series and remain on the fence, I hope I can shed some light on this for you. Let me start off by saying that in its entirety, the newest title for Deus Ex isnt ground breaking stuff. All the familiar mechanics are there, hacking is the same, the weapons are the same, 95 percent of the skills you unlock are the same exact skills. Due to an unfortunate event in the beginning of the game your augs end up having taken quite a blow And need to be reset. subsequently, you have to earn the majority of what you lost back. So strap in for doggie paddling even though you know the breast stroke And in honesty the new Augments aren't that impressive.
you have a "dishonored" like ability that behaves like a pseudo-teleport. There's  access to crysis like diamond skin reflecting bullets and absorbing emp. a weaponized mega manish arm cannon, only that it emits a sonic boom that puts people on their♥♥♥♥♥(visions of Aard) with further upgrades it can incapacitate. Furthermore, you have a tazer/blade launcher that can eventually be upgraded to target 4 seperate targets at one time. The odd choice with the aforementioned skill is that both lethal and non lethal options have their seperate development trees despite behaving in the same manner, and they don't use energy but instead ammo. Which seems a further strange choice not to just make it an upgradable weapon and just But that's just one dudes opinion. theres a knifty remote hack,  rather much more behaves as an emp that serves to temporarily disable small countermeasures, such as turrets, cameras, laser motion detectors, and highlights a sweet universal vehical dongle to remotely open any car trunk your heart desires. Last but not least, there's  enhanced focus *cough*bullettime*cough*.
So for the majority of your early to mid game you will indeed be reprogressing your former skills so that you can utilize the new ones in a practical fashion.
And that encapsulates  my only major gripe with this current installment. There's no exciting skill progression in my totally biased opinion.
With that out of the way, the game is worth playing, whether you pick it up on sale or full price is up to you. The storyline and voiceacting is top notch, albiet the animations for said dialogue is... creepy... at times. All cenimatics are unfortunantly rendered in 1080 but the actual meat of the game performed well in 4k.
Would you approach combat loud fast, brutal? cold, Meticulous, and percise? Or any mix in between? Perhaps you don't want to touch a single pixelated soul.
And the enviromentd are designed as Such To accommodate What ever So playstyle You Wish. Because of Deus Ex's "there's more than one way to skin a cat approach",
Whatever you choose, the game experience is rewarding. The environmental designs accommodate all player types with alternative paths and excellent level design.
On higher difficulty setting i was thoroughly immpressed with the enemy AI, Always looking for a flank and trying to pin me down with weapon fire or flush me out into a kill zone with grenades. It forces combat into remaining fluid instead of picking the gankiest corner and and waiting for the enemies to just come trotting up to a shotgun blast.
Instead you'll solely rely on your augs to spring up and away onto the nearest balcony or low hanging beam, shield up and return fire, roll into a cloak, blink on top of your grouped up enemies and come crashing into them with an icarus ground an pound only to mercilessly execute the half conscious remains with all too easy head shots.
Or you can get turned into Swiss cheese from the getgo due to an ever too easy miss-step.
All in all there's tons to explore, a hell a lot of attention to detail, and good ol AJ is about as badass as they come. I'd give it a 7 of 10 and that's only due to an unoriginal skill set, backed up with having to retrace just about everything you accomplished skill wise in the former title.
On a further note because it doesn't effect me, yeah there's in game micro trasactions, you don't have to buy them. and there's no blaring in game ad campaign begging you to do so. So I'm not too sure what people are on about.
I've had a few UI errors, a few frame rate drops, no crashes and only one temporary bug where text wouldn't disappear from the screen that i had to reboot the game for and I couldn't duplicate it. But please tell me when there was a pc launch where you never experienced one of the aforementioned and the game resulted in having zero patches...

If like me you're a Street Fighter refugee looking for a new fighting game to fill that void I can say this game is pretty good.
Give it a try, see if you like 3D or not - personally I found the movement/neutral game clunky and awkward (yes even after learning how to do korean backdashes etc which is easy as pie on a hitbox). That is just my opinion on 3D fighters - they're just not for me.
The netcode works pretty well in this game and online doesn't feel too different to offline, mainly in part due to the built in input delay (which is how fighting games generally deal with ping compensation).
Single player content leaves something to be desired if you're into that kinda thing but really the main thing with fighting games is to hop online and go play with humans. What this game is seriously lacking however is a robust tutorial system of some sort and information regarding frame data, how to back dash cancel etc being built into the game would be much nicer than me having to go online and research this for myself.
This game is pretty well optimised - I tested this on a thin 14in laptop I own with a Skylake 6500U processor with an integrated Intel 520 gpu. Short game with simple mechanics.
A very well defined art direction tells you a beautiful story of an impossible journey of two brothers. I'm always happy to find "universal" games where no language or actual text directions are needed. Always with voice sounds, gestures and common sense, this game will teach you and make you find your way through it's numerous challenges.
It is short, but do not let this decieve you, it last what it has to last. It is beautiful. If you like artistic and out-of-the-box games, this one is just what you need. If you liked Journey (PS3) this somehow falls into the same category (although both games aren't alike). Excellent game! Bravo!

This game keeps a fairly narrow focus, only trying to offer the player a few experiences. But everything it does offer is done perfectly. The story, puzzles, and visuals--the game's heart--are imaginative, beautiful, and enjoyable.
For a game which has no actual dialogue (the characters speak in a Sims-style gibberish), the voice acting pulls all the weight it needs to. The story is rich, leading the two main characters on a journey through varied and unique levels. The relationship between the brothers is emotional and meaningful. The tone varies from silly and whimsical to outright, unapologetically tragic.
The puzzles are intuitive (no insane adventure game logic) without being overly simple (no lazy adventure game logic). The level design allows you to solve puzzles in considerably broad ways using only the tiny amount of controls (one button, plus movement controls). Some of the challenge of the puzzles is just controlling both brothers at the same time. Simply put: the puzzles will be difficult enough to be fun, but not so difficult that you'll be frustrated and have to find a walkthrough.
And visually, this game is just beautiful. There are details worked in to every character animation, every puzzle, and even every distant background. The style is consistent but varied enough that you'll see levels that are worlds different from each other, but which clearly belong is the same world. I'm almost never one to care for visuals, but this game tackles it from the perspective of creating art, not just packing in pixels.
In three words, this game is imaginative, mystical, and gorgeous. My only quibble with the game would be the addition of a cooperative mode, though I can think of a few reasons that the developers decided against it. Truly, play this game. It's such a gem, and it won't disappoint.

It should be obvious with the news buzz the kind of things Take Two (and maybe Rockstar?) pull. Regardless, I'll review the actual game now that the storm has passed.
The game does have a fantastic world that is among my favorite ever crafted. The city, the mountains; it might seem small but it all fits in spots that feel right. The music, both score and licensed, is great. It's also fantastic looking. I have taken so many screen shots of sunsets and rises, the cityscape and the ocean and the wilderness. Initially out in 2013 and in it's current graphical updated release in 2014/15, if you want eyecandy this game has it in spades.
It's been a while since I've played through the story, so I don't remember all that much of it. At its core, that's really what it is: relatively unremarkable and not terribly memorable. But it felt fine and there were plenty of points to make you laugh, and it's worth a play through. Really though, you're getting the game to have a romp in the world.
That's where it excels. You can blow stuff up and have endless firefights through the city streets. Or you can nick a car off an unsuspecting lunch-goer in the middle of a drug-fueled rage. Spend ill-gotten gains on a really fast car and lap the state in less than 15 minutes. (The world's size starts to break down at high speeds, perhaps one of the few things that don't feel quite right.) Perhaps you'll find a bike and take it down the beach. Through the hills. Take it slow and go for a walk from Los Santos to Paleto Bay. The game pours life and charm and the world will absolutely capture you no matter what you decide to do.
So you decide to start an Online character. Your own character, your own story! More content! Friends! Better progression! What could go wrong?
Those things are true, but what's also true is the amount of grinding and back-watching you have to do. Yeah, I enjoy playing online because getting a new car or house feels like you earned it. At least, most of them. So many things are now far above resonable prices and require just a bit too much grinding, keeping you playing just a bit longer and wearing you down to spend some cash. Real cash. Because there are microtransactions, they drive the new content economy, and they suck. Hard. (Disclaimer: I lean on the side of cynicism when it comes to microtransactions. I don't think GTA's is a good implementation of them.) Don't worry, it's not pay-to-win, though. It's hack-to-win.
The back-watching I refer to is the fact that even though I like online for having my own character despite missing several bits and collectables from singleplayer, I only ever play on my own, or with friends. Public sessions are a near guarantee of griefers and other hacks. Efforts to stop this are entirely unsuccessful and result in unbelievable moves like we saw with OpenIV that don't actually fix anything.
So yeah. It's a fun game. I still fondly remember waiting for PC launch, strung out by Rockstar like a dog on a leash. I've certainly got my time out of it. It's also made me even more skeptical about AAA companies like Take Two and take a harder stance on microtransactions where they don't belong. It's an important, good game that everyone's going to remember for a long time, but it's also a damn good example of the pitfalls of money grabbing and other industry issues. Issues that turn a world that's more alive than the best movie or painting into a battleground between the art and business of game-making.

Did you love Sims 1, Sims 2? You'll love Sims 3.
...If you want to pay this much for very little... What made the previous Sims so fun? The excessive options in clothing, furniture, etc. With Sims 3, its a little different. You'll pay 40 for the standard, and being a Sims fan you'll spend another additional 20-40 bucks for an expansion.
What you think you get? A world full of options, diversity and the start of loads of fun.
What you actually get? A hollowed out game. Lacking content compared to the earlier games. The diversity of clothing, furniture, house options, etc, its been minimized. But, EA, being as lovable as they are will give you a chance to add some of that content back.
You want to use this piece of furniture? Yes? Pay extra money.
Oh you want to make use of the different towns in your options menu? Well, better pay some more money.
This particular shirt is featured today, if you want it.. you better pay more money.
Sims 3 will use any and all means neccesary to make you pay more money for stuff that should've been in the game in the first place. You buy the 'locked' stuff with points. These points can only be purchased with real money and there is no way to earn them.
You pay for a pedigree dog, and you get an emaciated mutt.
I love Sims 3, but dont bother buying it unless its on one hell of a sale.

After a decade of gaming, this is the first time I've felt compelled to write a review.
The gameplay is nice, graphics are pretty, story is... enough, I guess.
I'm refunding this game because of the microtransactions in singleplayer mode.
This is a business practice that is an absolute insult to anyone who buys this game at full price. This reminds me of an app game where they make you run out of resources and offer you a $5 bundle to solve all of your problems instead of.... you know, playing the game and managing your resources?
The severety of this issue may not be absolutely game-breaking in this title, but if we let a AAA release get away with these types of practices, it sets the bar so low and opens up this sort of slimy sales tactic to permeate otherwise great titles.
TL;DR - If I'm spending $60, I better be getting a complete title. Stop trying to squeeze 5 bucks out of me in a singleplayer environment. I enjoyed the first level of the game but I can't support this practice.

If people want to pay money to break the game for themselves then let them. Its their experience their potentially ruining.
It has not impacted my experience with the game or should it affect yours just because it's there. In fact, I didn't even know there were microtransactions until I saw all of you complaining. I don't like it either, but if whales (MMO term for people who spend a lot of money on micro transactions whether they are cosmetic, game breaking balance ,etc.) want to do that that's their choice nobody is forcing you to buy these anyway.
Now with that out of the way, I abolustely love Mankind Divided. I am running on a GTX 980 Ti and an i5 6600k and I'm getting mostly 60-70 FPS with my lowest being 54 FPS on mostly maxed settings without MSAA (turn this off it kills performance in all games, not just Deus Ex) and stuff like Contact Hardening Shadows off. The gameplay is much smoother since now you press F for cover instead of Right Click like in Human Revolution.
There are more augmentations and the same previous ones where you can build Adam around non-lethal stealth or lethal guns blazing (I prefer non-lethal stealth).  You are also encouraged to explore around the various areas throughout the game for some nice hidden goodies and there is a lot of hidden paths once you have more Augmentation upgrades. Overall with my 9ish hours into the game, If you love Human Revolution you will love Mankind Divided.

Torchlight II is a lovely, well-crafted game. Its colorful and inviting world is a pleasure to explore. The loot-driven fantasy-themed action role-playing game clickfest hasn't seen much change since the days of Diablo II. Torchlight II doesn't innovate and it doesn't surprise, and the genre may need an infusion of new ideas if it's going to stay vital. But Torchlight II serves up the old, irresistible recipe about as well as it's ever been done.

Not having much experience with point-and-click RPGs, I came into Torchlight II warily and was pleasantly surprised by an immersive and well-polished game. Although the story is not as intense and dark as others, the light atmosphere and cartoony characters are some of its major benefactors. You will get as much out of the RPG-aspect as you are willing to put in.
The characters are designed to be unique in skill-sets, and the dungeons are jam-packed with puzzles and tons of loot to keep you busy for a long time. I've just started the game, and I am already thoroughly enjoying the captivating environments doubled up with fun character customization. Definitely would recommend!

On the game itself:
-Yes, it can get very micromanage-y, but that's what the game is: a life simulator with architecture and interior design thrown in. It's been this way since the development of the first game, when playtesters enjoyed the Sims more than the actual building aspect.

-The lag can get monstrous at times. These spikes tend to last about 10 seconds for me.
On modding:
-There is a very active modding community that releases a lot of well made content.
-If you are running the game with a lot of user-created content, expect to get more lag than usual.
-Be prepared to sift through all the nude mods and band t-shirts.
On the DLC:
-You can have a lot of fun with just the base game.
-I agree that the content is overpriced, which is why I tend to only buy them during a sale.
-The major DLC packs (Pets, Seasons, Etc.) bring hours of new content, options, and possibilities. Most include bug fixes. While their normal prices are still high, they're not as outrageous as people claim.
-The stuff packs are overpriced no matter how you look at it, in my opinion. I recommend staying away from those.
My rating: 7.2/10

I've beaten Jack Black's Variety Hour at least 3 times now. It's easy to do because it's both short and really fun. The main character is Jack Black (as voiced by Jack Black), a Roady who is transported to a magical world modeled after various sub-genres of Metal. When Mr. Black arrives in Metal-land it's controlled by the Hair Metal faction. Without wishing to spoil anything, you eventually have to fight Tim Curry, reprising his role as Dr. Frank N. Furter, who after spending so long in prison on planet Transylvania, has grown cold, hateful, and more into his BDSM than he was when Brad and Janet first met him. It's clear that Meatloaf had an impression on Dr. Furter before his imprisonment. What once was a Wild And Untamed Thing has taken its Rock and Roll roots and twisted it into the Industrial Metal faction that Dr. Frank N. Furter now commands. I don't wish to spoil anything, but you also must fight an army of Death Metal enthusiasts before Jack Black is able to successfully Evil Dead 3 his way out of this magical Metal Land.
The story is OK, like I said it's very Army Of Darkness. The plot is your standard fare as well. The writing, however, is always where Double Fine shines. The dialog is fantastic, even the characters with 3 cutscenes are fleshed out well enough, and half of the fun is how Mr. Black interacts with the world around him. The decent Action/Adventure main game is blended with a mediocre RTS secondary game, but you can tell that all of it was purposefully built to serve the story and it's lovable characters. As Jack Black moves his army of Classic Metal around the game world, you really do yourself a disservice if you don't stop and look for side quests and conversions. As with Double Fine's other excellent Action/Adventure game, you can just stand near other characters and listen in on their conversations. I don't know about any of their games besides Psychonauts and Jack Black's Variety Hour, because I don't like Point And Clicks, but I assume the writing there is, as always, top-notch.

Rain-Slick 4 is an improvement on Rain-Slick 3 in almost every way. Once again, I played through the game on Insane difficulty. Due to the new monster ally mechanic, party member roles are not as rigid, and many battles require a different approach than using the same team composition over and over. While the overall challenge is slightly less than 3, it felt more rewarding to clear a hard encounter through modifying my strategy rather than just retrying and hoping my tank takes more hits; not to mention, there are still plenty of formidable opponents in the optional content.
Aesthetically, the lush landscapes and eccentric creatures of Underhell are far more delightful to behold compared to the streets and buildings of New Arcadia. Along with that, significant upgrades have been given to the music and sound effects, including a couple of really stand-out boss themes, which is excellent because boss themes are the most important aspect in judging a JRPG's quality.
My only criticisms are that, for most of the game, the focus switches between two separate parties with their own monster groups. Equipped items are not shared and money is rather scarce, so having to re-optimize after each swap can be quite irritating. The story is also barely-existent, essentially serving as "an event happened in the previous game and now you have to kill these things and then a final boss so the series can end." There are a few twists, but they are hard to care about because the characters are primarily vehicles for jokes rather than empathy. This was expected, as Penny Arcade has primarily been about comedy, but again it tends to be hit-and-miss. Personally, while many of the outlandish enemy designs and descriptions genuinely entertained me, the dialogue has a prevalence of snark, walls of text, CAPITALIZED SENTENCES WITH NO PUNCTUATION, "hitting stuff is funny," and "we all hate everything" that I can definitely see irritating certain audiences.
Still, this is Zeboyd's best game to date, and indeed, one of the most well-refined JRPGs I've played. An exceptionally good deal at $5 for ~15 hours of game time, and an absolute must for those who would rather think than grind.

It's like a linear version of Elder Scrolls if you've ever played one of them. Fully voiced, lots of lore, decent story, quests occasionally have options to alter the outcome, graphics are crisp, animations are mostly clean, there's detail in level design, lootz, crafting (optional) and a "double layered" level up system (able to tech into multiple trees and choose one passive perk). In a nutshell it's a dungeon crawler in 3rd person instead of top-down.
Perhaps my favorite part about Amalur aside from above is the feeling of not being tethered to the game in order to notice progression. I can play for just 15 minutes and actually accomplish something.
On a minor negative note, Amalur does not give the full freedom other games allow. The player can not jump and the player can not decide to step off a cliff on whim; there are set locations to allow dropping into water or down a cliff-side. Fortunately these limitations do not or hinder gameplay.
Combat is straight forward and fairly rewarding. Left click to continue swinging, instill a pause or hold the click to start a special attack. The player can also mix in magic or swap weapons on the fly to make some interesting combos and setups. Though combat may seem too basic the AI does its job in finding those holes in defenses and can manage to really take a chunk of health. While left clicking is easy, positioning amongst groups of enemies is where the player needs to maintain control even though the AI isn't the smartest.
I would recommend Amalur to anybody who likes leveling up and combining classes. The game actually feels like a dungeon crawler but from a behind the shoulder perspective.
I would also highly recommend downloading the YSA mod which balances the game to make Hard mode actually hard and Normal not such an cakewalk.
Additional Thought: It would be nice if Amalur was coop multiplayer though it does a great job as a singleplayer game. If War in the North mixed with Amalur...

Videogames are in love with themselves. Or rather, they’re in love with the monoliths of gaming history, the games that for many form a mesh of absolutes and ideals which other games continually seek to emulate. Sometimes this leads to the betterment of an idea, a concept first imitated and then refined so that it then becomes synonymous with this new game that did it better. Other times though the ways games so constantly seek to recreate their predecessors never extends beyond rudimentary or reductive replication, seeking success by playing to familiarity and nostalgia. This is where we are met with Oceanhorn: Monster of the Uncharted Seas, a would be Zelda clone that is the gaming equivalent to that off-brand action figure your grandmother mistakenly bought you for Christmas, on the surface indistinguishable from the original but whose inadequacy becomes immediately known once the disingenuous packaging is breached.
Oceanhorn mirrors not only Zelda’s style of play, but its aesthetic and structure. Its art design is inarguably seeking to reflect that of Zelda’s more cartoony iterations, specifically the nautically inclined Wind Waker and Phantom Hourglass. Oceanhorn’s world is bright and colorful, segmented into different islands you access by sailing on those supposedly uncharted seas, with a bouncy demeanor that is unable to distract from the overwhelming feeling of artificiality present in every aspect of Oceanhorn’s design. This isn’t wholly due to Oceanhorn’s status as a poor man’s Zelda, but the result of a world that feels entirely synthetic. The whimsical charm and history always so paramount to Zelda’s world design is entirely absent, replaced with a cold and alienating feeling of obligation. Oceanhorn’s world exists entirely for the sake of housing its plot, a plot which expands and shrinks in whichever way it finds convenient, pouring out backstory when it needs to feel grandiose and then receding into the background when it fails to back up its attempts at magnificence with anything more than words.
Where Zelda constructs its narrative to intersect and enhance its mechanics, Oceanhorn uses it as a crux. Things happen because the game needs you to move to the next dungeon. Plot is only ever employed for the sake of giving context to your actions, but the writing is so stale and inconsistent that it causes the game as a whole to feel even more so the product of recognizable but unofficial parts. Details are always given in terms meant to imply a storied history to this land, with caves and lost princesses being hidden away for thousands of years, and yet within minutes of arriving to these areas you are able to overcome whatever obstacle was standing in the way of the local inhabitants, often by such trivial means as to call into question whether anyone has actually cared even a little about the fate of their world until you arrived. There is an astounding level of pointlessness to Oceanhorn’s plot given how much time it dedicates to selling you on it, to the point I feel it would be better off simply tearing it all out and letting the mechanics speak for themselves.
It seems fair to say Oceanhorn’s main draw isn’t its plot but its mechanical similarity to Zelda, so its true test is in how well it manages to reconstruct a formula that has changed little over the years and yet remains incredibly well regarded and popular. In this Oceanhorn is…fine. It manages to mirror many of Zelda’s most recognizable aspects, from item based navigation puzzles to dungeon layouts and boss designs, but it never loses that feeling of being a cheap imitation. One of Zelda’s biggest strengths is in the multilayered design of its world and dungeons, where puzzles build upon themselves as your means of solving them becomes larger, each knew item bringing with it a host of immediate and secondary applications.
Oceanhorn in comparison is much less intricate in its design, presenting you with new items when it sees fit but never giving you much to do with them. There are puzzles here they are more like speedbumps than roadblocks, tending to hold you up for a moment but ultimately tedious to overcome and often of the same block-pushing variety. The lack of intelligent level and puzzle designs causes Oceanhorn to feel intensely segmented and linear, each dungeon serving to send you on the next but having little for you to actually do while you’re there. Exploration is nearly entirely absent both within levels and in the overworld, the former due to the narrow design of each island, and the later as the boat you use to travel between islands is entirely on rails.
Even as one of the few who enjoyed Wind Waker’s sailing, traveling between islands in Oceanhorn is excruciatingly obnoxious. There is so little to do in these segments that their inclusion is as worthless as the plot attempting to justify it. The ocean itself is tepid and lifeless and the only thing populating it an abundance of trash you need to clear away with your cannon, a task no doubt meant to keep you occupied until you arrive at your destination but only serving to make sailing even more annoying as you are then required to pay attention the whole time you are cruising along lest you bump into a mine someone carelessly left floating around. The monotony of sailing caused me to lose any interest I might have had to return to previous island to pick up a collectible I missed or finish up some of the sidequest objectives I hadn’t gotten around to, though these additions contribute so little to the game that the only real reason to pursue them is for the sake of completion.
Oceanhorn’s only truly alluring aspect is its novelty as the closest PC and mobile players can get to a native Zelda game. With so little like it on these platforms it is tempting to accept and justify Oceanhorn’s middling to bad attempts to replicate Nintendo’s iconic franchise, solely because it’s all we are likely to ever get. But for as hard as it might try, there is no mistaking Oceanhorn as anything but a knock-off, and not a good one at that. Its design is uninspired and meandering, a chore to navigate and a bore to solve. Even excluding comparisons to Zelda proper, Oceanhorn isn’t fun to play, and if it wasn’t for bearing such a striking resemblance to that series I doubt anyone would have paid it much attention in the first place.

The line above sums up the entire experience, sadly.
Oceanhorn is a really nicely presented game - the colourful, stylized graphics and really pleasant music are a highlight in the category of presentation - that brings the Zelda-like style of gameplay to PCs, but is nowhere near good enough to live to the reputation of aforementioned Zelda games. What we get instead is a stroll through several islands, hunt for collectibles and a story that barely does anything.
Let's start with the last on that list - while not overly complicated, and often obvious with its revelations/suggestions, the story of the game seems like an excuse thrown together without much thinking. The motivations and some connections are very sketchy, to the point where they don't get any explanation at all. Add to the fact that there is no real closure, the start and the end of the story feel almost random and... you have something that lives in the background, but that's about it. The big discrepancies in the performance of voice actors don't help - some of them sound like they just couldn't care for a single moment.
Unless we count shoe-horned insinuations of romantic interest and the like, which were as unnecessary and clunkily handed as possible.
Collectible hunt is actually fun, if you are after completing your games 100%, then this is a thing for you. There is plenty of exploring, bombing, jumping and otherwise figuring out how to get to that elusive last blood gem or chest. Coupled with the fact that the labyrinthine, complicated structure of the islands makes it interesting to poke your nose in every corner - it works well.
Which can't be exactly said about the puzzles, as they are divided into two categories, as far as I am concerned - relatively easy ones and those you will frown at because they are timed. Why would the latter be a problem? Because of how some of the control scheme works. The biggest offender here are Trencher Boots. For reasons I cannot fathom, aside from their primary function of jumping gaps (Zelda's ladder basically) they also have a roll function, which doubles the role of the dash the character has from the very beginning. Now, this roll can cause you to fall down from low-height platforms when you would rather jump from one to another, because both of these functions are tied to one button and which goes off is dependant on your position. And when you have a timed puzzle, you want to cut corners.
There are several more control gripes like that - throwing objects can be finicky, sword combat doesn't feel all too nice either. Bow has the same issues as throwing object which means... you will be okay, but sometimes it takes a wild guess whether you can hit something at all, and times when you will waste three arrows because you weren't just precise enough with turning your character around will happen.
All the issues and positives combined, Oceanhorn is... okay. You will probably enjoy yourself, spend 10-20 hours in it, then put back onto the virtual shelf. And forget about it, because what this game lacks the most, is anything that would make it leave a mark on your memories.
I would gladly give this game a neutral review if I could, but as it stands, a thumbs down is in order. Because the game isn't bad, but it is not worth recommending either.

Go into this game knowing that there's no way it's going to be like Gunz 1. Whether thinking it's a good or bad thing is up to you, but it surely is different. I personally think it's bad as the entire meta for the game is to simply knock you down on the ground and spam whatever spammable weapon you have. I'm guilty of doing it as well, and it feels more like a revenge tactic after I've been hit with that same move over and over and over again. It's dirty gameplay on everyone's part, and even though there are moves to recover from a fall they're not nearly as fast or as flexible enough to get out of the way of someone who's about to spritz you with bullets. As far as K-Style goes, you can chain your ground dashes and air dashes together to get to places faster, but that's as far as it goes from what I've been able to discover. You're also going to be dealing with a lot of "broken" characters, in that you're going to be hearing about how every character on the list is somehow broken from other players and they're not going to let you live your kill down for whatever reason. The truth is that they're all fine, but the mechanics of the game are broken. The dashing is far too short, you have to commit to your wallrun, and jumping off walls is broken. Remember in GunZ 1 how you were able to jump sideways from a wall? Can't do that here for some reason. Likewise the melee mechanics are maddening as well, where you have to commit to your attacks before you do anything else, and if you're out in the open and miss a slash in your chain you're pretty much dead. On the opposite end, if you're caught within someone else's melee chain then don't even fight it as you're going to die anyways. A lot of people seem to forget about blocking, but I think that's because blocking isn't as effective against gunfire as it was in the first game. Each character has a different melee weapon and they each have a range in which their blocks are effective agains gunfire, but it represents it through a bar rather than through an area of effect; essentially, it'll tell you that one weapon blocks less than the other, but the weapons are the exact same size so you just have to take the game's word for it. Even then, you can't completely block bullets in the area it does effect, so it's a moot point. Really awesome what the Roosterteeth guys are doing and so far loving the early build of the game. Although it isn't perfect and there are definite improvements that can be made, the potential is through the roof for this game. Initially I got a very bayonetta and KH vibe from the game just from the overall feel too it. It stays true to the hack and slash genre and incorporates a relatively basic attack system. The combat consists of 3 specials, a basic meele attack, and a ranged attack. In the future I hope to see a more combo oriented combat style with the requirements of being able to weave all three together. Another thing they NEED to add is a quicker way to level each special attack. A huge annoyance during my gameplay experience was being unable to level abilities without risking being KO'd. Another thing I would like to touch on with the combat is the grimm. I liked the mix of grimm chosen, each provided a different combat style you needed to recognize and adapt too. However it seemed to easy to dodge each Grimm's special moves, more noticably the Borbatusk and the Ursa. All you would need to do is stop attacking and press SHIFT (dodge) when the Grimm would flash white. In the future adding more difficult timing and a multitude of attacks for each Grimm would keep players on their toes and actually punish them for making mistakes. My final critique on the combat is the lack of teamwork needed to play this game. Although I don't expect it yet from such an early build, the addition of team attacks and combos would not only stay true to the show but make the overall experience more submersive. Currently it boils down to who can secure kills and steal the most XP possible. The leveling system is also very strange. I would personally like them to take a skill tree route rather than the MOBA like leveling they have chosen. It feels extremely akward and doesn't seem to work in a 4 campaign game. Overall the game needs work but for being such an early build the potential for it is extremely exciting! I recommend to buy the game only if you are a fan of Roosterteeth and RWBY. If not then I would wait until more changes and updates are added to help create a full experience. Overall I give it a 6/10 for an early access but the potential is through the roof.

PA'sOtRSPoD4 is the conclusion to the Penny Arcade 16-bit throwback RPG saga. It maintains the same look and gameplay as the previous game in the series. As with the previous game, the battle mechanics are unique and overall decent, plus there are tons of options and strategies to play around with. This time, Instead of having "pins" with special abilities that can be assigned to characters, you now have a zoo's worth of cutesy and/or weird Pokemon-esque monsters to do your bidding. Each monster has its own set of abilities and attacks, so you have no shortage of options to find a play-style and team combination that works for you. The main characters from the previous game all return and the story continues in the same strange and often amusing fashion. All is fine on that front, and the saga comes to a satisfying conclusion. Overall, the game seemed a bit easier than the previous one, but you have the option to change the difficulty at any time, in case you want a steeper challenge or can't get by a particular battle. In summary, this is a worthy conclusion to the series, assuming you have played and enjoyed the previous games. If neither of those things is the case, then I'm not sure I would recommend it unless you are a mega-huge fan of old-school RPGs and Penny Arcade. It's a passable game, but only has niche appeal. For existing fans of the series, I'd give it a solid B or B+, and for non-fans who are into 16-bit RPGs maybe a C or B-.

KINGDOMS OF AMALUR HERE IT COMES THE RECKONING
Kingdoms of Amalur was a surprisingly good fantasy game. It has a fluid and fun combat system. It has a generic but decent storyline. But best of all, it has good side quests. Some of them are even more interesting then the main storyline at times.
What I liked most about Kingdoms of Amalur, personally... was how you could build your character in whatever way you wanted. You were not tied down to any restricted class. But you could cross-class between three different trees. Don't like what you ended up doing? No problem. You can re-spec your character at any time during the game. Gold is no object, as there seems to be an over abundance of it in the game. I finished the game with over 6 million pieces of dosh. If that gives you any idea how much money you can make in this.
The story goes like this. Your character gets killed doing something he or she shouldn't have been. You come back to life by some mysterious means... and you have the ability to control fate. Now it's time for you to go off and save the world. So yeah that's cool and all. We've heard this kind of plot before. But what is best about the game is the journey through it and the quests you undertake throughout. This game has good beefy side quests with rich story and characters. You wont be wasting your time like with a certain other game that just recently came out.. something with Dragons. Dragon Day I think it was called. Anyway, you'll find that there is a ton to do in this game. If you're a nut about completion this'll take you a good 100 + hours to complete. SO clear you calender, ya dig?
Weapons are cool. Each weapon has its own unique style and use. I suggest dicking around with all of them and seeing what you like best. I personally enjoyed the chakrams cause you don't see them much in games, and the daggers because they're the only weapons you can do killmoves with on a sneak attack.
The game has a big flaw however and this is one I don't usually complain about with games.. but it was too easy. At level 20... 40 being the max.. I was nigh invincible. It's too easy! I played on normal difficulty, so I recommend maybe playing on Hard if you're not new to RPG's and third person action games in general.
The DLCs were both great. Teeth of Narnia & Dead Kenan & Kel had a great storyline and plenty of extra and new content. I'd totally recommend picking up the complete package when it's on sale!
So am I missing something? Probably. If you have any questions regarding the game, let me know and i'll answer them post haste.
Finale Verdict: (4.4 out of 5)

Crab Dub is about a lone crab going through three zones before fighting the very dangerous taco that you see on the zone select menu. Though, with a story obviously being apart of the game, instead of having random levels thrown in, nothing is really explained. Sure, there is a paragraph on the store page, but it is not given to us in any way in the game. So it just looks like a taco is weirdly placed on the level select screen and a rhino randomly smoking behind a desk when you do select a level.
So when you get into the game, you are met with three zones to select. Each having their own theme. The first zone will probably be the first one you play, and how confusing it is. Before you go into the game, you have to figure out how to actually get into it. Before you go into the first zone, specifically, you have a couple guns to choose from. Once you do that, there will be a button on the platform your crab is standing on, that when pushed, will let you start the level, instead of rather having a dedicated start button.
This is when you realize, this is not just a platformer, but a mix between a platformer and a point and click. The game never tells you this, only telling you how to jump and move. With how the first level of the first zone looks, it certainly does not show this well as the platform that holds, from what the game’s achievements call it, a magic pill looks close enough to jump to it. Instead you just stay on the platform you started on and click it rather than trying to jump to it thinking the crab needs to pick it up. The next level does do better, with the new information that you need to click, this also shows that there are other objects you need to interact with before you can continue. The rest of the levels are designed as platformers, though there are two things that do come up in these levels. There is another object you need to activate before continuing, but it is not something you click, but something you need to stand on it. Next, there is no cooldown for taking damage. You can be on the same area as something that can hurt you for a small amount of time that it can kill you easily. With health being scarce in the first place, especially during the bosses, I don’t see it as a problem. But as it is now, it only makes this game unfair. There is a double jump, but sometimes it just does not work, which can cause you to die.
The second zone puts you on a rubber duck and dumps you into a cylinder with green liquid. Again, only telling you how to move, but having elements where you have to click objects to survive. Missiles coming in from the side need to be detonated before getting to you, no matter if the cylinder should be cracked before it gets to you, while light blue blocks will keep floating in the liquid if you don’t click on it. Lastly, there is an apple that will bounce off of the cylinder’s walls. Clicking it does nothing, and you will always be hit by it. So how can you make the apple disappear? By clicking the liquid you are floating on to hit the apple, which in turn will lower the liquid level till more is added periodically. The only thing this is missing other than a proper tutorial is checkpoints.
The third, and last, zone is in space. The crab on a dog which can jump infinitely, but be sure to not go past the sparkling border or you will die. This is basically the same as first zone as you need to click on the magic pill to continue. Unless there are other objects you need to click before clicking the magic pill to continue. With pink balls, one that you can click to move and one you can’t that keeps soaring past the screen, will hurt you.
Before each zone ends is a boss. The boss being the same boombox throughout each zone. Depending on the zone you are in, the method to defeating them is different. After depleting the boombox health to 0, a very...weird sequence happens with a gullotine.
With the Boss zone dealing with the taco that you see the whole time. Taking place in space, with a gun in your crabby claws, the boombox constantly going after you, the taco occasionally sending out a circle of bullets, and the pink balls sailing through space threatening you. But having one thing that is different, and does not communicate well. You shoot the magic pill instead of clicking it to continue on to the ending “To Be Continued” ending screen.
Crab Dub is certainly not the worst out there, but that certainly is not a qualifier for telling if a game is good or not. Perhaps if this was handled more rather than stopping at putting in three different levels, Crab Dub could have been better. If more care was put into making this more enjoyable, putting in more than one music track, and an implementation of the story and how to play other than how to move. In contrast, the visuals are pleasing to the eye that it would still hold up if everything else was improved on. If you are an achievement hunter, then you will find this your kind of game to gather more achievements.

It has its fun moments, but this often feels like a jogging simulator. The maps are HUGE and the closest you're able to spawn usually means about three minutes of painfully slow jogging to the destination. And when you finally get somewhat near where you want to be, you'll probably get sniped and have to start over. Also, despite the super slow jogging to the destination, for some reason, there is an additional wait time to respawn (not a super long one, but still). Why? I have no idea.
My second issue is that it's very grindy. But it's not grindy in a fun way like Warframe or Monster Hunter or Diablo are. With the games that do grinding correctly, playing while underequipped is fun because it's still doable and fair (albeit tough). However, in this game, the maps are HUGE (as I mentioned before) so scopes are an essential, yet they take many hours to "earn." I spent most of my time dying from some sniper I couldn't even see or hit if I wanted to. It's not an even playing field when the enemy has the ability to zoom in on you 4x what you can and there's nothing you can do about it. You can earn a scope through lots of gameplay, but do you really want to sit through so many hours of boring running and dying? I played about 4ish hours and I can tell it'll be another 6 at least until I get a basic scope.
Oh, and thirdly, did I mention that this is just for the beginner gun? You can't even get the good guns until tons of grinding. Keep in mind that other players may very well have the good guns that you don't in the meantime.
My fourth problem is that matchmaking also takes a little while. That's understandable since the matches are with so many players though (30 or so I think).
My fifth issue is that the above problems are hightened by the maps often not being in broad daylight. When there is a nighttime map and there are massive dark hills in every direction, it's near impossible to spot a dark-dressed sniper. During the daytime, you stand somewhat of a chance.
I would like to add that I haven't even gotten to the tank or plane stuff yet. I didn't get that far.
What is fun in this game though (for me at least) is the first couple hours when you play in the much, much smaller map (although relative to other games, it could be considered a fairly large map) in the very beginner stage. It's close combat with cool areas to try to use as a defensive position and all your teammates and opponents are on about the same playing field as you in terms of equipment. The close quarters combat (and even the medium range shooting/sniping) is exciting and fun for sure.
Am I going to play this game more? No, I doubt it. Too grindy without much to keep me going other than the hope that one day weeks from now I might be able to compete with the other players. Fun for a little bit though. Adios!
