Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas was an iOS game ported to PC. This game pays homage to the Legend of Zelda series, specifically to Majora's Mask, Windwaker, and A Link to the Past. To me this game felt like it was a love letter to the LoZ series, a game that brings the same feeling with it's gameplay and great music, not on par with LoZ's music but something that you can listen to hours on end without getting annoyed. Though my hours on this version of the game says 2.1 hours, as of writing this review, I have already beaten this game on iOS and it was really fun to play on both versions each with their own good parts and bad parts.
The story for Oceanhorn is fairly straight forward, a big sea monster known as "Oceanhorn" has come to your island and your dad goes to fight against it while you sleep. As you awake you're left alone with your mother's pendant, that acts kind of like a guide, and you're off on your journey to fight against Oceanorn on your little boat, just like in Windwaker.
Though this game doesn't hold your hand and guide you through the game telling you which way to go, you're encouraged to explore around the different islands that you discover and sail to. You'll find interesting inhabitants, vast dungeons and enemies with their own unique design, though still looking very similar to their LoZ counterparts.
With just your sword and shield you'll fight off interesting bosses and solve some puzzles along the way. Now onto the controls, I highly recommend playing this with a controller, you can play with a keyboard just fine it's just gonna take a lil' while to get adjusted. The controls are a little loose but nothing too bad, especially noting that this was an iOS port, and the camera controls are a bit unnecessary since there is no use for it, especially since there is very little movement when you do move it.
The game itself has you fight off rather easy bosses, where you rarely take any damage, solve fairly simple puzzles and collect four elemental powers. Thought the gameplay doesn't have anything that really jumps out at you the islands make up for it with it's rich design making them immersive and best of all fun to explore. Sailing though is a bit of a let down, clicking on where you want to go without any controls, other than the gun that you fire later on in the game, but at least the amazing soundtrack helps pass the time while you sail from one island to another.
Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is a great and fun game to play, though it can be a bit too easy from time to time it's still something that I would recommend for someone to buy. As of writing this review Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is on available for $16.99CAD, about $13-$14 USD, and if you're planning on buying it I would say to wait until it's on sale for $10-$12CAD, $7-$9 USD.

Muddy Heights 2, without question, has attracted a lot of 'meme reviews', short-negative/positive-only reviews, and joke reviews. So I'll write a serious one to help out people who are currently considering to purchase this game.
Muddy Heights 2 is a short 'mini game' where you get to defecate from a rooftop and control your feces around with W/A/S/D/Spacebar. The main goal of the game is just to hit as many people as you can with your feces. You can either directly hit a person in the face or you can leave a slippery trail to tumble them down when they run over it. The more people fell down (or fainted?) caused by your feces, the more points you get. The more goals you achieve, the 'better' your feces will be (e.g. double jump, larger splatter, 'explosive' mode, etc)
The gameplay is very short - you'll get three levels to complete and that's it. For each level, you have certain goals you have to achieve in order to unlock the next level. Each level offers different possible humorous interactions with the environment - called 'secrets'. They will give you a word or a phrase as a clue and you'll have to find out that interaction by yourself. For example,
in the Theme Park level. The entire gameplay hours really depends on how smart you are on finding out those 'secrets' - if you're the type of person that always go after the 100% achievement. If you don't bother finding out all the secrets, you'll obviously finish and get bored of this game much quicker than what it has to offer.
Graphics are low-quality but very funny to see. The panic expression face are hilarious and the terrible animations made it funnier. Some of the interactions can be considered as a - excuse my language - 'WTF moment' and it's really worth it to find them.
As a humor-based game, this game has attracted a lot of gaming YouTuber to try them out - like PewDiePie, JackSepticEye, and Markiplier. I do not recommend you to watch their gameplay before purchasing this game. Spoilers will kill the 'WTF just happened' moments when you play the game. As Muddy Heights 2 is a short game, I personally do not want to miss out the initial natural reaction when I play the game.
Overall, it really depends on you whether this game is worth it or not. I saw a lot of negative reviews saying that this game isn't worth the price - so I took conclusion that not everyone enjoys these kind of games and not everyone find defecating from a rooftop as 'funny'. I personally think this game is worth the price. Even though the gameplay is very short, it gave me good tearful laughs and I enjoy the experience much better rather than watching others play it on YouTube.
As a gamer from an undeveloped country, I understand that not everyone can easily spend any money (even a dollar) on video games. If you do find it's not worth it to purchase Muddy Heights 2 - I highly recommend you to watch the gameplay from YouTube. Everyone deserves a good laugh - maybe Muddy Heights 2's gameplay can make your day.
That's all I have to say about Muddy Heights 2. I hope my review can be useful to you. Thank you for reading!

It's been a while since I last played the first GunZ, I have to say this game has gone a long way evolving from one generation to the next. It was a breeze of fresh air playing this game compared to the first one. Would totally recommend it.

Don't let those screenshots, and the tag of early access fool you! This game isn't going to change much, and it is nothing like those dolled up pictures. You'll be screaming about lag, and yelling hacks in just a few matches! I usually defend the fact games are "Early Access" despite tons of horrible reviews, but after playing this and having played the first, this is what I can "GUESS" will be the most viable review.
Even as an early access game I can guess they don't plan on changing a massive ammount of what I think is wrong with this game. The first game turned into a glitch/hack battle stadium from when I last played, which was probably 3-4years ago, and I have a feeling this is going to be about the same issue. I've played one campain map, but have tried to play 10 or so times. Only once has my ping been bearable enough to complete it. I don't like the fact that if the host is bad he has to manually change the host. Even after going through 2-3hosts the game still seems to have horrible ping so I'm unsure if matches are dedicated server based or not.  There is no real incentive to continue to play as the only way you can play in ranked is you play untill you reach level two. For the whole time i've played I've only reached level 6 probably would be at level 7 if I didn't try two other characters. So far the only way to obtain ingame money seems to be from leveling up or gaining achievements, meaning if someone is more interested in a new weapon they would be spending time trying to get an achievement rather than actually playing. Also the fact that leveling up and getting an achievement in one match means you will only get 2,000 of the ingame cash. A new weapon costs 15,000. So you could afford one fairly early, and maybe a second one around level 10. If you didn't want to try out a new character, which costs 10,000. So having 1 new weapon is more expensive than a new character, 3 new weapons, 2new skills, and a whole new skill tree. Through levels you also obtain crystal which 7 of get you a temporary weapon. If I had to guess you could also get money and crystals from ranked matches but like I mentioned you have to reach level 20 first. I would guess the equivilent of playing 100+ matches of normal.
The movement feels slow and clunky, even with a fast character. The guns feel like they are shooting everywhere but where you aim, and the Lag causes your shots to go through almost everyone unless you learn each persons personal lag based hitbox to aim infront of them for. The guns in the store are less powerful than the ones you can get from the premium crystal vendor, meaning people who achievement hunt are going to be more powerful, and if they add crystals to the store then the game will turn into pay to win. So in short I personally believe this game should have never had the chance to be put on steam. It should have stayed in the secluded corner of the net where people can play it and pretend they don't like they did with gunz 1. This is going to suck in tons of younger players, hackers, glitchers, and people who enjoy graphics/looking cool over gameplay.

Spelunky is the kind of game that keeps you on your toes. After dozens of times of dying to a miscalculated jump, a spike trap or just falling to the void, it keeps training you to do better. It took me ~200 tries to finally finish the game for the first time, but when I did, I truly felt accomplished.
It's a game that's easy to learn, but hard to master, and that's why I keep coming back to it. This isn't the type of game that takes the whole afternoon to play; most likely, you'll play it in small intervals, get♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥at the dumb reason you died, take a break and come back to it. Also, because of the random layout of the maps, each subsequent run will be different, which will ensure that you won't know the levels by heart, or some other cheap way to cheat yourself to victory. Each time you win or even get close to winning, it's all thanks to your skill and nothing else.
Even in my time playing this, I've never managed to finish it on "expert"; that is, by making it through the extra level in the very end. Even still, I keep coming back to it, which speaks volumes on how addicting the game is. I recommend this game to anyone who likes challenging platformers.

TL;DR – Great world and soundtrack, average gameplay and story. It's easy to look past the game’s issues and still have a good time.
Like most Tim Schaefer games, Brutal Legend is unique. It is completely focused on heavy metal and the subculture that accompanies the game. What amazes me is that the team at Double Fine created this game as a love letter to a genre that is rather obscure (to some), while also allowing outsiders to easily be drawn in and understand what is happening.
I’m not a metalhead. My taste in music leans more towards punk and hardcore. All I knew about metal before going in was the generic stuff that pretty much everyone else knows already. As somewhat of an outsider, I was immediately drawn in to the world and was able to understand with relative ease what the game was doing and referring to. The game brings you in to this world where the heavy metal subculture reigns supreme, and the player is able to instantly feel at home, even if he is familiar with it.

Another facet of the game that I loved was the game’s treatment of the game’s protagonist, Eddie (voiced by the amazing Jack Black, who is a perfect fit for this role), and how he is a roadie. Eddie is able to shred balls on a guitar and build a stage out of anything, but knows that his job is not out on the frontlines. He is always willing to stand back in the shadows and work as someone else gets the glory. It shows an understanding on Double Fine’s part of how bands work. All of the references Double Fine makes to the band culture and heavy metal never feel forced. They get all of these little bits just right. The player is able to tell that the developers understand heavy metal, but do not try to force it. This is the game’s greatest strength, in my opinion, and something that is extremely difficult to pull off effectively. The game is enjoyable from start to finish because the player never rolls his eyes and thinks “you’re trying too hard.”
With all of this in mind, it better have a soundtrack that is able to back everything else up. Thankfully, it does. Double Fine has amassed a collection of songs from well-known metal bands such as Judas Priest, Motorhead, and Black Sabbath mixed with songs from smaller, independent metal bands. The soundtrack always has something awesome pumping into your ears as you slay demons. Have you ever fought a final boss as Judas Priest blasts through your speakers? It just feels… right. As I mentioned before, I am not a metalhead by any stretch of the word, but this game got me to check out some of the bands on the soundtrack and I actually really like them (Brocas Helm, Iced Earth and In Flames being a few of my favorites). Now I wish more games had metal soundtracks because of how well the music compliments everything that happens in-game. My only complaint (and this is fairly minor) is that the song changes every time you do something in the game world (find certain collectables, die, get too far away from your car etc). I almost never heard a song all the way through.
***It is important to note, however, that if you are one of those people who recoil at the sound of metal and have some kind of argument along the lines of “it’s screamo!” or “it’s just a bunch of noise with some guy yelling” then this game is clearly NOT for you. Before you go into this game, you must at least have an open mind about metal.
Ok, all of that is well and good, but how does is play? Well, the answer is…average. The combat works, but it’s not super entertaining. It doesn’t flow very well. There are different moves you can do by inputting different button combinations, but they don’t lead into each other. I would have preferred a system similar to the Batman Arkham series. At least in those titles, the combat flows seamlessly and you can bounce between multiple enemies with ease. Brutal Legend requires you to focus on one enemy at a time, but oftentimes throws 4 or 5 at you at once. This can be frustrating, as you cannot do anything to attack any of the other enemies if they swarm you.
Another huge part of this game is the driving, which I felt was a bit clunky. It felt like a minigame that was added in as a fun thing to do on the side, not a key part of the gameplay. The control was not as tight as it should have been, and it can be difficult to line your car up for a jump if you are not given a small runway leading up to it.
The game’s story is also nothing special. It does make an effort to draw you in and invest you emotionally in the story with the death and/or betrayal of a few key characters, but it never quite worked for me. I never got super attached to those characters to begin with. When the game begins, Eddie is transported to this new world and immediately the “good guys” take a liking to him. There is no development of his friendship with these characters, and I did not feel any connection with them as a result.
When reading other critics reviews of this game, you will almost inevitably see mention of the real time strategy elements in this game. At first, I didn’t mind them because they were kind of fun. This all changed once I reached the final 2 missions, however. There is a sudden difficulty spike at the end that blindsided me. To my eternal shame, I had to look up a guide online on how to beat the penultimate mission. The battles until that point are relatively easy, but those final two missions completely changed how I felt about it. The game probably would have been better off without it, anyway. It doesn’t really fit in with the theme. The RTS elements aren’t introduced until midway through the game, and the sudden shift makes no sense when the game has been a brawler the whole time. Furthermore, you have this badass axe and guitar on your back that deal damage to enemies. I wanted to be in the fight slaying my enemies with the powers of rock, not directing the battle and ordering units around.
Overall, this game has tons of charm and can win you over fairly easily. It’s dedicated to something that very few other games have touched on, and none in a manner so focused like this. With all of that in mind, it becomes very easy to look past some of the game’s more minor flaws and still have a great time with this game.

Crab Dub is a 2D platformer with 3 different zones that all have a boss at the end. It's not very long and unfortunately it's not very good either.
Zone 1 lets you choose a weapon before you start - once you do, you play a bunch of levels where your goal is to click the object at the end. You can click on some other objects like hearts/bubbles and sometimes you need to click on another object before you can finish. These levels are decent but the controls aren't that great - you need to be clicking in the middle of an object for it to count and the double jump can feel unresponsive.
The second zone was my favourite as it plays more like a shooter. You have to survive in a tube that slowly fills up and click blocks and missiles before they hit you. The only time I have ever given a review on a game that was in Beta is when I know without a shadow of a doubt the game is going to fail. This could possibly be the exception. Once the servers are optimized and people aren't forced to play this FPS at 250+ ping (Seriously, this is unacceptable), the game will appeal to a much larger audience.  I was one of the few who played GunZ when it first came out and one of the many to stay with it until it became nothing more than a hackfest.
HOWEVER, I am still very concerned for the success of singleplayer campaign. In Campaign, 2 solid strikes from a melee unit and you're dead. Resurrection tokens cost money and there is no other way to purchase them, something that turns off a lot of players and is going to cost GunZ 2 in the long run in terms of playerbase.
The game has had a much needed change in the control scheme meaning that you won't have to worry about getting wrecked by people taking advantage of running on every surface imaginable as if gravity doesn't exist to gain an advantage over another player. Wall-running in multiplayer is kept to a logical minimum and isn't a game breaker. At the same time, I feel as if a cover system is in order as it is possible to die while trying to hide. EIther that or they need to reduce the amount of damage sustained fire can do to you.
Some guns also have a certain unfairness to them at certain points. For example, at close range the falemthrower demolishes everything. If someone happens to turn the corner while using a flamethrower into a tiny room, those in the room have little to no chance to survive. If people are forced down a tiny hallway, Rena's pistols when using her right click does a TON of damage to enemies who cannot strafe out of the way. Hopefully when they add more classes this will be more evened out, only time will tell.
TL;DR: This game will either be overhauled and massively added on to or it's going to fail in the eyes of the majority. I have never been wrong when I've made a statement similar to this, but I REALLY BADLY want this game to succeed.
MAIET, please, for the love of god, do something before it's too late.

The first thing that you'll notice about this game is that there's no real spoken dialogue. I mean the characters do make sounds and seem to have some verbal exchanges but it's more like Simlish. If The Sims has taught us anything in the last 20ish years though is that you don't need to understand the language to understand a story. This is actually the biggest lesson I'm reminded of as I live somewhere where I don't understand what 90% of the people around me are saying on a daily basis, but I digress.
Brothers features a beautiful rustic fantasy atmospheric adventure almost as if it was straight out of a fairy tale. You and your brother go on a journey across the land to find a tree that could save your dying father's life. Despite it being primarily about our two main characters and their journey you get to meet a lot of different inhabitants that help you along the way. Also you see the relationship and personalities between the younger and older brother in how they interact with each other and those they meet.
You'll find both have skills that move the game along. As we all know the older brother excels in strength you find out early on that the little brother also has some advantages due to his size and pulls just as much as weight as his counterpart.
Somewhere along the way though you'll find out that despite the cheery magical surroundings that the fairy tale aspect might be more ancient fairy tales where things don't always work out the way you expect it would and not the Disney type where people live happily ever after. That however, makes this game all the more compelling as at some point I was playing through tears. This isn't too much a spoiler but I think when a game can elicit emotional responses without saying a word that speaks volumes of the story and characters.
I was sad when my adventure finally came to an end but I felt satisfied and a real sense of growth in the characters without any leveling up system or super powers. Overall you have great graphics, a touching story with endearing characters. It was a pleasure to play, even with the sometimes unfamiliar controller mechanics where you're using each side to move both brothers simultaneously. I wholeheartedly recommend this game as one everyone should experience.

"Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" recounts the story of two brothers whose mother has passed away, on their journey to save their dying father. And it does so in a beautiful and sometimes surprisingly dark way.
Brothers owes much of its magic to the wordless storytelling that plays to your emotions, perhaps more than an old fashioned narrative could, accompanied by a soft background music. Not even the few glaring glitches* or the simple graphics (the settings are breathtaking nonetheless, even if the characters aren't) can hinder the game experience.
While the controls may freak you out in the beginning, learning to move and play both characters simultaneously will eventually come easier as you practice some hand coordination. I must say I didn't feel like this game *required* a controller, although I can see how it could make for better gameplay.
There was no boring moment - although I must admit there were times so troublesome and frustrating that I contemplated Alt+F4ing the whole thing (only for a brief second). It was the proximity with the young brothers and their quest, and the will to see them through this painful and exciting journey that kept me going until the very end, by which I dried off a tear and gathered what pieces I could of my just broken heart.

tl;dr: How to not make a fighting game in 2017. Not remotely worth the full price.
Read the full thing if you want to understand why you should not repeat my mistake of giving the devs a lot of money for this... thing.
To get this out of the way first:
This is Tekken, and if you always liked Tekken, you will like the combat in this one.
The controls are smooth and all the gamepads I tested worked well. And I heard some weirdos actually play this with keyboard. Okay... well, there you go, many input options!
The graphics are pretty good as well.
And Bob is in. I like Bob!
But this is 2017, and having only the very least possible content (1vs1 or tournament) in a fighting game is simply not enough when asking for this price.
Story mode? An utter joke. I'm not even as much disappointed as I am weirded out by it. Do you remember the nice mode in Tekken 6 (I think?) where you would get a playable story for each character with intro and outro video and some snippets in-between? In Tekken 7, you get some text, then one (!!!!!) easy fight per character, then a totally lame outro video and some more text. That's it.
And the main story has you playing through it with a fixed character in each level. When you thought you just had some moves down, there comes the next character. By the end of the story, things just become way too hard for any beginner, even with the "easy" moves. This is not a campaign that teaches a beginner how to play, it just teaches you how to be frustrated.
Oh... the "story" itself... I won't spoil it, it's just hilariously bad.
Please, compare this pile of junk mode to what games like Soul Calibur offered MANY YEARS AGO. A long story mode with varied fights & opponents, adjusted for each character, with decisions that branch it out for replayability. I won't even start comparing it with Injustice or the beautiful BlazBlue.
The only other things you can do in single player are practice (well, duh!), a boring and much too short arcade mode, and "treasure battle", which is basically fight after fight after fight, each giving some rewards (customization items mostly), until you decide you had enough. That's it! No dungeon-crawl-mode like in Mortal Kombat, no bowling, no other silly stuff. Just nothing.
And now to get to the meat of it all, the online mode:
Boy, oh boy... now THIS is disappointing. Ranked and unranked 1vs1, single or double elimination tournament. That's it.
No kind of co-op, no kind of team vs team, nothing except the very bare bones of a fighting game. Now, if anyone feels like whining "this isn't Tag Tournament!": Who cares? Get with the times! There is no technical or logical reason to keep that separation of Tag Tournament and "normal" Tekken. Especially in the face of a lot of competitors that offer so much more.
The online content is simply not enough.
And to make matters worse, there is no cross-play between PC and consoles, so good luck finding anyone to play tournaments with. I usually wait 10+ minutes. Ranked matches can be found relatively quickly.
Again, if someone wants to point out that this is a licensing issue: A great deal of other games manage to have cross-play at least with one console without any problem at all. This is not a valid reason, just mere incompetence on the dev side.
To make matters EVEN worse, tournaments are a technical and design desaster.
Instead of having the tournaments hosted on a server, a single player becomes the host (the one who opened the game). If this host leaves (rage quit or tech problems or just plain randomness), the tournament is off. No host migration.
You read right. Not only did they put the hosting on the player's shoulder (which is a joke, really, servers are cheap and I could code you a hosting app in a month of work), no, they also did not implement the bare minimum of host migration. I don't even...
Besides, if any player leaves DURING the tournament (again, rage-quit, it's just a sad fact of fighting games), the price money DROPS FOR THE REMAINING PLAYERS. The leaving player isn't punished at all (except not getting any money), yet the remaining ones are by getting less money.
I can hear your jaw dropping to the floor.
I can see you flipping the calendar pages to make sure this is really 2017.
I could go on and on and on, but the point is that this is a game that feels like it came about 10 years too late, ancient tech included (except the graphics, which are great).
Good at its core, but that's just not enough at full price when competing with the likes of Injustice 2 (which offers so much more than Tekken 7 it's not even funny).
Back to the drawing board, Bandai Namco.
If this series is to survive (and I sure want it to), you have to improve. A lot.

Brütal Legend is a typical Double Fine game in a sense that it picks a specific game design trope and tries to do something new with it. What we have here is a take on a GTA-style open-world game with RTS (sic!) elements. Except that the whole shindig is completely metal. I mean, just ponder the OST and the cast. Hell yeah, you are seeing it right, they did get Tim Curry, Lemmy Kilmister, Ozzy Osbourne and the rest. And you know what the ultimate move of the protagonist is? He brings down a burning zeppelin on his foes. So, to reiterate - completely metal.
Most of all, if you are a fan of Jack Black - then this is definitely a game for you. Otherwise you might not enjoy it so much, since the absurd and often childish humour of Tenacious D is not for everyone.
The game is solid. Lots of racing, lots of battling with a bit of unit micro-management, which seems like a mix of Overlord, C&C: Renegade and Giants: Citizen Kabuto mechanics. Some of the special attacks, namely the zeppelin summoning, reminded me of an old Shiny game called Armed and Dangerous. Plenty of awesome music. The plot is pretty standard, but the game does have a feel of the first Overlord game, since the lore is both familiar and original, sporting wild turns and twists on an overall common terrain. Even if you won't get the game do check out the lore. The video is called "The legends of Brütal Legend" and is epic (be forwarned that the last three legends contain major spoilers).
It shows that the game was designed with the intention of being marketed for consoles, but I didn't mind it that much, wasn't a bad port at all unlikely these new games.
Overall - the game is fun. It is well designed and is a good take on the all too familiar concept. Even though some of the elements don't work out to be stellar, in the end they still manage to deliver, as is often the case with the Double Fine games. Oh, and it is completely metal.
PS: I also feel obliged to give credit where credit is due. From a design point point of view this game has one of the best tutorials ever conceived, as in, you don't even notice that there is one. In a sense, the game essentially being a roadie-simulator, the tutorial here is the ultimate roadie. To quote the protagonist: "A good roadie stays out of the spotlight. If he's doing his job right, you don't even know he's there. Once in a while he might step on stage just to fix a problem, to set something right. But then, before you even realize he was there or what he did, he's gone".

Being a fan of the RWBY-series I was all hyped when I found out it would get its own game on Steam.
It didn't help with the trailer of the game, which made me look almost every day for updates about Early Access!
Finally it came out and I didn't even care about the costs, I just wanted the bloody game. And I was not disappointed. Being in Early Access stage I figured it would lack a lot of content and have several flaws, but just the little that was already done made me quickly recommend it to others. I love playing as Ruby, especially since she's my favorite character. Even more do I love to see places that I recognize and figuring out ways to handle challenging enemies like the bearlike Grimm (it's probably the deadliest one since I just can't interrupt its attacks).
The characters in this game varies in difficulty, which again varies from player to player. I've heard others say that Blake and Weiss are easy to handle, while Yang and Ruby are harder, while I have the opposite opinion. The skill-tree for each character is nice as it gives each player the opportunity to play in their styles. An example is for instance that I love the Crescentos-ability as it hits everyone around me and I'm quite good at entering a massive horde, activate Crescentos and then get some distance between me and the remaining Grimm, just to repeat it until a few are left standing, easy to take out.
What I miss is more ways to play the game. Currently it's pretty much straight forward and gets boring over time. And treasures and XP-boosts are always in the same places, meaning you can't get much excitement of "treasure hunting" and try to find the stuff before your companions, as everyone who's found the stuff before knows pretty much where it is.
As the game is still under development, one cannot really complain about the lack of content, only about the quality of the existing content. This is why I feel it is wrong to say that this game gets boring because it is short and repeatively. However I do hope that this game will give the player more variety in the future, perhaps even several game modes like participation in the Vytal Festival, missions with a separate team (like JNPR) and perhaps a social platform where one can explore the cities and do other stuff peacefully (or violently if you're of that type. Though I doubt it will happen in this game, it would be fun if people could create their own characters and form their own teams one day, for instance in a ranked contest or something.
Now enough of my crazy ideas, in overall I would give this a 7/10 as it still needs to work on some things to be one of the more "perfect" games.

This game is a zelda-clone, in particular a windwaker/phantom hourglass clone. However, it's a much shorter and smaller game. The gameplay and graphics are pretty decent, but the story, characters, and puzzles are relatively lackluster. Some of my favorite things about windwaker were the large, mostly open world to explore, the quirky characters and their accompanying side-quests, and the variety of items to use. However, those aspects were not really present in this game.
The sailing in this game is very boring to me. You're on a track to whichever island you choose as your destination and then there are a few obstacles you get to shoot in the 30 seconds or less it takes you to get to another island. No sunken treasures, outposts, or islands to discover(you just hear about them from other people and then go from point A to point B). The characters are not terribly memorable at all, although I did enjoy the designs of the rito and zora clones (owlbros and gillfolk). The only real items you get are bombs, arrows, and the ability to jump. There is also magic, but I think it could've been used more for the puzzles and bosses.
The story is about as cliche as it gets, but this time you're helping your dad instead of a princess.
That said, the quality is really nice for an indie game. The music is solid, but falls short of the glory of zelda soundtracks. The art is pretty and while the environments are blocky like in phantom hourglass, they're still made to look relatively natural. The combat works nicely and there are a fair number of enemies that you can't mindlessly hack and slash without first getting behind them or breaking their guard somehow. I'd recommend this for people who really like Zelda games, but expect a game about a third (or less) as long and half as good.

The short of it is that if you greatly enjoyed The Legend of Zelda: Wind Waker(or games like it), and you have a ton of free time on your hands, than you should give this game a chance. Otherwise, if you didn't, don't have that much time, or have access to Wind Waker, than you are better off skipping this game (and just playing Wind Waker instead).
The long of it is that this game is a mediocre adventure game with some charming elements to it, but lacks polish. Which is very disappointing since it is easy to see how this game could have been much better, had they just done a little bit more.  The lack of polish in this game is shown in nearly every part of it, but the two that I think best display it are these.
First, the game has a problem with visual cues, or to be more exact, it sometimes doesn't display any, or displays the wrong ones.  This happens at several places throughout the game, for example, sometimes there are floor tiles in a object moving puzzle section that will use the same texture as the border tiles, even though, you can slide things onto them. Not only is this confusing, but it is also very frustrating, since the solution ends up being very simple.  This visual inconsistence is bizarre, since at times it seems like it was done intentional. Like they wonder why no one else does this kind of thing (using the same texture for both a valid and invalid movement space) before, and they figure that they would.  Also, there a part in the game where the player run across a spiked gate. Not only does this looks goofy, but it doesn't make sense, since throughout the game spikes are used as a hazard.  Except in this one case, where it is the intended path.  These visual cue issues don't break the game, but they do happen enough to be a problem, which is disappointing, since they seem like they would be easy to fix.
Second, most of the game's puzzles, aren't challenging and feel meaningless, since they are just one step. For example, some time you'll run into a barred gateway, and to get past this gateway, all you have to do is use a switch. And most of the time the switch itself is within 20 feet of the gateway with nothing blocking you from using it. Other times you'll run into a pathway that splits into 2. Down one path is a locked door, and down the other is the key for that locked door. It is this simplistic design that makes most of the game's content feel shallow. There are no a-ha moments, no sense of achievement, and really nothing remarkable about running into a puzzle and then spending 5 seconds to get through it. In the end it feels like they have all the pieces that are used to make a puzzle, but missed the point of why gamers like to solve them.
Overall Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is a mediocre adventure game. It can be fun at times, but it usually isn't. The game has a decent foundation, but it execution of those ideas is lacking.  The game as is, isn't worth it, but I found its potential to be interesting.

"Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons" recounts the story of two brothers whose mother has passed away, on their journey to save their dying father. And it does so in a beautiful and sometimes surprisingly dark way.
Brothers owes much of its magic to the wordless storytelling that plays to your emotions, perhaps more than an old fashioned narrative could, accompanied by a soft background music. Not even the few glaring glitches* or the simple graphics (the settings are breathtaking nonetheless, even if the characters aren't) can hinder the game experience.
While the controls may freak you out in the beginning, learning to move and play both characters simultaneously will eventually come easier as you practice some hand coordination. I must say I didn't feel like this game *required* a controller, although I can see how it could make for better gameplay.
There was no boring moment - although I must admit there were times so troublesome and frustrating that I contemplated Alt+F4ing the whole thing (only for a brief second). It was the proximity with the young brothers and their quest, and the will to see them through this painful and exciting journey that kept me going until the very end, by which I dried off a tear and gathered what pieces I could of my just broken heart.
Beautiful, 8/10.

Blasted Road Terror is the second Steam game from indie developer, Tryzna83.
In Blasted Road Terror you take control of a small convoy of armed vehicles that is tasked with patrolling an area of ghoul-infested wasteland. Exactly how you ended up here, the cause of the wasteland, and the reason for the ghouls is not explained at all, but the game is still in Early Access, so that may all be coming. Even if it's not, you're given enough information to know that you're the good guys, and the ghouls, raiders, and other human scum are the bad guys. And that's all that really matters, right!?
At first glance the graphics in Blasted Road Terror don't look that impressive; they have a fairly zoomed-out top-down pixel-graphic look. But the more you pay attention the more you see. Each vehicle and weapon turret or rider looks different, each upgrade looks different, and they're all animated well, too. There are weather effects and various obstructions when you're out on missions, and the guys walking around the base are well done too. I'm actually very impressed.
There are some cool weapon effects, together with great flames and smoke from damage -- though the explosions look a bit weird, with strange box-like extents -- as well as different times of day, with some reasonably good-looking headlights, though they're not true dynamic lights. As your main vehicle gains abilities through levelling up it changes and starts to look pretty bad♥♥♥♥♥ and the different secondary vehicles you can acquire change as you progress through the game, too. Though they all have the same sort of feel to them, they're all unique and add to the game.
There's an opening cut scene, which is very basic, but sets the scene well enough. The grammar is absolutely terrible, though, both here and in various in-game texts. The game could really use a pass from a professional editor.
The soundtrack includes a number of different tracks, including some aggressive, drum-heavy beats as well as some really rather nice mellow, minimalist sounds when you're back in your base in The Valley. Sound effects are fine; nothing too exciting, but nothing too awful, either. A little bit more 'oomph!' in the explosions wouldn't go astray. There are some voices, but they're limited to unit confirmations, similar to a RTS game. They're reasonably well done; I didn't find any of them annoying enough to turn off.
There are no options whatsoever, but the sounds and music are well balanced and I didn't see any graphical slowdown, even with multiple explosions on screen. It's a bit disappointing that you can't turn off the music independently to the sound effects; though I quite liked the music, it's always good to be able to select your own soundtrack.
When I started up Blasted Road Terror for the first time I immediately thought of Convoy; the setting is obviously similar and the games share a number of gameplay elements. But Blasted Road Terror is not just a Convoy clone.
After the short introductory cut scene, the game proper begins with a battle. These are real time with no tactical pause. You can pause the game, but you can't actually interact with the game while it's paused so it's only useful for when real life intrudes. This can make the game frustrating on occasion, but when you stop thinking how it could be 'better' and instead focus on how to deal with your enemies, you'll realise that it's all part of the challenge, and it's all good fun.
Each combat shows your main vehicle -- your 'MCV' -- in the centre, with up to four supporting vehicles positioned around it. You can scroll the screen forward or backward a little and you can move the MCV directly (and very slowly) left or right off its default path in the middle of the road. Support vehicles are more interactive and are controlled like units in a typical RTS: left click to select and right click to move or attack. Each vehicle has an attack arc that depends on its equipped weapon and abilities. A typical combat involves a set number of enemy vehicles entering the screen from random directions and you positioning your support vehicles to take them out as efficiently as possible.
Each vehicle has hit points, armour, and 'fury', which acts as a shield. There are many different weapon types, which affect each of these values differently, but the basic idea is to reduce the enemy's hit points to zero as quickly as possible while maintaining those of your own vehicles.
Once combat is finished it's off to your safe zone in The Valley. Here you can repair or buy vehicles, weapons, accessories, and upgrades; hire expendable 'hero' vehicles; take on missions; level up your MCV; deal with the three factions in the game; manage your vehicle inventories; and more. The base can be upgraded, too, with resources earned by completing missions, and there's a trade-off between progressing in the game and grinding to gain levels, upgrades, and resources. I'm not sure if there are plans to expand to multiple safe zones or if you'll always be in The Valley.
There are a handful of different mission types, with more becoming available as you advance through the game. You can't always tell whether you'll be able to handle a mission until you try, but as long as you don't overstretch you can always buy replacement vehicles and weapons should the worst occur and not everyone makes it back alive. The game has some rogue-like elements, with random 'loot' and vehicles available each day and a sort of procedural generation at work in the levels, particularly in patrols. I hope further development plans include more of everything, though, because it does become a bit grindy.
The game is still in Early Access and it does feel rough around the edges, but the core of the game is solid and with ongoing work and expansion of some of the 'placeholder' type elements, it should be even better. There are some negatives, but I think many of these will be addressed with time.
The grammar is terrible throughout. Weapon and item bonuses don't change the displayed stats for your vehicles; I don't know if they actually work. You can't see a weapon's firing arc until you equip that weapon in the field; a way to view the arc before purchase would be useful. Vehicle pathing could definitely be better; you may have to intervene if obstacles are between your unit and its targeted position. I also did a mission with two NPC support vehicles tagging along, but they didn't seem to actually do anything; I'm assuming that's not intended.
The interface can also be rather confusing, though there is some advice in the very basic tutorial. The game doesn't give you nearly enough information about vehicle abilities (what does "Kinetic Dmg Mastery" mean, for example?), vehicle classes, or basically any other game component. This makes the learning curve steeper than it should be, but a couple of hours' play should see you getting the gist of most of it, anyway.
Pros:
+ Detailed pixel graphics
+ Plenty of upgrades and unlockables
+ Steam Achievements
Cons:
- Rough around the edges
- Some features need expansion
Blasted Road Terror is currently rough around the edges, but the core gameplay is fun and the infrastructure around it -- factions, unlockables, vehicle types, weapons, items, quests, etc. -- adds plenty of replayability. The game isn't Convoy, though it shares some elements with it, and that's a good thing. Some may find the real-time combat frustrating, and it does make for a challenge on occasion, but as long as you manage your resources and don't overreach, you can recover from even the most crushing defeat.
Blasted Road Terror is a very good game. With a bit more work during EA it should be an excellent one.

(I received this copy for free and do speak with the developer on rare occasions. However, this in no way influenced my decision to leave a review at all.) ( This review is of an unfinished product as well.)
Blasted Road Terror is solid mix of roaming tower defense, RPG and action with rogue-lite elements.
Hire vigilantes or permanantly recruit a team of 4 wasteland warriors to guard your convoy and  track down resources and supplys.
Level up by completing any of the various mission types. (Wasteland Assasination,Wasteland Escort,Wasteland Rescue and many more.)
Use your resources to build upgrades to your convoy, your garage, your medbay, your scout team, repair vehicles and more.
Use your XP to upgrade and add perks to your team.
While on missions you'll need to use your recruits in various ways to protect your main convoy truck. Position or move your team to various spots on and off the road to take down enemy vehicles as swiftly as you can.
Equip your team with a wide variety of weapons and armor.(1 gun and 1 piece of armor per vehicle.)
You'll need to strategize by staying under weight limits, picking the right weapons with differerent firing ranges and damage.
If you lose a vehicle during a mission, it's lost forever and loses any levels gained for that vehicle.
There are various mission difficulties that you'll have to scout for and unlock.
There are a ton of perks, a ton of vehicles, a ton of weapons and armor as well as a ton of mission types.
The graphics are great. The soundtrack is tense.
There's even a little bit of voice acting which is a great addition.
You'll use a mouse and keyboard to control your convoy, there's no controller support as of this moment,
but it really plays best with a mouse and keyboard anyway.
Overall Blasted Road Terror is a great experience and if you like
strategy, grinding, upgrading, blowing stuff up and so much more then I'd highly recommend this game.
Even in its unfinished state, it's well worth the current pricetag and even well beyond IMO.

TL;DR – Great world and soundtrack, average gameplay and story. It's easy to look past the game’s issues and still have a good time.
Like most Tim Schaefer games, Brutal Legend is unique. It is completely focused on heavy metal and the subculture that accompanies the game. What amazes me is that the team at Double Fine created this game as a love letter to a genre that is rather obscure (to some), while also allowing outsiders to easily be drawn in and understand what is happening.
I’m not a metalhead. My taste in music leans more towards punk and hardcore. All I knew about metal before going in was the generic stuff that pretty much everyone else knows already. As somewhat of an outsider, I was immediately drawn in to the world and was able to understand with relative ease what the game was doing and referring to. The game brings you in to this world where the heavy metal subculture reigns supreme, and the player is able to instantly feel at home, even if he is familiar with it.

Another facet of the game that I loved was the game’s treatment of the game’s protagonist, Eddie (voiced by the amazing Jack Black, who is a perfect fit for this role), and how he is a roadie. Eddie is able to shred balls on a guitar and build a stage out of anything, but knows that his job is not out on the frontlines. He is always willing to stand back in the shadows and work as someone else gets the glory. It shows an understanding on Double Fine’s part of how bands work. All of the references Double Fine makes to the band culture and heavy metal never feel forced. They get all of these little bits just right. The player is able to tell that the developers understand heavy metal, but do not try to force it. This is the game’s greatest strength, in my opinion, and something that is extremely difficult to pull off effectively. The game is enjoyable from start to finish because the player never rolls his eyes and thinks “you’re trying too hard.”
With all of this in mind, it better have a soundtrack that is able to back everything else up. Thankfully, it does. Double Fine has amassed a collection of songs from well-known metal bands such as Judas Priest, Motorhead, and Black Sabbath mixed with songs from smaller, independent metal bands. The soundtrack always has something awesome pumping into your ears as you slay demons. Have you ever fought a final boss as Judas Priest blasts through your speakers? It just feels… right. As I mentioned before, I am not a metalhead by any stretch of the word, but this game got me to check out some of the bands on the soundtrack and I actually really like them (Brocas Helm, Iced Earth and In Flames being a few of my favorites). Now I wish more games had metal soundtracks because of how well the music compliments everything that happens in-game. My only complaint (and this is fairly minor) is that the song changes every time you do something in the game world (find certain collectables, die, get too far away from your car etc). I almost never heard a song all the way through.
***It is important to note, however, that if you are one of those people who recoil at the sound of metal and have some kind of argument along the lines of “it’s screamo!” or “it’s just a bunch of noise with some guy yelling” then this game is clearly NOT for you. Before you go into this game, you must at least have an open mind about metal.
Ok, all of that is well and good, but how does is play? Well, the answer is…average. The combat works, but it’s not super entertaining. It doesn’t flow very well. There are different moves you can do by inputting different button combinations, but they don’t lead into each other. I would have preferred a system similar to the Batman Arkham series. At least in those titles, the combat flows seamlessly and you can bounce between multiple enemies with ease. Brutal Legend requires you to focus on one enemy at a time, but oftentimes throws 4 or 5 at you at once. This can be frustrating, as you cannot do anything to attack any of the other enemies if they swarm you.
Another huge part of this game is the driving, which I felt was a bit clunky. It felt like a minigame that was added in as a fun thing to do on the side, not a key part of the gameplay. The control was not as tight as it should have been, and it can be difficult to line your car up for a jump if you are not given a small runway leading up to it.
The game’s story is also nothing special. It does make an effort to draw you in and invest you emotionally in the story with the death and/or betrayal of a few key characters, but it never quite worked for me. I never got super attached to those characters to begin with. When the game begins, Eddie is transported to this new world and immediately the “good guys” take a liking to him. There is no development of his friendship with these characters, and I did not feel any connection with them as a result.
When reading other critics reviews of this game, you will almost inevitably see mention of the real time strategy elements in this game. At first, I didn’t mind them because they were kind of fun. This all changed once I reached the final 2 missions, however. There is a sudden difficulty spike at the end that blindsided me. To my eternal shame, I had to look up a guide online on how to beat the penultimate mission. The battles until that point are relatively easy, but those final two missions completely changed how I felt about it. The game probably would have been better off without it, anyway. It doesn’t really fit in with the theme. The RTS elements aren’t introduced until midway through the game, and the sudden shift makes no sense when the game has been a brawler the whole time. Furthermore, you have this badass axe and guitar on your back that deal damage to enemies. I wanted to be in the fight slaying my enemies with the powers of rock, not directing the battle and ordering units around.
Overall, this game has tons of charm and can win you over fairly easily. It’s dedicated to something that very few other games have touched on, and none in a manner so focused like this. With all of that in mind, it becomes very easy to look past some of the game’s more minor flaws and still have a great time with this game.

A very well made game, with a lot of potential and already great combat. The art style sticks to the show, as does the voice acting (however there is not much of it). The game is about an hour long, give or take, and currently only has one chapter, 2 zones and a handful of enemies. Yet it makes the most of it's limited content and does so very well.
The combat is reminicent to the traditional hack n slash and it feels very nice, but it is somewhat repetitive and half of the combo is useless, depending on the character you're playing, especially Blake. Still there are elements of synergy between the characters, mostly between the AoEs of Ruby/Weiss, Weiss/Yang and Ruby/Yang.
The characters themselves are polished to diffrent degrees. Ruby and Yang defintely have the most polish to them, with more detailed special abilities and normal attacks. Weiss is ok, but her ranged capabilities aren't really working well and Blake all in all being the hardest and least polished character, with a clunky and overly complex moveset. Nothing that can't be fixed though.
I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a good Hack n Slash, however it is to be noted that, at the time of writing this review, the game is in Early Access and by no means finished. The game itself can be enjoyed by fans of the show or just fans of the genre itself. It's easy to pick up and is very fun. However it can get repetitive after a couple hours.
Personally i'd like to see more diversity in the movesets of all characters, including more combos, more special attacks and diffrent perks, tracking on enemies, maybe Combination Attacks with other players? Another thing could be the addition of other characters from the series, Team JNPR and Team SSSN, maybe even the villians like Emerald and Mercury. And a larger amount of enemies, maybe even randomizing what enemies spawn to keep things from getting too repetitive?
All in all a very soild and well made game with a lot of potential and a dedicated team working on it. Defintely the best Early Access game currently available and better than several finished games on Steam in general.

Being a GunZ 1 player on and off for several years I couldn't wait to try GunZ 2. So, when the Beta finally opened for NA... well... I had to wait a few more days.
After the standard launch issues cleared up, I jumped in to see if it would live up to the hype.
First off I was disappointed to see that they had removed customization in favor of four preset classes.


Ivan wields a sniper rifle, katana, and SMG.
Rena duel swords, duel pistols, and SMG.
Elena a baseball bat, assault rifle, and nade launcher.
Max is equipped with a riot shield, mini gun, and flame thrower.
Each character does have a few sets of clothing and weapons to purchase, but it's cosmetic and slight stat variations. At least it means nothing is pay to win at the moment.
The shop does sell a few cosmetic items for real money at the moment.($15 for a hat!)
I picked Ivan and moved on to the lobby, which is your standard shooter lobby other than that(for the moment) there doesn't seem to be a way to select the room you join. You can queue up for 1-3 types of PvP.
-Team Death Match
-Team Elimination- Kill the entire enemy team. First to 5 wins.
-Time Assault- Destroy the enemy teams object within a set time.
or you can do the Co-op campaign.
I picked PvP.
So, now we can talk about combat.
In GunZ 1 I despised K-Style because of how it was implemented. It was basically a glitch that the developers didn't bother to fix. For GunZ 2 I was hoping for a more refined combat system. Something fast and elegant. Something that could match the good parts of K-style and remove the bad.
So did GunZ 2 deliver?
Well, it can be fast. Really fast. Not just movement but TTK is really low. If you get caught in a combo, you're stun-locked and dead.
I personally miss the epic battles from GunZ 1. Two equally skilled players could fight back and forth for minutes.
In GunZ 2 that's replaced by a lot mindless spamming. Blocking is made almost useless by special abilities that characters gain as the level up, meaning that combat in GunZ 2 is roughly the equivalent of Call of Duty with swords.
Despite the disappointment from the combat system, I decided to give the campaign a try. Surprisingly where the games shines. They're actually MMO instance quality missions. There are lots of waves but the require awareness, positioning, weapon and ability management to clear.
Bosses can feature multiple stages and well scripted abilities that require a bit of thought to counter.
I haven't finished the campaign yet but so far it's fun. The downside is there doesn't seem to be any form of reward. I have yet to get a shinny new gun or even a dirty sock. Cash gains from it are also slow in comparison to the PvP modes.
Overall, it's a fun game despite the fact the combat is frustratingly lacking of depth. I really hope they refine it a bit more and try to get a little closer to what I liked about GunZ 1 rather than a third person version of Team Fortress 2. Still, It's free the campaign is pretty cool. Give it a try.

I find it difficult to find an RPG that I can continuously come back to without getting bored of, and I have played Skyrim. In comparison to KoA, Skyrim is similar, but a little less immersive.
The world of KoA is beautiful. The lore and the main story are well-written, and make the playing even more enjoyable. And the combat is fluid, and fun.
Let's judge.
(COMBAT)
The primary and secondary weapon system makes it so much easier to transition from a long-range to close-range weapon, or a slow weapon to a fast, or any sort of pairing one can think of. The different types of weapon (Chakrams, Greatsword, Hammer, Longsword, Daggers, Staves, Scepters, Faeblades, and Bows) provide much entertainment in battle.
No complexity nonsense with the controls. Movements are fluid and there are only 2 buttons. Mashing doesn't always work-- dodging is a necessity, making it less lifeless and more active. I suppose it is a little repetitive, but I find it fun, personally. (I might be wrong.)
Also, the whole "you choose your own fate" idea makes it easy to go down whatever path you want to, whether it be finesse, sorcery, or might. You can even have hybrid combinations.
Cool note: your dodge, if you take the finesse/sorcery route, can be replaced by a short-range teleport, which can later deal poison damage if you teleport through enemies.
(LORE)
You have what I call "lorestones" scattered all over the world. The loading screens give you tidbits, and the cutscenes are, if nothing else, pretty. Dialogue with NPCs allow you to delve deeper into the story if you want to.
I love the whole fantasy-world-in-danger spin.
Also, you are "fateless".  You're bound by nothing at all. And you have an uber-super-cool special kill mode.
(GRAPHICS)
I love games with beautiful graphics. Some pixelated games, too, work well, but KoA is far from pixelated. The faces are smooth, the armor and weapons are pretty, and the world is vivid. Walking through the forests or the swamps or the cities is an immersive experience in itself.
(CRAFTING SYSTEM)
You can salvage items you don't feel like selling for components, which can then be used to forge the weapon of your dreams. Weapon customization at its finest. You can use gems as supplements, and (this is a small thing, but it's great) you can name your carefully crafted weapon, or armor. Name your longsword "Bootybuster" or something. Not that I would.
(THE FINAL VERDICT)

Everything wrong with surgeon simulator can be summed up in a single word: Depth.
Your hand acts like some kind of Flatlander trying desperately to rip out parts he can't see from a three-dimensional patient he can't look at properly while cutting with precision tools he can't grasp. Let's elaborate on that sentence, shall we?
1) Your arm is always in the way.
Movement in this game runs on a two-dimensional plane with mouse hold to descend, and mouse lift to ascend. This is insane. Your arm is the single most detrimental adversary in the game, with small glass beakers obstructing the path between you and your scalpel because Nigel can't be bothered to move his arm a few degrees to the right. Worse yet, pulling out organs is horrifyingly difficult because Nigel won't move his arm upwards, opting to strain his wrist while his arm rests on the patient, a clear oversight that leads to minutes of frustration when trying to tear out stuff that's deep in or at the bottom.
2) You can't see your patient from different angles.
This is crucial when it comes to saving your patient. How are you sure your saw is breaking their bones and not grinding their flesh into bleeding bits? How do you know your scalpel is hitting the right arteries? How can you be sure you've caved in a criminal's skull? Answer: You can't. Not to mention you may have bad depth perception, and will fail to grasp an organ or tool that isn't in your reach.
3) You can't grasp tools properly.
By far the worst part of the game. Moving your arm vertically and moving your wrist are mutually exclusive, which would be okay if your arm didn't retreat back to its default height the moment you let go of the left mouse button. This, in addition to depth perception and weak grasp, means that picking up a single object is a chore and you'll probably pick it up wrong anyway.
Honestly, the game is supposed to be a joke, but I can't laugh when gameplay is frustrating and unrewarding. We would love to play the game properly and kill our patients, get high, electrocute ourselves, jam laser beams into eyeballs, fly in space, stick Uber devices onto hearts, and replace the president's heart with a rock, BUT WE CAN'T ENJOY ANY OF THAT BECAUSE WE CAN'T GRASP ANYTHING PROPERLY.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Disclaimer: I watched the first two RWBY seasons a year ago and liked them. But I would't consider myself a "RWBY-fan".
I just watched the "red"-trailer and thought: "wow, that would make a great hack-and-slash-game.
So, I googled and found out that there was a demo were you basically play the trailer. Now I found out, that the game is actually released and bought it.
The first thing I noticed is, that this game is clearly made for fans of the series. (Or at least for People, who watched it)
You don't get any introduction to the story or the characters (not even an intro movie or anything)
I don't think that this is a bad thing but they should at least mention it in the game description.
(I will not mention the Coop because I didn't try it)
Now the Pros and Cons:
Pros:
-the graphics look nice, even at the lowest available option (also, it's the same graphic-style as the show has)
-Combos feel satisfying
-original voice actors from the series
-each character is unique with own skills and in my opinion, they all have a different difficulty
-the soundtrack is as good as in the show
-MOBA leveling
-you can destroy wood boxes (Half Life 3 confirmed)
and the Cons:
-the probably biggest Con is the Leveldesign. While playing I felt like the developers used mor invisible walls than actual walls. Some areas (especially in the 2 and 3 mission) looked like open world but in the end you still walked through hoses.
-the savepoints... I died around 3 times while my first playthrough, the first time I just respawned in front of the boss arena. But the 2nd and 3rd time I felt like I had to replay half of the level.
-the game was way too easy. But to be honest I don't know if H&S-games have to be easy, because this one is my first.
-some minor bugs: (It´s early access, so I won't include them in my rating)
the two I noticed the most are: 1. sometimes I saw white spheres in the trees and when I moved closer to them the spheres disappeared
2. when I stopped walking my character still has a walking animation for like 1 second
So now the most interesting question:
Would I recommend it?
If you are a fan of the series, Yes, of course you won't regret it
If you are completely new to RWBY, maybe, if you are interested in the universe but best thing would be to wait until the full game releases.
I would rate the game 7/10 atm. But this may change when the full game comes out.
So this was my first game review. I hope it isn't too bad.

Is good gaem. It's funny and I like how it doesn't take itself seriously. You can tell what the entirety of the game is going to be like in the first minutes... or can you? Well, you can definitely guess the ending, which was kind of underwhelming, but it did start to feel like the game's dragging on. I really enjoyed the main character (Jack Black) and some quips others have said here and there (not really fond of the characters themselves though, except for that one sound guy and of course the Killmaster and the guardian of metal). I have two issues with the game: 1. The "moba" kind of gameplay wasn't really my thing, and fighting with your character doesn't seem complex - it's simple, just to carry the story and the world along. 2. The story started to take itself more seriously as time went on, or/and the main character did. It's not a major thing, but the story felt really simple for the majority of the game only to drop some weak "twist" at the end which flew completely over my head. There was a bit of name dropping of characters you never actually interacted with but are just there to provide some background to the story, so I didn't really get it. I guess I'm stupid, or I wasn't paying attention. But to be honest it doesn't matter, since the game FEELS simple and enjoyable at it's own expense, so your own level of involvement in the story shouldn't impact the experience much.

Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning (KoA) had two obstacles from the start: the release date and a last ditch effort desperate to be a major to save 38 Studios.  Releasing at one quarter after Skyrim wasn't nearly long enough for players to be interested in a new RPG IP.  The rest is history.
Imagine if KoA was competing against Darksiders 2 in 2012's 3rd quarter instead.
KoA appears to be a great fusion of many RPGs, taking elements from the likes of Dragon Age, Fallout 3 and New Vegas, Darksiders, but the most obvious would be World of Warcraft.  KoA plays like a single player WoW, a huge game packed with content that you play at your own pace.  Despite the references, KoA executes its own flavors to make itself distinct.  There are many areas that are pretty stellar.
Combat: KoA uses an engaging third person hack and slash format at a speed that keeps the momentum high.  It rewards quick reflexes where you out-position your enemies by dodging and parry perfectly on block to negate any damage before making a reversal.  KoA quickly lets you fight fluidly right from the start, killing enemies in flashy ways, and variations increase further as you invest down your skill tree.  Every combo and spell/abilities rewards Fate, thus it's advised have a mix up of attacks.
Fate is used for a very memorable feature.
Fateshfit: Only useable with a full Fate bar, a mode with you slowing down time and increasing damage output for a short duration.  Killing an enemy during fateshift provides a detailed animation of your hero executing in the most lethal and merciless of ways.  This rush happens during the tutorial; KoA wastes no time to make you feel empowered.
Fateshift is the only mechanic that has a QTE, appearing at the killing blow as a button mash.  Across all games that use QTEs, KoA may be the only one that uses it with any real purpose.  Although optional, completing it rewards you up to 100% exp increase.  It's a prosperous cycle.  Mixing up attacks gets more fate; more fateshifts means more violent deaths; rapid leveling up gives more spells for mix ups.
Class Build:  Your class (Destiny) is based on the amount of points spent in three ability trees: Might, Finesse and Sorcery.  Players aren't restricted to spend only in one tree and resets are infinite.  Properly allocating in multiple skill trees will open up hybrid Destinies, and KoA gives some of the most powerful hybrids since each Destiny offers multiple passive effects that greatly enhance the playstyle.
My two heroes were Finesse/Sorcery and Might/Sorcery.  Hybrids take the best worlds of two (or three) trees and combine into one extremely powerful being because the crucial abilities are located in the mid tier.   Only pure builds could access the top tier abilities, but hybrids are amended by two or more competent mid tier skill trees, leaving no mediocrity in performance.
World of Amalur: Amalur is colourful as it is lively.  Every region has many reasons to explore -it may be loot, dungeons, towns, tales or quests.  You're always entertained.  Each region's beauty plays a different role, there's also an undeniable feeling of wonder when you reach the first city of KoA -like when you reached Stormwind City the very first time in WoW.  There are plenty of breathtaking sights that mesmerize, architecture that's curious, immersion is thick despite now-outdated graphics.  The tension is very apparent when you leave the relative safety of the forest of Dalentarth to the Plains of Erathell, a step closer to the realities of the war front.
Quests: There are many quests in every new region.  Although most quests involve killing, fetching, escorting, talking etc, each side quest is a story of its own.  Aside from reading books, quests are the core engine of storytelling.  Given that all NPCs are voiced, there are plenty of tales to be heard with the voice acting very competent and accurate.  Quests are also the motive to visit a dungeon, so raiding won't feel overbearing.  Faction quests, the best quests in game, serves as grand plot-driven stories with handsome rewards as the story progresses, and there are multiple factions in KoA.
Weapons/Armor Designs:  Aesthetically, nearly all the unique gear looks great.  KoA took a risk at introducing the use of Faeblades and Chakrams.  How many modern RPGs use them?  Which game can make you imitate Illidan or Xena -or both?
DLCs: 2012 was a time where DLCs had campaigns that at least go for 6-10 hours that were rewarding.
KoA easily hits the mark of a fun, huge RPG with hundreds of hours of content.  It doesn't need to be Skyrim because it stands out as its own individual game.  It's obvious how much love and respect was put into it.  However, KoA does come with flaws that holds it back.
Story: The main story is serviceable but unmemorable due to the generic plot of an unknown hero coming back from death to save the world.  The plot does have mystery, but there are loose ends that could evolve into deeper stories, the wonder of potential Amalur has yet to offer, but there won't be a sequel until EA wants to work more on this IP -especially those that ended off on quite a high note.  Look at EA's wisdom with Dungeon Keeper Mobile.  I'm left wanting more after KoA, yet it's a shame the potential won't be realized anytime soon -if ever.
Targeting, Ability Delays: If you're quick then it's often that your reaction time is faster than your hero is capable at switching targets.  Some abilities have too long of a start-up and/or recovery time.  You can't move until the animation is over.  Being unresponsive in the heat of battle outnumbered hampers momentum.  Dodging can only be used twice in succession before a recovery delay kicks in.  There's no point to make fights feel slower.
Game feels Easy: Humanoid enemies are most guilty of this.  Warriors and rogues lack close up aggression; archers lack suppression skills and mobility; mages lack a wide enough variety of attacks to confuse.  Humanoids aren't intimidating unlike some of the wildlife.
Repetition: More often than not, there isn't an unique boss with its own loot table and new strategy needed to kill at a dungeon's end.  With surroundings and enemies you've seen before, dungeons need better motivation.
Limited Player Creation:  For each race and gender, there are only 5 faces you could choose from.  A small choice of hairstyles don't help this.  A cool looking hero is still possible, but KoA's player creation falls short to other RPGs.
Loot: Despite having hundreds of gear, it still needs more end game gear to keep end game farming exciting.
Some things are just awful.

Bag Space: With a game that has hundreds of unique gear the max inventory space -without cheats- is 130.  That's too low.  A stash of 155 slots exists, but at 285 that's not even half the amount of gear KoA provides.  Since quest items can't be deleted, with bugged ones they will be stuck hogging bag slots forever.  When a great appeal to keep playing is to get more loot, it's foolish to have such a limitation.  I used cheats to remedy this.

Crafting: Blacksmith needs more than one design and colour scheme for every tier.  In single player RPGs it's vital that I look good.
The real flaw of Blacksmith is making too overpowered gear.  The two components that destroy any challenge are +X% Damage and +X% Damage Resistance -to all damage types.  Any gear you craft can add one or more of these parts.  Since damage scaling is multiplicative, the math will add up like this with you using +30% Damage parts in your gear: x(1.3^ y).  X is the base damage dealt, Y is the amount of +30% parts.  Your Destiny's passives aren't even calculated yet.  Damage Resistance works the same way.  This makes the other parts obsolete.
Final Verdict: 8/10
KoA's strengths are good enough that it feels great even with its flaws.  Give the KoA: Collection a try when it's on sale at $10, I assure that your time won't feel wasted.
This is a great RPG.  A huge world, great items, and cool art.

Story: 7/10. Can be compelling at times, and bland at other times. It can be a mess with so much going on, and it lacks emotional depth that would normally get you invested in the story.
Visuals & Sound: 7/10: It looks fairly good, but animations tend to feel repetitive after a while. Same goes for weapon and spell effects. It seems a bit uninspired considering how similar it looks to games like World of Warcraft, but if you're okay with that then no issues here. It definitely looks above average. The soundtrack is decent, nothing bad nor is it memorable.
Gameplay: Probably some of the most fun I've had in a combat RPG, ever! The skill progression system and character customisation (combat-based, that is) is spectacular. You can mix and match your character's abilities to range from a regular fighter, to a dirty rogue, to a mystical mage, and everything in between. This definitely has some of the most rewarding combat, level-up, and looting experiences in recent RPG games.
Conclusion: I would buy this game for the gameplay alone. Sure, it doesn't have the most amazing story or unique brand of visuals, but the gameplay value is stunning and will keep you coming back for more. If you enjoy combat-RPGs that give you the freedom to manuever around in combat and rely on your own reflexes and ingenuity to get by, then this is it.
