Deus Ex: Mankind Divided successfully does something with it's design many developers have been attempting for years. I'll use the "Witcher 3" as an example. Often times the sidequest felt much too artificial, especially when you'd visit a board to recieve them. Deus Ex does an exceptional job of creating an organic flow through it's narrative. Side quest are naturally stumbled upon & not forced down your throat. Often times I'd find myself not knowing rather a quest was part of the main story or a side bit untill I looked into my quest log. The downside, is that it's possible & sometimes easy to miss side-quest. The sidequest are the bulk of this game in such a way I wouldn't even call them "side"quest. This isn't a bad thing, as they are all well written, entertaining, & rewarding to the player.

The greatest achievement of Deus Ex: Mankind Divided is the way it goes about tackling the expanse of various paths & options you have to go about completing a task. In many games with systems that have multiple paths forward it often feels as if it's just a choice of, at best, Options 1-5, at worst, Option A or Option B. With Deus Ex: Mankind Divided your freedom feels so much greater. Often you stumble on to ways to advance a mission accidently, or while staking out other task. A mission can be completed through stealth, diplomacy, and force, & often times many combinations of them all. Your play will come down to your mood & for me my enemy. The story & narrative drives your play style, & I believe this is the best way to play Deus Ex: Mankind Divided, letting the narrative drive the gameplay.
At times it seems a bit easy. Even playing on the hardest difficulty. That could very well be the way I'm going about my first playthrough by avoiding much combat. When combat does happen the AI is quick & fairly effective. My only con right now is the mouse sensitivity in menu's versus in-game is really off, not huge but it's there & makes going through the inventory weird.

zero spoilers ahead
Pros
+ Level design: if there's one thing Mankind Dividied not only excels but also beats the original at, it's level design. Whether it's the huge Prague hub itself or any individual missions or thematic places, there are always many, MANY various way to solve problem, get to a point of interest, etc. Actually it's so good that on my first playthrough, I kept getting lost while (like always) trying to explore every corner of the world, always bumping into new points of entry and getting sidetracked
+ Graphics: the game is absolutely gorgeous, with amount of detail no other game can even compare with. As far as urban and interior environments go of course.
+ Updated augmentation, stealth and gunplay mechanics: the game not only looks like a perfect representative of this generation's games, it plays like one too.
+ Story and setting: while the ending of Human Revolution felt somewhat anticlimatic (not as much for WHAT's happend as HOW the game handled it due to budget and time issues), it left the world of Deus Ex in perfect state perfectly summed up by trailer's "The promise of golden age is over." HR rubbed my sci-fi nerdy parts right in the way how it presented the wonders of technological progression as well as beginnings of worldwide discord and systematic political oppression. MD now picks up after a major worldwide disaster showing the world at its worst. Posers say how it fails to be political, nitpicking on details, ignoring the fact the dystopian and technologically advanced future of Deus Ex can't be less related to real world problems. Thus, in it's own universe, Mankind Divided fits into original lore of far fetched conspiracies and enslaving technologies, builds upon it and expands it. And what's best, the game being kind of removed from reality, it still feels relatable. That being said though, the final fight is anticlimatic again, a bit of a let down after intense final levels.
+ Side quests and exploration: as opposed to the main story, the side quests of MD get better and better throughout the game. With tons of content to explore, any sneaky peeper will once again rejoice in reading other people's emails and PDAs and listening to their conversations.
+ Game longevity: my first playthrough took me about 32 hours, ten less than I spent with HR the first time around, but old and new features such as New Game+, Hardcore difficulty (one life) and Breach mode, as well as more ingame "collectibles", they all offer more gameplay than I had hoped for.
+ Prague: 'nuff said.
Neutral points
+/- Voice acting: professional as expected. American, British and Russian English is great. Czech is brilliant and probably most pleasant surprise about the game. It's where Czechs speak English the immersion got kinda broken for me. It's nitpicking but what can I do, I really wish they hired Czech voice actors for Czech as well as for Czenglish
+/- Story: As previously stated, the ending is cut-off really brutally. The entire story arc makes sense and is closed with just enough questions and a cliffhanger to make you look forward to planned sequels, but that doesn't excuse how weak the epilogue, until now one of the strongest suits of all Deus Ex games, feels.
Cons
- Voice acting: the constant eastern accent can get pretty annoying, especially in few cases of the real bad ones.
- Finale: While final level is probably one of the best, if not the best stealth mission I've ever played, the story feels like it ends mid-sentence and the final cinematic (Adam watching TV) completely fails to deliver the climatic ending all previous Deus Ex games had. However I only blame one party for this, and it is this ↓
- Square Enix: microtransaction store I can live with. It's not great but is (would have been) a feature easily ignored, despite its reinforcement of an increasing trend. But when half of the Season Pass and Preorder bonuses are single use only with the sole intention of boosting sales in aforementioned ingame store, that's where I draw the line.
There. The last point is the only reason I have to give my GOTY a negative review. Don't buy it. Get it from 'alternative sources' (bay of yarr-sayers), enjoy it, and praise how great it is everywhere you can, because it sure is. Maybe, just maybe, in time Square Enix will pull its head out of its collective♥♥♥♥♥♥and start practicing fair marketing. Until then...

Edit: - I played 21 solid hours of this game BEFORE going to the main story  (which I am now just starting) - so I am honestly, not sure what other people did if they only played 17 in total.  There is SO much to explore and do.
This is going to an AMAZING concept (not having the same aptitude to burn the witches, as others have displayed).  First thing first.
1.  Most of the negative reviews are under 2 hours of play.  This in and of itself is hilarous for what is primarily a STEALTH game - where you can shoot if you want to, but why, when there are plenty of FPS's out there to choose from?  So it takes, wait for it, wait for it..... TIME to play and appreciate.
2. Microtransactions are a CHOICE - I know right? Who knew you could decide these things for yourself??? I am utterly amazed !  And really, they are only there for people who want to make the easy difficulty, SUPER easy - for the rest of us, why bother (or moan)?
3.  I am playing non-lethal/stealth on Give me Deus Ex, as I always do, and finding it hard and darn rewarding.  There seems to be less stealth options than HR, which is awesome !!  Making it so much HARDER.
4. Graphics (always a very nice bonus) and the story (which matters SO much) are awesome - no crashes yet... so might just be lucky on that one (and I am only playing with a 970 on High).
5.  I DID ASK FOR THIS - and I have it, and every minute is **insert own choice of expletive** AWESOME !!
6.  I purchased the DLC - single use of an item in a single player game is extraordinarily odd /wrong - that one in all honesty does suck the proverbial egg and does warrant questioning.  Here's hoping that 'constructive' feedback may change Square Enix's decision with a patch (best thing ever about patches, constant improvements and constrcutive feedback can change outcomes).
7.  At this point however, I am still very excited by this game and am thorougly enjoying every moment, and shall be back playing it tomorrow evening after work - as soon as I walk in the door !  Woohoo... Did I mention, I am having a blast playing this game?

I honestly have to say that I went into this one a skeptic and came out on the other end a changed man. This game although difficult to explain, (it's somthing you just need to experience), delivers on levels I didn't know were possible for a game. I've been moved by a Mozart Concerto, a Vincint VanGough, and even an epic big screen masterpiece like Braveheart! I have never however, until today, been moved in such a way as to stir my very soul by such as a video game. Don't get me wrong, I've played some exiting titles, (believe me, I've played many) that evoked emotion within me to a degree. None of them even came close to what I experienced in my 4 hour playthrough of Brothers - A Tale of Two Sons! Everything about the game is spectacular from the art to the music and the short but effective narrative. The visuals in this game are breathtaking, often prompting the player to simply stop and look around in order to take it all in. I wanted to be there. I could feel the wind blowing on my neck, smell the refreshing mist of a mountain stream waterfall,  feel the warmth of fire, and the bitter chill of a cold dark night. The music was beautiful to say the least. It captured the emotion, surroundings and story of the game in ways I can't begin to describe. The story is simple yet complex in its messages and underlying theme . Even if one can't directly relate to the narrative, you feel for the brothers. You share their pain, their fear, and will even find yourself likley laughing out loud on occasion due to the small moments that make this story so rich and full. As wonderful as the game is, it is not without its small list of faults. First, this game doesn't hold your hand. There are no navigation markers etc. You simply have to explore. This is not difficult however, it just requires some patience. Personally this was not a negative for me, but I can see how it could be for some. Secondly If you need to have a game last for 20 plus hours in order to feel fulfilled then this game may not be for you. I played through in about 4 hours. This was after doing a fair bit of exploring but not being completly thorough. I for one feel that 4 hours was more than enough time to accomplish what it sets out to do. Thirdly, one must be mature enought to understand all the themes present in this masterpiece. In other words, for example, much would likely be lost on a 10 year old playing this. It would depent on the 10 however! In closing, if you want to experiece something beautiful, something a little off the beaten path, then this is it! If you are a skeptic like me, take a leap of faith. I promise, you won't be dissapointed!

- Motorcycle Club Businesses - 4 Motorcycle Deliveries sometimes bug out when you deliver 3, meaning you can randomly lose 25% of your profit, which can be up to 105 k.
- The system that kicks "idle" players that have been afk for 15 minutes sometimes kicks you out after 3 minutes when you're alt-tabbed.
- Following, joining a new session after being kicked sometimes takes literally 30 minutes.
- At certain angles, picking up your motorcycle from the ground causes you to die immediately and fly 100 feet away.
- Some motorcycles, when fallen, roll upside down and must be jumped over to turn them over again, otherwise you will be unable to ride on them again.
- In certain freemode missions in certain areas, such as resupply missions at Humane Labs where you must search crates, you will sometimes be completely unable to enter a vehicle, even the vehicle you brought in. These are just some bugs I've experienced, with an irrelevant copy-paste "it's your fault change your graphic settings" response from support the one time I contacted them about delivery missions bugging out and money disappearing. Yet another horror game where your only defenses are a flashlight, and the ability to hide.
What's good about The Hat Man? Well, it looks nice. It runs well. It's short, and has both achievements
trading cards.
The bad? Everything else. It's another typical 'try to survive with a flashlight' horror game, that takes elements from other titles without adding anything new of its own. You wander around the halls of an asylum collecting pages, and eventually a tall shadowy figure named
The Hat Man comes after you, slowly, so very slowly. Eventually, you'll collect enough pages to trigger the next part of the game.
Acting? Atrocious. Worse than the original Resident Evil, if you can believe it. There's no difference between playing as the mother and father, aside from the voice. Even the hand icon that appears when hovering over something usable looks manly, when playing as the mother.
It's supposedly based on a true story, but I can't find anything referencing the source material, other than a 'legend'. A legend is by definition something that can't be proven, so the whole "true story" is a misnomer.
Mm no. Not worth it. The lowest price the game has ever been is $0.19 (yes, 19 cents), so for that price, sure, why not. But the game is boring, bland, and rife with concepts that have been done long before and are long overdone.

***UPDATE***
tl;cba - Easy to sit on the fence for this one as there's a lot of negatives. Overall, the game is worth playing and I do recommend it.  If the game is ever on sale at 50% or less, you'd be a fool not to buy it.
- Game Time: I've finished the game and it took me more than 70 hours. I did a lot of exploring and I'm the kind of guy who leaves no witnesses, so perhaps that's one reason why I took so long.  I also got myself into some situations which were quite tough as I was a bit underpowered at the time. However, those were perhaps some of the best non-mission moments as you have to rely on what you've got and work out the best way to untangle yourself from your own mess :)
- DLC: The DLC is unintrusive, but it still feels like a cynical addition.  On top of that, any game that's released with DLC 'content' on day one, along with a season pass deserves the negative criticism as it feels like you're buying an incomplete game.  I don't object to anyone who gives a negative review because of day one DLC; the more people rage against such practices, the more chance there is of publishers stopping the blatant and cynical cash grab.
- Performance: There are quite a few bugs and CTD's.  The game ran fine most of the time although it does pummel your CPU. Optimisation is an issue and the centre of the main map will stutter due to the poor optimisation. Saying that, I got a good 60+ fps for the majority of the game, and never lower than 45fps except for that damned stuttering.  All in all, it's a standard lazy and slack port.
- Gameplay: The biggest positive of the game. I had a fantastic time and couldn't wait to get back into the game when I had some spare time, although I had to take a day off playing to give my eyes a rest :)  There's multiple solutions to every problem (don't forget to look up), and whilst some of the aug's are auto take (higher jumps, extra strength and improved Bio-Cells), I never felt stuck with my choice.  There are a few inventory items for those moments when you're in a rush or a bit stumped, and when the game presents you with a very specific task (such as hacking someone's computer), if you search hard enough, there'll be a way to circumvent the obvious method.
- Storyline: The side quests are the highlight for me. You can stumble upon some by accident, or by doing things that don't seem to have any immediate impact.  You can also kill characters, but the game still works without having to resurrect them.  I accidentally killed a good source of money, although he did catch me rummaging around in his lock-up. I also accidentally killed a major character, but the game still manages to cater for this.
At the moment, I'd give this game a thumbs up.  Works just fine on high setting using i5-3570 - 4.5GHz & GTX970 @ 1080p.  My PC is over 4 years old with the only upgrades being the GTX970 and all my hard drives are SSD's.
Game runs fine from 55fps in very busy areas (the notorious train station) up to 72fps (144Hz monitor using Adaptive Vsync @ 72Hz).
The only setting I have turned off are MSAA, Volumetric Lighting and Contact Hardening Shadows. My chosen FoV is 90 (100 max).
As long as you don't expect to be running Ultra setting with everything on at 4K you 'should' be fine.

Spelunky is a somewhat niche game. It's a difficult proceedurally generated platform game that has been out for a while for a while now but there's a certain something within it which keeps drawing me back.
The "difficulty" is actually very fair, it's simply a matter of understanding the mechanics of the game and with a fairly firm grasp of those, you're going to die, a lot! With that said, you do feel a sense of accomplishment when you figure out certain aspects of the game, or when you reach a new area, or alternatively when you actually finish the game, whether it is the main way or the hard way.
There is a local co-op mode which works well, especially if everyone is of a decent skill, but even if not, the players who have died can still help by triggering traps and moving items.
There is even a local deathmatch game mode which is, interesting, but I've not spent enough time with it to have formed much of an opinion of it.
Finally, and the most addictive thing for me is the daily challenge, time was that I would complete it and see how I did compared to my friends, they've moved on to other games and yet I still find the daily challenge fun to complete.

A stunning combination of modern graphics, old-school Zelda gameplay with modern Zelda goals, a touch of Windwaker islands, no restraints from fan-service and a clear amount of love and dedication to the format. This will be the best non-third-person Zelda game you've played for a long time, but don't let that comparison fool you as this game has so many good, well-followed-through ideas that you'll be left feeling Nintendo needs to catch up.
It's got everything you'd expect from the years of Zelda variations we've had: elemental relics, fish and bird people, arrows and bombs, heart pieces, and a silent protagonist. But it's also got a lot you woulds: XP and levelling up, fishing, built-in non-grinding acheivements that award XP, far more subtle secrets than Zelda's ever had, and persistent rooms that don't reset when you leave. This isn't some cheap indie cash-in. This was made with love, for the sole purpose of being a
game.
The further you get into the game, the more you see that this really is a shameless Zelda clone, which is very sad. It had so much potential to be special, but beyond simply a tribute game, they've stuck to the same old formula to the same detriment as Nintendo. The primary-coloured tunic, the carbon-copy Zora fish-people who are frozen and you save their princess, the legendary sword that looks identical to the Master Sword with a palette-swap, the three elemental gods whose elemental symbols you collect to gain their favour, refurring to Cuckoos by name (Zelda's name for chickens), and I mentioned it before but the silent protagonist is entirely unnessisary - characters converse with you like you're talking back, and this is a game where there is spoken, english dialogue, quite unlike Zelda.
Using an item to jump and casting ranged spells is a welcome change from the formula, but it's not the gameplay that's the problem - the fighting, puzzles and level design are all really fun. No, it's the strict adherance to creating an off-brand Zelda that really lets this game down. If you've never played a Zelda, then fantastic, but I imagine a lot of the people who bought this game were drawn to the aesthtic and familiar mechanics. This game could have been so much more and stood out on its own merits- the foundation is there -but its reverence to its inspiration is its downfall, highlighting all the stolen ideas and overshadowing the innovations.
If there's ever a sequel, and I would like there to be, I do hope they take a seperate path and turn this story platform into something unique.
If you okay with a straight up Zelda clone, this is the game for you.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

To be blunt, this game is a yes and a no. Why? Well, depends on how much you know and like about RWBY.
Granted, the gme is currently in its early development stage, which shows that it can become a promiing game for anybody who decides to pick it up. But, as it is now, it features four color coded girls with some crazy weapons destroying hordes of black creatures. That's... kind of what RWBY is in the first place. But, hey! I love it.
The game is an action packed beat 'em up with a feel similar to Devil May Cry, but not there yet. The game will be fleshed out later as it releases its full version. You pick one of four characters, each different but similar. They each have a standard combo, some which knock the enemy into the air and your character assaults it from there, and each has a ranged attack, which has the most variation of all of them. The special attacks are all similar as well, each character having an area attack, an attack good against single high level enemies, and a long ranged special. While they are all different in effect, visual, and feel, they all follow that same catagory. While this may seem like a negative thing, I find beautiy in this. While each character has their own quirks and battle style, I don't have to worry about whether or not I will be able to hold off multiple foes or be concerned with facing off against one. The characters all feel different, but they all have the same foundation; this is something I find intriguing and applaud the creator for doing (I can't remember his name...)
The game has it's pros, being fun, action packed fights that do indeed have a difficulty to them where I don't feel as though I reign as a god because the enemies attacks can hurt you if you don't pay attention. With an environment, storyline, and characters that has all RWBY fans whooping in celebration for one of the things they couldn't wait for, there are some negative quirks that will most likely be fixed. First off, your character level is not saved. You restart every time you play. The game is obviously a trial, as there are only four levels to play, after which you are whisked back to the main menu where you will either try again as another character or find something else to play. The game feels like it has a "rookie" feel, what from the visual aspect being a bit singular (there isn't a whole lot of detail or variation; a small thing, really), the characters movement feeling robotic (no acceleration; again, small detail), and some issues with targeting (no target lock, and I can't tell you how many times Ruby used Dust shot on Grimm that I wasn't even looking at). The grande scheme of the game looks fine, but if RT wants to make this a game that will win over not just RWBY fans but gamers in general, it has a bit of a ways to go.
Regardless, I loved the game. It was fun. I got to play as my favorite characters from my most favorite show. If and when RT makes this game bigger and more epic (I hope they wiil, at least), it will be one of my favorites as well. Personally, I wish this game had the combat of Kingdom Hearts + Devil May Cry, the open world of Far Cry, and craziness of Just Cause. Of course, gamers also want to see Half Life 3. I have a better chance than they, but still, chances are slim.

This is a great and funny game. The world is large and quite diverse, the music is cool, characters are cool. FFS Rob Halford and Ozzy are voicing characters here, that's really cool.
As for the gameplay, I have mixed feelings. It's decent hack n slash, and the main quest battles are real time strategy, which I'm not a particularily big fan of. But it's passible. The big battles can become tedious after a while, due to the fact that many of them are hard and require much time to complete. There are no tutorials introducing you in a nice way, so you have to figure out all that stuff yourself. The fact that you have to fight these battles like 7-8 times doesn't make it any better.
The quest and dialogues could use some work. Both of them are fairly repetetive. Main quests are mostly fighting the evil dudes and just progressing by fighting some armies here and there. When the main quests are done in one area, you know you'll most likely never return. Why is that? Because the side quests are very poor. No quests are "individual", they're all part of some story line, like the one with the hunter. Or the ambush quests which there are like 20 of. They weren't very entertaining at first, and certainly doesn't get better after many. And basically that goes for the other quests as well. The dialogue is decent, but is very repetive regarding side quests.
The multiplayer is basically meaningless. First of all, it's completely abandoned (even if it wasn't that when it came out as well). And the concept of fighting these large army battles doesn't really appeal to me in any ways, so the only reason to try them out is to get some achievments. Btw, if you're aiming at getting 100% completion rate of all your games, you shouldn't buy this. You will be forced to collect loads of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, like for example 120 serpents which would take a lot of ♥♥♥♥ing time.
Try to buy this on sale. It's a great concept with great characters. It's not too long either if you only focus on main quests, so you are able to complete this in a few hours. 6.75/10

DE:MD makes you think... carefully, if you don't investigate and plan you'll be punished, brutally. Even on the easiest level for a keen FPS player be prepared to slow down and think or you'll be punished, brute force will not help you and although initially frustrating the game forces you to try new ways of achieving your objectives and for that I'm truely greatful.
Graphically on ultra at 3440x1440 it's stunning - it's 21:9 support is nearly there with the usual 16:9 cutscene limitations and slightly overlooked onscreen damage/warning indicators also in 16:9 but nothing too shameful to worry about. FOV adjstment is also included along with Exclusive Full screen to allow Refreesh rate adjustment for those using G-SYNC - another thankyou to the developers.
It's a great continuatiuon of DE:HE but doesn't make you play it's predecessor to get the plot a useful optional 12 minute video at the start helps you out here.
In summary it's a slick thoughtful roleplaying game in a great looking FPS wrapper with a reasonalble narrative but if you are expecting FPS dynamics and simplicity prehaps watch some streams or gameplay footage before you decide to buy - might not be to everyones taste, but for me I'm a convert after just a few hours of being punished.

This is hands-down, no doubt about it my favorite PC game of all time! I play it almost every day, and I never get bored of it. If that's not a testament to how great it is (coupled with the fact that I've logged nearly 600 hours playing it), I don't know what else to say!

Fair warning: tall wall of text below.
I think if KoA was released an year before it's actual appearance, this game would become way more popular. It was flattened by stronger contenders, such as Skyrim, and didn't get enough recognition. Which, in my opinion, is unfair. This game deserves some love, because it is really well made.
The world is open and very large. It has many secrets to share. It's easy to get lost. But you don't get that "Bring me back" feeling, it is an experience - to explore new lands and watch out for new enemies and loot. NPCs are ranging from standart "good guys" and confusing, but adorable, midgets to psychos and evil mages with robes and whatever goes with typical villain appearance. Unfortunately, almost none of the are remarkable. You will often hear voice of the same person when speaking to NPCs in literally same exact location. Base models are quite often reused too. Slightly damages overall atmosphere of "everything new and unusual".
Quests are fun. Sometimes. Boring "go-there-and-speak-to-this-person-then-speak-to-other-person" quests are rare, but you will eventually stumble upon those. But even they always come with a twist. Speak to these four persons and find out how to place them in a column, so they won't kill each other, please. Quests are more like little adventrues, that will take you to the unexplored dungeons and cryptic castles (most of which would look exactly the same for you, but don't bother). All of them have stories behind them, but they seem rather... irrelevant. You don't feel the impact of your actions. You just helped that man, who claims to be the wolf, turned into humanoid by evil fairies. Now he thanks you and bids farewell. You will never see him again. And soon enough you will forget about him. Really rarely you get to see what have you done to others. Game simply erases it form the memory. The only reminder of that will calmly sit in your quest book. Strikethrough.
The combat on the other hand is developed amazingly. Strikes chain into beautiful combos, combos then develop into cascades of hits and then finishing blow. Rinse, repeat. Never mind that your character will do the same moves over and over. You will never get tired of them. There are tons of weapon types and all of them have their unique move sets. Not all of them will be unlocked at the beginning; it will take few levels and some skill points investments to unlock new attacks. Mixing them with generic weapon attacks will result in gorgeous sights and dead enemies. Charge the key and then... maelstrom of blades or magic envelops you. Truly amusing.
You also can kill any NPC that you don't like, ransack a wardrobe only to find peasant's tunic in here, pickpocket someone for sweet cash. Of course it comes with punishment. Of course local guards will try to stop you. And then you have a choice to bribe them, run away or go to prison like a good person (and then escape one moment later, brutally murdering everyone who stands on your way). Game doesn't stop you from being bad guy. You have your own path to follow, there is no set road. And I like it. And some quests actually reward that. So prepare your quick fingers, as a lot of stuff will stick to them quite soon.
Graphics are what you expect from 2011 game. Yes. they are not great, yes, they are cartoonish. But then you see a landscape and you finger automatically reaches the F12 button. Not always you will get breathtaking views, but when you do, you will be pleased. Architecture also deserves special mention. Sometimes reminds me of Warcraft, sometimes of Oblivion, other times feels like you were thrown into Witcher. There are many wonderful places, some of them will make you spend time simply staring on puzzling ornament on a wall, while you're being pursued by swarm of spiders. When it comes to NPCs. Most of them are bricky and not looking like someone who can breathe. But on the other hand, when you get used to it, you will skip this part and go straight sor details. And some persons you'll meet look really great. Maybe it's haircut, tattoos or eyes, or even mix of three at the same time, they catch your attention with their features.

Some basic tips for the Standard difficulty.
1) Do all the available side quests before advancing the main quests.
2) Do not mix Finesse and Magic trees unless you can find daggers equal to your level. They aren't nearly as common as they should be. Otherwise, you can't handle enough damage and don't kill things quickly enough.
3) Dodging is not as useful as the game claims for two reasons.
3a) Dodge doesn't give you any tactical positioning. In fact, most of the time you end up with your back to an opponent that's already turned to face you, so you end up repeat dodging just to get clear without getting it while they follow you.
3b) Certain bosses are too fast for dodging to be useful. Or they have AoE's that are too large to escape with a dodge. There's also fighting multiple opponents at once. They flank and they knock you off balance long enough to hit you again.
4) Amp your resistances up like your life depends on it. It does.
5) Load up on potions. Your life depends on these too.
If you leave any of these tips out, be prepared for frustration and loud cursing.
Oh, and don't count on the NPC's that sometimes accompany you to be useful. They're not. They can't deal damage worth sneezing at, and some of them spend more time rolling around than stabbing things.
Last Tip: The boss at the Hyperian is multi-stage. Be careful about using Fate Mode on him too early. This is the one that got me so frustrated I uninstalled the game.
Enjoy!

This is my second-favorite fighting game of all time, behind Soul Calibur II.
The visuals look great, the combat feels fluid, and the character designs (especially those of the women) are much better than MK9. The new characters are largely a good addition, although the military kids feel a bit bland at times. Like MK9, MKX has a great story mode (especially for a fighter) that lets you play as and get familiar with the new characters. While it's a bit short compared MK9, I still love to see story modes in my fighting games.
This edition of MK has seen a greatly improved version of the Krypt, which plays like a small spinoff of games like Legend of Grimrock. It contains a decent amount of collectables, although I'd like to see more "making-of" clips along with funny unlockables like the classic "Cooking With Scorpion." Mortal Kombat also features more online-integrated features this time around, like the Faction War system and Living Towers. Sadly, the Faction War system has very little depth and ends up just being a method of unlocking more player card items. The Living Towers, however, offer reasons to boot up the game each week and see something new. There are premium weekly towers like those for certain characters or holidays, along with towers which refresh daily and hourly. This helps keep the game more fresh, although MKX is missing a large challenge tower like MK9 had.
While many people have had seemingly endless issues with the PC port, I've been largely unaffected. The launch itself was terrible due to the streaming download feature, but it ran decently well for me. Over the past couple months, the game has had several patches which have brought the quality of the port much closer to that of the console versions. I get a consistent 60 FPS while in combat, which is a great improvement from the regular slowdowns I had right after launch.
I don't really play the game online much, but that has been a major issue I've heard. Apparently fight connection could have been greatly improved, and now there are very few PC players left from the bad launch. It appears that another company has begun patching the game instead of High Voltage Studios, so hopefully the quality of the port only goes up from here. Unfortunately, many of the patches the consoles receive don't seem to come to the PC until the major DLC character releases, so balancing and bonus costumes have been delayed consistently.
Overall, I really enjoy the game. It looks great, plays well, and has good depth with the variation system. While certainly not perfect, I'd definitely recommend this game to lovers of Mortal Kombat or the fighting genre itself.

After 23 years PC finally gets a release for Tekken, and its a very damn good release at that part as well! A lot of it is thanks to the Arcade version using UE4 and hardware similar to PC!
- In terms of offline content the game does a decent job at everything. Story mode is decent although I am not a fan of the narrator at all its around 4-5 hrs if you include the character story modes as well.
- Arcade mode isn't very good 5 battles and not even a special cutscene in the end.

-The treasure battles are pretty much the biggest part the single player content has to offer, it is basically countless battles with a CPU to unlock items to customize your character with and fight money. The type of items you unlock are really RNG, and it could come to the point that you are playing for hours just to unlock one item that would make your character look great! The only small issue I have with Treasure mode is that the AI can become very predictable even at the higher ranks but other than that unlocking the items is what makes the grindfest worth.
- Although many people complain that the cutomization options are less than what previous Tekken games have to offer it still has a crap ton of content to make and mix match many differnet custome combinations. You want Joker? You can make that! You want Ness from Earth Bound you can make that too, the combinations are endless and gives a lot of replayability alone and more costumes than you can get with DLC in any fighter!
- Training Mode is excellent if you know how to utilize it really well, btw don't get overwhelmed by the amount of commands on the stream a lot of them are either irrelevant, useless or jst basic stuff like F,F+1 (Foward, foward and Left Punch). In the trainnig mode you can preview all of the commands so you can see if you are actually doing them correctly or have an idea of the timings. You can also dictate the CPU to do different mixups and strings and you can practice countering them. Especially useful when you want to work on your poking game or punishing unsafe moves. One thing I really recommend is displaying the recovery animation. Good to see how safe your moves are/recovery frames in your moves and what move you can use to punish it. Unfortunately this game does not have a tutorial mode, which is something that can really overwhelm new players but thankfully there are tutorials online not only for the game but for the characters as well. Before doing anything in the game I really do recommend that you check out the tutorial mode first.
- Now onto the Online, the make it or break it for many of you. Well starting with the netcode I can say that its absolutely fantastic. WIth a moderate Nat (Type 2) I find so many matches at all times and all the games 3 bars and up were very fine! I almost never drop my combos and I lan most of my just frames which are pretty difficult (I play Nina) I even had 1 match with a player having 2 bars and it wasn't so bad at all still playable although every other match with 2 bars wasn't good at all. I even found matches with people far outsdie my area. I fought people from Italy, Spain, Indoneasia, Egypt, and even Colombia and all of the games went pretty solid especially colombia. My internet is very excellent though I must say 1gbps fiber internet extremely low ping ~90ms to Korea ~67 to South America ~70-80 around Dominican republic and im sure that does help.
- Whats terrible about the online is 1. Rage quitters yes they are in every game and this game is no exception. It is something that we all have to face, another is people dodging you based on your rank. If you're a certain rank with a low amount of wins (meaning you got there pretty ♥♥♥♥ing fast) they dodge you. IT started happening to me as soon as I became a Maurader. Also unfortunately tournament mode is dead but with good reason. A lot of the times the tournaments would disband when the host loses or they will kick you out the tournament if you take a game off them.
- Other than that the online experience for me has been great. 80 hours in (10 of my hours I played offline) so far I am really enojying Tekken 7.
* Im sure many of you reading this, if you're reading this are new players as am I and hoenstly before the game was released I was very skeptical on whether or not I should actually go out and purchase the game. I was plagued with the "This game has a very high ceiling curve" and "This game requires you to have a lot of understanding on the characters and the mechanics itself or you won't do very well" and this is so true. If you don't understand Tekken and go through the deep learning curve you will get blown up online. I was scared at first but then I went on youtube and watched plenty of tutorials to learn the mechanics of the game from KingJae and Aris respectively and I gained a huge understanding from the game just from that. Practicing in training mode for many hours and player matches (Offline and Online really helped me out as a new player and get better.) And I am defintiely seeing the results of my practice in player matches and ranked. If you put in the effort and work you will get better at this game. You aren't doomed on arrival just because you're a new player pitted against many veterans.
If you are looking for a fighter to play, especially on PC, definifelty recommend Tekken 7.

Neat little first person horror game that plays kind of like Slender along with some key items you need to find in order to proceed with the game. It's short, cheap, and bitter-sweet. In other words, it's alright.
The Bad:
The voiceovers for the journal entries were a bit dull to say the least, and even one of the entries completely didn't match up with the text, sounded like a different voice actor/cheaper microphone.
Opening doors and equipping items is like pulling teeth. For doors, you have to be extremely close, and your clicks don't even register half the time. As with items, there's delays and its unresponsive sometimes.
Jumping is literally useless, and leaning is too slow and doesn't go far enough.
The Good:
You will probably♥♥♥♥♥♥bricks at least once in one of your encounters, luckily for you, I have the worst colon in the world, so that's impossible for me. I did jump at least once though.
Eerie environments and sounds.
Bad AI makes enemies unpredictably scary (Something kind of like Afraid of Monsters)
The Objective:
Your goal is to get about 20 pages of your daughters journal, slowly uncovering the mystery of your missing daughter at an insane asylum, with the enemies getting more aggressive the more entries you pick up. You also need to find some key items to proceed throughout the game. You can save your game on TVs, unlike Slender. You must also avoid the shadowy figures chasing you down every now and then, or they will glue themselves to you and eat your face off faster than you can say "Game Over". After you get the 20 something pages and do a certain something, you've beaten the game.
Game isn't too difficult, and it lasted me about an hour with about 4 deaths.
So if you're a fan of horror games (like Slender), you might want to give this game a try.

The gameplay is a carbon copy of Human Revolution which immediately feels 5 years behind with half-life style sliding on glass movement, however they have at least enhanced and refined it somewhat. It's still clunky and works to the game detriment. I have struggled with ongoing crashing issues despite two patches thus far (MSI Afterburner needs to be turned off which sucks).  The shooting mechanics are still rather poor.  Thankfully the microtransactions can be avoided eaily enough, though the store is completely broken for me I guess that's a positive? [edit they fixed it...but not the game] All of this is not great, but I can get past it.
But what really dissappointed was the lack of care and attention to this game. If you haven't seen Jim Sterling's expose of Square-Enix's development of Mankind Divided please do before you decide to purchase this game. I do not support games that treat gamers like this, and it is unlikely I will be buying a sequel to this game.
This title is firstly a story driven game and it's presentation is subpar. The animation is worse than Human Revolution and after a year of titles like Witcher 3, Rise of Tomb Raider and even Assasin's Creed there is an expectation that a AAA title will look polished. If it was just 3rd party characters within the game world it may be less noticable and more excusable, but we have major plot points presented with some of the worst animation in the industry. The story is also terribly presented and it is very difficult to get invested in the purpose of Adam Jensen, it just feels like another day at the office. The story does eventually pick up and there are some great level design and gameplay sequences once you start the story proper, unfortuantely it's the only highlight here. To add insult to injury the story doesn't rap up and you'll need to pay for a season pass or the next game to see a conclusion.
All of this is a real shame. I have no idea what they have been doing for 5 years and a $70 million budget...but it's most certainly been wasted. Despite all this the game is still fun, even if on the hardest difficulty it's a walk in the park and dumbed down for the masses. Easily the worst entry in the series and I'd rather replay Invisible War. A huge missed opportunity but that's all Square-Enix seems to publish these days.

It is impossible to state how poor this game is, and that's not counting the excellent "translation". (Maybe it reads better in French or one of the other languages, but I somehow doubt the story is saner.)
- As a visual novel, the game is a debacle. The story is an atrocious mess of jargon which is apparently a side-story to the creator's epic "Dragon and Weed" (This is not a joke, it explains this in a heavily abridged form in a submenu you can find) saga that you can bet your♥♥♥♥♥♥I'm never going to look up. There are maybe 4 "branch points" in the game. They do nothing. Save and click either option! Nothing changes at all. As a result, you're just here to watch whatever strange superpowered wankfest this is play out over a few hours, with the occasional break in the form of...
- Quick-Time Events. No, seriously. Keep your hand on the keyboard and make sure you're familiar with french keyboard layouts, because that's what the keys are bound around. Earlier in the game there are more of these and then they just stop, like even the developer realized how dumb they were and didn't care enough to remove them. At least one failed to register for me until I restarted the game, so don't go in expecting them to be tightly-coded, either.
- The game says it runs in some sort of custom 3D engine! Probably to allow for the QTEs. It's not very good and somehow it crashed twice on me in the process of playing. A visual novel with no branch points crashed on me. Just take in how much of a wreck it is that this is a thing I'm writing. It wasn't a hard thing to test, fella.
- I don't speak the other languages to compare, but the English script is a debacle. Characters will repeat the same line back at each other randomly, some phrases are just entirely garbage (my favorite line in the game: "It's seems that Menkens hathwart someone he shouldn't. Men of the Bad Santass are here and not to joke..."), and more than a few lines just stopped a word in and continued on like the script wasn't matching up with timing somehow. Others were just still in French for no reason. Unlike a lot of VNs, there's no rewind function, so I hope you like being left in the dark or restarting entire chapters to figure out what the hell is going on. It's not going to help.
- The art is terrible. Action scenes don't feel kinetic, they feel like someone on Deviantart just learned Photoshop has filters. One of the climactic moments of the story has a man take off his shirt and then suddenly the screen is a mess of glowing red chains, because "he used to tame the tigers". It then cuts to black and suddenly he's beat up a little.
- I hope you don't want a soundtrack, because the only accompaniment the game has are some three-note "baby's first music" compositions, a lot of generic stock sound effects like gunfire or explosions, and most of the game is silent. Entirely silent.

This is my second-favorite fighting game of all time, behind Soul Calibur II.
The visuals look great, the combat feels fluid, and the character designs (especially those of the women) are much better than MK9. The new characters are largely a good addition, although the military kids feel a bit bland at times. Like MK9, MKX has a great story mode (especially for a fighter) that lets you play as and get familiar with the new characters. While it's a bit short compared MK9, I still love to see story modes in my fighting games.
This edition of MK has seen a greatly improved version of the Krypt, which plays like a small spinoff of games like Legend of Grimrock. It contains a decent amount of collectables, although I'd like to see more "making-of" clips along with funny unlockables like the classic "Cooking With Scorpion." Mortal Kombat also features more online-integrated features this time around, like the Faction War system and Living Towers. Sadly, the Faction War system has very little depth and ends up just being a method of unlocking more player card items. The Living Towers, however, offer reasons to boot up the game each week and see something new. There are premium weekly towers like those for certain characters or holidays, along with towers which refresh daily and hourly. This helps keep the game more fresh, although MKX is missing a large challenge tower like MK9 had.
While many people have had seemingly endless issues with the PC port, I've been largely unaffected. The launch itself was terrible due to the streaming download feature, but it ran decently well for me. Over the past couple months, the game has had several patches which have brought the quality of the port much closer to that of the console versions. I get a consistent 60 FPS while in combat, which is a great improvement from the regular slowdowns I had right after launch.
I don't really play the game online much, but that has been a major issue I've heard. Apparently fight connection could have been greatly improved, and now there are very few PC players left from the bad launch. It appears that another company has begun patching the game instead of High Voltage Studios, so hopefully the quality of the port only goes up from here. Unfortunately, many of the patches the consoles receive don't seem to come to the PC until the major DLC character releases, so balancing and bonus costumes have been delayed consistently.
Overall, I really enjoy the game. It looks great, plays well, and has good depth with the variation system. While certainly not perfect, I'd definitely recommend this game to lovers of Mortal Kombat or the fighting genre itself.

After 23 years PC finally gets a release for Tekken, and its a very damn good release at that part as well! A lot of it is thanks to the Arcade version using UE4 and hardware similar to PC!
- In terms of offline content the game does a decent job at everything. Story mode is decent although I am not a fan of the narrator at all its around 4-5 hrs if you include the character story modes as well.
- Arcade mode isn't very good 5 battles and not even a special cutscene in the end.

-The treasure battles are pretty much the biggest part the single player content has to offer, it is basically countless battles with a CPU to unlock items to customize your character with and fight money. The type of items you unlock are really RNG, and it could come to the point that you are playing for hours just to unlock one item that would make your character look great! The only small issue I have with Treasure mode is that the AI can become very predictable even at the higher ranks but other than that unlocking the items is what makes the grindfest worth.
- Although many people complain that the cutomization options are less than what previous Tekken games have to offer it still has a crap ton of content to make and mix match many differnet custome combinations. You want Joker? You can make that! You want Ness from Earth Bound you can make that too, the combinations are endless and gives a lot of replayability alone and more costumes than you can get with DLC in any fighter!
- Training Mode is excellent if you know how to utilize it really well, btw don't get overwhelmed by the amount of commands on the stream a lot of them are either irrelevant, useless or jst basic stuff like F,F+1 (Foward, foward and Left Punch). In the trainnig mode you can preview all of the commands so you can see if you are actually doing them correctly or have an idea of the timings. You can also dictate the CPU to do different mixups and strings and you can practice countering them. Especially useful when you want to work on your poking game or punishing unsafe moves. One thing I really recommend is displaying the recovery animation. Good to see how safe your moves are/recovery frames in your moves and what move you can use to punish it. Unfortunately this game does not have a tutorial mode, which is something that can really overwhelm new players but thankfully there are tutorials online not only for the game but for the characters as well. Before doing anything in the game I really do recommend that you check out the tutorial mode first.
- Now onto the Online, the make it or break it for many of you. Well starting with the netcode I can say that its absolutely fantastic. WIth a moderate Nat (Type 2) I find so many matches at all times and all the games 3 bars and up were very fine! I almost never drop my combos and I lan most of my just frames which are pretty difficult (I play Nina) I even had 1 match with a player having 2 bars and it wasn't so bad at all still playable although every other match with 2 bars wasn't good at all. I even found matches with people far outsdie my area. I fought people from Italy, Spain, Indoneasia, Egypt, and even Colombia and all of the games went pretty solid especially colombia. My internet is very excellent though I must say 1gbps fiber internet extremely low ping ~90ms to Korea ~67 to South America ~70-80 around Dominican republic and im sure that does help.
- Whats terrible about the online is 1. Rage quitters yes they are in every game and this game is no exception. It is something that we all have to face, another is people dodging you based on your rank. If you're a certain rank with a low amount of wins (meaning you got there pretty ♥♥♥♥ing fast) they dodge you. IT started happening to me as soon as I became a Maurader. Also unfortunately tournament mode is dead but with good reason. The Hat Man: Shadow Ward is an indie horror game, seemingly heavily inspired by Slender and similar games. You play as the father(or mother, depending on which you pick) of a young girl who was sent to an Asylum. You receive a message telling you that your daughter is missing and you decide to go look for her in the Asylum. Upon entering her room and opening her diary the Asylum changes, the diary explodes and the first Shadow person appears. You are now compelled to gather all the pages of the dairy as the games gets progressively harder with each page. Overall, the game is pretty graphically outdated(it's an indie game with a limited budget), but they were able to get the spooks pretty well(the SFX were nice, too). The voice-acting is either purposely bad or just bad, so it kinda makes it hard to get scared when the voice-acting makes you wanna laugh. There are some bugs and the Shadow people are pretty slow and you get rid of them quite easily. One of the biggest issues was the fact that upon dying I was cast back to the beginning, hence I'd recommend a way of saving the game or just more checkpoints. If you wanna get some creepy atmosphere going I suggest buying the game on sale, there are better titles out there, but it's still pretty solid.
>I'd give it a 5/10
>Pros: Spooky atmosphere, achievements, randomly generated map, allegedly based on real stories.
>Cons: Bugs, inability to save/rare checkpoints, the enemies aren't that tough, voice-acting, short, graphics are outdated, the rooms look almost the same but it isn't that bad.

Original Review:
It's basically more of human revolution with far shinier graphics and better combat. If you're a fan of DXHR, then this will be right up your alley.
Microtransactions are absolutely an insult to the franchise, but from what I've seen of them they are unnecessary and only really are appealing to those that have neither the time nor the patience to explore the levels and scavenge for their scarce resources (which IMO is actually one of the main pacing elements that really made DXHR). Buying them only really deprives yourself from enjoying the balance between combat and stealth that the game encourages.
Performance-wise, the game runs great on my GTX 970. While there are some settings (namely MSAA and volumetric lighting) that can literally cut framerates in half, using T-AA gets rid of most jaggies while not destroying shadow quality (I'm looking at you, Rainbow 6 siege). I get about 75-90fps, and in general my only complaint performance-wise is that the game stutters slightly in some of the hub areas every now and then- though this may very well be due to day-0 bugs. I'll try to update this if a performance patch comes out.
TL:DR
If you liked human revolution, this game is absolutely for you. This game fixes the glaring gunplay and combat issues that game had, while still bringing the same blend of story and gameplay that the franchise is famed for. Just remember to tweak your options settings before jumping right in- totalbiscuit's video on the PC version discusses the impact of settings in far greater detail that I can here, so go watch that if you don't like watching slideshows.
If you're new the franchise, it's a coin flip. The narrative in this game is amazing, and so long as you are fine with exploring evironments for supplies (like wolfenstein the new order) and general FPS mechanics, it's a shoe in. Some of the physics bugs with corpse dragging and other small parts of the game are annoying though, so if you're on the fence I would definitely suggest you wait for a couple weeks after release.It's basically more of human revolution with far shinier graphics and better combat. I only played this visual novel for a couple of minutes. Not because the story is bad, it starts out pretty good to be honest. But, there're just some serious grammar failures and some serious artwork errors.

Alright, I booted the game again. (Almost a year later) and although the developers said that they would fix the translation problem.., it's still a brutal mess. Most of the time I'm just so frustrated by trying to fix the mess I read on screen, it makes me feel like I'm taking somekind of grammar test; "Detect the 15  failures in the small block of text." That's how bad it is. This shouldn't even be released on Steam.

If you are going to sell a game as a visual novel, you should copy edit your text and review your translations. I can not speak for any of the other languages, but the English translation for
is embarassing. Not only does the vast majority of the script read like it was run through Google Translate without revision, it has enough typos to clearly indicate the writer/translator did not even bother to use spell check.
The terrible writing is not the only thing that muddles this story. The game uses so many acronyms that it can be difficult to keep track of them all. Some exist in the real world, some are made up for the game, but they all run together to combine with the incoherent translation in making the story extremely hard to follow.
The art ranges from appearing decent to looking like something a teenager threw together in Microsoft Paint. In some cases you can tell the artist reused a face asset which makes a character look like a mishapen freak of nature with two mouths.
The text is not always accompanied by sound. During my playthrough there were a number of long durations of text exposition that occurred in either total silence or with just some ambient white noise. The game has no voice acting, and most of the game sounds are just cheesy stock-sounding gunfire noises.
The interactive aspect consists of approximately ten quick time events that appear without warning and involves seemingly random keypresses. You never know when to expect them, what key you will have to press (either once or quickly in repetition), and they have a very short input window. When you fail the game goes back around 5 seconds for you to do it again once you know to expect it. Luckily you only lose those few seconds each time, since you will most likely fail them all at first (they also pop up at the top of the screen while you are reading the dialogue at the bottom). There are also two branching options that the player can choose from, but they appear to only affect a specific scene each and does not have any affect on the larger narrative.
The narrative itself, as difficult as it is to follow, ends as if this is the first chapter in an episodic game.  I don't know if this is the developer's plan, but even if it is, do not expect much satisfaction from the story. There are much better visual novels available on Steam. I suggest you exhaust as many other options as possible before purchasing this.

I'm a huge fan of the The Sims franchise, so it comes as no surprise that I enjoy this game. However, maybe this review is useful to someone already familiar with the series.
There are several aspects about this iteration of the series that I dislike and which make me continue to view The Sims 2 as my favorite. I absolutely abhor having to see paid content in-game without having any interest whatsoever in ever buying it. I already spent more than $100 dollars on the base game and DLC. Why would I be charged for more and what justifies charging for it? Server maintenance, updates, and the cost of a Community Team (does The Sims even have one?) should be more than covered by that. So, besides the major issues of microtransactions being forced down one's throat, it also appears that getting free community content is much more of a hassle.  For starters, there is no Body Shop that allows you to easily create Sims and package them. There is no denying that the new Create a Sim tools are much more evolved and allow for much more customization, especially the ability to modify a Sim's body type, and the addition of true personality traits and combinations are great. However, there doesn't appear to be an easy way to share and obtain community content outside of EA's platform. I could list various other things that bother me about the game (e.g. Why are younger Sims so ugly? Why add rabbit holes?), but I think the attempts at money-making and sharing limitations are the main downsides to me.
On the bright side, the graphics are beautiful and the exploration options endless, especially with the DLC (which, I am sorry to say, one still has to get for a more complete game experience).

Spelunky isn't the best game ever, nor is it my favourite. Yet it's perhaps the only perfect game that I've experienced. It is mechanically and conceptually brilliant, keeping things simple while allowing for emergent gameplay and moments that make you gape at the screen even after 150 hours of playtime. Lots of people can tell you that Spelunky is a roguelite, that it's unforgiving but rarely unfair, that the controls are tight, and so forth. But the discovery of all the content, tips and tricks are what make this gem shine.
You'll start out on your first playthrough, and think that bats are absurdly annoying. You'll keep getting tagged by falling spiders, wonder why arrow traps are so strong, and sprint in fear from the giant spider. Inch by torturous inch, you'll crawl relentlessly through the Mines. You'll try buying items to see what they do. You'll wonder what's stopping you from robbing the shopkeeper blind, before swiftly witnessing his particular brand of justice - no buckets on heads here. You'll kill yourself with bombs, fall on to spikes repeatedly, and curse dark levels for all they're worth. But...you'll make it. Into the Jungle.
Where a new brand of horror awaits. Tiki Traps, the bane of players both experienced and green, designed to instantly end a hurried run. Monkeys that lead you to your spikey demise, frogs that somehow always hit you. You'll start to get to grips with the emergent gameplay here - can you throw that caveman into that man-eating plant? Yes! Can the explosive frogs create a new path for you? Yes! Can the Tiki Traps be used to your advantage? I'll let you guess.
Gradually, you'll discover the playground that is Spelunky. You'll die hundreds of times before you get anywhere near the end of the game. Shortcuts will be earned, journal entries perused, leaping whip attacks practiced. Before long, you'll be skilled enough to reach the later areas, although not without difficulty, and start thinking about possibly comepleting the game. That, of course, is just the beginning.
After a while, you'll start seeing some of the genius in the game design. How there's always a solid path to follow, that Spelunky very rarely obliterates you out of nowhere - it always give you just enough rope (or lack thereof) to hang yourself in your hurry or greed. How certain items combine together perfectly, while others cripple a run. You'll find favourites, learn that dark levels are a goldmine, and laugh at bats as you swat them from the sky with impunity. You'll discover all the secrets the caves have to offer...
...but no matter how good you get, no matter how many arrows you whip from the air and jetpacks you covet, there'll always be another unique combination of traps and environments to bring you down. After all, in Spelunky, the beauty and madness are in the journey.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. With a title like that you must be in for a heartwarming story of brotherly love, right? Joke's on you friendo, this game comes from Sweden, where even the furniture is stark and depressing.
Admittedly I came to this game with a bit of an "okay, game, wow me" attitude, having heard nothing from gushing love from everyone around me. So to get the snarky negativity out of the way, I have some issues with this game, mainly relating to controlling both brothers at once. I see that the frustration is part of the game's storytelling, but there's a fine line between compelling storytelling through game mechanics and constantly having to adjust logistics because of the wonky keyboard mapping (admittedly, I should probably have played this with a gamepad, but I likely would still have to make the conscious choice to move each brother to their respectively mapped side of the keyboard to keep from disorienting myself). The worst moment came in one section where I literally was incapable of progressing due to overloading my keyboard with the number of keys I was pressing down at once, and had to remap them entirely. BAAAAAD. On a more nitpicky note, I also found the game a little manipulative in points, as if the story wasn't emotional enough without having to punch it up with histrionics.
But that stuff aside, I actually really, really liked this game. It tells a really engaging mythological narrative with absolutely no coherent dialogue or even text. There isn't even any kind of complex facial animation to show the emotions of the two protagonists through the journey, it's all pantomime and gibberish. The harrowing A-plot aside, you have a variety of little b-plots to get lost in, and what's fascinating is the lack of dialogue forces you to interpret the contexts for these stories by yourself.
The other big strength of this game is its absolutely incredible environmental design. If it seems a little bland and fantasy preset-y at first, don't worry, the imagery gets progressively more fantastical and surreal as you journey into the wilds and come across the castles of giants and crystalline ice lakes. The world itself tells stories that range from wonder inducing to downright horrifying (the valley of giants is one especially nightmarish moment with some gruesome puzzles to be solved). It may not be a world you have much freedom to explore, but nevertheless its one to be lost in.
It's perhaps best that the game's puzzles are all incredibly simple for the most part. You have enough on your plate managing two brothers, so complex puzzle mechanics are out. I have to say I wish there was more of a gameplay challenge if only to lend a bit more payoff at the end. However, there are some surprising moments toward the game's conclusion that make more sense of the decision to play as both brothers at once, both in terms of what tasks you will be controlling and what buttons you press to accomplish those tasks. Quite brilliant! Emotive even.
If you're an "always gameplay, never story!" sort of gamer, stay away. This game is linear and entirely based on narrative. If you don't mind that sort of thing, though, and I love it, then Brothers is a real treat. If you can get past the frustating elements, it'll win you over in a big way.

I received this as a gift, so I knew next-to-nothing about this game. I wasn't terribly disappointed, but I wasn't terribly surprised that I rated it lower than the overwhelmingly positive critic and user scores.
The Brothers Grimm-like environments and the seamless transitions akin to Miyazaki's Spirited Away impressed me, but the bad controls and the simplistic, repetitive puzzles didn't. The good idea of controlling two characters at once was marred by the mechanic of often holding down keys to save them from certain death, which struck me as lazy and unnecessarily frustrating difficulty. I would've much preferred cutting down that in half or to none in exchange for intellectually difficult puzzles that required at least *some* ambidexterity.
The untranslated gibberish for dialogue was odd, and it did work at times to enhance the atmosphere and story, but it backfired in the end. There wasn't enough characterization and back-story and too many immersion-breaking deus ex machinas to make me feel more empathetic to the younger brother's losses at the conclusion, and frankly they--the characters and story--aren't memorable. I expected to have multiple endings based on how you interacted with the world, which was wasted opportunity. I did like the part where the younger brother had to overcome obstacles that he couldn't before on his own, but that sadly didn't reach the depth and impact it could've been.
Sadly, I can't recommend this, especially in what I thought was a dissapointing story. If you must play this, wait until there's a steep discount.

What can I say about Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning?  It is an absolute and criminal shame that the company who put this game together dissolved before they could make a sequel.  The story line is decadent and entertaining, and the world has been robbed of a beautiful and engaging series by virtue of developers' bankruptcy.  Still, the only extant offering in the Kingdoms of Amalur series is definitely worth the price to play.  The game devs did not reinvent the wheel with regards to the RPG genre, but their ascendency comes from the wholly customizable class system.  Ever feel limited by the restrictive class system of other games?  Ever feel like your plate-wearing badass would also have access to sneaky, sneaky rogue tactics unavailable to your class?  Ever wonder if your mage would be just as adept at wielding a swords as at wielding magicks?  KoA allows you that opportunity and more with an imaginative and unique system that rewards your playstyle, whatever that might be, and if at anytime you regret your choice, just visit one of the many fateweavers in the game and change it all, for a token sum of coin of course.  Equally inventive are the skills, which are accessible regardless what "class" you've rolled.  All skills have utility: Alchemy makes potions ranging from health and mana to enchancing various types of damage done or reducing that received, blacksmithing creates armor and weaponry for every build, sagecrafting shapes gems to enhance your gear further, and those are just the tip of the iceburg.  Persuasion is decidedly worth the investment, but lockpicking is not, as only a skill point or two will carry you through the game, particularly as lockpicks are plentiful and the minigame is not difficult.  Speaking of difficulty, anyone just picking up the game would be well served to play it on the hardest difficulty setting; I was advised by a review to do so and never regretted it, as few of the encounters will shred your nerves, even on the hard.  If you want hard, go play Dark Souls.  If you want a fun take that shows the potential of what role playing games truly could be, try KoA.  This game is vast, with tons of quests and things to do in Amalur, helping the good people (or not, if you so choose).  I've spent over 200 hours in the game thus far, and there's plenty to indulge your completionist side.  Right now I'm seeking out the few remaining achievements after my first full play through.  The ending was a little lackluster, as though they ran out of time and money to finish the game properly, but the journey itself was rewarding.  Bottom line, for what it's likely to cost you to acquire this game, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a steal, but the real theft is that it's the only one of its line.

Well, this is an odd game to review as its often mistaken for what it is. It isn't Skyrim, at all. A game it is much closer to is Fable. I liked Fable, it's not the most in depth RPG but its fun and the combat is nice. Now, back to Kingdoms. The story line is a typical RPG story, you are seemingly a nobody, but something “happens” and you are now the key to everything. I don't want to spoil the game as the story is nice, but its nothing fancy. Serviceable with a hint of charm is how I would describe it. If you do not like the story, the game is built so you can skip that on and get to the combat. The combat is similar to Fable in how it works, but its much more advanced. You have the typical class choices, a big warrior, stealthy dual blades, wizard. They do differ a lot, and how you build them is up to you, although it doesn't offer THAT much of a choice that you would consider it important for multiplay through other than each class on its own.
The inventory system is not great, but it works fine enough if it is a little cumbersome. Plenty of lot to play about with, and a lot of side quests and mini-stories that do a good job of introducing you to the other elements of the game. I would happily say this game is a good weekend game, you would be hard pressed to dislike it too much. It is not as free as Skyrim and I think some people looking for that type of RPG fix might get a little put off with this game, but if you have ever enjoyed Fable you would do well to give this a shot.

I've been playing Mount & Blade since a demo in 2007.  The graphics are really dated, but the core game mechanics make this game the best mounted knight game I've had the pleasure to play.
Pros:
Combat.
Mount & Blade's core game mechanics make the game interesting in and of itself.  You guide your swings and strikes with your mouse view, meaning the sword will go where you are looking.  You can swing high to take down a knight riding at you or swing low to strike a peasant trying to gut you with a sickle.  You draw your weapon back by pressing LMB and you swing by releasing the LMB.  This means you can hold your sword high ready to strike and then let go at the precise moment your charging steed races by your enemy.
Archery is well modelled and decently realistic (I know, it's not realistic compared to Real Life (worst game evarr imo), but really, M&B does a very good job modelling the fundamentals of fighting with a bow.  I found myself adopting tactics actually used by the mongol hordes because they worked the best (circling an enemy formation on horseback while firing into them with my trusty bow).  Every arrow has is modelled as a separate object and has its own ballistics.  Remember that part in Braveheart where a storm of arrows came down on the Scottish lines?  Mount & Blade has you covered.  Damage is affected by character skill and the speed of your horse when your weapon hits your foe.  A well placed lance charge can outright kill even a tough enemy if you hit him at speed.
Battles.  You can recruit large armies and have mass battles.  You can give your troops basic command (charge, follow me, hold this position, etc.) but the AI does a decently OK job of controlling all the soldiers on the map.  The AI doesn't deal well with formations or tactics, and you have to help it by giving your troops commands.  Despite this battles are fun and even with a large army, the player is often makes the difference between victory and defeat.  Even if you just hang out and watch, your troops with engage the enemy.  Archers will form up and shoot, knights will charge, and your brave footmen will attack.  You can also attack towns and castles.  They're much like battles in a town or castle map, and they're fun too, but I prefer the open spaces.
Cons:
The game has a lot of potetial for RPG elements and greater storytelling, but it's never been really developed.  There's a basic plot of a land with warring kingdoms, and you can ally with one of the kings to rise through the ranks.  Mods can help with this. There are tons of great mods for Mount & Blade.
Graphics.  This is the big one.  The graphics weren't that great in 2007, and now they're very dated.  Thankfully, there are some graphics mods which can take the edge off the dated look, and once you get on the battlefield and start carving out a name for yourself, it won't matter that much.
Anyway, I really recommend Mount & Blade.  It's fun, and I keep coming back to it when I just want a simple fun battle game with intuitive fairly realistic combat with some light RPG storytelling.  I can't wait for Mount and Blade 2!

The big battles can become tedious after a while, due to the fact that many of them are hard and require much time to complete.
