When the main quests are done in one area, you know you'll most likely never return. Why is that? Because the side quests are very poor. No quests are "individual", they're all part of some story line, like the one with the hunter. Or the ambush quests which there are like 20 of. A classic. I've always had the Sims as my "go-to" for casual games. The Sims is extraordinary. EA is still money-hungry, so it's still super overpriced, but you won't regret the purchase.

I'm a huge fan of the The Sims franchise, so it comes as no surprise that I enjoy this game. However, maybe this review is useful to someone already familiar with the series.
There are several aspects about this iteration of the series that I dislike and which make me continue to view The Sims 2 as my favorite. I absolutely abhor having to see paid content in-game without having any interest whatsoever in ever buying it. I already spent more than $100 dollars on the base game and DLC. Why would I be charged for more and what justifies charging for it? Server maintenance, updates, and the cost of a Community Team (does The Sims even have one?) should be more than covered by that. So, besides the major issues of microtransactions being forced down one's throat, it also appears that getting free community content is much more of a hassle.  For starters, there is no Body Shop that allows you to easily create Sims and package them. There is no denying that the new Create a Sim tools are much more evolved and allow for much more customization, especially the ability to modify a Sim's body type, and the addition of true personality traits and combinations are great. However, there doesn't appear to be an easy way to share and obtain community content outside of EA's platform. I could list various other things that bother me about the game (e.g. Why are younger Sims so ugly? Why add rabbit holes?), but I think the attempts at money-making and sharing limitations are the main downsides to me.
On the bright side, the graphics are beautiful and the exploration options endless, especially with the DLC (which, I am sorry to say, one still has to get for a more complete game experience).

GunZ 2 is pretty much a remastering of a age old action TPS, GunZ. GunZ was a fast paced action TPS that involved either great amounts of skill, or great amounts of panicing. That game was fast paced, from the start to finish of any match.
Many advanced players would be sporting their respective fighting styles, and many newer players will be resorting to classic methods of run and gun. GunZ presented many ways to tackle problems; to rush in with your sword and come out like a bad♥♥♥♥♥ or have a heated gun fight and blow some lead into your opponent.
GunZ truly was a to the book, fun game. And here we have, GunZ 2 being released. Now at it's current stage, GunZ 2 is very much in it's early access/ alpha stage, so this review may not be valid if it so changes drastically, or proves me wrong in the future.  Granted, from the time I have played so far, here is what I have gathered.And this may all well just be an extended first impressions, so take it with a grain of salt.
From the get go, the first thing I noticed, was the uniquely different art style that GunZ 2 has. It's a lot less, "dark" shall I say than GunZ 1 in my opinon. But GunZ 2 does have slightly better graphics than GunZ 1, only, it would take a lot of time getting used to it. The style of GunZ 2 kind of reminds me of S4 league, not in any terms of art style, but just how they present their characters ,and how they move about and battle. But it just may be me. Either way, it's definetly a lot different than the original GunZ, but new players of the franchise probably won't get this feeling of disconnect from GunZ 2, which is a good thing.
Another thing I notice, is that the movements of the characters seem a lot less fluid. Granted this is probaly due to the Alpha effect, from the dashing and wall jumping, it just all feels a little clumpy, and even when I'm running around and hitting enemies. The epicness of actually landing my awesome combos in GunZ 1 isn't as evident in GunZ 2 at this current stage. Rather, landing a simple basic melee combo pretty much obliterates anyone and empting out maybe half your clip destroys anyone. Trying to land any fancy techniques could easily get yourself killed by an opponents team mate spraying you down. A very common experience I had was trying to chain a basic melee combo and then get gunned down and literally stunned since my opponent would then trap me in a melee combo himself and I would have no chance of escaping. At least in GunZ 1 I would have had some chance to escape since the basic melee combo didn't horribly trap me in place while taking all my hp away.
Other than some combat issues and some overall atmosphere feel, as GunZ 2 does not feel at all like GunZ 1, i admit it was still really fun to play. It was fun beign put back in the GunZ universe and to experience the fast paced TPS battles I once had. As a near end note, GunZ 2 also brings a lot of RPG elements into play.
The leveling system is actually used in conjunction to skills unlocked in actual combat, gear is now upgradable and has a durability system, and your loadout is preset towards certain gender locked characters during character creation. The RPG elements just seem like a little bonus feature and not much to fawn over, the real thing I want to see is for MAIET to bring back the good old GunZ feel back for us.
At the moment, GunZ 2 does not feel like a sequel, if I stretch it hard enough I could call it that, but it strayed so far from it's predessor in my opinion. Honestly, If they can improve on combat mechanics, combat play, fluid and actually useful movement plays (The dash is pretty much useless since it gets you nowhere, I've chased down plenty of people with my sword while they dashed away like it was nothing. Also, gunning them down with the dash was a piece of cake as well. Wall hanging was a nice thing to have, but it was pretty much just there for stealth players, I'd like them to incorporate a way to be able to shoot off walls. That would be an improvement. And don't get me started with wall running) then I think that GunZ 2 could be an amazing game.
But alas GunZ 2 is still in EARLY ACCESS (At the time of this review/first impression) So I will give MAIET the benefit of the doubt and press on. For all of you who haven't tried it out yet, I honestly will recommond it, give it a little taster, at least for a little while, even if you hate it later.

Having played the original Gunz: The Duel, I thought I had a pretty good idea of what to expect from Gunz 2- I thought the game would have moderately reactive inputs that could be chained in interesting ways to do all sorts of superhuman feats. Although the controls were generally tight, the magic element of the original Gunz- the ability to chain moves together in semi-broken ways to fly around the maps like Neo in The Matrix- is effectively gone, resulting instead in a dime-a-dozen third person shooter.
Unfortunately, Gunz 2 is not just a dime-a-dozen third person shooter; Gunz 2 is an incredibly bad dime-a-dozen third person shooter.  In fact, Gunz 2 is the worst game I have played in recent memory, if not my life.  The multiplayer is plagued by lag resulting from peer to peer connections, meaning that you have to lead all of your shots and that other players move choppily through the levels.  The spawn points for each team are static, meaning that the losing team will often get spawn camped, or that when you're fighting on the opponent's side of the map, someone may spawn in the middle of your duel to make it two against one.  Players are forced to choose their character right when they boot up the game without much indication as to the meaning of the choice, which results in 80% of the players playing as the default "dude with a sword, submachine gun, and sniper rifle".  To get another character, you have to spend a significant amount of in game currency... or real money, of course.  Furthermore, there is literally no character customization that doesn't cost some sort of currency, so the vast majority of people on the map at any given time are completely identical.  Some of the maps are the same as the original, which at first seemed to be a downside, but then I realized how bad the new maps were.  Since the games tend to devolve into a clusterf*ck of identical dudes jumping around with swords in a big bloody pile anyways, the maps almost don't even matter.
The campaign mode manages to actually be worse than the multiplayer.  In the original Gunz, the levels were quick and pretty fun, but here the levels are long, repetetive, difficult, and designed to squeeze your wallet.  The way the level I played (and I have no doubt many others as well) is structured is that you are in an area, you walk forward to a rally point, enemies spawn, you kill the enemies, walk to a new rally point, and repeat.  If you miss an enemy, the next rally point will not spawn, and you'll be stuck with no clue where to go next; this happened to our team, and we walked in circles for a short while before realizing there was a guy a long way back just staring at a wall. Since it's all peer to peer, even the AI lags around, making it almost impossible to hit them.  If you manage to shoot them, you will quickly find yourself running out of your very limited supply of ammo, especially since there are 2 ammo packs spawned after every couple conflicts - to a group of four players.  When you run out of ammo, you're forced to run into the mob of machine-gun toting enemies with your sword, which usually results in the player getting shredded in 2-3 seconds.  Once you're dead, you don't come back to life unless you or a teammate uses a Revival Coin to bring you back.  Realize that these levels last 15-20 minutes, and you could literally be stuck dead for that long. One guy in my party was stuck dead for about 7 minutes near the middle because one guy was unwilling to spend coins to revive him, which must have really sucked.  Although you get 3 Revival Coins daily, buying more than that costs $2.50 a pop.  Playing the first level, my party and I seemed to be doing pretty well, but we burned through all 12 of our new player Revival Coins in around 15 minutes (Buying that would be $30 worth of coins, kids!), mainly from getting cheesed by machine gun dudes.  We almost got to the end of the level, but were dropped into a tiny room where machine gun guys spawned almost on top of us, resulting in the death of the whole party and a game over.
I'm going to uninstall Gunz 2 after writing this review, deeply saddened that the sequel to a childhood favorite could have gone so wrong.

If you're looking for a good Zelda-esque experience, look elsewhere.
I know people really want a good PC Zelda-style game, but Oceanhorn is very mediocre.
I am honestly puzzled as to why Oceanhorn has so many positive ratings, given how many clear faults it has.
-Decent Music.
-Solid Controls.
-Environment visuals are ok.
-Extremely short dungeons.
-Uninteresting/Forgettable dungeon design. (Both in layout and visuals)
-Uninteresting items. (With the exception of Force Spell, and Trencher Boots.)
-No Overworld to speak of. (It's a glorified level-select)
-Boring sailing from island to island with almost no interactivity.
-No open exploration at all. (just level-unlocks hidden in other levels.)
-Terrible animation.
-One Spell has no animation at all.
-Bad voice-acting.
-Very limited enemy types.
-All of the enemies are too easy, including bosses.
-Late game enemies are very sword-spongy.
-Collectables take a long time to harvest, wasting time for no reason.
-No sense of urgency in the plot, ever. Because
: it does not actually progress at all until the absolute end of the game. (As an example: It is like if the entirety of "A Link to the Past" was spent just looking for your Uncle.)
-Shallow and uninteresting characters. (with the mild exception of the father due to narration on each island, but you never really get to know who he is, just that he did some stuff and has a kind of gravelly voice.)
-Painfully awkward "emotional" scenes, where you're supposed to really care about character(s) you've barely even seen before, let alone talked to.
With all of these Cons, Oceanhorn still might be worth getting if it's on a
steep sale, (ie. for $2.00 or less,) because the Dungeons are at least somewhat entertaining, and it is a mercifully short game. But it is
in any way shape or form, worth anything close to full price.
A poorly designed Zelda. Meh.

I bought Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas spontaneously, because I found the graphics interesting and because it reminded me of Zelda - I thought it deserved a shot, although I did think twice about buying it due it being slightly pricy. After two hours of playing it, I was hooked. I loved every bit of the game and I don't think my money could have been better spent.
What makes the game special? The parallels to Zelda games are numerous, but that doesn't have to be a minus. The game has its own charming character and still completely captures the fun of similar games. But I'm not here to talk about Zelda, I'm here to talk about what really fascinated me about Oceanhorn - the extraordinary art style, as well as the great atmosphere. Also, the puzzles in the game just had the perfect difficulty - not teeth-grindingly hard, but not pull-lever-and-win either. I've finished the game at 93% and have enjoyed 22 hours of wonderfully crafted exploration and RPG fun. Thank you Cornfox.
tl;dr: If you like Zelda, buy this game. If you like Zelda A LOT, don't get turned off by the games' Zelda-copying reputation. It has its own mind and it will give you the same magic spark as Zelda did. If you don't like Zelda, Jesus doesn't love you.

I highly recommend Torchlight II.
There are some people out there who would say the game is wortheless, others that it is perfect, and still others who would say it is alright, but fails to live up to other well-known ARPGs.
I say it is non of the above.
Torchlight II is an amazingly well-crafted game. Everything about it is perfect, except for the plot.
The gameplay is excellent. Fast-paced enough for there to always be some action if you want it, but not cluttered and overly fast to the point where there is no time for other things like simply enjoying the game, or inventory management (there's a lot). There is a balance of different abilities, and leveling up is never slow as in other games. And every time you level up, it is meaningful because you always have the opportunity to upgrade a spell/ability, and sometimes the opportunity to gain access to an item (by leveling your stats/skills). The abilities are all pretty fun. Some are more fun than others, and any combination you can think of works. There is no metagame for Torchlight II. You play your way, and it works perfectly. It's one of the highlights of this game.
There is a lot of inventory management, and it only gets worse as the game progresses. There are tons and tons of loot drops, and you will often find yourself going back to town to sell all the useless crap you have, sell some of the valuable items you picked up and stash something away for your other characters. There is a ton of loot. I mean, so much. A lot of it ends up being dupes of the same base item, but with different stat modifiers. I mean, holy crap. So much loot. Torchlight II truly has no metagame. Everything you want, you have. And it is all so-well balanced.
While I don't find the plot as bad as some do, it isn't amazing. It is interesting, yet it fails to motivate the player as some plots do. I wouldn't call it forgetful, and I will make a direct statement by saying it is much better than Diablo III, where the plot is just that a bunch of evil♥♥♥♥♥♥is coming out of hell, and you have to kill it all. Oh, and by the way Diablo is behind it all!
Torchlight II goes further in-depth, and the gameplay is much, much better (did I mention no metagame and even more loot drops than any other ARPG?).
Overall, I would rate this game an 8.5/10, simply because while the plot doesn't suck, it isn't amazing, and because the graphics, while not being horrible are not too impressive. But the art style is very pleasing.

There are a lot of Hidden Object games that do it right, sadly this isn't quite one of them.
I have Windows 10, and considering the release date for this game is listed as 2016, I consider it a significant failure of the developers to not support fullscreen gameplay. For those of us with huge screen resolutions this can be a significant turn-off as the game window will be tiny and can cause eye strain. We shouldn't have to force our monitors to a lower resolution.
While there is some great scenery, especially the intro where you are sent to the past, it is marred by the slow pacing and somewhat sluggish wait times for actions. The music got repetitive fast too, possibly fuelling my sleepiness. So by about a quarterway into the game I just wanted it to be over.
H/O scenes typically take the form of finding a list of items (some requiring additional action to reveal), or finding matching pairs based on their similarities (eg. a gold apple with a real apple, a needle with a spool of thread), ending with a short description of the final, useful item you want to find from the scene. It's a refreshing take on finding items in that you aren't told specifically what you are looking for, or simply handed the random item like other H/O games sometimes do, there is some working-it-out-for-yourself involved.
Unfortunately the story isn't great either. Voodoo mixed in with native Americans didn't make much sense to me, and I didn't understand why the Black Wizard (the evil guy of the game) was a voodoo doll running around pushing things over and stomping on things. Also, you bring all these friends over in the start and later you find them all sleeping in cupboards and wardrobes... maybe they had a booze-up hide-n-seek party while the protagonist was in the past.
One thing I love about other H/O games is collectibles and extras. ... Can you guess?! This game has ... none.

This is probably the only(?) good game EA has their name on.
Yes, I said it. EA has a game that doesnt have stupid microtransaction baits, terrible graphics that are 10 years behind everybody else or pay-to-win DLC.
Primarily, it is because the game is very, very easy. Not you-will-always-win easy, you are perfectly able to lose, but it does follow the somewhat shallow trend of "click this button and you´re doing good!" type of gameplay. Don´t be afraid to start off the first playthrough on hard, especially if you are used to RPGs or even brawlers. If you´ve played any of the recent Batman games, this combat will feel somewhat home-y to you. The Might tree is your "Warrior" playstyle, Finesse covers "Rogue" and "Ranger" and the third and final tree, Sorcery, handles all your Wizardry needs.
And because the game is this easy (due somewhat to the fact that healing potions are plentiful, even solely from drops/vendors and have NO cooldown despite being full heals unless you´re using the first ones at endgame) any player who can handle themselves will gravitate towards the Finesse tree to don the armors that boost damage the most. Magic especially has little merit since it really is just a Finesse Bow playstyle without the critical hits. Not to say that you can´t don a shield and robe and play through this game as a tanky wizard; There´s a specialization for that!
In fact, there are specializations for pretty much ANY playstyle. Whether you want to go for a "pure" playstyle of absolute wizardry, Teleport around in plate armor while firing lightning bolts or be a complete Jack of All Trades, the games Destiny card system will have bonuses that suit this playstyle. You can truly go into combat however you want and not feel like you're doing something the designers didn´t think of. (Unless you´re like me and just want the damn teleportation aspect without spending the points in Sorcery to get it ;~;)
That is probably also one of the selling points of this game, to start off with; The combat flow is GORGEOUS. Without a doubt, the spectacle of combat (At least dual-wield combat, from my playthroughs) and the flow between enemies is pretty much the same as in the Batman: Arkham [Word] games, only without the QTE prompts to avoid hits or change targets. Instead, abilities, dodge rolls or even teleportation lets you avoid big hits and zoom between enemies to perform more beautifully animated combos. You can feel the weight behind the heavier weapons, and the devs know exactly when to slow the game down and where to hold on a pose to get the most out of each hit. Even though you´ll be seeing the same exact hit combo throughout 95% of the game (the Main Story which I completed in 34 hours, with casual but active side questing in between) you won´t grow tired of seeing it.
As for the visual style, the game is best described as if World of Warcrafts art team had to design for Skyrim. You have large, beautiful world areas with lush forest, canyons with huge rock structures and shapes and wide open plains but still kept in a comic book-y, colorful palette that is almost like a childs imaginary world. The game is played in third person, but try and remember to turn the camera and look around, because it is indeed a beautiful game to immerse yourself into.
So,
SHOULD YOU BUY THIS GAME?
I would definately say yes. I got it for €20, and for that price it is well worth the fun you´ll get from the base game alone. If you´re the type of person who likes to replay the game, but in a different way, the Destiny cards definately allow for tons of fun here.
Now, there´s also 2 DLC areas, the Legend of Dead Kel and the Teeth of Naros. I´ll quickly cover these two;
THE LEGEND OF DEAD KEL DLC:
This DLC is very well suited for those who just finished the main quest line and want some more Kingdoms of Amalur, and get the best items. A big thing at the end of this DLC is that you gain very, very easy access to lots of Blacksmithing materials, which makes it a billion times easier to craft the best armor possible (Not needed in the slightest, but hey, if you want to catapult a giant across the map with a sneak attack, here´s the way forward!) once you complete the quests to own your own keep.
The story takes you to Gallows End, an island ravaged by Dead Kel. You meet a small town of survivors who seem to pray to an otherwise unknown god, and through ship stealing and offerings for human possesion, you´ll uncover who this god is, why Dead Kel is angry at everyone on the island and just how owning a pet rat is actually quite a neat thing.
The DLC is feels relatively short in terms of the main story, but considering the €10 price tag and all the side content that you have to enjoy, I´d say it earns the price tag. It´s not needed (nor is any other DLC) to enjoy Kingdoms of Amalur, but if you have the spare euros and want an evening or two of fun, then you can safely purchase this one. It´s just as good as the rest of the game, and even introduces an interresting AOE mechanic from a new mob (even if it is just a reskinned enemy skeleton). I reccomend to download and play this after reaching the level cap at 40 (or, if you are short a few levels and don´t want to spend an hour or two farming mobs, 35+) for the best rewards for your effort.
There is only one problem, and that is that the final quest has a somewhat buggy NPC AI that doesn´t always go where you need(read NEED) it to go to end the last main quest. Look on the unofficial wiki for a couple of easy ways to fix your NPC pathfinding at the end. As long as you don´t save once you´re standing on the beach with no NPC in sight to talk to, you should be able to reload the earlier (quick)save and fix it right up. Don´t let this scare you, just be aware of it :)
THE TEETH OF NAROS:
I feel this is really the one where EA might have shoved the content out without some proper QA. If you look this up on the unofficial wiki (AND YOU SHOULD!) you´ll realise there is a downright scary amount of bugs that can hardlock your character in this region. I reccomend saving outside the DLC area before and after going in (checking no bugs occoured of course) and only saving inside using F5 to quicksave and F9 to quickload. Look up every quest to be aware of potential bugs. As with the bug I just mentioned, they are avoidable with reloads, but there are so many you really want to look up what you´re doing.
The DLC feels a tad bit shorter than the Dead Kel DLC, but perhaps this is just because I rushed the main story for the reason I just mentioned above.
This area looks and feels very different from the rest of the game, with an obvious roman/greek influence. I feel the main selling point (besides some more KoA fun!) is the it offers the best core components for weapons in the game, better than the Prismere available otherwise. Perhaps best is that if you, like me, feel Prismere looks more like rock candy than deadly crystal, these components resemble the earlygame iron counterparts, but with better damage than prismere. If you´re sad that your OP weaponry looks horrid, this DLC fixes it!
Overall, if you don´t mind being careful with (quick)saves, it´s also worth another €10.
Oh, and as for the weapon pack, it´s not endgame related and NOT needed. Don´t waste money on it. You´ll get more fun out of throwing the bills out the window and watching the wind catch them as they fly away.

One of the most enjoyable RPG's I have every played, whilst not as visually attractive as games such as Skyrim, The Witcher and Dragon age, it offers a colourful environment which is very pleasing and interesting to view. Kingdoms of Amalur does the mechanics so well with easy to use menus to filter through armour, weapons and other items. Combat is fantastic, it is simple yet there are so many options available to you, with so many different types of weapons. Any 2 weapons can be equipped at one time and mapped to a single button, however this doesn't mean you have to choose between one hulking big hammer as your primary and a piddly dagger as your secondary, you can choose whatever you wish; two handed great sword and a warhammer sure thing! No waiting until the end of the game to unlock cool armour as its readily available from the start, and you will always find yourself picking up new and interesting weapons and armour pieces which makes you feel like you are always progressing. You can change your characters build pretty much when you want for a small fee and aren't restricted to certain weapons for a certain class. Everyhting is down to you and you can make the came play how you want. In addition the game is massive with so many places to explore and quests to complete, they are very samey however they never feel repetative due to the how well the rest of the game plays. Overall 9/10 my only real problem is the fact you can't instantly jump between your map and the quest log. Menus load fast and are super responsive and saving the game can be done in seconds and your back playing (useful when your saving every 5 minutes like me). EDIT: It saddens me that the developer has now gone, as I feel a sequel would have been hugely succesful and would have built on this games solid foundations.

I'm writing this review as of Patch #2 in early access (December 29th, 2015).
Let me get something out of the way first: I bought this game in Early Access purley because I love RWBY, and I wanted to support the development of this game.
As of right now I can tell you that the game looks amazing and has good music. As well it also has online co-op and a few levels. The combat is fun, you gain experience and upgrade your specials. The combat does need some work though, I've only played through what is here (4 levels) and it seems like just jump around and spam attacks and run if you need to heal, It can get a little challenging later on when more powerful enemies are introduced, but there isn't even a targeting system which most games of this genre have. And obviously the game is short of content. But hey, this is early access and is being worked on by a small amount of people. I hope these things are improved upon, and of course more content will be added.
As far as optimization goes, I don't know how it was on release but right now I can play it at ultra/1080p @60fps no problem, there may have been a few lag frames here and there but it wasn't any serious lag besides a few seconds when an explosion happened near a group of 50 enemies, So yeah, it runs pretty good for me.
Overall I'm excited to see what becomes of this game and can't wait for future updates. But because of the Early Access state, I only recommend it now for people who are huge RWBY fans and want to support development, as there is only about an hour of gameplay to play right now.

Brutal Legend is a game with identity issues. It can't seem to decide if it wants to be an open-world action-RPG, a real-time strategy game, or a driving simulator and due to that indecision none of those elements feel fully thought out or completed. The only thing that is thoroughly fleshed out is the Heavy Metal theme. There's sections that look like they were ripped right off of a Metal album cover, units that embody (or mock) fixtures of Metal culture, and a deep mythos that melds Norse mythology (the most Metal of all known mythologies) seamlessly with all that is Metal. Of all the shots Brutal Legend takes that just miss the mark, the commentary and the love of Metal is dead on. The game has the rare quality of producing lore that is instantly humorous but on a second look, is equally as capable of being taken seriously. That quality, and the fact the gameplay is switched up so often, makes it difficult to get too annoyed with its shortcomings. The familiar faces and voices of a couple stars in the world of Metal doesn't hurt either, even if they are overused to the point of parody.

Metal.  Pure and simple.  Brutal Legend is a combo of an RPG and RTS with a ton of driving in it.  The games art design, locations, characters, and literally everything else are based on heavy metal music album covers and bands.  The developers got several metal artists to do voicework, including Ozzy Osbourne, Rob Halford (Judas Priest), Lemmy Kilmister (Motorhead), Lita Ford (The Runaway's).  Jack Black voices the player character, Eddie Riggs.  If you're reading this review (or any of the others) I'm sure you knew about this game prior to seeing it here.
The game has an epic soundtrack, consisting of over 100 tracks from 75 bands.  Great voice acting.  Great story.  Gameplay is a lot of fun.  Driving around the map is absolutely AWESOME.  It's one of Double Fine's great games that probably won't ever see a sequel.  I highly recommend this to EVERYONE, but it is an absolute must buy for fans of metal music.

Gameplay-wise it's not exceptional - average, really -  and I found the story mode rather short.
However, the game makes up for that in other ways.
It's a game where a hot-rod built by titans races a taxi driven by a demon in a field of exhaust pipe cacti.
It's a game where half-naked amazons ride fire-breathing sabertooth gorillas into battle against gangs of emo zombies.
It's a game where you play literally face-melting riffs against a spider composed of chromed engine parts.
It's a game where every scene and landscape looks like it belongs on the cover of a 70s or 80s heavy metal album, the story feels like it came from the song lyrics of said album, roadies are ninjas (it makes sense in the context), and there are cliffs built out of giant loudpeakers.
Yes, it's that kind of game - set in a delightfully insane world, full of tongue-in-cheek humor, quirky characters, and (how else) plenty of METAL.
It's the most f***ing metal game you'll ever play, and you'll love every minute of it.

Even though I'm a huge fan of Farsight's Pinball Arcade for the PC (having logged over 233 hours on that game) as you can see I've only played Stern Pinball Arcade for about 15 minutes before posting this negative review.  It is Sep 2017 and I just learned that this Stern version of Pinball Arcade even existed.  I never knew I even had a reason to look since a handful of Stern tables did gradually show up in the good ol' Pinball Arcade.
As exited as I briefly was to learn about a 'new' Stern Pinball Arcade with amazing and much newer Stern tables like AC/DC etc - and that it was free to download and try out on Steam, my dissapointment with this 'new' Stern version of PA was immediate and a bit painful.
While downloading Stern PA, I took time to read many of the reviews on Steam and was suprised that most were negative.  I silently hoped that maybe the reviews were older and that they had fixed those problems by now.  Once I started the game though I figured out that most of the reviews were sorely true even at the time of this writing (09/10/17).
First though - Some good things.
1) Early reviews mentioned many serious glitches.  Starting problems, crashes, ball rolls around like their crawling through mud, etc.  I didn't experience any of that on my launch.  The game runs perfectly on my mid level gamer PC, the audio is excellent and in sync with the action on the table.  The interface to get to the games is doable.  A lot of people complain about the interface - and I agree with them and their many suggestions for improvements - but, once you get into Farsight's mentality about navigating an odd interface, its not so bad.  It will get you where you need to go.
2) I assume Farsight has struck a deal with Stern to reproduce Stern's newer tables, but only if Farsight can make a new product/game licensed solely to Stern.  I understand why Stern did this - Stern want's a premium price for their new virtual tables to complement their actual machines, they want to steer the virtual fans to real pinball machines (where the money and fun is) and they wan't to make a profit - virtual or real - because they are still in business, unlike others.

So much for the good - now the bad and the ugly
1) Oh My! Configure the game for the highest resolution your new monitor supports and it looks horrible.  Farsight just pixelates and stretches the screen to match its highest supported resolution which appears to be about 1024 X 768.  It looks horrible, unplayable, almost a joke.
2)  Original Pinball Arcade allows me to play my old Williams/Bally games (and a couple Sterns) in high resolution and those games are beautiful, playable, winnable.  Not so with Stern PA.  original Pinball Arcade lets me set my monitor to portrait, which I flip 90 degrees to give me a large size top to bottom playfield in 1920 * 1080 and it looks awesome.  Not available in Stern PA.  Not even an option.  All you get is 1024 X 768 cartoonishly stretched to your post 2007 computer LCD flat screen.
Some people blame Stern for handicapping Farsight's efforts.  I don't see it happening that way.  Farsight promised a good popular product to Stern to license those machines, and Stern took a chance hoping to take their skills to jump into the virtual space.  Stern is charging a premium for those tables that they pass onto Farsight and us, the consumer.  I'm all for it, I've got some money, but Farsight is making Stern look bad - the Stern machines in this rendition are unplayable, ugly, ameaturist.  Its not Stern's fault except that they approved this project to go ahead.
Farsight, for the love of God, please improve your game (resolution/quality).  New tables are nice and all, and I want to play them.  My wallett is busting with game money but I can't send a cent to your coffers till you up your game.

While tables prices in Stern Pinball Arcade are quite steep compared to the already not exactly cheap Pinball Arcade tables, ACDC and Star Trek are two absolutely brilliant tables. Both modern Steve Ritchie designs, they have amazing depth and are highly playable, with flashing shots clearly indicating what to hit next as well as very crisp and powerful audio - ACDC with the booming sound effects and thumping hard rock (I´m not even into hard rock but ever since the Guns´n´Roses table it´s my favorite theme for pinball!), Star Trek with a dramatic soundtrack and satisfying jingles.
The interface is quite odd and rather counterintuitive, and I wish I could make the table itself darker compared to the table LEDs. However, once I´m playing the tables those downsides just melt away.
Mustang, despite looking quite garish, is actually a very nice, deep table with a ton of fun modes and a nice soundtrack-picking option, so that´s a great freebie!
I absolutely love the normal Pinball Arcade, but with the way more recent Stern designs I´m amazed that pinball still keeps improving, with industry veterans still pumping out fantastic tables. Yes, the tables are rather expensive, but they are also very much worth it for enthusiasts.

I don't know where to start. I guess I should start by saying that I really like Farsight's Pinball Arcade game, so I largely ignored the negative reviews and went ahead and downloaded this. To say I'm disappointed would be an understatment.
There are a host of technical issues, ranging from crashes to poor controller support, but the most glaring and obvious is the way the game stretches what appears to be a (1024x786? maybe?) letterboxed window into a 1920x1080 screen if "fullscreen" is selected, and uterrly ignore the resolution settings in it's own configuration panel. The result is an image that is blurry, pixellated, stretched AND letterboxed to the point of almost comical ugliness.
Added to this is a UI that is completely inscrutable. As I said before, I'm a big fan of Pinball Arcade, but that game's UI is pretty terrible. That being said, Pinball Arcade's UI is a masterpiece of visual clarity and usability compared with the Stern-branded product. It feels like it was designed by a programmer with no UI/UX experience and went through no testing before being unleashed upon an unwitting populace. Clunky with a mouse or touchscreen, but completely opaque with a controller.
Finally, the branding and messaging. I'm really confused. Why does this product exist? Why does it need to exist? Farsight already makes the vastly superior Pinball Arcade, which has a number of Stern tables in it. I would love the rest of these tables to join them in PA. Why not release them there instead? If the issue is that they need to be released outside the established "season" model to be financially viable, so be it. Even if there is some market or licensing reason why this second product is needed, why on earth not simply reskin PA and avoid the need to reinvent the wheel or maintain multiple codebases (as seems to be the case here)?
The thing that is clear is that there needs to be some kind of communication from Farsight about what is going on. Educate me as a consumer on why I should want to have both and why there need to be two so obviously overlapping products.
At the moment, this seems to be a huge overreach by a small team that already struggles with the technical support of all their PA skus. Adding a second product, particularly one that is so obviously not sufficiently product tested, does Farsight a huge disservice in the long run. I'm certainly not going to buy pinball tables for THIS game, and the lack of communication regarding how this affects PA makes me more reluctant to continue investing in their flagship product as well. A strategic misstep all around.

A lot of people tend to compare Oceanhorn with past installments of The Legend of Zelda series. I can understand why, but in my opinion, it evokes far fonder memories of an old beauty called Landstalker. The platforming style used in Oceanhorn mixed with it’s gorgeous graphics and expansive world make it a pleasure to play. Find our more in our Oceanhorn Monster of Uncharted Seas Review!
Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas’ storyline is fairly basic. Boy’s father sets out to slay a twisted beast, boy heads out to find father, boy learns he needs to collects emblems of Earth, Ocean and Sol to help defeat said beasty, boy makes friends along the way, finds beefed up equipment to help him with his journey etc.
However, I feel that the true beauty of Oceanhorn isn’t the story. The storyline plays second fiddle to the satisfying exploration and combat system. The most enjoyment when playing Oceanhorn is from the many different islands you’ll visit and landscapes you’ll explore.
Environmentally speaking, each island is beautifully portrayed. One such island is covered in abysmal fog and rain, whereas another depicts an incredible rocky landscape. The islands are all unique and each hold their own secrets for you to uncover.
Some players notice when playing Oceanhorn that the whole thing really is quite reminiscent of Zelda games. The enemies are similar; certain characters seem to have walked straight in from another franchise; and the sailing mini-events that take place whilst traversing the ocean waters will have you thinking you’ve accidentally launched another game.
However, I implore you to ignore the feelings that you’ve played this before. Overlook the fact that some concepts seem borrowed, and think more along the lines that Oceanhorn is a culmination of different concepts brought together into one vast gaming experience.
Oceanhorn easily holds strong in today’s gaming world and delivers a fulfilling experience from both it’s gameplay and design.
When playing the Steam version of Oceanhorn, the main character is controlled via the ‘WASD’ keys, whilst aiming and attacking is controlled by your mouse and mouse buttons.
Various equipment can be acquired throughout your journey that, not only plays an integral part in combat, but also helps in gaining access to areas of the game that would otherwise remain inaccessible. Such items come in the form of bombs that can be used to blow away boxes or rubble; and a bow and arrow that can be fired at strategically placed targets which act as buttons to open doors or move pillars out of your way.
There’s also a few spells to procure along the way, such as fire to melt ice, or a force spell which summons objects to the area you’ve aimed your cursor. There’s even a secret spell to unlock by obtaining a certain amount of items known as bloodstones. If you’re lucky to chance across one, it can be acquired by hacking away at it with your sword until it gets added to your inventory.
Box puzzles await your brain and act as a nice little break between taking on constantly respawning enemies. When completed, these box puzzles will reveal pathways to destinations unexplored or drop treasure chests that contain a nice little bonus of gold or XP.
Gold doesn’t seem to play much of a role in Oceanhorn but it’s still handy to accumulate. Merchants provide the service of stocking up your extra items, I.e. bombs, arrows etc. and they can also sell you extra hearts to increase your maximum health.
Levelling up is great fun because each level you reach will unlock a little extra bonus for the game. Some of these bonuses are gaining a gun to shoot monsters or obstacles when sailing around the world, or decreasing the amount of stamina used when blocking attacks.
Another thing I quite like about levelling up is the title rewarded with each level. For example at level ten, you’ll be given the title of “Voyager” and eventually you’ll work your way up to “Legend”.
But one of the most fun additions to journeying through your quest is fishing! Yes!! Everyone loves fishing in a game!
Basically at a certain point in the game you are awarded a fishing rod. Take this good ole fishing rod down to a body of water and commence your new adventure!
You’ll catch different kinds of fish and you’ll also be catching fish of differing lengths. The bigger the better.
Catch all species of fish and I wonder what happens…?
The combat in Oceanhorn is simplistic in nature and does away with all the bells and whistles seen in some hack’n’slash games. Left click swings your sword; right click utilises whichever extra weapon/item you’ve got equipped; the ‘f’ key casts whichever spell you’ve equipped; left-shift brings up your shield to act as defence against attacks; and space-bar toggles sprint, picks up and throws an item or acts as the action key.
If you’re expecting a massive challenge from Oceanhorn, you might be a little disappointed. Monsters found throughout Oceanhorn aren’t that difficult. Some of them will do a lot of damage when they hit you, but you can always block those attacks with your shield. Most enemies will wait a few seconds before commencing their first attack which usually buys enough time to defeat them quickly.
Some enemies are a bit more dastardly and will manage to get a few hits in before you kill them. This will result in a heart or two of your health being taken away. Health can always be replenished from hearts that drop from monsters, or are found when destroying an object like a vase or cutting down grass. If you do end up dying, you’ll respawn at a previous checkpoint.
Thankfully, bosses happen to be quite engaging and fun! Each boss will tend to follow certain patterns or require you to perform a specific action before being allowed to damage them. However, bosses found earlier on in the game can be quite easy and you’ll find yourself being able to handle them with little difficulty. When you get further on in the game, the bosses become more challenging and you’ll be relying on your reflexes, as well as your gear, to dispatch them successfully.
Graphically, Oceanhorn shines brightly. The environments and colours found throughout are gorgeously detailed and display beautifully on a sharp screen, be it computer or iPad.
Enemy design is well thought out and you can see that a lot of love has gone into their creation. Boss design is brilliant and each one brings it’s own flare to match the area you’re traversing perfectly.
The music is nice to listen to but certain areas might have you reaching for the mute button. In particular the Hermit’s Island. Sound effects aren’t too bad but some sounds, such as when your character runs out of stamina and starts puffing, come across as a bit forced and sound like it could have been done better.
Voice acting isn’t that great. The actors sound wooden and devoid of emotion. That’s why I preferred to play with subtitles on so I could still follow the story without having to listen to the dull voices.
In summary, Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is a splendid release from both FDG Mobile Games GbR (iOS version) and Cornfox & Bros. (Steam version). The whole game is a joy to play and would be best enjoyed by younger gamers as an introduction to RPGs.
The game’s main story takes around ten to fifteen hours to complete, but if you want to fully explore everything and get one-hundred percent complete, you’ll probably find yourself investing quite a few more hours.
Beautifully designed and superbly created, you’ll find yourself wanting to jump back into the world of Oceanhorn quite often. Definitely worth a look!

A very fun, if often fairly easy, Zelda-like puzzle game that is absolutely worth your time to play. Set in a world following a huge magical war, you set off in search of your father, who in turn is hunting a massive sea monster known as Oceanhorn. Follow in his footsteps as you gather some strange relics in order to finally have the power to confront the beast and perhaps find your father.
The story is fairly lighthearted and quirky, with a very Zelda-like feel. Characters are all sketched out very quickly and loosely, and you're expected to really like people quickly. I didn't always find this to always be the case, but warmed to what the story was aiming for pretty quickly. I'm about 2/3rds of the way through the game at time of speaking (as far as I can tell), and am looking forward to diving even further in to what this game has to offer.
Pros:
- Lighthearted, fun story, with a rich backstory and lore
- Controls are really solid for PC, especially with it being a mobile port (don't let that scare you off, the game looks and plays like a PC native game, and the price is more than fair)
- There's plenty of content to explore, lots of fun secrets, and cute puzzles
- Great unlocks as you progress, opening more of the game to you and rewarding players who note down places of interest earlier in the game.
- Interesting monsters to fight, with tactics to learn as you move forward.
- Some really fun boss fights!
- Graphics are charming
Cons:
- Your character's attacks are sometimes a bit unresponsive about specific directions
- The storytelling can be a bit weak sometimes
- Puzzles are occasionally quite unclear, and solutions are sometimes just finding a hidden button under some breakables
- Sailing is often pretty dull, which is a shame
Overall, this game is a solid 7.5/10 so far, and is well worth picking up and playing. The asking price is more than fair, but getting on a sale is just icing on top. Will update if necessary when I finish this game!

This game is a kick in the eye to everyone who believes 8K 144fps is the ultimate gaming experience. It is equally so to everyone who believes gaming's golden age was during the 16-bit era. As far as I'm concerned, Spelunky is damn close to a perfect game.
Notice I didn't say
because if that's what you're looking for, you're missing the point. Spelunky is just a game, and that's all it's trying to be -- one that does its job exceedingly well.
This has perhaps the best gameplay mechanics of all time. At its core, it's a rogue-like platformer. You explore caves, and they change each new time you play. You grab gold and gems. You throw bombs. You climb rope. You kill enemies. You try to find the next exit.
Okay, that's par for the course but what makes this so good is all the mechanics that are meant to be discovered. What happens if you whip the gold statue? What happens if you grab a ledge while in a freefall? What exactly do those goggles do anyway?
Because this is a rogue-like, so much about this game is based on chance. Yet, as you play again and again, the skills you learn really do matter. Unlike many similar games, there's a clear sense of progression as you move forward, and even the slightest victory seems monumental.
This is easily the weakest part of the game. There isn't much story apart from collecting gems and trying to make it to the next exit. Rescuing the girl and being awarded with a kiss (and thus a life) is such a tired trope, I really wish developers thought of something else.
But if you're looking for a story, you're missing the point. This game is about chance and skill: at the intersection is whimsy. And to highlight just how much this isn't about whimsy, you can select from a broad selection of characters, many which will be unlocked as time moves on.
As already implied, you don't need a GTX 1080 Ti to run this game. This is a 2D rogue-like platformer, and it looks like a 2D rogue-like platformer.  That said, I'm exceedingly glad that this game isn't trying to look "retro". There's little overt pixelization of sprites. Everything looks clean and crisp.
Of course, I realize earlier versions did have a "retro" style -- and that version can be acquired as freeware. If you're going to pay money for this game, it
look better than the freeware version, and it does. Even so, the revamped graphics keep the spirit of the game alive.
From the opening screen, you know you're in for something special. The 80s-inspired soundtrack pumps you up. I found myself humming along as I traversed the levels. You just feel so much is on the line.
The sound effects are a work of
. When you capture gold or kill an enemy, the sound just gives you a fine sense of accomplishment. When you hear everything, you know you're in a world of fun.
Many PC users scoff at the idea of using a controller, but in this case, you absolutely should. This game has a certain rhythm that cries for an XInput controller. That said, if you're the kind of person who only has a keyboard, that won't keep you from enjoying the game. Keyboard works flawlessly. It's just that a controller is a nice enhancement.
If you have almost any PC made in the last 10 years, you should be able to use this fine. It may be possible that those cheap sub-$100 tablets won't be able to handle it. But then again, why would anyone want to game on those devices?
One thing I don't understand is why there isn't an official Mac or Linux port. It's not as though this game is hard to port. In fact, there's several unofficial ports flying around the Internet. So why not love for users that prefer an OS other than Windows?
Sure, I have quibbles, but those are slight. This isn't just a classic, but arguably one of the best games of all time. Certain gamers may take issue with my assessment but the proof is in the pudding: despite having almost no fanfare at initial release, the community grew by word of mouth. People still pour hours of time despite this game being nearly 10 years old. This is because the gameplay mechanics are just so damn good.

This is my favorite game ever made. It is a "perfect game." Being on a Mac, I found some weird wine port that stopped working after a while, then I had to play Spelunky classic after that. Finally I installed Windows on my Mac for the sole purpose of playing this game, and to this day this game is the sole reason I ever turn on that side of the computer. Anyway...
If you're a fan of platformers, stop reading this review right now and just buy the game already! The game is like Mario. In fact it's inspired directly from that, and handles much like it, from player proportions to the feeling of movement. There are even direct parallels to goombas: the snakes that move back and forth and splat when you jump on their heads. Now that I think about it, all that's missing is some parallel to koopas - an enemy you can jump on and then kick t0 have it bounce around destroying blocks.
Spelunky combines that classic formula with another (roguelikes). All the levels are randomly generated so you can pretty much play the game forever. Since the walls are always shifting, you cannot memorize a route, but must always be thinking on your feet to judge the situations. Due to the perfect stun system, health system, and emergent, interacting elements, you can and will die a million different ways. But that makes winning all the more special. In all my hours of Spelunky (possibly triple what it shows on Steam) I have beaten hell only twice and both times were amazing.
There is a soft time limit (the ghost) that is often criticized by inexperienced players possibly coming from the min-maxing hell that is Isaac. After 2:30 in a level (plenty of time for even the slowest players to make it through the level and still have time to spare), an invulnerable ghost will appear and follow you, and if it touches you, you die. Noobs will complain that they can't fully explore the level, but the solution as it stands is perfect and elegant and would be boring otherwise, and forces you to, as said earlier, think on your feet. Just trust Derek Yu knows what he's doing on this; he runs TIG Source and knows more about game mechanics than probably anyone.
A very elegant solution to the modern rogeulike (unlike say Isaac).

So for me there was lots of random clicking to see what things do, and in one case I was instructed to find something in the picture that I had no clue what was because I hadn't visited the location in the game where the thing goes yet. But no penalty for misclicks or anything so I just guessed.
The game only took me just over 4 hours to finish, so I'm glad I got it on sale.
Biggest problem I had with this game was I suffered a couple of Fatal Errors while I was playing, requiring me to relaunch the game to continue. Seemed to do it at points where it autosaved, so I rarely lost any progress. Though in one case it set me back about five minutes of play time. Not too bad, but still annoying to have to repeat steps I'd already taken.
Overall, if there hadn't been those gamestopping Fatal Errors, I might've been confident recommending this game to some HOG players for the interesting story alone, but getting dumped out of the game randomly makes me hesitant to do that.

An Honest Aussie Review:
Is this game beginner friendly?
Yes and no in a way, its easy to spam moves against the cpu and other low leveled players online however that changes when you rank up online so then it becomes more of a challenge in blocking and punishing moves that take long to recover from. I'd rather go and try something like Marvel Vs Capcom or Street Fighter which is probably a litlle easier to understand as the move list is rather small in comparision.
Player Base?
Player base isn't that big as you can imagine, if you have a console i'd recommend you play on that instead if you want to find a quicker match, however the matchmaking or 'NetCode' is fairly good for the PC version as you would imagine.
Story good?
Story is meh, personally im not found of story modes in arcade fighters but if you are theres enough button mashing and content to keep you entertained for a while but dont expect hours as it is a fighting game of course and Tekken isnt really known for its full long story gameplay.
Bruh Roster Trash?
Tekken 7's roster is great in my opinion as it brings new fighters into the mix, meaning new moves and play styles to make online fighting more interesting and difficult. You of course have some of the iconic characters like Jin, Yoshimitsu,Kazuya, Eddy, Kuma, Law, Paul while also bringing new fighters such as Master Raven 'Similar to Raven in a sense' Claudio, Lucky Chloe, a new Jack, Akuma from Street Fighter and many other uniquely designed characters.
Gameplay?
Similar to all the other Tekken games before however it now has the new Rage system which acts similar to Street Fighters special bar but instead is only gained once throughout a round when your health is low enough. You can use it to extend a combo or create an opening or just use it to gain some space getting away from a wall and so on. Moves are updated from Tekken Tag 2 and some new moves have been added along as well.
Overall i would recommend this game to all Intermediate fighting game players and potentially Beginners depending on much time you are willing to spend in order to get familar with the mechanics and long move lists and no be scared away from the game due to move spammers and silly loses.

If you don't like 'Brothers', then you simply don't like video games at all. Well, okay, maybe that's not entirely true and I may be a bit melodramatic when saying that, but I really can't figure out a reason why someone would dislike this game, other than the fact that it's pretty short. Although making this game longer would most likely deter from it's beauty. Simply put, this is one of the best and most original puzzle games that I have played in a while, and although it's not exactly the most difficult, the reward is in the storytelling. It's not easy to portray emotion in a video game without saying a word, but this game pulls it off in style.
While I agree that all video games, no matter how bad or good they are, are a form of art, this game is a shining example of it. Emotional storytelling combined with controls that make sense not only to the gameplay, but say even more on a narrative level, 'A Tale of Two Sons' shines the most when it comes to how we interact with the characters. By giving players the opportunity to control both brothers at once by utilizing the dual sticks on your gamepad, 'Brothers' takes storytelling through gameplay to a new level. This may sound difficult to control at first, but after a few minutes you'll get the hang of it and will often forget that you're controlling two people at the same time without much thought.
This game more than deserves the amount of praise that it has been given and I hope to see more video games that utilize this control concept. The art style here is fantastic, the variety in gameplay will keep you entertained the whole way through, and the puzzle elements although simplistic are incredibly fun when combined with the controls. The asking price may be a bit high for such a short game, but the next time this one is on sale, I would recommend picking it up to pretty much anyone.

Okay. Hello, if you are reading this, then you may be wondering why I gave it a thumbs down. It's simple.
Though I love the game, it is in need of some early design changes and more development.
First of all, the script. I feel that the character interactions are pretty genuine "for the most part" with some cheesy lines here and there but the problem is, is that the conversations are very brief and there's a lot of silence. I'm not talking about the bugs where some of the audio doesn't play or the filters don't turn off, I mean those moments where your running around and theres nothing. Though the world is expansive, I think there needs to be a lot more cutscenes and conversations. That would be the same with battles as well because there isn't a "WOW, it's battle time" or "OMG, so many grim, quick get ready", it's just "grim, fight, defend." so I feel a lot more should be added there in how they are presented and to show off the characters relations more.
Next is the battle system. Combined with hints of RPG elements, I honestly think it's a bit bare and very much hack and slash. I would say it needs to be changed up a bit more and there should be options for stance changes so that guns have a use in the middle of melee combat rather than just being "a thing" and so players can focus on dealing with groups or an idividual enemy in a style that suits them.
A minor issue I have with this game is that despite being a team, RWBY doesn't do much other than hack at the same enemy so I think more Utility should be added in with the abilities rather than "USE TO WIN" because said abilities honestly feel weak after a while, make health pick ups/life steal a thing and also, reduce the amount of staggers the enemies have on you and make them a genuine threat. I would also suggest adding a system so that teammates can shout out commands to guide each other but also so they can shout at the grim to lead them away and have an alley sneak of to help their downed friend.
So far, it feels like a 6/10 but it could be much better.

Oceanhorn is one of the best games I´ve played recently. Whereas most games have lovely ideas but lose the big picture, this game has, well, only a small idea but nails it. The idea: to make a smaller and indipendent version of "The Legend of Zelda". Some reviews compared it to The Wind Waker and they´re probably right. From the first to the very last moment you won´t get rid of the feeling that a certain Triforce and a green hat are missing. Nevertheless I´ll leave out comparisons and focus on the things that hit my eyes.
This game is not for hardcore adventure gamers, I fear, as it misses the great challenges. However, for beginners or "easy players" this game will be a great experience. You should read my notes under this assumption.
+ short game time: A fact I like most of the times is if a game doesn´t take too much time to complete it. There may be some collectables left, but I finished most of the game and the story after around 9 hours.
+ appropriate graphics: The game is designed lovely and nice to loook at
+ easy and accurate controls: Played on a controller, there were no difficulties and the buttons are occupied cleverly
+ easy puzzles: Whenever a chest is hidden or the way blocked, it won´t take a lot of experimenting to find the solution
+ lovely music: well-composed, supporting the settimg - you will love to listen to it
+ cute settings: suitable even for children
+ easy boss fights...
- ...which are really too easy. Once you found out the right tactic you can´t fail
As I said, Oceanhorn will not be the right game for hardcore gamers, however, fans of "The Legend of Zelda", beginners in the field of Adventure and lovers of cute stories will definitely have their fun with the game.

Most people here complain about terrible performance without bothering to turn framerate killers like MSAA and volumteric lighting off and/or setting textures to high(very little difference between high - very high - ultra textures). I personally run on high - very high settings with a GTX970 and i5-6600k (both not overclocked atm) and get 60fps most of the time.
As for the annoying DLC and season pass ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t, I hate that too, but you can just ignore it for the most part. However, I really hope this trend doesn't continue - singleplayer games with microtransactions suck.
As for the gameplay, It is basically very similar to Human Revolution. You can play the game how you like, be it stealth, guns blazing, non-lethal or lethal, your preference. Obviously I can't say much more than that since I haven't played for that long yet. This review is mostly to debunk some misinformation that is being spread.

At this point and date, it's just sad that people are OK with full priced games being broken and/or incomplete. I see "turn X off, turn Y off, keep Z below ultra for better performance" everywhere. Umm, if your game only works when I turn some a visual option off, what's the point of you "developing" it? This is not acceptable for a AAA game, let alone a game of the Deus Ex franchise.
I have seen a guy who was OK with lip sync being horrible just because "devs didn't hide it was horrible beforehand". So that's it, huh? Devs can just say "yeah we screwed up lip sync in a game where dialogues are the main part" and get away with it, and you're still OK with paying full price to a game that doesn't bother trying to deliver a better experience.
I have refunded the game because it didn't even start without me disabling all the pre-purchase DLC's  which are, by the way, apparently for single use only. Trying to force microtransactions in a full priced SINGLE PLAYER game is not even funny guys, come on. This, yet again, is another stain on the great franchise that is Deus Ex.
Still, I am a huge fan of the series. But my 5 years of hype disappeared faster than Adam doing an Icarus Dash, so I will play this game at some point in the future.

As a forewarner, this game has quite possibly the worst netcode in existence. Seriously, if you aren't the host (it uses *peer-to-peer* hosting in 2014), your shots register about three-fourths of a second behind where you are currently looking, making it impossible to hit people whom are usually dashing about incessantly, meaning any character not focused on AoE or wide-arc melee will be left missing well over two-thirds of the shots tehy would have otherwise rightfully hit with. To test this yourself, play games until you get host, and notice your accuracy and kill ratio skyrocket astronomically when the game registers your shots properly.
The classes are an awful change to the GunZ system. Players are given little to no detail about each class other than a vague single-word descriptor like "heavy" or "gunslinger". When a player chooses a class, they are effectively locked into that class until they grind enough gold (which admittedly isn't hard) to try another class. Weapons are locked on a per-class basis, so to try all weapons in the game, you'll have to grind ~70000 gold (around 60 wins, up to over 100 losses) to unlock all the classes, and then an additional 15000 gold per weapon, plus upkeep costs, because there is a tumor-like durability system built into all weapons purchased with in-game money.
Most of the weapons are, according to their stat bars, objectively worse than other choices. There is usually one weapon other than the default that is considered "good", with the others having severe deficiencies that make them frustrating to use. Ranged weapons, as per the awful netcode, are basically spray-and-pray with little to no skill involved, as the mental gymnastics of seeing the future to land a hit is, understandably, a bit much to ask of any human being.
The melee is overstated and overemphasized. Melee combos are unbreakable, meaning that once you've been staggered by one attack, if the enemy is in range, they are free to melee you until the comobo ends, usually with an automatic knockdown, whereupon they are free to pull out automatic weapons and spray you down for what very little of your health is left afterwards, because melee does way too much damage. As a result, you will often find yourself literally losing to knives in a gunfight because melee is basically a free 1v1 win as soon as they land one hit and lead into a combo with you being left staggered and unable to get out of the way because the netcode is so awful that by the time you've gotten down the timing to dodge out, they'll already be registering a hit on you on their screen, and then it has to go through a P2P host network, and by that point everything is a complete crapshoot except for the fact that you will automatically lose if you don't have your melee weapon out before they start hitting you. But really, if you need to have your melee weapon out before a melee gets to you because ranged weapons are severely ineffective, you might as well exclusively play Ivan and swing a katana, because by god it's the most reliable way to get a kill.
The only way to get permanent weapons is through either level-up reward crystals or through cash-shop currency, both of which run on a luck-based lottery system prevalent in many korean F2P games.
Overall it's a frustrating mess of a game and wouldn't reccomend it to anyone. It's a buggy, sloppy, laggy mess of a game and  will probably be dead within half a year in its current state.

"The perfect videogame" isnt a term that should be thrown around lightly, yet so very, very many times now I have heard it applied to this one game.  In addition to that, Spelunky is also one of the games that is responsible for kicking off the whole trend of adding roguelike elements to games.  Enough time with the game.... and it doesnt take much... and chances are, you'll see just why both of these ideas might apply here.
Spelunky is nice and simple to start with.  At it's heart it's a platformer with a nice, simple goal:  climb downwards through each level, and reach the exit without getting murdered by something.  The simplicity also extends to just how you play it, as the controls are very streamlined and easy to learn.  Jump, whip, pick up and throw things, and use bombs or ropes.  There's no complicated combos here or the need to select items from an inventory or anything like that.  The controls are very much what you'd expect out of a classic-style platformer.  So it's nice and easy to get into, and will just feel great the whole time.
And that's a good thing, because one of Spelunky's stand-out traits is the sheer difficulty of it.  You will die.  Often.  Even once you've performed the ancient ritual of GIT GUD, you're still going to die often.  If you watch even the best players out there, they still die alot.  Spelunky is a game that wont hesitate for a moment to stomp you into the dirt.  You cant take much damage in this game... you start with only 4HP, and getting more health is very difficult, requiring you to rescue a "damsel" and take them to the exit without getting them killed, at which point you'll get exactly one more point of health once the level is over.  Which is great and all, but it only helps so much, because lots of things either do a good bit more damage than just one point, or they just instakill you.  In fact, the number of ways the game can insta-kill you is really high, even compared to other games of this type.  Maybe you'll get crushed by something, or fall on spikes (which are everywhere) or even have a teleporter mishap and blink yourself directly into solid rock.  Or a billion other things that can go horribly wrong.  And even things that arent "instant" kills can still end your run pretty much instantly anyway.  Psychic projectiles, fired by certain exceptionally powerful foes, dont instakill you... but they do a whopping 10 damage per hit, and can hit you multiple times.  Similarly, bomb blasts also do silly amounts of damage.  Or perhaps you'll get stunlocked.  Most forms of damage will cause your character to become stunned for a time, just laying there, but you have no invincibility during this.... you can be hit again, and this will reset the stun.
With dangers this brutal, the game may sound a bit unfair.  However, this is not so.  At no point is the game genuinely unfair.  Nor are the odds as stacked against you as they may seem.  One of the biggest reasons for this is a major concept that the game uses, which is that if it seems like a particular interaction SHOULD be possible for a particular entity or thing, it probably IS possible.  Take the shopkeepers for instance.  Friendly at first, they'll go absolutely bonkers if you try to steal from them, turning into a geriatric tornado of shotgun pellets and murderous rage.  They are extremely fast, leap around like maniacs, have high HP.... but something like spikes will insta-kill them just like it does to you.  Hit them with a simple rock, and like you, they will be stunned.  Like you, they'll drop the item they're carrying (their shotgun) which you can then grab for yourself.
The rules that apply to you apply to everything (with a couple of extremely specific exceptions).  Enemies cannot damage each other via simple contact damage, but other than that, the level is just as dangerous for you as it is for them.  Traps for instance, which are very common throughout the game and take a great many forms, dont give a flying fart about who or what the target is:  They simply activate when the conditions are right and try to kill their target.  The nasty arrow traps in the mines for instance fire a single super-fast arrow forward when something crosses their line of sight (fortunately they can only fire once).  In most games, this would only happen to you.  But in this, even a bat or a spider can get splattered by these.  Or maybe a caveman gets stuck between a Tiki Trap and a wall, and gets stunlocked into oblivion by it's deadly spikes.  Understanding how the interactions in the game work, and putting them to your advantage, is an important part of dealing with the problems the game will throw at you.
It's also a huge source of fun here.  Often, events will play out like some sort of deranged Rube-Goldberg machine, with one thing causing a chain reaction that causes all these other things to happen.  In the ice caves for instance, a yeti might step on a landmine.  This explodes, sending a nearby rock through the air, which flies across the room, knocking you (or someone else) over the edge and into some spikes.   Your failures are many, but they're often so darned funny that you're just not going to get too bothered by them.  There is a saying that is often applied to Dwarf Fortress, which is "Losing is FUN!!!", and this saying can apply here too.  The developer did everything to make sure that the game gives off a sense of constant fun and hilarity no matter what is happening, and it works brilliantly.
Of course, none of this would matter if the game's content weren't up to par.  But it is.  In here you'll find a wild variety of items, objects, and monsters to deal with, as well as fun-yet-deadly levels to go through.  These levels are fully destructible, too, able to be blasted apart with your bombs (or some other things), which of course can bring about even more chaos.  In each level there are also plenty of things to find.  You're in this for the money, after all, so finding gold and other treasures is part of what it's all about.  You may also find useful items hiding away in crates.  And of course, you can buy things from shops.  And these items are just FUN.  There's lots of entertaining things to find and use, and even when it comes to items that might be "bad" in alot of ways... like the camera... you'll likely find yourself using them anyway simply because it's fun to do.  There are many, many ways to play Spelunky, and you absolutely dont have to be approaching it in a super-serious way all the time.  Players have come up with TONS of ideas for special "challenge runs", just because they can.
Of course, your initial goal should just be beating the game, and this leads to the one real issue:  The game's difficulty really is very high, and it's likely to seem like a rather cruel wall at first.  Chances are, you will struggle to even get out of the mines, the first of four major areas.  And even once you get out of there, the next zone, the jungle, will absolutely murder your face. LOTS of players get stuck on the jungle.  But it's a testament to the game's design and the sheer fun of it all that even the most beseiged players usually never give up.  Even if the game keeps trashing them, they just keep coming back for more.
And dont let the apparent simplicity of the game fool you:  This is a game about depth and skill, and you have many options in terms of how to deal with any situation.  Making choices about how to handle things is a huge part of the game.   An arrow trap in your way, but no rocks or skulls around to set it off so you can pass?  Stun that nearby caveman, pick him up (yes you can pick up stunned enemies, just like you can pick up everything else) and chuck HIM into the trap's deadly gaze.
And I've ran out of space.  Yet there's so much more to say!  Suffice it to say...this is a good one. One of the best, even.  If you even slightly enjoy platformers... you need this one.  It's a classic in every sense of the word.
