My brief take on KoA: I recommend this game if you enjoy action RPGs in fantasy settings.  Having said that, I should point out that I haven't actually finished the main quest, and have been on a hiatus from the game for a couple of months, but I am looking forward to getting back to it in the not too distant future.  I've started the game with a couple of different characters in order to see how different choices and character builds affect progress, and I feel like doing that has been reasonably rewarding, although there are not many choices with significant ramifications (they typically relate to which reward you get for completing a task or side quest).
I do recommend you wait to get it and its DLC on sale.
My less brief take:
For me, this game's strengths are an open world that's fun to explore and nicely designed, a combat system that encourages players to try different combat styles, fairly engaging stories within the main quest and the factional side quests, and some interesting/funny NPCs, particularly in those factional side quests.  I'm sure I could have finished the main quest in the amount of time I've played, but I really liked doing the factional quests and spent a lot of time on the Legend of Dead Kel DLC.  That was among my favorite storylines in the whole game, at least so far, which is why I recommend getting the DLCs in addition to the base game.
The most noticeable weaknesses are that the simple side missions can get repetitive, inventory and crafting could have been designed better and crafting is not very useful until you've leveled your crafting-related skills up somewhat, and there'll come a point where your character and weaponry is leveled up past the point where combat is very challenging in most instances.  (On that last point, take a look at the article on the Amalur wiki that describes the "Area-Level Cap" - apparently you can compensate for this to some extent if you want to amend your play style to do so.)
I bought a discount bundle containing Steam keys for the base game and the two story expansion DLCs from another online retailer; I paid about 25% of the current full price of $40 for the collection.  I certainly feel I've got my money's worth so far; I'm not sure I'd recommend paying full price for it, but it does go on sale on Steam pretty often, and it's definitely $20 worth of entertainment if not a bit more.
If you're considering buying the game, you may be wondering why the game doesn't have a great deal of name recognition, and whether that lack of recognition reflects the overall quality of the game.  While it has shortcomings, I think the game was unlucky in that (a) it was somewhat overlooked upon release because it was viewed as competing with Skyrim, though the two games are pretty different in terms of tone and overall experience and (b) the developer went bust in a very public fashion not too long after release, which I think cast something of a pall on the game's ongoing reputation, or at least did not help it any.  If you like open world action RPGs and are willing to overlook some minor flaws, I think you'll be pleasantly surprised by this game.
If someone buys the game's intellectual property, I'd love to see either a sequel in similar format, or further development of the idea for the MMO that was supposed to succeed KoA.

Should you get RWBY at this stage?
No.
Should you keep an eye on it?
Yes.
The game, as it stands, has a good start to everything. decent level design, decent character design, good fighting, fun to play.
but... theres just so very little of it, and a couple design decisions so far I view as detrimental to the fun:
-Less than a hour of gameplay
-The combos are unpolished and don't string together as good as they should. Ranged combat and close combat don't flow together very well in combos, though you feel they should in many instances.
-The enemies are mostly fun to fight, but a lack of variety and invunerability frames make them sometimes a bit of a nuisance.
-The invunerability frames deserve their own mention. In my opinion, and in no way a objective statement, the invunerability frames are entirely unecessary considering the quantities they are used in (4/7 enemies use them), and could easily be replaced by simply being un-knockbackable when doing attack.
-Invisible walls, oh the invisible walls. Good luck jumping over anything that isn't a destructible crate.
-Boring story that isn't silly enough to laugh at, or delivered seriously enough to want to know more about at this stage.
-the characters lack mobility. If you watch the show, theres so much mobility with characters using recoil and agility fly everywhere. In the game, recoil is a afterthough, and characters really only have a boring dodge roll to rely upon to move around.
-The characters sometimes don't play as you feel the characters should (looking at you Weiss >.>)
-The levels feel very uninspired. All the cool parts of the levels that you WANT to interact with are locked behind invisible walls, leaving you with current-realm textured "corridors" and empty wide fields to fight the enemies in. It certainly isn't bad, and some areas like the underground actually have a couple of interesting spots. But so far, combined with the invisible wall problem, just isn't anything to write home about.
Normally, I'd say 15 dollars would justify the small amount of content, but considering steam sales...
I'd say, if your a huge fan of the show, its worth it at this stage to bounce around as your favorite character.
If your not, follow the games development and watch the forums. Early access is like kickstarter. Any money you put down should be considered a investment, like the stock market. Sometimes you win, sometimes you lose. And for a first time developer, the risks are high. Keep an eye out for this one, its either gonna be great, or it will be a alright game that can't compete to its rivals in the genre.
Remember, this is my subjective opinion, and as someone who's not tried a huge amount of spectacle fighters, take my word with a grain of salt. But I would definitely recommend waiting at this stage unless you like to late alpha-test games.
Edit: Initially, i put this as recommended, but upon second review I changed it to no. Not a no entirely... just not at this stage unless your just DYING to play something, anything RWBY related at this moment. also added a bit more opinion to the review.

Headbanger or not, you owe it to yourself to feel the tough metal love coursing through the veins of this game. Made by talented and imaginative people from Double Fine, Brutal Legend tells two stories: A story about the adventures of a roadie called Riggs in the wild, dangerous and breathtaking land of Ormagöden. It is also a tribute to the glory of Metal as well as being alone on the unknown road, heading to the unperceivable fate.
The story is near perfect, with varied main missions that don’t get boring, as you drive, hack and command your troops to victory with many music legends that have voiced the memorable characters that you meet on this unforgettable ride. There’s chase, fury, standoff against insurmountable odds, there’s laughter, sadness, love, betrayal and payback time. The graphics are still standing well, with the land of Ormagöden that remains one of the very best fantasy settings ever created; its landmarks and the trip through it will take your breath away on a regular basis.
And then there’s the Deuce, the most important character in the game, the one that you’ll spend most of the time hanging out with, a hell-bent and timid car that you’ll drive and try to subdue all the time with its touchy and sensitive response. It can be and will have to be upgraded and molded into the death dealing machine if you intend to survive. You also have a trusty axe and a set of flashy moves that you’ll learn to implement on the skulls of your enemies, God of War-like style. If that’s not enough, there is a full-on, fast and furious RTS as well, where you’ll control your troops and resources as you try to take down the enemy stage. Loyal headbangers are your army, fans are your resources, and your music stage is the center of power. There’s even some meta-jab at the necessity and the power of merchandising that did not go unnoticed. There’s multiplayer that is still active with frenetic and quick battles, if you want more Brutal Legend after you are done with the single player experience.
It all sounds well and majestic, and for the most part Brutal Legend truly delivers. But there are some problems under the hood: vehicle and fighting controls are very touchy and best suited for an analogue controller, side-missions do become a busy chore after a while, and the real time strategy bit is good but not great due to overall complexity and a mix of game genres. I have to mention that Giants: Citizen Kabuto did strategy-action-drive mix much better. You’ll do just fine with a mouse and a keyboard, but there will always be that nagging feel at the back of your skull that you’re somehow being tied down.
Brutal Legend is not perfect; it has an attitude and a greater that life character. But man, what a ride this game is… It’ll slap a wide smile over your face that won’t come off until you are done playing. Get it, feel it, love it :D

The gaming world is awash in fantasy RPG-style games that all look, sound and play exactly alike. For that reason alone, it's hard not to give BRUTAL LEGEND an enthusiastic thumbs up for its refreshing originality (a Double Fine signature) and the sheer coolness of what it's aiming for here. I am reminded of FULL THROTTLE and this is a worthy successor to that classic.
However, in practice the gameplay is more exhausting than fun. The hacking, slashing and electrifying all work great, but most of the other controls are kind of funky -- I am having particular difficulty with the damn car, and when I think of how beautifully the vehicles work in the BORDERLANDS series, for example, I know that Double Fine could have done a better job with this crucial element. The map is another example -- it took me ten minutes to figure out how to get from the map back into the game... which you DON'T do by pressing the same button that got you into the map in the first place. Frequently, the game plunks you down into an action setpiece with no guidance and no clues as to what you're supposed to be doing.
It just seems that there are unnecessary awkwardnesses that could have been ironed out with just a little more time in development. And all these little things conspire to suck a lot of the fun out of what's otherwise a really unique and original game. It looks great, it sounds great, it's got style and spirit, but the controls and (so far) the lack of a really fully realized Open World keep BRUTAL LEGEND just shy of greatness.

Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a very moving, powerful game. This is a game that will in a sense, keep you on the edge of your seat, not so much due to QTEs, or huge set pieces ala Tomb Raider, where your adrenaline is pumping, rather more in the vein of the emotional sense. Brothers is a puzzle game at its core, but one that is highly story driven, despite the game only taking three to five hours to complete; it is one of the games that I have played that has left such an impression that I don't think I am like to forget this game anytime soon...or ever.
Set in the Medieval Ages, this game finds two brothers who set out on an adventure (I can't stress this word enough adventure! This is no mere quest as we so often find within RPGs today and of yester-year.) The two brothers embark on an adventure in order to save their father by journeying to the tree of life. Along the way these two brothers will face many obstacles, they'll encounter great beauty and many dangers. The two often go hand in hand, which makes this adventure feel even more like an epic adventure. I think I liken this to the 1984 film “The Neverending Story” in many aspects. The two brothers will come across and meet many people and creatures along the way. Some of these moments are more memorable than others, like passing through a village with a little girl who has a ball. You can take the ball and pass it back and forth or play keep away, you can even drop it down a well if you're feeling mischievous. The human element in this game is one of its greatest strengths, I would say it is its greatest strength. As I have said this game focuses on emotions. You'll feel a wide array of emotions. I personally never really ever felt anger or the need to kill anyone in the game. If such a part came up, I only felt that I had to for self preservation. Starbreeze Studios captured that emotional pull very well, all while managing to never invoke that feeling of vengeance, anger, or hatred. What you will fell is sadness, joy, excitement, compassion, and a slew of other emotions swirling around in a pot. The language is akin to what you would hear in the Sims, so while you aren't able to understand what is being said, the body language and facial expressions more than make up for it. This, I feel adds even more so to that layer of emotion.
Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons is a game that everyone should play once at the very least. Mind you this game doesn't really have any replay value, still it should be experienced by everyone. This is a game about humanity and human interactions. The way you interact, the choices you make (which are few) all coalesce into the overall experience of what this game is about rather well. It is a jaw dropping experience!
I'd  would really like to go on and on about the game to tell of my adventure, but this is a special game, and so it is far better for you to experience this adventure for yourself than it would be for me to tell you about it.
Now, the art direction of this game is phenomenal! Your eyes will be treated to some of the most beautiful level designs I have seen in any game. The game is powered by Unreal, so don't expect the graphical fidelity that you would see in Far Cry 4 or Shadow of Mordor. The way the art team handled this game, though makes it absolutely beautiful amidst the backdrop of the story. The striking beauty clashes with the deaths in the game, so much so that many of the deaths you see look peaceful and beautiful, again only invoking sadness and compassion, not anger. The texture quality for the caliber of this game and its particular art direction is more than satisfactory. I had no issues with the textures, I experienced no pop ins or anything of the sort. It should be noted that there is no graphical options other than resolution and gamma, but honestly that is all you need in this game anyway.
The other very noteworthy factor of Brothers is the the sound design. It complements the art direction. The audio is quite rich and flavorful. The ambient sounds can be heard clearly and I did not experience any muddled audio. The score is also very well done. The developers and the composer implemented each score at just the right time to maximize whatever emotion they wanted the player to feel at that ime. Damn good job on their end.
As for the gameplay. It is fun and exciting, it never grows dull as this adventure really does take you to unexpected places. The developers added the right amount of freshness to prevent a dull experience, however, the gameplay is not flawless. I had some issues with the controls, with getting one or both of the brothers to do what I needed them to do. I felt that the controls could have used some more work. This is the only gripe that I have with this outstanding title and it is a minor one, as the gameplay is pretty solid, just not as perfect as the other aspects of Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons. I experienced no bugs or glitches during my playthough, and while the game is quite short by today's standards, I was very pleased and felt the QA team did a good job as did the programmers. I must confess that I look forward to Starbreeze Studios' next IP. They have certainly developed a game that will stay with you.

Spelunky is easily one of the best rogue-likes ever made. It's brutally difficult - the tiniest mistake, or the slightest whim of not progressing carefully, can result in an instant death, or at the least, harsh punishment. I've put about 20 hours in at the time of writing, and I've not gotten even REMOTELY close to winning. Not even halfway.
What makes the game great, beyond it's difficulty? Well, it's fair, almost always. Your deaths are your fault - you didn't look carefully enough, you reacted too slowly to a bad situation, you hurried too much. There is the occasional death from just... the most unfortunate circumstances, such as a glorious moment in which you're knocked around 3 or 4 times in hitstun, straight into some instant kill spikes, but I'd say that's rare.
What makes Spelunky so... replayable, is that it is QUICK. You boot up the game, you can press a button to skip the main menu entirely, straight into the "level select" area, in which you can take shortcuts to areas after you have reached them a couple times and met some prerequisites. However, you can not win the game if you do this - it's impossible. When you die, you can press a button to immediately get back into the action, we're talkin less than 2 seconds. It's... addicting. Just one more run... I'll do better this time. It's a great time-killer, since unless you're pretty good, most runs don't last more than 5-10 minutes. It's an amazing, well built cycle of throwing yourself at the brick wall in the best painful way.
It's just plain fun. Rage inducing? Sometimes. But even with my BIGGEST rage quits, I'm often back within the hour. The gameplay loop is just that satisfying.
Do you want a great rogue-like game with infinite replayability, a satisfying gameplay loop, and kills a lot of time, without much actual time commitment? Buy this game. It's easily worth full asking price. Just get it.

As I glance through some other user reviews I see a lot of positive comparisons to some of the leaders of the RPG genre: Skyrim, Guild Wars 2, Fable, Diablo and Torchlight. Personally I saw the closest resemblance to World of Warcraft with its visuals and questing system. However, this is no clone of a game. It has a unique identity that, in part, is made from borrowing successful traits from these other titles. What stands out most strongly to me about Kingdoms of Amalur is its narrative and world lore. It presents fresh ideas and throughout my 95+ hours (including 210 quests completed) with the game it always felt consistent, like the developers shared a unified vision of what they wanted this world to be.
Without discussing any specific plot points, I'll say that things begin on a high note and intrigued me right off the bat with a mystery surrounding who this character you are playing as is. It is a special feat in my mind to be able to have a personalized, voiceless protagonist that you are expected to project yourself into also have a predetermined, very interesting back story of their own. Too often these types of characters are just a boring blank slate.
My sense of progression through this world was wonderful. Your journey begins far from a major warzone and consequently you merely hear stories about it. As you advance closer you begin to see more immediate effects like sons and daughters gone off to fight or altered local economies. Eventually you'll see large refugee camps causing overcrowding problems and burned down towns before reaching the warfront itself. By and large, the settings you visit along the way stand apart from each other both visually and in local story. The exceptions to this are some of the dungeons that look and play very similarly, just with different layouts and quest objectives to fulfill. For a game already so big I think it would have benefited from cutting some of them out.
All dialogue is voice acted and of good quality. There is some noticeable reuse of voice actors among NPCs, but that is excusable for a game of this size. I would rather see good voice actors reused than bad voice actors brought in in greater numbers.
Combat, unfortunately, is just adequate. There isn't enough depth here to stay compelling throughout. There is a nice mix of weapon types that all control very differently, but you're likely to pick one or two early on and stick with them. Magic brings some cool spells to the fray but are very limited in number. Leveling up is a good, customizable system that does gradually add new abilities, but not enough to keep things from going stale. To be clear, I never got to a point of hating battles. However, a combination of things getting too easy by the end, the long length of the game and repetition of enemy types eventually sucked a lot of the enjoyment out of it. I will warn you that it is possible to become over leveled if you do all side quests as you find them. Google "Amalur Wiki overlevel" to find a guide for avoiding this.
I'll wrap things up with a few more minor critiques. Loot is dealt out in such volume that inventory management becomes a chore (similar to many Diabloesque games). Despite this abundance of gear it was surprisingly infrequent how often I found something better than what I was wearing. Also, before long I had more money than things to do with it. I play most games on Normal difficulty, including this one, but didn't find enough challenge here so I suggest playing on Hard to most players. The orchestral score was competently produced but lacked the artistry to make it memorable.
Overall, Kingdoms of Amalur: Reckoning is a fantastic, expansive experience that could have benefited from seeing its great length reined in a little bit.

There are already several excellent in-depth reviews here on Steam so I'll keep this short.
I really enjoyed playing through this game. The story is done well and offers some fresh takes on your standard fantasy fare, the world is huge with plenty of places to go and things to do. The DLCs are worthy expansions that add new world areas with yet more places to go and things to do, along with some nice loot for your troubles. There is a tremendous amount of content here.
You don't pick a class for your character, like in the elder scrolls games you build your class up from skills, and you can mix and match pretty much however you want. The skills can be easily be reset at any point for a nominal fee if you want to try something different.
Combat is fast and fluid, nothing turn-based here. You need to learn to dodge and hit your enemies from behind, or use a ranged weapon or magic and blast them from afar. It's also possible to get a teleport dodge that does damage as you pass though enemies. You can equip two weapons at a time in any combination and switch between them fluidly in combat. Once you've filled a gauge, you can unleash awesome kill moves to quickly take down difficult enemies.
The graphics are bright and colorful and look good, with an art style that reminds me of WoW. The animations and effects are well done so combat is fun to watch.
There's a few cons, the biggest one being game balance. Early on, the game is fairly well balanced, but each zone has a level cap on the monsters and loot which spawns there which you can easily exceed before finishing all the quests in that area. This makes the later parts of the game laughably easy unless you've just been rushing through the main story missions. Also, the developer unfortunately went bankrupt making this game so there will be no fixes, sequels or additional content, which is a real shame given how great this game is all things considered.
Overall, an excellent game with a few small issues that can be easily overlooked. Make sure to get the DLC as well.

CONCLUSION:
PROS- Great gameplay, compelling characters.
CONS- Lazy ending, microtransactions.

Before launching I decided to take a quick look at the Steam reviews. The endless negative reviews were not encouraging. The problem however is even if the reviewers were experiencing no performance issues they were providing a negative review simply because on the Main Menu, under a Store Sub menu you can waste your money buying extra praxis and credit points. If not for the million silly thumbs down reviews for this I would not have even looked under the store page.
As of early morning Aug 24 using the most current Nvidia drivers 372.54 and a GTX 1070, Win 7 64 bit, 32 GB Ram I'm experiencing No Performance Issues. Running at 1440p with Motion Blur turned off, MSAA turned off as many are recommending, and Volumetric and Contact Shadows at On as many are recommending. Everything else is at Ultra. With these settings the game runs great and looks excellent. Fortunately the youtube videos I had seen before the launch didn't do the game justice. It looks very good.
UI / Keybinding highly customizable. You can turn off many notifications, rescale the UI (how many games give u that option?) and can have dual bindings for everything.
For those that can't figure out where your DLC / Pre-Purchase items are - There is literally an In-Game Guide telling you exactly where they are and how to use them. Tab -> Shows your inventory -> on the left is a tab that says storage -> this is all your extras.
The one major con I do have right now is it even tells you these items are one Save series use. That is if you use them in this save and start a new game they will not be available for that new game. This is completely inexcusable, particularly with how Deux Ex tends to encourage either Lethal or Non-Lethal play throughs where many people will have at least two separate games. I've been reading that this may get changed as it should be and hopefully soon before such pointless nonsense blemishes the game. Fortunately this may only apply to consumable items like praxis and ammunition and not weapons - i have not tested it myself yet.
Ultimately Square Enix could've and should've saved much face by avoiding cheap cash grabs with a totally avoidable menu-linked store & one time use DLC. I also see they launched a Deus Ex Go App (paid) that lets you get more in game praxis. These are all ridiculous and provide cheap targets for an otherwise so far solid game.
If you're actually interested in playing a Deus Ex game and not finding reasons for false outrage you'll probably have a good time. Have a decent card, download the latest drivers, use above recommend settings and adjust as necessary. Performance will only get better as new drivers & patches come out.

Blah blah Zelda Blah Blah
Oceanhorn takes place in an archipelago inhabited by several sentient races. From fish dudes to eagle people. From several types of humans to even machines. Also the occasional demon. There're also ghosts in the postgame dungeon. Like all video games, it starts out peacefully but everything turns to hell and some random kid with a destiny has to save the world. To do that, you hunt an ancient relic from the technologically advanced past named Oceanhorn but there's a twist...which I'll save for those who play the game.
The main character is the aptly named Main Character (or Hero). At the start of the game, his father writes a note saying how his (the father's) destiny is linked to Oceanhorn, which also means the Hero's destiny is too because that's how video games work). He then goes to attack a giant robotic crab. The Hero then wakes up on a different island inhabited by one guy named Hermit who sends you on your way to avenge your father and save the world. All the while a Black Boat stalks you from just off screen except when plot demands otherwise.
The game then continues like all action games: you visit scenic locals; a desert, a dense forest, some ruins, a quaint little town, a floating rock, etc. and you upgrade your gear, learn to use magic, and learn just how special you are because your parents are doubly special. Once in a while, you fish or throw plants at the head of their gardener/Hero's love interest because you (as the player) are a sociopath.
The controls are exceptional for a game that was originally an iOS game – at least with an X-box controller. The only issue that can, and totally will, happen is how easy it is to fall off a ledge and have to redo entire sections of dungeons again. It's not game breaking but it can be annoying having to back track several screens because you were pushed off a small walkway or you just got to close to pick something up or to avoid another thing. It's great that being able to jump down ledges is a thing – it allows for a bit of a different type of exploration – but it's frustrating to no end when you've done it too many times. Other than that, combat is fairly fluid. Arrows and magic go where you send them and there are never too many enemies on screen to make one have to panic. The puzzle aspects don't interfere with combat when they're intermingled (meaning boss battles).
Sadly, the plot isn't all there. I'm not saying there are any plotholes but some of it just feels rushed and just didn't feel deep to me. A random girl suddenly being your love interest is the most obvious one. It's not a main plot in the story so it might just be something that bothered me slightly and you might be totally fine with it. The game is all narrative which, is fine, but it's easy to miss things or important information can be easily forgotten. For example, if you don't talk to the correct people or find certain bottles then certain side quests aren't going to be available to you. Nothing story related is missable but you might not get to full health, arrow/bomb capacity, or challenge completion (if you're into that though, you're probably using a guide). The game keeps going after you beat the main boss so even then, you can go back and find what you want to. Nothing is permanently missable. Some of this might just be mobile limitations that unfortunately show in this PC port. I don't do a lot of mobile gaming so I'm not sure what is and what isn't great.
Music is a very subjective subject but I can say that I found it to be perfect. It fits the mood and helps provide immersion. Nobuo Uematsu wrote a track for the OST so that's all you really need to know. I like to add official sources where one can preview it so here's a link.

Probably the best battle simulator I played. The main "plus" is a competent AI (both friendly and enemy). The main "minus" is no tutorial or explanation. The graphics are minimalist--just enough to give you the info you need. The GUI takes some getting used to. And so the game is "hard work" ... but rewarding when your plans succeed. The player must study the map, study the Order of Battle, and consider how best to make use of time & space. The scenarios appear pricey, but you can be replaying them for years.

One of the best and most unique war games ever made. It is very much not a board game masquerading as a PC game as many war games tend to be. It actually makes you think like a commander, looking at the overall picture and reacting to a rather solid AI.  It is less “solve the puzzle” and more “art of war”.  This game will pull you out of your comfort zone of war gaming. You set an order to your HHQ and watch the AI plan and execute the whole battle. Or, you can micromanage an armor battalion and try to overrun defensive positions. The game rewards combined-arms tactics so don’t be afraid to mix up your OOB and attack with a infantry and armor battlegroups. The AI is rather adept at planning your tasks but you are free to tweak paths, formations, supply preference and even pre-attack build up points.
Wishlist: I wish the map overlays would update without pausing the game.
The base game is free, so you have nothing to lose. Make sure you RTFM.

From an art style point of view you will struggle to find a more beautiful and original game, but when that game also gives you "the feels" it becomes something truely special. Like rereading a favourite book from when you were a kid, it is both as exciting as a it was when you remember reading it, but also nostalgic and familiar for its sense of old fashion story telling.

A wonderful and emotional story told without words (At least, not real ones).
Beautiful visuals, great music.
Controlling the two main characters will take a bit of time to perfect, but becomes second nature near the end.
Some small puzzles are added in, nothing too difficult.
The only downsides to this game are the price and the length.
The game tops out at just over 3.5 hours, and that's with getting all the achievements.
The current price (at this time, $15 USD) may be a bit much for some to spend on a short story (even if it is good).
If you don't mind a short emotional story, get it when it's on sale.
If you're a cold hearted person that feels no emotion, or you're too "macho" or "manly" to have normal human feelings, go play something else.

This game is unique thanks to its absence of dialogues, you can only guess what the characters are trying to say from their nonverbal communication. It doesn't hurt the story though, instead of listening to cliche phrases you can imagine your own conversations.
The Two brothers complement each other in order to overcome obstacles and puzzles. The puzzles are not particularly challenging, but that keeps the story flowing and frustration at bay. Instead of trying hard and being mad at the game, you can admire the beautiful environment, scenery and music. Also this game convinced me to buy a gamepad. You can play it with keyboard too, but the controls are much more intuitive and immersive with a gamepad.
Game is fairly short but i think the length is just right to keep the story intense. Also the game mechanics are not complex enough to keep you interested for longer period.
Although the game seems peaceful, you will get your share of adrenaline and fighting.
In my opinion the main strength of the game is it's streamlined and polished feel, that lets you fully embrace the emotions this game stirs up.
All of the above makes a very immersive game that now holds a special place in my heart.

This game has grown to become one of my favorites. The play time reflects only how much I've played the PC version, and it was purchased only a few weeks prior to writing this review. Prior to that I played the game a lot of PS4 and did not hesitate to buy it for PC since the asking price is low compared to how much someone who really likes this game will actually play it.
And there's the catch. Not everybody will like the game. It's extremely difficult. You will have the perfect run, and you'll be screwed over one little thing going wrong, triggering a chain reaction to strip your health and end your run. This is a roguelite with permadeath, so when you screw up, you have to start over again from the beginning. But that's the beauty of roguelites. They are different each time thanks to procedurally generated levels and balanced, but varied powerups that never appear in the exact same configuration two times. So the incentive to play again is that you have no idea what to encounter next time, or the time after that, and so on...
You'll die a few hundred, perhaps even a thousand times before completing the game the standard way. But that is just the beginning. There is also a hard way, really hard way to complete the game that will keep you playing.
Then you can choose to play what I like to call "terrorist mode" where you just gun down the shopkeepers so you can grab all their stuff and not have to risk your life collecting gems to pay for it. That carries with it heavy consequences, but also ups the adrenaline and is a lot of fun! It also gives you the shotgun early on, which is rare to obtain when you play it the "lawful" way.
This game is proof that platforming and roguelites can work very well if made by someone competent. The balance is very well, moreso on the punishing side. I guess he wanted to make sure you get a hard time rather than take the chance a lucky RNG could break your run.
Would I recommend this game? Yes, this is a fantastic game! But if you get frustrated easy or want more of a casual experience that has a lot of instant gratification, steer clear of this. Don't get this game if you have anger problems! This game WILL make you angry. Angrier than you thought you were capable of. That's how punishing it is. It will dangle the carrot before your eyes before pulling the rug away from under your feet without warning. You'll be "so close!" time and time again. Get this only if you can handle it!

This is NOT a game for everyone. It's highly challenging and the learning curve is very steep. Those who want an easy game or those who just want to play for the plot won't find that in Spelunky. Those who want to torture themselves again and again, this game is for you.
It's got immense replay value. It's got procedurally generated levels, so that every time you die, and every time you beat the game, and every time you start over, you'll get an entirely different experience. Even with 3000+ attempts under my belt, I still run across situations that I've never been in. And that makes the game challenging even now. For those who are interested: Spelunky is entirely worth your money. I've played no other game as much as I have Spelunky, and if you're one of those who wants to try their hand at the learning curve, I can guarantee that this $15 will last you for a VERY long time.

Series veteran for 15+ years here.
So far the game looks and sounds great, and runs just fine with default settings. I turned a few extra options up, but only enough that I can keep it at 30FPS+.
I am using an Intel i7-4770K 3.50 GHz CPU (8 CPUs), 16GB of RAM, and a Radeon R9 200 card with 4GB of RAM on Windows 7.
The game seems to be completely stable and I have not had a single problem yet with crashes or glitches of any kind.
So, why is the response so negative? There are some questionable decisions made by Square-Enix regarding monetization--You can spend money in real life to buy praxis points and in-game credits, but these purchases can only be credited to a saved game once. THIS INCLUDES THE IN-GAME BONUSES FROM THE DELUXE and 0-DAY EDITIONS (Seriously?!). It is certainly repugnant, but I don't think it meaningfully impacts the core game enough to matter. It's just a way for them to make some extra cash from people who have too much money and want to make the game easier for themselves.
They have added a difficulty level which does not unlock until you have beaten the game once, which adds permadeath to the game. This is probably where people are going to end up spending real-life money on Praxis and credits.
I think that it is slightly ridiculous that people are rating this so negatively when the game has been out on PC for less than a day.
Certainly, it should be said that mainstream companies need to be more considerate in the future with how they treat their fans when they are charging ~$90 for a "deluxe" digital edition with a season pass where the bonuses only work on once saved game. I am sure they will listen to my suggestion as they count my money in their mansions made of gold.
So far I am digging on the gameplay and the story, and spirits remain high.
I will keep this review updated as I spend more time with it.

This is probably the first time I wish I could write a neutral review. I haven’t played much of Mankind Divided yet, but from what I’ve experienced so far, it’s absolutely fantastic from a gameplay perspective. Primarily the new Dawn Engine and larger levels to explore have made this feel like “the next” Deus Ex game.
However there are many reasons I’m writing this review so early, and that’s because there are many concerns I have after such a short period of time with this game.
1.) Micro-transactions have no place in Deus Ex, or any single player AAA game release. They dilute the experience for me. Here I am wanting to enjoy this creative masterpiece, but it’s stained by the fact that clearly there are some seriously greedy people involved with its distribution. It’s completely unreasonable, and I won’t support it.
2.) I also have several minor issues with the state of this PC port. It was handled by Nixxes, who have proven they are competent at dealing with PC ports for Square Enix games in the past. However there are a few too many issues for me with this port. The in game inventory was clearly designed for consoles. Hitting TAB to enter your inventory should also exit it right? Nope, you have to either hit the escape key or find the “Back” button at the bottom of the screen with your mouse. It doesn’t seem like a big deal, but after a couple hours it was making me open my inventory less and sometimes wish I didn't have one.
Mouse acceleration is also a concern. There are currently no options for turning it off, so I have to try and play even though it doesn’t feel comfortable when I look around.
3.) Performance isn’t great. While fairly well optimized on lower settings, there are still many areas that get massive frame drops even with my system that is more than capable of running this on Ultra (at least based on in game recommendations).
Add all of these problems together, and my Deus Ex experience isn’t what I hoped it would be. There’s a hidden gem under all this nonsense, I just hope I can bring myself to play it to completion. Either wait for a much needed patch, or accept it in this state.

Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas is an isometric RPG clearly inspired by the Legend of Zelda series, at least the isometric/Game Boy versions. Everything from the lock-on sword play, the story about a hero gaining three valued artifacts of power to overthrow a growing evil and much of the visual design shows that inspiration in spades. Due to that inspiration, the comparisons to the Zelda series are easy to make. I hate to say this but more often than not, Oceanhorn doesn’t compare well. Whether by limitation of the iOS platform or the inexperience of the developers, a lot of ideas and mechanics were pale imitations of what’s been done before.
The story is ok at best. It’s a traditional story of a young boy who goes out to find the three magical Emblems of the Elements and put a stop to an evil entity. At first, we’re introduced to Father, who goes out to fend off a living fortress known as Oceanhorn and what happens to him is ultimately unknown. After gathering Father’s sword & shield as well as preparing yourself for sailing, Hero goes out to gather these circles. He has Father’s journal with him which will narrate a little bit every time you visit an important island. Hero goes to a forest island, a desert island and an island in the sky to collect all three magical sources of power. Along the way, Hero meets two different races that have fallen into ruin due to the evil machinations of Mesmeroth and some of minions. So, through some dungeon crawling, Hero will eventually right those wrongs done and those races will eventually rise from defeat….in maybe another game. Once the pieces of the puzzle are assembled, with help from Hermit along the way, Hero will go to Father and fight Mesmeroth once and for all. During this quest, a few side characters will come in and out of the story but otherwise, Hero is on his own for this journey. Having only the guidance of Father’s journal and the power of the elements to “guide” him. The emblems are only in the game to push the story along, nothing else.
The combat has the worst problems. Using a sword and shield most of the time, you’ll have a lot of slap fights with bullet-spongy (sword-spongy?) enemies in the game. They will often require a ton of hits to bring down and there are a lot of enemies per level which also happen to respawn rather quickly. It definitely feels like grinding through a level, if the experience system didn’t make that particularly obvious. Bloodstones in particular, while not enemies, seem to require 20 or so sword attacks to collect. Why? I don’t know but I thought that was a waste of time. As far as blocking projectiles/attacks with the shield, this seemed to be hit and miss on which attacks would and wouldn’t be blocked, leading to a constant source of frustration while fighting. As a whole, the system works and you can get through the game. But it’s not going to be a whole lot of fun. Oh and there are spells which are used for some puzzles and can be used for the fights. However, I found they often used far too much mana so I usually only used them for puzzles. This is thanks to the lack of an adaptable inventory system. There’s no bottles you can hang onto to replenish health or mana, everything has to be found in the levels. It makes boss fights a lot less interesting as well.
It’s got a pretty OK selection of options. You have four different graphic presets including low to ultra. There’s a bunch of different options that turns various objects including clouds and soft shadows on/off. V-sync and anti-aliasing is included. Fullscreen and borderless windowed are here as well with a reasonable choice of resolutions. FPS can be set to 30 or 60 FPS locked/unlocked. In the pause screen, you can adjust speech, effects and music with individual sliders. You might want to consider lowering the music slider which I’ll explain later on. Keyboard and mouse work ok with Oceanhorn but it feels off. Not that controller is a lot better either. Some of the action keys can be rebound but the implementation limits where they can go. Mouse keys can only be rebound to other mouse keys and the same goes for keyboard ones. Why did we decide this was a good idea? No clue. It’s a big no-no.
Ultimately, the frustrating part about Oceanhorn is how much this game treads the same ground so many others have in this genre. Sure, it’s one of the better iOS to PC ports I’ve seen in a long time. There’s nary a mention about touching the screen or buying microtransactions in the App Store and I respect that. Unfortunately, the game still suffers problems inherent to the mobile platform. It’s a mechanically boring game that’s a chore to get through rather than an experience to be enjoyed. The gameplay is filled with repetitive and somewhat unresponsive gameplay that completely lacks meaningful feedback to hook the player in. The optimization is questionable too. The story, honestly, the story feels like it was missing a chunk of itself. There are two dimensional characters abound and its hard to stir myself into getting interested while I’m playing.
Oceanhorn was just a drag to get through, especially towards the end. The entire time, I was constantly reminded of what this game could have been instead of what it was doing. I was constantly disappointed every time a new mechanic was introduced or an area shown. Most of the time, what they had implemented was done on the most basic of levels, giving me nothing to sink my teeth into. Other reviewers constantly talk about how much this is like Legend of Zelda except on an iPad. This, at best, is a passing imitation to that series. I myself cannot recommend Oceanhorn: Monster of Uncharted Seas.

Good game, looks good and gives provides a decent amount of fun. Still, I am not so happy with it as other reviewers. This is a Zelda clone, ok, maybe the story is original, and the voices are pretty good too, but there are so many things just exactly like you would find in a Zelda game, chests, heart containers, mirror shield, coins, even a tryforce reference. I'm fine with subtle references, but this is too much, it's not that hard to come up with something different and original. Then there's also the dungeon and puzzles design, which are kind of dull, but it gets better later in the game.
Another annoying thing is the controls, which relies too much on the physics engine, the player moves around kind of slow and it feels weird when going up stairs, because the weight and gravity makes the character move slower and even it seems like it gets stuck. You get used after a while, but still feels weird.
I understand that this game was made by very few people, but that doesn't justify anything, this game needs more polish.
Despite all that, I liked it and I would recommend it, as I said, the game is fun and the story is not bad.

Oceanhorn immediately caught my attention as an IOS game. I eagerly awaited the Android release because of the rave reviews and many comparisons to Zelda. When it came to Steam, I said "good enough" and made the purchase. Mistake.
On its face, Oceanhorn has a cute art style and interesting Zelda-like premise. Evil monster, father killed, dungeons, items, puzzles, bosses, you get the drift. But from the moment you set foot on your home island the first time, the game clobbers you with a very un-Zelda feel.
To say this game's controls feel clunky, does not really convey the true badness of how this game plays. Moving your character around is a chore, and dodging enemy attacks is almost impossible. Fortunately, that is not really an issue, because 90% of the enemies are dumber than a bag of hammers and so slow to act that there are no attacks to dodge. The few enemies who are actually a threat to you are easily dealt with using items that are far too powerful to make any part of this game a challenge.
The boss fights are really the true disappointment. In almost every boss fight, the game switches perspective to lock the camera so that it always faces the boss. This was kind of interesting, but when most of the bosses have no attacks except to charge at you in a way that almost feels like they're bored, it really lets down. I never took a single point of damage from a boss until about 3/4 of the way through a game when a boss pleasantly offered a real challenge. This boss, the lone exception, features battle mechanics that require weakening him and avoiding his counterattacks. Part of the challenge comes from the camera always changing perspective while he's shooting at you, but hey, I'll take it.
There are more annoying gameplay elements, like the completely-extraneous boat travels scenes between islands that took 3-6 minutes of firing an infinite-ammo gun at every single thing that isn't water. The challenge is so low for this part that I don't understand the point. It is not fun and adds nothing to the game or story.
The plot for this game is plagiarized from Generic Adventure Game. Literally nothing surprising happens. Ever.
Comparing this game to Zelda is like comparing a Ferrari California to a Chevy Cobalt. Yes they are both sports cars, but that hardly puts them in the same category. Save your money.

This game is incredibly fun and very easy to navigate. The controls are simple and straightforward, which is a major plus for someone coming into the game blindly. Right now there's only one campaign and it makes me sad actually. The gameplay is so addicting, it makes you want more! I want more levels! Speaking of combat, it's very simple to learn both keyboard and gamepad controls yet very addicting.
Online play is really spot on. You can join people in the middle of matches and re-connecting to games is very easy and simple to do. An offline mode would be nice, but you're suppose to play this game cooperatively anyway so it's not a big deal.
A few warnings though:
If you've never seen RWBY, you might want to watch at least the first volume before playing. This game doesn't continue from the main story in the show, but it is hard to understand what is what if you've never seen the show. Basically, if you've never seen the show and don't plan to, you probably shouldn't buy the game. Especially considering it's still in Early Access. However, if you're a hardcore RWBY fan like myself and are desperate to play this game, go right ahead! Lastly, again, the game is in Early Access still so there's not a lot of content at the moment. If you're skeptical about it, just wait for the game to be finished. It'll probably be a lot better by then.
TL;DR
I highly recommend it to fans of RWBY and even hack and slash fans. It's very addicting and fun and easy to get into!

Ok, this is a bitter sweet review; I loved the game overall. It was a thrill that brought me back to Dark Cloud, Legend of Zelda, and even a few moments feeling like I was questing in World of Warcraft (the good and the bad). There is so much to speak on yet so little time....As always this review is by a disabled gamer and phyically challedged. The base line stats are as followed...This has been one of my highest reviews to date; hopefully the game nazis will be sated, doubt it though....
My base stats for this game:
Sound: 60% out of 100
Graphics: 90% out of 100
Controllers: 92% out of 100
Replay value: 80% out of 100 (will go into detail on this with controls, again.)
ADA (Americans with Disablities 508 complience) friendly: 95% out of 100%
Overall Score is a 83.4% (taking all averages then getting the overall average of the combined)
Sound and Graphics: I have a hard time overlooking the repeative music , over and over again. The same damn tune...Ruined the time that was taken for the lovely landscapes. This is trully a game that has taken the concepts of Dark Cloud, mixed some minecraft, and put thier own polish to it. It was quite breath taking to see just how everything from monsters to NPCs look so whimical yet enchanting. The PGWs are each it own sandbox as you portal from one to the next.
This game is not for a lightweight i3 or i5...I can see even some i7 cpus getting killed by this game. Do not waste your time running this game on a large sandbox save you are running Xeon 6 to 8 core or a Ryzen 5 1600 or better. This game is surprisingly light on the GPU for the quaility of the skins but generating the worlds on a 4 core 8 thread is laughable unless you are going a small box. This is one reason why I love the game becuase it puts to use the more up to date cpus with heavier core counts. Not once did my Ryzen 7 1700 chug or lag. I believe this is the real recommended spec.
Controls and ADA compilance:  Wish Keen / 505 would do a 5-0 on Batterystaple and teach them how to build an engine that allows for full customization as Portal Knights has shown. I have been able to play this game with controller, mouse only, keyboard partial only, and been able to play within my limitations with little to no issues. The only place I was struggling was being able to see drop off for the trees. If we could gets a partial transparency as we get under so muchcluster it would make the game that much more polished. Aside from that it was an amazing romp in this "dungoen crawling" wonderland! I rearely can say that about many games. This game feels like it was developed by Nintendo, Capcom, or another AAA in the 90s
Replay value: This game...If you start you may not stop, it is that level of addictive crafting, grinding, mission crawling, portal seeking adventures in this game that really make Portal Knights feel like a AA in the making. I have not even tried co-op yet and still very impressed with just how marvelous the come back draw is in this game. It seriously what Minecraft was lacking and still lacks. Add some new tunes, get the pitfalls so you can see them coming and this will be a game that will be a masterpiece.
Overall: This game deserves more attention then what it has been recieving. Other developers should take notes of why this game is as good as it is. It takes alot to get above an 80% from me,  this game has that place in my ranks.

Brothers A Tale Of Two Sons is a touching experience.
Unlike other games (which i still love) such as "Heavy Rain" or "Life Is Strange", this one is a proper game in the most classic sense of the therm, but it also adds so much to the rather simple gameplay.
The player guides two brothers in a quest to find a cure for their illed father; each character is controlled with a half of the controller, so you are often asked to solve short and easy puzzles by moving both characters at the same time with the analog sticks.
The thing that makes "Brothers" interesting is the experience.
The strongest component of the game is the sense of exploration; you wander through a series of magical and very well designed landscapes, which become really breath-taking towards the end.
The game istelf doesn't have an actual narrative, but the music, animation, atmosphere and setting help to create a truly dreamy and oniric experience which captivates the gamer's attention and strikes directly to the heart, also because of some emotionally intense moments.
Considering the very low price this game can be found at it's a very well deserved purchase, specially if you want to see what the gaming medium is capable of, from time to time.

In my opinion CO2 is one of the greatest wargames ever made.
It simulates war without an artificial turn-based structure or exaggerated and unrealistic micromanagement. The chain of command and different levels of headquarters are superbly integrated in the overall concept of the game. It's really a unique feeling playing this game. It feels like the real thing: You give orders to subordinated headquarters or units and they try to execute the mission within the parameters you set for them, but at their own discretion. Like it would be in the real world. But you also have the freedom to intervene and do some micromanagement when it's needed.
It has a steep learning curve, okay, I give you that [by the way: everybody who says the game is too complicated and played it for less than an hour can't be taken serious. RTFM!]. The AI isn't as smart as it should be, regarding the fact that the game is built around the concept that the AI acts as subordinated commanders and executes the orders given by the player. But that's about it on the negative side.
I hope this game will be further developed. I'd like to see some scenarios outside the WWII-Environment. Some Cold War stuff perhaps? The engine should be adjustable!

Note: This review was written straight after launch. If updates fix this game, I will note this in an edited review. For the moment, though, this is where we stand.
This game is not ready for primetime. I am a massive fan of The Pinball Arcade and have sunk hours and hours on various devices. This is not a worthy sequel. The decision to "enhance" the presentation with an un-necessary arcade backdrop is one I don't like, but I would make peace with it if not for the fact that it slows the game down horrendously and there is no option to turn it off. There is no Direct X 9 support, and the Direct X 11 version is a slideshow on my machine which is to reccomended machine specs. The keyboard control doesn't work which means I can't play it in a cafe or anything where I don't have my gamepad. (Yes, you can play it with the mouse in theory, but no, you can't actually play it with the mouse if you want any enjoyment out of it). The DLC doesn't work, so you can't even buy the new Stern tables, you can only play the 1 free "Mustang" table (I somehow suspect this will be the first thing they fix, as it's preventing money for DLC flowing their way). The camera on the Mustang table is a mess - no matter what resolution I set it to, I can't see the whole table. You also can't "demo" the tables you don't own as you can in TPA.
Positives...well, the DLC crosses over with TPA, meaning that the Stern tables from TPA that are in the game are automatically unlocked in this if you login with your TPA account. That said, with the game in this state, I cannot imagine any reason that you would want to play those tables in SPA rather than TPA.
I cannot reccomend the original Pinball Arcade enough. It is full of classic tables and it runs really well, emulates pinball as well as if not better than any other game out there, and I have had almost nothing but positive experiences with it. This is a buggy, stuttery mess and the fact that you cannot buy any DLC currently may almost be a blessing in disguise for the developers, as they at least won't be overwhelmed with demands for refunds.
The most sensible thing to do would be to release the SPA exclusive tables as DLC for the original TPA, which works, and put this sorry mess behind everyone. I suspect this is unlikely to happen. For the moment, either make sure you have a beast of a PC, well above reccomended specs; or wait for the game to be release with a DX9 version. This release is in an unacceptable state.

This is one of the best open world RPGs I have ever played.  I am also a fan and have played hundreds of hours on the Elder Scrolls series, the Fallout series, and even World of Warcraft.  The story, mechanics, depth, and on a simply level - the quantity of content presented are all on par with such games.
Some neat things that not every massive RPG can say they contain:
- Total voice acting for every NPC (you very seldom hear the same thing over and over again, and if you do then you are probably returning to old areas to offload gear, etc).  Also, I am never able to point out the same actor between areas and in questing - which is an amazing feat for the actors or for the quantity of people brought in for the performances)
- Very little to no mindless grinding.  The main storylines and side quests almost never have collection duty type quests, everything is story-driven and somehow makes sense - quite a feat for any Action RPG.
- While I have not finished the game (and at about 80 hours, I think I'm about half way through), I already have the sense that the story is consistently building on itself and adding more as well - building towards what will hopefully be a grand and satisfying conclusion.
- The graphics are right on par for 2012 when the game was released, but the game also runs quite well on my ultrabook system, better than WoW - and it is based on an base game engine released in 2005.
Those are just some of the things I love about the game, I highly recommend it to any open-world fantasy RPG fans out there.

If you are looking for a continuation of GunZ: The Duel, please note not to get your hopes completely up. GunZ 2: The Second Duel added upgraded visuals, sounds, weapons, classes and accessories. Also the addition of Matchmaking was added. But at the same time things have been removed or changed for better or for worse.
*PLEASE NOTE* This is based off what I have seen, I am not out to bash the game as it is still early access. Don't let this review put you off towards playing it for yourself and seeing whether or not you appreciate the changes.
Matchmaking - Getting paired against people who are over 15 levels higher than you is to be expected (If your fresh to the game).  And by that time you going to see that even with high skill level, someone who has full gear sets and is used to the game is going to prove to be a difficult challenge to kill.
Host lobbies can be hit or miss. Sometimes they are playable and others it is just a mess. When opening the score board and looking at you ping rate seems to just be a lost cause. I have been in lobbies where everyone is 30/40ping and the game is unplayable for all.
Classes – The adding in classes was a cool idea, however not being able to switch after you made your choice is really frustrating. In order to get a different class you need to pay for them. And certain classes have certain class specific weapons and gear. Unlike the previous Gunz, you cant just switch to a gun or armor set depending on how you want to play that day, but you need to purchase and level up other characters. I guess they did this so you have more to work towards, (which can improve game life) However not being able to switch classes without paying disables the F2P feature.
Weapons + Gear – Weapons look and sound cool, and are based more off real weapons. There is a good variety that don’t look exactly like another model which is nice, but it is still Early Access so there will probably be a bigger selection in the future. There are no entry guns though, meaning as you level up you chose what statistic you want higher on your gun, not just an overall better gun. So the price for everything is the exact same. No really everything is 15,000 Gold. So the feel of advancing just isn't as in depth or exhilarating.
Visuals – Visuals are excellent especially for a F2P. Some of the maps that were brought back don't look as nice though. The Gothic feel of Mansion is gone and is just to much yellow. And the character model scales seem to be off a bit (I think your shorter than you should be compared to the maps :P ). But the game plays smooth and looks great.
Gameplay – Now this is where it comes to completely opinion base and whether or not you like or dislike the changes. Dash has been nerfed, no more sword climb, and sword battles seem to be more about standing still and spamming left click. I feel as if the block system needs fixing as I can never seem to deflect an opponents attack, or maybe its a connection thing. Moving around seems clunky in battle and is hard to tell if your hitting an opponent or not. (GunZ: The Duel, you would get a sound indicator and the word HIT would appear) Overall I think they didn't focus on sword gameplay as much as the game is called GunZ after all. But Sword Styled gameplay was probably the biggest factor of the first game and it will be missed as time goes on.

So here's my review of Deus Ex Mankind Divided
TL;DR : The Game itself is a great game, if you played Deus Ex Human Revolution, this IS DE:HR but better (story Sucks tho)
Personal Advice : Grab it on sale
I will try my best to avoid spoilers in the review and also, i will compare the game to DE:HR
Long Version:
This is going to get messy
~ 8/10
Graphics is Gorgeous in this game, you can feel it after jumping right into the game, the lightings, sharp visuals and also the atmosphere takes you right into the game setting itself, but the issue is with the lip-syncing, I don't feel that the developer is doing their best with the lip-syncing, it feels sort of, strange, ever watch a dubbed foreign movie?, it felt like that.
The HUD is really user-friendly, you got the option to fade it in the option, or turn it off for total immersion or just for taking cool looking screenshots so Kudos to the developer on this one
The details look amazing, clearly a lot of effort has been put into the Graphics (Except Lip-Syncing).

TIPS : Turning off MSAA will boost the performance of the game
~ 9/10
If you played DE:HR, you will notice different things, 1st, the upgrade system has been revised, meaning you need to explore more and collect what you need, the way you  "Augment" yourself has been revised, this small changes is what makes the game interesting, you also have the option to play the game like DE:HR which gives you the Augmentation you used to, but the new Augmentation is DOPE.
The Side Quest in this game is ABSOLUTELY Amazing, in DE:HR, The side Quests didn't have much weight on the story, but in this game it actually gives you the opportunity to see what’s going on in the streets of Prague and what’s going on with the Augmented Citizen and the Length of it makes it feel like it’s actually a main mission, Moral Choices also applies, You can always play as the Good-Cop or the Bad-Cop, or if you don't want to get your hands dirty, you can always make others do it for you, with CASIE of course.
Another thing: If you have Deus Ex GO on your phone, you can link it to the game and Get free Praxis point for playing it
~ 5/10
The mouse Acceleration is completely unacceptable and also the sensitivity slider is also clunky that it won’t give an exact number I want, I also turn it so low so my mouse stop accelerating but you can still feel the acceleration when you aim down the sight.
And why it doesn’t have any [Toggle] option, this should be mandatory in the game, I personally find this really annoying since I like to hold down the crouch button instead of press it once
And also, where is the option to remove key-bindings, you can change key-bindings but not remove it, what the-
~ 8/10
I don't know if others have had the same experience as me, cause its buzzing and choppy but I bet it’s just my sound driver, anyway, to the music, The Music is Amazing, as soon as it plays, you will be immersed in it directly, you will feel the Cyberpunk and Tense feel in it, i will gladly swap my Phone Ringtone to one of the OST, i don't have much complain on the sound & music side.
Why I didn't recommend it
I don't know why people put Micro-Transaction in a singleplayer story-driven game, i mean,this is not a competitive game, This is outrageous, i don't know why people even bother to pay for 5 praxis kit for $3.99 when you can get all of those by progressing the story of the game, I don't blame the developer on this one but the publisher needs to get their things sorted out.
Remember Guys this is a
This is completely unacceptable
Who the hell think that changing the DLC name and the content on the launch date is a great idea, a lot of buyers especially those who pre-order this game is completely♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥by this decision, not only that, they announce that you can't claim the consumable repeatedly, which means, if you claim those consumables in one play through, you won't be able to use it in the next play through, the information itself is not disclosed before the Launch, which left many users in disappointment.
This review should be finished 2 days ago but because of me experiencing a game breaking bug, which is fixed by the patch yesterday, so, lets continue the review then,
Thank you for all of the support that has been given by marking this as a helpful review, your support has been really helpful
And thanks for the Great Comments
~3/10
Well,
So, how should i say this, The game main story itself, could be finished in about 10 hours, not only that it's short, it is also not a memorable one, it doesn't even gave you the chance to love the character, which is a shame, in DE:HR, the story actually gives you the chance to love the character eventhough it is short (My Fav Character is David Sarif and Frank Pritchard), and also the ending doesn't leave you hanging, which means that the ending in DE:HR actually gives you a conclusion to the story, in DE:MD however, you will be left wondering, pondering as if the games is actually over or not. Imagine if LOTR : The Two towers actually ends when the Battle of Hornburg is about to start. It feels somewhat like it.
It Cuts the story right as it was starting to get good
Another thing is that the game concludes after fighting a villain which has no ulterior motives or what so ever that could justify their action. Shame.
What is worse about it that the real ending might be placed behind a DLC Paywall.
The Gameplay mechanics is great, The Graphic and music is great, but without a great story to support it, it won't be a memorable game,
especially after an amazing experience with The W*tcher III
So for those who don't really care much about the story, this game is great and worth picking up, but try a gun-blazing gameplay, it is more rewarding than stealth gameplay.
For the others who wanted to buy the game for the story, i suggest that you stay away from the game till they applies some discount or if possible wait for the "FULL DIRECTOR CUT" edition instead
Thank You for the support, this concludes my review for Deus Ex Mankind Divided, i hope you enjoy it, and the last but not least

Compared to the original demo, and the "first look" demo that Rooster Teeth published on its website a year ago for its sponsors, this Steam version is extremely lackluster. Sure the graphics are there, and it looks like the show (which I do love, for the record), but the gameplay doesn't feel nearly as tight. It's way too easy to mow down hundreds of Grimm with no skill involved. If your Aura (health) is low, just run away for two seconds and it's full again.
Besides Yang, each character's fighting gameplay is really similar. Only their animations are all different (duh). The only gameplay differences happen when you level up multiple times to get the maxed-out versions of the special attacks, but that shouldn't be the case. Crescent Rose shouldn't feel the same as Myrtenaster.
Combos aren't up to player control anymore, whereas in the demo you had full control over what you were going to end up doing with the certain way you attacked. Ruby, the only character in the demo, had a plethora of special moves and combos, and it feels like they're just automatic here with no player input. The game is way too easy and, as a result, boring and not fun.
The voice acting seems really effortless as well. Yeah they're the same voice actors, and I'll give credit where credit is due on that front, but only Ruby and Professors Port and Oobleck seemed to care about anything they were saying.
All of that being said, Rooster Teeth Games are claiming 8-10 months of Early Access development, so I'm refunding the game and hoping to see a lot more out of Grimm Eclipse further down the line. Maybe I'll pick it up again if everything gets improved. As it stands right now, I had way more fun with the old devoid-of-story-content demo than this easy snoozefest.

Turkey, they are always the butt of European and Arabic jokes, because Turkey is in both areas and yet part of nether. How many great things can a person name, that has come out of Turkey. Struggling, well here are a few to get you started.
1. Ratah Lokum (aka Turkish Delight)
Not the Cadbury’s mock attempt but the real thing (shove that glass and a half up your…..!). Absolutely delicious, it truly earns its nickname of rāḥat al-ḥulqūm (Throat comfort).
2. Troy in all those Homer epics (the Greek guy, not the yellow cartoon idiot).
If you did not cheer during that epic Bana V Pitt your a heartless ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥!
3. TaleWorld Entertainment.
Who? I hear you exclaim. Well sit down Lads and Lasses and let me tell you.
If you have not heard of a game called Mount & Blade, you can be forgiven. This was a sleeper hit in 2006. If Total War and Elder Scrolls had a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ child then Mount and Blade was it. Ugly and stunted yet majestic and beautiful at the same time. Then came its siblings, M&B: Warband, M&B: Fire and Sword, M&B: Nepoleonic Wars and soon we will have M&B: Bannerlord.
This series of games put you at ground level (literally) of control of your destiny. You can choose to  become a Merchant, Bandit Lord, Knight, Sell-sword, Bounty hunter or you could go straight to the top and fight for the right to wear the crown of all Calradia. It is less open world but more open life style. You can anchor yourself to one of five separate kingdoms or to none of them and create your own slice of Medieval heaven.
GAME PLAY
Up front is the customisability of both your character and skills, told through a story style intro, though you do get to fiddle with sliders and skill points before hitting the game proper.
Face slider physics are nowhere as pretty as Skyrim or Fallout but it gets the job done and you will get a fairly decent face out of it (BannerLord looks to have improved on this, so fingers crossed).
Skill points are dished out between abilities, general skills, fighting skills and weapon skills. Making your character unique from game to game. Once done you pick a starter town or if it is your first time a training arena. Get your lights punched out (if you suck at fighting) and then you get your first quest, find your attackers.
There is the world map where you travel from town to town, chase/track/avoid bandits or armies or even sail up and down the coast singing sea shanties. Cities will give you quests, trade routes, major supplies and major NPC recruitments; towns will give you minor quests, minor supplies and recruits; Castles will give you refuge from enemies (as long as they are not your enemy). If you are a Lord or a self made King you can own any and all of these.
When in Cities, towns or engaged by an enemy you go to personal view (1st person/3rd person/over the shoulder). You can talk one-on-one with town folk or if in battle/siege, command your troops. It is here in battle where M&B really sets itself apart from other war games.
You get to personally command hundreds of on field troops AND fight yourself, like a real general. You can give general orders covering all your troops or individual orders to select groups like your archers or cavalry. Field strategy and troop make-up is paramount as the AI is no slouch (its not too bright on easy but will still give you a run for your money) and can mow down your veteran Knights with mobs of peasants with sound tactics. Each faction too will have their elite troops and cannon fodder and there is nothing wrong with sticking to a set faction, but if you really want to wipe your enemies aside, mix and match your troops. For example, Khergit horse archers can pick enemy from a distance, yet evade with lightning speed, follow them up with a charge of Swadian Heavy Knights and sweep everyone off the board. Defensibly, have a line of Nord berserkers backed by Rhodok spearmen, with Vaegris Archers at the back.
How many troops you can field will depend on your computer but you can get up to 300+ men on the field at any given time. So battles and sieges will be hectic and epic!
THE CANDY
Under the hood M&B’s graphics is sub-par compared to other titles but again, they do the job and do it well. Trees, people buildings and horses are pleasing but not beautiful. BannerLord will be a step up from this but all in all great graphics don’t always makes a great game.
Out of the box there is no voice acting so boohoo, start reading princess. Sound effects are pleasing  but at times repetitive and musical scores are nice and at times authentic but again repetitive.
Having never played Multi-player I will be side-stepping this but from what I have read and heard, it is top notch.
IN A NUTSHELL
TaleWorld’s Mount & Blade series is not the prettiest nor the ugliest girl at the fair but she is the best fun you will ever have this side of Turkish Delight. Yes, giving commands to troops is a little finicky and sluggish and there is no actual story (lineal or otherwise), save the overall story arch, you have to make your own as you go. But there is a huge Modding community that have ways of fixing her blemishes, placing you anywhere in the historical time line, anywhere in the known or fictional world, including Star Wars, G. R. R. Martin or Tolkin universes.
Now if that doesn’t have you spinning faster than a Dervish Dancer, then when M&B: BannerLords hits the shelf, you may as well be just like the people of Troy sitting behind your walls, because that wooden horse is about to blow our minds once again!
