Fighting games aren't normally my sort of thing, I just can't seem to get into them enough to get good, but having played and thoroughly enjoyed NetherRealm Studio's last fighter (Injustice: Gods Among Us), I thought I'd give it a go as I've always liked the look of the Mortal Kombat series.
The story mode is as can be expected from a game of this type, essentially 4 hours of cutscenes interspersed between quick-time events and actual kombat.
Needless to say, the story hasn't exactly been the feature that has been bringing fans back time and time again, it's relatively dull in fact, but the characters and scenery are attractive enough to keep it interesting. There are a few chartacters I've had brief experience with from past MK games which are missing from the line-up, but I should think these are likely to be added as DLC further down the line. One feature that has been sure to bring fans back, is the gratuitous gore. This game had me wincing from disgust more frequently than I expected - which can only be a good thing as I've long considered myself desensitised from years of gaming. Kudos to NetherRealm Studios for that.
The way 'koins' are earnt throughout the various game types adds enjoyment to being able to unlock extras. Koins are spent in the Krypt, and all sorts of extras can be unlocked at random by exploring it. This is something I would have liked to have seen in Injustice as I'm more of a fan of the DC universe. Maybe next time.
The game wasn't without its share of bugs, none of which cause any real problems, but still annoying nevertheless. This coupled with a distinct lack of SLI support means this game has a little room for improvement. Both issues should have been resolved before release.
For a first foray into the world of Mortal Kombat, I greatly enjoyed the experience of MKX, and would recommend it to anyone looking for an entry to the series. However, I'd wait until it's a little cheaper as unless you're willing to invest a lot of time getting beaten to a pulp in the online multiplayer, the story mode just isn't long enough to justify the cost.
Edit: Netherrealm have ceased to support the PC version of MK X, meaning no more characters or content which will be released on consoles. Despicable behavior by Netherrealm and Warner Bro's.

From my childhood I maintained a sensible and close relation with fairy tales. Later on that turned into an affection for cartoons, providing an enchanting athmosphere for the never-to-grow-up child inside of us. If you have ever longed for grasping that feel of the ancient lovable fairytales in a game, this title is ment for you.
Brothers places together all the parts necessary to build up a story around you that will stick you down into your chair. You start with a sick father and two worried brothers, setting out for the journey to get the cure which can save the old man. The game is basically made for co-op play on one machine, but it can be a tricky  finger excercise for single player as well. We have played through the whole adventure with my girlfriend in two days. That might seem a bit short, but considering the common adventure, it turned out to be just the right amount of time to delight the both of us. The game mechanincs are quite simple: one brother suitable for the first move of the puzzle goes ahead while the other will depend on the former's help to push through. One striking feature is the storytelling without a single articulate word. The characters behave and talk in a way that will surely make you understand whatever is happening at the moment. Among such circumstances imagery will take the leading role and that is another remarkable aspect of the game. Every last frame of it is well-planned and all of the screenshots you take would make a nice picture in your bedroom (believe me, or look it up in my screenshot section - spoilers at later pictures!!). The textures, tones and camera settings build up a marvelously charming athmosphere, leaving you stunned for several seconds with the scenery. You can practically feel the hours of carefuly artistic work put into the job all throughout your adventure. Not only is the artistically composed masterpiece a memorable experience, but it also hints you slightly with fable like qualities. I would hate to say too much, I suggest you jump right into it.

This game really surprised me! I had little expectations for it when I got it in a bundle, and it took a long time and a lot of boredom for me to give it a try, but I'm glad I did! The way you control the two brothers independantly from each other, and at the same time is a pretty cool experience. Because of this, it is manditory that you have a dual analog gamepad, it's the only way the game really works well.
The story line is interesting as well. The characters don't speak in English, and there are no subtitles, so you gather what is happening through expressions, inflections of voice and hand gestures. Even though the language is unintelligable when by itself, the story as a whole is quite intuitive.
The graphics of the game are gorgeous, everywhere you go in the game is a work of art. There are many benches throughout the game that you can sit on to rest, and capture breathtaking views.
My only gripe with the game is that it's very short. I beat the whole thing in just under 2.5 hours. Because of this, I can't really recommend the game at full price, but I do recommend you add it to your wishlist, and wait for the Steam Summer Sale! I was wrong to ignore this game for so long, the couple hours I played it were thoroughly enjoyable, and I'll be sure to return to it again someday.

Pros:
+The port is good, nothing obvious is missing.
+The game is very balanced.
+The music is the best since Tekken 5 in my opinion.
+Big roster of characters to choose from. All unique in their own way.
+Decent costumization but not quite as much as previous games yet.
+The game is Tekken with some adjustments. If you like Tekken in general you will like this one.
+Big nostalgia trip if you haven't played a Tekken game in a while.
Cons:
The online mode, while having a solid netcode, still has some problems.
- Can't always reliably connect to players.
- Finding players with 5 bars of connection can be hard depending on your region.
- Harder to escape grabs/CGs when playing online.
- Rage quitters and lag switchers exist though not common.
- Cosmetic weapons are not banned in ranked play. ( They are usable and while not very effective, can catch you offguard
The single player content including the story is very mediocre.
- Game includes a short Story mode, Arcade mode ( 5 battles + a boss ), VS mode and Treasue Battle ( Survival mode that unlocks cosmetics )
You get all the unlocks for win/losing 2000 matches online or offline doesn't matter.  Making Treasure battles semi pointless.
There's also short character stories, and by short i mean a single battle of 2 rounds followed by a small cutscene.
Lastly there are some characters missing from the old games, so you might want to look up the roster to see if the characters you played are missing before buying the game.
Conclusion:
Now that sounds like a lot of negatives but overall the game is very solid. Each character is a lot of fun to mess around with. If you have friends to play with then you're looking at hundreds of hours of fun. Online play, while not perfect is still enjoyable. However if you're looking for a lot of single player content you might want to wait.

It's hard to explain what is so enjoyable about this game. Whilst the map feels vastly underpopulated and it is obvious from the design of the surroundings that this was intended to be a MMORPG, I think that adds a certain charm. Feeling tiny in a world so huge is part of the experience.
It did take me a while to get fully into the lore, and I wouldn't say I'm quite there yet, but you can certainly play the game without understanding the fuss about these 'Fae' or why everyone argues over this 'Mitharu' fellow.
The DLCs are absolutely fantastic and expand what is already a vast, multi-faceted world. The creativity behind this game is evident in every last corner.
Though the character customisation is limited, that is probably a good thing, as I like to spend hours upon hours getting my hero's eyebrows JUST RIGHT.
It's also worth mentioning that the customisation extends into gameplay; the class system is, in my opinion, without fault. It's user-friendly, it enables users to play whatever combination of skillsets they choose, and it has a system of specialisation that other RPGs, I felt, were missing.
All in all, buy the game. Just buy it. Now.

Kingdoms of Amalur is such a weird game because on one hand it's amazing, and on the other it's a giant mess. What should be a 9/10 near-perfect game is muddied with just a handful of bugs and a sordid real life backstory. Its writing and triple-A voice acting are especially of note for an RPG of this size, and this game like no other makes the player feel like an actual hero (or villain) in its immersive fantasy world.
So many game elements feel bittersweet if you're familiar with the development fantasy surrounding this game, where its engine and mechanics were actually developed to support an Amalur MMO that never saw the light of day. What we're left with is a mostly-solid single-player experience that rivals similar mature-themed action RPGs. Amalur's brilliant expansions even hold their own against the main campaign, with exceptional voice acting and writing indistinguishable from the core game.
The action is fun and fluid, with variety and skill for veterans and novices alike. The abilities to reimagine your character's appearance at nearly any part of the game, rebuild an entirely customized class, or to create armor and weapons that you can name yourself, give the player an unprecedented amount of freedom in Amalur. Most won't even notice the subtle shift away from directly focusing on attribute numbers to simply more playing the way you want to naturally. Instead of leveling up and micromanaging how many points you put into Strength or Dexterity, for example, you simply spend your skill points on the types of skills you're interested in and the gear you choose will augment your numbers accordingly. More than anything, playing Kingdoms of Amalur can be a very
experience where other games find themselves tedious, and this kind of thoughtfulness bleeds into nearly every aspect of the game.
Despite its few bugs (and the fact that they will never be patched), Kingdoms of Amalur is still a fantastic game and well worth its price. A console port done right.

Tips for noobs:
~ Skills ~
-Alchemy, lockpicking, persuasion, and stealth are useless skills.
-Up to 5 levels of each skill can be found or bought in the game (6 with DLC).
-Detect hidden should be invested in immediatly. I've found Purples and Yellows in hidden chests.
-Blacksmithing is incredibly OP.
-Fateweavers reset all skills. Use this to maximize your training potential (You can be too overleveled in a skill to train it)
-Mercantile is excellent for early game. Once you have 2mil+ gold, reallocate those points to something worthwhile.
~ Combat ~
-Bows with the 7 charged shot ability can one shot bosses when fired at close range.
-Invest early in +health/second gear. This keeps you from overusing health pots.
-Weapon damage stats may be misleading. A Dagger with 30 phys and 30 piercing will read 60 damage. Another dagger with 20 Phys, 20 Piercing and 20 poison/5 seconds will also read as 60 damage.
-Use Reckoning often; it's quick to recharge. Combine with experience potions for exponentially more exp.
~ Misc ~
-Quests are black and white regarding moral choices. These have little repercussions.
-You will outlevel the available gear considerably.
-Many zones and quests will be skipped.
-NEVER repair via a blacksmith. Always use repair kits, it's astronomically cheaper this way (even with 0 Blacksmithing skill)
-Explore early. This aids greatly when fast traveling from redundant quest to redundant quest.
-You can buy back EVERYTHING you've ever sold in the game. Only sell to the Fence in Star's Camp. That way you can buyback anything you want (even if you stole it) if you choose to respec.
This game is addicting if you like RPGs. Very fun, though a little bit slow at first. The story and the DLC's will suck you in fast, though, and is definitely worth a play.

Fighting games aren't normally my sort of thing, I just can't seem to get into them enough to get good, but having played and thoroughly enjoyed NetherRealm Studio's last fighter (Injustice: Gods Among Us), I thought I'd give it a go as I've always liked the look of the Mortal Kombat series.
The story mode is as can be expected from a game of this type, essentially 4 hours of cutscenes interspersed between quick-time events and actual kombat.
Needless to say, the story hasn't exactly been the feature that has been bringing fans back time and time again, it's relatively dull in fact, but the characters and scenery are attractive enough to keep it interesting. There are a few chartacters I've had brief experience with from past MK games which are missing from the line-up, but I should think these are likely to be added as DLC further down the line. One feature that has been sure to bring fans back, is the gratuitous gore. This game had me wincing from disgust more frequently than I expected - which can only be a good thing as I've long considered myself desensitised from years of gaming. Kudos to NetherRealm Studios for that.
The way 'koins' are earnt throughout the various game types adds enjoyment to being able to unlock extras. Koins are spent in the Krypt, and all sorts of extras can be unlocked at random by exploring it. This is something I would have liked to have seen in Injustice as I'm more of a fan of the DC universe. Maybe next time.
The game wasn't without its share of bugs, none of which cause any real problems, but still annoying nevertheless. This coupled with a distinct lack of SLI support means this game has a little room for improvement. Both issues should have been resolved before release.
For a first foray into the world of Mortal Kombat, I greatly enjoyed the experience of MKX, and would recommend it to anyone looking for an entry to the series. However, I'd wait until it's a little cheaper as unless you're willing to invest a lot of time getting beaten to a pulp in the online multiplayer, the story mode just isn't long enough to justify the cost.
Edit: Netherrealm have ceased to support the PC version of MK X, meaning no more characters or content which will be released on consoles. Despicable behavior by Netherrealm and Warner Bro's.

Pros:
+The port is good, nothing obvious is missing.
+The game is very balanced.
+The music is the best since Tekken 5 in my opinion.
+Big roster of characters to choose from. All unique in their own way.
+Decent costumization but not quite as much as previous games yet.
+The game is Tekken with some adjustments. If you like Tekken in general you will like this one.
+Big nostalgia trip if you haven't played a Tekken game in a while.
Cons:
The online mode, while having a solid netcode, still has some problems.
- Can't always reliably connect to players.
- Finding players with 5 bars of connection can be hard depending on your region.
- Harder to escape grabs/CGs when playing online.
- Rage quitters and lag switchers exist though not common.
- Cosmetic weapons are not banned in ranked play. ( They are usable and while not very effective, can catch you offguard
The single player content including the story is very mediocre.
- Game includes a short Story mode, Arcade mode ( 5 battles + a boss ), VS mode and Treasue Battle ( Survival mode that unlocks cosmetics )
You get all the unlocks for win/losing 2000 matches online or offline doesn't matter.  Making Treasure battles semi pointless.
There's also short character stories, and by short i mean a single battle of 2 rounds followed by a small cutscene.
Lastly there are some characters missing from the old games, so you might want to look up the roster to see if the characters you played are missing before buying the game.
Conclusion:
Now that sounds like a lot of negatives but overall the game is very solid. Each character is a lot of fun to mess around with. If you have friends to play with then you're looking at hundreds of hours of fun. Online play, while not perfect is still enjoyable. However if you're looking for a lot of single player content you might want to wait.

Spelunky is a roguelike dungeon exploration game that is very difficult. Your character must work his/her way down to the bottom of the dungeon to defeat the boss whilst also collecting as much gold and killing as many enemies as possible.
Not really any story in Spelunky other than what is described in a few "cutscenes" and whatever else you can read in your journal. The main experience is in the story you find yourself along the way to your final destination.
The gameplay is the core of the game. It's fast, action-packed spree to get as many items as possible before escaping to the exit. This game is easy to learn but extremely difficult to master. The tutorial gives enough depth into what you'll be doing throughout the game. You will definitely struggle your first 10-20 runs (you might die a lot in the first 1-2 levels), but the game's easy replay action makes you spring back into action to start your run over again. Your objective of the game is to reach the bottom of the dungeon and beat the boss. Along the way you have to collect item to improve your character and what it can do. There are many upgrades and only few ways to get it: Shops (the most common, but also difficult to get if you want to steal it), Crates (big dice roll for specific items), or in very specific locations such as certain knives and lazers.
There are four main areas in Spelunky with some altnerative layers within these areas. These include: The Mines, The Jungle, The Ice Caverns and The Temple. Although every level is rather difficult, the variey of enemies and traps increases the further you go. Which is why you're encouraged to collect as many items as possible before you reach the harder levels as these items will make your experience easier. You have a very limited supply of items and damage points you can take each run; items will definitely improve your survivability. Things like weapons, jetpacks, ropes, bombs etc. will make you feel overpowered; however, you never are. As one wrong move can lead to your death, no matter how many good items you have.
As stated before, Spelunky is not an easy game; it's quite difficult even for the experienced players. This doesn't just come down to Randomly Spawning Levels either (these just make it so you don't feel like you're playing the same level over and over again), the enemies you encounter - although you can learn their patterns - will always remain a nuisance no matter where you encounter them. The further you progress, the more difficult the game becomes and the final level will really test your gameplay skills (no, it's not The Temple). The final level is an excellent challenge that will you make you excited for the final boss.
Spelunky is a tough, yet enjoyable game with a good level of difficulty and depth to make a great experience.

This game tries to blend rpg elements within the popular build/craft genre. Only it failed to accomplish satisfying any real desire to play either. For starters if you prefer using a controller then I strongly urge against this game. The inventory and crafting interfaces feel extremely restricted with a controller. It's slow, clunky, and often times counter-intuitive which is made worse with flawed game mechanics. For example, in order for you to use an item it has to be activated in your hotbar. You can't just select a potion in your inv. and use even though there is a drop down menu for each item. It has to be moved to your hot bar, then activated from there
The combat system also suffers from poor design. You are allowed the option of 1st person or 3rd person views. If you opt for 1st person then you will find frustrating when the game forces you into 3rd person when locked on in combat, which is understandable considering how locked on combat works. The issue arrives in between fights. You have to manually enter 1st person yourself, after every fight. Or when you pick up health. Or when you pick up mana. Or when you grab air bubbles underwater.
Also in the 15 hours that I have played, I was not able to find a way to reset my character. If you choose a class, that's it, no toying around with alternative roles without making a new character. Which is not terrible, albeit a bit obnoxious, what is terrible is the inability to reset attribute points that were mispent, or spent trying to test certain class builds, even though those too are very limited. Again I must say I did not find a way in my 15 hours a gameplay.
Lastly there is the load time in between worlds. It would not be a problem if I didn't have to travel to multiple worlds to grab varied materials. The fact that certain materials can only be found on certain worlds is a mechanic the I not only agree with, but I enjoy. However it gets old real quick when Im trying to build up my home island and I have to endure multiple load screens as I gather the necessary compenents.
For some of you reading this and scoffing at how I am complaining about minor issues, consider that, although these are little things, little things do add up. And this game is full of little, irritating issues. This game would have done very well perhaps 5 or more years ago, when minecraft was still young. But now, in 2017, everything you can find here can be found in countless modpacks available for minecraft, with proven and successful mechanics, and far less resistance to ones personal gaming style, and easy to configure files for fitting ones gaming style. So yeah, like I said, makes me wanna play minecraft.

Mount and Blade: Warband Is a third person "open world" game. I say "Open world" Because you are not walking around freely around the world like in The Witcher 3. It's more an overhead view where you look down on your little character walking around the world. When you meet an enemy or enter a town you get to a little map where you can walk around in third person.
Gameplay: The gameplay may seem basic at first and it is, but it is extremely easy to get sucked up into this game. You pretty much run around with your little army killing any enemies you find. The combat system is pretty simple where you have directional attacks and blocks to defeat your enemy. You can also command your army to a certain extent where you can ask them to form lines give them certain attack orders or just make them charge in
Bugs: There are a few bugs with item names and quests
Story: You are put in the continent of Calradia a fictional world resembling medieval Europe. You can coose to swear fealty to a king or kickstart your own kingdom. The story is your own and all the factions have their own military units with pros and conns.
Mods: What makes this game interesting for many is the modding scene you can mod the game into everything from a survival zombie game to westeros there are a lot of mods and it is fully supported by the devs.
Multiplayer: The multiplayer is what keeps a lot of people interested. You can join sieges deathmatches to full on battles and free for alls. There are also clans for those who are interested. The multiplayer function supports mods as well.
Verdict: The game is addicting and if the singleplayer is not for you there is always the multiplayer. My biggest problem with the game is that sieges are not that great and after you level up your character a few levels you turn into an unstopable killing machine were 1v50 turns into a cakewalk if you have a horse.

The game really does appeal to almost every sense of a great fantasy game: combat, exploration, interaction, etc. The camera could be a bit tricky as it did tend to fling around easily, but later in my playing I found that to be beneficial and detrimental to me in combat as pushing a key in the direction you want to attack and not the way the camera faced could be confusing at times, but I adapted.

Striking multiple enemies and moving between them all in between swings feels extremely satisfying and really does give you a feel for that fanstical combat with monsters. The animations for many of the weapons are strong indeed, the only weapon I truly disliked were the hammers. Slow, clunky and short range. Staves, chakrams, and faeblades all look and feel very cool to use. Attacking and switching between weapons cancelled combo's and would allow you to be much more variable in combat.
The only things that I felt lacked were indepth, meaningful conversation with people, romance and how empty and underused many towns were. Now, no romance isn't necessarally a bad thing, but for rpg's it should be a given- everyone likes it and if you don't, well, you're wrong.

Prepare to die screaming…or more likely laughing at the horrendously bad voice acting of ‘The Hat Man: The 20+ Pages’……wait….wrong game (and more on the voice acting later).
Alas, just as has happened with so many other indie horror games in recent years and with the advent of the Slender series, ‘The Hat Man: Shadow Ward’ (the ‘for real’ name) falls victim to the same ‘collect quest’ gameplay mechanic. This means that you need to find a set number of pages from your daughter’s diary to complete the game. Ultimately, that’s the basis of the game: you either play as the father or mother in search of said daughter, who has gone missing from the seemingly empty asylum she was committed to which is now populated by shadow people/The Hat Man (BTW – the idea of shadow peeps is based loosely on fact and there are many documented cases, and even some decent movies, about people that have seen or had encounters with these so-called ‘Shadow People’). Thankfully, you don’t just search for pages as you also need to find some other items to progress deeper into the asylum and defeat The Hat Man (who I guess is like the pimp of the shadow peeps) to get your daughter back.
One of the more unique attributes of this game (though it’s been done before) is that sound is utilized to pinpoint the location of pages/other items you need by means of whispery voices. Also, the sound design of this game isn’t half bad for being a budget title, with some of the sound effects/ambient music being pretty creepy in my opinion.
Now as promised, I must go back to my earlier comment about the voice acting. Granted, this game is super short and can be beat in less than half an hour, so you may think that voice acting wouldn’t be too important in such a game…..but it kinda, sorta totally is. Essentially, it’s hilarious. No, seriously, I’m not joking. I mean, it’s so stupendously bad that it’s good (I don’t know how that works; it defies the human intellect to comprehend how that can be) but it’s true. I figure most people will laugh at it, though some may actually want to cry at how bad it is. And for all those 100% achievement unlock Steamers out there – prepare thine selves!! There is actually an achievement for listening to your daughter reading the pages of her diary as you collect them. Sure, this game can fairly easily be ‘100%’d’ and the aforementioned achievement is easy enough to unlock, but don’t go joy-puking your faces off just yet as I seriously believe that listening to all of the pages may very well land you in an asylum. I personally just barely managed to keep my sanity intact while unlocking this achievement, so don’t say I didn’t warn you.
This game can be fun for like 2 hrs tops, but I wouldn’t recommend it at full price, even if it is a budget title. With decent voice acting, who knows, perhaps this game could have been terrifying. As it is, it will likely be overlooked by most gamers, but it is somewhat interesting and good for a laugh….or cry, so give it a shot.

I’ll admit I maybe spent longer studying The Hat Man: Shadow Ward’s death screen than it deserved. But it so nicely summed up the game for me that I couldn’t help but appreciate that I was being handed a focus point for my review without even having to look for it.
But let’s step back for a moment because it’s not just the death screen important here, but how you arrive at it. After scurrying through a twisting, self replicating maze of stock textures and out of place items, you’re inevitably caught the titular Hat Man in all his floating jack-o-lantern glory. And what’s this? He’s opening his mouth and- oh, I guess that wasn’t supposed to happen.
And just like that we’re transported to a perfectly flat, perfectly bland death screen featuring three buttons, each drawn with the same ugly font and taking up almost the entire screen. I realize it’s a screen that didn’t need to have much detail, but what’s here is such a pitiful excuse for a menu I couldn’t help but laugh at it.
I suppose I can give The Hat Man that much anyway; it made me laugh. First at the ridiculous voice acting that I want so much to believe was intentional. Then when turning around and laying eyes on what I think was supposed to be a terrifying demon but looked more like a blazing smile.
And finally at the death screen, which I saw many times and eventually decided was a good enough place to give this game a rest. After all The Hat Man is just doing his job haunting this asylum, and doing it damn well at that, so I’ll just leave him be and go do literally anything else to try to forget this ever happened.

Break down:
Graphics: 8/10
Solid graphics, again extremely "Zelda" in nature but enjoyable none the less. It has a simple cartoonish style similar to  Zelda Windwaker without the cell shading.
Music and audio: 6/10
It's not bad by any means. The music is okay, but is not memorable. It serves its purpose without adding much more. Voice acting is similar in that it gets the job done, but I did not find it memorable or overly well done.
Controls/Playability: 8/10
I played with a controller, and I'd recommend playing it that way. Controls are responsive and natural. There were only a few times I was frustrated with the ability to aim at objects in the distance, otherwise the game will largely correct aim on your behalf.
Do I recommend it:
Heck yes. My biggest complaint is the length, beating it in just 8 hours of total play time without referencing any outside guides. I'd like to of have given more of such a good thing.

My nameless little Link clone handles well on foot. Combat feels good, I never felt like I got killed by something because of the way the game is designed. I do wish I had more control over the camera, that isometric perspective is sometimes hard to navigate. The animation is a tad rough in some of the cutscenes/enemy animations. And there's voice acting. I'll let you decide if that's a good thing or not.

Overall this is a fairly good game and I enjoyed most of my time playing it. The main story happens at a reasonable pace and doesn't involve too much backtracking. Going for the 100% completionist, though, stretches out the gameplay to the point where it starts to become tedious and less enjoyable.
The general combat is fairly decent though it's not very responsive, dynamic, or varied. Hack n' Slash is holy writ for the most part. One
gripe I have with general play is that enemy loot doesn't spawn until a second or two later when the enemy bodies have despawned; this means you have to force yourself to wait around after killing something, backtrack, or ignore the loot. On the plus side the experience "drop" is an automatic pickup even if in the grand scheme of things not worth much (you get most of your XP from
stuff, not
stuff.
I greatly appreciated that there wasn't One Way to defeat bosses, largely because that way would result in longer and more tedious fights. Many of the boss fights had a particular gimmick to disarm them based on the arena but this effect could be replicated by bombs, arrows, and/or magic. On the other hand there isn't much depth to any of the fights except the very last one as all the others are just 'disarm, bash-bash-bash-bash-bash, disarm, bash-bash-bash-bash-bash, disarm, bash-bash-bash-bash-bash, done'. Despite that I'm still not sure how I beat the final boss (deus ex machina, literally).
Its style shares vague similarities to Wind Waker but it lacks a certain depth that Zelda games tend to have. There's only basic gadgets, half of the spells are unnecessary, and the fishing mini-game is largely there just to pad the XP growth potential (you can't sell the fish, they can't be used in any way, and none of the NPCs care what happens, but you get tons of extra XP the first time you catch a fish type).
My personal recommendation is to get it on sale, play through the main story, maybe track down some heart pieces for the final boss, and leave it at that.

It's a zelda-clone, and a damn good one. The game it most heavily reminds me of is Legend of Zelda: Phantom Hourglass, mostly because of the setting and usage of some of the items. It has it's flaws, the magic spells are a little too expensive for my tastes and gold suddenly becomes really common after about the halfway point, but besides that this is well worth purchasing.

The Good:
- Art design and music lend perfectly to the genre. The game obviously emulates Zelda, but it also reminds me of other classics like Landstalker (Genesis) and Alundra (PS1).  If you’re into these types of games, you’ll definitely enjoy what Oceanhorn has to offer.
- Certainly, the upgrades and variety of gadgets could have been more robust and there could have been more towns to explore, but as a five hour experience (if you're just focused on the main story), Oceanhorn didn’t need these extra elements to be enjoyable.
- Unlike other reviewers, I really liked the sailing segments. It’s essentially an on-rails shooting gallery that gives the player an opportunity to refill their inventory and health before reaching a new island.
The Bad:
- For the most part, Oceanhorn ran smoothly; however, there were a few times during my play through that the frame rate plummeted. This occurred mostly when entering the towns, but thankfully it only lasted for ten to twenty seconds before returning back to normal speed.
- This game desperately needed an active mission hint system to give the player suggestions on where to go or how to accomplish certain goals. For me, this would have been helpful after major segments of the game as it took a bit of trial and error to figure out where to go next.
- Boss fights ranged from tedious to overly convoluted.
- If you’re an achievement hunter this game is not hard to fully complete. But, some of the fishing challenges (The Botfish) were ridiculously frustrating.
Final Verdict:
I recommend this game, but only if it’s on sale. While there are numerous positives to Oceanhorn, there are design and game play elements which unquestionably detract from the overall enjoyment of the game.

It has been 17 years (!!!) since I last played, and I feel incredibly old, yet very happy, to be writing this.
Police Quest: SWAT 2 is one of the early old-timers to introduce tactical, real-time squad-based gameplay to PC gaming, and was first released by Yosemite Entertainment for Microsoft in 1998. Which means that I was 6 when this came out. 6!
The series spanning the original SWAT to SWAT 4, has been a rather broad, somewhat eclectic mix of genres including Strategy Adventure (SW 1), RTS (SW 2) and FP Tactical Shooter (SW 3/4) spanning separately across the four titles, but SWAT 2 remains my firm favourite.
The game features two separate campaign paths in which you control a SWAT team or infamous terrorist organisation 'The Five Eyes,' and go head-to-head, from a static isometric view of California, Los Angeles and the surrounding 'off the grid' area. In total there are 30 missions, 15 for each respective campaign and each storyline is independent of the other, though some scenarios are similar. Based on the individual mission requirements, you can select a team of officers or terrorists and negotiate, neutralise or manhandle your way to success.
The game is not without flaws, but many veteran players will look toward this title with rose tinted specs and forgive the overly complicated interface, micromanagement and janky artificial intelligence.
I hope that this allows you to re-experience and thoroughly enjoy the game as I did/am, and bask in all the sentimental energy that has collected between your wizened ears over the years.
It remains as one of my all-time favourite games, and I was delighted to find it available on Steam earlier this year as a nostalgic addition to the RTS section, and for all fans of tactical squad-based gameplay, and I am sure it will be appreciated and welcomed by new and older gamers alike.

Spelunky is a roguelike dungeon exploration game that is very difficult. Your character must work his/her way down to the bottom of the dungeon to defeat the boss whilst also collecting as much gold and killing as many enemies as possible.
Not really any story in Spelunky other than what is described in a few "cutscenes" and whatever else you can read in your journal. The main experience is in the story you find yourself along the way to your final destination.
The gameplay is the core of the game. It's fast, action-packed spree to get as many items as possible before escaping to the exit. This game is easy to learn but extremely difficult to master. The tutorial gives enough depth into what you'll be doing throughout the game. You will definitely struggle your first 10-20 runs (you might die a lot in the first 1-2 levels), but the game's easy replay action makes you spring back into action to start your run over again. Your objective of the game is to reach the bottom of the dungeon and beat the boss. Along the way you have to collect item to improve your character and what it can do. There are many upgrades and only few ways to get it: Shops (the most common, but also difficult to get if you want to steal it), Crates (big dice roll for specific items), or in very specific locations such as certain knives and lazers.
There are four main areas in Spelunky with some altnerative layers within these areas. These include: The Mines, The Jungle, The Ice Caverns and The Temple. Although every level is rather difficult, the variey of enemies and traps increases the further you go. Which is why you're encouraged to collect as many items as possible before you reach the harder levels as these items will make your experience easier. You have a very limited supply of items and damage points you can take each run; items will definitely improve your survivability. Things like weapons, jetpacks, ropes, bombs etc. will make you feel overpowered; however, you never are. As one wrong move can lead to your death, no matter how many good items you have.
As stated before, Spelunky is not an easy game; it's quite difficult even for the experienced players. This doesn't just come down to Randomly Spawning Levels either (these just make it so you don't feel like you're playing the same level over and over again), the enemies you encounter - although you can learn their patterns - will always remain a nuisance no matter where you encounter them. The further you progress, the more difficult the game becomes and the final level will really test your gameplay skills (no, it's not The Temple). The final level is an excellent challenge that will you make you excited for the final boss.
Spelunky is a tough, yet enjoyable game with a good level of difficulty and depth to make a great experience.

I'll try to keep this nice and short for easy of reading.
This game has some pros and cons as most games do.
Pros: There is a lot to do if you really want to delve into all the game has to offer you. Make your own base, house castle dungeon, spaceship. Really there is little limits to what you can construct, however furniture do is a bit limited.
Different fighting styles ranging from melee to physical ranged to magic. with variations on how your character works, crits, multistrike, tanking and so on based on the equipment used.
Cons: I'll start with the elephant in the room. The game is very poorly optimised, I have a computer capable of running any game well optimised on either high to ultra settings no problem but this gets very laggy, even more annoying is that the sound gets all choppy when it lags and in reallity there should be no reason for this, the game is not graphically intensive enough to justify these problem, it's just poor optimisation. I'll note as a disclaimer that the only thing my computer is missing is an SSD, maybe these problems won't occur if you use one however consider that the majority of the people still do not use SSDs and probably a major shift into SSDs won't occur until people can get half a terbyte for less than 100 bucks.
Unbalanced content. Hard mode bosses are completly unbalanced if you are doing solo play. In a group it would appear it is fine, however solo they are huge damage sponges so a fight lasts anywhere from 15 minutes to 20 and don't forget you chug a buff potion every 2 minutes so it's also a huge resource drain. They also do ridiculous amounts of damage where most characters will be oneshot unless they have some heafty investment into getting more life or lots of resistence.
Poor end game. Once you reach end game, all there is left to do if probably build more or level up another class of character. The existing end game content is one dungeon which is a little bit maze like though still doable without getting completely lost and the 3 hard mode bosses which as I refered previously are fights that are not fun, balanced or worth the eforth.
Very RNG prone. Now don't get me wrong, I don't have a problem with RNG except when it gets on the ridiculous side, when you have to kill the normal bosses douzens of times for that one drop or when you do certain content like farm mummies and ancient mummies for example to try and get some vanity item and despite having killed hundreds, one of the 3 drops still hasn't occured.
The Idea of events was good to help break the monotony, but many of them are just nothing but a waste of time because you are looking for things that maight have spawned in completely ridiculous location like little islands above the main island. In fact the procedural generation while generally a good idea, was poorly done with many things generating incomplete or in ridiculous places. It definitely needs a tweek.
Conclusion: All in all I'd say it's not worth buying. I got to make myself a really big house, do all of the content except farming hard mode bosses because they are unbalanced and get most of the recipes in the game save for seasonal ones in just a few days. The game really is low on content and the poor optimisation really is a deal breaker. Maybe if you find this on a huge discount then just maybe it might be worth the few hours of gameplay you'll get out of it.

UPDATE
So Eidos / Square Enix reacted with two patches less than a week after launch - I'm pleasantly surprised. The first one fixed some issues I wasn't affected by, but the second one actually fixed my main big problem - the sensitivity for the X and Y axis can now be set independently, and I can finally aim properly. Therefore I can now confidently recommend the game. The smaller flaws mentioned in my original review still apply, but they are massively outweighed by the atmosphere and the overall gameplay. The exploration aspect is huge - I'm about 15 hours in by now, and still have only barely touched the main storyline, while just doing side quests and exploring Prague. If you're a fan of Deus Ex, or RPGs, or stealth shooters, or exploration games - get it right now.
Feel free to read my original review below, but keep in mind it's a bit salty because of the initial problems ;)
------------------------------------------
ORIGINAL REVIEW
The game itself is great, but the PC port is an absolut POS. And I'm not even talking about all the fuss about microtransactions - as long as the game is balanced without them I don't care, and as of yet it seems that's the case.
The single worst thing about this port is the negligence of the KB+M control scheme. First and foremost, the mouse sensitivity. It is WAY too high, the slider only adjusts in weird steps instead of at least pretending to be continuous. On top of that, the acceleration/sensitivity seems to be different for the X- and Y-axis - up/down-movements are way slower than left/right-turns. This is f***ing frustrating. I'm quite good at shooters, but the one time I got into a firefight in this game as of yet, I could not hit a single enemy. In Human Revolution I could cast headshots on enemies a good distance away with the pistol with the standard crosshair, in this game I'm lucky to even hit their body when they're standing right in front of me. I had to reload that firefight a couple of times until I got lucky and managed to sneak around it instead of fighting it out. So much for the highly praised improved combat in this game.
It might be way more fun with a controller now, but with M+KB it's basically unplayable.
Other nitpicks about the controls: You can't move the camera with the mouse in the hacking minigame, you have to move it by wasd. Bonus points for including keyboard shortcuts for capturing/fortifying a selected node, though. When you enter the in-game menu via Tab, I, M or whatever key for any of the screens, you can't use that same key to get out of it again quickly, you have to reach for ESC. Same for the weapon customization.
So, because of that messed up mouse sensitivity making proper aiming impossible, for now I'm basically going completely stealth. Now, this gets hard too when the ragdoll physics cause every second unconscious body I try to move out of plain sight to get stuck in a window, or some random cover object, or just the f***ing floor.
The optimization of the port also is not the best, but it's nowhere near the desaster that Arkham Knight was.
Okay, rant over. The above things make me wish I weren't already over my two hours so I can't refund, so I'm writing this negative review instead.
But as I said in the beginning, apart from these issues, the game still does a lot of things very well.
The graphics are beatiful, the stealth system is a lot better once your are used to it (quite similar to the cover system of Watch Dogs, just with different keybindings), and the atmosphere and feeling of Deus Ex is definitely there and enjoyable.
But because of the terrible port, I can't recommend it yet - I will update the review when/if these issues get fixed.

I’ll admit I maybe spent longer studying The Hat Man: Shadow Ward’s death screen than it deserved. But it so nicely summed up the game for me that I couldn’t help but appreciate that I was being handed a focus point for my review without even having to look for it.
But let’s step back for a moment because it’s not just the death screen important here, but how you arrive at it. After scurrying through a twisting, self replicating maze of stock textures and out of place items, you’re inevitably caught the titular Hat Man in all his floating jack-o-lantern glory. And what’s this? He’s opening his mouth and- oh, I guess that wasn’t supposed to happen.
And just like that we’re transported to a perfectly flat, perfectly bland death screen featuring three buttons, each drawn with the same ugly font and taking up almost the entire screen. I realize it’s a screen that didn’t need to have much detail, but what’s here is such a pitiful excuse for a menu I couldn’t help but laugh at it.
I suppose I can give The Hat Man that much anyway; it made me laugh. First at the ridiculous voice acting that I want so much to believe was intentional. Then when turning around and laying eyes on what I think was supposed to be a terrifying demon but looked more like a blazing smile.
And finally at the death screen, which I saw many times and eventually decided was a good enough place to give this game a rest. After all The Hat Man is just doing his job haunting this asylum, and doing it damn well at that, so I’ll just leave him be and go do literally anything else to try to forget this ever happened.

I've just played less than an hour. Nonetheless, I was amazed by what I experienced. Here's a basic skeleton of pros and cons.
Pros:
-The attacks feel powerful but not too powerful. I have as much a blast fighting enemies as I'm sure the actual characters would have had.
-Skills complement, not replace your basic attacks, although you may end up preferring a certain skill tree for one character and create your playstyle around that.
-Movement doesn't feel bad. I'll explain later why I don't say it's good.
Cons:
-My computer isn't a dedicated gaming computer, but it's still decent given that I don't feel the absolute need to enjoy all games I play on ultra high settings. However, when I play this game, I get slight but frequent frame drops - right? that's the term? - although my control inputs do make it into the game in a timely fashion.
-As a result of that, when moving around, I can't expect to see my character move fluidly because of game performance. I know they move unawkwardly, though, because I don't feel stiffness during combat or when walking to the next area. This, along with the first con, will most likely be TEMPORARY CONS because this game is only in Early Access, and the devs are in the process of putting out optimization patches.
-Skills are mapped to 1, 2, and 3, which means I have to take my hands off WASD to use them. Not a big deal, and the devs will mostly likely let you map your own keys later anyways.
Here's what I liked most about the game:
-Combat feels great, it feels like a constant struggle against the evil forces, although when you're playing with 3 other people the hack'n'slash gives a bit of its seat to the feeling of teamwork.
-Speaking of which, it's not specific to this game, but very often you'll join a team in a mission and you'll magically and inexplicably work together like 4 meshing gears, straight out of the box. Speaking of which: don't forget to revive dead teammates! It makes you feel a bit better, and they're not wasting useless time staring at their corpse and the chaotic fighting happening around.
Miscellaneous notes:
-Story is present but sparse. Expect much more as the game emerges from Early Access. This game was focused around Hack'n'Slash anyways.
-Four characters currently to play as. More may be added. Heck, more content will be added overall. MORE CONTENT!

The game really does appeal to almost every sense of a great fantasy game: combat, exploration, interaction, etc. The camera could be a bit tricky as it did tend to fling around easily, but later in my playing I found that to be beneficial and detrimental to me in combat as pushing a key in the direction you want to attack and not the way the camera faced could be confusing at times, but I adapted.
The greatsword is by far the most fun weapon to play with in my opinion. I love games where they truly allow a greatsword to shine- where, when the blade hits something, it hits something. Striking multiple enemies and moving between them all in between swings feels extremely satisfying and really does give you a feel for that fanstical combat with monsters. The animations for many of the weapons are strong indeed, the only weapon I truly disliked were the hammers. Slow, clunky and short range. Staves, chakrams, and faeblades all look and feel very cool to use. Attacking and switching between weapons cancelled combo's and would allow you to be much more variable in combat.
The only things that I felt lacked were indepth, meaningful conversation with people, romance and how empty and underused many towns were. Now, no romance isn't necessarally a bad thing, but for rpg's it should be a given- everyone likes it and if you don't, well, you're wrong.

After reseach on the internet, I found a solution :
FIXED :
Causes of this Error
This error has been known to occur as a result of one or more of the following:
Cause 1: Access rights are set incorrectly
The most common cause of this error is a Windows application that is unable to access the other files that are necessary for it to work.
Cause 2: System files are damaged or corrupt
The other common cause is a Windows system file that became corrupt because of a disk write error.
Fixing “0xc0000022” on Windows
Fix #1: Check for permission issues
If the 0xc0000022 is trigged by a specific application and you’re able to identify which application was it, check for its permission configuration to make sure they are set correctly.
To do so, follow these steps:
Right-click on the application that triggered the error. This can either be the shortcut on your Desktop or the .exe file of the application installed, available in My Computer.
Choose Properties
Go to the Security tab
Change permissions for all the Administrators, Power Users and System to Allow Full Control
Click Apply
Fix #2: Check for DLLs with accessibility issues
If the error is caused by a DLL file, you can identify which file triggered this error by installing and running the Process Monitor tool from Microsoft:
Download and run the Process Monitor tool
Run the application that triggered the 0xc0000022 error
Wait for the error to appear
Click File
Select Capture Events
Select Filter (or you can press the CTRL and L keys) to open Processs Monitor Filter
Filter out all the lines that don’t belong to the application that caused this error
Search for events with the result column as ACCESS DENIED
Once you’ve identified the DLL file with ACCESS DENIED, follow these steps:
Go to the folder where the application that caused this error is installed
Right-click on the DLL file
Select Properties
Go to the Security tab
Click Continue
Click Add
At Enter the object names to select, type users
Click Check Names and then OK
Set the access levels for the new added user to Read & Execute and Read access

Well, this is a fun game nonetheless but it's difficulty is too heavy on randomness. Some skill is involved into making progress but most of the times you die by having a bad luck, e.g. shopkeeper beats the living out of you or some yeti slaps you all over the screen and you fall into endless pit(game over).
First map pack (mines) is cool and has a lot of charm. Second map pack (jungle) is also very colorful and most of the times without cheap deaths and enemies that can instakill you. Third map pack (ice caves) is just way too random. Half of the level  is composed of platforms hanged in air, the other half is a pit that when you fall into you die. Ah, and there are also a lot of mines(explosives) that expolode, a lot of yetis that throw you away like crazy and probably into the pit and flying aliens that when hit explode like a bomb. Crazy.
And the last level pack (temple) is just insane. No way to beat it without being super prepared with having most of utility items, cape, crysknife, kapala and lots of health. You have like 4 HP at the beginning of each game. One hit from one fly that some mummy generate in numbers like 5-6 every like 2 seconds take about 2HP. Just do the math yourself. There is also a flying anubis type monster that generates some magic balls of player rage that spawn every second, are locked on player and deal like 10 HP damage every second. Good part that they are slow albeit that's a weak deal.
Anyways, I've beaten Olmec the Last Boss and guess what? I died because some of some random action like being hit by dead body of an enemy (that I've killed second before with anubis magic stuff), being stun locked and thrown backwards just conveniently into a pool of lava.
You know what? This game is a masterpiece from a technical point of view but from gameplay point of view it's pointless unless you like loosing. Like loosing is fun. Dwarf Fortress is fun although it's fun because of loosing that's inherently entwined within it. Spelunky is fun untill you see that no matter how hard you've prepared yourself you'll probably die because of some random stupid action that escalates quickly and eats your HP or instakills you no matter how many HP you have.
It's not even following the GIT GUD philosophy of Dark Souls. DS is fun because you hone your skill, prepare ahead and mix that with a lot of dexterity.
In Spelunky the GIT GUD philosophy goes to the thrash. You play carefully? You'll lose. You play rashly? You'll lose, just faster.
If you like to play games in which the way to the goal is more important than the goal itself then you'll probably like Spelunky very much. In other case, like me, there is a high chance that you'll see no point in a game like this.
Your buck, your choice.

I love this game.
I'm biased, the original Sims was the first normal PC game I'd ever owned and I loved it.
Now that that's out of the way, I never played 2 but everything I wanted from the original is here, you can walk outside of your lot and explore the neighborhood and you can age or go to another neighborhood for college.. You can even make friends with service workers because they're all Sims that exist in the town. It's amazing! If your Sim is a criminal you might see him rob another Sim if you aren't playing as him too!
All the inter-connections they've made are just a lot of fun. You can even eliminate having to micro-manage their needs almost entirely if you so wish to maximize time on progression.
I really can't list all that you can do because there is so much.
So quickly... Lots of job choices including work-at-home, expanded families and trees, option to have aging or not, ability to either micromanage all Sims in a town or let them follow their own will, and you can build basements! Not to mention all the other 'towns' your Sims can go to as vacations, trips, or education.
I do have some negatives about the game though. First, initially loading time is really long, understandable but still they could optimize it instead of the current 2-5 minutes it takes before you even get to play. Second, HUGE push towards their content marketplace. Users can still make their own content but the game pushes their own pay-for content more and it's not cheap (new towns can cost around 20 USD and items are usually 3-5 USD and more for sets of items) so be prepared to spend a lot of you want extra bits and pieces.
Finally, this is The Sims, even with the first series expect a lot of expansions. Thankfully, this game and all its expansions go on sale at least once a quarter so if you exercise patience you can get them all for 40-60% off which will save a tremendous amount of money.

One final note, save often because the game can and will crash during long sessions.

At first glance I thought this cubic-world themed game would be another disappointing Minecraft wannabe that does little to separate itself from the dozens of other clones in a crowded genre. Oh how I was wrong.
I bought this game on sale when a few friends recommended it to me, but after playing it religiously for the past week I would've been happy paying full price for it. The game is incredibly easy to get into and understand, yet there is enough content there to keep you occupied for dozens of hours. The class system and portal mechanics really make Portal Knights stand out amongst similar games and gives you a rewarding sense of progression and as if there's always something to do. Playing with friends is definitely the way to go, as completing in-game dungeons and events becomes twice as fun, but the solo experience holds up quite well on its own, although can get slightly grindy at times.
The only negatives I would have lie within the core prinicple of the game - the portals, which you use to traverse between different biome-like worlds, can force long loading screens of up to 4-5 minutes if playing online with long-distance friends. In single player this is barely an issue, but things can get a little janky once online. I've also experienced a crash or two in my online world with my friends, which erased all our progress in the world (but our characters inventory and levels were unaffected) and set us back a few painful hours. Other than that, the game holds up very nicely and there is little left to criticise.
If you like the Minecraft sandbox/cubic-world genre of games then Portal Knights should definitely be on your radar. It offers elements both for players who like to quest and adventure and players who like to take it slow and invest in building. At the perfect price, I highly recommend you give it a try.

Alright, let me start out and say I LOVE this game! I was a big fan of the first one, and this one is just as good. Below I will list some pros and cons and then below that I will go into some of the details for each point.
PROS:
Good story line!
Easy / improved controls
Improved gui since last game
Lots of tooltips and a towel
Pretty decent fps
CONS:
No Running?
Combat System (read more)
Now I will elaborate on some things!
1. The storyline picks up pretty much where the last game ended, so I definately reccommend playing the first game before this one to get an understanding of your character.
2. The controls (At least on controller) are pretty easy to grasp and learn quickly. In my opinion, they have definately improved since the first game!
3. The interface menus are pretty sleek and upgraded in this game! By holding RB, a map overlay will come up along with your current mission and where it is located! Also, lootable drawers, fridges, etc., now just put everything into your inventory instead of making you enter a gui!
4. If you are ever lost, then you're doing something wrong! There is pretty much a tooltip for everything! Also, Towlie (character from the Southpark show) will pop up from time to time to give you information about new mechanics you unlock.
5. I have a pretty high end computer, so if you have a budget build or a mid tier computer, I can't really say what your framerate will be like, but if you have a 1080 ti (what I have) then you shouldn't have any issues!
6. So apparently there's no running in this? I haven't finished the game, but unless you get the ability to run halfway into the game, you cant run in this! Not really a big deal cause you're not like SUPER slow, but I would like to get around the map a lot faster then currently available.
7. Okay, now the combat system isn't technically a con, it's actually pretty decent BUT, in terms of the combat system in the first game, I prefer that one instead! The combat system in the first game was simple and easy to understand. The combat system in this game is a little hard to understand at first and I still, after like 30 battles, am trying to understand a couple things about my attacks. When learning what to do when you select an attack, there's no help, you just have to learn what to do which was pretty annoying! Overall it's pretty good and really I'm just salty about not getting to use the old system, but that's just me.

On sale for $0.19, so well worth it to try it out, but I'm gonna have to give this a No.  I love giving horror games a fighting chance since I'm one for jump-scares and usually people giving reviews call those out as a negative thing.  As far as being scary, this game does an okay job.  The feeling of vulnerability with no weapon and the ability to lose the game by getting "caught" is a little nerve-racking, but otherwise, this game isn't quite there.
The weapon you DO get is immediately used up.  You can't pick it up after you use it, which I find weird since it doesn't look hard to pick back up if it were real life.
The Journal Pages you need to collect don't add much to the spookiness of it, and are slightly broken.  You get some voice-over for the Journal pages, but some of the pages have text and voiceover that don't match, like the voice is for a completely different page, crushing the illusion.
You don't really know where to go and just hope you're going in the right direction.  No maps or anything.  This would be fine, but the scenery you get lost in is repetative, so it gets old after a while.
Clicking to open things seemed un-respsonsive.  "Click to Open" with a hand icon on the screen, but clicking doesn't do anything unless you click like nine times.
When you first get the ability to scare away shadows, it's creepy and works well.  When you encounter the Hat Man, however, you get the impression that it's supposed to work, but ends up failing, making you move too slowly to get away.
I DID like how it stops you if you "miss something".  The game actually says "You missed something" if you don't pick up a vital item, which I thought was a nifty touch.
Anyway, like I said, not a loss at all for 19 cents, but that's where I'd draw the line.

RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is a must-have for those fangirling over RWBY everything (show, manga, merch, etc.).  It truly combines the traditional hack-and-slash genre with the pulse-poundin world of Remnant.
The fighting style is fluid and the controls are very easy to pick up; upon purchase of the game I immediately threw myself into a Quick Game mode and familiarized myself with the controls and different combinations in a few minutes.
This game truly brings out it's mettle when joined with three other online players (and feels all the more authentic when each player in your team is one of the main characters from the show).  Each character has their own unique set of characteristics that can control how the battle flows.  For example, one person may be a more in-your-face type of player while another may be more of a support, and hence those two teaming up can effectively destory the enemies that have their difficulty raised/lowered depending on how well the entire team performs.  Plus, it also looks really cool when you are able to free your teammates from being surrounded by using a well-timed special attack.
Being still in development, there are the occasional bugs and doo-dads that need fixing, and the characters need to be refined(as well as more characters need to be added) to really flesh out the world of RWBY.
In short, RWBY: Grimm Eclipse is one of my favorite games to play, and if this is how the game is at it's Early Access stage, I cannot wait to see how the game will be once it is fully released.  Thanks to Roosterteeth and all those affiliated in bringing this game to life!

Review as of 12/22/15
This game is in Early Access and is subject to change periodically, so much so that within even one update that this review could potentially be completely outdated.
Length:
An important thing to mention is that the first campaign is rather... short, which is honestly an understatement. I beat it twice in under an hour, and if we assume that the other campaigns are as long, we're talking around a maximum of 3 hours for all three campaigns. Either more levels (in terms of areas and character strength) are needed, or the current ones should be extended. In my honest opinion, the campaigns should really be longer. It doesn't matter if this game has the worlds greatest combat; it's going to get really stale and tiring to see the same locations over and over (albeit they are absolutely freaking GORGEOUS).
Combat:
The combat holds up remarkably well, but as of right now, it has the potential to get extremely repetitive. This issue is easily fixed by boss fights and enemy varity. A current problem I have ATM that I don't see mentioned a lot, was that throughout the first campaign, the levels ended with waves of enemies instead of a boss fight with an incredibly powerful Grimm, which would be awesome. Gives us a chance to understand exactly how powerful these suckers can get by fighting them in the game, and thus in turn would change how we view certain Grimm in the show. Currently, the game feels a little too Dynasty Warriors, which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but nearly every fight suffers because nearly every Grimm feels identical. Granted, there are two Grimm in particular that I really like, (forgive my ignorance on the names) the Boar and Bear Grimm.
The Boar is an extremely quick powerhouse that can easily overwhelm a single player if they aren't careful. Kiting the Boar and working as a team to tire it out before striking is the way to go, which I love. It provides a minor layer of depth and tactics in the combat. Do you divert your attention from the main swarm and risk getting overrun, or do you ignore the Boar and run the risk of getting knocked flat on your butt and in need of a revive?
The Bear is also an interesting foe. Due to it's thick skin and armor, it is immune to ranged attacks (without the armor piercing upgrade), which forces everyone to fight it in melee combat. The Bear gives as much damage as it can take; if you aren't careful, it WILL take you down in 1-2 swipes. These two enemies, when combined, are a fearsome duo. They add an extreme amount of danger and difficulty and everyone is going to have to work together to take them down.
However, those two are the only enemies where mashing the attacking button isn't really a viable option. Nearly every other enemy requires no thought to take down; you simply mash the attack button and use your abilities over and over until they die. This coincides with a small combat issue: the combo meter. The only way to get your special back is by striking enemies over and over without getting hit. If you get hit, it's back to 0. However, this can be pretty damn annoying if you are in the middle of destroying a group of enemies and you get run over by a Boar you didn't see from off-screen, ending the combo and your chances of refilling your special meter for several seconds. Almost every enemy except for the Boar, Bear and Beowulf (that name I know) is there for the sole purpose of getting the crap beat out of it so your special meter can fill up. Personally, I think this should be changed into one of two possible new systems.
1. The combo meter can stay, and it keeps its functions with one key difference: the special meter passive refills itself like mana, albeit very slowly. You can get upgrades so it fills back up faster, so there are more customization and build options.
2. A high-risk, high-reward system where your Aura fuels your special abilites. So not only is the Aura your shield, but it is also your weapon. This forces you to THINK very carefully about whether or not you should use an ability, and if you do, will you be punished for it? Such a simple addition will add a new layer of depth to combat, keeping you constantly on your toes and forcing you to PAY ATTENTION to your surroundings.
Various other things to be considered for combat:
1. Upgrades to your weapon and attack damage. I noticed right away that ranged attacks seem to be lacking in nearly every way, and are only good for making sure your combo meter doesn't run out of time by shooting a far away enemy. Melee attacks also seemed to slightly fall off near the end of the final level, where you are swarmed by Bears and Beowulfs with extremely high HP and defense. It's better to ignore them altogether and just focus on fueling the bomb, which isn't something you want to happen in a game about combat.
2. Customizable skill loadouts. Every character should have about 4-6 skills, and it is up to the player which ones they will use. When they play Ruby, will they use a long-range sniper build, or perhaps a more balanced melee and ranged attack combination? Or will they focus on AOE damage and crowd clearing? The choice is theirs and it further deepens combat and negates repetitiveness. Players will be incentivized to experiment with different combinations of skills.
3. Upgrades to your defense, allowing your Aura to take more hits (and if combined with the system of Aura fueling your skills, use more skills) before being subject to defeat.
Appearances:
This game, visually, is stunning. It needs a little work here and there, but the style of RWBY really shines in the form of a video game. The animations are a little strange and clunky ATM, and even some animations are missing, but remember that this is an Early Access review. You honestly should expect these kind of things. In terms of art design, this game NAILS it.
I don't really have much else to say at the moment, but I am really excited for the future of this game. I'm sure everyone here wants to see it get better and improve, ka?
At the moment, I both recommend and DON'T recommend this game. I recommend it due to the low price, which will eventually go higher as progress continues, and the several hours of playtime you can knock out of it to try out the core features. HOWEVER, I do NOT recommend nearly everything else. The game is still really early in development, and it needs to be better polished. Everything changes, in due time, and with the developers listening eagerly to the community, I have no doubt in my mind that this game will be a great one, true to the RWBY series and what makes it so grand. If I rated games solely on who developed it, this game would get a solid 10/10.

It's almost impossible to talk about this game without comparing it to others in the same genre, so I'm not even going to try. So if you don't want to read a lengthy comparison of Torchlight 2 and Diablo 3, I'll save you the trouble, put the bottom line right here, and say that you should probably play both, because they're both very good games.
Torchlight 2 is a huge improvement over the first game. More varied classes, areas, and enemies for starters. I didn't get that sense of having seen the exact same layout a couple areas back nearly as often in Torchlight 2 as I did in the first Torchlight, and aesthetically, it recycles a lot less than the first game. My first playthrough, I set off as my Berserker, Scruffy the Everything Slayer, and her trusty sidekick, Anthony Stewart Headcrab (a.k.a. Giles), and found no difficulty whatsoever figuring out what I was supposed to be doing, or having fun doing it.
So the comparisons. I would've had no problem saying Torchlight 2 was a better game than Diablo 3 prior to the rebalancing and auction house closures undertaken by the latter. Now, they're on pretty even ground, and mechanically, Diablo 3 even occasionally makes Torchlight 2 feel sort of dated. Cooldowns on potions were an excellent idea. They forced players to think a bit harder about how they play rather than trying to tank through all the challenging bits, chugging potions. The challenge of Torchlight 2 suffers immensely from the ability to just chug potions one after the other. My first playthrough, I defeated the last boss on my first try. I'm not exceptionally good at this style of game, despite playing a lot of them, but I was a little disappointed how successful you could be in this game without really thinking much about what you're doing. I might think differently after playing through at higher difficulties and also finishing New Game +, so I'll probably update my review once that happens, but Normal mode: probably equivalent to other games' easy. Also, I wish the crafting systems had been a lot more robust in Torchlight 2.
Also, Runic's lack of transparency with the Mac community about this game has been fairly frustrating. Sort of wish they'd have actually made sure they were able to release a Mac version before saying they were going to. Unfortunately, it didn't happen that way, and it's led to an angry Mac community, and still no Mac version. A fairly minor gripe, but still, annoying. Especially since there is a Mac version of Diablo 3 already out.
On the other hand, Torchlight 2 has the benefit of not being always-online, which means none of that annoying single-player lag you get in Diablo 3, not to mention that it's not dependent on the profitability and security of someone else's servers. It's moddable, which is also absolutely huge, has a more interesting visual feel (highly subjective, I know, but that's my personal opinion, and I'm sticking to it), and pets, which are much less annoying than constantly hearing the same conversations with your followers in Diablo 3. Whereas with Diablo 3, you easily get what you pay for, with Torchlight 2 at a fraction of the price, you get a lot more.
